part_subtitle: The road remembers what people deny.

chapters.chapter_title: THE VILLAGE THAT DID NOT USE A NAME
paragraphs: Buck refused the bridge before the village refused its name.

The horse stopped with both forehooves in the brown water where the road had sunk, ears flat, wet mane stuck to his neck like torn weed. Rain moved over the valley in patient sheets, too patient to be called a storm and too stubborn to stop. It made the river smell of thawed mud, old reeds, and something warmer under the cold, a buried breath rising where no breath had any right to be. Jack Morningstar sat in the saddle and let the refusal tell him more than the signpost had.

The signpost stood at the road's fork with its arms hacked clean. Someone had taken an axe to the village name and left only the direction marks, north to Crow's Perch, south to the river crossing, east to a place no one wished to be counted as entering. The cuts were fresh, showing pale wood under rain-dark bark. Fresh cuts lied differently from old ones. Old damage weathered itself into fact. New damage wanted to be noticed and denied in the same breath.
"You saw it first," Jack said.

Buck moved one ear, which was not agreement, but from Buck it was more courteous than most men deserved. The horse had carried him through three flooded ditches, one abandoned Nilfgaardian camp, and a toll bridge where two men in mismatched mail had argued for half an hour about whether a witcher counted as taxable livestock. Buck had taken the ditches without complaint, tried to bite one taxman, and now would not place a hoof on a village bridge made of old pine and older guilt.

Jack dismounted. Mud accepted his boots with a soft pull, like a mouth considering whether to keep what it had been given. The Wolf medallion against his chest remained still, heavy under leather and rain. The other necklace, the one he wore beneath the armor and did not show unless something had already gone wrong, lay colder against his skin. The barbed star had always known how to be silent. It had known that longer than he had.

The bridge had been repaired in five places. Not maintained. Repaired. Different wood, different hands, different seasons, each layer set over rot instead of cutting it out. Jack crouched and pressed two fingers to the boards. The top was cold with rain. The seam between planks breathed warmth.
Buck snorted.
"I said I saw it. I didn't say I liked it."

The village waited beyond the bridge with the careful stillness of places that had rehearsed innocence. Smoke climbed from chimneys, but no one stood under eaves. A red hen scratched beside a trough and pretended not to be watched by three faces hidden behind a shutter. The houses leaned inward around a lane paved in broken stone. At the far end, where the ground dipped toward the river, an old mill turned with no grain in its throat.
The wheel moved slowly, pushed by water that looked black under the sky. It creaked once every turn. The sound arrived late.

Jack led Buck across by the reins. Halfway over, the horse stopped again and put his weight backward. Jack did not pull. Pulling a frightened horse was for fools, noblemen, and people who later wondered why they woke up without teeth. He waited until Buck placed one hoof forward, then another, and the warmth under the bridge shifted against the soles of Jack's boots.

The first man to meet him had alderman's hands, soft at the knuckles and ink in the nail beds. He wore a fur hat too fine for the weather and a belt with a brass buckle polished bright, implying honest administration, which was rarely a sign of honest administration. Behind him came a priest with a candle lantern and two villagers carrying boar spears. The spears had been cleaned. The men had not.
"Witcher," the alderman said.
Jack looked past him to the shuttered windows, the mill, the child watching from behind a broken door, and the black river sliding under its skin of rain. "That was on the notice."

The alderman blinked. "I am Odrik, elected alderman by common assent and royal continuance, under the terms of local settlement confirmed before the late war and unaffected by present vassal adjustment."
"Congratulations."
The man with the left spear coughed into his fist. The priest did not smile. Priests had training for that sort of thing. Jack respected it in the way one respected a locked door.
"You came quickly," Odrik said.
"Your notice said livestock. Then two missing men. Then a child. Notices get more expensive when they improve."
"The child came back," the priest said.

His voice was soft and dry. He was young in his piety and old in his use of it as furniture. The candle in his lantern burned with a yellow, untroubled flame despite the rain. Jack watched it lean toward the mill.
"Alive?" Jack asked.
"In body," the priest said.
"Try not to be poetic until after I know who is paying me."

The spear-man coughed again, this time badly, hiding a laugh. The alderman turned a look on him that would have fined him if looks had seals. Jack had seen villages arrange themselves by fear, by hunger, by old women, by pigs, by priests, and twice by geese. This one was arranged by what it would not call itself.
"Payment is as posted," Odrik said. "Seventy crowns on proof of removal. Additional ten if the mill is preserved."
"No."
The alderman frowned. "No?"
"No additional ten. If the mill is part of it, the mill goes where it needs to go."
"The mill belongs to five families."
"Then five families should have built it somewhere else."
The priest lifted the lantern a fraction. "The mill is old. Older than most claims."
"So is rot." Jack looked at the hacked signpost behind him. "What's the village called?"
Three faces vanished from three windows.

Odrik's lips tightened. The priest lowered the lantern. The child in the broken doorway remained where he was, thin as a post, hair too light for his dirty face, one hand pressed hard around a wooden toy horse. Buck blew air through his nose and turned his head toward the boy. The boy did not move.
"We do not use the name," Odrik said.
"I noticed the axe work."
"Superstition," Odrik said too quickly. "After the war people became... suggestible."
"Respect for the dead," the priest said.
"Those are different lies," Jack said.
The rain filled the space after the words. A dog barked once from somewhere behind the houses and then thought better of the matter.
Odrik's face reddened in a disciplined way. "You were hired for a monster, not for an inquiry into local grief."
"I charge extra when grief bites."

The priest faced him then and truly saw past the swords, past the armor, past the dark leather and the white hair wet against his brow. His gaze caught on Jack's eyes and stopped. People always did that eventually. It was one of the few reliable things about them. They saw the crimson, the slit pupils, the way low light gathered in them as if invited, and they remembered all at once that hiring a witcher meant bringing another frightening thing close to speech.

"The first cow vanished six nights ago," the priest said. "Then two goats. Then Toman the miller's nephew. Then Berek, who went looking for him. The child, Miro, was taken yesterday before dawn. He returned before noon and has not spoken since."
"Where was he found?"
The priest did not answer. Odrik looked toward the mill.
"Useful," Jack said. "We're improving."

The woman at the mill watched him from the open half of a stable door. She was old, but not with the fragility city folk liked to imagine when they used the word. She had river-old shoulders, hands bent by work, and the kind of eyes that had outlived pity because pity had never carried water or buried a son. A blue kerchief held back hair the color of stove ash. She did not cross herself. She did not spit. She watched Buck's hooves first, then Jack's hands, then the place under his collar where the hidden necklace lay.
"Who is she?" Jack asked.
"Edda," Odrik said. "The miller's widow."
"Which miller?"
The priest's fingers tightened around the lantern handle.
Jack turned to the old woman. She gave him no answer. That, at last, was something honest.

The mill yard was churned by men trying to look brave after the useful portion of fear had passed. Tracks overlapped tracks, boot heels through goat blood, spear-butts in mud, ash scattered in clumsy circles around the threshold. Someone had poured salt at the door, then crossed it twice. Someone else had nailed three horseshoes over the lintel in three different directions, which proved the village had at least three opinions and no plan.

Jack walked the perimeter first. He did not ask questions while the ground was still speaking. Mud kept records better than frightened men. A dragged mark began at the goat pen, stopped near the well, resumed ten paces away, and then vanished not at the river but at the mill's north wall. The gap mattered. Gaps were where lies stood when they had no boots.

The missing cow's blood had not dried properly. It had steamed in cold air, leaving a dark crust around the stones. The mill wheel creaked. Under that creak, faint and out of rhythm, something clicked as if teeth were being counted.
Jack knelt beside the well. The rope was scorched halfway down.
"Lightning," Odrik said from behind him.
"In a covered well?"
"It was during a storm."
"Storms have standards. Low ones, but standards."
The spear-man made a small sound again. Odrik turned to him. The spear-man became interested in his boots.

Jack drew a knife and scraped the scorched fibers into a fold of oilcloth. The burn smelled wrong, not woodsmoke, not pitch, not witchfire. Hot iron and wet stone. He put the oilcloth away and went to the mill wall, where frost clung in the sheltered cracks despite the thaw. Frost on the surface. Heat in the joints. The medallion twitched once, not a proper warning, more like a sleeping dog kicking at a dream.

Inside, the mill had the warm damp smell of grain gone sour. The grindstones sat in silence though the wheel moved outside. Flour dust lay over the floor in old drifts, disturbed by boot marks, animal tracks, and one broad smear where something heavy had been pulled inward. Jack followed the smear to a trapdoor hidden beneath sacks and a floor plank newer than the others. The iron ring had been wrapped in cloth to keep it quiet.
"Cellar?" he asked.
"Storage," Odrik said.
"For what?"
"Grain. Tools. Winter stores."
Jack lifted the cloth from the ring. It was warm.
"And guilt," he said.
The priest drew a breath. Outside, the old woman Edda spat into the yard.
Jack watched her through the doorway. "How many times has the mill been rebuilt?"
No one answered.
"Three," the old woman said at last.
Odrik turned sharply. "Edda."

"Four, if you count the war winter," she said. Her voice had the flatness of river stones. "But they don't count that. Didn't get permits for war work. Hard to file improvements when half the men have run to the woods and the other half are hiding grain from whichever army asks politely with torches."
The priest closed his eyes.
"Who died under it?" Jack asked.
Edda studied the trapdoor. "Depends which prayer you believe."
"I don't use prayers for counting."

"Seven men during the old fire. Two deserters, one tax rider, one girl dressed as a boy, three we never named. Later, when the foundations sank, we built over them. Priest before this one said disturbance would invite worse. Alderman before this one said digging cost money. Both were right, which is how wickedness usually survives."
Odrik's face had gone the color of old pork. "Those are not established facts."
"No," Jack said. "Established facts cost money."
The old woman almost smiled at him. It did not improve her face. It made it less lonely.

The trapdoor opened with a sigh of stale heat. The smell that came up was not decay. Decay was generous. It told you what it was. This smell was cooked mud, iron, roots split open, and old grain fermented in something that had once been a body. Jack took a cat potion from his belt, rolled the vial between gloved fingers, and hesitated.
The boy Miro stood at the doorway.
No one had heard him cross the yard. He stared at the trapdoor with the whole of his thin body, not just his eyes. The wooden horse hung from his hand by one leg.
Jack turned. "He shouldn't be here."
"He follows the sound," the priest said.
"Then stop making the sound."
"What sound?"
Jack studied the mill wheel. It turned and creaked, turned and creaked, and under it the hidden clicking grew softer, as if something below had learned to listen.
"Clear the mill," Jack said.
Odrik lifted both hands. "Now, witcher, if this is a bargaining posture, it is a poor one. We cannot empty five households because a hired mutant dislikes a noise."

Jack unsheathed his steel sword. The clean sound of it did more for persuasion than reason ever had. "Clear the mill. Clear the houses nearest the river. Put everyone uphill. No lamps near the ground floors. No children near wells. Tie your pigs or lose them. If anyone stays because they think property outweighs breath, I charge the same to carry what remains."

For a moment the room held its shape around the threat. Then Edda moved first. She took Miro by the shoulder, not gently, but with the competence of someone who knew the difference between care and softness. The spear-men followed. The priest lifted his lantern, looked at Odrik, and finally said the most useful thing he had said all morning.
"Do as he says."
Odrik did. He made it sound like his own decision, which was the privilege of office.
Before the hunt, Jack walked the hill where the villagers had gathered and made them show him what fear had edited from their first telling.

It took an hour. It should have taken ten minutes. People made poor witnesses when they were frightened, and worse ones when they were ashamed, because shame gave them the energy to arrange facts into furniture. The missing nephew had not gone into the mill alone. He had gone with two friends to pry old iron from the lower supports, because iron sold well after armies passed and because hunger made thieves of sons whose fathers had once called thieves vermin. Berek had not gone looking for him out of bravery.
Berek had gone because the nephew owed him money for a pig, and money made grief practical to approach.

Miro had been playing near the old sluice when the ground opened. No one said playing. Odrik said trespassing. The priest said wandering. Edda said the boy had been watching the mill because everyone watched what they were told not to watch, children simply had less training in pretending otherwise. Jack listened to all three and took from each the useful portion: the sluice mattered, the boy had seen something, and the adults had spent more effort controlling his location than understanding his survival.

The child would not answer questions. Jack did not force him. Men with authority forced speech and then mistook the result for truth. Instead he crouched near the stone wall, held Miro's wooden horse by its carved tail after the boy pushed it toward him, and examined the mud packed in its wheels. The toy had been dragged through warm silt. Not river mud. Not yard mud. The silt from under the mill had small black grains in it that glittered when broken open, as if coal dust had learned to grow.
"He took it down there," Edda said.
"No," Jack said. "It was returned with him."

The priest made the sign of the flame by habit, then remembered which goddess his village officially favored and changed the gesture midway. It did not improve the theology. Odrik saw Jack notice and looked away.
"Something brought the boy back," Jack said.
"Mercy," the priest said.
"Wrong smell."
Edda's gaze sharpened. "Then why?"

Jack turned the toy horse over. Under the belly, in the place where a child's thumb had worn the wood smooth, a streak of black silt formed a crooked line. Not a mark, perhaps. Not a rune. Only pressure and dirt. But the barbed star under his shirt chilled as he studied it, and Buck, standing three paces behind him, stamped once.
"It returned him because it had learned him," Jack said.
No one liked that. It was useful to know which truths made a crowd stop breathing.

By dusk, the village that did not use its name had climbed the hill above itself. Rain thinned into mist. Lamps burned behind blankets in upper rooms. Animals complained from fences dragged uphill. Odrik stood under a bent apple tree with a ledger held under his coat, trying to record an evacuation as if records could make it orderly. The priest moved among the villagers with his candle lantern and murmured comforts that Jack could not hear. Edda sat beside Miro on a stone wall and watched the mill. Buck stood near them, wet and offended, one rein looped loosely over a dead branch.
He had refused the old stable with such force that Jack had respected the opinion.
Jack worked alone.

He salted the yard where salt mattered and ignored the horseshoes. He set three snares of chain and hooked them to the mill's support beams, then cut two beams halfway through with measured strokes. He wedged an old plough-blade under the wheel brace, coated the trapdoor ring with oil, and laid a path of pig blood from the cellar mouth toward the marsh beyond the north field. The marsh was a skin of reeds and black water over ground that had forgotten whether it was land. It would hold weight badly. That made it useful.
Useful things often had poor manners.
The alderman came down once before full dark, carrying a purse and a face arranged around official concern. "If the mill is destroyed without necessity, we shall have to revisit the terms."
Jack did not look up from sharpening the last stake. "Bring a shovel when you revisit."
"I am trying to preserve what little these people have left."
"No. You're trying to preserve what proves you didn't know."
Odrik went quiet. Rain ticked on the broken boards. The mill wheel creaked behind them, slower now. Jack could feel the warmth through his boots.
"My father built one of those beams," Odrik said after a while.
"Your father built over a grave."
"Men did what they had to do during the war."
Jack tested the edge of the stake with his thumb and watched a thin line of blood appear. "They always do. That's why the ground keeps accounts."
Odrik left with the purse still under his coat. The extra ten crowns would not survive the night. Jack had known that from the bridge.

When darkness came, it came from the river first. It moved up through the reeds, took the mill yard, climbed the walls, and sat under the eaves. Jack drank the cat potion and felt the world sharpen with its usual cruelty. Darkness turned blue and silver. Raindrops became needles. The warm seams in the floor shone faintly, not with light, but with wrongness. His pulse slowed. His mouth filled with the bitter mineral taste of alchemy.
He opened the trapdoor.
Heat breathed up. Something below clicked twice.
"Come on, then," Jack said.
The mill answered by stopping.

The silence was immediate and muscular. All day the wheel had given the place a false heart, creak and turn, creak and turn, a sound people could pretend belonged to water and work. Without it, the mill became a mouth held open. Under the floor, mud shifted. The sacks along the far wall sagged inward though nothing touched them. A thin crack ran across the flour-dust floor and closed again.
Jack stepped backward along the blood path, sword low. The cellar remained black. Then the trapdoor frame buckled upward and something that had learned the shape of roots reached out.

It was not large at first. That was the insult of it. A narrow head pushed through, blind and pale, plated in patches of mud-hard skin and old wood slivers. Its mouth opened sideways. Too many small teeth clicked against one another with the sound Jack had heard beneath the wheel. Two forelimbs followed, one ending in claws, the other in a flattened digging plate wrapped in rope fibers and bone. It had built itself from survival, pressure, and everything the villagers had given the ground by refusing to open it.
The creature paused at the threshold. It tasted the air. Then it turned its head toward the hill where the villagers waited.
"No," Jack said.
It came for him instead.

The first rush broke the trapdoor apart. Jack cut across the plated snout and felt steel scrape without biting deep. The creature recoiled, not from pain, but calculation. It had fought men with spears. It had pulled goats through walls. It knew resistance as a pattern and had learned that anything standing its ground could be undermined. The floor under Jack's left boot softened.
He moved before it opened.

The boards collapsed where he had stood. Mud erupted, warm and black, swallowing the stake he had left there. Jack rolled across flour dust, came up beside the first chain snare, and drove the hook into the creature's digging limb as it lunged. The chain snapped taut. The beam groaned. Above, the cut he had made in the support began to widen.
The creature clicked. The sound changed pitch.
From the hill, someone shouted. The creature turned toward the voice again.
Jack cut the blood path with his own palm and let fresh blood fall onto the floor.
The barbed-star necklace under his armor went cold until it hurt.

For one breath, the warmth beneath the mill pulled toward him. Not toward the blood, not exactly. Toward the old hidden place under his ribs where something had slept all his life with the patience of buried fire. Jack's vision tightened. The crimson in his eyes caught the dark and held it. The creature froze with its blind head tilted.
Then the pull passed.
Jack exhaled through his teeth. "Not tonight."
The creature lunged.
He let it drive him through the north wall.

Rotten planks burst outward. Rain hit his face like thrown gravel. Jack rolled in mud, shoulder burning where old nails had caught leather and skin. The creature followed, dragging the chain, support beam tearing loose behind it. The mill screamed. A good sound, if one had the right taste in architecture.
Jack ran toward the marsh.

The thing came low and fast, using forelimbs and body weight, digging through the upper mud rather than over it. It was quicker in open ground than it had any right to be. It had learned from footsteps. It had learned where men placed weight and how they turned when frightened. Twice it cut him off before he adjusted. The second time its claw opened his thigh through the armor seam, hot pain flashing down to the knee.
Buck screamed from the hill.
"Stay," Jack muttered, though the horse was too far to hear and too wise to obey if he chose otherwise.

The first snare pulled free behind the creature, bringing half the mill's north frame with it. The second caught as Jack reached the edge of the marsh. He turned there, boots sinking, sword in both hands, blood moving warm under rain-cold leather. The creature slowed. It knew soft ground. It knew traps. It had survived because men assumed hunger was stupidity.
Jack took one more step backward and let his injured leg buckle.
The creature came.

It hit him chest-high. The force drove air from his lungs and pushed him into the marsh with its mouth opening near his throat. Jack jammed his left forearm across the jaws and felt teeth grind against reinforced bracer. The digging limb slammed down beside his head, sinking past the wrist into the black mud. He drove his knee upward, shifted, and thrust the silver sword he had drawn in the fall into the soft seam beneath the creature's jaw.
Silver burned where steel had only argued.

The creature thrashed. The marsh accepted it. Jack twisted the blade, not deep to kill, deep to anger. The thing reared, dragging him half upright, and the second chain went taut around the limb still caught in the mill frame. Up the slope, the weakened beams gave way at last.
The mill collapsed like a verdict.

One wall folded into the wheel. The wheel tore free, spun once without water, and dropped into the river with a great dark splash. The chain jerked. The creature screamed, a high wooden sound that sent birds bursting from the reeds. Mud opened under it, not a hole, but a swallowing. Jack rolled clear as the marsh took the weight, the chain, the beam, the creature, and part of the bank in one patient inward breath.
The thing tried to climb out. Jack got to his knees. His injured leg shook. He cut the last support rope with his knife.
The old millstone, dragged from its place by the falling frame, slid down the bank and struck the creature across the spine.
That ended the argument.
The marsh closed slowly. A few bubbles rose. Then nothing remained but reeds, rain, and a warmth fading under the ground as if a fever had broken.

Jack stayed on one knee until he was sure. The cat potion made the villagers on the hill too clear: Odrik with both hands over his mouth, the priest's lantern lifted, Edda standing now, Miro beside her with his toy horse held against his chest. Buck had pulled free from the branch and stood halfway down the slope, trembling with the effort not to come farther.
"Good horse," Jack said.
Buck tossed his head. The opinion was plain. Good witcher remained under review.

By morning, the village had a ruin where a mill had stood, a trench through the yard, and seven old bones laid out under a blanket because Edda had brought a shovel before anyone in office remembered burial. The priest said prayers over them. This time he used no poetry. Odrik counted coins with shaking fingers and tried to subtract the mill. Jack held him there until arithmetic became less ambitious.
"Seventy," Odrik said.
"And five for the rope."
"Rope?"
Jack pointed to the marsh. "Mine's gone."
The spear-man laughed before he could stop himself. Odrik paid the five. The coins were damp and clipped, but not so badly that another conversation could grow from them. Jack counted them anyway.

Miro approached while Jack was checking Buck's left foreleg. The boy moved carefully, not because he feared the horse, but because fear had become a habit in him and habit was slower to leave than monsters. Buck lowered his head and breathed into the child's hair. Miro shut his eyes.
"He likes you," Jack said.
The boy opened his eyes. "He thinks I'm sad."
His voice was cracked from disuse. The priest went still behind him. Edda put one hand to her mouth and looked away as if speech were a private indecency.
"Horses are rude that way," Jack said.
Miro looked toward the ruin. "It sang under there."
"No. It listened. There's a difference."
"It said the ground was hungry."
Jack buckled the strap on Buck's tack and made himself do it once, not three times. "The ground doesn't get hungry. People put things into it and expect it not to remember."

Miro considered that with the grave seriousness of children who have been given more truth than adults intended. Then his attention reached Jack's face. Rain had washed most of the mud away. The cat potion had faded, but the crimson remained. It always did.
"You're the red-eyed wolf," the boy said.
"No."
"You stopped the ground."
"No. I dropped a mill on a thing that had poor judgment."
"That isn't how I'll tell it."

Jack held on him for a long moment. The boy looked back, pale and stubborn, one survivor already becoming a witness, one witness already becoming a story. There was no malice in it. That made it worse. Malice at least knew it was lying.
"Tell it cheaper," Jack said. "Stories with too much embroidery attract tailors."
The boy frowned. "What?"
"Never mind."

Edda came then with a cloth-wrapped bundle. Inside was bread, hard cheese, and smoked fish. Payment villagers gave when coin had already been paid and pride wished to pretend it was not gratitude. Jack took it because refusing would make her thank him with words.
"The name," he said.
Edda studied the hacked signpost beyond the bridge. "It was Willenford once. Before the fire. Before the tax riders. Before men decided names made accusations easier."
"Willenford," Jack repeated.
Several villagers flinched. The world did not end. No door burst open. No buried thing called from the marsh. Only the river moved, carrying away pieces of the mill wheel.
Edda's eyes grew wet, which seemed to anger her. "There."
"There," Jack said.

He mounted with more effort than he liked and less than anyone else noticed. Buck stepped onto the bridge without stopping this time. Halfway across, Jack looked back. Miro stood in the lane beside Edda and the priest, already telling the story with both hands. The boy's palms shaped something larger than what had happened. Something with eyes and a wolf's back and a ground that opened because a witcher had ordered it to.
Jack touched the purse at his belt, the wound in his thigh, the cold hidden star at his chest.
The road took him before the gratitude could.
By the time the first version reached the next village, the mill had been swallowed whole by a red wolf with a sword in its teeth.
By the time it crossed the river, the wolf had spoken the dead name and the earth had obeyed.

By the time a clerk in a brown coat wrote it down on poor paper with expensive ink, the witness was described as reliable, the phenomenon as localized, the witcher as unidentified, and the ground itself as responsive under pressure.
Under remarks, the clerk added one line and sanded it dry.

Subject displays unusual field effect in post-contact witness narrative. Recommendation: retain statement pending narrative correction. Potential recurrence should be observed under controlled contract conditions.
The first repeated phrase appeared on a whitewashed post outside a hamlet that had lost three geese, one drunk, and its sense of proportion.

Jack read the notice while Buck cropped dead grass from the ditch and pretended the geese were not staring at him. The paper had been nailed too high for most villagers and too low for officials with self-importance, which meant the man who placed it had wanted it seen by travelers, not locals. The hand was neat. The spelling was better than the hamlet deserved. At the bottom, under the usual promise of payment upon proof, someone had written localized instability in a style that did not belong anywhere near missing poultry.
"Geese," Jack said.
Buck chewed.
"Localized instability."
Buck swallowed and reached for another mouthful.
"You're right. Geese explain most of it."

The geese did not explain the drunk. That was the trouble with honest mockery. It never survived the corpse. The drunk had been found in a drainage ditch at dawn, folded in a way that suggested either great malice or extremely focused ignorance of joints. There was pondweed in his mouth, though the nearest pond had frozen over weeks before and thawed into mud instead of water. His widow wanted ten crowns and revenge. The alderman wanted five crowns and no attention. The priest wanted to say it was punishment for drinking.
The geese wanted the world kept as it was, which made them politically aligned with most priests.

Jack followed the tracks to a culvert half-choked with reeds, old bones, and the remains of a military boot. It was a drowned dead, but altered by hunger and cold, with fingers hardened into hooks and river silt packed into the sockets. It had been feeding on small animals, then learned that drunk men fell more slowly than geese and screamed less usefully than pigs. Jack killed it in the culvert after lying on his back in six inches of black water for twenty minutes while it crawled across the stones above him.

The widow paid in coins wrapped in linen. The alderman asked for a certificate proving the death was natural to the monster and not actionable against the hamlet drainage committee. Jack gave him a look instead. The alderman accepted the look, perhaps sensing it carried fewer administrative obligations.
The notice disappeared before sunset.

The second phrase appeared two days later in a town with a market square, a cracked shrine to Melitele, and four men who had taken to calling themselves a militia because bandit sounded less civic. They had posted three monster notices on the same board: one for a barn gnawer, one for a night screamer near the tannery, and one for suspicious lights by the old plague pits. All three notices used different local seals. All three used the same ink. Under witness instructions, all three said witness control advised until field residue can be assessed.

Jack stood before the board with rain sliding from the edge of his hood and felt the road tilt slightly under him. Not magic. Habit. The body sometimes understood pattern before the mind had finished being reasonable.
A clerk watched him from under the eaves of the tax office.

He was narrow, damp, and badly shaved, with sleeves that had been mended carefully at the cuffs and ink stains that no amount of washing had persuaded to leave. His boots were polished only in front, a man hoping desks would hide the rest of him. When Jack turned, the clerk looked down too late.
"You wrote these?" Jack asked.
The clerk swallowed. "I post what is submitted."
"That wasn't the question."
"No." His gaze moved from the board to the militia men by the shrine, then to Buck, who had pinned his ears at the smell of tannery runoff. "Some. The older notices. Not those."
"Name."
"Rian Wedeck. Assistant clerk under temporary reassignment to market administration and requisitional postings."
"That sounds contagious."
Rian's mouth twitched and failed to become a smile. "After the war a man takes the title that arrives with bread."
That could stand without help.
Jack took one of the notices from the board. The nail came free too easily. "Who submitted it?"
"Riders. Different days. Different offices."
"Same ink."
Rian's eyes flicked up. "You noticed."
"So did you."

The clerk rubbed one thumb against the side of his forefinger. Ink had settled there permanently. "There are only three suppliers in this part of the vassal north with lampblack that fine. Two sell through Novigrad merchants. One sells through military stores. These sheets were cut from office stock. Not village rag."
"You're nervous for a man who only posts paper."
"Paper gets people hanged. Usually by men who say they only carried rope."
Jack folded the notice and put it under his belt. The phrase looked worse when kept. "Who pays you?"
Rian's attention went to the tax office door. "Officially? The district."
"Unofficially?"
"My mother still thinks I copy grain tallies."
"That wasn't the question either."

For a moment Rian seemed to become smaller inside his coat. Rain tapped from the eaves between them. Across the square, one militia man tried to make his spear spin and nearly removed his own ear. It made the world briefly more honest.
"A courier brought supplemental fees for notices involving irregular field concerns," Rian said. "I did not know what that meant. I still don't. They were sealed properly."
"Everything terrible is sealed properly now."
Rian assessed him then, not the eyes first but the swords. A clerk's survival instinct. Tools before myths. "Are you taking the contracts?"
"One. Maybe two."
"The barn gnawer is real. The tannery one is probably dogs. The plague pit lights are boys trying to scare each other or something worse using boys as cover."
"You read more than notices."
"So do you."
It was the first useful answer. Jack almost liked him for it, which meant the man would likely become inconvenient.
The plague pit lights were boys, as Rian had guessed, but the thing using them as cover was not childish.

Jack found the first lantern buried under wet leaves with a string tied through the handle, the other end running to a ditch where three bootprints overlapped in comic incompetence. Boys, then. Village boys with more nerve than judgment and no proper instruction in the difference between frightening each other and providing camouflage. Beyond the ditch, past the place where the first boy had retched from too much cider, the grass bent outward in a circle. Something had watched the lanterns swing and decided swinging lights made useful bait.

He followed the circle to the plague field. The graves there had been dug shallow during the bad winter, when the earth was hard and people were tired of breaking tools on grief. A narrow creature had opened three of them from underneath, feeding upward through the backs of coffins and leaving the upper boards intact. Clever, and still hidden. Hungry, and willing to risk the lantern game. Jack salted the grave mouths, waited in the rain until his cloak froze at the hem, and killed the thing when it rose under the fourth coffin with a child's shoe in its teeth.

The boys watched from behind a linden tree after being told three times to leave. One fainted when the creature opened. The other two claimed afterward that they had remained as tactical support. Jack charged their fathers for the extra hour. The fathers complained until he placed the shoe on the table between them. Complaint then collapsed into coughing, cheaper than argument and harder to answer.
The tannery dogs were dogs, but the dogs had been eating a man who had been dead before they found him.

That man had a district tag in his boot, a broken fingernail packed with sealing wax, and a mouth full of black thread. No monster had done that. Monsters rarely cared about silence after death. Jack took the thread and the wax, burned the corpse until the dogs lost interest, and told the tanner that his problem had solved itself. He did not tell the militia. Their leader had the bright eyes of a man waiting for legal permission to be cruel. Such men could turn a dead messenger into a civic occasion.
By the time he returned to the market board, the three notices had been replaced with fresh copies.
Rian stood beneath them with a hammer in one hand and misery in the other. He had hammered the top nail crooked. That offended him more visibly than the conspiracy. Clerks had their gods.
"These came while I was gone," Jack said.
"Yes."
"Same rider?"
"No rider. They were in the office when I arrived."
"Doors learn to write now?"

"If they do, they will be promoted above me by spring." Rian lowered the hammer. "The district seal is correct. The local notation is wrong. It calls this township Heddel's administrative ring. That name has not been used in six years, except in archived tax rolls. Someone is copying from records, not roads."
Jack read the phrases again. Localized instability. Field residue. Narrative correction. Witness control. All the words sat politely in the rain, pretending they had not crawled from the same hole.
"You could leave," Jack said.
Rian gave him a thin look. "With what money? To what office? Under what reference?"
"People leave without references."
"People with swords leave without references. People with mothers, rent, and handwriting samples require more planning."
That, too, could stand. Jack took the notice and handed Rian the nail. The clerk accepted it automatically.
"If another copy appears," Jack said, "don't post it."
Rian stared at the nail. "That would be a violation of duty."
"Yes."
"A small one, perhaps."
"Practice."
The clerk's mouth moved as if he had discovered that treason could begin with stationery. Then he put the nail in his pocket.
Mara and Rian knew each other, which made the room more complicated before anyone admitted it.

Rian came to the infirmary after the garkain was burned, carrying a sealed packet and the expression of a man trying to decide whether loyalty belonged to law, fear, or the woman who had once set his broken fingers after a cart wheel crushed them. Mara saw him in the doorway and did not invite him in. He entered anyway. That was how Jack knew the packet mattered more than manners.
"They requested confirmation," Rian said.
Mara's hands stopped over a row of clean needles. "Who?"
"Supplementary field office. Same phrasing. Different seal. Better paper."
"For what?"
Rian glanced between Jack and the bloodied cloth in the basin. "Subject response."

The word reached the room before he could regret it. Subject. Not patient. Not witcher. Not contractor. Mara's face tightened and then smoothed out with effort. Jack watched the effort. He trusted effort more than instinct. Instinct came free. Effort left marks.
"He is sitting three feet away," Mara said.
"I know."
"Then use the noun you would use if he were armed."
Rian looked miserable. "He is armed."
"Good. Begin there."
Jack almost liked her again. He should have distrusted that more.

Rian placed the packet on the table as if it might hatch. "I can delay a day. Two if the road floods. More if the seal is damaged, but damaging seals is a hanging matter in some districts and a promotion matter in others, depending on who needed it damaged."
"Delay it," Jack said.
"Yes," Rian said, then blinked as if surprised by his own obedience.

Mara took the packet. The wax bore no crest Jack recognized. Only a black oval pressed so deeply that the paper around it had bruised. She did not open it. She put it in a drawer, locked the drawer, and kept the key in her fist.
"There," she said. "Now all of us have done something stupid. The evening can proceed honestly."

The barn gnawer had eaten through three stalls, a winter store of turnips, and half a man's face. It was not a gnawer. It was a garkain, young or starved past caution, hiding in the hayloft above a cow that had died standing up. The fight took less than a minute and left Jack paying for every careless inch. The creature dropped from the rafters with one wing torn and one claw already slick. Jack met it with silver, took the first strike along the ribs, and drove the blade through the chest when it opened its mouth to scream.

The scream came anyway. It filled the barn, shook dust from beams, and sent one cow into a panic so violent that she broke her neck against the stall door. The owner cried harder for the cow than he had for the hired man. Jack did not judge him. Grief followed profit in villages because profit fed the surviving children.
The woman who owned the dead cow asked whether witchers gave discounts when livestock died during the saving of other livestock.
"No," Jack said.
"Priests give discounts for funerals when half the family goes at once."
"Priests have steadier roofs."
She considered this and spat into the straw. "Fair."

Her name was Brana, and she had the square face of someone who had spent twenty years being disappointed by weather and men in equal measure. She did not like Jack. She liked the dead garkain less. Commerce could proceed. While Mara prepared the needle, Brana argued over the cow, the hired man's face, the price of smoke-wood for burning the monster, and whether a damaged barn counted as damage caused by the witcher, the beast, or poor initial construction.
"Poor construction," Jack said.
"My brother built that loft."
"Poorly."
Brana surveyed the broken rafters, the corpse, and her brother, who had arrived late and was trying to appear bereaved in a way that did not invite repair work. "I always said so."

For a moment the barn became almost ordinary. Money, blame, family, a dead cow, rain leaking through bad thatch. Then Mara lifted the cloth from Jack's ribs and the room remembered blood. Brana stopped bargaining. Her brother stopped breathing through his mouth. Rian held the notice as if its letters might rearrange themselves into a kinder profession.
Jack preferred the bargaining. It had rules.
Later, when the barn had emptied of everyone except the dead thing and the people with reasons to stay, Jack examined the damaged wing.

The bone had not been broken by impact. It had been cut and healed wrong. A strip of dark leather still clung near the joint, too narrow for a trapper's snare and too carefully punched for chance. Someone had bound the creature, kept it hungry, then released it near town, where people were easier to find than wild meat. The garkain was not innocent. Innocence was a word people wasted on things that did not understand ledgers. But it had been used, and used things often became more vicious than wild ones.
Mara watched him wrap the leather strip in cloth. "That is not part of the contract."
"No."
"Will you be paid for following it?"
"No."
"Then why?"
Jack took in the rafters, the broken loft, the cow lying stiff in the next stall, Brana arguing outside over smoke-wood and compensation. "Because someone else already was."
By evening, the wound along Jack's ribs had begun to burn in the wrong way.
That was how Mara Veyr found him.

She came into the barn with a leather satchel, a lantern, and the expression of a woman already angry at the patient for being difficult before the patient had earned the courtesy. She was not tall, but moved like someone used to making taller men step aside by failing to notice them. Her hair was dark blond, pinned without softness. Her sleeves were rolled to the elbow. Her hands smelled of spirits, comfrey, and old blood.
"You the medic?" Jack asked.
"At present."
"What's your profession when the present improves?"
"Optimist, apparently." She crouched beside him without waiting for permission and lifted the torn edge of his armor with two fingers. "That needs cleaning."
"It had rain."
"So do gutters. I don't drink from them."

Rian, standing uselessly in the barn door, made a small sound that could have been admiration or fear. Mara did not look at him. She examined the wound, then Jack's face, then the wound again. Her gaze paused at his eyes and continued its work. That put her ahead of most people.
"Garkain?" she asked.
"Young. Hungry. Wing damaged before it reached town."
"Field residue notice said possible carcass instability."
"It was a monster. Not a philosophy."
"Most forms are monsters after too many revisions. Hold still."

The needle went in before she finished speaking. Jack's fingers closed around the edge of the bench. The wound had started shallow and become personal. Mara cleaned it with spirits with the manners of something that could remove paint from a door. She worked quickly, not gently, but without waste. Her touch had the practical confidence of people who had learned that sympathy did not stop bleeding.
"You run hot," she said.
"Potions."
"This isn't potion heat."
"Then bad manners."
"Those are usually colder." She pressed a cloth into the wound and watched his reaction too closely. "How long since the cut?"
"An hour."
"It has already started closing."
"Witcher."
"I have treated witchers."
Jack met her eyes. "Where?"
Mara tied the bandage with one clean pull. "Where they bled."
Rian found something very important to inspect outside.

Jack could have pressed. The question stayed between them like a knife left on a table. Mara had not lied. That mattered. She had answered in a way that protected the place, not the facts. A different thing.
"You work for the town?" he asked.
"I work where field irregularities outpace local hands."
"Another title with bread attached."
Her hands paused. "Rian told you that?"
"He looks hungry."
Mara's mouth tightened. "Most of us are."

Outside, rain began again in earnest. It hit the barn roof, the yard mud, the dead garkain's stretched wing. It made the world smell of wet hay and copper. Mara sat back on her heels and studied the creature. Professional curiosity sharpened her face.
"You didn't burn it."
"Not yet."
"Why?"
"Wing was damaged before it attacked. Bone sheared. Not by a villager. Not by a fall. It was driven here."
"By what?"
"That's the expensive question."
"And the cheap one?"
Jack glanced at Rian's notices tucked under his belt. "Who knew I would answer it."
The packet Rian brought had no title on the outside, which meant the title inside would be worse.

Mara opened it after he left and after Jack had forced down bitter tea meant to keep him from looking as if pain mattered. The first page was a routing slip. The second was a list of terms under a heading so dull it could have hidden a massacre: Irregular Field Guidance, Transitional Use Only. Rian had made a copy in haste, and the letters leaned where fear had moved his hand. The words did not lean. They sat straight and clean.
Localized instability.
Witness control.
Containment viability.
Narrative correction.
Internal custody review.

Jack read them once and then again, slower. The phrases had no blood on them. That was how they managed to smell of it. He had seen villagers lie over graves, soldiers lie over plunder, aldermen lie over ledgers, and lovers lie over things they were not ready to name. This was different. This was language designed to make lying unnecessary because the person reading it would no longer have access to the older question.
"Who receives these?" he asked.

Mara stood beside the table with one arm folded across herself. "District medics. Some clerks. Field assessors. Anyone likely to encounter contamination after the war. That was how they described it. Contamination."
"Convenient bucket."
"Very. You can put anything in it if you dislike touching it."

He studied the bottom of the copy. The signature line had been removed, but pressure from the original page had left a faint groove. Not ink, only the memory of writing. S. V. perhaps. Or S. Y. The second letter had a hook.
"You saw this before you treated me."
"Parts. Not the custody section."
"Mara."

The single word did what accusation would have overplayed. She closed her eyes, opened them, and met his gaze. "I saw what I needed to know the office wanted more than fever mapping. I told myself wanting more did not mean taking more. That is the kind of sentence people make when they are tired and afraid of unemployment. It sounded better yesterday."
Jack folded the page. "Most things do."
"You should hate me more cleanly."
"I don't do much cleanly."

The answer made her look away. Rian had gone into the rain. The packet lay open. The garkain corpse burned somewhere under wet wood and bad chanting. The room held three people even after one had left: a witcher, a medic, and the institution standing between them in perfect grammar.
Jack put the copied guidance into his pouch.
"That is theft," Mara said.
"Practice," he answered.
The town's infirmary had once been a fuller's shed, and the walls still remembered lye.

Rain pressed the smell inward until the room seemed to breathe in damp wool, bitter herbs, old soap, iron tools, and the sour patience of timber that had absorbed too much human trouble. Wet cloaks hung from pegs near the door. Bundles of comfrey, mint, and yarrow dried from the rafters above a table scarred by knives, needles, and the small black rings left by metal cups set down too hot and too quickly. A single stove made more smoke than warmth, and the lantern on the table guttered whenever wind found the gaps in the boards.
Each time the flame bent, it leaned toward Jack.
Mara noticed. She did not mention it.
"Take off the armor," she said.
"I thought you stitched it already."
"I stitched what I could reach through leather, mud, and your charming refusal to fall over. I would like to clean the rest before infection develops ambitions."
"Infections usually do."
"So do men who think not complaining is the same as healing."

He removed the upper straps. The armor came away with reluctant sounds, dark leather wet and heavy, metal reinforcements catching candlelight along scratched edges. Under it, the shirt had dried into the wound. Mara's expression changed by less than a finger's width. Jack saw it anyway, because pain made most people look away and she had not given herself that mercy.
"I'll do it," he said.
"You won't." Her hand came down over his. "If you tear it, I sew more. Sit."

The command should have annoyed him. It did, which was different from disobeying. Jack sat on the edge of the cot while Mara warmed water in a dented basin and added something so bitter it made the air taste medicinal. She worked the cloth free slowly, using patience where a careless hand would have used speed. Fast pain could be answered. Slow care had no proper enemy, and that made his body distrust it before his mind could form a cleaner objection.

Her shoulder brushed his once as she leaned in. The contact was accidental until neither of them corrected it. She was close; he could smell soap beneath the spirits on her hands, and fatigue beneath both. Not weakness. Fatigue had weight, not shame. It sat in the angle of her neck, in the way she kept her jaw steady while the wet fabric peeled loose from blood and skin.
"You should sleep after this," she said.
"Should is a crowded word."
"Then let me phrase it medically. If you ride tonight, you will reopen the wound, bleed into your armor, frighten your horse, and perhaps die in a ditch with impressive discipline."
"Buck won't be frightened. He'll be angry."
"Good. Someone should be."

The cloth came free. Jack let the breath leave through his nose, but not all of it. Mara's eyes lifted to his mouth and returned to the wound with unnecessary speed. The infirmary became smaller around them, filled by rain, stove-smoke, wet leather, and the bright, precise pain of being handled by someone competent. Competence made trust appear practical, which was worse than charm.
"You are very calm for a man who has been routed through three notices in six days," she said.
"Calm is cheaper than panic."
"That is not the same as trust."
"I didn't pay for trust."
Her fingers slowed at the bandage. "No. You paid for thread."

The answer landed more softly than either of them expected. Outside, a wagon passed through mud, wheels sucking deep. Someone cursed at a mule. Somewhere beyond that, Rian was likely copying something he wished he had never read. The world remained ugly and insistently organized. Inside the shed, Mara tied a final knot and let her hand rest against Jack's ribs a moment too long.
His skin was warmer under her palm than it should have been.
"You feel it," he said.
"Yes."
"And?"
"And I am deciding whether to pretend I don't."
"Useful habit."
"The kind men should fear." She withdrew her hand. The absence of it stayed. "There are men collecting reports about unusual field effects. They do not call themselves hunters. That may be worse."

Jack looked toward her satchel. A corner of folded paper showed under the flap. Field residue. Containment viability. Narrative correction. Words that smelled cleaner than the barn and fouler than the garkain.
"Do you work for them?"

Mara did not flinch. That made the answer worse before she gave it. "I file medical observations through a district office. I thought it was disease mapping after the war. Mutations, monster-borne fever, battlefield contamination. I thought useful work still existed."
"Does it?"
She returned to the basin. The water had gone pink. "Sometimes. That is how they keep people like me."

The rain thickened until the roof seemed to be counting every wrong answer in the room. Jack should have stood. The wound had been cleaned. The room had begun asking for answers he did not give and warmth he had not paid for. Instead he watched Mara cross to the stove, pour bitter tea into two cups, and place one beside him without ceremony. Her sleeve had slipped to her wrist. There was a burn scar there, old and pale, in the shape of a small hand.
"Child?" he asked.
Her face closed. "Not mine."
"Sorry."
"Don't be. She lived. That was the point."

For a while they drank in silence. The tea tasted like bark, iron, and poor judgment. It eased the pain anyway. Mara sat on the stool across from him, not close, not far, hands wrapped around her cup as if warming them after years of not admitting cold. She looked older in the lantern light and younger at the same time, not because the light softened her, but because exhaustion sometimes stripped people back to the first version of themselves that had ever hoped work might save anyone.
"You shouldn't be alone tonight," she said.
Jack turned to her.
"Medically," she added.
"Of course."
A faint color touched her face, which annoyed her into making him almost smile. "If you mock the woman who sewed you closed, I will use thicker thread next time."
"There will be a next time?"
"With your profession? I would wager my good scissors."

He inventoried the door, the windows, the latch, the shadow under the herb shelf, the line of knives within her reach, the satchel with its folded paper, the lantern flame still leaning toward him. No second presence. No hidden movement. Only a medic who had helped file him badly and then studied the damage as if paperwork could bruise her too. The room had its risks. So did the road. The road, at least, did not put warm cups into a man's hand and make leaving feel like an answer chosen too early.
"One hour," he said.
"Two."
"One and a half."
"You are bleeding on my cot. Two."
"That is not bargaining."
"No. That is medicine."

He lay back because the room tilted slightly and because Buck was under shelter behind the infirmary and because exhaustion, ignored too long, became another predator with better patience. Mara checked the bandage once more. Her fingers brushed his side, paused, and remained with open, careful permission. She did not pretend the pause was professional. That would have made it smaller than it was.
Jack caught her wrist, not hard. The pulse under his fingers moved quickly.
"Mara."
"Yes."
"Decide before you touch me like that."

Her breath changed. Barely. The room felt it anyway. The rain filled the shed with its patient noise, and the stove answered with a small settling crackle. Her hand stayed where it was, warm through the edge of the bandage, and her eyes did not leave his. She could have turned it into humor. She could have called it fever, loneliness, shock, the usual cheap disguises people gave desire when they wanted it near but not accountable. She did none of that.
"I decided before I touched you," she said.

The first kiss did not arrive like hunger. It arrived like an argument that had run out of safer subjects and found one more fact waiting beneath the table. Mara leaned down slowly, giving him the chance to turn his head, and Jack did not. Her mouth was warm and faintly bitter from the tea. The contact stayed measured for one breath, then another, until her hand settled at his shoulder and the steadiness broke into something more human.
She made a sound against him, soft and unplanned. "Mm..."

It should have been too small to matter. It mattered anyway. Jack's hand lifted to the back of her neck and stopped there, fingers barely closing over the damp tendrils of hair escaping her pin. He could feel the heat under her skin, the tension she carried like armor no one had taught her to remove, and the sudden uncertainty in the strong body of a woman who was not used to being met with restraint. She drew back first, breathing unevenly, eyes darker in the lantern light.
"This is a bad idea," she said.
"Most ideas that happen after bleeding are."
"That should help." Her mouth almost found a smile and failed. "It does not."

He let go of her wrist. She did not move away. That was the second decision, and it was harder than the first because staying required more honesty than crossing a room. Mara's fingers touched the side of his face this time, not the wound, not the heat, not the evidence, but the scar at his cheekbone. Her thumb paused there. Jack held still because movement would have been easier than being seen.
"Tell me if this is only pain making a liar of you," she said.
"Pain usually makes me quieter."
"That is not an answer."
"No," he said. "It is not only pain."

The second kiss was hers, less careful and more honest. It deepened until the infirmary seemed to fall quiet around them, rain turning distant, stove settling into embers, the world outside reduced to water, boards, and the sound of breath changing between two people who knew better. Jack did not rush her. He held her with the restraint of a man used to measuring force in finger-widths and consequences. Mara answered that restraint with a hand pressed flat against his chest, not to stop him, but to confirm he was there and still under her choice.

Her breathing grew audible. Not loud. Not theatrical. Simply no longer hidden. Each breath warmed the space between them, unsteady in a way that betrayed her and steady in a way that kept choosing. When he brushed his mouth to the corner of hers and waited, she made a sharper sound, half gasp and half refusal to retreat.
"Ah... don't make a habit of listening that closely."
"Too late."

Her fingers tightened once in the cloth near his collar. The movement tugged the wound. Pain answered. Jack's breath caught, sharper than wanting. Mara stopped at once, and that, more than the kiss, made the room sharpen. Care had a way of entering where desire could be held at the door.
"There," she said softly. "That is why two hours."
"You kissed me to improve compliance?"
"If I had, you would be asleep already."

For a moment they remained so close that speech had to pass through warmth before becoming words. Her mouth brushed the corner of his again, slower this time, not asking for more than the night could honestly hold. He let his hand settle at her waist, careful, still over fabric, and felt her answer with a tremor she did not apologize for.
"Mmh..." It was barely more than breath. It stayed anyway.

Then she drew back. Not far. At the distance where choice became boundary and boundary became real. Her hand remained over his chest, above the wrong heat under his skin, while the room slowly remembered the rain, the papers, the garkain smoke, and the district office waiting somewhere beyond the wet road.
"Sleep," she said.
It should have been a command. It came out almost like a plea.

Jack closed his eyes. The room kept its smells around him: lye in the boards, bitter herbs, wet wool, iron tools, Mara's soap, smoke from the cheap stove. When the pen scratched later by lantern light, careful and reluctant across a page, he did not wake to ask what she wrote. He already knew. Care could be true and still become evidence.
In the morning, the wound had closed too much.
Mara noticed. Rian noticed the missing corner of one copied notice. Buck noticed Jack's mood and tried to kick the stable door. Everyone, in their own profession, proved competent.

Field Observation, District Medical Addendum. Subject: unnamed Wolf School witcher, probable age twenty to twenty-five. Wound response exceeds expected witcher range after garkain contact. Tissue heat persistent. No fever presentation. Eye coloration anomalous. Recommend cross-reference with host suitability vocabulary in irregular field guidance. Do not disclose to local authority pending internal custody review.
The contract for the Broken Crown arrived on dry paper in a town where every roof leaked.

That was the first insult. Rain had followed Jack for nine days, softening roads, swelling streams, turning graves into soup and soup into arguments. Paper suffered in such weather. Notices curled, ink ran, seals bled, and honest village complaints became dark smears under thumb marks. This notice remained crisp on the board outside Heddel's Ferry, its corners square, its ink black, its seal pressed deep into red wax that smelled faintly of cloves.
Buck smelled it and sneezed.
"Agreed," Jack said.

The notice offered one hundred and twenty crowns for removal of a subterranean threat beneath the hill-fort locally known as the Broken Crown. That was too much. It specified metallic auditory phenomena, livestock distress, and localized structural hazard. That was too clean. It requested that witnesses be held for statement collection after contract resolution. That was too familiar.
At the bottom, in smaller script, someone had written containment viability uncertain.
Jack took the notice.

Heddel's Ferry had a tavern with a roof that leaked into three bowls and one man's hat. The common room smelled of onion broth, wet dog, horse sweat, and the private despair of travelers who had hoped the next village would be better. A group of charcoal burners sat near the hearth. Two soldiers without colors played dice with the serious hatred of men losing money they had stolen. Behind the bar, a woman with forearms like hams watched Jack read the notice and made the sign against evil after she noticed his eyes.
"You know where the Broken Crown is?" Jack asked.
"Hill north of here," she said. "Old fort. Bad stones. Worse memories."
"Specific."
"Specific requires another coin."
He put a copper on the bar. She regarded it as if it had insulted her lineage. He added another. The insult became tolerable.

"Fort was Temerian once," she said. "Then Redanian, then Nilfgaardian for half a week, then no one's because everyone with sense stopped wanting it. Crown shape on the ridge. Three towers left, if you count leaning as standing. Folk say metal grinds under it at night. Sheep won't graze near the throat."
"The throat?"
"Pass between the rocks. Wind goes through like a man swallowing nails."
One of the colorless soldiers looked up. "Don't go there, mutant. Crown takes what wears steel."
"You've been?"
"My cousin went."
"Returned?"
The soldier showed brown teeth. "Parts."
"Which parts?"
The smile went away. Good. Stories liked details until details became work.

A man in a dark travel cloak sat near the back with his hood low and a cup he had not touched. His hands were clean. His boots were muddy only at the soles. He did not look at Jack, which was often how watchers announced themselves to anyone worth watching. Jack marked the man, finished the weak beer he had not wanted, and went outside through the kitchen instead of the front door.
Rian Wedeck was waiting in the rain beside Buck.

The clerk looked worse than when Jack had left him, which suggested either conscience or poor lodging. His coat had been turned inside out to hide a district patch. His hair clung to his forehead. He held a leather packet under one arm with the desperation of a man sheltering a child or evidence.
"I was told not to speak with you," Rian said.
"You should try following instructions. It may soothe whoever gives them."
"They sent a query after the garkain report. Then another after the mill story. Then one asking whether your eyes were naturally crimson or reactive under stress."
Jack checked Buck's girth. It did not need checking. His fingers did it anyway. "Who is they?"
"The office names change. The phrasing doesn't."
"You followed me to say office names change?"
"I followed you because the Broken Crown notice was copied before the shepherd reported the noise."
Rain ticked on the saddle leather. Buck turned his head and pushed his nose against Rian's shoulder hard, making him stumble. The horse disliked fear that stood too close.
"Before," Jack said.

Rian nodded. "By two days. Maybe three. The date was adjusted. Not well. Whoever corrected it knows forms, not postings. Postings have local weather marks, different folds, thumb grease. Forms stay clean in offices."
"You notice many romantic things."
"Ink is steadier than people." He swallowed. "There will be witnesses."
"There are always witnesses."
"Too many. Too early. The notice requests statement collection after resolution. I saw three riders leave this morning toward the hill. Not villagers. Clerks, perhaps, or men pretending to be."
Jack studied the packet. "What's that?"
Rian held it out and then seemed to regret having hands. "Copies. Phrases. Seals. I don't understand them. I know what I need to be frightened."
"Sensible range of knowledge."
"If I disappear, my mother lives in Devenford. Her name is Lyska. She thinks I am still in grain tallies."
Jack took the packet. "If you disappear, being right will comfort her less than you hope."
Rian's mouth trembled into something like humor. "Yes. I thought that might be so."
The back door of the tavern opened. The man in the clean cloak stepped out, saw them, and looked surprised with professional neatness. Jack mounted. Buck moved before the man's second breath.

The road north climbed through wet fields where old siege lines had become ditches full of brown water. Blackened stakes still jutted from one hill like rotten teeth. A shrine to a local saint had been repaired with Nilfgaardian boards, the imperial stamp planed off but not fully erased. Politics lived like mold in every join. Jack rode past a burned wagon, two scarecrows dressed in soldier coats, and a row of graves marked with spoons because no one had spare wood after the winter.
By afternoon, the Broken Crown came into view.

The hill had once been a fort and had since become an accusation against engineers. Three broken towers stood along the ridge in a jagged line, their tops torn so that from the road they looked like points of a cracked circlet. Below them a narrow cleft cut through the rock, dark even under gray daylight. The wind moved there with a low metallic groan. Sheep bones lay in the grass, clean and scattered in circles.
Buck stopped fifty paces from the cleft.
"I know," Jack said.

The horse's skin trembled under the saddle. Not fear of predators. This was deeper, the refusal he had shown at the bridge in Willenford but sharpened into anger. Jack dismounted and led him to a twisted hawthorn well away from the cleft. He loosened the reins and did not tie them. If Buck chose to leave, rope would not improve the decision.
The ground near the hill was cold. The stones were warm.

Jack put one hand against a fallen block and felt heat pulsing through it in slow intervals. Not fire. Not spell. Pressure. The medallion shivered, stopped, shivered again. Silver in the scabbard warmed against his back. When he drew a small blade and touched it to the stone, the tip sang faintly, a thin sound that made his teeth ache.
Anchor-site, some later part of him would call it, once he had names to give what his body had already understood. For now it was only wrong.

He climbed the outer slope. Tracks crossed the mud near the ruined gate: sheep, goats, villagers, two horses with iron shoes, one cart with narrow wheels, and three sets of boots too new for hill work. Witnesses, as Rian had promised. One set had paused beside a boulder with a view of the cleft. The boot heel had a crescent nick. Jack had seen the same mark in tavern mud behind the clean-cloaked man.
The cleft did not descend like a cave. It descended like a wound reopened badly.

Jack entered deep into the ruin, where old tool marks scarred the stone and later hands had tried to hide them. Iron had once been set into the walls at intervals, not for doors, not for torches. Restraints. Some had been pried out. Others remained, sunk deep and black, their surfaces sweating in the cold air. When he held the lantern close, the flame narrowed to a blue thread and pointed inward.
Ten paces down, the passage widened into a throat-shaped chamber where water dripped upward.
That stopped him.

Drops gathered from cracks in the floor, trembled, and rose a finger's height before bursting into mist. Not all of them. Only those near a shallow groove carved through the stone, a line that curved toward the deeper dark and then vanished under rubble. Jack crouched beside it. The groove was old, softened at the edges, but inside it a black residue clung like tar. He touched it with the tip of his knife. The residue shrank from the iron and stretched toward his glove.
The barbed star under his armor turned cold.
"No," he said to the empty chamber.
The chamber did not argue. It waited. Waiting was worse.
Behind him, the district clerk called down, "Master witcher, procedure discourages unsupervised descent."
"Then procedure can come hold the lantern."
No footsteps followed.

At the far end of the chamber, behind a fall of stone, something breathed without lungs. Jack heard it once, then only felt the interval where the sound had been. He placed one palm against the wall. Heat moved there, slow and circular, as if the hill had swallowed an enormous animal and trained itself to deny digestion. Beneath that heat, faint and regular, metal scraped.
The creature was not sleeping. It was being held until the right audience gathered.
The old fort still kept human traces under the monster sign.

A child's bead near the south wall. A strip of blue cloth knotted around an iron ring. Scratches in the lower chamber, not claw marks, but counting marks made by someone with a nail or a bit of wire. Thirty-one lines in one group, seventeen in the next, then a space where the hand had either escaped or stopped needing numbers. Jack stood over them longer than the investigation required.

People liked to say monsters moved into ruins. It comforted them. It let them believe ruins began empty, innocent, waiting for fangs. The facts were usually meaner. Ruins were built by people, filled by people, misused by people, and only then inherited by things honest in their biting and free of proclamations.

Near the counting marks, he found a patch of wall where soot had been scrubbed away. Not washed. Scraped. Under it remained a symbol too damaged to read properly: three short lines meeting a circle, or a crown, or a gate drawn by a shaking hand. When Jack touched the edge, the skin of his fingertips tightened. His medallion trembled once and went still, as if whatever slept beneath the hill had turned its face away to avoid being seen too clearly.
He scraped a flake of soot into oilcloth and put it in his pouch. Evidence did not explain itself. That was why officials liked it. They could arrive later and offer assistance.
Jack returned to the surface and saw the audience waiting exactly where fear, greed, and instruction had arranged it.
The hill was not empty.

He counted seven villagers in the lee of the broken south wall, though the contract had not asked them to come. Three men, two women, one old shepherd, and a girl with a bandage around her hand. They held lamps despite the daylight. The flames leaned toward the cleft. Behind them stood two men in district brown, tablets tucked under oilskin. One had a little writing desk strapped over his chest like a poor man's armor. The other held a sealed tube.
"You were told to remain downhill," Jack said.
The old shepherd spat. "By who?"
"Common sense."
"Never met him. Does he pay for sheep?"

One of the brown-coated men stepped forward. "Master witcher. Under district safety ordinance, witnesses to the matter have been retained for post-resolution statement consistency. Your cooperation will be noted."
Jack studied the writing desk. "Will my lack of it get a nicer verb?"
The man's smile had no weather in it. "Our office prefers accuracy."
"No office prefers accuracy. It makes work."
The shepherd chuckled. The clerk did not.
Before entering the cleft, Jack made the witnesses tell him the hill's stories separately.

The girl with the bandaged hand was called Nessa. She had been sent to fetch a ewe that would not come down from the ridge, and she had returned with three fingernails broken, a burn along her palm, and the conviction that something under the hill had called her by her grandmother's name. The old shepherd said the hill did that to women sometimes. The district clerk said auditory hallucination was common near unstable stone. Nessa said nothing after that, but her bandage reddened whenever the wind moved through the cleft.

A charcoal burner claimed he had heard armor marching underground. His brother said it was not armor but a forge. A third man, who had lost two sheep and a son to different wars, insisted the Broken Crown had been used to hide prisoners when the flags changed too quickly for proper paperwork. That last story made the district men exchange a glance. Barely. But it carried.

Jack walked the old curtain wall while they spoke. The stones bore marks from three occupations and one unofficial repair. Temerian mason cuts under Redanian mortar. Nilfgaardian wedge marks near the gate. Local hands closing murder holes with fieldstone because after armies left, people used fortresses for sheep and secrets. Under the south tower, he found iron rings driven low into the wall, half-hidden by moss, too small for horses and too strong for doors.
Kept, he thought again, before he knew what had been kept there.

The cleft itself breathed in intervals. When the wind entered from the west, it should have whistled. Instead it ground. Jack set a coin on a flat stone and watched it tremble toward the dark, pause, then tremble back toward his boot. A place that pulled both ways. No proper portal did that. No ordinary curse either. It reminded him of traps Vesemir had made with two doors and no safe room, designed to teach boys that choosing quickly was not the same as choosing well.

The clean-cloaked man watched from the boulder with the crescent heel mark near his boot. He pretended to study the clouds. Jack pretended not to know. The exchange had the elegance of two thieves passing in a chapel.
"Seen what you need?" the old shepherd asked.
"No."
"You witchers ever say yes?"
"When paid."
"Good trade."
"Not lately."
The shepherd hawked and spat neatly between two stones. "My wife said never trust folk who come with forms before funerals. She died before the war. Clever woman. Poor timing."
Jack glanced at the district men. "Your wife would be popular today."
"She hated being popular. Said it attracted requests."
The exchange made Nessa almost smile. The smile vanished when the cleft groaned again and her hand began to bleed through fresh cloth.
Jack crouched before her. "When it called you, did it use your name?"
She shook her head.
"Your grandmother's?"
A nod.
"Was she buried here?"
Another shake, sharper. "She served here. Before I was born. In the kitchens, they said. Not prison. Kitchens."
The old shepherd looked away.
Jack understood the shape of that lie too well. Kitchens, prison, garrison, occupation. Words changed when families needed descendants to sleep.
"Go downhill," he said.
Nessa turned to the district clerk. The clerk consulted procedure. Procedure looked back and found no blood in itself.
Jack stood. "Now."
She began moving before the clerk decided whether to forbid it. That saved her life for nearly six minutes.
A boy from the charcoal burners tried to sell Jack a charm before the fight.

It was a nail wrapped in red thread and dipped in candle wax, which put it above most charms in effort and below most knives in usefulness. The boy held it out with the expression of a merchant expecting mockery and needing coin badly and enduring it. His sleeves were too short. His wrists showed winter rash. Behind him, his father pretended not to watch and failed with parental thoroughness.
"Against the Crown," the boy said.
"Does it work?"
"No one carrying one has died there."
"How many went there carrying one?"
The boy hesitated. Honesty fought commerce and lost only partly. "None."
Jack gave him a copper and did not take the charm.
The boy frowned. "You forgot it."
"No."
"Then why pay?"
"For the statistics."

The boy turned that over, decided adults were a poorly made species, and ran back to his father. The father nodded once to Jack. Not gratitude. Recognition. The small, bitter fellowship of men who knew children watched what fear made of them.

Later, after the red pressure had bent the lamps and broken the hill's throat, Jack would find the charm in Buck's mane. The boy must have tied it there while pretending to admire the saddle. Buck had allowed it, which meant either the boy had excellent hands or the horse had decided one useless charm would not worsen the day. Jack left it there until the next river crossing.
Superstition deserved no respect. Children sometimes did.
The metallic groan under the hill stopped.
Every lamp flame went sideways.
