Jack turned toward the cleft. A sound rose from below, not loud, but intimate, as if someone were dragging a crown across stone under the earth. The girl's bandaged hand began to bleed through the cloth. She stared at the cleft and whispered something Jack did not catch. The old shepherd crossed himself, then cursed himself for doing it.
"Move them downhill," Jack said.
The district man lifted the sealed tube. "Procedure requires proximity sufficient for witness verification."
Jack stepped close; the man smelled the cat-potion bitterness still living faintly in his breath from old use and the leather oil in his armor. "Move them downhill."
The man saw Jack's eyes and discovered procedure had legs. "A measured withdrawal may be acceptable."
"Run, if you like shorter phrases."
The first scream came from under the south wall.

Stone burst upward. Not outward, upward, as if the hill had swallowed a fist and decided to make it everyone else's concern. A creature dragged itself through the broken floor with iron rings embedded in its hide. It had a draconid shape ruined by imprisonment: long jaw, plated shoulders, forelimbs too powerful for the starved body behind them, wing bones fused under scar tissue, eyes filmed white. Chains hung from its neck and ribs, each link black with old rust. Where the chains scraped stone, sparks jumped blue.
It wore part of a bit in its mouth.
Not wild, Jack thought, and the thought came cold. Kept.

The creature lunged at the nearest villager. Jack crossed the distance in three strides and met it with Aard. The Sign struck the jaw sideways. The creature hit the wall, recovered too quickly, and came again. Silver left the scabbard in a pale arc. Jack cut along the neck, felt scales part under the edge, and smelled blood like hot coins.

The villagers ran badly. Most people did. Fear made them children and kings, certain the world would notice them individually. One woman fell. The old shepherd tried to pull her up and lost his lamp. The flame hit wet grass and burned blue instead of dying.
The chains on the creature tightened by themselves.
Under the hill, something pulled back.

Jack saw it then. The creature was not the contract. It was bait tied to the contract. The chains ran into the broken floor through a crack too narrow to have admitted them unless the stone had grown around them. Each time the creature strained, the hill groaned. Each groan drew the villagers' lamps sideways. Each sideways flame leaned toward Jack.
The district man with the writing desk had not run. He was writing.
Jack swore.

The creature slammed into him. He caught the jaw on the crossguard, boots skidding, injured thigh from Willenford flaring. Teeth snapped inches from his face. Its breath smelled of blood, rust, and long confinement. He drove a knee into the plated chest, rolled under the forelimb, and cut the first chain. The link broke with a sound like a bell dropped into water.
The hill answered.

Pressure moved through the stones. Not a tremor. An inward breath. Jack felt it in his teeth, in the healed scar on his cheek, in the hidden necklace under his armor. The barbed star went cold, then hot, then cold again. For a moment he saw not the hill but lines under it, angles and points, old pressure routes like veins through black stone. He blinked and the world returned.
The girl with the bleeding hand stood at the cleft.

She had stopped running. Her eyes were open and empty, fixed on something below. Blood ran from her bandage and dripped onto a stone carved with three shallow notches. The lamps leaned harder. The creature screamed and turned toward her, not to feed, but to obey the pull.
Jack threw his silver sword.

It struck the ground between the girl and the cleft, blade sinking into mud, wolf pommel shivering. The sudden silver line broke whatever had held her. She gasped. The old shepherd caught her around the waist and dragged her backward.
The creature came at them.

Jack met it with steel because silver was in the ground and there was no time to be elegant. Steel skidded from scale. He used the impact to turn, slammed his shoulder into the creature's neck, and drove it away from the shepherd. A claw opened his left arm. Another tore the strap at his chest. The hidden barbed-star necklace slipped free under the loosened leather and struck the air.
The hill went silent.
Every eye found him.
The creature. The clerks. The villagers. The lamps. The frost gathered in the cracks of the warm stones. Even Buck, down the slope, threw his head up and screamed once into the rain.
The barbed star lay against Jack's chest, dark metal around a red center that had never shone before.
No, Jack thought, but the word had no handle.
The creature lunged. The chain under the ground pulled. The girl's blood steamed on the notched stone. The hill took a breath through him.
Crimson answered.

It did not glow. Glow was for mages showing off and cheap lantern glass. The air around Jack thickened with red heat, dense and low, like summer seen through blood. Frost vanished from the stones in a circle at his feet. Torches and lamps bent sideways toward him, their flames drawn flat as banners in a storm no one else felt. The silver sword in the mud trembled. The chains inside the hill pulled tight and then, impossible and slow, pulled inward.
Everyone heard something.

The old shepherd heard a hunting horn and fell to his knees. The girl heard a woman singing in a language she would never know. The clerk with the writing desk heard metal gates closing and wet himself without noticing. The creature heard its master, or its prison, or the difference between the two, and broke its own jaw trying to scream.
Jack heard a heartbeat that was not his.

The pressure moved into his bones. His eyes burned. The hidden places in the hill unfolded in his sight: a throat of stone, a hollow chamber, chains knotted through old anchors, a black residue clinging to the links like thought. The creature was only meat around a hook. The hook wanted blood. Not the girl's now. His.
He took one step forward.
The ground cracked.
"Run," he said.

He did not know if the word carried. The villagers moved anyway. The old shepherd dragged the girl. The woman pulled the second woman. One district clerk ran with them. The other kept writing until a stone split beside his boot and persuaded him literacy had limits.

Jack reached the silver sword and closed his hand around the hilt. Pain flared through his palm. The blade was too hot. The crimson pressure wrapped around it, not obedient, not separate, like two animals forced into the same cage. He lifted the sword and drove it into the first anchor-notch.
The hill tried to swallow him.

Mud, stone, air, sound, all pulled inward. Jack dropped to one knee and felt the world narrow to the sword, the notch, the chain below, and the thing in his blood that knew how to hold. Not open. Hold. The distinction arrived without language and left claw marks behind. He twisted the blade. The anchor cracked.

The chained creature convulsed. Its body folded around the chain as the chain pulled back through it. Jack saw ribs snap inward. He saw the draconid's white eyes clear for one breath, not intelligent perhaps, but aware, and terrified. He cut the second chain. The creature collapsed.
Below the hill, something struck the inside of the stone.
Not the creature. Bigger. Older. Farther away than distance should allow. A pressure-front against a closed door.
Jack's blood answered again, harder.

The red heat burst outward. Not fire. Not spell. The lamps shattered. Rain hissed into steam before it touched the stones. The three broken towers of the fort groaned, leaning toward the cleft as if bowing or being dragged. Jack's vision went white at the edges. He drove the sword deeper and felt the anchor break.
Silence fell so suddenly that the rain seemed embarrassed to continue.

The creature lay dead. The chains had withdrawn into stone, leaving black grooves and a smell of burned iron. The cleft no longer groaned. The flames that had survived stood upright again, small, yellow, ordinary, and frightened. Jack remained on one knee with one hand around the sword hilt and the other pressed against the ground because if he removed it, he was not certain the hill would remain where it was.
The crimson heat faded into his skin.
It left marks.

Thin red lines crossed his palm where he had gripped the sword. On the notched stone, a blackened shape remained, five points around a center, not carved, not burned, but remembered into the surface. The barbed-star necklace was cold again. It hung against him as if it had never done anything in its life.
Jack stood slowly.

The witnesses stared from the slope. Their faces had the blankness that came after survival, before gratitude, before stories, before men with papers taught them what they had seen. Buck pulled free of the hawthorn and came to him, reins dragging. He pressed his head hard against Jack's shoulder, nearly knocking him sideways. Jack put one blood-marked hand on the horse's neck.
"I'm standing," he said.
Buck breathed against him, unconvinced.
The first officer was local and frightened, mistaking speed for authority.

He came up from Heddel's Ferry with one cart, two scribes, a medic, three armed men, and a coat too clean at the cuffs. He did not look first at the girl. He studied the red mark on the stone, Jack's burned palm, and the dead draconid with its chains withdrawn into black grooves. The medic went first to the corpse. The old shepherd saw it too. Sometimes contempt was the only language strangers shared.
"My granddaughter is bleeding," the shepherd said.
"She will be seen," the clean-cloaked officer replied.
"Pretty phrase. Means nothing, but it is pretty."
One armed man stepped forward. Jack shifted his weight. Buck bared his teeth, yellow and exact. The armed man discovered a sudden interest in remaining useful elsewhere.
"You maintain an unsafe animal," the officer said.
"So do you. Yours wears boots."

The old shepherd barked a laugh. Nessa, pale and shaking, pressed her bandaged hand against her chest and looked at Jack as if laughter near fear were a new weather. That look would become part of the story. He knew it before she did.

A woman in a gray veil had ridden with them and not dismounted until then. She approached the notched stone with the care of someone walking toward a sleeping snake. Her gloved hand hovered above the five-point mark, then withdrew as if heat had reached through leather. She spoke to the officer in a low voice. Jack caught only three words: internal, pressure, unsuitable.
Unsuitable for what, he wondered.
The officer heard the question in his silence. Men trained for paperwork often mistook silence for absence. Better ones heard the blade inside it.
"You are injured," he said.
"Often."
"Medical assistance can be provided."
"I have bandages."
"Specialized assistance."
"I have better bandages."

The officer's polite mask thinned. The rain made a small bright line along his jaw and failed to make him look human. Behind him, the gray-veiled woman had taken out a wax tablet and was sketching the mark without touching it.
"This need not become adversarial," the officer said.
"Then stop finding long words for cages."

That line reached the witnesses. Jack saw it move from face to face, not fully understood, fully felt. The officer saw it too. The balance shifted by a hair. Too many eyes. Too much mud. Too fresh a rescue. The state had arrived quickly, but too late to own the first version.
That was why the purse came out.
Payment first. Classification later. The old order and the new one, briefly forced to share a road.

The district clerk with the writing desk approached first. He had lost his hat and gained humility, both temporary conditions. His hands shook, but the stylus remained between his fingers. Men like that could be terrified and still useful to the people who terrified them.
"Master witcher," he said. "For purposes of accurate classification, would you describe the manifestation as voluntary?"
Jack faced him.
The clerk swallowed. "No, then."
The old shepherd spat into the mud. "He saved us, you paper-faced tick."
"That can be included as secondary outcome," the clerk said, which was when Jack decided he disliked him and remembered his face.
From the road below came the sound of wheels.

Not a cart. Three carts. Iron-rimmed, moving fast despite mud, escorted by riders in dark coats with no local colors. They arrived before the corpse cooled, before Nessa stopped shaking, before the hill's warmth faded. One rider carried a black tube sealed at both ends. Another wore a sword that had never chopped wood or butchered meat. The third had gloves too clean for travel.
The local officer saw them and went paler. That was useful. Fear, like ink, had grades.
The man in the clean cloak from Heddel's Ferry dismounted first.
He bowed with the perfect moderation of someone who had practiced respect in a mirror. "Jack Morningstar?"

The name hit harder than the question. Jack had not given it at the ferry. He had not given it to the district clerk. Rian knew it, perhaps Mara. Few others did. Fewer still used the surname unless they wanted to see what happened.
Buck's ears went flat.
"Depends who is asking," Jack said.
The man's smile did not move his eyes. "An officer empowered under provisional cross-border safety memorandum regarding anomalous threats, field residues, and public-risk persons."
"No, then."

The old shepherd laughed once, wild with relief and fear. The laugh made two of the riders look at him as if laughter ought to be licensed. Nessa did not laugh. She watched the black tube. Clever girl. Children who had nearly been used by old stone learned quickly which objects had teeth.
The officer opened the tube and withdrew a document. The paper was dry. Of course it was.
"You are not accused of any criminal act at this time," he said. "Your cooperation is requested for preliminary classification."
"Classification of what?"
The officer looked at the red mark on the stone, the dead draconid, the witnesses, Jack's burned palm, the crimson eyes. He did not call him witcher. He did not call him man.
"Of the public-risk anomaly presently associated with your person."

Jack's face did not change. Inside, something that was not anger yet arranged itself with care. Anger came hot. This came cold. It had drawers. It had labels. It had a place ready for men who said associated with your person because saying you would have forced them to admit the person was still there.
"I fulfilled the contract," he said.
"That is not disputed."
"Then pay me."
The officer paused.

It was a small pause. Good quality. Expensive. The kind of pause institutions made when a living person insisted on being treated under the older, cruder category of worker rather than the newer, cleaner category of subject. Behind the officer, one of the carts opened. Inside were iron bands, folded canvas, a medic's chest, and three wooden boxes with ventilation holes too narrow for comfort.
The old shepherd saw them too. His mouth shut. Nessa's good hand closed on his sleeve.
The officer recovered. "Payment can be arranged after statement consolidation."
"Payment now. Statements later. Consolidate that."

The district clerk made a helpless noise. The officer's eyes moved to the witnesses. Too many. Too public. The story had not been corrected yet. Jack could see the arithmetic move behind his face and arrive where all frightened arithmetic arrived: not justice, not decency, but delay.
The officer nodded to a subordinate. A purse changed hands.
Jack counted the crowns. One hundred and twenty. None clipped. He had to admit, in that narrow matter, the paperwork had manners.
"We will require a statement," the officer said.
"You have seven witnesses."
"Witnesses are unstable after phenomena of this class."
"So are hills. Write to the hill."

He mounted despite the pain in his palm and the weakness crawling up his legs. Buck moved before anyone decided to stand in front of him. The officer did not try to stop them. Not yet. That was the important part. Jack rode down the slope with the hill behind him, the dead creature cooling, the witnesses being gathered, and the red mark on the stone already drying into evidence.
At the bottom of the road, Rian stood half-hidden behind a birch tree, white-faced.
Jack did not stop. He dropped the copied packet as Buck passed. Rian caught it badly, fumbled, clutched it to his chest.
"Go home," Jack said.
"Too late," Rian answered.
That was probably true.

Jack did not look back at the hill until the road bent. When he did, the officers were already arranging people into lines, separating the shaken from the useful and the useful from the inconvenient. Nessa sat on a stone with her grandfather's coat around her shoulders while the gray-veiled woman questioned her from too great a height. The girl's mouth moved once. The woman wrote twice. That was how fact became a draft.

Buck felt the change in him and slowed without being asked. Jack touched the horse's neck with the hand that was not burned. The other hand throbbed in time with the hidden star under his armor. Behind them, the Broken Crown had stopped breathing. Ahead, every road sign looked suddenly less like direction and more like permission someone else had granted.
The report traveled faster than Jack did.

By nightfall, it had become a hill-fort instability with anomalous thermal displacement. By dawn, it had gained a subject. By noon, three witness statements had been corrected for hysteria, one girl's account had been retained under restricted access, and one shepherd's statement had been marked unreliable due to age, local superstition, and repeated use of the phrase "paper-faced tick" in reference to authorized personnel.
In a clean office two districts away, a clerk copied the senior examiner's initials at the bottom of the page.

Preliminary Field Classification. Subject: Jack Morningstar, unregistered Wolf School derivative, status irregular. Associated manifestation: crimson thermal-pressure event, non-standard Sign, non-standard curse, non-standard sorcery. Public-risk anomaly confirmed. Senior review requested under S. Veyrane. Recommended language pending: voluntary cooperation preferred, containment viability undetermined.
Mara Veyr had moved the infirmary before Jack returned, which meant she had expected him to survive or had feared he would.

Both possibilities irritated him. Hope made people careless. Fear made them thorough. The new room stood behind a cooper's shop in Devenford, above a yard full of barrel staves and rainwater hoops. It smelled of oak shavings, boiled vinegar, bruised mint, and the dry mineral odor of powdered medicines. A narrow window overlooked the alley. A second door opened onto a stair that led to the yard. Mara had chosen well. Two exits, poor sight lines from the street, no loose boards near the bed, knives within reach of the table but not the patient.
He had reached Devenford by the back roads, avoiding the main toll not because he feared tolls but because toll collectors remembered faces for coin and faces for men who paid them to remember.

The ride had made the Broken Crown wound reopen twice. The palm was worse. It did not bleed much after the first hour. It heated. Heat pulsed under the bandage in slow intervals, answering things Jack did not see: an abandoned shrine beside a flooded road, a stone culvert where Buck refused to drink, a black crow with one white feather that followed them for three miles and then dropped from the air as if struck. Jack buried the crow because leaving it visible would have made some farmer invent a prophecy by supper.

Buck hated the cooper's yard on principle. Too many hoops, too much hollow wood, too many places for cats to claim tactical advantage. He allowed himself to be stabled only after Jack checked the stall, water, hay, roofline, latch, and the suspicious bucket near the door. The horse then pressed his head against Jack's chest hard, making the burned palm throb.
"I'm not dying in a cooper's yard," Jack said.
Buck blew warm air through his nose.
"Fine. Not planning to."
That did not satisfy the horse. It did not satisfy Jack either.

Climbing the stairs behind the shop took longer than it should have. Each step reminded him of the creature at the Broken Crown, the chain, the anchor, the way the world had folded inward through his blood. He had spent years understanding his body as a disciplined instrument with inconvenient modifications. Now it felt like a locked room in a house he had never owned. Something inside it had heard a knock and nearly answered in a language older than consent.

At the landing, he paused with one hand against the wall. Oak dust clung to his glove. Through the door came no voices, no movement, only the faint scrape of paper being turned and the hush of someone who had stopped breathing to listen.
Mara knew how to wait.
He knocked once because entering without warning would have made the night easier and the room less honest.
Jack noticed all of it before he noticed her.

She stood at the table with both hands flat on either side of a ledger. Her hair had been pinned too tightly. Her sleeves were rolled, but not because she had been working. There was no blood on them. No herbs under her nails. A woman preparing for argument, not medicine. The lantern between them threw her shadow against the wall and made it look larger, which was a kindness lamps sometimes offered without permission.
"You should not be here," she said.
"I get that often."
"This time it is excellent advice."
"Then it will be expensive."

Her gaze dropped to his left hand. He had wrapped it himself, badly, because riding with one hand, bleeding through the palm, and arguing with Buck about direction had left limited room for artistry. The bandage had gone dark at the center.
Mara's face changed. Anger stayed. Worry arrived behind it and disliked being seen.
"Sit down."
"After you answer."
"Sit down before you fall down, and I will consider answering with fewer insults."
"That your medical oath?"
"No. My medical oath has more threats."

He sat because the room had begun leaning toward him and because refusing care was not independence when infection had already been invited. Mara crossed to him with a basin and scissors. Her movements were sharper than before. She cut the bandage with unnecessary precision, peeled it away, and went still.
The wound was not healing like a cut. It was sealing like a brand.

Five red lines crossed the palm from the sword grip, thin and bright under the skin, radiating toward the wrist in a shape too close to the barbed star hidden under his shirt. The skin around them was not burned. It was changed. Mara touched the edge with a wet cloth. Heat rose into the room.
"What happened at the Broken Crown?" she asked.
"Your reports didn't say?"
Her hand stopped.
There it was. No need to draw steel. The right words could enter cleanly between ribs and sit there.
"Jack."
"Don't soften it now. It becomes harder to classify."
She set the cloth down. "I did not know they would use my notes that way."
"You knew someone would use them."
"Yes."
The answer was immediate. Honest. Too little.

Rain whispered against the window. Below, the cooper's yard creaked as wet hoops shifted. Somewhere in the alley, a man sang the first two lines of a soldier's song and forgot the rest, which made it almost tolerable.
"They arrived before the corpse cooled," Jack said. "With forms. With iron. With a cart that had air holes."
Mara's face tightened around the last detail. "Gods."
"No. Men. Gods have worse handwriting."

She turned away, then turned back because guilt had not become cowardice in her yet. "I filed wound temperature, recovery irregularity, and eye response. I marked it for medical review. I did not write public-risk anomaly. I did not write containment."
"But you had seen the words."
"Yes."
"And kept working."
"Yes."
He stood. Too fast. The room narrowed. Mara reached for him and stopped before touching. Good. She was learning where care became permission and where permission had to be asked.

"People keep working," she said. "That is the ugliest thing I know, and I know quite a few. A clerk copies a phrase because the seal is correct. A medic files heat because fever kills villages. A ferryman asks no questions because his children need bread. Then a cart arrives with air holes, and everyone says they did not build it."
"Did you?"
The question should have been cruel. It came out tired.
Mara studied the ledger. "I helped with the hinges."
Silence gathered.

Jack could have left then. The part of him trained by Kaer Morhen, by winter walls and old men who taught boys to sleep with knives near their hands, had already measured the distance to the stair. Take the copy if there was one. Burn the rest. Leave before tenderness made anything ambiguous. The road was cleaner than rooms. It lied less.
Mara lifted a folded paper from under the ledger and placed it on the table.
"This came after your first treatment," she said. "I was asked to confirm whether old Wolf School terminology applied. I did not answer. I copied it. Then I moved."
Jack did not touch the paper.
"Read it," she said.
"You read it."
"I want you to know I can say it aloud."
That mattered in ways he disliked.

Mara unfolded the page. Her hands were steady. "Supplemental requisition, irregular field subject. Possible unregistered Wolf School asset. Morningstar designation uncertain. Previous concealment probable. Vesemir reference requires archive cross-check. If subject presents voluntarily, medical custody preferred. If subject resists, witness correction recommended before seizure."
The room lost warmth.

Vesemir had been dead so long grief had settled into objects. A cup at Kaer Morhen no one used. A whetstone with the old man's thumb groove. A phrase in memory spoken too dryly to be comfort and too kind to be anything else. Hearing his name in requisition language made Jack's burned palm close before he chose it. Pain flashed red.
Mara reached for his hand. This time he let her.
"I am sorry," she said.
"Don't spend it all at once."
"It is not payment."
"Then what is it?"
She looked up. "Too late."

The words should have broken the room. Instead they steadied it. Too late was at least a place. People could stand there. They could not live there forever, but they could stand there and decide which ruin mattered.

Jack sat again. Mara cleaned the wound in silence. The heat under the skin resisted the salve, then accepted it with a faint sting that moved up his arm and into the scar along his cheek. Her fingers were careful now, not with fear, but attention. The argument remained between them. So did the kiss from the infirmary, the rain, the report, the cart. Nothing canceled anything. That was what made the room difficult.
When she finished wrapping his palm, she did not let go.
"I thought you had died there," she said.
"No."
"You keep saying that as if it answers the thing being asked."
"Usually does."
"Not tonight."
The lantern flame moved. Not toward the wound this time. Toward the narrow space between them.
Jack studied her hand around his. He could feel her pulse through two layers of bandage and one layer of reluctance. "Mara."
"I know."
"Do you?"
Her mouth shifted, almost a smile and then not. "No. But I know what I am choosing badly with open eyes."
"That is not encouraging."
"It was not meant to be." She leaned closer, then stopped. The stop mattered more than the movement. "Tell me to move away."
He did not.
She had tried to pack before he arrived.

He saw it after the first argument, after the confession and before the kiss changed the room's grammar. A traveling bag stood under the table, half-filled with rolled linen, two vials wrapped in wool, a spare dress, a packet of dried apple, and a small framed drawing turned face down. The bag had been closed once and reopened. That told its own story. People who intended to flee packed cleanly. People who intended to stay near danger kept reconsidering socks.
"Where were you going?" he asked.
Mara followed his gaze and gave the bag the look one gives a witness who has spoken too early. "South, perhaps. West if the roads were watched. Nowhere clever. Clever roads require money."
"You could still go."
"So could you."
"I am."
"No." She touched the folded requisition with one finger. "You are following a line someone else drew and hoping to arrive before it tightens. That is not the same as leaving."
He disliked that because it was accurate. Accuracy from someone who had touched him kindly and harmed him accidentally was harder to dismiss than insult. He studied the facedown drawing.
"Not mine," she said before he asked.
"You said that about the handprint scar."

"Same child. Her name was Lenne. Fever after a rotfiend pit broke open near the refugee camp. She lived. Her mother did not. I kept the drawing because keeping the dead's things felt greedy and keeping the living's things felt like proof."
"Proof of what?"
Mara's mouth twisted. "That useful work still existed."

There it was again. The phrase under every ordinary compromise. Useful work. Useful bodies. Useful notes. Useful silence. The world did not begin by asking people to be wicked. It asked them to be useful and sent better forms each year.

Jack picked up the drawing. A child's hand had made a horse with four uneven legs and a head too large for its body. Buck would have found it flattering, which proved Buck's vanity had room for mercy. In the corner, a woman with yellow hair held a green bottle. Mara, perhaps, seen by a child who could mistake medicine for magic and magic for kindness.
He set the drawing down carefully, face up.
That was when she kissed him the second time.

The decision to stay one more minute happened several times before either of them moved toward each other. It happened when Mara poured water over his burned palm and did not pretend not to see his fingers tremble. It happened when Jack noticed her bag under the table and said nothing for three breaths longer than accusation required. It happened when thunder moved far beyond the roofs and both of them turned toward the window as if expecting riders, not weather.
Each small delay built a room inside the room, one where the door existed, the road waited, the danger remained, and neither of them was yet willing to grant danger every inch.
"If this is goodbye," Mara said, "it is poorly structured."
"Most goodbyes are. People leave the important parts until the horse is saddled."
"And you?"
"I usually saddle first."

She faced him then with something like anger and something like grief, though grief had not yet earned the right to use its name. "Of course you do. The horse, the exits, the coin, the wound, the next road. Everything in order except the thing that matters."
"The order is why I survive."
"No." Her voice went lower. "It is why you can leave."

The words held him more effectively than a hand on his arm. He could have answered with cruelty. He had several available. He could have said she had no right, that her notes had helped put him on a page, that wanting him now did not absolve what she had sent before. All of that would have been true. All of it would have been cowardice wearing armor.
So he said nothing.

Mara crossed the space slowly. Not cautious. Deliberate. She stopped close; he could feel her warmth through the damp chill of his shirt and the fevered ache of his own skin. Her eyes dropped once to his mouth and returned to his. The lantern between them made gold of the rain on her hair and put every tired line of her face where he could not pretend not to see it.
"Tell me to move away," she said again, but this time the words had changed. They were not a challenge. They were a door left open.
He left it open.

The second kiss came with the taste of argument still in it. It was not gentle at first. It could not be. Gentleness would have lied. Mara's mouth met his as if she were angry at herself for wanting what she wanted and angrier still that wanting had survived fear. Jack's good hand rose to her jaw, thumb resting against the place where her breath moved unsteadily under the skin. He felt the tremor she refused to give her voice. He let her feel the restraint in him, the measured force, the choice not to take one inch more than she gave.
She drew back only until breath could fit between them. Her forehead touched his, and the sound that left her was small, broken at the edge. "Mm... gods, I hate this."
"Which part?"
"That you ask." Her fingers tightened in his shirt. "That you would stop. That it makes me want you more."

The room before them had been built for repair, not comfort. The bed was narrow. The table was scored by knives and rings from hot cups. Oak shavings clung to the floorboards where the cooper's work had followed boots upstairs. Outside the window, rain slipped down the glass in thin crooked lines, and the alley beyond was all shadow, wet stone, and the occasional passing boot. Inside, the lantern made a small country of gold around the table and left the corners to keep their secrets.

Jack stood slowly, giving the dizziness time to pass and Mara time to change her mind. She did not. She watched him with the fierce concentration of a woman who had spent too long being useful to other people's systems and had chosen, for one night, a desire that no form had requested. When he reached for her, she came into his hands with a breath that caught and then deepened.
Nothing happened quickly after that.

His hand settled at the back of her neck. Her breath warmed his mouth. The next kiss softened not because the need was less, but because both of them heard the danger in haste. Mara's hands moved over his shoulders, careful of bandage and bruising, then less careful when his mouth found the line beneath her ear and she forgot to be composed.
"Ah..." The sound surprised her. He felt the surprise under his lips, felt the way she almost withdrew from it and then did not. Her fingers closed in his hair. "Don't make me regret being honest."
"That depends what you regret."
"Not this." She said it against his mouth, not loudly, not like a vow. Like a fact she hated and trusted anyway. "Not this."

He lifted her onto the edge of the table because the bed was too far and the world had narrowed to the lantern, the rain, the heat under his skin, and her knees bracketing him with chosen pressure. The papers scattered. One slipped to the floor. Neither of them acknowledged it. For once, paper lost authority.

Mara's breath changed first. It grew uneven, audible, less disciplined than the hands that had sewn men closed and measured fevers while villages lied around her. Each time Jack paused, each time his touch held still enough for her to answer, her body gave another truth before her mouth could dress it properly.
"Mmh..." Her eyes closed. The sound stayed low in her throat. "Yes. Like that."

He moved with care, not delicacy. Care was stronger. Delicacy pretended the body was glass. Care knew the body could hunger, shake, bruise, heal, ask, refuse, and still deserve reverence. His wounded hand remained protected between them. The other traced the shape of tension up and down her back, drew it out slowly, felt her loosen by degrees she would deny in daylight.
Outside, someone passed beneath the window. Both of them went still.
The boots moved on. The rain covered them. Mara laughed once under her breath, unsteady, almost wild, and the laugh became another sound when Jack kissed her again.
"Mm... Jack."

His name in her voice did something the crimson heat had not. It entered without violence. That made it harder to refuse. He answered by pressing his forehead to hers until both of them breathed the same narrow air.
"Say stop," he said.
Her eyes opened. "I won't."
"Say it anyway."

A flicker crossed her face, pain and respect so close they could have been the same wound under different light. "Stop if I say stop. Move if I ask you to move. Stay if I ask you to stay. Is that clear enough for a man who distrusts paperwork?"
"Clear."
"Good." Her hands slid to his face, then to his shoulders, then lower, not searching blindly but learning him with deliberate attention. "Then stay."

The rest of the room fell away by inches. Fabric loosened, shifted, slipped from shoulders and hands in small practical movements that mattered less for what they revealed than for what they admitted. Heat gathered where they touched. Breath became the measure, in and out of the narrow space between them, back and forth between restraint and need. Mara's sounds came softer at first, caught behind teeth, then less contained when Jack's restraint taught her there was room to answer without being used by the answer.
"Ah... mmh..." Her hands held his arms, not stopping him, grounding herself. "Gods. Wait. No, don't wait. Just..."
He waited.

That broke something in her more completely than urgency would have. She leaned into him, laughing once, almost angry, and the laugh dissolved into a long, trembling breath as he kissed her throat. Her pulse beat hard under his mouth. The lantern made her skin look warmer than the room, warmer than rain, warmer than anything the road usually permitted to remain.

For all their heat, they remained careful with the wound. That care might have been absurd in another story. In this one, it became the measure of whether the night deserved to exist. Mara shifted when his breath caught for pain rather than wanting. Jack angled his burned hand away from her skin. Once, when her knee struck the table leg and she made a sharp sound, he stopped at once. She stared at him through the lantern glow, irritated and moved in equal measure.
"It was the table," she said.
"Tables don't get exceptions."
"You are impossible."
"Often."

She pulled him back with both hands, and the kiss she gave him then was not gratitude, not absolution, not escape. It was permission renewed in the middle of danger. That made it worth more than any first yes. Anyone could say yes before the body learned the room. Fewer could say it again after being heard.

Time thickened. It did not vanish. Jack remained aware of the door, the stair, the alley, the knife on the table, his injured palm, the paper on the floor with Vesemir's name folded into requisition language. Awareness did not leave him. It made the choice sharper. He was there with her inside danger, not outside it.
Mara understood that. Maybe that was why her voice changed.
"Ahh..." It slipped free of her, fuller now, no longer hidden. Her fingers tightened. "There. Stay there."
He stayed.

The table creaked softly beneath her. Rain moved over the window. The cooper's yard below gave one deep wooden groan as staves settled in their racks. In the small gold country of lantern light, Mara stopped performing control. Her head tipped back. Her breath broke into small sounds, wordless and human, each one drawn from contact, pressure, restraint, and the terrible relief of being answered carefully.
"Mmh... ah... Jack."

He kissed her again before the name could become too much. She answered with both hands, with a sound into his mouth, with a shiver that moved through her and into him. Heat built and held. Neither of them hurried toward its end. Haste belonged to fear, and fear had already taken its share.

The sound changed again when he slowed. That was the strange mercy of it. Speed would have let them pretend this was only need, only bodies taking warmth before the road took everything else. Slowness made witness of them both. Mara's breath came open against his cheek, each small sound caught by the low rafters and the rain-heavy glass, and Jack felt every one of them as a decision renewed rather than a surrender.
"Mmh... do not make this gentle just because it hurts," she said.
"Gentle is not the same as careful."

"Then be careful badly." Her laugh broke on the last word. It became a softer sound when he answered her with his mouth, not hurried, not obedient, but present in the way she had asked him to be. "Ah... yes. Like that."

For once, the room gave them no clean name. The papers on the floor remained papers. The requisition did not stop being a threat because it had been kicked under the table. His burned palm still pulsed. Her notes still existed somewhere below them, copied in a hand that would become evidence by morning. None of that vanished. It only lost, for a brief and difficult while, the right to be first.

When release came, it did not arrive as violence. It came like a rope loosening after holding too much weight. Mara's breath caught, broke, and spilled into a softer sound against his shoulder. Jack held her through it, his own control narrowing to the simple work of not crushing, not taking, not losing the line between hunger and care. She clung to him as if gravity had become negotiable and she had chosen him as evidence.

Afterward, the room returned slowly: the rain first, then the lantern, then the ache in his palm, the burn along his ribs, the smell of oak, mint, and warm skin. Mara remained against him, breathing unevenly. One hand rested at the back of his neck. Not holding him in place. Confirming he had not become rumor.
"That was not gratitude," she said.
"No."
"It was not forgiveness either."
"No."
Her mouth touched his shoulder, barely a kiss. "Good. I would hate to have wasted it on something clean."
He almost smiled. Almost.
She salved the wounds afterward because bodies did not become symbolic simply because desire had made them briefly less lonely.

The table had been cleared, the papers gathered, the bed used at last for sitting rather than what both of them had refused to name too neatly. Mara worked by lantern light, wrapped in a blanket, hair loose now and falling forward each time she leaned over his arm. The intimacy of treatment after intimacy was different from before. More difficult. Before, care had been a bridge. Now it was evidence that neither of them had disappeared into wanting.

Jack watched her apply salve to the red lines in his palm. The marks had faded slightly, but not by much. Under the skin they still held a shape. Mara's mouth tightened each time the heat rose through the ointment. She had been vocal a little while ago, breath and broken sounds and his name caught in the low rafters. Now silence returned to her like a discipline she could still put on, but not comfortably.
"This is not ordinary burn tissue," she said.
"No."
"Not spell backlash. Not Sign strain. Not alchemical reaction."
"No."
"Your talent for detailed medical collaboration is astonishing."
"I've been praised for less."
Her eyes lifted. The softness from the bed had not vanished, but it stood now beside fear and work. The three did not get along well. "Does it hurt?"
"Yes."
"You considered lying."
"Briefly."
"Flattering."
"Efficient."

She tied the bandage and sat back. The barbed-star necklace lay visible against his chest. It had slipped free again, dark metal catching lantern light in hard points. Mara studied it the way she had studied the wound: as something that needed a name and would punish the wrong one.
"I asked before," she said. "About that. You didn't answer."
"I don't know."
"That is an answer."
"Not a useful one."
"Few honest answers are useful at first." She reached toward the necklace, then stopped before touching it. "May I?"

Jack studied her hand. He remembered Vesemir's fingers closing around the signet years ago, old eyes narrowing, Geralt in the doorway saying nothing because he was younger then and silence had not yet become retirement. He remembered being told to keep it hidden. He remembered not being told why.
"Yes," he said.
Mara touched the edge of the star. The lantern flame bent toward it.
She withdrew her hand slowly. "Cold."
"Usually."
"Usually," she repeated. "Comforting word. Sounds as if the impossible has habits."
"Everything has habits. Monsters. Men. Paper."
"And you?"
"Especially me."
The answer settled badly. Mara folded her hands in her lap. The blanket had slipped from one shoulder. She did not fix it. That small refusal to be embarrassed made the next words harder.

"The requisition mentions Vesemir," she said. "If the office has his name, they have old records or stolen summaries. Maybe both. It also mentions a Wolf School reference and concealment. I do not know who can explain that to you."
"I do."
She understood before asking. "Geralt of Rivia."
Jack nodded.
"Toussaint, then. Corvo Bianco, if rumor is right."
"Rumor has been very busy."

"This one came from wine merchants, not state offices. Safer class of liar." Mara reached under the pillow and withdrew a second folded sheet, smaller, copied in a hand not hers. "I took this from the packet before they collected my field notes. It has a routing mark. Not full origin. It showed the requisition passed through an office that also handled old Kaer Morhen material after the pogrom records were consolidated."
Jack took it. The paper felt harmless. Paper excelled at that.

Cross-reference request: unregistered Wolf School asset, possible Morningstar designation. Vesemir file fragments to be reviewed against historic concealment categories. Surviving associate: Geralt of Rivia, present location believed Toussaint, Corvo Bianco. If subject moves toward associate, observe voluntary contact pathway before intervention.

The name of the vineyard looked wrong in that hand. Too clean. Too accessible. Geralt had earned peace in the unlikely way some men earned scars: by failing to die through repeated administrative oversight. Seeing that peace written as present location in a requisition made Jack want to break the table more than the table deserved.
"They are not only following me," he said.
"No."
"They are mapping who knew."
"Yes."
Mara's voice nearly broke on the word and did not. He respected the effort. It asked more than tears.

Jack stood and reached for his shirt. His body objected in several languages. He ignored the eloquent ones and listened only to the useful pain. Mara rose too, blanket gathered around her, bare feet soundless on the boards.
"You cannot ride tonight."
"I can."
"That was not my meaning."
"I know."
Her attention moved over the bandage, the necklace, the copied paper, then his face. "If you go to him, you bring this to his door."
"It is already on the road. I'm only trying to arrive before it knocks."
"And if he does not answer?"

The question found an old place. Geralt had taught him sword angles and how to hear lies under politeness. Vesemir had taught him when to leave a village before gratitude curdled. Both had taught him silence so thoroughly they had mistaken it for safety. Jack did not know what Geralt would say when the papers arrived wearing Jack's name. He knew only that the road to Toussaint had become the safer danger.
"Then I ask badly," he said.
Mara's laugh was small and wounded. "That I believe."

At the door, he stopped. The room behind him held heat, paper, guilt, and a tenderness neither of them could afford to make noble. Buck waited below in the yard, stamping once, impatient with human delay. Rain had eased into mist. Dawn had not arrived yet, but the night had already lost its privacy.
Mara came to him and placed one hand against his chest, over the hidden star. Not ownership. Not farewell. A witness.
"They will make you something," she said. "Risk. Asset. Door. Weapon. Whatever frightens them least."
"Men like that prefer many names. More places to hide."
"What are you, then?"

Jack weighed the stairs, the alley, the road south, the road west, the long stretch toward Toussaint, and the old man in a vineyard who had helped hide him before the world had learned what hiding demanded. He had many answers and none that would survive being written down.
"A witcher," he said.
Mara's fingers tightened once. "For now."
He left before she could apologize again and before he could want it.
By noon, Devenford had produced three rumors.

In the first, the crimson-eyed witcher had seduced a district medic and stolen her secrets, which was nearly flattering and therefore unlikely to survive official interest. In the second, the medic had poisoned him and he had ridden away dead, which would comfort several men until contradicted by hoofprints. In the third, the witcher carried a star that burned cold and made official ink run backward.

Rian Wedeck heard all three while hiding in the back room of a chandlery. He wrote none of them down. That, he thought, might be the bravest thing he had ever done, which was not comforting because bravery felt much like nausea.
At dusk, two polite auditors came to the door.

chapters.chapter_title: THE MAN WITH TOO MANY PAPERS
paragraphs: Rian had always believed torture would begin with shouting.

This was because he had an honest man's imagination, which was to say a limited one. Shouting belonged to soldiers, drunks, cheated husbands, and market inspectors who had discovered three pigs declared as two. Real pressure, he learned in the back room of the chandlery, arrived with clean cuffs, warmed wine, and a man who apologized for the inconvenience of asking questions that were not questions at all.
Before the auditors arrived, Rian had tried to prepare a lie and discovered that good lies required more sleep than he possessed.

He had spread his papers across the chandlery table in four piles: true, dangerous, already known, and possibly edible. The last pile was small but emotionally significant. Candle stubs surrounded him like mourners. His landlady had knocked twice to ask whether he was praying, because no honest renter used that much light after midnight. He had told her yes. It was not entirely false. Clerks prayed to sequence, margin, and the mercy of not being asked where copies had gone.

The copy he had not given Jack lay under the loose floorboard near the stove. It contained only routing numbers and one partial name, Veyrane, S., but it had begun to weigh on the room like a body. Rian had taken it out three times, read it four, and put it back each time with less confidence. He did not know whether keeping it was bravery, stupidity, or the common clerkly compromise of postponing disaster until morning.
Morning came with two auditors and no mercy.

The first auditor was called Merrow. The second did not offer a name, which made Rian think of him as the Margin, because he stood just beyond the reach of the lamp and corrected nothing except the room's willingness to breathe. Merrow sat across from Rian with a little writing board on his knee. He had kind eyes and the hands of someone who had never pulled a body from a ditch. The kindness made everything worse.
"You are not accused of misconduct," Merrow said.
Rian nodded. He had worked with paper for years and knew not accused meant already placed in a category whose name had not been selected.
"You have performed useful service under difficult transitional conditions," Merrow continued. "The administration recognizes that postwar posting offices often operate under irregular pressure."
The Margin shifted slightly.
Rian looked at the cup of wine they had poured for him. He had not touched it. His throat ached with wanting it.
"I copied notices," he said.
"Of course."
"I posted what was sealed."
"Naturally."
"If a seal is proper, an assistant clerk is not empowered to reject the instrument."
"A sound principle," Merrow said. "Very sound."
Rian understood then that they would let him build the rope himself if he kept talking. It was polite of them. Administration often was.
Merrow turned one page. "We are interested only in consistency. You spoke with the witcher known as Jack Morningstar."
"He asked who wrote the notices."
"And you answered?"
"I said I posted what was submitted."
"A cautious answer."
"A true one."
"Those occasionally overlap." Merrow dipped his pen. The nib made a small wet sound. "Did he ask about ink?"
Rian's hands wanted to fold together. He kept them flat on his knees. Flat hands looked innocent if a man did not watch them tremble. "He noticed the ink."
"Before or after you directed his attention to it?"

The room seemed to tilt toward the answer. Rian saw the market board again, Jack's white hair darkened by rain, the crimson eyes, the notices with their identical phrasing. He thought of his mother in Devenford, who believed grain tallies were dull and safe. He thought of the packet he had given Jack and how little courage had improved afterward.
"Before," he said.
Merrow wrote. "Good. Good. Independent pattern recognition. That aligns."
"Aligns with what?"
Merrow smiled as if Rian had made a charming procedural error. "We are not here to burden you with interpretive weight."
The Margin spoke for the first time. "Where are the copies?"
The warmed wine steamed softly between them.
Rian swallowed. "Burned."
Merrow looked disappointed. The Margin looked unsurprised.
"By whom?" Merrow asked.
"Me."
"Why?"

The fact was that he had burned some, hidden others, given one packet away, and eaten one narrow scrap in the privy behind the chandlery because panic made men discover unexpected dietary commitments. The answer available to him was less dramatic.
"Because paper gets people hanged," Rian said.
Merrow's pen paused. "That is an interesting phrase."
"It is also true."
The auditor's kind eyes softened by a fraction. "Truth is not our enemy, Master Wedeck. Unstructured truth is merely hazardous."
Rian thought of geese, garkains, warm stone, a witcher's burned palm he had not seen but already imagined because the road made pictures faster than reports. "To whom?"
Merrow closed the folder.

The Margin stepped fully into the light. He had a scar along his chin, old and white. His coat was district brown without a district badge. His gloves were gray leather, fitted too well. He placed a document on the table and turned it toward Rian.
"Read the final line."
Rian read because clerks were trained into obedience before they learned resistance had grammar.
The asset's self-description is not legally determinative.
The line sat on the page with calm obscenity. No blood. No threat. No curse. Just words arranged so cleanly that the person under them had already been removed.
"I don't understand," Rian said, and hated himself because he did.
"That is why you are useful," the Margin said.
Mara's questioning took place in a room that had once stored apples.

The smell remained under the limewash, sweet and brown, fruit memory turning slowly into vinegar. A table had been brought in, along with two chairs, a basin, a clean cloth, and a pitcher of water no one drank from. The woman across from her introduced herself as Senior Field Interviewer Halbreck. She wore no weapon Mara could see. That meant there would be one outside.
"You treated the subject after the garkain encounter," Halbreck said.
"I treated a witcher after a monster contract."
Halbreck made a note. "You prefer occupational terminology."
"I prefer accurate terminology."
"Of course. Accuracy is our shared concern."

Mara had always disliked people who said shared when they meant confiscated. She folded her hands to keep them from reaching for instruments that were no longer in the room. They had taken her satchel. Politely. They had left her scissors. Also politely, after removing the hinge screw that made them useful.
"Describe the wound response."
"It is in my report."
"Reports summarize. Bodies elaborate."
That was almost a good sentence. Mara resented it.

"Accelerated closure," she said. "Persistent heat without fever. Unusual tolerance for pain. No delirium. No signs of infection. Subsequent burn or pressure marks after the Broken Crown event, not yet examined by me in official capacity."
"But examined."
Mara turned to her. "Not in official capacity."
Halbreck smiled faintly. "A useful distinction for your conscience?"
"No. For your file. Conscience rarely respects margins."
The smile faded. Good. Not victory. A scratch on varnish.
"Did the subject display attachment behavior?" Halbreck asked.
The room cooled around the question.

Mara thought of the infirmary, the rain, Jack's hand catching her wrist not to hold but to ask, the way he had said decide before you touch me like that. She thought of his burned palm on her table, his face when Vesemir's name became requisition language, his body against hers with restraint so precise it had been more intimate than hunger. Attachment behavior. The phrase made tenderness sound like an insect pinned for study.
"He displayed pain," she said.
"That is not the same."
"No. It is more diagnostic."
Halbreck set down the pen. "Mara Veyr, you are not accused of obstruction. Your work has been valuable. It may continue to be valuable if framed correctly."
"And incorrectly?"
"Then it becomes emotionally contaminated."
Mara almost laughed. It would have been a poor sound. "You people are afraid of the strangest words."

"We are afraid of wars caused by unmanaged anomalies. We are afraid of mage catastrophes, mutational escapes, draconid events, cultic misuse, and public panic after an apocalyptic winter most citizens barely survived. Fear, properly organized, becomes policy."
It was the first honest thing Halbreck had said. That made it the hardest to survive.
"And people?" Mara asked.
"People benefit from policy."
"That is not an answer."
"It is the answer institutions are built to provide."
Outside the apple room, someone moved. A boot scraped. Mara turned her head before she could stop herself. Halbreck noticed. Of course she noticed.
"You hope he is far from here," the interviewer said.
Mara looked back. "No."
"No?"
"I hope he is faster than you."
The pen resumed. "Emotional contamination confirmed."
Mara said nothing. Some facts deserved no assistance.
Miro's statement was taken in Willenford under the apple tree because Edda refused to let the boy enter Odrik's house.

The interviewer disliked that. He disliked the damp bench, the chicken droppings near his boot, the old woman with the shovel across her knees, and the way the boy kept looking past him toward the place where the mill no longer stood. He introduced himself twice. Edda told him both times that names mattered less than conduct. Miro said nothing and held the wooden horse in both hands.
"Tell me what the witcher did," the interviewer said.
Miro turned to Edda.
"Tell him what you saw," Edda said. "Not what he wants to buy."
The interviewer smiled without warmth. "No one is buying anything."
"Then your purse will be relieved."
Miro's thumb moved over the horse's belly, where a black stain still sat in the grain of the toy. "The ground listened to him."
The interviewer wrote. "You mean the creature responded to his movements."
"No. The ground."
"You were frightened."
"Yes."
"Fear alters memory."
Miro considered this. Children, when not bullied into speed, could be brutally fair. "So does wanting a different story."
Edda made a sound in her throat that might have been pride. The interviewer placed a small copper coin on the bench. Miro did not take it. Edda did. She bit it, spat once, and handed it back.
"Clipped," she said. "Like your questions."
The final statement described Miro as imaginative, trauma-affected, suggestible, and contaminated by village superstition. It did not mention that he had refused the coin.
The old shepherd from Broken Crown proved harder.

His name was Luthan. He had three living teeth, seventeen sheep, one granddaughter, and no respect for ink that had not first been useful on a weather report. When the correction clerk arrived with two guards and a prepared statement, Luthan invited them to sit on a wall that had recently been used by goats. The guards remained standing. The clerk sat and regretted it.
"The statement says you observed a dangerous uncontrolled manifestation," the clerk said.
"I observed a witcher saving my Nessa while your man wrote so fast it might catch fire."
"Both matters can be true."
"Then write both."
"The public version requires clarity."
Luthan leaned on his stick. "Public version. That's a fine phrase. Means lie with shoes."

The clerk tried three more times. The final statement marked Luthan unreliable due to age, grief, and local hostility to authorized procedure. It did not include his answer when asked whether he feared the crimson-eyed witcher.
"Course I fear him," Luthan had said. "I fear deep wells too. Doesn't mean I let fools piss in them."
That sentence traveled without paper.
The office of Sorel Veyrane had three windows, two locked cabinets, one cold fireplace, and no personal portraits.

It did have maps. The walls were covered with them, not proudly like a general's room or beautifully like a merchant's fantasy, but functionally. Roads, rivers, border changes, quarantine zones, old battle lines, rumored monster migrations, known mage safehouses, abandoned witch-hunter cells, vassal jurisdictions, disputed toll roads, and villages whose names had been corrected in three different colors. Pins marked locations. Threads connected pins. Black ink marked events that had become administratively real.
Sorel stood before the map of the vassal north and read the Broken Crown report for the fourth time.

He was not old, though the men who feared him tended to remember him that way afterward. Fear aged its owners in other people's accounts. His hair was dark, worn close, his face narrow and composed. He had the hands of a scholar and the posture of a soldier who had learned the greater strength of not reaching for a weapon. His coat was well made, unadorned, and dark enough that ink stains vanished into it.
Sorel's belief in order had not begun as cruelty.

Cruel men were easier. They could be bought, trapped, shamed, or killed with comparatively little paperwork. Sorel had met plenty of them in the long aftershocks of the wars. Officers who burned villages and called it denial of supplies. Priests who found heresy in houses with silver spoons. Mages who described peasants as necessary test conditions. Bandits who became local law because no one with a banner wished to ride through mud. Their motives bored him. Appetite, vanity, fear, profit. Old animals wearing hats.
The frightening ones were those who had seen too much chaos and craved clean categories with the devotion of saints.

Sorel had been young when a sealed relic under a provincial archive opened because a magistrate refused to evacuate until ownership could be established. Forty-one people died in halls built for records, their bodies found arranged alphabetically by the first letter of their surnames. The report had been suppressed, then misfiled, then summarized so gently that the dead became an incident of structural collapse. That was when he had learned the first law of governance: if horror was not classified by those who understood it, it would be classified by those who needed votes, tithes, revenge, or sleep.

He did not hate Jack Morningstar. Hatred would have simplified the matter and Sorel distrusted simplification. He hated preventable catastrophe, which was a nobler phrase and therefore required more suspicion. Under that suspicion, he still believed it. The continent had survived the White Frost by miracle, blood, and people whose names were already being turned into songs or secrets. It would not survive every dangerous body being allowed the romance of self-definition.
This was the thought he did not put in the file.
Files worked better without confession.
On his desk lay three files.
Willenford: unnamed village, ground response narrative, juvenile witness, phrase infection beginning with red-eyed wolf.
Devenford sequence: repeated notices, garkain displacement, medical anomaly, field warmth, irregular recovery, attachment risk through field medic.
Broken Crown: public crimson thermal-pressure event, draconid-adjacent bait organism, anchor-site reaction, non-voluntary manifestation, seven witnesses, one uncorrected shepherd.
The shepherd annoyed him.

Not personally. Sorel reserved personal annoyance for poor wine, sloppy handwriting, and officials who used emergency powers as a substitute for thought. The shepherd annoyed the structure. Old men with foul mouths were hard to classify as hysterical when everyone knew old shepherds cursed at weather, sheep, kings, gods, and their own knees with equal vigor. His phrase paper-faced tick had already spread through one tavern. It would become a joke before becoming sedition, and jokes moved faster than warrants.
Sorel touched the pin at Broken Crown.
"He was not summoned by name," Halbreck said behind him.

She stood at the edge of the carpet, file in hand. Merrow stood beside her, looking pale from travel and interviews. Odran Bracc, field captain, occupied the left wall with the resentful stillness of a man who thought chairs were moral decline.
"No," Sorel said. "He was summoned by profession. The name followed from response."
"Then the routing works."
"Partially. It attracted him. It did not contain him."
Odran shifted. "Give me six men and authority not to care about witnesses."
Sorel turned from the map. "If I wanted a massacre, Captain, I would hire cheaper men and call it weather."
Merrow looked down. Halbreck did not. Odran accepted the correction with a small movement of the jaw. Useful man. Limited, but useful. Limits were not sins when correctly labeled.

"The subject is armed, trained, socially adaptive, and resistant to conventional intimidation," Halbreck said. "He displays attachment to his horse, possible attachment to Mara Veyr, and practical concern for civilians under threat. He accepted payment after the event, which suggests continued occupational self-definition."
"He still believes he is a witcher," Sorel said.
"He is a witcher."
Sorel turned to Merrow.
The junior auditor flushed. "Legally, I mean. Mutated, trained, medallion-bearing, contract labor pattern."

"Legally, he is whatever jurisdiction can sustain under pressure." Sorel returned to the desk and opened the oldest file. It contained copies of fragments, some badly damaged, some translated from older hands, one carrying a name that had been underlined three times by a dead researcher: Morningstar. "Occupational identity may be retained in preliminary language if it eases voluntary approach. It must not control classification."
Halbreck placed Mara's interview summary on the desk. "The medic is compromised but not useless."
"Compromise is often how usefulness becomes visible."
"She may warn him again."
"Good."
Odran frowned. "Good?"

"If she warns him, he will follow the oldest emotional road available. Vesemir is dead. The old Wolf records are broken. He will seek Geralt of Rivia, because hidden boys become men who look for the hands that hid them when the hiding fails."
Merrow's pen paused over his notebook. "Do we want him near Geralt?"

Sorel considered the question. Want was an ugly word in policy, but not always useless. Geralt complicated every file he touched. The witcher had a history of transforming local crises into continental embarrassment, often while claiming reluctance and accepting payment. He had ties to sorceresses, dwarves, bards, monarchs, vampires if certain reports were not entirely drunken, and the Empress-designate of Nilfgaard through bonds no court had successfully categorized. Near Geralt, Jack Morningstar would become harder to seize quietly.
He would also become easier to map.

"We want the network to reveal itself," Sorel said. "We do not yet know whether Morningstar is a weapon, a key, a carrier, or a containment remnant. We know only that uncontrolled contact produces public phenomena and that older documents anticipated something like him."
"A person," Halbreck said.
The room changed by less than a candle flicker.
Sorel turned to her. "What?"

She held his gaze with professional steadiness. "You asked whether he is weapon, key, carrier, or remnant. The field evidence also supports person. He chooses civilians over tactical advantage. He bargains. He jokes. He counts coins. He asks consent, according to the medic."
Odran's mouth twisted. Merrow stared at his notes as if hoping to disappear into grammar.
Sorel sat. The chair made no sound. "Your objection is noted."
"It was not an objection."

"No. It was evidence offered with moral emphasis. That is an objection in field clothing." He folded his hands over the file. "I do not dispute personhood as a theological or social category. I dispute its sufficiency under emergency doctrine."
Halbreck went very still.

Sorel did not enjoy this part. Enjoyment belonged to amateurs and sadists. He had seen what unmanaged anomalies did when given the courtesy of delay. A mage child in Aedirn who turned a village well into a vertical river and drowned twenty-three people in their beds. A cursed noble line in Redania protected by inheritance law until the fourth bride began eating servants. A relic under a chapel near Ban Ard that sang soldiers into cutting out their own tongues because no one wished to offend the bishop by calling it alive. The White Frost had taught the continent scale.
It had not taught mercy. Mercy remained local. Policy had to survive distance.
"Personhood does not answer blast radius," he said.
No one replied.

He took up his pen and wrote beneath the preliminary classification. His handwriting was clean because he believed carelessness in language became violence in action. Violence, when necessary, should at least know its own name, even if the public version required gentler nouns.

Directive addendum. Subject to be approached through occupational identity until voluntary cooperation becomes structurally unnecessary. Avoid martyr language. Avoid monster language unless local fear requires steering. Do not call subject dragon-blooded in public channels. Maintain witcher terminology in rumor layer. Preserve Morningstar designation for restricted review.
He sanded the line and continued.

Risk matrix: armed mutation, unknown hereditary function, crimson pressure manifestation, potential draconic anchor interaction, public witness contamination, emotional network expanding. Classification phrase approved: anomalous witcher asset. Secondary internal phrase: hereditary infrastructure under destabilization.
Halbreck read upside down. Her face revealed nothing. Good training. Poor work.
"You dislike the phrase," Sorel said.
"It is obscene."
"It is accurate."
"Many obscene things are."
For the first time that day, Sorel almost smiled. He did not. Humor in offices encouraged memory. "Accuracy will have to serve until kindness can be made operational."
Odran looked toward the map. "Orders?"

Sorel capped the ink. "Let him ride. Tighten roads behind him. Collect Willenford again, especially the boy. Correct the shepherd if possible and discredit if not. Keep Mara Veyr under soft watch. Offer Rian Wedeck useful employment somewhere far from posting boards."
"And if he refuses?" Merrow asked.
"Then he becomes an example of how fear makes men unreliable. Handle gently. His kind break better under gratitude than pain."
Merrow nodded, too quickly.

Merrow had begun his career believing the empire's great cruelty lay in conquest. Later he learned that conquest was loud and therefore remembered. The quieter cruelty came afterward, in rooms where good handwriting decided who had been moved for protection and who had been taken.

He watched Sorel read the files and felt the old discomfort that had kept him useful but not promoted. Sorel did not enjoy harm. That was what frightened Merrow most. Men who enjoyed harm became sloppy. Sorel remained precise. He could put a person in a sentence and remove the personhood without raising his voice. He could also remember the names of dead villagers from reports no one else had opened twice.

Halbreck knew it too. That was why she challenged him carefully, never from softness, always from evidence. Odran did not know and did not care. Odran thought policy was a sheath for action. Merrow envied that simplicity for exactly three seconds and then despised himself for the envy.
On the desk, the Morningstar file waited with its fresh tab. New files always looked innocent. They had not yet learned the weight of what would be put inside them.
"What of Geralt?" Merrow asked.
Sorel did not look up. "Do not touch him. Not directly."
"Because of his associations?"

"Because men like Geralt of Rivia are most dangerous when offered a simple enemy. Give him one villain and he becomes useful to every ballad writer in the North. Give him weather, law, old guilt, and a young witcher who does not know what he is, and he must spend time choosing which blade to draw. Time matters."
Halbreck's eyes moved to Sorel's face. "You are using affection as delay."
"I am using known relational pressure to prevent uncontrolled escalation."
"That is the same sentence after washing its hands."
Sorel dipped his pen. "Then let us hope it washed well."
Merrow wrote that down, then crossed it out. Some lines were too honest for minutes.
Sorel also ordered a song.

Not openly. Open songs could be traced to patrons by anyone with a drunk singer and a patient dwarf. This would move through small purses and smaller vanities: a verse given to a peddler, a chorus hummed by a carter, a soldier paid in ale to remember the line incorrectly but with enthusiasm. It would not name Jack at first. Names gave a man shape. The song would begin with the burden of dangerous bodies, with the kindness of wiser custody, with villages saved only when fearful people surrendered private judgment to public hands.
Halbreck read the proposed refrain and set the page down as if it had dirt on it.
"This is poison," she said.
"Most medicine is," Sorel replied. "Dose matters."
"And who is the patient?"
"The public."
"Convenient. The public rarely gets to refuse treatment."

Sorel did not answer immediately. Outside, a courier bell rang twice in the lower yard. Another rider leaving with another sealed thing. The whole continent, some days, seemed made of riders carrying papers that would make strangers worse to one another by supper.
"Refusal," he said at last, "is a privilege of those who understand the threat."
Halbreck studied the Morningstar file. "That sentence will excuse anything."
"Only if used carelessly."
"No," she said. "Especially if used well."
For a moment the room allowed the disagreement to stand without disguise. Then Sorel took back the song sheet and placed it in the outgoing stack.
By morning, a ferryman three crossings away would be singing about the red wolf who saved villages by proving why wolves needed chains.
Sorel opened a fresh folder. On the tab, in neat letters, he wrote MORNINGSTAR, JACK. Then he paused and added beneath it, in smaller hand, CORVO BIANCO PROBABILITY.

Outside the office, rain tapped on the windows. The world was wet, hungry, frightened, and full of people who believed being afraid excused imprecision. Sorel Veyrane had built his life against that belief. Fear did not excuse imprecision. Fear required structure. Fear required forms, witnesses, routes, language, leverage, and men willing to become unkind before panic made cruelty popular.
He looked once more at the map.

A red thread now ran from Willenford to Devenford, from Devenford to Broken Crown, from Broken Crown toward Toussaint. It looked almost delicate against the paper. A child's line, perhaps, if one did not understand maps.
"Begin narrative correction," he said.
Merrow gathered the files. Halbreck remained a moment longer.
"And if he truly is containment rather than threat?" she asked.

Sorel looked at the empty space on the map east of the known roads, where older notes dissolved into guesses, deserts, dragons, and names Northern scholars spelled three ways because ignorance often wore confidence as a hat.
"Then we cannot allow him to belong to himself," he said.
The horror of the sentence lay not in anger, because there was none.
It lay in how carefully everyone in the room understood it.
The soft watch on Mara began before the lamp in the apple room went out.

A cooper's apprentice, paid two crowns and told he was serving district safety, took a place near the yard and pretended to mend a hoop for three hours. A woman selling onions stood at the alley mouth with no onions worth buying. Two boys were given sweets to report whether the medic's window showed light after midnight. None of them knew what they were part of. That was the elegance of the method. A cage could be built from errands if each errand was small, innocent-feeling.

Mara saw the onion woman first. Then the apprentice. Then the boys, because children sent to watch windows always watched the watching more than the window. She did not run. Running would confirm a category before she knew which one had been chosen for her. Instead she made tea, sharpened the hinge-screwless scissors out of spite, and burned the scrap of bandage that still held Jack's heat.
The ash rose red for one breath.
No one outside saw it. Mara did, and wished she had not.
At the last toll before the road divided, a tollman tried to charge Jack for two swords, one horse, one dangerous profession, and a surcharge for traveling after irregular events.
"Which irregular events?" Jack asked.

The tollman glanced at the notice pinned inside his booth, then realized too late that Jack had noticed it. The paper was fresh. The ink was not local. No name appeared on it, only a description: pale hair, crimson eyes, Wolf medallion, possible public risk. The tollman had underlined possible three times, perhaps hoping uncertainty could be made profitable.
"Road safety contribution," the man said.
Jack leaned from the saddle and removed the notice. Buck showed the tollman his teeth with professional timing.
"How much for stealing government paper?" Jack asked.
The tollman studied Buck. "Waived today."
"Generous."
"War's over," the man said weakly. "We're all trying to be generous."
Jack rode on with the notice folded in his coat. Behind him, the tollman lowered the gate for an empty road and looked relieved when nothing ancient happened.
By the time Jack crossed the last northern toll road before the long way south, three songs had already begun in taverns behind him.
One made him a hero. One made him a monster. One, paid for in good coin and sung badly by a man with clean boots, made him a public burden.
Buck disliked the third. He tried to bite the singer.

Jack paid for the broken stool, refused to apologize for the horse, and rode before dawn toward Toussaint with Vesemir's name folded against his heart and Geralt of Rivia waiting at the end of a road that had already started writing him down.

part_subtitle: Peace is a house with old swords still within reach.

paragraphs: Buck disliked Toussaint before Jack saw the first vineyard.

The horse made his opinion known at the border post by stopping under a whitewashed arch, lowering his head, and breathing suspiciously at a painted cherub nailed above the toll window. The cherub smiled down through peeling gold leaf with the cheerful emptiness of objects made by people who had never had to sleep in rain. Buck disliked it. Jack could not fault the judgment.

After weeks of wet northern roads, clipped coins, corrected witnesses, and songs that arrived in taverns before he did, the sudden appearance of plaster saints, clean arches, and officials with polished buttons felt less like peace than a trap that had learned manners.

Toussaint smelled wrong for a hunted man. Lavender grew beside the road. Grape vines ran in disciplined lines over hills that did not look as if armies had recently used them as butcher tables.
