Stone walls carried sun even after afternoon rain, and every little bridge seemed built by someone who expected people to admire it. Beauty, Jack had learned, was not innocence. It was only another surface that could hide a blade, a debt, or a witness paid to say he had seen what he had been told to remember.
In his inner coat, Mara Veyr's copied requisition sat folded around Vesemir's name, the paper softening from evidence into summons.

The tollman read the notice with one eye on Jack and one eye on Buck's teeth. He had been given a copy, of course. Pale hair. Crimson eyes. Wolf medallion. Possible public risk. The paper was folded inside a local permit ledger as if danger became more respectable when kept between vineyard tariffs and fish transport permissions.
"Road maintenance contribution," the tollman said.
"For the horse or the risk?"
The tollman studied Buck. Buck showed him one yellow tooth with private eloquence.

"For the road," the man said, revising policy in the presence of evidence. "Everyone pays for the road. Even knights. Especially knights, when the Duchess is in the right humor. Or the wrong one. Hard to tell sometimes. Very refined country. Unwise refinements."

Jack paid because arguing would leave more memory than coin. He took the folded notice from the ledger before the tollman decided whether to object. The man watched it go with the expression of someone seeing official paper choose a worse master.
"That is district property," the tollman said.
"So am I, if the right fool reads it. Consider us reunited."
The tollman opened his mouth. Buck shifted one hoof. The mouth closed.

Beyond the post, the road curved between low hills and pale villas with red roofs. Jack rode with the hood down despite the mist. People remembered hoods. They invented faces under them. Better to give them the true one and let fear do a more accurate job. His palm ached beneath the bandage, not sharply now, but with the slow pulse that had followed him since the Broken Crown. Sometimes it answered stones. Sometimes it answered official seals.

Once, passing a chapel whose saint had been given new paint over old cracks, the mark in his hand warmed so suddenly that he almost drew steel. Nothing emerged. A nun sweeping leaves studied him, studied Buck, and went back to sweeping because lifelong devotion had apparently taught priorities.
By the third hill, the songs had caught up with him again.

Two boys in a cart were singing the red wolf verse while delivering empty bottles to an inn. They had the tune wrong, which improved it, and half the words wrong, which made it more dangerous. In their version, the red wolf had eaten a fort, kissed a medic, and promised to surrender his chain to wiser hands if the countryside behaved itself. One boy made the chain noise with his tongue. The other saw Jack, struck the first boy in the ribs, and both discovered a sudden need to inspect the road behind them.
Jack rode past without comment. Comment fed songs. Silence fed them too, but at least silence did not pay for its own rope.

Corvo Bianco announced itself with cypresses, clean walls, and a view so carefully arranged it might have been evidence in a case against grief. Late sun broke through the clouds and touched the vineyard slopes in gold. The manor house stood pale against the green, its shutters blue, its roof warm red, its courtyard swept. Somewhere beyond the stables, workers were laughing at something ordinary. The sound reached Jack badly. Not because it was false. Because it was not.
He stopped at the outer bend of the road.

Buck stopped with him and did not argue. The horse's ears were forward now, not flat. He knew the smell before Jack let memory name it: oiled leather, horse sweat, old steel, rosemary near the kitchen door, grape skins crushed under cart wheels, and beneath it all the faint bitter trace of witcher potions kept in a place too domestic to deserve them.
Geralt of Rivia was in the yard, arguing with a barrel.

Not loudly. Geralt rarely wasted volume on objects unless they were trying to kill him, and even then he tended to sound disappointed rather than alarmed. He stood with his sleeves rolled, white hair tied back, one hand on a wine barrel that had shifted in its rack. A young worker held a wedge. Another held a mallet and the expression of a man wishing he had chosen poetry, crime, or any trade that did not involve being corrected by a retired witcher about the emotional life of cooperage.
"The wedge goes under the lower hoop," Geralt said.
"Master witcher, Master Barnabas said the upper hoop."
"Master Barnabas likes standing uphill from problems. Lower hoop."
Jack watched him for three breaths before moving. Three was all memory could steal before the road demanded payment. Geralt turned before Buck's first hoof struck the courtyard stones.

It was not dramatic. No start, no shout, no hand going to sword. Geralt looked first at the horse's gait, then at the rider's seat, then at the way Jack kept the wounded left hand out of the reins. Only after that did he look at the face. Recognition moved through him without permission and left almost nothing behind for strangers to see.
"Your left stirrup is too long," Geralt said.
Jack let Buck walk into the courtyard. "You look older."
"I am older. Your stirrup still looks stupid."

The worker with the wedge looked from one witcher to the other and decided this was either affection or a dispute about saddlery beyond civilian understanding. Geralt stepped closer. The sun caught the scars on his face, the yellow of his eyes, the older weariness around them. He looked retired in the way a sword looked retired when hung above a hearth within easy reach.
"You rode hard," Geralt said.
"Road was soft."
"Hand?"
"Attached."
"That used to be your standard for acceptable gear too. It was bad then."
Jack almost smiled. Almost. The old shape of it tried to return and found a different mouth. Geralt saw that too. Of course he did.
"Stable first," Geralt said. "Questions after the horse drinks."
"I came for answers."
"So did the horse, probably. His are simpler."

Buck approved this order of concern and stepped toward the stables before Jack asked. Geralt took the reins without making a ceremony of it. He ran a hand along Buck's neck, checked the sweat pattern under the saddle, and clicked his tongue at the girth.
"You rode with a wound and a shifting strap."
"The strap held."
"So did you. Neither is praise."
The courtyard worker, still holding the wedge, whispered, "Are all witchers like this?"
Geralt turned to him. "No. Some talk more."
"Gods save us," the worker said, then realized he had spoken aloud and went pale.
Jack let the ordinary joke stand in the yard. It did more for his balance than the saddle had done.

The steward came from the house with a ledger tucked under one arm and authority worn like a clean apron. She was a round woman with silver in her dark hair and the sort of gaze that inspected boots, intentions, and future laundry all at once. She looked at Jack's armor, the mud dried into seams, the torn strap, the blood stiffening at the bandage, and then at Geralt.
"I assume this is not a wine buyer," she said.
"No," Geralt said.
"Good. Wine buyers bleed less on the stones but ask worse questions." She turned to Jack. "Food, bathwater, or physician? Choose two first. The third will follow when your pride gets tired."
"Horse first," Jack said.
Her face softened by less than a coin's edge. "Then he has manners. I am Malva. Do not die on the courtyard. It upsets the household and stains unevenly."
She left before he could answer, which proved she had survived Geralt's retirement by learning speed.
Triss Merigold came after the horse drank.

Jack heard her before seeing her: light steps on stone, a pause at the stable door, the small intake of breath of someone told only what would make fear stand upright. She wore travel-dark green, sleeves rolled back, hair bright as a banked fire under the stable's shadow. Her face held warmth first, then intelligence, then calculation, but the calculation did not replace the warmth. It stood beside it, armed.
"Jack Morningstar," she said.
"Triss Merigold."
"Geralt said you were trouble."
"He says that about weather."
"Only accurate weather." She stepped inside and held out both hands, empty, visible. A mage announcing care without threat. Good. Better than most. "May I see the hand?"
Jack turned to Geralt. Geralt was busy pretending to inspect Buck's hoof while listening with his whole spine.
"You told her?" Jack asked.
"I told her someone I should have warned sooner was riding south with official trouble behind him."
"Efficient version."
"Left out the worst parts. I assumed you brought them."
Jack unwrapped the palm.

Triss did not reach immediately. She looked first. That mattered. The red lines under the skin had darkened with the ride, five thin strokes radiating from the center of the palm, not a burn, not a rune, not a scar. Her eyes narrowed. The stable seemed to cool around her attention.
"Not Sign backlash," she said.
"No."
"Not a normal curse."
"No."
"Not normal anything," Geralt said.
"Helpful," Jack said.
"You're welcome."

Triss touched the edge of the mark with two fingers. The contact was brief. Her own fingers warmed, then she withdrew them and looked at the stable lantern. Its flame had leaned toward Jack without wind.
"Where did it happen?" she asked.
"Broken Crown. Hill-fort north of Heddel's Ferry. Draconid-adjacent bait. Old chains. Witnesses placed before the fight. Officials arrived before the corpse cooled."
Triss's expression changed at officials before the corpse cooled. Geralt saw it and stopped checking Buck's hoof.
"What kind of officials?" she asked.

Jack took the folded notices and requisition copies from his inner pouch. Mara's last copy sat among them, creased along the line where old Wolf School terms had made the road unavoidable. The paper had warmed against his chest during the ride and cooled in his hand now. He gave them to Triss. She read standing beside Buck's stall, the scent of hay and horse surrounding words that wanted colder rooms.
The first page took her attention. The second took her color. By the third, her mouth had gone still.
"Geralt," she said.

He was beside her before the name finished. He read over her shoulder. Jack watched the old witcher's face, not for surprise, because Geralt had trained surprise into something private long ago, but for the small failures that came when privacy broke. Vesemir's name did it. The line unregistered Wolf School asset did more.
Geralt took the page from Triss and read it again.
"Where did you get this?" he asked.
"Mara Veyr. Medic. Not innocent. Not architect."
"Alive?"
"When I left. Watched by then."
Geralt folded the page with care too exact to be calm. "And Rian?"
Jack turned to him.
Geralt did not look away. "Rian Wedeck. Clerk. Brown coat. Nervous hands. You didn't say his name. The report did."
"You read fast."
"I've had practice with bad news."

Triss took the page back before either man could use silence as a weapon. "This is not a bounty. It is not even surveillance in the old sense. It is classification work. Public-risk language, witness correction, voluntary surrender preferred, medical custody."
"You know it," Jack said.

"I know its relatives." She looked toward the open stable door, where the vineyard lay in gold and green as if law could not cross beauty without wiping its boots. "Mage purges used softer versions. Kovir bankers use similar sentence shapes when they want a person to become a liability before becoming a debtor. Redanian investigators used worse ones, but less elegant. This is cross-border. Organized. Afraid of sounding cruel."
"Useful flaw," Geralt said. "Cruelty that wants good diction."
Jack leaned against Buck's stall with the tired caution of someone deciding whether the wall deserved trust. "They used Vesemir. They had fragments. Old ones."
Geralt's jaw moved once. "We'll talk inside."
"Now."
"Inside," Geralt repeated. "Food first. Bandage after. Then answers. If you fall over in my stable, Malva will blame me, and she'll be right."

Jack wanted to argue. The old habit rose quickly: refuse care, keep moving, reduce every room to exits. It met three things at once. Buck's head pushing against his shoulder. Triss watching the papers instead of his eyes, choosing the threat over spectacle. Geralt holding Vesemir's name in one fist and anger in the other, saying food because he could not yet say fear.
"Fine," Jack said.
"Good," Geralt said. "Your stirrup still needs fixing."
"Touch it and Buck bites."
Geralt glanced at the horse. Buck looked back with measured professional interest.
"He might," Geralt said.
"He will," Jack said.
Triss, still pale from the papers, laughed once under her breath. It was small and not happy, but it kept the room human.
Corvo Bianco fed people before it interrogated them.

This was Triss's influence, perhaps, or Malva's, or Geralt's late discovery that questions landed better in a room with bread. Jack found himself at a long kitchen table rather than a council chamber. There was stew with white beans, coarse bread, goat cheese, olives, and a red wine that tasted of sun and old stone. The room smelled of rosemary, woodsmoke, hot iron from the stove, and paper because Triss had spread the requisitions beside the food despite Malva's objections that documents had no table manners.

Geralt sat opposite Jack. Triss sat at the table's end with the papers arranged into three piles: field reports, official language, and things she had not yet sworn at because Malva was present. Malva moved between stove and table, refilling bowls and pretending not to hear words like containment and seizure. Her pretending was unconvincing. It was also merciful.
"Start with Willenford," Geralt said.
Jack did.

He kept it short at first, because short was safer. A nameless village, warm ground under frost, the mill rebuilt over buried dead, a child returned by something that had learned him, the creature drawn into the marsh, the mill dropped because some buildings deserved no gentler ending. Geralt listened with both hands around his cup. Triss interrupted only to ask about the warmth under the ground, the medallion response, and whether the child had touched the barbed-star necklace.
"No," Jack said.
Geralt's eyes moved to the chain at Jack's throat, hidden again beneath the repaired shirt. "It reacted?"
"At Willenford, cold. Broken Crown, more."
"More," Geralt said.
"Red center. Heat. Then the hill." Jack studied his bandaged palm. "It answered through me. Not by me."
Triss wrote that down. Geralt saw her do it. She looked up before he could object.
"This is not a Black Ink report," she said. "This is ours. There is a difference."
"Black Ink?" Jack asked.

"Not official name. Mine for now." She tapped one page. "They leave black ovals, redact origin, use terms like narrative correction. Until they introduce themselves properly, they can suffer a nickname."
"Careful," Geralt said. "Nicknames become songs."
"Then I will send Dandelion a better one before the wrong song gets comfortable."
Jack looked from one to the other. "You're involving Dandelion?"
"Rumor is already involved," Triss said. "Dandelion can at least tell us who is paying it to sing."
"He'll make it worse."
Geralt took a sip of wine. "Usually before making it useful."

The second telling came slower. White Post, Black Ink. Rian. Mara. The garkain with its damaged wing. The packet. The moderate care in the infirmary, described without the parts that belonged to the room and no one else. Triss noticed the omission and did not ask. Geralt noticed because Geralt noticed almost everything and asked even less when asking would be unkind before useful.
At Broken Crown, Jack's voice flattened.

He told them about the staged witnesses, the chained draconid, the girl called by a dead grandmother's name, the anchor notches, the chains under the hill, the red pressure, the heartbeat that was not his. Triss stopped writing halfway through. Geralt put down his cup.
"Say the last part again," Triss said.
"It held," Jack said. "Whatever was under the hill wanted to pull. The blood answered by holding."
"Not opening?"
"No."
"Are you certain?"
He met her eyes. "No."
Honesty made the room colder than certainty would have. Malva, at the stove, muttered something in Toussaintois that sounded religious and insulting. No one asked for translation.
Geralt leaned back. The chair creaked. "Vesemir knew the necklace was trouble. He didn't know this."
Jack's attention sharpened. "You knew to hide me."
"Yes."
"From mages. From courts. From Ciri."
Triss's hand stilled over the page.
Geralt did not reach for wine. "Yes."

The word stood alone and did not defend itself. That gave it weight. Jack had expected evasion, perhaps anger, perhaps the kind of explanation that began with you have to understand and ended with a man excusing his younger cowardice in older grammar. Geralt gave him one word. It was worse.
"Why?"

"Because the first month after Vesemir brought you in, a man came to Kaer Morhen asking about a barbed-star signet. He claimed to be a relic buyer. He had soldier's feet, mage-silver under his nails, and a priest's letter in his boot. We found two more on the road a week later. One dead from wolves. One not dead, and still lying."
"You never told me."
"No."
"Vesemir?"
"No."
Jack let the silence stretch. It had teeth.
Geralt studied him across the table. "We thought discipline would keep you alive longer than answers."
"Did it?"
"You're here."
"So are the papers."

That struck. Not visibly, perhaps, but the room shifted around Geralt's stillness. Triss looked down at the documents not to avoid the pain but to give it space. Malva stopped pretending to arrange bowls and left the kitchen without a word.
Geralt's voice roughened. "We were right to hide you. We were wrong about what hiding takes. Both things can be true."

Jack looked at the bread, the wine, the papers, the repaired strap of his armor hanging near the hearth. Family, he had once learned, was not a word for blood. It was a word people used when they wanted debts to sound warmer. Yet the kitchen did not feel like a trap. That made him more wary of it.

Triss broke the silence with a kindness sharp, and useful. "They believe Geralt matters. That means old records matter. Kaer Morhen matters. Vesemir's notes, if anything survived. But we do not go running north without understanding who else has been told to wait for you."
"We," Jack said.
"Yes," Triss said.
"You don't know what I am."
"Neither do they. That is why we should be less foolish than they are."
Geralt's mouth moved slightly. "She does that."
"Says obvious things?" Jack asked.
"Makes them sound like orders."
"Someone has to," Triss said.

The kitchen breathed again. Not safely. Safety was for people with fewer files. But the first shape of a plan moved through the room: letters, routes, names, old contacts, the difference between hiding and choosing privacy, the difference between help and custody. Jack felt the old instinct resist all of it. Help became leverage. Leverage became a handle. Handles let men carry you where they wanted.
Then Geralt stood, took Jack's saddle strap from the hearth, and began repairing the weakened stitching with a needle too small for his hands.
No speech. No oath. No declaration. Just thread through leather, slow and ugly and steady.
Triss watched him do it. Her face softened for one second, then returned to the papers.
"I need the cellar," she said. "And ordinary ink. Not mage-channel first. Someone may be watching disturbances."
"Write to who?" Jack asked.
"Yennefer," she said. "Dandelion. And someone near Ciri who can read danger without turning it into imperial property."
The last name entered the room without being spoken.
Geralt's hands stopped on the saddle strap.
Jack understood then that the road behind him had not only brought him to Geralt. It had brought him to every person Geralt had once hidden him from.
That night Jack slept in a room with two windows, one door, and a chair he moved under the latch despite knowing Geralt would notice.

The bed smelled of sun-dried linen and lavender. The luxury of it was nearly offensive. Rain had not soaked the blanket. No one coughed behind a plank wall. No horse shifted uneasily on the other side of the room, because Buck had been given a stall with clean straw and had accepted it with the wary dignity of a visiting ruler. Somewhere below, Triss moved through the house with a candle. Somewhere farther, Geralt's boots crossed the courtyard once, paused near the stables, then returned.
Jack lay awake with the bandaged palm resting on his chest.

The barbed star beneath the cloth had gone quiet. Not safe. Quiet. He had learned the difference from monsters, men, and old keeps. A sleeping threat breathed differently from an absent one. It made room for itself in the dark.
Near midnight, he heard Geralt outside his door.
No knock. No entry. Only the pause of a man deciding whether concern gave him rights. After a while, the floorboard eased and the steps moved away.
In the morning, Jack found his saddle strap repaired. The stitches were uneven. Strong, though.
Geralt did not mention it.
Before breakfast ended, Corvo Bianco tested him with kindness in smaller ways.

A stable boy brought Buck an apple and asked permission before offering it. A kitchen maid placed a folded cloth beside Jack's plate without touching his wounded hand. Malva sent up a basin of hot water and a shirt that had belonged to no one in particular, which was how houses with histories pretended not to make gifts personal. None of it looked like threat. That made Jack look harder.
Geralt noticed from across the table. "No one poisoned the shirt."
"You checked?"
"Malva would be offended if I did."
"That wasn't the question."
"I checked the basin."
Triss lifted her cup. "Romance is alive in this house."
"Caution is alive," Geralt said. "Romance was last seen arguing with laundry."
Malva, passing behind him with a tray, said, "Laundry won."

Jack ate because his body had become too persuasive to ignore. The bread was still warm. The butter had herbs in it. Both facts seemed excessive. He had eaten worse things than stale bread while sitting on worse floors than this kitchen could imagine, and hunger had never offended him until comfort made it look like a diagnosis.

Triss watched him notice the room. Not stare. Not pry. Simply watched with the trained softness of someone who understood that a hunted person measured safety as if safety might later be called as witness.
"The house has exits," she said.
Jack met her eyes.

"The kitchen door. The cellar stair. The east hall. The service passage behind the pantry. Window above the herb beds if someone is either small, desperate, or Dandelion." She buttered bread calmly. "I am not telling you so you can leave. I am telling you because if you have to count them all morning, you will eat less, and Malva will become political."
Malva said, "I have always been political. I merely express it through soup."
Geralt looked at Jack over the rim of his cup. Something like apology moved behind the yellow eyes and did not ask to be received. "She counts them too," he said, meaning Triss.
"I know," Jack said.
Triss's smile was brief. "Good. Then we can all stop pretending doors are invisible."

After the meal, Geralt took Jack through the house. Not as host exactly. Not as father, certainly not yet. As a man showing another man where trouble might enter. The sword rack near the west door. The old cellar that could be barred from inside. The guest rooms that looked over the courtyard rather than the road. The narrow stair to the upper gallery, useless for servants with baskets, excellent for someone needing height and shadow.
"You made a home with defensive depth," Jack said.
Geralt shrugged. "Toussaint has vampires, knights, auditors, and guests. A man plans."
"In that order?"
"Depends on the guest."

In the study, Jack paused before a shelf where two of Triss's books sat beside an old whetstone, a half-repaired glove, and a wine ledger with Geralt's handwriting in the margins. The objects did not match. That was why they looked true. Lives rarely arranged themselves by theme unless someone had died and a curator arrived.
"You stayed," Jack said.
Geralt stood near the doorway. "Looks that way."
"Hard habit to start."
"Harder to believe after starting."
Jack touched none of the objects. The old instinct told him to leave no prints where belonging might be inferred. "Does it work?"
Geralt looked past him toward the vineyard light. "Some days. Other days I wait for the road to call me a coward."
"Does it?"
"No. Roads don't care. That's mostly our vanity."
That was almost useful, almost wisdom. Jack disliked it for arriving in a room with curtains.

When they returned to the kitchen, Triss had the papers arranged and the warm part of the house had narrowed again around words that wanted to be cold. The day moved toward the cellar, but for a small hour before that, Corvo Bianco had shown Jack its ordinary machinery: bread, ledgers, insults, boiled water, horses, and people who disagreed without drawing steel.
He did not trust it.
He remembered it.
Near sunset, Jack went to the stables again and found the toll notice Geralt had taken from his coat pinned open on a tack board.

Geralt had not pinned it as evidence. He had pinned it beside a cracked horseshoe, a list of feed measures, and a note from Malva forbidding anyone from storing onions near saddle soap. That placement did something to the notice no counterargument could have done. It made the official phrasing look ridiculous, not harmless, but smaller. Possible public risk sat under bran mash proportions and above a reminder to repair the north stall latch.
"You put it there," Jack said.
Geralt was sharpening a hoof knife near Buck's stall. "Yes."
"Why?"
"Wanted to see how it looked in a useful room."

Jack read the notice again. The words were still there. Pale-haired itinerant mutant. Possibly traveling under witcher identity. Report discreetly. Yet between leather, straw, horse breath, and Malva's handwriting, the sentences had lost some of their borrowed authority. They had not become false. They had become made.
Geralt tested the hoof knife on his thumb and seemed satisfied. "Papers work by making rooms feel like they already belong to the paper. Don't let them."
"That Vesemir's lesson?"
"No. Mine. Learned late."
Buck pushed his head over the stall door and tried to eat the corner of the notice. Geralt lifted it out of reach.
"No," he said. "Bad for the stomach."
"His or the paper's?"
Geralt narrowed his eyes. "You do make jokes."
"Under duress."
"Most good ones are."

It was not reconciliation. It was not even trust. But the notice remained on the tack board all night, reduced by proximity to things that had work to do. In the morning, Malva wrote beneath it in strong black hand: NOT TO BE USED FOR WRAPPING CHEESE.
Jack kept that memory longer than he meant to.
One more thing made him stay the second night.

It was not Geralt, or Triss, or the promise of answers. It was Buck. The horse slept properly in the lower stable after deciding the straw was acceptable, the water unpoisoned, the mare dignified, and the grooms educable. Jack found him stretched almost loose, one ear moving toward the door without waking. A horse that slept like that had judged the place safer than the road.
Jack stood outside the stall longer than needed.
"Traitor," he said.
Buck opened one eye, considered him, and closed it again.
That settled the matter more effectively than conversation.
The next morning, Jack found the word guest written beside his name on Malva's breakfast list.

He stared at it longer than the word deserved. Guest was safer than subject and warmer than asset. It made no legal claim beyond food and sheets. For that reason alone, it unsettled him more than several threats had.
Guest, he decided, was a word one could accept for a night without surrendering the road. That was perhaps why it mattered.
He did not say that aloud. Some thoughts lost shape when given to air, and others became promises by accident.

By the third morning, he had learned the estate used names with careless decency. Guest on a breakfast list. Jack in Malva's mouth when she wanted him to move before soup cooled. Witcher when a groom forgot himself around the swords. None of the words tried to own him, which made them harder to refuse than subject had been, harder even than asset, because kindness could enter through a door no enemy bothered to guard.

He kept the old notices folded in his pouch anyway. A house could make paper look ridiculous on a tack board, but the world outside still believed paper could become rope if enough frightened men signed the knot.
Triss chose the cellar because beauty lied less convincingly underground.

Above her, Corvo Bianco prepared itself for morning with the calm arrogance of a house that had survived its own happiness. Servants moved through halls, shutters opened, dishes clinked, and somewhere in the courtyard Geralt told a vineyard worker that if a barrel rolled downhill again, he would begin charging it rent. The worker laughed, which meant he did not understand Geralt was only half joking. Sun warmed the stones outside. Grapes waited in disciplined rows. The world looked almost healed from a distance, and distance was precisely where most lies preferred to live.

The cellar offered better company. Stone, damp, wine dust, old oak, and the smell of ink. Triss sat at a narrow table between two racks of Beauclair White and a row of red vintages Geralt had threatened to label according to which guests made him need them. A lamp burned low. Its flame stood straight unless one of Jack's papers came too near. Then it leaned. Just slightly. The cellar seemed to notice with him.
She had divided the documents again before dawn.

Field language went left. Medical language went right. Rumor language sat in the center because rumor, unlike documents, could not be trusted to remain in its pile. The requisition with Vesemir's name lay by itself. Triss had not yet decided whether that was respect, caution, or fear of what Geralt's face did each time he saw it.

Jack stood at the far wall near a wine rack, not because he cared about the vintages but because the position gave him sight of the stairs, the table, the second door to the store passage, and the small ventilation window above the barrels. He had been in the cellar for twenty minutes and had already mapped it as if barrels might testify against him. Geralt sat on a cask with a cup of coffee he disliked and drank anyway. He looked older in cellar light, less silver and more bone.
"Read the phrase again," Triss said.
His attention settled on her. "Which one? There are several trying to win prizes."
"Voluntary surrender preferred."
Geralt's cup stopped halfway to his mouth.
Triss tapped the paper. "Preferred. Not required. That means the legal theory already permits removal without consent. They simply want a cleaner record if you walk into it yourself."
"Considerate," Geralt said.

"No. Efficient. Consideration wastes itself on people. This is for future review boards." She turned to another copy. "Witness correction. Not witness collection. Correction. They expect statements to be modified until useful. Public-risk anomaly is the outer phrase. Internal custody review is the working phrase."
"And host suitability?" Jack asked.
The cellar seemed to listen.
Triss had delayed that phrase. She had hoped delay would change its meaning. Hope had been a poor scholar since Thanedd and had not improved in private life.

"That is older," she said. "Or made to sound older. Mages used host in possession cases, cursed lineages, plague carriers, and certain relic infections. Nilfgaardian military science uses it for bodies that carry something strategically inconvenient. Redanian witch-hunters used it for women they wanted to burn with official tenderness."
Geralt looked down into the coffee. "Any version not terrible?"
"No."
Jack's expression did not change. That was not proof of calm. It was proof of labor. Triss had seen Geralt do the same thing until stillness became almost loud.
"They don't know what he hosts," Geralt said.
"No. That is why they are testing terms. Asset, anomaly, subject, host, infrastructure. They are not only tracking Jack. They are trying to discover which word gives them the strongest right to him."
Jack turned slightly toward the ventilation window. Dust moved in the thin light. "Words don't give rights."
"They do in courts," Triss said. "And offices. And sermons. And songs. Usually before anyone asks the person under them."
Geralt turned to her then. A brief look, old and grateful and tired. Triss felt it and set it aside because the page in front of her required the harder part of love, which was staying useful.
She took out three sheets.

Not enchanted parchment. Not message crystals. Not anything that might flare in a place being watched for resonance. Ordinary paper, ordinary ink, ordinary seals with ordinary lies ready to sit on the outside. Magic would move faster. Magic would also announce that people worth watching had begun to move. Triss had survived too much politics to mistake speed for safety.
"Yennefer first," Geralt said.
"Yes."
"She'll be angry."
"She reads better angry."
Jack looked between them. "You trust her."
Geralt answered too slowly for the sentence to remain simple. "Yes."
Triss dipped the pen. "And I trust her to notice when language around a body starts smelling like the old crimes. Especially if Ciri may be pulled into the shape of it later."
Geralt's jaw tightened at Ciri. Jack noticed. Of course he noticed. The cellar gained another old ghost.
"Does Ciri know about me?" Jack asked.
The question had been waiting since last night. It arrived without surprise and still found the one place on Geralt's face left unguarded.
"No," Geralt said.
"Did she ask?"
"She didn't know there was a question."
"Convenient."
"No," Geralt said, voice low. "It was many things. Convenient wasn't one of them."
Triss did not rescue either man from the silence. Rescue, in some rooms, became theft. She began the first letter and let the scratch of the pen give everyone a place to look.
My dear Yennefer,
The problem is not yet named, which is why I am writing before someone else names it for us.
She stopped. Too soft. Yennefer would smell apology and tear it apart before breakfast. Triss crossed it out and began again.
Yennefer,

A containment apparatus of unknown origin is moving through the vassal north. It uses public-risk language, witness correction, medical custody, host suitability, and possible cross-border authority. The subject is a hidden Wolf School witcher, human-born and mutated, carrying a barbed-star signet tied to Vesemir's old concealment records. He survived a public crimson pressure event at a site with draconid-adjacent symptoms and old anchor behavior. Geralt is involved because Vesemir was involved. I am involved because the language is already building a cage.
That was better. Yennefer liked clean wounds.

Triss continued, choosing each phrase with the care of someone placing stepping stones over deep water. She did not write Jack's full condition. She did not name Corvo Bianco on the main page. She used three substitutions Yennefer would catch and anyone else would file incorrectly. The rose glass meant Ciri. The cold cellar meant Geralt's home. Old ash meant Vesemir. Sorceresses had written under threats before. Codes were not romance. They were scar tissue with grammar.
Geralt stood and came behind her. Not too close. Close; he could read it if she allowed him, and she did. His hand rested on the back of the chair for one breath, then moved away.
"Add that he didn't choose the manifestation," he said.
"I did."
"Add it again."
Triss looked up. "She will understand."
"Add it for me, then."
So she did.

The manifestation appears non-voluntary. I am repeating this because men with documents often erase the difference between dangerous and guilty, and because erasure is easier when the erased person has already been renamed.
Jack said nothing. But his bandaged hand flexed once, and Triss wrote that into her own private file, the one that did not leave the room.
The letter to Dandelion required more cruelty because Dandelion was most useful when frightened for the right reasons.

Triss stared at the blank page and listened to the cellar breathe around her. Writing to Yennefer meant telling a blade where the throat was. Writing to Dandelion meant convincing a peacock that the mirror was on fire and that no, this was not the time to compose a stanza about it.
"How much can he know?" Jack asked.
"Then act," Geralt said. "Too little to perform."
Triss gave him a look. "That is not how Dandelion works."
"I know. I was being hopeful."
She wrote.
Dandelion,
Do not sing about this.
Geralt made a small sound that might have been approval.
Triss continued.

And because I know that sentence has already injured your professional instincts, read the next one twice: someone else is already paying singers to shape the story before the man at its center understands what is being done to him.
There. That would reach him.

She told him to listen for verses about a red-eyed witcher, a crimson wolf, a dangerous body, wise custody, chains offered as mercy, and villages saved by surrendering fear to public hands. She told him to let Priscilla hear the phrasing, not only the melody. Priscilla understood the violence songs could do before a crowd knew it had been wounded. She told him to send for Zoltan if paper, wax, tavern debt, dock freight, or paid witnesses appeared.
"He will enjoy being told not to sing," Jack said.
"He will hate it," Geralt said. "Then he'll understand why. Then he may enjoy hating it."
"That sounds inefficient."
"Dandelion is many things. Efficient only by accident."
Triss smiled despite the papers. "He is also loyal, which neither of you mentioned because witchers become embarrassed around useful affection."
Geralt studied the coffee again. "The coffee is cold."
"A devastating counterargument."

Jack watched them. Triss saw the watching and understood some of it. He was not admiring their banter. Not exactly. He was studying how disagreement moved between people who shared a table and a bed and still had separate spines. Geralt and Triss did not agree easily. Their love did not need that. It had domestic friction, old tenderness, political memory, and the practical courage of not leaving the room when history entered through the door.

Jack had been hidden from that kind of ordinary complexity. Kaer Morhen had taught loyalty, certainly, in the ways hard places could. But loyalty there had smelled of stone, winter, sword oil, and boys learning not to cry because crying wasted breath. Corvo Bianco's version smelled of ink, wine, stew, and Triss telling Geralt he was wrong without fear that wrongness would break the house.
That, perhaps, was why he distrusted it.
Triss sealed Dandelion's letter with plain wax and no crest.
"If the courier is stopped?" Jack asked.
"It reads like gossip about a jealous patron trying to suppress a song cycle. Dandelion receives letters like that twice a week."
"Three times in festival season," Geralt said.
Triss ignored that with the dignity it deserved.
The third letter was the hardest.

Not because of Ciri. Because of everything around her. Titles made people expensive to love. Ciri was twenty-one, alive after the White Frost, walking toward Nilfgaard's throne by a choice that had taken another life she might have lived. She was Geralt's daughter without blood and Yennefer's daughter without permission from law. She was Elder Blood to scholars, heir to emperors, symbol to armies, and a young woman who had earned the right to be tired of being described by what others could use.
Triss did not write to Ciri directly.

That would put Jack's name too close to imperial channels too soon. Instead she wrote to Ilyra Sarn, a quiet intelligence contact attached to Ciri's transitional household, loyal to Ciri, useful, and politically cautious in the precise way usefulness required.
The opening took five tries.
Madam Sarn,
You once asked how to recognize the moment a safety apparatus becomes a hunting machine. I have a practical answer now.
Triss paused. Too sharp? No. Sharpness had its uses when writing to people who read between threats for a living.

She did not name Jack. She named phrases. Bloodline custody. Host suitability. Voluntary surrender preferred. Unregistered witcher asset. She named Geralt indirectly, by reference to the wolf who bought peace among vines. She named Ciri only as your principal. She warned that the language resembled the same moral machinery once used by courts, mages, elves, and emperors when speaking about Elder Blood without saying girl.
Geralt rose and walked to the far rack.
Triss let him. His back said more than his face would have. Jack saw that too and, for once, did not press.
"Will she tell Ciri?" Jack asked.
"If she is wise, she will prepare the ground first," Triss said. "If she is loyal, she will not bury it. Ciri hates being protected by omission."
Geralt's voice came from the wine rack. "Yes."
The single word carried more history than the cellar could comfortably hold.
Triss sanded the letter, folded it twice, and sealed it with a mark that meant nothing to anyone who had not spent years learning which meaningless things kept women alive.
Then the lamp bent toward Jack again.
Not far. Not dramatically. Only a small lean, like a listener turning in a crowd.
Jack studied the flame. So did Geralt. Triss looked at the papers instead, because sometimes the evidence that did not move was worse than the flame that did.

A brown stain had appeared on the lower corner of the Broken Crown report. It had not been there before. Not water. Not wine. It spread slowly through the fibers, forming a line of five points and a center, faint as a memory pressing from the other side of the page.
"Don't touch it," Triss said.
Jack had not moved.
Geralt stepped closer. "What is it?"
"I don't know." Triss hated the answer before it left her. "A reaction. The page was near his hand during the night?"
"No," Jack said. "It was in the kitchen."
The stain darkened, then stopped.
Triss took a clean slip of paper, placed it beside the report, and waited. Nothing. She moved the Yennefer letter closer. Nothing. The Dandelion letter. Nothing. The Ilyra letter. The mark warmed.
Geralt's eyes narrowed.
"Ciri," he said.
"Not Ciri herself," Triss said quickly. "The channel. The subject. The wording. Elder Blood proximity, maybe. Or political custody language. Or all of it touching the same old wound."
Jack studied the mark. "You said she hates being protected by omission."
"She does."
"Geralt?"
Geralt did not answer immediately. That, more than anything, made the cellar feel underground.
"She should hear it from someone who loves her," he said at last. "Not from a file."

Triss turned to him, and the old pain of their shared life passed between them without accusation. Geralt had made choices around Ciri before. Some had saved her. Some had hurt her. The worst had done both.
"Then we make sure the file does not arrive first," she said.
Malva found them near noon and announced that if strategy did not come upstairs to eat, lunch would be reclassified as evidence and removed.

Jack followed because the body had begun making arguments the mind could not defeat. The household above had continued being alive without permission from the documents below. Bread had been cut. Plates laid. Someone had brought flowers from the garden and placed them in a jug that had once held vinegar. Geralt noticed Jack noticing and said nothing. Triss noticed Geralt noticing and also said nothing. Corvo Bianco, Jack began to understand, was full of skilled silences.
At table, Malva served soup and interrogated no one directly, which made her more effective than several officials.
"The mare in the lower stable is near foaling," she said. "If your horse decides to take offense at childbirth, tell him the estate cannot afford drama before harvest."
"Buck respects mares," Jack said.
"Does he respect grooms?"
"Depends on the groom."
"Sensible beast."
Geralt tore bread. "He tried to bite a tollman."
"Also sensible," Malva said. "Tollmen count wheels as if wheels chose taxation."

For a few minutes, the world became soup, bread, horses, tollmen, and Geralt being told by his steward that no, he could not sharpen a knife at the table simply because the table had seen worse. Jack ate more than he intended. Hunger, when given actual food, sometimes became a betrayal. Triss watched without making a point of it. That was kind. Geralt pushed the bread basket closer with one finger and looked away. That was worse.
After lunch, a courier arrived.

Not one of Triss's. Too soon. This man wore local colors, rode a sweating bay, and carried a sealed notice for Geralt of Rivia, owner-resident of Corvo Bianco estate, titled in local script with all the ornamental flourishes Toussaint used when politeness wished to trip its reader. The courier looked deeply relieved to hand it over and deeply sorry that Geralt existed to receive it.
Geralt broke the seal in the courtyard.
Jack stood beside Buck. Triss stood under the arch. Malva stood in the doorway with her arms folded. The courier tried to become smaller than his horse.
"Read it," Triss said.
Geralt read aloud.

"Notice of advisory caution concerning a pale-haired itinerant mutant of unknown jurisdiction, crimson-eyed, armed, possibly traveling under witcher identity, associated with recent instability in northern districts. Local authorities request hospitality providers report presence discreetly for public reassurance. No direct confrontation advised."
Silence followed.
Malva said, "Hospitality providers. How charming. We are inns now."
The courier examined his gloves as if they contained a route out of the yard.
Geralt folded the notice once. "Who else got this?"
"Estates, inns, toll posts, some parishes," the courier said. "It came through Beauclair dispatch, master witcher. We just carry what is sealed."
Rian's sentence, wearing southern manners.

Jack held out a hand. Geralt gave him the notice. It was copied from the same family of phrases but dressed in local lace. Possible public reassurance. Not risk. Not custody. They were learning the shape of the region before entering it.
"They know where I went," Jack said.
Geralt looked toward the road beyond the cypresses. "They know where they wanted you to go."
Triss's expression tightened. "Then my letters must leave by three routes. Now."
Malva turned to the courier. "You will eat before you ride back."
"Madam, I should return at once."
"You carried bad paper into my courtyard. You will repair the universe slightly by eating soup."
The courier turned to Geralt. Geralt studied the road. Jack studied the notice. Buck looked at the courier's horse with interest that might have been romantic or hostile.
"Eat the soup," Geralt said.
The courier ate the soup.
By evening, the three letters were gone.

One traveled with a vineyard account book bound for a merchant who thought he was smuggling untaxed wine and would therefore be too busy feeling clever to read the hidden fold. One left in the prayer book of a pilgrim who owed Triss a favor from a winter fever and believed the favor involved herbal advice. One went with a girl from the kitchens whose uncle drove cheese to Beauclair and whose innocence was so convincing that Malva said it should be taxed before officials noticed.
Jack watched each departure from different windows and hated the logic of needing other people.
Triss found him after the last cart left.
"You look as if you want to chase all three," she said.
"Want is crowded today."
"That happens in houses. Roads let a person pretend fewer things matter."
He glanced at her. "You giving advice or diagnosis?"
"Both. I charge more when they overlap."

Below, Geralt crossed the yard toward the stables with a small lamp. He stopped to check the latch on Buck's stall. Buck allowed it, which either meant the horse had accepted Geralt or was planning something more sophisticated than biting. Geralt adjusted the latch, then stood there a moment longer than the task required.
Triss watched too.
"He should have told you more," she said.
Jack's hand tightened on the window ledge. "Yes."
"He knows."
"Knowing doesn't repair it."
"No. It only changes the next thing."
That sounded like the kind of sentence people said after too many mistakes had taught them not to promise repair where only consequence existed. Jack respected it. He disliked respecting it.
"Why are you helping?" he asked.

Triss kept looking at Geralt. "Because I know what files do to bodies. Because Geralt cares for you and has not yet found the words that will not embarrass him. Because Vesemir's name in that document makes an old debt new. Because if this reaches Ciri as imperial policy before it reaches her as truth, it will hurt her in a way none of us deserve to pretend we did not foresee." She paused, then added, "And because you asked that as if help always hides an invoice. I object to the principle."
Jack looked out at the vineyard. The last light had softened the vines into dark lines. "Usually it does."
"Then read ours carefully," she said. "It may be poorly itemized."
At the stable, Geralt put the lamp on a hook and checked Buck's water though the bucket was full. The horse pushed his nose into Geralt's shoulder, not rude, but impossible to miss.
Geralt stood still.
Jack watched longer than he meant to.

Somewhere beyond the hills, letters moved. Behind him, the papers in the cellar waited with their clean obscenity. Ahead, Kaer Morhen had already begun to feel less like a place and more like a question sharpening itself in the dark.
The letters did not leave cleanly because nothing important ever did.

The first courier refused the sealed account book when he learned the road had received advisory notices. He did not refuse loudly. Refusal in servants and hired men often came wrapped in apologies because hunger had taught them which tone survived. Triss listened to his fear, paid him for the distance he had already ridden to reach the estate, and did not shame him for keeping his skin. Geralt watched from the doorway and said nothing until the man was gone.
"We are losing time," he said.
"We are not gaining loyalty by punishing fear," Triss answered.
"I didn't say punish."
"No. You only looked like winter."
Geralt grunted. "Winter worked."
"On wolves, perhaps. Not couriers with three children and one horse nearly eligible for alderman."

Jack stood beside the cellar table while Triss chose new routes. He had expected annoyance from her, perhaps urgency sharpened into blame. Instead she revised. Cleanly. A merchant account became a prayer request. A prayer request became cheese transport. The failed courier's name was crossed out not with anger but with care, as if a person who refused danger should not later be mistaken for someone who had betrayed it.
"You forgive easily," Jack said.
"No," Triss said. "I distinguish. It saves time."
"Between what?"
"Cowardice that protects a life and cowardice that sells one." She folded the letter again. "Most institutions confuse them when convenient. I try not to."
Geralt turned to her then with the small, quiet expression of a man reminded why a house had become possible.

The second courier was the kitchen girl, Lena, who had freckles, good boots, and the bland face of someone who had learned that looking simple made adults say complicated things nearby. She accepted the cheese invoice, listened to Malva's instructions, and asked only whether the danger would be worse if she knew the content.
"Yes," Triss said.
"Good," Lena replied. "Then I do not know it."
Malva looked proud and ready to deny it in court.

The third route required Geralt to write the outer note himself. Not because his hand was elegant. It was not. His writing looked like a crow had survived a knife fight on the page. But certain merchants owed Geralt favors from Blood and Wine days, and favors written in his hand moved through Toussaint with less inspection than favors written in a sorceress's. The note said nothing about Jack. It complained about cork.
"Cork?" Jack asked.
Geralt sanded the page. "Everyone in Toussaint complains about cork. Safest subject in the duchy."
"People might read it."
"They will. Then they'll argue about cork and forget the fold."
Triss took the note and looked amused despite herself. "There are days I remember why you survive."
"Charm."
"No. Local misdirection and unreasonable luck."
"Charm helps."
"No witness has confirmed that."

The banter landed lightly, but Jack heard the tension under it. Every letter out widened the circle of risk. Every person trusted became another name a man like Sorel Veyrane could write in a column. Yet doing nothing would let the official version grow alone. Silence, Triss had said, was not neutral when others had ink.
By dusk the letters had left by wine, cheese, and cork.

Only then did Triss sit down. She pressed both hands flat on the table and lowered her head for one breath too long. Geralt moved as if to touch her shoulder, stopped, then touched it anyway. She covered his hand with hers without looking up.
Jack saw it and turned toward the stairs, not so quickly it seemed he had seen nothing, not so slowly it seemed he had chosen to watch.
"Jack," Triss said.
He stopped.
"This is the price help names before anyone asks for blood." She looked up. Tired, warm, sharp. "Remember it. People who offer clean help are either lying, ignorant, or not close yet."
He had no answer that would not make the room smaller.
So he nodded.
For Triss, that satisfied the question.
After the couriers left, Triss made one more copy by hand and did not send it.
Geralt noticed. "For who?"
"For the room that survives us if we are stupid."
"That's cheerful."

"It is practical." She folded the page, sealed it without address, and wrote only one word on the outside: IF. "If I vanish, if you do, if Yennefer arrives and finds this house quiet in the wrong way, if Jack rides before the rest of us can catch up, someone should know which words came first."
Jack studied the small sealed letter. The word if looked too light for what it carried.
"Where will you keep it?" he asked.
Triss smiled without humor. "Somewhere no man will look because the object seems domestic."
Geralt glanced around the cellar. "That could be anything. I have been accused of missing several domestic objects."
"Accused fairly," Triss said.

She placed the letter inside a small box of candle stubs near the stair. Jack nearly objected, then understood. A house survived through things no spy thought to search first. Wax ends. Mending thread. Dried orange peel. Spare buttons. The empire had conquered provinces with cavalry and ledgers, but most homes kept their private histories in drawers men with authority considered beneath them.
"You hide evidence in rubbish," Jack said.
"In maintenance," Triss corrected. "Rubbish is only maintenance that has lost an argument."
Geralt turned to her with admiration so plain it would have embarrassed him if named.

Jack looked at the candle box and thought of Kaer Morhen's hidden compartments, of Vesemir keeping notes where boys would not look because boys disliked chores. Perhaps all households had archives. Some called them records. Some called them kitchens. Some called them shame.
The cellar retained the smell of their choices after the candles were snuffed.

Ink, wax, old wine, paper ash, and the damp mineral breath of stone. Triss paused at the stair and looked back once, making sure nothing had been left in the open that could wound the wrong eyes. Jack watched her do it. A person who cared about papers that way understood what papers could become.
"You sleep?" he asked.
"Sometimes," she said. "I am told it is restorative."
"By who?"
"Liars with beds."
He almost smiled. She saw it and did not claim victory.

The sealed IF remained in the candle box when they left the cellar. Triss did not look back again. Geralt did, which made the hidden letter feel less hidden and more like a small witness waiting among wax scraps.
Jack remembered where it was without meaning to.
Yennefer received Triss's letter in a room where three candles burned and none of them behaved.

The inn called itself The Silver Comet, which was ambitious for a building with a cracked roof, sour wine, and a stable boy who feared mules with more theological intensity than he feared sin. It stood two days north of Brugge on a road used by merchants, pilgrims, spies, and travelers who wished to be mistaken for one of the first two. Yennefer had chosen it because the room was private, the food edible, and the owner discreet in the specific way that meant he accepted coin before conscience could ask questions.
On the table lay four dead beetles, a blackened sprig of rosemary, a shard of stone warm, leaving a mark in the wood, and Triss Merigold's letter.

The beetles were not from the inn. They had fallen from the rafters that morning in a chapel two miles east, each one split cleanly along the back as if hatched from within by heat. The rosemary had come from a shrine where a woman claimed the saint's statue had whispered red door into her husband's ear for three nights, which might have been marriage, madness, or magic, and Yennefer had no patience for guessing when residue could answer. The stone shard had been taken from a dry well whose bottom steamed in the rain.
Then the letter arrived.
An unidentified holding mechanism is currently traveling across the northern vassal states.

Yennefer read it once for facts, again for omissions, and a third time for Triss. The third reading mattered. Triss wrote warmly when afraid for people and coldly when afraid of systems. This letter was cold. Surgical. That meant fear had already passed through warmth and found bone.
The old wolf's past actions are what pulled Geralt into this. My participation comes from seeing how the bureaucracy is constructing a prison out of words.
The middle candle leaned toward the page.
Yennefer lifted one finger. The flame straightened because it had not been granted permission to be poetic.

She read the line about non-voluntary manifestation twice. Men with documents often erased the difference between dangerous and guilty. That sounded like Triss and not like Triss. Better phrasing than Triss normally used when writing in haste. Either Geralt had asked for it or the hidden witcher had made the distinction with his body. Both possibilities irritated her in different ways.
Old ash. Cold cellar. Rose glass.
Vesemir. Corvo Bianco. Ciri.
Yennefer folded the letter and unfolded it again. There were times when anger became too crude a tool. This was one of them. Anger would come later, dressed properly. First came examination.

She passed her hand over the warm stone. No curse pattern. No standard draconid residue. Something older in the pressure, not raw magic, not gate logic. When she brought the stone near Triss's letter, the heat intensified. Not toward Yennefer. Toward the phrases: host suitability, bloodline custody, old anchor behavior. Language did not usually activate stone. Unless the language described a structure the stone remembered.
That was inconvenient.
She went to the mirror and found it had fogged from the inside.
A single line appeared in the mist before fading: red pressure, northern girl, wolf hidden.

Yennefer studied herself in the clearing glass. Violet eyes, black hair, controlled mouth, a face that had been called beautiful by men who thought naming beauty gave them access to it. The mirror offered no further advice. Mirrors, unlike people, could be trained.
She burned the outer wrapper of Triss's letter, kept the coded page, and packed in thirteen minutes.

The innkeeper's wife met her at the stairs with a question halfway formed and thought better of it. Wise woman. Yennefer gave her coin for the room, coin for silence, and an additional coin because the stable boy had not cried when the portal flare startled the mule. Courage in children deserved better than life usually paid.
Outside, the road smelled of wet leaves, horse piss, and rumors that had not yet learned her name.

Yennefer drew the portal in the air with two fingers. The opening flowered black, then blue, then white at the edge. Before stepping through, she looked once toward the north. Somewhere there, someone had decided a living body might be better understood as infrastructure.
She had heard that kind of thought before.
She stepped into it with murder in excellent posture.
The temperature at Corvo Bianco changed before the portal opened.

Geralt was in the courtyard teaching a vineyard worker how not to lose fingers under a barrel rack, a subject he had developed opinions on since acquiring a house where barrels outnumbered monsters and seemed nearly as determined. Jack stood near Buck's stall with a brush in one hand, performing the sort of work that allowed men to avoid rooms where papers waited. Triss came out of the house with her sleeves rolled and ink on one finger.
The air tightened.
Geralt straightened. "Yen."
Jack weighed him for a breath. One word, no surprise, too much history.

The portal opened beside the cypress walk, tearing a clean oval through the afternoon. No smoke, no theatrical lightning, no nonsense. Yennefer of Vengerberg stepped out as if the world had been arranged for her arrival and was fortunate to be correct. Black and white, severe lines, raven hair untouched by travel, violet eyes moving once across the courtyard and retaining more than most men could write down in a day.
The portal closed behind her.
No one spoke for one breath.
Triss did first. "Yennefer."

"Triss." Yennefer's gaze rested on her, not warmly, not coldly, but with adult recognition. Whatever lived between them had survived too much to fit inside jealousy. "Your code has improved. Your handwriting remains sentimental in the lower loops."
"I will notify my pen."
Geralt made a sound that did not become a laugh. Yennefer turned to him then.

There it was, entering without permission: old love, old anger, old knowledge of each other's silences. Geralt stood in a sunlit courtyard with vineyard dust on his boots and Triss's ink still drying somewhere inside the house. Yennefer saw all of it. Jack could tell by the exact stillness around her mouth. The room between them, though they stood under open sky, filled with what had been and what no longer had the right to behave as if it had vanished.
"Geralt," she said.
"Yen."
"You look disgustingly well housed."
"I'm trying to make it look accidental."
"You have never been that skilled."
"I had help."

The smallest glance toward Triss. Not apology. Not declaration. A fact. Yennefer's eyes followed it, returned, and did not flinch. Triss remained at the foot of the steps. She did not leave the room merely because the room had become a courtyard and history had entered it in black and white.
Good, Jack thought. Then wondered why the thought mattered.
Yennefer turned to him.

The assessment was immediate and impolite in its completeness. She took in the silver-white hair, the crimson eyes, the healed cheek scar, the bandaged palm, the left side he favored by half a breath, the hidden necklace's shape under the shirt, the swords, the set of his shoulders, the way he kept Buck between himself and most of the courtyard without seeming to. Her gaze did not linger on beauty. It went straight to function, damage, risk, and refusal.
"Jack Morningstar," she said.
"Yennefer of Vengerberg."
"You have been badly described."
"Common problem."
"Not for long if I can help it. Show me your hand."
"Ask better."

Geralt turned to Jack. Triss turned to Yennefer. The vineyard worker, still holding the barrel wedge, discovered an urgent need to be somewhere else and escaped with the instincts of a surviving species.
Yennefer's eyebrow rose a fraction. "May I examine your hand?"
Jack held it out.

Geralt's mouth moved. Triss nearly smiled at him. Yennefer unwrapped the bandage herself, not because she lacked gentleness, but because she distrusted intermediate incompetence. Her fingers were cool, precise, and did not touch the wound until she had looked enough. When she did touch, magic passed through the contact like a blade under silk.
The red lines flared.
Buck stamped. Geralt's hand moved toward his sword and stopped before hilt. Triss stepped closer, one palm ready. Yennefer did not release Jack's hand. Her eyes sharpened.
"This is not draconid residue," she said.
"No?" Triss asked.

"Not only. Draconid residue leaves appetite, territory, heat. This leaves pressure. Containment pressure. But the contamination inside it is hungry." Yennefer turned Jack's palm slightly. "You did not produce this. It passed through you and left a road."
Jack's voice stayed even. "Where to?"
"That is the question people die around before they learn to ask it accurately."
"I prefer short answers."
"Then you have chosen the wrong problem."
She released his hand. The red faded. The afternoon returned reluctantly.

Yennefer looked toward Triss. "The stone shard I carried reacted to your letter. Not to my magic. To the language. Host suitability, anchor behavior, bloodline custody. The words match a structure older than the paper."
Geralt's face hardened. "Meaning?"

"Meaning someone with fragments is using administrative procedure to grope toward a magical truth they do not understand." She glanced at Jack. "Or they understand only what lets them become worse than ignorance."
"That's reassuring," Jack said.
"I am not here to reassure you."
"Good. The position was crowded."
Something in Yennefer's expression shifted. Not amusement. Recognition of teeth. "You are Geralt's student."
"Hidden mistake, according to the papers."
Geralt flinched. Barely. Yennefer saw. Triss saw. Jack saw all three seeing and disliked the arithmetic.
"Papers are often written by people too frightened to touch the facts," Yennefer said. "Do not accept their cowardice as biography."
That line entered him before he could stop it. He said nothing.
Triss moved first, saving everyone from gratitude. "Inside. The cellar has the documents. Malva has threatened lunch. I cannot guarantee which is worse."
"I remember Malva from your last letter," Yennefer said. "She has excellent instincts for tyranny."
"Domestic governance," Triss corrected. "Tyranny requires worse soup."
Geralt looked between them. "This will be pleasant."
"No," Yennefer said. "But possibly useful. You often confuse the two when cornered."
They entered the house together, not comfortably and not dishonestly. That was something.
Yennefer read every page in the cellar without sitting.

She stood at the table with one hand resting near the lamp, black sleeve close to flame, violet eyes moving line by line while the others waited. Triss watched the reading rather than the reader. Geralt watched both and pretended not to. Jack stood near the same wine rack as before because habit rarely respected new guests.
Yennefer paused at Vesemir's name.
No one spoke.
She continued.

At host suitability, her mouth tightened. At unregistered Wolf School asset, it went still. At hereditary infrastructure, she lifted her eyes from the paper and looked at Jack with a sharpness that seemed almost cruel until he recognized the direction of it. Not at him. Around him. Toward every hand already reaching through language.
"There," she said.
"There?" Geralt asked.
"The intention. Not custody for safety. Ownership for use. They are not merely afraid of what Jack may do. They are considering what can be done with him."
"You got all that from one phrase?" Jack asked.

"I got all that from a continent that repeats itself and men who believe new nouns absolve old sins." She placed the page down. "Hereditary infrastructure is not a phrase one uses for a man one intends to let walk away."
Triss folded her arms. "Ilyra needs to see that."
Yennefer's gaze cut to her. "You wrote toward Ciri."
"Toward Ilyra. Coded."
"Good. Direct channels are likely watched."
Geralt's eyes narrowed. "Likely?"

"Certainly if Emhyr's people have half the competence they claim and twice the paranoia they deserve. Ciri's transition has made every ambitious clerk in Nilfgaard discover an interest in protecting her from truth until it becomes policy."
Geralt looked away. Yennefer saw the movement and softened by not softening at all.
"She will be told," Yennefer said.
"I know."
"By us if possible. By someone who loves her if necessary. By a file only over my dead and spectacularly inconvenient body."
Triss nodded once. Adult alliance. No warmth needed. Warmth would come later if it survived work.

Jack watched the three of them and felt the shape of a family he had been kept outside of and now risked damaging by entering. Geralt had once loved Yennefer. Geralt now shared this house with Triss. Ciri belonged to both old history and current danger. Jack did not know Ciri, yet his existence had already begun moving toward her through coded letters. He had been hidden to avoid one kind of burden and arrived carrying another.
Yennefer turned to him. "Do you have the necklace?"
"Yes."
"May I see it?"
At least she asked now. He drew it out.

The barbed star fell against his shirt. The cellar lamp bent sharply toward it, then away, as if regretting curiosity. Triss inhaled. Geralt did not move. Yennefer's face altered in a way too controlled to be called surprise.
"Do not touch it," Jack said.
"I was not going to."
"You were."
"I revised myself. Do try to keep up."
The corner of Geralt's mouth moved. Triss looked down at the papers. Jack let the almost-joke stand.

Yennefer circled once, slowly, studying the star from angles. "Not a standard signet. Not merely jewelry. It is a key, but not to a door in the common sense. It responds to pressure and witness language. It may also be hiding itself from certain readings."
"Can you identify the maker?" Triss asked.
"No. Zerrikanian influence, perhaps, but older or deliberately archaic. The barbs are not decorative. They mark direction. Inward, not outward."
Jack looked down at it. Inward. The word carried the Broken Crown back into his palm.
"Can you remove it?" Geralt asked.
Jack's gaze snapped to him.
Geralt met it. "I didn't say we should. I asked if she can."

Yennefer answered before anger could become useful. "I would not remove it without knowing what duty it performs. It may be a lock. It may be a warning. It may be both. I dislike both without diagrams."
"Vesemir had sketches," Geralt said. "Maybe. Old ones. Hidden."
Jack let the silence answer first. "You know that now?"
"I know where he hid things when he felt guilty and careful. Not what survived."
"Kaer Morhen," Triss said.
The room arrived there together. Cold stone, old ashes, empty beds, Vesemir's omissions waiting where death had left them unanswered.
Yennefer turned to Geralt. "You will go."
"Yes."
"With him."
"Yes."
"And leave us to letters, rumor, and the pleasure of being underestimated by bureaucrats."
"You say that as if you don't enjoy the last part."
"Only when it ends badly for them."
For one second, Geralt and Yennefer almost smiled at the same memory. Triss saw it. She did not punish either of them for having lived. Jack saw her not punishing and understood why the house held.
Geralt and Yennefer spoke in the vineyard after supper because houses had ears and vines were at least honest about what they wrapped around.

The evening had gone blue. Corvo Bianco's windows glowed behind them. Somewhere inside, Triss was preparing duplicate letters and pretending not to be tired. Jack had gone to the stables with Buck, which meant he wanted either privacy or something living that did not ask questions in words. Yennefer walked beside Geralt between the rows, black dress brushing leaves, her presence making the vineyard look briefly like it had been included in a sharper world.
"You should have told Ciri," she said.
Geralt looked ahead. "Yes."
"I had prepared a longer accusation."
"Use it anyway. You traveled far."

She glanced at him. Age had settled on him with irritating dignity. Not softness. Never that. But he had a home now. A real one. Vines, barrels, a steward who bullied him, Triss's books in a study, his swords not hidden but no longer always demanding movement. Yennefer had told herself, quite reasonably, that she had accepted this. Acceptance, she found, remained less tidy when standing inside the proof.
"Why didn't you?" she asked.

"Because Ciri was hunted by too many things. Because Jack had things following him even before we knew what they were. Because Vesemir said two fires draw more moths than one. Because I agreed. Because it was easier than imagining what happened if I was wrong." He paused. "Choose one. They all hold."
"And insufficient."
"Yes."

They walked past a row where grapes hung heavy and dark. The air smelled of leaf, soil, and the faint sweetness of fruit not yet cut. Too peaceful. Peace always angered her a little when arriving late to people who had needed it sooner.
"Triss has built you a good house," Yennefer said.
Geralt's steps slowed by a fraction. "We built it badly together. Then Malva fixed it."
"That sounds like Triss. And like you. And like a sensible steward."
"You and Triss are being..." He searched for a word, which was always dangerous. "Civil."
"We are not children, Geralt. And even when we were, we were never that kind of stupid."
"No."

She stopped at the end of the row. The valley opened beyond them, lights scattered along the lower road. Somewhere out there, letters were moving, songs were mutating, and a machine of polite custody was learning the shape of their lives.
"She is good for you," Yennefer said.
Geralt stood very still.
"Do not look as if I have offered to cut out my own tongue," she added. "I can observe facts without endorsing every cosmic decision that made them necessary."
"Yen."

"No." The word came sharper than intended and therefore honest. She corrected the edge without softening the blade. "Not tonight. We have a young man in your stable who may be a living component of something old and catastrophic. We have Ciri walking toward a throne built partly from knives. We have documents learning how to call a body infrastructure. Our history can stand in the vineyard without asking to be fed."
Geralt's face shifted, old ache under discipline. "Can it?"
"It has done worse."

That was cruel. It was also true. Their past had crossed deaths, wishes, betrayals, rescues, a daughter found by destiny and kept by choice, and the terrible labor of learning love did not guarantee a shared future. If it could not survive standing beside vines while Triss worked in the house, then it deserved less poetry than people had wasted on it.
Geralt looked toward the stables. "He's angry."
"He should be."
"At me."
"Also correctly."
"You're enjoying this."
"No. I am simply refusing to provide you the comfort of being unfairly judged. It is important to let men suffer accurate guilt."
This time he did almost smile. Then it faded. "I don't know what he is."
"He is a man. Start there before the rest of the world makes it optional."

Geralt received the sentence like a blade turned flat against his ribs. It did not absolve him. It did something less comfortable and more useful: it gave him a first instruction plain enough that guilt could not decorate it.
Geralt nodded slowly.

Yennefer looked back toward the house. Through one window she could see Triss moving past the lamp, hair bright, shoulders set in concentration. Not young anymore. None of them were, not in the ways that mattered. Good. Youth was overrated by those who had forgotten how much of it was terror and poor decisions with better skin.
"The language around him reminds me of Ciri," Yennefer said.
Geralt's face closed.

"Not the magic. The ownership. Vessel, blood, duty, destiny, state. New nouns, same appetite." She turned back to him. "If Ciri learns of Jack from an imperial dossier before she hears it from us, she will not forgive the shape of that silence. Nor should she."
"I know."
"Then act as if knowing does not solve it."
He turned to her. "You going to tell me what to do?"
"I just did. Keep up."
For one brief moment, old laughter moved between them and did not ask for anything more.
Jack found Yennefer in the stable before dawn.

She stood outside Buck's stall, not touching the horse, which proved intelligence. Buck watched her with ears forward and the wary respect he reserved for mares, sorceresses, and dangerous bridges. Yennefer had a lantern in one hand and one of the copied papers in the other. She looked entirely too composed for a woman who had probably not slept.
"Your horse dislikes me less than most animals do," she said.
"He respects threats that announce themselves."
"Then he has better politics than several kings."
Jack leaned against the door frame. "You came to talk about the necklace."
"No. I came because Geralt is asleep in a chair, Triss is asleep on three papers, and you are doing an excellent impression of a man who thinks leaving early is a strategy."
Buck snorted. Betrayal, apparently, had hooves.
"I wasn't leaving," Jack said.
"You were measuring how much food you could take without it being noticed. That is leaving with administrative restraint."
He said nothing. Correct accusations did not improve when denied.

Yennefer set the lantern on a hook. "You distrust being helped. Sensible. You distrust tenderness. Less sensible, but understandable. You distrust rooms where people know your name. That will become impractical by noon."
"This your bedside manner?"
"I reserve bedside manner for beds. This is stable manner. It includes more hay and fewer lies."
He almost smiled again. It was becoming a problem.

Yennefer studied him. Not like Halbreck. Not like Mara with fever instruments. Not like Triss with documents. Yennefer's attention moved as if it could cut the strings attached to a subject by naming who held them.
"Do not mistake my interest for ownership," she said.
"People usually don't warn before owning."

"Better people do when they fear the habit." She looked toward the courtyard, still dark. "I have watched the world try to make Ciri into blood, gate, heir, weapon, bargaining chip, prophecy, and daughter when daughterhood suited someone's speech. I will not assist the same crime with a different body and better stationery."
The words entered the stable and settled hard.
Jack looked at Buck because Buck did not require an answer. The horse was busy chewing hay with the seriousness of someone unaffected by metaphysics.
"I don't know Ciri," Jack said.
"No. But your enemies are already borrowing her vocabulary. That will make her know you before she meets you."
"Is that good?"
"No. It is useful. Try not to confuse the two."
He looked back. "Geralt taught you that?"
"Geralt has taught me many things. Usually by accident, rarely in the order he intended."
A faint sound came from the house, some servant beginning the morning fires. Dawn pressed pale light against the stable door.
Yennefer picked up the lantern. "Stay until we have a plan that is not simply a road with panic wearing boots. Then go north if north remains necessary."
"And if I choose otherwise?"
