"Then I will call you an idiot with accuracy and decide whether stopping you would make me useful or merely another person taking your choice. I dislike that calculation, so avoid forcing it."
Jack watched her leave.
Buck chewed.
"Don't start," Jack said.
The horse's ear moved. Too late.
By breakfast, Yennefer had moved into the problem as if she had always owned a chair at its table. She did not own the chair, Jack reminded himself. She had simply made the chair afraid to disagree.

The first new report arrived with a vineyard boy before the bread cooled. A ferryman near the north road had sung about a red wolf who saved villages by proving wolves needed chains. The boy sang the refrain before realizing every adult in the room had gone silent.
Yennefer listened once.
Triss closed her eyes.
Geralt turned to Jack.
Jack folded his burned hand slowly around the cup until ceramic creaked.
"Dandelion," Triss said.
"Yes," Geralt said. "Before the song grows legs."
Yennefer's mouth hardened. "Too late. It has teeth."
Outside, Corvo Bianco shone under a clean morning sun. Inside, the old world had entered the house and wiped nothing from its boots.
Later, Yennefer and Triss worked together in the cellar, which made the air behave as if it had been asked to hold two storms politely.

They disagreed over the first test before the first candle was lit. Triss wanted a passive reading: paper, stone shard, Jack's bandage, the barbed-star signet placed near but not touched. Yennefer wanted a pressure response with controlled provocation. Geralt, leaning against a barrel, said controlled provocation sounded like a phrase used by people who later apologized to architecture. Jack said nothing because the argument concerned his body and had not yet asked whether it intended to become another cage.
Yennefer heard the silence before the others did.
"You may refuse," she said.
Triss's attention snapped to her, then she nodded. "Yes. You may."

The correction mattered. It did not make the cellar safe, but it changed the shape of the table. Jack looked from one sorceress to the other. One severe, one warm, both dangerous, both aware that asking could become theater if refusal carried too high a price.
"What do you need?" he asked.
"Need is a greedy word," Yennefer said. "I want to know whether the signet reacts to your blood, to the wound, to the phrasing, or to the intention behind the phrasing. Those are different crimes."
"And if it reacts badly?"
"Then Geralt will do something dramatic and ineffective," she said. "Triss will save the furniture. I will be irritated."
Geralt turned to her. "Good to know the roles are assigned."

They began with distance. The signet on the table. The Broken Crown report near it. The Ilyra letter sealed and set three handspans away. Jack standing at the wall. Nothing moved. Then Triss read aloud, not the whole report, only the phrases: host suitability, hereditary infrastructure, voluntary surrender preferred.
The signet cooled the room by a breath.
Yennefer's eyes narrowed. "Again."
Triss repeated the phrases. This time she added Jack's name.
The lamp bent toward the signet, then toward Jack, as if uncertain which object had the stronger claim.
Geralt pushed himself off the barrel. "Stop."
"Not yet," Jack said.

The words surprised them. They surprised him less. He had spent too many days being described by people who did not ask. If the table meant to learn him, he would rather stand in the room while it tried.
Yennefer picked up a blank paper. "Write the same phrases," she said to Triss, "but change the subject."
Triss wrote: unnamed cursed object, possible containment hazard, voluntary surrender preferred.
Nothing.
She wrote: unidentified mage relic, host suitability unknown.
The lamp trembled once, then steadied.
She wrote: Jack Morningstar, hereditary infrastructure.
The signet struck the table hard, cracking the wax beneath it.
No one breathed.
Jack felt it in his teeth. Not pain. Recognition without warmth. The red lines in his palm lit under the bandage and faded before anyone could speak.
Yennefer's face had gone pale with anger. "It knows the name. Or something using the name knows where to pull."
"Which is worse?" Geralt asked.
"Both are competing."
Triss set down the pen. Her hand shook once, then stilled. "Then the papers are not only describing him. They may be teaching the structure where he is."
"Every file as a bell," Jack said.
Yennefer turned to him. "Yes. A bell written by fools who think sound belongs to the ringer."
Geralt picked up the signet only after Jack nodded. He wrapped it in cloth and returned it to him with the care of a man handing back an organ.
"Kaer Morhen," Geralt said.
No one argued that time.
Before Yennefer slept, if the two hours of stillness in the guest room deserved so generous a word, she wrote her own note to Ciri and did not send it.
Ciri,
That was as far as she came for some time.

There were many ways to begin badly. My dear daughter would be true and useless, because letters that began with tenderness before danger always made Ciri look for the knife under the ribbon. Your imperial handlers are idiots would be satisfying, but not informative. Geralt has once again made a family out of secrets might have been accurate; the paper might have burned by itself.
Yennefer put down the pen and listened to the house.

Geralt's steps crossed below once, paused near Triss's study, moved on. Jack's door remained silent. Triss coughed softly in the cellar, where she was still pretending fatigue could be negotiated with. Corvo Bianco at night was not quiet. It ticked, settled, breathed through walls full of people trying not to wake one another with fear.

Yennefer had lived in palaces, towers, inns, war camps, bathhouses, prison cells, and rooms that men thought became theirs because they paid for them. This house was none of those. It had a center. That made it more vulnerable than fortresses and more dangerous to anyone who mistook comfort for weakness.
She took up the pen again.
Ciri,

A matter has arisen that resembles old language used around your blood. I am not sending this through the first channel because I would rather offend speed than feed a machine. Geralt is alive, Triss is competent, and a young witcher you have not been told about is becoming a category in someone else's records. This sentence already contains too many failures to address in one letter.
She stopped there. Too much. Too little. Exactly the part that hurt.

In the end she sealed nothing. She folded the blank page around the written one and placed both inside her travel case. Some facts should not be sent before the room was ready to receive the wound. Some silences were cowardice. Others were simply timing sharpened until it cut the person holding it.
Yennefer hated the distinction.
That was why she would not let Geralt use it too easily.
When the cellar emptied, Yennefer remained behind with the cracked wax beneath the signet.

She touched the break with the tip of a silver pin and watched the wax split farther into five small lines. Not heat. Not pressure. Pattern. The thing did not merely react to Jack. It remembered how to make the world arrange itself around him. That was worse than a curse because curses usually had authors. This had architecture.
Triss paused at the stair. "You found something."
"No," Yennefer said. "I found the shape of the not yet. I despise it."
"That sounds like something."
"Then let us both be irritated accurately."

Yennefer also despised that the young witcher had thanked no one for the warning. Gratitude would have been easier to file under manners. His silence forced her to respect the fact that respect itself could become another demand if dressed too warmly.
Dandelion received Triss Merigold's letter while correcting a singer who had rhymed crimson with imprisoned.

"It is not that imprisoned is inaccurate," he said, one hand raised with the patience of a saint who had mislaid his sainthood in a brothel. "It is that the stress falls like a drunk through a stairwell. Crimson, prison, vision, decision if you must become philosophical after wine, but imprisoned? My dear Poldi, no audience deserves that much ankle."
Poldi, who had a voice like warm honey poured over gravel and the literary instincts of a mule, looked wounded. "Crowd liked it."
"Crowds like executions and fried onions. We do not build civilization by surrendering to enthusiasm."
From the corner table, Priscilla looked up from tuning her lute and said, "You once rhymed passion with fashion, compassion, and a baron's ration in the same verse."
"Youth," Dandelion said. "A fevered country. We all survived it differently."

The Chameleon breathed around them with the late-afternoon vigor of a tavern pretending not to be an intelligence office. Cups struck tables. A merchant from Cidaris complained that Novigrad dock fees had become indistinguishable from piracy except for the paperwork. Two students argued about whether a man could be in love with justice if justice had a face and several wealthy relatives. Near the door, a Temple Guard veteran with a missing ear listened too carefully to jokes about priests and pretended not to.

Dandelion saw all of it, as a good performer saw: entrances, exits, who laughed after the beat, who did not laugh at all, who paid in clipped copper but wore boots with new soles. People thought bards noticed beauty first. Amateurs did. Professionals noticed danger, appetite, and which table would pay for another round if given a chorus with sufficient flattery.
The messenger arrived badly dressed as a cheese factor.

This was not a criticism. The disguise had commitment: the smell, the ledger, the offended expression of a man whose entire life had been reduced to whey. Unfortunately, he held the satchel too high and looked at the stage before looking at the bar. A real cheese factor would have located beer, exits, and anyone who might owe him money before art.
Dandelion finished insulting Poldi's scansion and received the folded letter behind the curtain near the back stairs.
"From a lady with red hair," the messenger said.
"My dear man, half the women who write to me either have red hair, claim to have red hair, or accuse me of once preferring someone who did. Be precise."
"From a lady who said you would say something like that and that I should tell you the third line of your ballad about the Duchess of—"
"Stop," Dandelion said quickly. "A sacred correspondence. Profaned by detail."
Priscilla, who had appeared beside him with the quietness people forgot performers possessed, held out her hand. "Triss."
"Obviously."
"You went pale at sacred correspondence."
"I am a man of emotional range."
"You are a man who once used sacred correspondence as a euphemism in a song that had to be banned in two districts."
"Three, if one counts the village that banned all rhymes ending in -ence as a precaution."
She gave him the look that made his vanity sit up straighter and pretend to be intellect.
He broke the seal.
Do not sing about this.
Dandelion gasped. "Cruel woman."
Priscilla took the page when his face changed.

The letter did not waste time. Red-eyed witcher. Paid songs. A body built for trouble. Wise custody. Chains as mercy. Villages saved by surrendering judgment to public hands. Watch for repeated phrases. Let Priscilla hear the hooks. Send for Zoltan if money appears. Do not make him hero or monster. Both are cages.
Priscilla read silently. The tavern noise seemed to pull away from their corner, not because it lessened, but because the words on the page had their own weather.
"This is already happening," she said.
"You've heard one."
"Three."
Dandelion turned to her.

She folded the letter carefully. "One at the fish market yesterday. A woman selling eel pies sang about the red wolf taking coin to frighten children into obedience. She did not know the verse's second half. One near St. Gregory's Bridge, about a monster with a man's face who gave his chain willingly to kinder masters. One here, last night, after you left, from a student who claimed it was from a new military satire."
"Why didn't you tell me?"
"Because until now it was a bad song. Novigrad produces twenty bad songs before breakfast."
"Thirty if Parliament has met."
"Now it is a pattern."

That sobered him more than insult could. Dandelion took the letter back, read again, and felt a familiar chill unrelated to drafts. He knew the birth of songs. Not the pretty version poets told patrons, all inspiration and moonlight and women with implausibly patient husbands. The real birth was dirtier. A phrase paid for in one tavern. A line simplified by a carter. A refrain moved from jest to proverb because it fit the mouth of frightened people. Songs did not need truth. They needed repeatability, emotional permission, and someone who benefited from the crowd humming before it understood.
"Who is he?" Priscilla asked.
"Triss says hidden Wolf School. Geralt is involved."
"Then he is already someone's wound."
Dandelion regarded her. "That is a good line."
"Do not steal it for a song."
"This is a moment of crisis, Priscilla. Accusing me of theft is hurtful."
"It is preventive medicine."
Below the stage, Poldi began trying imprisoned again.
Dandelion closed his eyes. "We must save the continent quickly. Art is suffering."
The first paid verse came from a man with clean boots and dirty fingernails.

Dandelion disliked the combination. Clean boots meant money, self-regard, or a recent carriage. Dirty fingernails meant labor, disguise, or a man who handled things he wanted others to think he did not. The singer sat in the corner of The Bent Pike, a dockside tavern where the beer smelled of ropes and regret. He had a decent tenor, no soul, and the confidence of someone paid before performance rather than after.
He pitched the song to be overheard, but not challenged as entertainment.
A wolf came red from northern rain,

Priscilla listened with her hood low. Dandelion stood at the bar and made himself look offended by the beer, which required no acting. A dwarf dice-player tapped one finger on the table in time with the refrain. Two dock hands picked it up by the second repeat. That was the danger. The melody was simple, built for people carrying loads. The line wiser hands must guard us all fit the breath exactly.
"Hook one," Priscilla said when they stepped outside. "Fear offered relief."
"Hook two," Dandelion said. "He saved a child. They keep the good deed so the chain sounds fair."
"Hook three. No name. Only wolf. Easier to own an animal in song."

The alley smelled of fish scales, hot tar, piss, rain, and fresh ink from a printer's shop around the corner. Novigrad was commerce wearing a prayer and sin wearing better shoes. It could move rumor faster than cavalry because rumor did not need hay.
They followed the singer after his third tavern.

He was not difficult to follow. Paid amateurs rarely were. He walked like a man told he was in danger and convinced danger had office hours. At a corner near the canal, he received a small purse from a woman selling ribbons. The woman then sold no ribbons for ten minutes and disappeared into a dyer's yard. Dandelion bought two ribbons from the abandoned basket because he believed in supporting narrative evidence and because one was blue and flattering under winter light under winter light.
Priscilla did not comment. That was how he knew she was worried.
At the fourth tavern, the verse had changed.
A wolf came red through mud and flame,
Dandelion's skin tightened under the linen at his cuffs.
"No mother, no father," Priscilla said. "They are preparing the crowd to accept he belongs to no one."
"And therefore to everyone."
"No," she said. "To whoever speaks first."

Dandelion thought of Geralt, of the many times the white-haired bastard had insisted he wanted no ballad and then proceeded to live in ways that made ballads both necessary and impossible. He thought of Ciri, whose name had been sung by people who loved her, hunted by people who wanted her, and whispered by people too frightened to understand the difference. Now another hidden wolf was being turned into an animal before the man had entered the song.
"We need Zoltan," he said.
"Yes."
"And we need to keep you from singing this anywhere near a crowd," Priscilla said.
Dandelion placed one hand over his heart. "You wound me."
"You harmonize when anxious."
"Only because anxiety should not be allowed to win unaccompanied."

She smiled then, barely. The smile had work in it. Her voice had never fully returned to what it had been before cruelty damaged it, but she had learned to make the changed instrument cut where sweetness once carried. Dandelion admired that with a tenderness he did not place in public, because public tenderness became currency in cities like Novigrad.
They returned to the Chameleon by the alleys.
A boy was chalking a wolf on a wall near the back door. Red brick dust for eyes. Black line for a chain. He could not have been more than nine. Dandelion caught his wrist gently.
"Who taught you that?"
The boy looked ready to bite. Good instinct. "No one."
Priscilla crouched to his height. "No one paid you?"
He turned from her to Dandelion's ridiculous hat, and chose the safer adult. "A man said wolves bring luck if chained. Gave me a copper. Said draw it near taverns."
Dandelion gave him two coppers. "Draw cats instead. Cats answer to no empire and improve most walls."
The boy considered this. "Cats are harder."
"Art requires sacrifice."
"Can I draw ugly cats?"
"All cats are ugly if you ask them honestly."
The boy ran.
Priscilla studied the red-eyed wolf on the wall. "It has begun in children's hands."
"Then it is already faster than us."
"Not faster than fear," she said. "Nothing is."
Zoltan Chivay was found where all sensible men should be found during a crisis: near money, beer, and someone else's argument.

He sat in a back room above a cooper's warehouse, playing cards with a halfling, two dock factors, and a woman whose smile suggested she had knives hidden in both boots and perhaps a third in her theology. Zoltan had a cigar clamped between his teeth, a pile of coins near his elbow, and the expression of a man listening to lies for recreation while waiting for one worth charging for.

"Dandelion," he said without looking up. "If you've come to borrow money, I've lost tragically. If you've come to sing, I've won tragically and deserve mercy. If you've come about the red wolf nonsense, sit down and stop standing in the doorway like a magistrate with prettier cuffs."
Dandelion sat. "You heard."

"I drink in places where men think whispers are private because beer is loud. Course I heard." Zoltan laid down a card. The halfling swore. "Someone's paying decent coin for bad verse. That offends me twice."
Priscilla gave him Triss's letter.

Zoltan read with his lips moving slightly only when angry. Halfway through, he took the cigar from his mouth and crushed it in the tray. At witness correction, he looked up. At wiser custody, he spat to the side with admirable precision.
"Clean words," he said. "Filthy work."
"Can you trace the purse?" Dandelion asked.
"I can trace purses, wax, paper, and fools. Fools are plentiful, but they breed messily." Zoltan folded the letter. "Who is this poor bastard?"
"Jack Morningstar," Priscilla said. "Hidden Wolf School, if Triss's letter says what it appears to say. Geralt is with him."
Zoltan's face changed at Geralt. Not dramatically. Dwarves had their pride too. "Of course he is. White-haired whoreson retires to wine country and trouble still finds the address."
"It may have been sent there," Priscilla said.
"Then trouble has better penmanship than usual." Zoltan stood. "We start with wax. Songs are air once sung. Paper and wax have bodies. Bodies have sellers. Sellers have debts. Debts have names."
"That is almost poetry," Dandelion said.
"Say that again and I charge you."

They left through the warehouse yard. Rain had started, thin and cold, turning the boards black and making the canal smell of old rope. Novigrad hunched around them in layers: steeples, warehouses, bridges, alleys, the Chameleon lights behind, the Eternal Fire temple ahead like a warning nobody had paid to remove. Every window seemed capable of holding a listener.
Zoltan moved through it as if the city owed him money and he intended to collect without haste.

The wax-seller was a widow named Brelka who had opinions about everyone and invoices to prove some of them. She sold sealing wax to guilds, couriers, small courts, rich hypocrites, and poor hypocrites buying on behalf of rich ones. Zoltan bought nothing. He placed a broken black seal on her counter, the impression copied from one of Triss's pages.
Brelka studied it once. "No."
"That was fast."

"Fast saves time. Time saves money. Money saves fools from thinking too loudly in my shop." She pushed the wax impression back. "This came from south stock but not local purchase. Clove oil in the mix. Too much lampblack. Whoever ordered it wanted black to look black in poor light. Amateur's vanity. Professional's caution. Hard to tell."
"Who bought clove-black last month?" Zoltan asked.
"Three churches, one counting house, two noble bastards, and a man pretending not to be from a medical office."
Priscilla leaned forward. "Medical office?"
"He asked for wax that would not crack in damp field conditions. Only officials and grave robbers worry about damp field conditions before they arrive at the field."
"Name?" Zoltan asked.
Brelka smiled. "Names charge."
Zoltan placed coins on the counter. Dandelion placed fewer because his relationship with money had always been more lyrical than practical. Priscilla placed none and watched Brelka's eyes.
The widow took Zoltan's coins and pushed Dandelion's back. "Keep yours, bard. Last time you paid here, the coin had a love poem etched around the edge and I had to explain it to a tax clerk."
"Art moves in mysterious circles," Dandelion said.
"Art nearly got me fined."
She wrote one line on a scrap: Valden Rue, purchasing agent, South Quay Counting House, medical freight designation.
Zoltan took it. "Knew I liked widows."
"Widows outlive men with opinions," Brelka said. "Try to become one, Master Chivay. It improves judgment."
Outside, Priscilla said, "We have wax."
Zoltan nodded. "Now paper. Then debt. Then some bastard discovers dwarves dislike being paid to misname cages."
Dandelion touched the blue ribbon in his pocket. "Should I prepare a counter-song?"
Priscilla and Zoltan answered together.
"No."
He sighed. "Civilization continues to wound itself."
That night, the Chameleon did not sing about the red wolf.
It did something worse.

Priscilla took the small stage after supper, when the crowd had softened with drink and before the cruel hour when men began remembering debts. She wore plain blue, hair braided back, lute held low. Dandelion stood near the side curtain with both hands folded over his cane and the expression of a man voluntarily not speaking in public, which several patrons took as evidence of severe illness.
Priscilla sang an old road song about a nameless bridge.

Not Jack. Not wolves. Not chains. A bridge that charged every traveler a different toll because the keeper changed the names of things as they crossed. A widow became cargo. A soldier became weather. A child became debt. A horse became property of the road because it had stepped on it too often. The melody was simple enough for a market and sad enough for a church. By the third verse, the room had begun listening with its mouth closed.
No one heard the counterargument until it was too late.
When she reached the last refrain, she changed one line.
Name a man a burden, and the bridge will learn to own him.
The room held still.

Then a dock hand cursed softly into his cup. Someone near the back said, "That's true enough." The Temple Guard veteran with the missing ear looked at the door. The phrase did not tell people what to think. It made a place in them where thinking could begin. That was better and slower and therefore more likely to survive.
Dandelion understood why Triss had written let Priscilla hear the hooks.
Hooks could be removed only if one knew where they had entered.
After the song, no one applauded for three breaths. Then applause came, uncertain, growing, not festive. Good. Festive applause forgot quickly. Uneasy applause went home and became conversation.
Backstage, Priscilla set down the lute.
Dandelion kissed her hand, not theatrically. "Brilliant."
"Necessary."
"Those occasionally overlap."
"Do not quote me to me."

Zoltan entered through the rear door with rain in his beard and a grin that had no warmth. "Found the paper. Counting house bought stock under medical freight. Same stock used for notices in at least six districts. Paid through three accounts and one charity for war widows. Charming touch."
Dandelion closed his eyes. "Please tell me the charity is real."
"It is. That's how they hide it. Good lies feed someone."
Priscilla looked toward the stage, where people were still murmuring the bridge line. "Who controls the accounts?"
Zoltan held up the scrap from Brelka, now damp and folded. "A South Quay office. We go tomorrow. Tonight we let the crowd chew."
Dandelion listened to the room beyond the curtain. Already the line had changed in one man's mouth.
Call him burden, bridge will own him.
Shorter. Better for survival. Songs were beasts. One could train them a little. Never fully.
He took out paper and began his reply to Triss.
Triss,

You were right, which I write under protest because admitting it without witnesses would be morally insufficient. The song exists. Worse, it is competently made in the manner of poison hidden in broth. Priscilla has begun removing the hook without naming the fish. Zoltan is tracing wax and paper. Someone is paying through medical freight and widow charity, because villainy has developed bookkeeping and a sense of irony.
He paused, then added the part he would not make into performance.
Tell Geralt the story is moving faster than a horse. Tell the young wolf, if he allows himself to be told anything, that silence will not protect him from becoming a song. Only better witnesses may.
He sanded the page.
From the tavern floor came a drunk voice, trying the red wolf refrain. Another voice cut in with Priscilla's line about the bridge. The two songs collided, stumbled, and became an argument.
Dandelion smiled without joy.
"There," he said. "Civilization, limping but audible."
Before dawn, a pamphlet appeared under the Chameleon's front door.
No title. No illustration. Only four lines printed in black ink on cheap paper that had been bought in bulk and cut cleanly.
A wolf that saves may yet devour.
Dandelion read it in his nightshirt while the cook stared at the hallway and crossed herself so often she risked starting a draft.
Priscilla came down wrapped in a shawl. Zoltan arrived from the back room with an axe in one hand and a boot in the other, having apparently decided footwear was secondary to tactical readiness.
"Printer," Zoltan said.
"Obviously," Dandelion replied. "And a bad one. Doom is unforgivable."
Priscilla took the pamphlet. Her thumb paused on the third line. "Old stone's call. They know about the hill. Or they know what they want people to think about the hill."
Zoltan's face darkened. "Then we start with the paper shop now."
"You have one boot," Dandelion said.
"I'll kick half as much and twice as hard."

By sunrise, Novigrad had begun waking around a new phrase. Wiser hands. It appeared on a wall near the fish market, chalked by someone with adult handwriting. It appeared in the mouth of a baker's assistant who did not know where he had heard it. It appeared in a priest's aside during a sermon about public burdens and private pride.
The story had teeth, as Yennefer had said miles away.

Dandelion sent the reply by two routes and kept a third copy hidden in a false songbook labeled Early Erotic Failures, Volume IV. No thief with taste would touch it. No official with dignity would admit to opening it.
Then he dressed, adjusted his hat, and prepared to do something he considered morally heroic.
He went to find an accountant.
Dandelion did try, briefly and privately, to write the forbidden song.

He did it at three in the morning with one candle, two cups of bad wine, and the guilty expression of a man committing treason against his own better judgment. The page began well enough, which was the problem. A man with red eyes riding through rain, a horse that distrusted bridges, a village that forgot its name, a hill that breathed through chains. Good material. Unwise material. Material that leaned toward heroism the way drunk patrons leaned toward balconies.
He wrote four lines and hated them.
The young wolf came where old roads bled.
No. Too grand. Too clean. Too likely to make Jack sound like a symbol and symbols were precisely the disease.
He crossed it out.
Priscilla entered without knocking because performers respected privacy only when convinced it would improve the performance. She turned from the page to him.
"You wrote it."
"I investigated the possibility."
"You wrote it."
"I wrote a diagnostic fragment."
"Dandelion."
He sagged. "I wrote it. Badly."

She sat across from him and took the page. Her hair was loose, her shawl crooked, her face tired in the unadorned way that came after pain had become part of the room rather than an event. She read the crossed-out line and did not smile.
"This makes him arrive as answer," she said. "He should arrive as person."
"Persons do not scan as easily."
"Then work harder."
That should have stung less from anyone else. From her, it became law.

They spent the next hour not writing about Jack. They wrote around him. A song about bridge tolls, as she had sung. A tavern verse about a clerk who classified his own mother as grain to avoid visiting her. A mocking couplet about wise hands that always seemed to reach for other people's purses. Humor, not reverence. Doubt, not worship. The public did not need a saint to replace a monster. It needed suspicion with a tune.
"You're asking people to think," Dandelion said at last. "It is an ambitious demand before ale."
"No," Priscilla said. "I am asking them to laugh at the hand reaching for the chain. Thinking may follow after embarrassment."
He faced her and felt the old ache of loving someone whose courage had become quieter after the world damaged the instrument it first admired. "That is better than my line."
"Yes."
"You might pretend otherwise for romance."
"No."
"Cruel woman."
"You collect them."

By dawn, they had three anti-hooks. Not counter-songs, not declarations, not praise. Little knives. A line about how every wolf called dangerous had first been counted by a shepherd who sold wool. A line about wise hands being surprisingly fond of locks. A line about bridges that charged names as tolls.

Dandelion copied them without signature and sent them into the city through buskers who owed him favors and one who owed him an apology. He gave each a warning: sing lightly, never twice in the same tavern, and do not let anyone call the subject Jack.
"Why not?" asked one girl with a fiddle and more courage than years.
"Because a name is a door," Dandelion said. "And at present, several bastards are paid to listen for hinges."
She accepted that with the seriousness of young artists who believed metaphor was probably taxable.
By midmorning, wise hands had competition.
Not victory. Competition. In Novigrad, that counted as weather change.
The Chameleon became more useful after midnight, when the respectable patrons left and the people who actually moved the city arrived.

A laundress brought a melody from the Temple quarter, hummed low while pretending to ask about ale. A cobbler's apprentice brought chalk dust on his cuffs and a wolf sketched on the sole of an unfinished boot. A river pilot brought three names, two false and one expensive. Dandelion paid for all of it, sometimes in coin, sometimes in wine, and once with a promise to remove a verse about a fishmonger's sister from public circulation. The sacrifice nearly broke him.

Priscilla sorted the reports by hook, not location. Fear. Custody. Blood. Gratitude. Chain. She used wine corks as markers because the Chameleon had an abundance of failed corks and Dandelion said they deserved a meaningful afterlife. By the end of the night, the table looked like a child's game invented by a magistrate with nightmares.
"Gratitude is the worst one," she said.
Zoltan, who had arrived with rain in his beard again and a pastry he refused to share, grunted. "Fear's worse."
"Fear makes people step back. Gratitude makes them step forward into the knife and thank the hand holding it."
Dandelion raised one finger. "As a lifelong recipient of gratitude, I object to being implicated in stabbing."
"You have stabbed several reputations with couplets."
"Reputations heal badly because they refuse proper care."

Priscilla tapped the cork labeled gratitude. "The songs always begin with rescue. The mill. The child. The hill. The girl. If the public accepts that he saved people, then custody sounds benevolent rather than punitive. That is the trick. They are not saying he is evil. They are saying he is too important to remain free."
Zoltan set down the pastry. That was how Dandelion knew the matter had become severe.
"Then the answer isn't to say he's harmless," the dwarf said. "No one believes harmless saves folk from hills. The answer is to say useful is not owned."
Priscilla turned to him. "That is the line."
"What line?"
Dandelion had already found paper. "Useful is not owned. Zoltan, you magnificent granite-hearted accountant of the human soul."
"Call me that in public and I will make you useful."
By dawn, the phrase had entered three mouths not belonging to any of them. It was not pretty. That helped. Pretty phrases attracted vanity. Useful phrases found work.

Near the fish market, a woman selling eel pies said it to a dock guard who had called the red wolf a public burden. He had no answer prepared. The pause was small, but in cities pauses were where counter-revolutions hid.
By the next evening, Dandelion had discovered a grief particular to restraint.

People praised the counter-lines. They bought him drinks for verses he had not signed and could not admit. A fishmonger slapped his shoulder hard, threatening artistry and said, "Useful is not owned. That's yours, ain't it?" Dandelion opened his mouth, saw Priscilla's stare across the room, and said only, "It belongs to the city now. Try not to let it embarrass us."
The fishmonger nodded as if entrusted with a kingdom.
Dandelion later described this as personal martyrdom. Priscilla called it professional maturity. Zoltan called it not before time.
The line traveled poorly at first, which reassured Priscilla. Perfect travel meant a patron. Bad travel meant people had begun carrying it themselves.

Dandelion watched the phrase stumble through three versions before noon and resisted the urge to correct it. That resistance, he informed Priscilla, was a spiritual achievement. She said nothing, which was either agreement or mercy. He chose the kinder interpretation and was almost certainly wrong.
Zoltan Chivay believed every mystery became less mystical once someone had to pay for it.

This did not make him unimaginative. It made him experienced. Men spoke of destiny when the bill was hidden, of patriotism when the invoice was delayed, of faith when the collection box had no names attached, and of public safety when iron bands were purchased through a medical freight account. Zoltan had survived monarchs, pogroms, false friends, true friends with worse judgment than enemies, and Dandelion's attempt to invest in a perfume venture based on the phrase emotional musk. He trusted coin because coin lied with weight.

The South Quay Counting House stood between a spice warehouse and a chapel dedicated to a saint who had supposedly fed three hundred poor people with one loaf and then founded a guild to regulate bread. Novigrad loved miracles that ended in fees. The counting house door was painted green, its brass polished, its windows barred from inside and out. A sign above the door read VANDER ROGH AND SONS, DISCREET ACCOUNTS, LAWFUL TRANSFERS, MEDICAL FREIGHT, CHARITABLE TRUSTS.
"Any business that advertises discretion above the door deserves burglary," Zoltan said.
Dandelion adjusted his cuffs. "We are not burgling in daylight."
"Why not?"
"Because daylight exposes me to criticism from lesser dressed men."
Priscilla regarded both of them. "We are asking questions first."
"Fine," Zoltan said. "But I reserve burglary as an instrument of civic improvement."

Inside, the counting house smelled of ink, wax, dust, and fear so well managed it had become policy. Clerks sat behind high desks, copying numbers into ledgers with the soft scratching sound of a hundred small creatures eating accountability. A portrait of the founder hung on the wall. He had the face of a man who had discovered compound interest and mistaken it for virtue.

The front clerk looked at Zoltan, then at Dandelion, then at Priscilla, and made a rapid calculation. Dwarf with money or trouble. Bard with scandal or debt. Woman with eyes that missed nothing. He chose procedural contempt because it was safer than honest alarm.
"Appointments are required," he said.
"Good," Zoltan replied. "We require one."
"With whom?"
"Someone who knows Valden Rue."
The clerk's pen stopped.
Zoltan smiled. Dwarven smiles were excellent tools when built correctly. This one suggested both friendliness and a cellar where friendliness could be reconsidered.
"Master Rue is not available," the clerk said.
"Busy?"
"Absent."
"Dead absent, hiding absent, or promoted to a room with better locks absent?"
Dandelion placed one elegant hand on the desk. "My associate means to say we are concerned for Master Rue's health."
"No, I don't," Zoltan said.
"He means to say he has a rich emotional life and poor phrasing."

Priscilla leaned in. "Master Rue purchased clove-black wax under medical freight designation and paid singers through accounts attached to a widow charity. If he is absent, someone should know whether his absence is accounting or anatomy."
The clerk lost color in a way that made Zoltan's morning worthwhile.

A door opened behind the desks. A woman emerged, perhaps forty, perhaps older, with gray at her temples and a chain of office over a dress the color of wet slate. She had the composure of a person who had fired men for sweating on ledgers.
"I am Mistress Vander Rogh," she said. "You will lower your voice or leave."
Zoltan looked around the quiet room. "This is my lowered voice."
"Then we will move to my office before your natural state damages the furniture."

Her office contained two chairs for guests, one chair for power, and a locked cabinet that hummed faintly when Priscilla passed it. Zoltan noticed. Priscilla noticed him noticing. Dandelion noticed a small bronze statuette of a goat on the mantel and seemed briefly tempted to make a comment. Priscilla stepped on his foot.
Mistress Vander Rogh sat. "Valden Rue worked here on temporary contract. He handled medical freight pass-throughs from several districts. If he has broken law, take the matter to magistrates."
"Magistrates eat paper and burp seals," Zoltan said. "We prefer digestion."
"Then you prefer trouble."
"Only when it pays better than patience."
Dandelion produced Triss's copied seal impression, Priscilla's pamphlet, and the wax scrap from Brelka. He placed them on the desk without flourish, which for him constituted a spiritual sacrifice.
Mistress Vander Rogh studied the papers. She touched none. "I do not know this pamphlet."
"You know the wax," Zoltan said.
"I know many waxes. I am tragically worldly."
"Clove-black. Damp field condition. Paid through charity."
Her eyes moved once to the locked cabinet.
"There," Zoltan said. "That little glance spent your dignity. Spend the rest wisely."
Mistress Vander Rogh leaned back. "You are an unpleasant man."
"I've trained."

Priscilla's voice entered softer. "Someone is using your accounts to prepare a crowd for custody language. A man is being made into a burden in song before the state approaches him in law. If this was done without your consent, you are being used. If it was done with your consent, you are in worse company than you think."
The office quiet deepened.
Mistress Vander Rogh looked at Priscilla longer than she had looked at the men. "You understand performance."
"I understand injury that reaches a room before the knife."
That did it. Not completely. It opened the door.
The accountant stood, unlocked the cabinet, and removed a narrow ledger bound in gray leather. She placed it on the desk and kept one hand on the cover.

"Rue brought letters under seal. Proper seal. Cross-border medical relief designation. Postwar irregularity fund. War widows attached because those accounts move without questions from men who enjoy appearing charitable. I processed transfers. I did not write songs."
"Names," Zoltan said.
"Numbers first. Names later if I decide not to have you removed."
"Madam, if removal were easy, you'd have started there."
For the first time, her mouth almost smiled. Accountants respected correctly stated difficulty.
She opened the ledger.

Numbers. Dates. Amounts. Paper stock. Wax. Courier fees. Tavern credit. Payments to singers under performance stipends. A printer near St. Gregory's Bridge. A medical supplier in Devenford. A district office near Heddel's Ferry. And there, near the bottom of one page, an account notation abbreviated in a clean hand: S.V. discretionary channel, public reassurance layer.
Dandelion whispered, "S. Veyrane."
Zoltan turned to him. "You know him?"
"No. But I dislike him already."
"Don't rush. Dislike matures better with evidence."
Priscilla copied the line. Mistress Vander Rogh let her. That was not absolution. It was a woman choosing which danger might leave her business with fewer teeth marks.
"Where is Rue?" Zoltan asked.

"Gone. Two nights ago. South by river. He left a debt here. That suggests he expected protection or lacked time to settle accounts. Men expecting death sometimes settle debts. Men expecting promotion often don't."
"Clever woman," Zoltan said.
"Widow," she replied. "We have advantages."
Valden Rue had not gone far because men who trusted protection usually forgot weather.

They found his rented room above a lamp-oil shop, empty in the ordinary ways and full in the useful ones. The bed had been slept in badly. A travel cloak was missing. The washbasin held black grit under the water. The window latch had been repaired from inside after forced entry, which meant either Rue had locked himself in after being visited or staged a visit with poor carpentry. On the table lay a heel of bread, a smear of goose fat, and three grains of red sealing wax that did not match the clove-black.
"He ate before leaving," Dandelion said. "That suggests confidence."
"Or hunger," Zoltan said. "Never build philosophy on goose fat."
Priscilla examined the windowsill. "Someone stood outside. Mud on the ledge. Narrow boot. City make. Not dock."
Zoltan grunted approval. "You're wasted on music."
"So are most listeners."
The room's best evidence was in the stove.

Rue had burned letters and still left too many. Men in haste trusted flame the way fools trusted kings: by reputation rather than inspection. Zoltan sifted ash with a knife and recovered three half-charred scraps. Dandelion held the lamp. Priscilla read.
...retain wolf terminology in public layer...
...avoid dragon-blooded designation pending senior review...
...Vineyard probability increasing. Do not engage Rivia directly...
Dandelion lowered the lamp until wax dripped on his fingers. He did not notice until Priscilla took it from him.
"Vineyard probability," he said.
Zoltan's face went hard. "Geralt."
"They wanted Jack to go to him," Priscilla said.
"Or expected he would," Zoltan said. "Difference matters. One is bait. One is accounting. Both stink."
From below came the creak of a stair.

Zoltan put one finger to his lips. Dandelion, whose instincts under danger had improved over decades of being Geralt's friend and worsened by being Dandelion, reached for a candlestick. Priscilla moved to the side of the door with a knife she had not been holding a moment earlier.
The door opened.
A boy entered with a tray of cold tea and immediately regretted adulthood.
"Rue sent you?" Zoltan asked.
The boy shook his head so hard tea spilled. "Man downstairs. Said bring it. Paid me."
"What man?"
"Brown coat. Gray gloves. Said if anyone asked about Rue, say he went east."
"And did he?"
The boy looked at the dwarf, the bard with a candlestick, and the woman with a knife. His sense of audience adjusted. "He went south. I saw him from the roof. Toward the medical barges."
Zoltan gave him a coin. "For honesty."
Dandelion gave him another. "For trauma."
Priscilla gave him the cold tea back. "For returning the tray."
The boy fled with the dignity of someone paid from three moral systems.
At the medical barges, they found Rue's coat.

Only the coat. It had been folded and placed under a rope coil as if its owner had removed it neatly before vanishing from the world. In the pocket was a permit stamped with a black oval, a list of taverns where the red wolf song had been seeded, and a smaller list of names under the heading possible emotional witnesses. Mara Veyr. Rian Wedeck. Miro of Willenford. Luthan and Nessa of the Broken Crown. Geralt of Rivia. Triss Merigold. Yennefer of Vengerberg, uncertain arrival probability. Ciri, restricted, do not activate without senior approval.
Priscilla read the last line twice.
Dandelion made no joke.
Zoltan folded the list. "Now we have blood in the accounting."
"Rue?" Priscilla asked.

He studied the river. Brown water moved under gray light, carrying straw, oil, and one dead rat with democratic indifference. "Either protected, promoted, or drowned. We won't know until someone needs one version more than the others."
Dandelion found his voice. It had less ornament than usual. "We send this to Corvo Bianco."
"Copy first," Zoltan said. "Send one by road, one by river, one through the dwarf carriers. Keep one hidden where no romantic idiot will open it for dramatic effect."
"I resent the specificity."
"Improve and I'll generalize."
Zoltan wrote the practical part of the message because Dandelion's idea of urgency still wore embroidery.
Geralt,

Someone is paying for the songs, the paper, and the wax through South Quay accounts dressed as medical freight and widow relief. Clove-black wax. Office stock. Printer near St. Gregory's. Account notation S.V., public reassurance layer. They know the vineyard is likely. They do not want you engaged directly yet, which means either they are frightened of you or have grown temporarily intelligent.
He stopped, chewed the end of the pen, and continued.

List found in Rue's coat names witnesses: medic, clerk, boy, shepherd, girl, you, Triss, Yennefer, and Ciri under restricted note. This is no longer rumor only. It is mapping. If the young wolf thinks leaving keeps others safe, hit him with something heavy but not fatal. Preferably a chair you dislike.
Z.
Dandelion read over his shoulder. "Elegant. Brutal. Unmarketable."
"Good. Means you won't sing it."

Priscilla added a second page in a cleaner hand, describing the lyrical structure of the paid verses, the bridge counter-song, the phrase wiser hands, and the way crowds accepted rescue before custody. She wrote with a musician's precision and a survivor's anger. Dandelion added a third page despite objections, because witnesses mattered and because tone sometimes carried what facts could not.
Geralt,

You once told me, with your usual grace, that poets made monsters of men by preferring shape to truth. I objected at the time because you were rude and because I had just written a very good couplet about a noonwraith. I object less now. They are shaping this Jack before he arrives anywhere as himself. Monster will not be the first cage. Hero may be worse. A hero can be chained in public and thanked for the honor.
Priscilla is brilliant. Zoltan is unbearable and correct. I am, as ever, indispensable underappreciated civilization.
D.
Zoltan scratched out underappreciated. Dandelion wrote it again smaller. Priscilla let it stand. Morale, she said, was sometimes cheaper than medicine.

The messages left Novigrad under three covers: a wine invoice, a dwarf freight note, and a prayer request to a saint of lost livestock. Dandelion considered the last one inspired. Zoltan considered it blasphemous only if the saint read accounts.
Then they waited, which none of them did well.

Waiting in Novigrad did not mean stillness. Zoltan visited dockmasters, bought beers for men he disliked, threatened a printer with a discussion about unpaid dwarf labor histories, and discovered that two singers had been paid from the same purse by different hands. Priscilla listened in markets and chapels, tracking how the red wolf song mutated. Dandelion performed old favorites and inserted small, careful changes into the spaces where crowds expected easy answers. No red wolf. No crimson chain. Bridges, names, burdens, and wolves that refused collars for reasons entirely unrelated to current affairs, naturally.
By the second night, someone tried to follow Zoltan home.

This was unwise for several reasons, beginning with the fact that Zoltan did not go home when followed. He went to an alley behind a cooper's yard where the cobbles tilted, the lamplight failed, and two friends from Mahakam were repairing a cart wheel with hammers built to make moral arguments brief.
The follower entered after him and stopped.
He was young, human, brown coat, city boots, gray gloves. Clean face. Frightened now. Fear improved him.
"Evening," Zoltan said.
The young man turned to leave. The two dwarves with hammers adjusted the cart wheel in a way that closed the alley.
"Wrong way," Zoltan said. "Happens in cities. Streets confusing. Men paid to follow dwarves often get lost right before learning useful things."
"I don't want trouble."
"Then you're in the wrong profession. Who sent you?"
"No one."
Zoltan sighed. "Bad start. I respect many vices. Laziness in lying isn't among them."
The young man's eyes moved to the hammers. "Odran Bracc. Field captain. I was to note contacts only. Not engage."
"Wise. For a man who sent you, not for you."
"I don't know anything else."

"Course not. They pay little men to know little things so big men can call it structure." Zoltan stepped closer. "Listen carefully. You will report that Dandelion is vain, Priscilla is recovering, I am drunk, and the money trail ended in a widow's bad memory."
"They won't believe that."
"Make it uglier. Truth sounds too neat when frightened."
"And if they ask about you?"
Zoltan smiled. "Tell them I bite."
The young man nodded rapidly.
"One more thing," Zoltan said. "If you go near the boy in Willenford or the girl from Broken Crown, I will discover which account paid your boots and charge interest on your bones."
The follower believed that. Good.
When he was gone, one of the cart dwarves lowered his hammer. "You letting him walk?"
"For now. A frightened messenger carries more than a corpse."
"Softer than you used to be."
"Richer in strategy, poorer in patience. Don't confuse maturity with mercy."
The next pamphlet did not mention wiser hands.
It asked questions instead.
Who decides when a mutant ceases to be a man?

No signature. No crest. Printed on cheap paper from a shop that owed Zoltan money by morning and owed him gratitude by noon. Priscilla argued the phrasing. Dandelion improved the rhythm. Zoltan paid the printer and threatened him with a discount if he bragged.
"We are now propagandists," Dandelion said as they watched the first copies move through the market.
"No," Priscilla said. "We are making room for doubt. Propaganda closes the room."
Zoltan grunted. "Also ours scans better."

The pamphlet spread less quickly than the red wolf song. That was expected. Fear sprinted. Doubt walked with a limp. But it walked. At the fish market, one woman refused to sing the chain refrain after reading it. Near the chapel, a student asked whether wise custody had ever been wise for the person being held. At a tavern, a drunk claimed he had always hated wolves, chains, and government in equal measure, which was not coherent but showed civic movement.
That evening, a courier arrived from Corvo Bianco with a note in Triss's hand.
Received. Yennefer present. Ciri channel warmed. Kaer Morhen likely. Continue tracing S.V. Protect witnesses where possible. Do not turn Jack into a hero. Do not let them make him a beast.
Below it, in Geralt's cramped hand, another line:
Zoltan, if Dandelion writes a song called Wiser Hands, break the lute first.
Dandelion clutched his chest. "He wounds because he loves."
Zoltan took the note and smiled for the first time that week with something like warmth. "Good. Old bastard understands."
Priscilla looked toward the Chameleon's common room, where two songs and three arguments were currently damaging one another in useful ways. "Do we?"
"No," Zoltan said. "But we know where the money went. That's more understanding than most prophecies deserve."
He folded the note and placed it inside his coat.

Outside, Novigrad rained ink, smoke, and rumor. Somewhere far south, a young witcher with crimson eyes was being pulled toward an old keep by a dead man's name. Somewhere behind him, Black Ink was learning which witnesses had resisted correction. Somewhere ahead, a vineyard held too many histories under one roof.
Zoltan ordered another beer and began a new list.
War widows account. Medical freight. Clove-black wax. Valden Rue. Odran Bracc. S. Veyrane. Vineyard probability. Ciri restricted.
He underlined the last one twice.
Then he wrote one more line at the bottom.
Find who paid for the first bad song.
Because every song, like every crime, had a first coin.
The printer near St. Gregory's Bridge had ink under his fingernails and terror under his collar.

His name was Fennec, which Dandelion declared too literary to be trusted. The man printed prayer sheets, debt notices, marriage bans, political lies, and occasionally poems when poets paid in advance and accepted that art looked better if folded badly. His shop smelled of oil, metal, wet paper, and nervous justification. Zoltan found the pamphlet type still locked in a tray beneath a cloth, because Fennec had hidden it the way a child hid broken pottery: so thoroughly it proved guilt and so poorly it insulted anyone searching.
"I print what comes with payment," Fennec said.
"A noble creed," Zoltan said. "Used by hangmen, whores, and tax farmers, though usually with better shoes."
Dandelion examined the type. "Doom really was your choice?"
Fennec blinked. "What?"
"The rhyme. Wiser hands than doom. If you were coerced, blink twice. If you chose it freely, I may need to sit down."
Priscilla lifted one of the proof sheets. "Who brought the copy?"
"A clerk. Brown coat, gray gloves. Paid double. Said it was a public reassurance notice adapted into verse for easier comprehension."
"Did he give a name?" Zoltan asked.
"Bracc. No first. He said the account was guaranteed."
Odran Bracc. Another line connecting to Sorel Veyrane's structure.
Fennec's wife emerged from behind a stack of paper with a baby on her hip and fury in both eyes. "He also said refusing would make our license interesting."
"License interesting," Zoltan repeated. "That's city poetry."

The wife pointed at a locked drawer. "He kept the scrap. I told him to burn it. He said evidence protects printers. I said evidence gets printers drowned. He said I lacked respect for professional risk."
"Does she?" Priscilla asked.
Fennec turned from his wife to Zoltan. "No."

The drawer contained the original copy, three payment chits, and a tiny smear of black wax. It also contained a list of distribution points, each chosen not for size but for repetition: fish market, bridge tavern, shrine steps, laundry lanes, ferry queue, student quarter. Places where people repeated what they heard because their hands were busy and their minds had room for borrowed fear.

Priscilla copied the list. Dandelion, with visible moral struggle, did not correct the meter in the original verse. Zoltan paid the printer's wife rather than the printer and told Fennec that if another gray-gloved man threatened his license, he should remember licenses burned better than families.
Outside, Dandelion said, "That sounded compassionate."
"It was practical. Families complain longer."
They went next to the charity office.

The widow fund operated from two rooms above a candle shop, with three clerks, one locked strongbox, and a painted sign showing a woman in tasteful grief accepting a loaf from a hand descending from clouds. Zoltan disliked the sign immediately. Divine hands rarely balanced accounts.

The clerk in charge insisted the fund was clean. She was right in the narrow way that made lies durable. Money had entered under proper donation categories. Money had left under relief disbursements to musicians, printers, couriers, and medical observers, each transaction small, avoiding scrutiny, and virtuous in a way that discouraged curiosity. No widow had been cheated. That was the cleverness. The lie did not steal from grief. It stood beside grief and used its doorway.
"Good evil," Zoltan said after reading the ledger. "The irritating kind."
"Good?" the clerk asked.
"Competent. Don't preen."
There, in the third book, they found a recurring notation: S.V. review, no crest, routed through Rue.
Dandelion studied the initials. "He likes being abbreviated."
"Power does," Priscilla said. "It turns men into weather."

Zoltan copied the page and left two dwarves to watch the office. Not threaten. Watch. Threats made people dramatic. Watching made them careful, and careful people often preserved evidence by accident.

By nightfall, the trail had become a body with bones: Sorel Veyrane at the head, Odran Bracc in the field, Rue moving money and paper, Fennec printing fear, singers turning it into air, charities making it clean, and witnesses being gathered like loose thread.
Zoltan looked at the map they had scratched on the back of a tavern menu and tapped the line toward Toussaint.
"Now we know what to tell Geralt."
Dandelion studied the menu. "We should copy it before someone orders stew on our conspiracy."
"Too late," Priscilla said. "The stew is part of the evidence now."
"At last," Dandelion said. "A meal with narrative function."
The dwarf carriers refused to take the first packet until Zoltan told them exactly why it mattered.

That was their rule, older than most city charters and better built. A sealed thing could be carried for coin. A sealed thing of that kind required kinship, debt, or truth. Zoltan met them in a warehouse where iron tools hung from rafters and the smell of coal dust lingered in the cracks. Three dwarves listened while rain tapped the roof and Novigrad shouted beyond the doors.
"Geralt's involved," Zoltan said.

That earned attention, but not assent. Geralt had done much for dwarves and also brought trouble with the reliability of mold in damp cellars. Gratitude did not cancel risk. Dwarves, unlike several human governments, understood accounting.

"Young witcher," Zoltan continued. "Hidden Wolf. Red eyes. Some smooth-handed filth wants him named as public burden before they put hands on him. Papers, songs, wax, charity accounts. They are making a lawful chain."
The oldest carrier, Yarpen's cousin by some route no one had time to diagram, scratched his beard. "Human problem."
"Starts that way," Zoltan said. "Then someone remembers nonhumans are useful categories too. They always do."
That moved the room.

He laid the copied ledger line on the table. Medical freight. Widow charity. Public reassurance layer. S.V. The dwarves read slowly, not because they lacked wit, but because they respected paper and distrusted haste. When the oldest looked up, his expression had changed from caution to old anger.
"We carry one," he said.
"Three," Zoltan replied.
"One through our route. One through a cousin route. One through a route I do not tell you, so if you get drunk and poetic beside the bard, you cannot betray it."
"I am never poetic."
The old dwarf studied him.
"Fine," Zoltan said. "Rarely. Under provocation."

They stamped the packets not with a crest but with a trade mark for cracked hinges. No clerk would care. Every dwarf carrier from Novigrad to the upper crossings would understand it meant the hinge might look broken because it had been built to open only for the right hand.
When Zoltan returned to the Chameleon, he found Dandelion arguing with a patron about whether burden rhymed with certain.
"It does not," Dandelion said.
"Near," the patron replied.
"Near is how civilizations get tax law and syphilis."
Zoltan placed the stamped receipts on the table. "Packets are moving."
Priscilla touched the trade mark. "Cracked hinges?"
"Doors again," Zoltan said. "Everyone's got a theme whether they want one or not."
For once, no one made a joke after that.
The first bad song had cost six crowns.

That offended Zoltan more than almost anything else. Not because six crowns was much. Because it was little. A man's future public cage had begun at a price low; two fair boots might have bought it, a week of cheap rooms, or one fine dinner for a fool trying to impress someone clever, gone before dessert.
They found the payment in a tavern ledger under entertainment sundries. The tavern keeper, a woman with one cloudy eye and a memory sharpened by poverty, remembered the man who paid.

"Not the singer," she said. "Singer was a reed with boots. The payer stood near the door. Brown gloves, not gray. Spoke like a clerk trying not to. Paid in new coin. Told the singer to keep the wolf brave in the first verse and dangerous in the last. Said crowds like fairness before fear."
Priscilla went very still. "Crowds like fairness before fear."
"That is not a singer's thought," Dandelion said.
"No," Zoltan said. "That is a handler teaching poison to taste balanced."

The keeper produced one of the coins from a jar behind the bar, saved because new Nilfgaardian minting remained rarer in that quarter than bad debt. Zoltan weighed it on his palm. Legitimate coin. Southern route. No clipped edge. A state, a bank, or a thief with standards.
"Can you trace it?" Dandelion asked.
Zoltan closed his fist around the coin. "Coin wants to be traced. That is why it changes hands."
"That sounds like philosophy."
"It's accounting with dirt on it. Better."

By the time they left, the tavern keeper had agreed to forget which patron asked and remember which song had made her room uneasy. Zoltan paid her for the remembering. Dandelion tipped for the offense done to music. Priscilla thanked her for noticing the instruction hidden inside the verse.
Outside, the rain stopped. Novigrad steamed. The city smelled of ink, fish, and old lies getting wet, showing seams.
Zoltan wrote the amount beside the other figures and circled it. Six crowns. A cheap beginning was not a small beginning. It was proof the machine understood scale.
Geralt knew the council had begun badly when no one touched the wine.

This offended him in principle. Wine had once been a luxury he distrusted on grounds of price, taste, and the kinds of people who described it with words better saved for weather or lovers. Owning a vineyard had complicated the matter. He had learned that good wine could be work, bad wine could be useful, and certain conversations required a bottle on the table if only to prove civilization had not fully surrendered. Now a fine red from his own cellar sat breathing in the middle of the study while five people stared at paper, wounds, and one another's failures.

The room had been built for estate business and had become, by force, a war room pretending to remain domestic. Ledgers shared space with Black Ink copies. A vineyard map lay under a Novigrad money trail. Triss's letters sat beside Zoltan's account notes and Dandelion's dramatic testimony, which had been written in a hand that seemed to bow between sentences. Yennefer stood near the mantel because she preferred positions from which she could watch everyone and insult the furniture if needed. Triss sat at the desk, sleeves rolled, ink on her finger again.
Jack stood by the window with Buck visible beyond it in the courtyard, as if the horse were an argument for leaving.
Geralt sat because someone had to demonstrate faith in chairs.
"Read Zoltan's list again," Yennefer said.
Triss did. "War widows account. Medical freight. Clove-black wax. Valden Rue. Odran Bracc. S. Veyrane. Vineyard probability. Ciri restricted. First bad song pending."
"Ciri restricted," Yennefer said.
The two words had been sharpening themselves since the message arrived. Geralt felt them in the old places. Not scar tissue. Deeper. The place where a father kept every moment he had arrived late.
"Means they know enough not to move her yet," Triss said. "Or she understands what moving her may trigger."
"Or they are waiting for us to do it for them," Jack said.
Everyone turned to him. He did not turn from the window.
"Explain," Triss said.

"They routed notices before the reports. They placed witnesses before the flare. They expected Geralt before I came. They seeded songs before the story had legs. Maybe they don't need to touch Ciri. Maybe they need us to warn her, and the warning proves the connection."
Yennefer's expression became unpleasantly approving. "Good. Paranoia with evidence. A rare masculine achievement."
"You think he's right?" Geralt asked.
"I think ignoring him is how people die."

Triss leaned back. "The Ilyra channel warmed before any answer. That may be magical resonance, bureaucratic surveillance, or the mere fact that every road to Ciri is lined with people who believe loving her gives them rights."
"Some of us earned the belief," Geralt said.
Triss's face softened toward him. That was worse than anger. "Yes. And we must still be careful what we do with it."
The room quieted.

Geralt found Jack by the window. The young witcher had cleaned his armor that morning until the dark leather looked ready rather than polished. His white hair was tied back. The scar on his cheek caught the lamplight. His bandaged hand rested against the sill, fingers loose, too loose. Geralt knew forced ease. He had practiced it for decades and never mastered it as well as he pretended.
"We need Kaer Morhen," Geralt said.
The words did what names of old homes did. They opened doors in the room without moving walls.
Jack turned. "Why now?"
"Because Vesemir kept things. Notes, sketches, old letters, names of men who came asking. If Black Ink has fragments, we need the pieces they don't have."
"And if the pieces say he knew more than you said?"
Geralt met his eyes. "Then we read them."
"That's not an answer."
"No. It's the only honest plan."
Yennefer crossed her arms. "Kaer Morhen is a logical step. Also an obvious one."
"Meaning they may expect it," Triss said.
"They expect everything with enough roads leading to it," Geralt said. "Doesn't make the road vanish."
Jack's mouth tightened. "Roads can be traps."
"So can rooms. You're still standing in one."

For one second they looked less like mentor and hidden student than two wolves arguing over which cliff had better footing. Then Malva entered with a tray and ruined the tension by saying, "If no one drinks the wine, I will consider it insult, waste, or both, and adjust supper accordingly."
Yennefer glanced at her. "You must be Malva."
"And you must be the famous sorceress with the voice like a knife wrapped in velvet."
Geralt closed his eyes.
Triss made a small choking sound that might have been suppressed laughter.
Yennefer looked at Malva for a long moment, then said, "That depends who has been speaking."

"People with ears." Malva set down the tray. "There is bread. Cheese. Apples. Eat if you plan to make decisions about dying, traveling, or inconveniencing the household. Empty stomachs are poor counselors."
"She's right," Geralt said.
"Do not hide behind my steward," Triss said.
"I was admiring governance."
Malva pointed at him with the bread knife. "You may admire by eating."

Jack was the first to take bread. Geralt saw it. So did Triss. The act was small, practical, and more important than anyone admitted. A man preparing to bolt did not eat in front of witnesses unless hunger ambushed him or trust had begun its quiet treason.
"Good," Malva said. "The pale one has sense."
"Which pale one?" Geralt asked.
"The one not arguing with the furniture."
Yennefer looked from Malva to Geralt. "I like her."
"She likes being paid on time," Geralt said. "Be careful."
Malva left them with bread, wine, and a room slightly less willing to turn into a funeral.
The practical questions took two hours and left the wine half gone.

Routes north. Which roads would be watched. Which names could be used. Whether portals would announce too much. Whether Jack's resonance responded to Yennefer's tracking spells. It did, but badly. The test cracked one wineglass, warmed the iron latch, and made Buck slam a hoof against his stall until Geralt shouted that no one was dead. The horse remained unconvinced and bit a groom's hat for emphasis.

They decided against portals for the first leg. Yennefer disliked the decision but did not overturn it. The resonance and the barbed-star necklace made fast magic too visible. Triss would maintain courier lines from Corvo Bianco through Kovir contacts and Dandelion's network. Yennefer would move between Corvo Bianco and her own disturbance trail until the evidence demanded she travel north. Geralt and Jack would ride quietly toward Kaer Morhen, not by the fastest road, but by one with fewer official mouths.
"Quietly," Yennefer repeated. "With two white-haired witchers, a horse that assaults hats, and every tavern from here to Pontar humming about red wolves."
"I've done worse," Geralt said.
"That is not a standard. It is a confession."

Triss spread three maps over the desk. "If you avoid Beauclair's main dispatch road and cut through the old quarry route, you can reach the river crossing without passing the estates that received the advisory notice. From there, small ferries. No major tolls until after the Angren branch."
"Small ferries gossip more," Jack said.
"Yes, but they sell gossip locally. Major tolls archive it."
Jack nodded. "Fair."
Yennefer watched him. "You accept tactical advice when it is sound."
"I accept maps. They lie less than people."
"Maps lie constantly. They simply do so with scale."
"Then this house is full of dishonest paper."
"At last, agreement," Geralt said.
Triss marked the route with a charcoal line. "No heroics on the road. No public contracts unless unavoidable. No red displays, if you can help it."
Jack studied his palm. "If I could help it, the first one would not have happened."
"I know." Triss's voice softened. "I meant no bait accepted. They may stage distress again."
"People may die if ignored."
"Yes," Yennefer said. "That is why bait works."
That sentence sat down heavily among them.

Geralt remembered Ciri at every age he had failed to protect her in. A child in a ruined kingdom. A girl training in snow. A young woman chased by kings, elves, mages, ghosts, destinies, and men who loved her badly and made choices for her. He looked at Jack and saw a different shape of the same trap: danger made visible, personhood made negotiable, everyone around him tempted to call their fear care.
"If there is bait," Geralt said, "we decide case by case. On evidence. Not panic."
"We?" Jack asked.
"Yes. You and me. If I start deciding for you, hit me."
Yennefer's eyebrow lifted. "Generous."
"Not fatally," Geralt added.
"Coward," she said.
Jack held Geralt's gaze for a long moment. "And if I decide wrong?"
"Then I say so. You may still decide wrong. That is how choices work. Annoying feature."
Triss looked at Geralt with something like approval, something like grief. "Good. Remember that when he does."
"I will try."
Yennefer's voice cut in, quieter. "Trying will not be enough in the end. It never is. But it is where we begin when no one has a clean answer."
For once, no one argued.
Jack found Triss in the study after the maps were folded.

She had remained behind to copy routes and burn the scraps she did not want carried. The room smelled of paper ash, wine, and orange peel from Malva's tray. Through the open window came the sound of Geralt and Yennefer in the courtyard, not words, only the cadence of two people who knew how to disagree without losing track of the shared threat.
"You wanted something," Triss said without looking up.
"Not sure."
"That is allowed. In some rooms."
He stood near the desk, feeling too large for the domestic quiet. "Geralt and Yennefer."
Triss set down the pen. "Yes."
"You don't mind?"

She looked up then. Not offended. Not naive. Older than warmth alone. "Of course I mind. Sometimes. I am human, not a moral illustration. But minding something does not tell me what is true, what is kind, or what the situation needs."
Jack considered that. "Most people use jealousy as permission."

"For cruelty? Yes. It is fashionable. Usually badly fitted." She leaned back. "Geralt loved Yennefer. Loves, in some old shape that does not ask my permission to have existed. She is Ciri's mother in everything that matters. She would burn a city to keep Ciri from becoming a tool again. That makes her necessary here before it makes her uncomfortable."
"And you?"

"I am Geralt's present partner. I choose the life we are building. I read letters in cellars, argue with old lovers, and tell stubborn witchers when their emotional habits are endangering logistics." Her smile was small. "It is a rich position. Poorly salaried."
Jack almost said something easy. He did not. Easy would insult her.
"You make it sound simple," he said.
"No. I make it sound chosen."
The distinction landed. He looked toward the courtyard voices. "Choice seems to be everyone's favorite word until someone dislikes the result."

"That is why it needs witnesses who are not owners." Triss reached for a sealed packet and handed it to him. "For the road. Poultice for the palm, fever draught, and a powder that will make you vomit if you take it with witcher potions, so do not be heroic and stupid in the same hour. Geralt has separate supplies because he prefers his stupidity familiar."
"You always talk like this?"
"Only when frightened."
His attention settled on her. She let him see it. Not all of it, perhaps, but the shape.
"Why?"

"Because Geralt is about to ride toward a dead man's secrets with a young witcher he helped hide, while Yennefer and I try to keep Ciri from being turned into either bait or policy, and a man named S. Veyrane is making moral ugliness sound like civic sanitation." She pushed the packet into his hand. "I am very frightened. I am also very busy. Busy is preferable."
Jack took the packet. "Thank you."
"There. Not fatal."
"Unclear."
She laughed softly.

In the courtyard, Yennefer's voice rose with elegant irritation. Geralt replied with two words. Whatever he said made her go silent for exactly the length of time required to choose between murder and maturity. She chose, apparently, continued conversation.
Triss listened and smiled with more sadness than envy. "History is loud in quiet places."
Jack studied the packet in his hand. "So is paper."
"Then we make sure bodies speak too."
Geralt found Jack in the stables late that night.

He had expected that. Jack had made the expectation easy by cleaning Buck's tack with the focus of a man trying to polish thought into something manageable. The horse stood loose in the stall, head over the half-door, watching both witchers with an expression that suggested neither was as subtle as believed. Geralt brought two cups and a bottle.
"Wine?" Jack asked.
"No. Water. Triss says if we drink more wine before discussing travel, Malva will make breakfast educational."
"I don't know what that means."
"Neither do I. That's why we're obeying."

Geralt handed him a cup. Jack took it with the unbandaged hand. For a while, they drank in the stable's warm dark. Horses shifted. Hay breathed. Outside, crickets tried to convince the world nothing official existed.
Geralt studied Buck. "Good horse."
"He knows."
"Bad trait in a horse."
"Worse in a witcher."
"Depends on the witcher."
That was as close to ease as they came before the old wound returned.
Jack set the cup on a barrel. "Why did Vesemir keep the necklace on me?"
Geralt had expected that too. Expecting did not help.
"He tried taking it off once," he said. "You were fevered after the second trial. Breathing badly. The medallion wouldn't stop shaking. He thought the signet was feeding it. Cut the chain."
Jack's hand stilled on the strap.
"What happened?"

"You stopped breathing. Not long. For years." Geralt studied the stall wall. The wood grain was easier than the young man's face. "He put it back. You breathed. After that, he said we wait until we understand it. Then he died before understanding what it meant."
"And you didn't tell me."
"No."
"Because discipline keeps boys alive longer than answers."
Geralt closed his eyes briefly. Hearing his own failure repeated in Jack's voice made it uglier. Good. It deserved the shape.

"Because I was afraid answers would send you looking before you were ready," Geralt said. "Because Ciri was hunted and I thought hiding you both from each other kept two dangers from touching. Because Vesemir asked me to trust him. Because I wanted him to be right."
Jack turned the strap over. "Was he?"
"Sometimes." Geralt turned to him then. "Not always."
The answer stood between them without excuse. Buck chewed hay with impressive disregard for inherited guilt.
"Ciri," Jack said.
Geralt's chest tightened. "What about her?"
"You hid me from her. Did you hide her from me?"
"Yes."
"She know you make habits of that?"
Geralt almost smiled. It hurt too much to last. "She has opinions."
"Good ones?"
"Usually. Loud ones. Sometimes with a sword."
Jack nodded as if cataloging weather. "You think she'll hate it."
"I think she will recognize it." Geralt leaned against the stall. "That's worse. Ciri survived because people helped her. She nearly died because people thought helping meant deciding for her."
"And you?"
There it was. Clean blade. No wasted motion.
Geralt drank water he did not want. "I did both."

Jack held him in silence for a long time. Not forgiving. Not condemning. Measuring, perhaps, but with less coldness than before. Geralt would have accepted hatred. Hatred gave a man a wall to stand against. This was worse because it left doors.
"I don't want to be managed," Jack said.
"I know."
"Yennefer will try."
"Yes. She'll call it strategy. She may even be right."
"Triss will soften it."
"And sharpen it where needed."
"You?"
Geralt looked at the repaired saddle strap hanging over the door. His stitches held, ugly and strong. "I'll try to remember I don't own the choice just because I'm afraid of it."
Jack's mouth tightened. "That sounded rehearsed."
"It was. Triss yelled at me earlier."
For a moment, the stable allowed a real smile to nearly exist between them.
Then Jack said, "If Kaer Morhen has answers, they may not be kind to Vesemir."
"I know."
"Or you."
"I know."
"Or me."
Geralt watched him without blinking. "That's the part I'm worried about."
Jack looked away first.
