Outside, a night bird called from the vines. Buck lifted his head, decided the bird had no jurisdiction, and returned to hay.
The message from Ilyra Sarn arrived an hour before the decision to leave became final.

It came through the least impressive channel available: a cracked jar of preserved cherries delivered with a wine order and a complaint that the fruit had turned sour. Malva opened the jar, smelled it, declared the complaint accurate, and found a waxed strip of paper tucked beneath the cloth seal. Triss read it in the study while everyone else pretended not to crowd her shoulder.
The note was short.

The vocabulary is known to us. Similar phrases have appeared in advisory summaries near Her Highness, not naming your subject but describing bloodline custody concerns and potential destabilizing association with northern witcher networks. I have not shown her the file. I will not keep it from her long. If you intend to tell her as family, move before policy learns to speak first.
No signature. Only a small mark in the corner, a crescent cut through a line. Ilyra.

Geralt took the note after Triss and read it twice. Yennefer did not ask to see it; she simply held out her hand, and he gave it to her. Jack watched that exchange with a strange attention. Trust, in this room, passed through gestures so old that even anger did not fully interrupt them.
"They are circling Ciri," Yennefer said.
"Not touching yet," Triss said.
"Circling is touching with patience."
Geralt looked at the vineyard map, though nothing on it could help. "Then Kaer Morhen faster."
Jack folded his arms. "Or I ride away from all of you."
The room went still.
It had been waiting for that sentence since he arrived. Triss closed her eyes. Yennefer's face went knife-still. Geralt did not move at all.
"Say it properly," Geralt said.
Jack turned to him. "If connection is what they need, I break the connection. I leave before Ciri is drawn in, before this house becomes evidence, before your old friends become witness lists."
"And go where?"
"Roads exist."
"So do hunters."
"I have handled hunters."
Yennefer's voice cut cleanly. "You have handled men who wanted you dead, paid, frightened, or quiet. You have not handled a system that wins by making your isolation look like your choice."
Jack's eyes hardened. "And staying does not make me managed?"
"It might," Triss said.
Everyone turned to her.

She did not blunt the fact. "It might. If we become frightened enough, if Geralt confuses guilt with authority, if Yennefer confuses strategy with ownership, if I confuse care with arrangement, then yes. We could become another beautiful cage. That is why we name it now."
The honesty struck harder than reassurance would have. Jack's anger had expected resistance and found an open door with a knife beside it.
Geralt stood. "I don't want you here because you're useful."
"Want does not build the bridge," Jack said.

"No. So here's the rest. If you leave alone, they still have your witnesses, your medic, your clerk, the boy, the girl, Ciri's file, my name, Vesemir's fragments, and every song already moving. You don't break the chain by taking yourself off one link. You only make the next person easier to pull."
Yennefer watched Geralt with rare approval. "Adequate."
"Thank you," Geralt said without looking at her.

Jack looked toward the window. Buck stood in the courtyard below, flicking flies away with his tail, unaware or pretending to be. Freedom, Jack thought, should have looked more like a horse and less like choosing the least dishonest road.
"Kaer Morhen," he said at last. "But I ride beside you. Not behind."
Geralt nodded. "Beside."
"And if I say we stop, we stop."
"Unless stopping kills us."
"Then you may argue."
"I was planning to."
The room breathed again, unevenly. Triss set Ilyra's note beside Zoltan's list. Yennefer folded her hands. Geralt looked suddenly tired, which made him seem more honest than strong.
Jack took the cherry jar from the table and sniffed it.
"Sour," he said.
Malva, from the doorway, replied, "At last, a man reads the true report."
It was too small a joke to save anyone. It saved the minute. Sometimes minutes were the only honest currency left.
Packing for Kaer Morhen made Geralt clumsy.

Not in the ways that mattered to survival. The blades were checked, oils sealed, potions wrapped, maps folded against damp, coin divided between obvious purse and hidden seams. His hands knew the old work. It was the domestic objects that betrayed him. He put a vineyard key in the saddlebag, took it out, put it back, then stared at it as if it had asked a question.
Triss saw. She came beside him and took the key from his hand.
"The house will be here," she said.
"I know."
"That was not the part you were doubting."
He met her eyes. "No."
She closed his fingers around the key again. "Then take it. Not because you need it on the road. Because you need to remember you have somewhere to return without earning it again."
Geralt's face changed in the small, painful way of men who had been handed tenderness with instructions. He kissed her forehead. Not dramatically. Too little for ballads. The room accepted it anyway.

Across the courtyard, Jack tightened Buck's girth and pretended not to see. Yennefer stood near the steps and pretended not to see him pretending. Malva saw everything and ordered two servants to carry oats, because oats were less embarrassing than grief.
When Geralt mounted, the vineyard key rested in his inner pouch beside a whetstone and Triss's route note.
It weighed more than either.
They left after breakfast, which was less suitable for ballads and more suitable for people who understood that horses, fear, and kitchens all became disagreeable when rushed.

Malva gave Geralt a list of household matters he was not to use as excuses to turn back, then gave Jack a packet of dried meat and pretended it was for Buck. Triss checked the route packet twice and then a third time because worry had hands. Yennefer placed a small charm on Jack's saddle and told him not to thank her because it was experimental and might offend her by working.
"What does it do?" Jack asked.
"If a tracking spell catches on the tack, it will make the caster taste vinegar for an hour."
Geralt looked impressed. "That's petty."
"It also burns the trace. The vinegar is for me."

Triss embraced Geralt in the courtyard without drama. He held her a moment longer than a man leaving for a simple road would have. She did not tell him to be careful. Careful was too small. Instead she said, "Come back with answers you can stand to hear."
"That's optimistic."
"I did not say like."
Yennefer stood a little apart, arms folded. When Geralt turned to her, she inclined her head once. Old blessing, old challenge, old refusal to soften in public. Then she turned to Jack.
"Do not let him confuse silence with wisdom. He does that."
"I noticed."
Geralt muttered, "Wonderful. Alliance."
"Temporary," Yennefer said.
"That is how most ruinous ones begin," Triss said.
Jack mounted. Buck shifted under him, eager for road and suspicious of farewell. Geralt adjusted Roach's reins, then checked Jack's saddle. His eyes narrowed.
"Girth's loose."
"It isn't."
Geralt checked anyway.
It was not loose. He tightened it by a fraction no horse required. Jack watched the old witcher's hands do practical fear badly. Geralt's face gave nothing away. The hands did.
Triss saw. Yennefer saw. Malva saw and, mercifully, told a groom to stop gawking at family business.
Geralt stepped back. "Now it isn't."
Jack faced him from the saddle. Something passed between them that was not forgiveness and not refusal. A road, perhaps. Narrow. Muddy. Better than no road.
They rode out under a sky scrubbed pale by rain.

Behind them, Corvo Bianco stood in the morning light with its shutters open and its swords still within reach. Triss watched from the steps until the road bent. Yennefer remained beside her, black and white beside green, old history beside present choice, neither woman leaving the other alone with fear. Malva pretended to inspect a rosebush and wiped her eyes with the irritation of someone discovering emotion had poor discipline.
At the bend, Jack looked back once.
Geralt saw but did not comment.

Behind them, letters moved through wine, prayer, freight, and song. Triss and Yennefer remained at Corvo Bianco with the cellar papers, the unsent Ciri note, and the kind of alliance that did not need warmth to be loyal. Dandelion and Zoltan hunted wax, singers, and accounts in Novigrad. The roads had become too many for one horse, even Buck, which offended Buck only because no one had asked his opinion.

For the first mile, Toussaint tried to make the departure beautiful. It gave them pale road dust instead of mud, poppies along the ditch, and a little chapel whose painted saint looked too cheerful for any profession involving miracles. Jack distrusted all of it. Geralt seemed to distrust it too, which was one of the first useful comforts the morning offered.

The comfort did not last. At the vineyard boundary, a local patrol had nailed the hospitality notice to a post beside a list of orchard pests and missing goats. Someone had drawn a careful red dot over the word crimson. Someone else had written under it in a larger hand: if threat, why warn politely? The question had already gathered three different opinions in charcoal below it. That was how public fear matured: not as fact, but as handwriting.

Geralt tore the notice down and folded it without reading the rest. Jack watched the gesture, then looked at the road ahead. He could have said it was too late, that paper had already done its work, that tearing one sheet only made the next one more official. He said none of that. Geralt knew. Knowing did not stop the hand from tearing. Perhaps that was the point.
Buck sniffed the empty nail holes and sneezed. It was the most honest review the document would ever receive.
Before they crossed the first ridge out of Toussaint, Geralt stopped and looked back.

Jack let him. The road bent below them, pale between vineyards, then vanished behind cypresses and stone walls. Corvo Bianco itself was hidden by distance, but the hills still carried its shape: tended rows, morning smoke, the promise of a roof that did not ask a man to justify sleeping under it. Geralt had spent most of his life distrusting places that promised return. Now one waited behind him, which made the road ahead feel older and less obedient.
"Forgot something?" Jack asked.
"Probably."
"Important?"
"Only if Malva is judging."
Jack looked down the road. "She is."
"Yes."

Geralt turned Roach north again. For a while they rode with the ridge wind at their backs and the first rougher country ahead. The silence between them had changed from the silence of accusation to the silence of men conserving strength. It was not forgiveness. It was not trust so complete it became foolish. But it could carry weather.
At the bottom of the ridge, Buck snorted and tossed his head.
Geralt measured him from under his brows. "What now?"

Jack studied the mud beside the road. A hoofprint where no horse had passed them. Fresh. Narrow shoe. Behind it, nearly lost under gravel, the half-moon nick he had seen once before near men who watched too cleanly.
"We have company," Jack said.
Geralt's mouth tightened. "How many?"
"One close. More if he is stupid."
"Most are."
"Not this one."

The old ease vanished. Swords did not come out. Not yet. Geralt adjusted his reins. Jack shifted Buck half a step to the right. The road continued ahead, innocent as all roads looked before someone tried to own what moved on them.
"Beside," Geralt said.
Jack glanced at him.
"You said beside," Geralt repeated. "So ride beside."
Jack drew level with him.
Together, they entered the trees.

part_subtitle: The past is not buried if someone kept the key.

paragraphs: The watcher in the trees had good boots and poor discipline.

Jack noticed the boots first because mud took impressions before men took credit. Narrow iron shoes, southern make, expensive, suggesting a sponsor, and worn with calculated neglect to make the man look less rich. The half-moon nick in the right heel had followed them from Toussaint into rougher country, disappearing whenever the road hardened and returning whenever rain softened the edges. A careful man would have changed shoes. A clever man would have walked where the cart wheels chewed the ground first. This one had done neither, which meant he was either nervous, arrogant, or a clerk wearing courage badly.

Geralt noticed two miles later and said nothing for another mile because old habits respected useful silence. Roach kept to the left of the track, Buck to the right, the two horses sharing the road with the narrow dislike of professionals forced into partnership. Pines thickened around them. The air lost the lavender and warm stone of Toussaint, taking on wet bark, old leaf rot, iron in cold water, and the far winter smell that always waited in the North even when the calendar pretended otherwise.
"One man," Geralt said at last.
"One close," Jack said. "Second farther back. The first is meant to be found. The second is meant to count what happens when we find him."
Geralt looked ahead through the trees. "Could let them count rain."
"Generous."
"Retirement improved me."
Buck snorted. Roach flicked one ear with the grave contempt of a mare who had heard too many men announce self-knowledge.

They did not stop at once. Stopping taught watchers what mattered. Geralt led them through a logging track that had not been used since the thaw, then down a stony wash where water had cut the soil bare. Jack dismounted before the wash bent west. He handed Buck's reins to Geralt without explanation. Geralt took them without question, which was almost worse than trust because it proved old training had survived both distance and resentment.
The first watcher entered the wash seven minutes later.

He had a brown cloak, a short sword, a crossbow wrapped against damp, and a face that would have been forgettable had fear not made it honest. He crouched at the edge of the stony ground and stared at the missing tracks. For a moment he looked less like a spy than a man who had misplaced an argument. Jack stepped from behind a black pine and put the point of his steel sword against the man's kidney.
"Quiet," Jack said.
The man became quiet with admirable speed.
Geralt appeared on the far side of the wash with the horses. He had not drawn a sword. That frightened the watcher more. Men understood blades. They became nervous when violence remained optional.
"Name," Geralt said.
"I carry road advisories," the man said.
"Bad name," Jack said.
"Tervan," the man answered. "Tervan Milt. Contract courier. I was paid to observe direction, companions, injuries, and whether the red manifestation recurred. I was told not to engage."
"Good instruction," Geralt said.

Jack reached inside the man's coat and removed a folded slate wrapped in oiled cloth. The handwriting on it was not a field man's. It was neat, instructional, and careful with nouns that should have been left to priests and executioners. Observe whether subject relies on Geralt of Rivia for route selection. Confirm whether voluntary escort is familial, custodial, or tactical. Note any resistance to northern travel.
Geralt read it once. His face did not change enough for Tervan to notice. Jack noticed because he had been trained by that same face.
"Familial," Jack said. "Custodial. Tactical. They like tidy boxes."
"Boxes stack," Geralt said.
"So do corpses."
Tervan swallowed. "I only copy what I am given."
"That has become a popular defense," Jack said.

Geralt folded the slate back into the cloth and put it in his saddlebag. "You saw two witchers ride north. Then you lost them in weather. The road was bad. Your horse threw a shoe. You were frightened of wolves."
"There are no wolves here."
Geralt watched him without blinking.
"I was frightened of wolves," Tervan said quickly.
Jack stepped back. The courier did not run until Geralt told him to. That was good. Fear that waited for permission had an office behind it.
They let him go south. They rode north.
They did not leave the wash immediately.

Geralt crouched where Tervan's knees had pressed two dark cups into the mud and followed the prints with one finger. Jack watched him read the ground, old and unhurried, and remembered being twelve years old in a lower trail at Kaer Morhen, ordered to explain a track before hunger made his answer stupid. Vesemir had stood behind him then with a stick in one hand and patience in neither. Geralt had stood farther away pretending not to help, which was how help often entered Kaer Morhen, sideways, poorly named, and carrying a lecture if caught.
"Second watcher did not come close," Geralt said.
"He was told to let Tervan be caught."
"And?"
Jack studied the water moving over stone. "He wants to know whether you protect me from people or protect people from me."
Geralt's mouth tightened. No one needed the sentence finished.

The second watcher had crossed the ridge above them, not down the wash. Good discipline this time. Better boots too, with wrapped soles to break the print. Jack found one thread from the wrapping caught on a thornbush, black wool soaked clean of scent by rain. Geralt found the place where the man had lain on his belly and watched. Buck found a patch of grass the watcher had pissed on and made his opinion known by refusing to step near it. Roach flicked an ear, perhaps in agreement, perhaps from professional contempt.
"We follow?" Geralt asked.
"No."
"Why?"
"He expects that. He wants direction confirmed. He wants us late enough for the keep to receive whatever message went ahead."
Geralt studied the northern slope. "Then we take the old quarry road."
"That road collapsed."
"Most things called roads in Kaedwen have collapsed. This one did it with dignity."

They rode the quarry road because dignity, in Geralt's usage, meant stones that could tear a horse's shoe and turns built to break a cart axle. By noon, rain had become wet snow. The trees closed in and the world lost color: black trunks, gray rock, old white patches under roots. Jack's palm ached whenever the path passed old boundary stones. Three of the stones had wolf marks carved on them, nearly erased. One had a newer cut beside the wolf, a clean black oval scored into lichen and smeared with ash.
Geralt saw it and stopped.
"Black Ink?" Jack asked.
"A man with their habits."
"You make habits sound like knives."
"They are easier to conceal."

Geralt scraped the ash into a cloth. Under it the stone carried an older scratch, not a letter, not a rune, only two short crossing cuts. Kaer Morhen boys had used such marks to show a trail was unsafe after snowmelt. Jack knew that because Vesemir had made him memorize every private mark before he was allowed to take the lower pass alone. The black oval had not erased the old warning. It had used it. That offended him more than fresh threat would have.
"They found a Wolf sign and wrote over it," Jack said.
"No," Geralt said. "They wrote beside it. They want us to know they can read enough."
For the first time that day, the road felt less like a route and more like correspondence.
Kaer Morhen announced itself by refusing welcome.

The mountains held the keep in old stone hands, not protectively but because ruins, like guilt, were difficult to set down once lifted. Snow lingered in the high cracks though the valley below had begun to thaw. The road climbed through broken walls, pine roots, and patches of ice darkened by soot from fires long dead. Jack had ridden it as a boy with a child's hatred of cold and a survivor's gratitude for walls. Returning as a hunted man made the place seem smaller and more hostile, which was probably closer to fact.
Buck stopped at the outer gate and refused to step under the arch.
"He remembers," Geralt said.
"He was never here."
"Horses remember other horses being unhappy. It saves time."

Buck looked at Geralt as if considering whether agreement required violence. Jack dismounted and led him by the bridle. The old gate stones were split in three places. Grass grew through the cracks where boys had once bled into snow and been told they were learning balance. The wolf medallion on Jack's chest gave one slow tremor and went still. The barbed-star signet beneath his shirt remained colder than the mountain air.

The courtyard smelled of rat droppings, leather oil, old ashes, damp straw, and steel that had not been sung to in too long. A training post lay on its side near the wall. Someone had repaired the well cover with a piece of shield painted in flaking Nilfgaardian black, which meant either Lambert had been practical or angry and found no reason to choose. One shutter banged in the wind, stopped, banged again. The sound was almost speech and too unkind to be memory.
Lambert stood on the steps with a crossbow in his hands and a face arranged around irritation because grief would have looked too expensive.
"You're late," he said.
Geralt looked up at the keep. "Road was watched."

"Roads do that. Usually with eyes less expensive than yours." Lambert's gaze moved to Jack. He did not look at the scar first, or the swords, or the crimson eyes. He looked at the hands, the stance, the way Jack had positioned himself between Buck and the courtyard. Then the expression sharpened into something uglier than suspicion. "So that's him."
"Jack," Geralt said.
"I know the name. Vesemir wrote it in places he thought none of us would search because he mistook guilt for architecture." Lambert descended two steps. "He forgot who he trained."
Jack did not answer. He had learned that Lambert used words like other men used knives thrown in taverns: not always to kill, often to see who ducked.
A woman's voice came from inside the hall. "He also forgot rats. The lower archive has enough rats to constitute a voting bloc."

Keira Metz emerged behind Lambert wearing travel wool under a cloak far too elegant for Kaer Morhen and boots that had already decided they hated the mountains. Her hair was pinned in a way that suggested the pins had been threatened into service. She looked at Jack with open curiosity, then at the courtyard, then at the sky, as if judging which part of the ruin was most likely to insult her intelligence first.
"Geralt," she said. "You look exactly as cheerful as your letter."
"You came."
"Lambert shouted at the letter for ten minutes and then packed. I came to make sure he shouted at the right people. Also, your hidden witcher appears to be biologically rude."
Lambert turned. "Biologically what?"

"Rude. To categories." Keira stepped down into the courtyard. Her eyes moved over Jack's face, paused at the bandaged palm, then flicked to the chain beneath his collar. "Mutation profile, eye color, recovery, resonance reports, and whatever that is under his shirt do not fit any tolerable table. I dislike intolerable tables. They imply someone else was interesting before I arrived."
"A tragedy," Jack said.
Her mouth curved. "He speaks."
"Under duress."
"Most useful things do."
Lambert made a disgusted sound. "If you two plan to flirt, do it away from the door. Some of us are trying to be angry at the dead."
"You've had years of practice," Geralt said.
"And still the dead keep earning it."
The sentence struck the courtyard and stayed. Geralt turned to Lambert. Lambert looked back with the hatred of a man who had found a moral wound and refused to dress it prettily.

Another horse entered through the gate before either could speak again. It was a big chestnut with a white blaze and the resigned posture of an animal attached to a sensible man. Eskel rode under the arch without hurry, cloak wet at the hem, sword hilts plain in the mountain light. His scar pulled one side of his face into severity, but his eyes softened when they found Geralt. Then they moved to Jack and held there with steadier sadness than Lambert's anger allowed.
"Road was watched," Eskel said.
"Yes," Geralt answered.
"Bad watcher. Worse second watcher. I sent the second south with a broken stirrup and improved manners."
"You broke his stirrup?" Lambert asked.
"Only after he tried to draw."
"Soft."
"The horse was innocent."
Buck lowered his head slightly toward Eskel. It was not approval. It was a treaty opening.

The old courtyard breathed around them: four witchers, one sorceress, two horses, a keep full of missing boys, and the winter-long shadow of a dead old man who had hidden answers where love and fear had worn the same gloves.
Geralt surveyed the hall. "Inside."
"No," Lambert said. "Here first. Where the dead can hear."

Keira's amusement vanished. Eskel set his reins over the chestnut's neck and came down from the saddle. Jack did not move. Geralt did, one step forward, which was not threat and too much to be nothing.
"Say it," Geralt said.
Lambert lifted one hand toward Jack. "How many?"
"What?"

"How many boys did Vesemir hide in cracks because he decided the rest of us were too damaged, too loud, too angry, too inconvenient to know? How many names are under stones in that keep? How many files burned because someone said protection and meant control?"
Jack studied the training posts. Snowmelt had gathered around the fallen one and made a dark ring in the dirt.
"One that I know of," Geralt said.
"Comforting."
"No," Geralt said. "It isn't."
Lambert's anger had expected defense. The absence of it left him with nowhere clean to put his teeth. He turned on Jack instead because Jack was standing and Vesemir was not.
"And you? Did you know?"
"No."
"Nothing?"
"Only that I was trained. Hidden. Sent out at nineteen. Told too little."
"That makes two of us, then," Lambert said.
Jack met his eyes. "You were not hidden."

"No. I was sold. Then trained. Then told the Path was freedom by men who locked gates behind children and called it survival. Don't split hairs with me in the yard where boys learned to stop screaming."

For a moment the keep became exactly that yard again: not legend, not stronghold, not beloved ruin, but a place that had survived by hurting children into tools sharp and trained to outlive it. Geralt's face closed. Eskel looked down. Keira, for once, said nothing.
Jack took the anger because it had weight and a right to exist. "I'm not the ledger you're angry at."
Lambert's mouth twisted. "No. You're the page they kept."
The words landed. Jack did not flinch. Geralt did.

Eskel moved then, not between them, but beside the argument. His talent had always been that. "We search first. Fight after. If the keep gives us enough truth, there may be room for more accurate anger."
"Your optimism is moldy," Lambert said.
"It has survived you. That proves quality."

Keira clapped her gloved hands once. "Excellent. We have established that the ruin is morally compromised, the dead are guilty, the living are defensive, and the horse dislikes the arch. Can we now enter the building before my fingers freeze into academically useless hooks?"
Buck snorted again.
"See," Keira said. "The horse agrees with good methodology."
The lower archive had survived fire by being inconvenient.

Kaer Morhen's upper halls had known violence openly: cracked stone, scorched beams, broken beds, training scars along walls, and the old laboratory stains no amount of scrubbing had ever persuaded to become history. The archive beneath the west tower was different. It had been reached by a stair too narrow for armor, hidden behind a shelf of cracked jars, and protected less by locks than by the assumption that no sane person wished to spend hours bent double under leaking stone among rats and ledgers written by men who considered boys experimental inconvenience with names.

Geralt led with a lantern. Lambert carried a crowbar. Eskel carried chalk, because Eskel believed in marking exits and proving old corridors wrong with quiet competence. Keira carried three candles that burned blue at the wick and silver near the base. Jack carried nothing visible. The mark in his palm pulsed under its bandage with each step, slowly, as if something below counted him.
"If this collapses," Lambert said, "I want my bones labeled correctly."
"By who?" Geralt asked.
"Anyone not Vesemir. He'd put me under miscellaneous behavioral difficulty."
Keira leaned to avoid a hanging root. "A generous category."
"Careful, witch. I can still leave you to the rats."
"Lambert, dear, the rats have been more welcoming."
Their voices made the corridor less holy. Jack preferred that. Ruins that became holy usually did so by making their crimes decorative.

The archive door was oak bound with black iron. The lock had been cut out long ago and replaced with a wedge, three nails, and a strip of leather stamped with a wolf's head. Eskel touched the leather first.
"Vesemir," he said.
Geralt nodded. "He used old bridle straps for things he wanted us not to throw away."
"Emotional misdirection through tack," Keira said. "Crude, but effective on men who prefer horses to conversations."
Jack faced Geralt.
"She's not wrong," Geralt said.

Lambert pried the wedge loose. The door opened with a smell of dust, damp paper, rat nest, old ink, and the bitter ghost of alchemical preservatives. Keira's candles bent inward. Jack's palm heated sharply, then cooled as if whatever had recognized him decided to hide again.

Inside, shelves leaned under account books, winter stores ledgers, apprenticeship rosters, formula scraps, monster diagrams, toll records, false tax notes, old letters, and a surprising number of empty bottles hidden behind medical inventories. Lambert found those within thirty seconds.
"Aha," he said. "Secret archive. Historic truth. Evidence of conspiracy. And Vesemir's peach brandy."
"That's not peach," Eskel said.
Lambert uncorked one, sniffed, and closed it again with reverence. "No. That's regret with fruit nearby."
The joke worked for half a breath. Then Geralt found the first missing shelf.

Dust told the story. A rectangle paler than the surrounding wood, three finger widths high, twelve long, behind a row of old contract copies. A small packet had sat there for years and had been moved recently or moved long ago and never dusted over properly because the air inside the archive was stingy. Geralt touched the mark and said nothing.
Jack watched his hand. The fingers had gone still.
"There was something here," Eskel said.
"Yes."
"Taken?"
"Or hidden better." Geralt looked toward the west wall. "Vesemir did both when he couldn't decide which truth deserved more shame."
They searched for two hours.

Keira grew more interested when ordinary papers began misbehaving. A training roster from 1256 curled away from Jack's hand. A formula correction written in Vesemir's cramped script warmed when placed near the barbed-star signet. Three pages of weather notes stuck together around a water stain that had dried into a five-pointed shape. Lambert muttered that even the mildew had become pretentious. Keira told him mildew had better survival strategy than most kings and should not be insulted without data.
Then Eskel found the false stone.

It was low in the wall, behind a broken crate of rusted stirrups. Too poorly hidden for treasure. Too careful for rubbish. Eskel tapped around it with the handle of his knife, listened to the hollow reply, and looked at Geralt.
"You knew?"
Geralt stared at the stone. "No."
Lambert laughed without humor. "Good. Hate to think the rest of us were the only fools in the room."
Jack crouched and touched the stone with his unbandaged hand. Cold. Ordinary. He put the bandaged palm against it.
The stone drank heat from him.
Not much. The signet answered anyway. The red lines under the cloth tightened like strings being tuned. Jack pulled back and found the bandage faintly smoking.
"Do that again," Keira said.
"Ask better," Geralt and Jack said together.

Keira's eyes brightened. "Oh, that is unpleasantly charming. May I request that you do that again under controlled conditions, assuming controlled conditions can be manufactured in a hole under a murder school?"
Jack studied the stone. "No."
"A pity. I admire boundaries when they inconvenience my curiosity."
Lambert wedged the crowbar into the seam and levered. The stone shifted with a soft crack. Behind it lay a narrow cavity wrapped in oilcloth. Geralt reached in, hesitated, then let Jack take it.
The packet was heavier than paper should have been.

Jack unwrapped it on the nearest crate. Inside were three folded sheets, a brass key green with age, a child's leather wrist strap, and a thin black disk marked with a barbed star so worn the points looked more like wounds than ornament. The wrist strap had been cut, not broken. Jack knew it before touching. Boys cut straps when they outgrew them. Men cut straps when they could not bear to unbuckle what they had done.
Geralt picked up the strap.
No one spoke.

Keira, gentler than she looked comfortable being, lifted the first sheet with two fingers. "This is not northern notation. The geometry is eastern. Zerrikanian or something trying to be mistaken for it by people who do not know the desert from a spice cupboard."
"Read it," Lambert said.

"I can read the mathematics. Not the prayer, if it is prayer." She turned the page toward the candle. Lines crossed in a lattice of five outer points and a dark center. Several words had been translated in Vesemir's hand around the margins: anchor, blood, soft ground, carrier, morning star, not crown. Beneath one phrase he had written three question marks and then scratched them out so hard he tore the paper.
Geralt measured Jack's face. Jack studied the diagram.
The barbed-star signet under his shirt began to warm.
"We stop for today," Geralt said.
"No," Jack said.
Lambert looked between them. "We're already pretending this is a family discussion? Fast work."
Jack lifted the black disk. The room's candles leaned toward it, then toward his chest, then away from both as if reconsidering their loyalties.
"This belonged to me?"
Geralt's throat moved. "Maybe."
"Wrong answer."
"True one."

Jack closed his fingers around the disk. The mark in his palm answered through the cloth, not with pain exactly, but with pressure. Somewhere above them, Buck struck a stall door hard; the echo moved down through stone.
Keira's face had gone still with professional hunger and personal alarm. "Whatever that is, it recognizes the signet. And your wound. And perhaps your name."
"Names are doors," Jack said.
"Some are locks," Keira replied.
Geralt took the second sheet and read Vesemir's marginal note aloud because delaying it would only make the room crueler.
"Found in eastern ruin. Child alive. Signet not removable by force. Do not expose to mage inquiry. Do not expose to court inquiry. Do not expose to Ciri."
Lambert stopped moving.
The last sentence lay between them like a bone no one wanted to identify.
Jack's expression did not change. His control was beginning to look less like strength than architecture under siege.
"Archive search," he said. "Relational conflict. Efficient."
Keira turned to Geralt. "He becomes very tidy when wounded."
"Yes," Geralt said.
"You taught him that?"
"No."
Jack folded the page with care and put it back on the crate. "Someone did."
Keira insisted on the diagnostic in the old infirmary because the room already knew too many bad ideas to be offended by one more.

The infirmary had not been used properly in years, but proper use had never been its moral strength. Its shelves held bottles with labels eaten by damp, clamps wrapped in cloth, old scalpels rubbed bright at the grips, cracked basins, and a chair with straps cut through rather than unbuckled. Jack chose the chair first. Keira noticed. So did Geralt. Lambert noticed last because he had entered the room already angry at it and had to sort the new anger from the old.
"No straps," Jack said.
"I was not going to suggest straps," Keira said.
"You saw them."
"I look at many things I do not intend to use. Lambert, for example."
Lambert leaned against the door frame. "You use me constantly."
"Mostly as a warning to civilization."
Eskel set two lanterns on the sill and opened the narrow window. Cold mountain air entered with a smell of snow and pine sap. "Fresh air," he said.
"Superstition," Keira replied.
"Useful one."

Jack sat on the edge of the table, not the chair. Keira accepted the choice without comment, which made the acceptance more noticeable. She laid out objects between them: the black disk, Vesemir's diagram, a silver needle, a bowl of water, three strips of linen, and a small mirror covered in cloth. Geralt disliked the mirror at once. Mirrors in rooms with sorceresses, old secrets, and bloodlines rarely behaved as furniture.
"Rules," Jack said.
Keira's brows lifted. "You are wonderfully presumptuous for a patient."
"Subject, if the wrong office writes it."

That made her expression sharpen. "Fine. Rules. No restraint. No trance. No spell entering your mind. No blood taken without you watching the instrument and agreeing. If anything answers through the signet rather than through your body, I stop. If it answers through both, everyone runs except Geralt, who will attempt heroism, and Lambert, who will insult death until it loses interest."
"I never agreed to be useful," Lambert said.
"No one ever does. It happens to the unlucky."

Jack held out his left hand. Keira unwrapped the bandage herself, slow enough that the room could see the pause before every touch. The red lines had thinned since Novigrad's first reports but not faded. They lay under the skin like heated wire buried in wax. Keira did not make a soft sound or offer a healer's comfort. She leaned closer, and her curiosity warmed the air almost as much as the wound did.
"Beautiful," she said.
Geralt's jaw moved. Lambert muttered something obscene. Jack watched her until she glanced up.
"Beautiful things can still cut," Keira said. "I did not say harmless."
"People often do. Then reach."

"I am reaching because you have allowed the test. If you withdraw permission, I stop and remain intellectually deprived." Her mouth curved. "Do not mistake deprivation for death. I survive disappointment several times before lunch."
She touched the outer edge of the mark with the silver needle.
The water in the bowl rose in a thin trembling dome.
No one moved.

Jack's breath caught, then steadied. The signet under his shirt turned so hot it showed its shape through the fabric. Keira's pupils widened. For one sharp heartbeat the old infirmary seemed to lean inward, shelves, straps, bottles, rusted instruments, all listening to a word just beyond hearing.
"Stop," Geralt said.
"Not yet," Jack answered.

Keira turned to him, and the charge in the room changed. It was not desire alone, though desire had come in on quiet feet and stood there smiling at the wrong time. It was recognition of danger shared knowingly. Her fingers remained close to his palm, not touching now, and the heat between skin and silver made her breath slow.
"You can feel where it wants to go," she said.
"Down."
"Into what?"
"Stone. Names. The center of things that pretend they are walls."
"That is medically offensive and magically inconvenient."
"Write that down."
"I intend to embroider it."
Keira's diagnostic did not end when the water cracked.

It should have. The rules had been made, the reaction observed, the room warned. Sensible people stopped after a bowl of water rose, froze, and split itself open on a table in a keep with a history of turning curiosity into graves. Kaer Morhen had never been a place where sensible people governed for long.
Keira asked for one more reading.

She did not touch him at first. That mattered enough for Jack to notice and for Geralt to stop halfway through forming an objection. Keira warmed her hands over a candle, not because they were cold, but because cold fingers made lies of reflex. Then she looked at Jack, not the mark, not the signet, not the instruments.
"Your choice," she said. "No witty phrasing. No pretty science. I need proximity to the pulse at your wrist and the signet's line of pull. If you refuse, I will be cross, educational, and alive."
"And if I agree?"
"Then I will be cross, educational, and possibly wrong in a more useful way."
Lambert made a sound from the door. "She calls that charm."
"And yet," Keira said without looking at him, "you remain fascinated."
Jack held out his hand.

The room changed before her fingers settled. Not magic first. Breath. Keira's, carefully slowed. Geralt's, stopped and then resumed through his nose. Lambert's, sharpened into annoyance because fear embarrassed him. Eskel's, quiet, almost lost under the old window draft. Jack's own breath became the loudest thing in his body because the heat under his skin did not behave like pain anymore. Pain argued. This waited.

Keira placed two fingers at his wrist, light as a physician and steadier than desire had any right to be. Her thumb hovered above the red lines in his palm without touching them. The nearness drew heat between them. The candle flame bent, then bowed lower, thin and blue at the edge. Jack felt the signet at his throat pull inward, as if the chain had shortened by a breath.

Keira's eyes darkened. Not with fear only. Curiosity, yes. Attraction too, perilous because she understood danger and did not mistake it for permission. A small sound left her, not a moan, not pain, only surprise before pride could dress it.
"Ah. There you are."
Lambert's head snapped up. "Keira."

"Do not bark. I am using both hands and all my judgment, which is more than most institutions can claim." Her gaze never left Jack. "It is not moving out of him. It is moving through the idea of him. Name, blood, old stone, witness. Four pressures. Maybe five."
"What is the fifth?" Eskel asked.
Keira's fingers tightened once around Jack's wrist. It was almost nothing. His pulse answered like a struck string.
"Need," she said.
That word made the infirmary colder.

Jack drew back before the room could decide what need meant. Keira released him at once. No clutching, no objection, no last little theft of data disguised as concern. The release steadied him more than the touch had. She wrapped the wrist again herself, slower than before, and for once her mouth held no joke.
"You can be drawn by need," she said. "Not only by blood. That means every staged rescue is also a leash if they understand enough."
Geralt looked toward the door as if he already saw the next trap standing somewhere in a city square, smiling with paperwork.
"Then we make sure they understand less," Lambert said.
Keira studied him. "No. We make sure we understand faster. Ignorance is not protection. It is only a room without windows where men congratulate themselves on not seeing the fire."
Jack flexed his bandaged hand. Heat remained where her fingers had been. Not ownership. Evidence.
"Write that down," he said.
Keira's smile returned, faint and tired. "I intend to embroider it on Lambert's pillow."
"Burn the pillow," Lambert said.
"Sentimental already."

The bowl cracked. Water spilled across the table and froze before it reached the edge. Keira withdrew at once. Jack closed his fist. Geralt took one step nearer and stopped because stopping mattered. Lambert's eyes had lost all humor. Eskel covered the mirror with one large hand as if the cloth alone might not be enough.

Keira wrapped Jack's hand again. Her touch, when it returned, was professional and slower than before. "You are not a source," she said, quietly enough that it nearly escaped the room. "You are a hinge. Something pushes from both sides."
"Hinges are owned by doors," Jack said.
"Only until someone removes the door."
Lambert turned to her. "Is that optimism?"
"No," Keira said. "It is vandalism with a theory."
For the first time since the courtyard, Jack smiled properly, and Geralt saw the boy inside the man. It was gone quickly. That did not make it less real.
Geralt had always hated how neatly Vesemir wrote when afraid.

The old man's ordinary hand had been cramped, economical, and impatient with decorative tails. He had written shopping lists like tactical orders and alchemical corrections like personal insults. But fear made him careful. Fear straightened his lines, rounded his letters, slowed the pen. The pages on the crate were careful in a way that hurt.

He did not read them all at once. Reading was not the same as understanding, and understanding had a habit of arriving after a man had already used the wrong tone. Geralt took the three sheets to the old refectory because the archive air had become too small and because the refectory, at least, had held arguments before. Lambert built a fire with too much force. Eskel cleared the table. Keira set wards at the doors and complained about drafts in a voice that meant she was listening to the walls.
Jack stood near the window where the winter light fell thinly across his face and made his crimson eyes look less like flame than old blood under ice.
The wrist strap lay beside the papers.
No one touched it now.
"Start with the clean page," Eskel said.
"There is no clean page," Lambert said.
"The least dirty, then."

Keira sat at the end of the table and spread the first sheet with the flat of her hand. "This is not a full record. It is a field reconstruction. Vesemir was comparing something he saw to something someone told him, then adding guesses he disliked. See the changes in ink?"

Geralt saw them. Brown-black for the original note. Iron-gray for later additions. A third ink, nearly faded, written in smaller letters between lines: found after Jack's first Trial fever, not before. He remembered that fever. Everyone remembered the fevers they survived and the ones other boys did not.
Jack said, "Read it."
Geralt did.
Geralt remembered more when the page made him.

Memory did not come whole. It came as weather, then smell, then the shape of Vesemir's hand closing around the child's necklace and failing, for once, to look old enough for what he had found. Wet snow had fallen through the broken roof of the ruin and vanished on stones still warm from fire. The tower had leaned like a drunk listening at a door. Roach had refused the courtyard. Geralt had thought of drowners, ghouls, deserters, bandits. He had thought of everything that fit the road before the world had the discourtesy to become stranger.

The cellar was half filled with rubble. Vesemir had gone first despite the bad knee he refused to name. Geralt had followed with silver drawn and steel ready. Beneath the fallen beam was a strip of red cloth, a small hand closed around nothing, and a boy whose white hair was dark with soot. The child had not cried when Vesemir lifted the beam with a grunt that sounded like prayer in a man who hated needing gods. He had only opened his eyes.
Crimson.

Not fever-red. Not potion-red. Geralt had seen monsters with kinder eyes and kings with less hunger in theirs. The boy watched him as if the world had already proven insufficient and he was waiting to see whether Geralt would join it.
"Alive," Geralt had said, because simple facts were the only ones his mouth could carry.
"Yes," Vesemir had answered.

The old witcher touched the necklace then. The barbed star burned through his glove. Vesemir did not curse. That was how Geralt knew it frightened him. He only wrapped the chain in leather, cut nothing, pulled nothing, and looked at the dead around them with the practical horror of a man counting how many explanations had failed.

There had been a woman near the stairs. Not old. Too young to have deserved what was done. A blade in her hand, black hair burned short on one side, fingers broken around the hilt. Vesemir covered her face with a cloak before Geralt could ask why. A man in Nilfgaardian underleather lay two paces from her, no insignia, no banner, a wound through the ribs and another through the throat. His body had been placed between the cellar mouth and the child's hiding place.
Geralt knew now that they had been Helena and Jacob. Back then they had been dead people with no names and too much courage.
"We take him," Vesemir had said.
"To Kaer Morhen?"
"Where else? A temple? A court? A mage?"
Geralt had looked at the child's eyes and hated that the question answered itself.
"Ciri," he had said, though she was not there, though that name already turned every decision into a blade.
Vesemir's face had closed. "No. Not her. Not with this."
"You do not know what this is."
"That is why not her."

The memory ended there because the page in front of Geralt ended there, and because the rest had been years of repeating the same decision until it looked less like a decision and more like architecture. A hidden lower trail. A boy trained off record. A false fever when Ciri came. A door closed before two children could ask why it was never opened at the same time.

Geralt looked at Jack in the refectory and saw not the silent child under stone, not the young witcher with a burned palm, but the line between them, taut as wire and dark with all the things adults had called protection because the alternative word would have named them.

Field note. Winter cache designation: J.M. Do not place with general School records. Signet recovered on subject at ruin site east of old Temerian military road, map unreliable. Child alive despite crush injuries, smoke inhalation, blood loss, and cold exposure. Necklace resists removal. Cutting chain caused fever spike. Do not repeat.
The room listened in the way old rooms did when people finally spoke what they had been holding in their floors.
Geralt remembered smoke.

Not the theatrical smoke of burning castles in ballads, all orange light and heroic silhouettes. This had been winter smoke, low and black, pressed down by wet snow. He and Vesemir had found the ruin because two wolves had refused the road near it and because Roach, younger then and less patient with human mistakes, had kept turning her head toward the trees. The castle had not been a castle anymore. A tower, half a wall, a cellar mouth, stones split by old fire and newer violence. Bodies under snow. Too few bodies for a garrison. Too many for bandits.
The child had been in the cellar under a fallen beam, not crying.

That was what Geralt remembered most. Not the blood in the snow. Not the necklace at the small throat. Not Vesemir's face when he saw the barbed star. The silence. Children in pain made noise until the world taught them noise did not help. This child had already learned too much or had gone somewhere inside himself where noise could not follow.
"You found me there," Jack said.
It was not a question. Questions asked for kindness. Jack had no use for kindness until it proved whether it could survive accuracy.
"Yes," Geralt said.
"How old?"
"Three. Maybe four. Hard to tell. You were small for either."
Lambert leaned against the hearth. "Vesemir told us you found a ruined nest. Monster killed. No child."
"He told you later," Geralt said. "After we brought Jack through the lower trail."
"Through the chute?" Eskel asked.
Geralt nodded.
Lambert laughed once. "Of course. Smuggled a child into a witcher keep through the goat chute. Dignified."
"It wasn't used for goats."
"It should have been. Would explain the smell."
The joke reached no one who needed healing. Lambert let it die and looked at the wrist strap again.
Keira turned the second page. "This one has diagrams. Poor diagrams. Do not take offense, Geralt. Your father figure lacked architectural grace."
"He wasn't my father."
"No," Keira said. "Of course not. That would be far too simple for this room."
Geralt turned to her. She looked back without apology. Keira, for all her vanity, had a gift for cutting soft lies before they grew sentimental. It made her useful and difficult to thank.

The second sheet showed a star with five barbed points connected by cramped lattice lines. Along one edge Vesemir had copied words phonetically: Zerrikant, Zerrikanter, Morning Star House, Black Crown, holding blood, east survivor unknown. Several translations had been crossed out. Beneath the black center he had written not power. Then, later, not only power. Later still: key? wound? bait?
Jack read over Geralt's shoulder. He smelled of cold leather, damp wool, and that faint mineral heat that had entered his body since the Broken Crown.
"He didn't know," Jack said.
"No."
"He knew what mattered."
Geralt studied the page. "Yes."
Lambert pushed away from the hearth. "That is becoming your favorite word."
"Because it fits too many things."
"Try a fuller answer. The boy has earned more than syllables."
Jack's eyes moved to Lambert. Something passed there, not friendship, not even agreement, but recognition that anger could occasionally stand in useful places.

Geralt sat because standing had begun to feel like avoidance. The bench creaked under him. Once, years ago, a boy had carved a crude wolf into its edge. Another had altered it into a pig. Someone had then added Lambert beneath it in a hand too neat to be Lambert's. He noticed it now because grief made cowards of attention; it ran to smaller things.

"Vesemir knew the signet was hunted," Geralt said. "He knew men had come before us. The dead at the ruin were not all one side. Some had eastern blades. Some had Nilfgaardian gear stripped of marks. One wore a priest's cord. One had mage-silver dust under his nails. None carried papers. That frightened Vesemir more than papers would have."
"Because no papers meant someone important had already learned cleanliness," Keira said.

"Yes. Two months later a man came asking about a barbed-star relic. Vesemir lied. I followed him. Found two more outside the valley. One had a list of names. Mine. Vesemir's. Ciri's. Not Jack's. Not yet."
Jack's hand tightened once around the back of a chair.
"So you hid me from her," he said.
Geralt could have said yes again. Lambert's eyes dared him to try. He did not.

"Ciri was already a fire every moth in the world wanted," Geralt said. "Elder Blood. Cintra. Emhyr. Mages. Elves. Prophecy. Men with songs. Men with knives. Vesemir thought putting you near her would make two trails cross and teach every hunter to follow both. I agreed because I was tired of children being chased by destiny dressed as necessity."
"You decided for her."
"Yes."
"For me."
"Yes."
"And called it protection."
Geralt held his gaze. "Sometimes protection is deciding for someone before they can consent. That is why it rots if you keep doing it after they can speak. We kept doing it too long."
The fire shifted. A small log broke inward and threw sparks. Lambert opened his mouth, then closed it. That was rare; Eskel glanced at him.

Jack did not forgive him. Geralt could see that in the straightness of his shoulders, in the careful absence of heat from his voice, in the way he looked at the paper rather than the man who had helped make it true. He also did not condemn him. That was worse in a more generous way. Condemnation ended a conversation. Jack left the conversation alive and bleeding.
Lambert did not stay for the whole reading.

He left after the Trial page, which was Lambert's way of not throwing the table at the wall. The door slammed hard, waking dust from the lintel. Keira closed her eyes for the duration of one breath and did not follow him immediately. That restraint scraped at her. Jack saw it. Geralt saw Jack seeing it. Eskel, who had made a profession of noticing pain without staring at it, gathered the pages before the draft took them.
"He will come back," Eskel said.
"He always does when leaving would make the anger look frightened," Keira replied.
Outside, steel rang in the yard.

Not practice. Punishment. Lambert striking the post with a blunted sword, the sound too hard and too regular to be training. Jack listened through the wall. One strike. Then another. Then a third that split old wood and made a horse stamp in the stable. The keep did not echo it kindly. Kaer Morhen had heard too many boys learn anger by hitting things that did not answer.
Jack rose.
Geralt watched him without blinking. "You don't have to."
"I know."
That was why he went.

Lambert stood in the yard with his coat open to the cold and his breath coming white. The post had taken four cuts. The fifth would break it. Jack stopped ten paces away, outside sword reach and inside insult range.
"Come to defend the dead?" Lambert asked.
"No."
"Good. The dead have too many advocates."
"I came because you called me a page."
Lambert's grip tightened. "And?"
"Pages can be read wrong."
That checked him more than a challenge would have. Lambert lowered the sword a fraction, irritation fighting the unwilling respect men sometimes had for sentences that did not waste themselves.

Jack studied the broken post. "I do not remember the ruin. I remember rooms I was not allowed to enter. I remember footsteps stopping when I came near. I remember Vesemir saying some roads were not mine and Geralt looking away because he knew the road's name. I thought that was discipline. Now everyone wants the hurt to be more useful if it has a better explanation."
Lambert said nothing. Snow moved in small hard grains across the yard.

"You are angry because boys were turned into tools," Jack said. "So am I. You are angry because care and cruelty wore the same coat here. So am I. You are angry because Vesemir decided who could know, who could grieve, who could help, and called it survival. So am I."
"You say it very calmly."
"Calm is where I put things until I can kill something that deserves it."
Lambert stared at him, then barked one laugh. It was not kind, but kindness would have been a worse lie.
"Careful," he said. "Talk like that and I'll have to stop hating you on principle."
"Use a different principle."
"I've several. Most poorly maintained."

Keira appeared in the doorway behind them, wrapped in her cloak, watching Lambert as if she could see where fury bruised him under the skin. She did not call his name. Good. Men like Lambert sometimes needed to return from themselves without being dragged by tenderness in front of witnesses.
Lambert tossed the practice sword point-first into the snow. "Tell Geralt I am still angry."
"He knows."
"Tell him anyway. It improves the acoustics."
Jack turned to leave. Lambert's voice stopped him once more.
"And Morningstar?"
Jack looked back.
"If they try to make you grateful for the cage," Lambert said, "bite the hand explaining the lock."
It was not comfort. It was not brotherhood. It was a useful curse.
Jack nodded once and went back inside.
Keira saved them with ruthlessness. "The third page is newer. I suspect Vesemir returned to it after the Trials."
Geralt picked it up.

Trial response irregular. Mutagens bind too fast, then resist. Body rejects expected sterility markers. Fever presents with crimson ocular flare. Skin temperature rises near signet. Subject hears stone under laboratory floor during seizure. No stone below that floor. Lambert not to be told. Eskel not to be told. Geralt knows too much and too little. This is not a boy the School can explain.
Lambert stared at the page.
"Lambert not to be told," he said softly. "Kind of him. Saved me the inconvenience of caring."
"He thought you'd be angry," Geralt said.
Lambert's face went bright with contempt. "I am angry. Look how well prophecy works when written by old bastards."
Eskel took the page from Geralt, read the line again, and placed it down with a care that made the movement feel like burial. "He was afraid."
"He was always afraid," Lambert said. "He just called it prudence because prudence got cleaner boots."
"Fear kept some of us alive."

"Fear also built that table." Lambert pointed toward the old laboratory wing beyond the door. "Fear mixed mutagens and called dying boys necessary losses. Fear took children and taught them to be grateful for surviving what was done to them. I am tired of fear receiving medals for outliving its victims."
No one answered quickly. Some rooms deserved the decency of not having their truth handled at once.
Jack looked at Lambert as if seeing him more clearly than before. "You hated this place."
"Hate," Lambert said. "Present tense. I also come when Geralt writes, because apparently I collect contradictions."
"Useful habit."
"Don't start liking me. I charge."
"In what?"
"Complaints. Interest is ruinous."
Eskel rubbed a hand over his scarred cheek. "The diagrams point beyond Kaer Morhen. See the lower mark."

The lower corner of the second sheet carried a partial stamp. Not Vesemir's. Not witcher. A black oval, faint as if copied from another page. Around it was written Novigrad confiscations, post-purge lot, healer ledgers? Beneath that, in Geralt's hand from years ago, there was a line he did not remember writing: Ask D. about auction records.
"Dandelion," Jack said.
"Or another D," Lambert said. "The world contains several idiots."
"This idiot has auction friends," Geralt said.
Keira tapped the stamp. "Black Ink, perhaps?"
"Before Triss named them?"

"People rarely wait for nicknames to exist. The black oval could be a precursor, a sealed office, or a collector's mark. Novigrad confiscated half the magical world during the hunts. Mage ledgers, relic catalogs, patient books, charlatan scrap, cursed heirlooms, anything that could be sold or sanctified. If Vesemir saw a matching stamp, someone in Novigrad had a piece of the Morningstar trail."
"And Black Ink found it," Jack said.
"Or bought it. Or became it. Institutions have childhoods too, unfortunately."
Geralt stood. Decision arrived because standing still had become another lie. "We go to Novigrad."
Lambert frowned. "We?"
"Jack and I. You, Eskel, Keira, finish here. Copy everything. Look for missing dust, loose stones, old tax marks, anything Vesemir hid because he thought his shame was private property."
"Orders," Lambert said.
"Request."
"Sounds better after washing its hands."
Geralt almost smiled despite himself. "Learned from a clerk."

Jack folded the wrist strap in oilcloth and put it in his inner pouch. Geralt watched the movement and felt the old guilt shift shape. Not lessen. Never that. It changed from a stone into a tool he had not asked to carry but could no longer set down.

Before leaving the refectory, Jack stopped near the wall where swords had once hung for boys to take down with hands too small for the hilts. Only four pegs remained. One had a notch carved beneath it: J.M., tiny, almost hidden, the sort of mark a boy made when he wanted proof he had occupied space without inviting someone to ask why.
Geralt had never seen it.
Jack touched the notch once with two fingers and then moved away.
That was the answer he gave Kaer Morhen.
They stayed one more night because the mountain refused haste by making the lower road ice over after sunset.

Geralt found Jack in the old training yard near midnight. No moon. Thin stars. Snow crust shining faintly along the wall. Jack stood before the fallen post with his hands bare despite the cold. The red lines in his left palm glowed under the skin, not brightly, but with the dull persistence of coals buried in ash. He had placed Vesemir's black disk on the post. It did not move. That was almost disappointing.
"Keira said not to test alone," Geralt said.
"She said not to test without her. Different sentence."
"Meaning?"
"She dislikes missing interesting mistakes."

Geralt came to stand beside him. The yard looked smaller at night. No boys running. No Vesemir correcting footwork. No Ciri exploding with temper because Geralt had told her to repeat the same movement until her wrists hated him. The empty yard made memory feel too loud.
"Ciri trained there," Jack said.
Geralt looked at the patch of hard ground near the east wall. "Yes."
"I was kept from the yard on days she was here?"
"Mostly. Sometimes you were sent to the lower trail. Sometimes to Eskel's old traps. Sometimes Vesemir said you had fever."
"Did I?"
"Often, until the lie became useful."
Jack nodded once. "Efficient."
Geralt hated that word now.
"She deserved the facts," he said.
"So did I."
"Yes."
Jack picked up the black disk. It warmed his fingers, then cooled. "Vesemir taught me that a locked door was an argument waiting for evidence."
"Sounds like him."
"He was the lock."
Geralt said nothing because some answers would only defend the dead from a man they had wounded.
After a while, Jack put the disk away. "Lambert is right."
"Often by accident."
"Not about this."
"No."

The cold made their breath visible. Geralt could smell snow, old stone, and faint smoke from the refectory fire. Somewhere inside, Lambert cursed at a rat. Keira answered with a threat involving transformation and civic improvement. Eskel laughed once, quiet and brief.
Jack listened. "You have family here."
"What's left of it."
"It sounds like an argument."
"Usually."
"Maybe that is why it works."
Geralt turned to him, but Jack was watching the empty yard.
"Ciri survived because people helped her," Geralt said. "She almost died because people thought helping meant deciding for her. I was both kinds of people. Remember that when I sound certain."
Jack's face remained unreadable for a long moment. Then he said, "You sound certain often."
"Old habit."
"Expensive one."
"I know."
This time the words were not enough, but they did not pretend to be. They stood together until the cold entered their boots and the keep behind them became less a wound than a witness.

In the morning, Eskel gave Jack a repaired strap for Buck's saddle. Lambert gave him a knife and said it was only because the one Jack carried offended several traditions. Keira gave him a vial wrapped in silk and told him not to drink it unless his blood started singing in a language he did not know, or unless he was bored with ordinary mortality.
"What does it do?" Jack asked.
"Perhaps nothing. Perhaps prevents your heart from trying to negotiate with architecture. We will learn if you survive."
"Comforting."
"I am rarely employed for comfort."
Lambert turned to Geralt. "Bring him back."
The sentence came out wrong for Lambert, too naked and therefore instantly punished by his own mouth. "Or don't. But if he dies before I decide whether I hate him, I'll be irritated."
Jack mounted Buck. "I'll consider your schedule."
"Do that. I am very busy being charming."
Keira turned to Eskel. "Is he?"
"No," Eskel said.

Geralt swung into Roach's saddle. The keep rose behind them, cold and scarred, no cleaner for what they had found inside it. Yet as they rode under the gate, Jack looked back once. Not long. One look could carry the whole keep.
Kaer Morhen had not given him home.
It had given him evidence.
After the others slept, Geralt returned to the archive alone and found Eskel already there.

This surprised him less than it should have. Eskel had always preferred arriving before a man could pretend he did not need company. He sat on an overturned crate with a lantern beside his boot and Vesemir's old bridle strap in his hands. The leather was cracked but still strong. Vesemir had kept useless things if uselessness had once worked hard. That was one of the old man's more tolerable hypocrisies.
"Lambert asleep?" Geralt asked.
"Angrily."
"Keira?"
"Writing. Also angrily, but with better posture."

Geralt sat beside him. The archive smelled colder now, as if opened secrets had let winter in through the shelves. He picked up an old ledger at random and saw a list of boys by year, not names at first, only weights, fevers, reactions, survival markers. Later, someone had added names in the margins. Perhaps Vesemir. Perhaps another man who had decided too late that numbers could not bury children deeply enough.
"We made a lot of ghosts," Eskel said.
"We inherited most of them."
"Inheritance still has to be carried."
Geralt closed the ledger. He thought of Ciri, of Jack, of how often adults called survival a gift after handing children a world honed to cut them into usefulness. "Lambert is right."
"He will be unbearable if you say that aloud."
"I won't."
"Good. Mercy has limits."

Eskel handed him a scrap he had found beneath a loose shelf board. It was not one of Vesemir's main notes. A personal fragment, perhaps never meant to survive even as hidden record. The writing was careful, therefore afraid.

If the boy lives, the lie lives with him. If the boy dies, the lie dies with me. This is not comfort. Geralt will understand the practical part and hate the rest. Lambert would call me a coward and not be entirely wrong. Eskel would ask what the boy needs. That may be why I cannot tell him.
Geralt read it twice.

The page did not absolve Vesemir. Nothing should have. Absolution was for priests and people who liked clean endings. But the scrap put a hand-shaped mark on the old man's fear. It reminded Geralt that Vesemir had not hidden Jack because he did not care. He had hidden him because he did, and because care in Kaer Morhen had often been trained to walk with cruelty until even the men using it forgot which foot belonged to which.
"He knew you would ask the useful question," Geralt said.
Eskel looked toward the ceiling. "I might not have asked the right thing."
"You would have asked more than I did."
"Maybe." Eskel folded the scrap along its old crease. "You cannot fix that by bleeding over every road now."
"Wasn't planning to."
"You were. Quietly. With competence."
Geralt almost smiled. "You become unpleasant when accurate."
"Lambert practices louder. I practice better."

They sat in the archive until the lantern burned low. Above them, the keep settled around its winter bones. Jack slept somewhere in Vesemir's old room because no one had known where else to put him and because the cruelty of the choice had become visible only after it was made. Geralt had almost changed it. Jack had said nothing and taken the room, which was perhaps worse.

Before dawn, Geralt placed the scrap with the other notes. Not to protect Vesemir. To keep the contradiction intact. Jack would need the whole wound if he was ever to decide what scar it deserved to become.
The first Black Ink copy reached Kaer Morhen before the snow finished melting from their boot tracks.

It came by raven, which offended Lambert because ravens had belonged to gloom long before bureaucrats discovered them. The bird landed on the broken tower at midmorning with a copper tube tied to its leg and an expression of professional contempt. Keira took the tube after bribing the raven with a strip of dried meat from Lambert's pack.
"That was mine," Lambert said.
"You were slow."
The message inside bore no full seal, only the black oval and a notation in a clerk's hand.

Northern ruin inquiry: possible archive retrieval at wolf-site. Monitor for relational interference. Do not engage Lambert of the Wolf School directly unless provoked; subject profile suggests provocation likely and unproductive. Keira Metz present by association. High curiosity risk. Consider false alchemical lead if containment review requires delay.
Keira read that line and became delighted for exactly the wrong reason.
"High curiosity risk," she said. "Finally, an institution recognizes my gifts."
Lambert took the page. "They think I am likely to be provoked."
"They think correctly," Eskel said.
"By cowards using grammar, yes."

Geralt folded the page and felt the road to Novigrad shorten under his feet. Black Ink had looked toward Kaer Morhen. That meant the keep was no longer archive only. It had become active ground. Every person in it had become a line item.
Jack looked at the raven, then at the message, then at Geralt. "They are fast."
"Too fast."
"They had someone waiting for us to come here."
"Yes."
"Because Vesemir's records were not a secret to them."
Geralt did not answer. He did not need to. The raven croaked from the tower and took wing, black against the gray sky, carrying nothing now and still managing to look accused.
Dandelion was standing on a table when Geralt entered the Chameleon.

This was not unusual, which said unkind things about the Chameleon and accurate things about Dandelion. He wore burgundy velvet despite the hour, one sleeve rolled because ink had attacked it, and a hat with a feather so blue that it seemed to have survived by bribery. One boot rested beside a half-written song. The other pinned down a stack of pamphlets threatening to escape into the common room, where three patrons were arguing whether a man could sue a bridge for emotional injury.

"A bridge cannot be sued," Dandelion declared from the table. "It lacks property, personhood, and the capacity to look ashamed. A bridge keeper may be sued. A city may be sued if one has coin, patience, and a death wish. A troll may be negotiated with. A poet should be paid in advance because civilization is fragile."
"Get down," Priscilla said from the corner.
"I am conducting public education."
"You are avoiding the ledger."
"The ledger is hostile to art."
Zoltan Chivay, seated beneath the table with an account book open before him and a knife holding one page flat, did not look up. "The ledger says art spent twelve crowns on feather maintenance."
"A moral investment."
"A structural failure."

Geralt stood in the doorway until the room noticed him. Jack stood just behind him with his hood down because hoods had become more memorable than faces, and because if the wrong song had already described him, hiding from it only gave the song imagination. The tavern noise thinned. Not stopped. Novigrad never stopped. It merely lowered its voice to listen more profitably.

Dandelion's performance fell away so quickly that only people who loved him would have noticed what it took. He stepped down from the table, crushing no pamphlets through luck or divine incompetence, and crossed the room.
"Geralt," he said.
Geralt studied the hat. "The feather got worse."
Dandelion embraced him anyway.

It was brief. Geralt endured it with the resignation of a man submitting to weather. Then Dandelion held him at arm's length and looked past him to Jack. For once, he did not speak immediately. His gaze took in the white hair, the crimson eyes, the scar, the stillness, the Wolf medallion, and the way Geralt had not stepped aside until he knew the room had done its first arithmetic.
"Jack Morningstar," Dandelion said. "My apologies. The city has been describing you with far less restraint than reality deserved."
"It usually does."
"Yes. Reality, poor thing, has no publicist. I have offered repeatedly."
Zoltan closed the ledger and stood. "You're taller than the songs."
Jack considered him. "Songs measure badly."
"Good. You'll do." Zoltan pointed toward the back. "Room's ready. Beer is bad but honest. Wine is better and lying. We recommend the beer for strategy and the wine for despair."

Priscilla came forward with quieter grace. Her voice, when she spoke, had the careful strength of an instrument repaired rather than restored. "The back room is watched by three people who think they are watching other people. Two are ours. One is stupid."
"Which one?" Geralt asked.
"The one who believes Dandelion when he says he has lost money."
"That narrows it poorly," Zoltan said.

They went through the curtain behind the stage, down a passage smelling of candle smoke, old perfume, wine vinegar, and damp wool, then into a room where Novigrad's public soul had been pinned to a table. Pamphlets, copied verses, debt slips, wax impressions, paper samples, dock tallies, chalk sketches, church notices, bridge songs, counter-lines, merchant marks, and one eel pie wrapper covered the boards. The wrapper had been labeled in Priscilla's hand: witness says refrain was sung while pastry cooled. Dandelion had added: pastry criminally over-salted.
Jack stopped at the table.
Before the ledger could speak, Priscilla made them listen to the street.

She opened the back window a finger's width. Novigrad came in at once: cart wheels, gulls, rainwater under hooves, a woman bargaining over lamp oil, a priest's bell, a fishwife insulting ancestry with the authority of scholarship. Beneath it, woven through the ordinary noise, came the new phrases. Wiser hands. Old stone's call. Red wolf. Useful ain't owned. No one sang a full verse. That was worse. Full songs could be found, mocked, interrupted. Fragments hid in errands.
"That is the state of the battle," Priscilla said.
Dandelion looked wounded. "My dear, I had prepared a stirring summary."
"Exactly."
Zoltan snorted into his beer. "She loves you. Cruelly, but well."

Priscilla ignored both men because she had survived worse than performance and had learned not to spend voice where a look would do. She placed three copied scraps before Jack. On one, a Black Ink phrase had been repeated almost exactly: dangerous bodies must rest in wiser custody. On another, a tavern singer had changed it to dangerous wolves need wiser hands. On the third, written in a child's wide chalking hand, was only this: wise hands take.
"That last one is ours," she said. "Not because we wrote it. Because the city answered back."
Jack touched none of them. "A child wrote that."
"Yes."
"Children should not be in this."
Geralt gave him a look so old it had traveled through too many forests. "Children are always in it. Adults just file them under consequences."
Dandelion's face went still. The feather in his hat trembled from a draft and, for once, seemed embarrassed by itself.

Priscilla continued. "Black Ink wants the crowd to rehearse custody before seeing custody. We cannot win by saying Jack is harmless. He is not, and people know lies when they are offered for comfort. We win by teaching the crowd to ask who benefits from calling another person's body public property."
"That scans poorly," Dandelion said.
"Then shorten it."
Dandelion looked at the scraps, then at Jack, and the professional mask settled over something deeply human. "No chain is held by wisdom alone."
Priscilla considered. "Too noble."
"Wise hands like other men's locks."
Zoltan pointed at him. "That one."
"Of course that one," Dandelion said. "It has both moral clarity and a vulgar aftertaste. My finest territory."

They laughed, not because anything was funny enough, but because the room required proof that dread had not rented it outright. Jack watched them turn fear into phrases, phrases into tactics, tactics into errands. He had thought songs were air. He had been wrong. Songs were knives with handles shaped for crowds.
Dandelion saw him understanding and did not make it a lesson. That, Jack decided, was the bard's rarest talent.

His silence changed the room more than surprise would have. Dandelion watched him look at the public version of himself: wolf, burden, rescue, chain, wiser hands, dangerous body, grateful surrender. Each phrase had been copied in at least four hands. Some were expensive. Some childish. Formal on its face, fit to pass through doors. Several included no name. That was the clever part. A name could be challenged. An animal shape could be fed fear until it grew.
"They are making me without me," Jack said.
Priscilla nodded. "Yes."
No pity. Good. Pity would have made the room uglier.

Zoltan opened the ledger again and stabbed one entry with a thick finger. "Wax first. Clove-black. Bought under medical freight by South Quay Counting House through three accounts and a charity for war widows. The charity is real, which makes the lie better and the bastards uglier. Paper came from a printer who usually handles church indulgence blanks and municipal pest notices. Paid in silver clipped Redanian style, laundered through a barge owner's debt."
"Witnesses?" Geralt asked.
