"Bought through old debts," Zoltan said. "Not coin handed to liars in alleys. Too crude. They pay a widow's rent, settle a son's tax, forgive a tavern slate, return a confiscated permit. Then the witness remembers the useful version because gratitude wants to be clean."
Jack studied a copied deposition. "Useful is not owned."
Dandelion brightened with pain. "Ah. You heard that line?"
"Two towns south. Spoken by a man selling boots. He had changed it to useful things bite owners."
Zoltan grinned. "Better."
Dandelion put a hand to his chest. "I am wounded by democratic editing."
"You didn't write it," Priscilla said.
"I suffered near it. Art is communal when credit is unavailable."

Geralt moved through the papers slowly. Jack noticed how the room treated him. Dandelion made space without asking. Zoltan placed the heavier ledger where Geralt's hand could reach without needing to request it. Priscilla stopped a lamp from guttering near his sleeve. Small movements, old ones. No ceremony. No one announced friendship. They worked around him as if he belonged among their inconvenience.
That, Jack thought, might be how families avoided admitting what they were.
Dandelion cleared his throat. "Kaer Morhen found something?"
Geralt placed Vesemir's copied note on the table. Dandelion read it. The feather in his hat seemed suddenly absurd in the hard silence, which perhaps was why it belonged there.

"Confiscated mage ledgers," Dandelion said after a moment. "Post-purge lots. I know three men who bought such things and four who lied about not buying them. One is dead, one is pious, one is married to the printer's sister, and one owes me money. Naturally, we begin with the last."
"Naturally," Geralt said.

Zoltan turned a page. "Already did. The debtor sold a box of pre-purge ledgers to Vander Rogh and Sons six months ago. Same counting house. The box contained patient records, relic sketches, tax seizures, and a red-bound book with no title. The clerk handling it vanished. His apartment was cleaned by men who did not understand poor people keep important things under kitchen bricks."
Priscilla lifted a small packet. "We found one page."

It was brittle, water-stained, and marked with the same black oval from Vesemir's note. The page showed a fragment of a diagram: five barbs, a center, and a line of text in a hand not Vesemir's. Jack read the translation someone had added below it.

Specimen mark corresponds to eastern Morning Star custodial signet. Do not identify publicly as royal, draconic, or priestly. Public frame should remain mutant, witcher, or public-health exception until senior doctrine established.
Keira's phrase returned: names are locks.
Geralt's hand closed slowly on the table edge. Dandelion saw and, for once, did not make a joke.

"There is more," Priscilla said. "The public story shifted yesterday. Not just safer chains. Now the songs say the wolf belongs to old stone. That phrase did not come from tavern invention. Someone added it after Broken Crown or after another site like it."
Jack felt the mark in his palm pulse. "Another site?"

Zoltan nodded toward the window. "There was a disturbance near Hierarch's Square this morning. Not public yet. A contract board was replaced before dawn. Four notices appeared with the same handwriting, different seals. One offers payment for a beast in the old drain under St. Luthar's well. Too much payment. Too clean paper. We didn't pull it because pulling it tells them who reads."
"Trap," Geralt said.
"Aye," Zoltan said. "But not just for you. For the room around you."

Dandelion leaned over the table. His voice changed, the stage velvet replaced by the bare planks beneath it. "Sorel or whoever holds his leash does not need you to be guilty. He needs the city to watch you become necessary to restrain. He needs rescue to look like evidence against freedom."
"Then we don't go," Jack said.
"Then he hurts someone else," Geralt said.
"Yes."

The bluntness made Dandelion wince. Geralt did not. Jack's eyes were on the diagram. Dandelion, who knew crowds, saw the danger in that stillness. A man who could accept strangers dying because a trap was obvious was one thing. A man forcing himself to say it aloud because the alternative was being used was another. The second kind usually bled later in private.

Priscilla set down a counter-song sheet beside the Black Ink phrase. "Both saint and monster are cages," she said. "Geralt told Dandelion that in a letter. He was right. We cannot make people love you out of fear of what fear will do. That becomes another chain."
"Then what do you make?" Jack asked.
"Witnesses who know the trick before the trick is played."
Zoltan tapped the ledger. "And debt. Good debt. Ours, not theirs. We find the people they bought with favors and give them a reason not to be grateful to bastards."
Dandelion sighed. "It is very inconvenient that morality now requires accounting."
"Morality always required accounting," Zoltan said. "Poets just hide invoices under metaphors."
Zoltan's money trail required walking, which Dandelion considered a deliberate attack on lyric intelligence.

They began at a paper merchant whose shop smelled of wet linen, glue, and moral compromise. Zoltan asked for invoice copies. The merchant denied knowledge. Zoltan placed three names on the counter: a widow whose rent had been mysteriously paid, a dock porter whose son's fine had vanished, and a printer's apprentice suddenly eating meat twice a week. The merchant's denial lost weight with each name. By the fifth, it lay dead on the counter and no one mourned.
"I sell paper," the merchant said. "I do not ask what people print."
"Convenient," Zoltan said. "I sell axes and ask why a man wants one if he is standing in my shop covered in someone else's blood. Makes life less profitable but easier to sleep through."
Dandelion leaned over a stack of uncut sheets. "Do you at least ask whether the poetry is competent?"
The merchant blinked. "No."
"Then you are damned twice."

Geralt found the watermark before the merchant found courage. A small press mark near the lower corner, nearly invisible unless held against window light: three reeds and a little crown. Zoltan knew the mark. Of course he did. Dwarves, Jack was learning, treated supply chains the way witchers treated tracks, with less reverence and more profanity.
"South Quay stock," Zoltan said. "Bought cheap after a plague office closed. Official paper without current office. Perfect for bastards who want authority to smell secondhand."

The merchant gave them a ledger page. Not because conscience bloomed. Because Zoltan explained that the alternative involved a public conversation about tax stamps, false weights, and the private room above the shop where the merchant's brother stored confiscated hymnals. Morality did not always begin with nobility. Sometimes it began with leverage pointed in a healthier direction.

They went next to the widow permit office, then to a pawn stall, then to a cellar where a former witch hunter kept account scraps in a flour barrel because he believed flour made paper smell honest. Geralt did not strike him. That took effort. Jack saw the effort in the set of his jaw and the way his hand remained open at his side.

The former witch hunter had been paid to stand near the board and say, only if asked, that he had seen red light before the creature attacked. He had not seen it. He had, however, received back a seized permit allowing his sister to sell soap. The sister knew nothing. That was the cruelty of the method. Black Ink bought lies by rescuing people from other small violences. Then gratitude did the rest and called itself reasonable.
"If you expose me, my sister loses the stall," the man said.
Zoltan turned to Jack. "Your call."
Jack hated that. Not because he could not choose, but because each choice arrived already dirtied by someone else's hand.

"You tell Priscilla exactly who asked you," Jack said. "You tell it before witnesses. You say you lied because the man who paid you also held your sister's permit. You keep the stall. If you lie again, Zoltan handles the poetry."
The man turned to Zoltan.
Zoltan smiled. "I rhyme with hammer."
"Poorly," Dandelion said.
"Loudly," Zoltan corrected.
The man agreed.
Outside, Geralt gave Jack a look that might once have been praise if Geralt knew what to do with praise before it became uncomfortable.
"What?" Jack asked.
"Nothing."
"That sounded like something."
"You did not take the easy blood."
Jack looked down the alley, where the merchant's watermark gleamed faintly in the wet on the ledger page. "Easy blood leaves stains other men can sell."
Geralt nodded. He did not say Vesemir would have approved. That was good. Jack might have hated him for it.
Novigrad in the afternoon smelled like fish scales, hot tar, incense from churches trying to drown out the docks, piss in alleys, wet stone, cheap perfume, and fresh ink.

Jack walked through it with Geralt and felt the city try to name him. Eyes moved from hair to swords to eyes and then away too quickly. Some people recognized the song before the man. A washerwoman near the canal whispered wiser hands and then looked ashamed when the boot seller beside her said, "Useful ain't owned." Two children chalked a wolf on a wall and argued whether the chain should go around the neck or the paw. One drew no chain at all. The other told him that was not how the song went.
Geralt heard it too. His face did not change. His hand adjusted the strap of his sword, though the strap needed no adjustment.
"You lived here?" Jack asked.
"No one lives in Novigrad. They survive it while claiming rent."
"Dandelion does."
"Dandelion inhabits attention. The city is incidental."

A man selling devotional candles called out blessings for dangerous journeys and discounts for bulk repentance. Geralt bought none. Jack stopped at the edge of Hierarch's Square where the contract board stood beneath a statue of a saint with one hand extended in mercy and the other suspiciously close to a purse. Four notices had been nailed in a perfect row. Too perfect. The old board around them was scarred by weather, knives, lost dogs, missing apprentices, and prayers written by people who had no paper. The new notices looked like clean teeth in a rotten mouth.
Jack read them without touching.

One for a beast under St. Luthar's well. One for unusual heat in the old drain. One for a pale dog with a black tongue. One for a public advisory concerning itinerant armed mutants traveling under professional title.
"They put the advisory beside the contract," Jack said.
"So anyone who sees you read one sees you inside the other."
"Clever."
"Yes."
"I hate clever."
"You are clever."
"I am professionally offended by competition."
Geralt glanced at him. "Lambert is rubbing off on you."
"Then kill me quickly."

A woman at the edge of the crowd crossed herself, then uncrossed herself, then muttered something about plague carriers. Geralt stepped half a pace to Jack's left. Too little to shield him. Still, the crowd adjusted its attention. Jack noticed and said nothing. Practical care was more difficult to reject when it arrived in geometry.

At the opposite side of the square, a man in gray watched with a book under his arm. No Black Ink seal. No sword. No obvious power. That made him more dangerous, or at least better trained than the courier in the trees.
"We pull the contract," Jack said.
"We pull the witnesses first," Geralt answered.
"Dandelion's idea?"
"Priscilla's. Dandelion claimed it afterward with decorative language."
Jack almost smiled. Almost.

They did not take the notices that day. They bought lamp oil, watched who watched the board, followed two clerks to a print shop, and let Zoltan's people begin the ugly work of finding the debts hidden behind witness gratitude. By evening, the Chameleon back room held names. By midnight, it held more fear than names. By dawn, the first witness changed his story before anyone official asked for it, not because he had become brave, but because Zoltan had paid the tax on his mother's stall and then threatened to make him explain in public why he preferred gratitude to truth.
Jack watched this machinery with discomfort.

Blades were cleaner. Contracts uglier but narrower. This was a fight of doors, debts, songs, rooms, and ordinary people choosing whether their relief belonged to whoever paid first. It made him understand why Black Ink liked paper. Paper could hold violence in a form that did not sweat.

Late that night, Dandelion found him in the empty common room. Jack sat near the stage with Buck's saddle strap across his knees, repairing a tear that had not been there in the morning. Geralt had gone with Zoltan to inspect the old drain route. Priscilla slept upstairs. The Chameleon breathed around them, chairs upturned, candles guttering, city noise pressing faintly at the shutters.
"Geralt used to sit there," Dandelion said.
Jack did not look up. "Did he repair tack too?"
"No. He glowered at it until leather reconsidered."
"Sounds efficient."

Dandelion sat without invitation, which Jack decided not to punish because the bard looked suddenly older without his audience. "He finds family by accident. Then denies the accident has implications. I have watched him do it for years."
"I am not his family."
"Of course not. That is why he rides beside you, lies badly about worry, and looks at doorways before you enter them. Complete stranger behavior."
Jack pulled the thread through leather. "You talk too much."

"I am a bard. That is both trade and diagnosis." Dandelion glanced toward the shuttered window. "You should understand something about songs. Silence does not stop them. Refusing to be described does not prevent description. It only leaves the work to people with worse motives and weaker rhymes."
"So you describe me better."
"No. I make the crowd suspicious of anyone describing you too easily. That is different. Less satisfying, unfortunately. Harder to sell. More likely to help."
Jack tied the stitch and cut the thread. "Why?"
"Why help?"
Jack let the silence answer first.

Dandelion's answer arrived without performance. "Because Geralt would. Because Triss asked. Because Priscilla heard the poison before I had the sense to fear it. Because Zoltan hates paid lies. Because I once watched a girl become a story before she had finished being a child, and by the time the world learned her name, half of it wanted to own her."
Ciri entered the room through absence.
Jack looked down at the strap. "I don't know her."
"No," Dandelion said. "But the people hunting you are using a grammar she has bled in. That will serve."
The city bell struck three times. The third note sounded cracked.
By morning, the trap was ready.
So were they, which was not the same as safety.
The man who owed Dandelion money lived above a printer's shop and had decorated his room with unpaid confidence.

His name was Pavo Lutt, though Zoltan called him Ledger Pavo because he kept four sets of accounts and believed that made him clever rather than merely flammable. Pavo had a thin mustache, a satin waistcoat gone shiny at the elbows, and the distracted terror of a man trying to decide which lie was currently cheapest. He opened the door at the sight of Dandelion, began to smile, saw Geralt behind him, saw Jack behind Geralt, saw Zoltan below the window with a hammer, and achieved spiritual clarity.
"I was about to send payment," Pavo said.
"A beautiful intention," Dandelion replied. "Several religions are built from less."
Zoltan came in last and shut the door. "Records."
"Which records?"
"The ones your eyebrows just lied about."
Pavo returned to Jack. Jack said nothing. Silence did the work. It often did, when a man had rehearsed speeches and found no audience for them.

The room smelled of hot ink from below, candle smoke, stale wine, and panic. Priscilla moved to the desk before Pavo could. She lifted a stack of playbills and found a ledger under them. Dandelion looked wounded.
"Under my announced revival of The Sorrowful Duchess? That is not hiding. That is commentary."
"The market commented first," Pavo said weakly.
"You wound me twice. Continue."

The ledger had coded entries, but the code had been designed for tax clerks, not dwarves with grudges. Zoltan broke the first layer in three minutes and the second by asking where Pavo stored his real ink. The answer, under the bed, produced a smaller book bound in red leather with no title.
Jack felt the signet cool.
Geralt saw his hand move toward his chest. "This one?"
"Yes."

Pavo began speaking too quickly. "It was part of a lot. Confiscated papers. Witch-hunt seizures, old mage ledgers, nonsense mostly. I sold the originals to Vander Rogh and Sons. Kept extracts because extracts have value. Not treasonous value. Scholarly value. Commerce, really. Civic preservation."
"You are making me miss silence," Jack said.
Pavo closed his mouth.

The red book contained copies of copies. Relic sketches. Patient notes. A diagram of a barbed star labelled eastern non-human containment emblem. Three witness statements from the purge years mentioning a burned woman with desert scars asking about a child. A tally of payments to a field doctor attached to irregularities. A name in the margin: S. Veyrane, junior review.
Geralt turned to Zoltan.
"Before he was senior," Zoltan said. "Bastards have childhoods."

Priscilla read one of the witness extracts aloud. "Woman asks for child with white hair and red sickness. Burn scars. Speaks Northern poorly. Carries bone knots. Refuses payment. Threatens clerk with knife after phrase state custody. Escaped before questioning."
Jack looked toward the street below. People passed outside without knowing a lost portion of his life had been stored above a printer's shop by a man in a bad waistcoat.
"Asha," Geralt said.
"Seems so," Zoltan answered. "She was searching before the songs. Before Broken Crown. Before Black Ink found the nerve to print."
Dandelion leaned over the page. For once he looked less like a performer than a man watching history remove makeup. "We need her."
Jack's jaw tightened. "Need is becoming crowded."
"Crowded rooms are harder to raid," Zoltan said.
"Easier to betray."
"True. So we pick useful bastards and watch their hands. Welcome to friendship."
Pavo made a small sound.
Zoltan turned to him. "Not you."
The red-bound book was not hidden well.

That was the insult. People imagined dangerous books buried under altars, chained in towers, guarded by curses, wrapped in oaths. This one sat inside a box of damaged playbills beneath a stack of sermons no one had paid to hear. Its cover was cracked red leather, its corners blackened, its spine unmarked. A dead fly had been pressed between the first two pages so long that it had become part of the account.
Pavo Lutt swore he had never opened it.
Zoltan opened it and found the page edges cut clean.
"Your innocence is improving," the dwarf said. "Now it has tools."

The book was a catalog, or what remained of one. Confiscated materials from the years when witch hunters had dressed theft in holy language. Mage patient records. Relic sketches. Private letters. Things seized from dead men, frightened women, bankrupt families, and anyone foolish, owning an object that hummed near the wrong priest. Most entries had been crossed out as sold, burned, transferred, cleansed, returned to authority, or lost. Lost appeared often. Lost was a wonderfully useful word. It meant someone had stopped wanting accountability.
Halfway through, Jack found the page.

Morning Star signet, eastern custody class uncertain. Associated infant survivor. Northern retrieval believed. Do not label draconic in public listings. Potential buyer interest: medical, military, theological, imperial.
A second hand had added beneath it: If the carrier lives, the object may locate him under pressure.
The room narrowed.

Geralt took the book and read the line. His thumb stopped over infant survivor. Jack knew he was seeing the ruin again. Smoke. Snow. A boy too quiet. Perhaps Geralt would see that room every time a file learned how to say child without using the word.
Dandelion lowered himself onto a crate. "Medical, military, theological, imperial. That is nearly everyone with furniture."
"Not everyone," Priscilla said from the door.
"My love, this is not the hour for optimism."

"It is not optimism. It is target selection. Whoever wrote this knew which appetites to list and which to omit. No banking notation. No academic notation. No collector's private mark. This was not being sold to curiosity. It was being routed toward authority."
Zoltan gave her open approval. "You should frighten more accountants."
"I intend to."
Jack studied the book. "Take it."
Pavo made a strangled sound. "That book is worth a considerable sum."
Geralt turned his head.
Pavo reconsidered the market. "Spiritually, I mean. As evidence."
Zoltan took the book.

As they left, Dandelion paused beside Pavo and pressed one finger to the man's satin waistcoat. "If anyone asks, you sold us sermons. Boring ones. If you become creative, I will write a verse so memorable that your grandchildren will be born owing money."
Pavo went pale.
Jack understood then that bards, like witchers, could be hired against monsters. The monsters simply preferred applause.

They took the red book, three ledger leaves, and a list of payments. Dandelion also took the playbill from The Sorrowful Duchess and claimed it was evidence of aesthetic persecution. Priscilla told him it was evidence of mercy if the production remained unperformed.

Outside, Jack paused under the printer's sign. Fresh sheets hung from lines in the workshop, drying in rows. Words repeated in black across cheap paper. Sermons. Prices. Notices. A city could become a hunting dog if ink taught it which scent mattered.
"Paper is fast," he said.
Geralt studied the drying sheets. "So are fires."
"That an option?"
"Not yet."
"Pity."

From somewhere near the market came a child chanting useful ain't owned in a skipping rhythm. The line had become uglier, smaller, and therefore stronger. Jack listened until the chant dissolved under cart wheels.
Dandelion watched him. "That one is not ours anymore."
"Good."
"You say that as if surrendering authorship is not agony."
"I have no authorship."
"Exactly. That is why you must be careful who gets it."
The contract board had acquired an audience before sunrise.

That was how Jack knew Sorel Veyrane had manners. A cruder hunter would have sent men with nets, blades, and a cart with air holes. Sorel sent a crowd first: bakers' apprentices, former witch hunters pretending to be concerned citizens, dock laborers paid through forgiven debts, two priests with different gods and the same fear, three clerks, a widow who had been given back her confiscated permit, and a boy selling hot chestnuts who kept glancing at the wrong men for instructions. Violence arrived more cleanly when people believed they had gathered by accident.

The square woke around them. Shops opened shutters. Carts complained over stones. A beggar with one leg cursed at a pigeon for professional reasons. The statue of St. Luthar looked down with chipped mercy and a pigeon stain on his sainted brow. Above the contract board, the four notices remained in their perfect row.
Jack stood at the edge of the square with his hood down. Geralt stood beside him. Not behind. Not ahead. Beside. That, too, was a message for anyone paid to classify posture.
"Crowd's wrong," Geralt said.
"Too many eyes. Too few errands."
"The chestnut boy is real."
"Yes."
"Hungry."
"Also yes."
"Don't use Igni near the cart."
Jack turned to him. "That your strategy?"
"I like chestnuts."
The humor helped because it was too small to lie.

Dandelion had placed three singers in nearby alleys, none of them singing about wolves. Priscilla watched from a linen merchant's upper window with her hood low and two students beside her copying crowd phrases. Zoltan's people moved where practical people always moved: behind stalls, near carts, under awnings, at exits, beside anything that could become a barricade. Geralt knew the map because Dandelion had drawn it badly and Zoltan had redrawn it with insulting accuracy.
Jack knew another presence before he saw her.

The air at the north side of the square changed. Not colder exactly. More disciplined. Yennefer stood beneath the shadow of a church arch in black and white, one gloved hand resting on the head of a cane she did not need. Triss was not beside her. That meant Triss was somewhere more useful. Yennefer's eyes found Jack across the square, then the notices, then the crowd, then the drain cover near the statue.
She had read the magic before the trap introduced itself.
A city clerk mounted the low steps beside the contract board and unrolled a notice.

"Citizens," he called. His voice had been trained for smaller rooms and larger lies. "By advisory authority of municipal safety coordination and inter-district irregularity review, all persons are requested to remain calm during professional assessment of a possible public-risk anomaly presently associated with itinerant witcher activity. No accusation is made. Cooperation preserves civic reassurance."
The crowd did not understand all the words. That was part of their design. People became easier to frighten when meaning passed above them but tone stayed near their throat.
Geralt murmured, "Civic reassurance."
"Sounds edible," Jack said.
"Probably poisonous."
The clerk continued. "The armed mutant known in certain unverified reports as Jack Morningstar is invited to present himself voluntarily for preliminary classification."
There it was. Invited. Voluntarily. Classification. Three links of one chain.

Jack stepped forward before the crowd could start looking for him. Geralt moved with him. Murmurs ran over the square, not one sound but many small transactions: red eyes, him, witcher, saved a girl, killed a cow, dragon blood, wiser hands, useful, not owned, dangerous. The chestnut boy stopped selling. His brazier smoked.
"I am here," Jack said.
The clerk looked relieved and terrified. Men liked procedures more before procedures answered.

A gray-coated officer came from beside the church, carrying no visible weapon. His gloves were clean. His hair had been clipped recently. His face had the even mildness of an instrument that did not think itself cruel because someone else held the handle.
"Master Morningstar," he said. "Your cooperation is appreciated."
"Then pay for it."
A ripple of laughter moved through the front of the crowd before fear remembered its duties. The officer absorbed it, which proved training.
"This is not a contract matter."
"Everything is."
"You are not being detained."
"Then I may leave."
"After preliminary civic questions."
Yennefer's voice carried from the arch, precise, cutting through market noise. "Questions asked after the exit is removed are not civic."

The officer turned. He recognized her. His posture changed by less than a coin's thickness, but the change moved through the clerks. Yennefer of Vengerberg had entered the procedure, and the procedure had not budgeted for her.
"Madam," the officer said.
"No."
"I have not asked anything."
"I am saving time."
That was when the drain cover screamed.

Not a sound made by iron. Iron complained, shrieked, rang, tore. This screamed with a throat it did not have. The cover lifted half an inch, dropped, lifted again, and burst upward as steam blew from the old drain beneath St. Luthar's statue. The chestnut boy froze. The crowd pulled back badly, each person certain space would make itself for them because terror had never learned arithmetic.
Jack moved toward the boy.
The officer arrived before the creature, which made him part of the creature.

He wore municipal blue over a breastplate polished too carefully for a man expecting ordinary paperwork. Two clerks followed him with tablets. Three former witch hunters stood nearby, each pretending he had become a concerned citizen since fire lost its legal uniform. A woman with a prayer wheel murmured about public safety. The widow with the restored permit held her permit so tightly that the paper buckled in her fist. Dandelion's students copied the crowd's phrases from the upper window. Priscilla did not look at the crowd. She studied the people feeding it words.
"Jack Morningstar," the officer called.
The square liked the name. It moved through mouths before anyone knew whether they had permission to use it.
Jack did not step forward. "You have me at a disadvantage."
"Captain Orvan Slett, municipal special appointment under provisional safety cooperation."
"Long name. Does it bite?"
A few people laughed. Not many. The sound made Orvan dislike it.
"You are advised to submit to questioning regarding repeated anomalous manifestations in proximity to civic danger sites."
Geralt said, "Questioning usually starts with questions."
"Master Geralt of Rivia, your cooperation is welcome but not required."
"That true?"
"Legally, yes."
"Then your law is badly made."
The crowd enjoyed that more. Crowds weaponized that. They could be frightened into cruelty and joked into courage, sometimes within the same minute.

Orvan unrolled a document. Yennefer's eyes narrowed from the church arch. Jack saw her read the page from across the square not by sight, but by the way her anger found posture before words. The officer held the writ high for witnesses and low for the finer text to hide from the wind.
"Voluntary cooperation is preferred," Orvan read.
"By whom?" Jack asked.
"By competent authorities."
"Name one."
This time the laughter was larger. Zoltan's people shifted at the exits, ready for the mood to turn. Humor bought time. It did not buy safety.
The chestnut boy watched the wrong man again.

Jack saw it. Geralt saw Jack see it. The wrong man, a former witch hunter with a scar across the chin, touched two fingers to his sleeve. The boy, confused and frightened, reached to stir the brazier so the coals would glow brighter. Beneath the statue, the drain cover clicked once.
Yennefer moved her cane one inch against the stones.
The drain cover clicked again.
"Move the child," Jack said.
Orvan did not look at the boy. "No civilian is under threat at this time."
The drain cover lifted.

The creature came out of the drain in pieces that decided, halfway into the light, to belong to the same body. First a long forelimb, scaled and blackened, claws scraping sparks from stone. Then a narrow head plated in scorched horn, one eye sealed with milky scar, the other too bright and wrong. Then wings, useless and folded tight against a rib cage that had been cut, healed, cut again. It was draconid-adjacent, as Yennefer would later phrase it with professional hatred. Not a true dragon. Not a wyvern. Something starved, burned, driven through old stone, and taught to follow pressure instead of prey.
It went for the chestnut brazier because heat lied to it.
The boy stood between heat and teeth.
For three breaths, the fight belonged to the crowd.

Not to Jack. Not to Geralt. Not to the creature clawing itself into daylight. To the crowd, because fear first makes owners of whoever sees it. A baker's apprentice shoved a woman into a stall and then tried to pull her back, already ashamed. A priest lifted a charm and dropped it when the creature's good eye rolled toward him. One former witch hunter drew a blade against a beast he had helped arrange and discovered that arranged danger still had teeth.
Then training took the fight away from them.

Geralt threw the chestnut boy under the cart and kicked the cart's wheel brace loose so it sagged into a shield. Jack cut the brazier stand in half before the coals could scatter toward the boy. Yennefer sealed the northern alley with a snap of black light that looked less like a wall than a refusal. From somewhere behind the board came Triss's voice, sharp and warm at once, ordering civilians left, not right, because right had become a funnel.
The creature struck where Jack had been.

Stone split. The contract board shook. Four notices tore free at the same time and spun through the smoke like birds with broken wings. One slapped against Jack's chest and stuck there, not from damp. From heat. Words pressed into the leather for a heartbeat: subject proximity, necessary custody, response event. Then the paper blackened at the edges.
Jack ripped it away and saw the creature's attention follow the motion.

It had been hurt before, but not to the point of ending its use. Its wing bones had been cut close to the joint. The scars were stitched with wire so fine only a rich man or a laboratory would waste it on cruelty. Around its throat the skin had been burned in a ring. No chain remained, but the burn remembered one. Its breathing rattled with old metal. Each time the creature lunged toward Jack, the drain below answered with a wet grinding sound, as if the city itself dragged an unseen hook through stone.
"It is following the writ," Yennefer said.
"Writs don't smell," Geralt said, cutting at the forelimb when it swept toward a fallen clerk.
"This one does."

Jack heard her because the square had become terribly clear. The creature's claws. Geralt's boots. Triss tearing a seal from the board. Dandelion shouting from a window that anyone who ran toward the church steps would be immortalized as a cabbage in a heroic ballad. People obeyed because fear, apparently, still had standards.
The mark in Jack's palm opened heat under the bandage.
Need, Keira had said.

The boy under the cart began to cry. Not loudly. Worse. Quietly, as if he had already learned that panic should not bother adults. The sound reached Jack before the creature's next movement did. The old pressure in his blood answered with a red pull so sudden he nearly stepped toward the child instead of the beast.
There was the leash.
Staged rescue. Staged fear. Need made into a hook.
Jack planted his boots.
"Geralt. Boy."
"Already."

Geralt dragged the child farther back by the collar and shoved him toward a cabbage seller with arms like harbor rope. The seller caught the boy, looked around for someone to charge, and then did the right thing for free.
The pull changed. Frustrated, the creature twisted toward Triss. She had the writ now, half torn and smoking in her hand.
Jack moved.

He did not think of heroism. Heroism wasted time. He thought of angle, weight, footing, and the little gap under the jaw where pain had kept the creature from healing cleanly. He took the cut across his arm because avoiding it would give the beast Triss's throat. He stepped inside its reach, inside the reek of burned scale and laboratory vinegar, and drove silver up with both hands.
The blade met bone. Stopped. He twisted his wrist. The red lines in his palm flared through the hilt.
For one instant, the creature's good eye cleared.
Not human. Not pleading. Aware at the end, released from obedience and terrified by the mercy of ending.
Jack drove the sword deeper.

Jack reached him first. He caught the boy by the back of the coat and threw him toward Geralt. Geralt caught him with one arm, shoved him under the chestnut cart, and drew steel in the same movement. The creature hit the brazier. Coals exploded across the stones. The crowd screamed. Jack drew silver.
The officer with clean gloves shouted, "Remain where you are!"
No one did. This improved the square's intelligence.

The creature turned toward Jack before Jack struck. Its good eye fixed on his bandaged hand. Not hunger. Recognition corrupted by pain. The mark in Jack's palm answered with red heat, and every notice on the board curled at the corners as if the paper had been put too close to a fire.
"No," Jack said.
The creature lunged.

He met it low, blade angling under the jaw, but it twisted with unnatural speed. Silver scored scale. Black blood hit the stones and steamed. Geralt cut across its flank to keep it from the crowd. Yennefer lifted one hand. The space between the creature and the fleeing citizens hardened, invisible and absolute; three men struck the barrier and bounced back with the offended confusion of drunks meeting walls.
"Left," Geralt said.
Jack moved left. The creature did not follow. It went right, toward the contract board.
Toward the notices.

Triss appeared from behind the board with a wet cloth over her mouth and one hand full of torn paper. She had used the confusion to take the writ. The creature's head snapped toward her. Flame from the scattered coals leaned flat in Jack's direction. His palm burned. The signet at his throat woke like a coin heated in a forge.
He crossed the square in three strides and slammed Aard into the creature's shoulder.

The Sign should have moved it. Instead the space around it buckled inward. The creature skidded, not away from Jack, but toward him. Red pressure gathered behind his eyes. The square sounds warped: screams became distant, bells too close, breath loud as leather tearing. The creature's chains were not visible, but Jack felt them. Not iron. Phrases. Writs. Names. Contract. Anomaly. Custody. Morningstar. Each word a small hook thrown into old blood.
Yennefer saw it. "Jack. Release the pressure. Do not answer it."
"Trying," he said through his teeth.
"Try with more talent."

That almost made him laugh. The laugh did not come, but the shape of it loosened something. He let the red heat pass through the sword instead of the palm. Not out. Down. Into the silver. Into the creature's wounded shoulder. It screamed, and the scream was not only pain. For one breath the draconid's good eye cleared.
Then Geralt killed it.

Not beautifully. Not ceremonially. He stepped inside the reach of the forelimb, took a cut along the arm, drove his sword up under the skull, and twisted once. The creature collapsed across the stones, knocking over the chestnut brazier and one city clerk who had chosen the worst possible place to regain procedural dignity.
The square became aftermath.
Aftermath always revealed the real design.

Black Ink men moved first toward the witnesses, not the wounded. Zoltan's people moved faster. A fishmonger with shoulders like a door shoved one statement-taker into a cabbage cart and apologized to the cabbage. Dandelion's singers began a tavern refrain about wise hands dropping purses when beasts appeared, light, letting people laugh before fear settled into obedience. Priscilla's students copied names. Geralt stood over the dead creature, blood dripping from his sleeve. Jack stood before the board, breathing hard, his palm smoking through the bandage.
The crowd tried to become a verdict as soon as the body stopped moving.

That was what crowds did when fear had no clear instruction left. They looked for a shape to pour themselves into. Some saw rescue in the dead creature. Some saw Jack's smoking glove and found proof for every paid warning. Some saw the boy and remembered he was alive. Some watched the clerks, because clerks were already writing, and writing gave fear permission to pretend it was accuracy.
Priscilla reached the square before Black Ink's statement-takers did.

She did not sing. That would have been too clean and therefore wrong. She walked from witness to witness with two students at her shoulder and asked one question first: what did you see before the monster appeared? Not during. Not after. Before. The question struck people oddly. It pulled the trap backward. A woman remembered the boy being told where to stand. A fish seller remembered the brazier moved closer to the drain. The cabbage seller remembered the former witch hunter touching his sleeve.
A priest remembered the officer reading the writ before the drain opened and hated remembering it because it made his god less useful than timing.

Zoltan's people took the witnesses who had remembered too much and moved them through alleys the city had forgotten to tax. Dandelion gave directions in the wrong voice twice so the wrong men followed the wrong hat. One student spilled ink on an officer's tablet and apologized so extravagantly that everyone nearby became involved in the apology and no one noticed the permit widow leaving with Priscilla's cloak around her shoulders.
Geralt saw all of it while pretending to check the creature's corpse.
"Your friends are thieves," Jack said.
"Useful ones."
"That is still not owned."
"No. It is borrowed with gratitude and returned with complaints."

Yennefer came to stand near the board. Her gaze moved over the creature, then the drain, then the half-burned writ in Triss's hand. Triss had soot on her cheek and fury in her eyes. She looked less like the warm woman from Corvo Bianco and more like a medic deciding which limb to cut before rot became law.

"It was not only drawn to him," Triss said. "It was instructed through the legal language. The writ names him, the event type, and the expected response before the event. The paper is part of the spell, or part of the spell's imitation."
"Not spell," Yennefer said. "Procedure wearing magic's corpse."
Geralt glanced at her. "That worse?"
"Much. Magic admits when it hungers. Procedure asks you to sign the plate."

Jack studied the contract board. One notice remained nailed there, lower than the others. Public advisory. Pale-haired armed mutant. Possible witcher identity. Report discreetly. A drop of creature blood had landed over the word discreetly and made it unreadable.
He almost laughed.
The sound did not come. It turned colder and went somewhere else.
Orvan tried to recover authority by stepping onto the base of St. Luthar's statue. He managed height. Not authority.
"All witnesses will remain for correction," he said.
That was the first true sentence he had spoken.

Dandelion, from the steps of a fish stall, put one hand to his chest. "Captain, as a public artist and therefore professional witness to civic embarrassment, I must ask whether you mean collection. Correction sounds so... pre-edited."
The crowd shifted.
Yennefer smiled as if someone had laid a throat neatly on a table.
"Do answer him," she said. "Slowly. Many people here have recently learned to listen before the monster appears."

Orvan looked around and found his crowd no longer entirely his. That did not make him harmless. It made him harder to stop later. But later was not the square, and the square, for the first time that morning, belonged partly to the people who had survived it.
Triss unfolded the writ she had stolen and read rapidly. Her face changed.
"They had this prepared before the creature emerged," she said.
"Of course," Yennefer said, coming toward them. "The creature was punctuation."
The gray-coated officer approached with two armed men. He had recovered his face. Not his position.
"This area is under civic safety review," he said.
Yennefer fixed him with that winter-black stare. "This area is under my patience. It is a smaller jurisdiction and far less forgiving."
"Madam, the writ authorizes containment measures in the event of non-standard manifestation."
"The writ precedes the manifestation."
"Precautionary authority permits preparation."
Triss held up the page. "It also names the manifestation type before anyone here observed it. Crimson pressure event with draconid anchor response. That phrase appears in no municipal code."
The crowd, still terrified, heard what it needed. Phrases could wound officials when repeated aloud in the wrong weather.
Geralt stepped to Jack's side. "You brought the beast."
The officer's eyes flicked to the dead creature. "We responded to credible risk."
"In advance."
"Civic protection sometimes requires anticipation."
Jack faced the officer. His voice was quiet enough that the nearest witnesses leaned in without meaning to. "You put a child beside a brazier and hoped I would choose fast."
The officer's face did not change. No one needed the sentence finished.
Yennefer moved then.
She did not raise her voice. She did not throw fire. She simply stepped closer until the officer understood that dignity had become poor armor.

"Listen carefully," she said. "You may write that Jack Morningstar killed the creature. You may write that Geralt of Rivia assisted. You may write that Triss Merigold confiscated an unlawful writ, and that I called your superior a coward with clerks. What you may not write, if you value the continued flexibility of your fingers, is that a man protecting civilians from a staged ecological horror thereby consented to custody."
The officer watched her hand. So did everyone else.
Yennefer smiled very slightly. "Good. Literacy survives."
Asha watched from the linen merchant's roof until the second story began to defeat the first.

She had not come for the fight. She had come for proof that the last bearer was not merely the strongest thing in the wrong room. Strength was cheap. Vharakthul had turned valleys into ash and still called it balance. Empires were strong. Black Ink was strong in the way mold was strong, through patience, damp, and finding the joints in houses. Strength told Asha very little.
Choice told more.

The witcher had felt the leash. She saw the moment of it. Need pulled at him through the crying child, through the wounded beast, through the public danger arranged like bait. He had almost moved where the hook wanted him. Almost. Then he had placed his body between the pull and the child, not because anyone ordered him, not because a prophecy lifted his hand, but because restraint had reached the choice before hunger did.
That mattered.
It did not absolve him.

Asha studied the dead creature and saw old ash wearing new skin. The wing scars were not Northern. The wire at the joint had passed through hands that knew draconid tissue and did not respect it. The burn ring around the throat was a broken imitation of an anchoring collar described in Faithel warnings to frighten children away from clever cruelty. Northern fools had found fragments and reinvented sacrilege badly. That did not make them harmless. Bad sacrilege often killed more people because it did not understand the doors it rattled.

Below, Jack Morningstar stood with blood on his sleeve and smoke rising from his glove. Geralt was beside him. Yennefer and Triss were already turning the room of the square against the file-makers. Dandelion and Zoltan moved witnesses like stolen coin. It still left the wound open. It was more than Asha had expected from the North.
She touched the bone charm beneath her collar.
The charm warmed.
Not for the first time. But this time the heat did not point toward rumor, ruin, or old paper. It pointed at the man himself.
"Helena," Asha whispered, too low for even the gulls to steal. "If he is cruel, forgive me. If he is kind, forgive me more."
Then she climbed down to become the next unwelcome answer.
The Chameleon became an infirmary, a court, and an argument before noon.

Triss stitched Geralt's arm in the back room while Geralt complained about the thread, the light, the chair, and the general decline of professional standards. Triss ignored the complaints with the serenity of a woman who had learned which noises meant pain and which meant male pride requesting witnesses. Yennefer spread the writs on the table and pinned their corners with knives. Dandelion objected to using stage knives as legal weights until Zoltan reminded him stage knives had contributed less to justice than cabbages that morning.

Jack sat near the wall because the wall had fewer opinions. His bandage had been replaced twice. The red lines in his palm had darkened, extending toward the wrist in thin branches that vanished when stared at too directly. Keira would have wanted to see them. Jack was grateful she was still in Kaer Morhen and annoyed at himself for the gratitude.
"The creature was not summoned," Yennefer said.
Triss looked up from Geralt's arm. "Drawn?"

"Driven and drawn. There are old anchor residues under St. Luthar's well, likely from a pre-city drainage foundation or something older the city built over because cities are arrogant and seldom dig down before charging rent. The draconid had been injured elsewhere and released into a route where Jack's presence would pull it toward the board."
"Ecology and paperwork," Zoltan said. "That's new."
"No," Geralt said. "That's old. We just used to call one of them monster and the other mayor."
Dandelion, despite himself, reached for paper.
"No," Priscilla said.
"It was a good line."
"It can survive unrecorded."
"Many things cannot."
Jack studied the writs. "What did they gain?"

Yennefer's expression hardened. "Jurisdiction. Too little to take you cleanly. Still sufficient to circulate amended advisory language. You manifested under public stress near a draconid event. They will omit that the event was staged. They will emphasize that people saw the pressure."
"Then people saw me save them."
Priscilla shook her head. "That helps them if gratitude is the hook."
The room knew it. The songs from earlier had prepared exactly this shape: rescue as evidence of dangerous usefulness. Fear did not have to deny kindness. It could weaponize it.

Zoltan tossed a small bag onto the table. Coins spilled out, mixed silver and copper, each marked with a tiny scratch near the rim. "Paid witnesses. We caught three before statement-takers got them. Two took money, one took debt relief, all three thought they were helping public safety by confirming phrases already written. I offered an alternative public service."
"Which was?" Triss asked.
"Remembering what happened before I introduced them to a canal."
Geralt stared at him until Zoltan found something else to do with his hands.
"Metaphorically," Zoltan said after a pause. "Mostly."

Dandelion handed Triss a cup of water, then looked at Jack. "You need to understand the next problem. The city will now hold two stories at once. One: Jack saved a child and killed a beast. Two: Jack's blood pulled a beast into a public square. Both can feel true, and people will choose whichever helps them sleep."
"Truth as menu," Jack said.
"Novigrad's oldest cuisine."
The door opened before anyone knocked. Asha entered as if she had decided the room had delayed her beyond tolerance.

She was tall, dark-haired, and scarred along the left side of her neck in a pattern that seemed at first like burn damage and at second like script written by fire with poor mercy. Her cloak was travel-stained, but the stitching along the hem held a repeating star pattern so subtle Jack saw it only when she moved. Her eyes went to him first. Not to Geralt. Not to Yennefer. Him.
Every candle in the room leaned away from her.
Yennefer stood. "You are late."
Asha turned to her. "You do not know when I began."
Jack rose slowly.
The woman's gaze moved to his palm, then to the hidden signet beneath his shirt, then to his face with something like grief disciplined into duty.
"Jack Morningstar," she said. "At last, the road stopped lying."
That was when the room learned the trap had opened more than one door.
Merrow watched the square from behind a shutter and did not write for twelve full breaths.

That was dereliction by office standards. It was also the first honest thing he had done that morning. Below, the draconid-adjacent carcass lay cooling under a canvas. The canvas was too short. One claw protruded, black and curved, scraping the stone whenever people moved near it. The chestnut boy had survived. The officer had not secured custody. Yennefer of Vengerberg had humiliated municipal procedure without technically obstructing it. Geralt of Rivia had behaved exactly as Sorel predicted, which somehow made the prediction less comforting. Jack Morningstar had flared and then forced the pressure downward instead of outward.
Merrow did not know how to classify that.
He knew how Sorel would.
Controlled response under public stress. Demonstrates training, restraint, and potential directed application. Increased utility. Increased risk.
The words formed by themselves. That was the horror. After years of service, the office could write through a man before his conscience found ink.
He opened his notebook.

Field observation, unsent duplicate. Subject protected child before self-preservation. Manifestation appeared involuntary at onset, then partially directed into weapon conduit. Crowd response divided: fear, gratitude, suspicion of state handling. Recommendation in official channel will likely emphasize public manifestation. Private note: custody attempt during rescue will radicalize hostile witnesses if exposed.
He stopped at private note. Too exposed. Too true. He tore the page out, folded it into the inner lining of his coat, and wrote the acceptable version on the next leaf.

Below, one of Zoltan's men escorted a witness away through the fish market. Not forced. Persuaded with a loaf of bread in one hand and a threat in the other. Good method. Less elegant than Black Ink's, but perhaps more honest because the threat admitted it had teeth.
Merrow saw Jack look up once toward his shutter.
Not directly. Too little to prove he had been seen. Still, it made Merrow step back and feel, absurdly, like a boy caught taking apples from the wrong tree.

By evening, the official report had already begun to change. The child became minor bystander. The prepared writ became precautionary document. The creature became emergent threat responsive to subject proximity. The rescue became uncontrolled intervention. The crowd became emotionally contaminated.
Merrow copied what he was told.
Then, when no one watched, he made one error in the courier routing.
A duplicate page went to a spice pouch bound for the Chameleon. It was not courage, he told himself. Courage was a large word. He had only misplaced paper.
Paper, in his experience, did worse things every day.
Triss found Jack after the second bandage change and did not begin with the wound.

That was why he let her sit. The back room had emptied for an hour, leaving only the lamp, the table, the smell of blood under spirits, and Novigrad pressing against the shutters. Triss carried a bowl of clean water, fresh linen, and a face that had decided not to make sympathy louder than usefulness.
"Geralt's arm will heal," she said.
"He complains like it won't."
"He complains because it will. Men who think they may die become quiet or poetic. Men who will heal become tyrants about thread."
Jack held out his hand. She unwrapped the bandage. The marks had branched again. Not much. So much that her mouth went still.
"Keira should see this," she said.
"You sound unhappy about that."
"Keira enjoys interesting things before asking whether interesting things are suffering. She often asks eventually."
"You ask first."
"Not always." Triss cleaned the edges with warm water. Steam rose though the water had cooled. "I have been young, ambitious, frightened, and useful to the wrong rooms. I try to ask sooner now."
Jack let the silence stand between them. The honesty did not ask him to comfort her. That made it easier to respect.
"Does the house know you blame yourself for things I don't know?" he asked.
She smiled faintly. "The house keeps several ledgers. Geralt is in many. Yennefer pretends not to be. Dandelion signs his in decorative ink."
"And you?"
"I hide mine in practical tasks. People rarely search bandages for guilt."
He let that stand. She wrapped the hand again, not too tight, not too loose. Good work. Quiet work. The kind that kept people human without asking whether humanity had signed a receipt.
"Today will become a file," she said.
"Everything does."
"Not everything. Some things become people first if we are fast enough."
Jack looked toward the stable beyond the wall. "Fast is not always clean."
"No. But clean has begun to frighten me more than quick."
She tied the final knot and set his hand down on the table with care. Not ownership. Placement.
The distinction mattered.

chapters.chapter_title: THE WOMAN WHO SURVIVED THE FIRE
paragraphs: Asha had watched Jack kill the draconid and decided not to trust him.

This disappointed her. It also kept her alive. Hope had killed better guardians than disbelief, and Asha had inherited the duty of distrusting hope before breakfast. From the linen merchant's roof she had seen the square arrange itself around a staged kindness: a child placed near heat, a beast driven through sickness, officers waiting with paper, singers waiting with counter-songs, a sorceress in black, another with red hair, Geralt of Rivia beside the white-haired witcher, and the man himself standing in the center while the world tried to decide which noun would fit around his throat.
He had moved first for the boy.

That mattered. It did not absolve him. Cruel men could save children if the saving made them useful. Vharakthul's first priests had fed villages before counting who belonged in the ash. Balance required evidence beyond instinct, and instinct, Asha had learned, was often grief wearing a faster body.
So she followed him after the Chameleon.

He left by the kitchen door near dusk, alone except for the horse that came with him into the alley like a threat pretending to be livestock. Buck's ears shifted toward her hiding place before Jack did. Good horse. Annoying horse. She had always respected animals who distrusted destiny.
Jack stopped beneath a clothesline heavy with damp shirts. "Come out or stay useful."
Asha stepped from the shadow.

The alley smelled of rainwater, kitchen ash, fish guts, wet wool, and stale beer. Above them, a woman cursed at a leaking roof. Somewhere nearby, a man sang the first line of the wise hands song and was immediately told by three voices to put the wise hands somewhere unprintable. Novigrad was learning resistance badly, which was still resistance.

Jack stood with one hand near his sword, but not on it. The restraint was deliberate. Asha marked it. Restraint could be theater. It could also be training. His eyes were as the old rites had warned and failed to describe: red not like rubies, which belonged to merchants and court fools, but like banked heat under iron after a blade was pulled from coals. Human eyes altered by more than mutation.
"You named me in the room," he said.
"Others have named you worse."
"That does not answer why."
"No. It refuses to hurry."
Buck stepped between them by half a pace. Jack put one hand against the horse's neck without looking. The animal settled, but only to the level of considering murder later.
Asha drew a small cord from her sleeve. Five knots. Black thread around red. At the end hung a sliver of pale bone carved with a barbed star.
Asha did not begin with names because names were doors and the North had become a nation of locksmiths.
She began with a cup.

Not wine. Not tea. A bitter black drink from a packet she took from inside her coat, mixed with hot water in the Chameleon's back room while Zoltan watched as if foreign herbs might pick pockets. The scent filled the air slowly: smoke, salt, dry leaves, and a mineral sharpness like stone warmed by sun. Jack recognized none of it. The barbed-star signet recognized something and cooled against his chest.
"Drink," Asha said.
Geralt's eyes narrowed. Yennefer lifted one hand before anyone else could turn suspicion into theater.
"No compulsion," she said after a brief pass of magic. "No trance agent. Bitter in a way that qualified as assault, but not sorcery."
"Comforting," Dandelion murmured. "I have always preferred my assaults well reviewed."
Asha ignored him. "The drink is for memory. Not yours. Mine. I will not speak dead names with a dry mouth among strangers who treat history as salvage."
Jack studied the cup. He did not drink because she told him to. That was wise. He lifted it, smelled it, then offered it first to Asha.
Her eyes changed.
Good, she thought. Not obedient.

She took one swallow and did not grimace because she had been raised better than to insult discipline in public. Then she handed it back. Jack drank. The taste made his mouth tighten. It did nothing else for a moment. Then heat settled low in his chest, not the crimson heat, not the anchor pressure, but a human warmth, foreign and old, a campfire kept alive under desert stone.
"What is it?" Triss asked.
"Bitterleaf, ash salt, and water carried in a goatskin that has seen too many miles," Asha said. "A poor ceremony. It will have to serve."
"Ceremony for what?" Jack asked.
"For refusing to make your origin sound like an answer."
That silenced the room more effectively than a spell.

Asha placed five objects on the table. A bone charm. A strip of burned red silk. A cracked bead of blue glass. A small iron ring scorched black at one side. Last, a flattened button from a Nilfgaardian field coat, the imperial sun scratched off by a knife.
"These are not proof enough for courts," she said. "That is why I trust them more. Courts prefer evidence that can be owned. These survived people who did not."
Jack studied the button longest.
Asha marked that too.
Jack's palm lit under the bandage.
He drew his sword before the light finished moving.
Good, Asha thought. Not because she liked being threatened, but because a man who did not answer pain with readiness had been broken somewhere too deep for duty to use.
"Put that away," he said.
"The cord or the thing tied to it?"
"Start with the cord."
She let it drop into her palm and closed her fist. The red in his bandage dimmed. "You feel the call but do not reach for it."
"I do not reach for things I don't understand."
"That is almost wisdom."
"It is suspicion with better posture."
For the first time, Asha nearly smiled. The expression hurt the burn scars along her neck, so she let it pass.

"I am Asha var Faithel," she said. "Last sworn ash-reader of the western remnant, former guardian of a house your northern records call dead, former prisoner of men who believed duty could be extracted by heat, and the woman who has searched for the signet at your throat for longer than you have known its name."
Jack did not soften. "Everyone arrives with a title when they want something."
"I want nothing from you in an alley. That would be poor ritual and worse manners."
"Then why follow me?"
"To see what you do when no one watches for a file."
He looked toward the street. "People are always watching for a file now."
"Yes. That is why I chose the alley. Fewer clerks. More rats. Rats are less offended by truth."
Buck breathed loudly. Jack's mouth moved by less than a smile.

A man entered the alley from the far end carrying a basket of laundry. He saw Jack, saw Asha, saw Buck, and remembered an appointment elsewhere. Asha waited until he had gone. Jack did not fill the silence. Another mark in his favor. Men eager to be believed usually spent their first chance destroying it.
"You tested me," he said.
"Yes."
"Result?"
"Incomplete."
"Useful. I like being graded by strangers in alleys."
"Do not mistake irritation for oppression. You will need your anger for better enemies."
His eyes sharpened. "You know Veyrane."

"I know his kind. Some wore temple colors. Some wore imperial black. Some carried scholar seals. Some came smiling to burning houses because people save ledgers before children when trained correctly."
The alley became narrower around the last sentence. Jack noticed the scars again, not with pity. With calculation and respect.
"You survived the fire," he said.
"One of them."

Asha opened her collar and revealed the rest of the burn pattern. It ran over her shoulder in branching lines, not random damage, but a symbol interrupted by pain and healed badly by necessity. Jack's expression changed at last. Barely. Asha saw it.
"Faithel," he said.
"You know the word?"
"Vesemir wrote it badly. Keira pronounced it worse."
"Mages do that to most things east of their vanity."
Buck's ears shifted back. Someone approached the alley mouth again. This time the footstep was too regular to be laundry. Jack turned to Asha. She nodded once.

The man who entered wore a city watch cloak and the face of a paid afterthought. His hand rested near a whistle. He had two others behind him, one visible, one trying not to be. The visible one carried a cudgel. The hidden one had a crossbow. Poor spacing. Good intent. Bad future.
"You there," the watchman said. "Public safety inquiry. Remain where you are."
Jack held Asha in silence. "Yours?"
"No."
"Pity."
"Why?"
"I would have judged your training."

The watchman brought the whistle to his mouth. Asha's cord snapped out. Not magic in the northern style. No gesture, no word, no light. The knots struck the whistle hand, and the bone charm touched skin. The man froze with his mouth open, not charmed, not controlled, simply remembering every oath he had ever broken in the same instant. His knees gave way. The cudgel man rushed. Jack hit him with the flat of his sword hard, ending the charge without ending the man. Buck turned his hindquarters with professional economy and introduced the third man to a wall.
The crossbow bolt went into a hanging shirt.
Jack inspected the damage. "Laundry casualty."
"Novigrad will mourn," Asha said.
They tied the three men with the shirt line and left them in a row beside the fish barrels. Jack checked the first man's pulse. Asha watched that too.
"Still incomplete?" he asked.
"Less so."
The Chameleon back room received Asha poorly, which was wiser than receiving her warmly.

Yennefer stood the moment Asha entered. Triss put down her cup. Geralt's hand went near his sword and stopped because Jack's had not. Dandelion looked delighted until Priscilla touched his wrist, which suggested she had heard something in the room he had not. Zoltan looked at Asha's boots and then at the burn scars near her collar.
"Desert stitching," he said. "Old. Expensive. Not for decoration."
Asha turned to him. "You know cloth."
"I know what people pay for when they pretend not to. Sit. Or don't. But if you plan to speak in riddles, speak loudly. I hate asking twice."
"Good," Asha said. "Riddles are for cowards who want applause for withholding maps."
Dandelion placed a hand over his heart. "I feel attacked by the geography of that sentence."
"You probably deserve it," Asha said.
Geralt turned to Jack. Jack gave no warning, no reassurance, only a small nod that meant he had decided Asha was dangerous in ways worth hearing.

Asha remained standing. Duty did not always sit when invited. "Your North has fragments. Stolen sketches. Sick translations. Black Ink summaries. Vesemir's frightened mercy. Mage guesses. Bard songs. Useful, perhaps. Not doctrine."
Yennefer folded her arms. "And you have doctrine."

"I have broken doctrine, ash memory, survivor names, and enough truth to make every comfortable room worse." Asha's gaze moved to Jack. "Helena Morningstar was your mother. Jacob was your father, Nilfgaardian by birth, oath-blade by choice. They died in 1249 when the remnant houses were struck. Zerrikanterment, Last Warden, died there as well. Vharakthul, the Obsidian Crown, did not die. He was already prisoned. The strike was not meant only to kill guardians. It was meant to poison the key that would one day maintain the lock."
The room took the names badly.
Not because they were grand. Grand names could be laughed at. These names arrived with the weight of people who had been kept from Jack not by fate, but by fire, ignorance, and deliberate violence.

Jack's face went still. Geralt saw the stillness and went quieter. Yennefer did not interrupt. Triss's eyes softened and sharpened at once, as if she were already arranging where grief would need support later.
"Key," Jack said.

Asha nodded. "Not ruler. Not chosen sword. Not dragon prince. Not prophecy's pet. Key, wound, and carrier of corrupted seal-force. Your blood was meant to help keep a lock shut. During the massacre, the enemy rite contaminated that blood. Zerrikanterment saved you by compressing his last Cinder into the line, but he sealed the poison in with the protection. Crimson resonance is the grinding of both."
"You said you disliked riddles," Jack said.
"I do. This is the plain version."
Lambert would have made a joke. Dandelion looked as if he wanted to and had temporarily misplaced the cruelty needed for it.
Yennefer's voice was low. "You are telling him his body is a battlefield."
"No," Asha said. "The world already told him that. I am telling him whose dead stand under the field."
Geralt took one step toward the table. "Why now?"

Asha's eyes cut to him. "Because you and Vesemir hid him well; it broke my trail. Because Faithel rites read resonance through anchor-sites, not tavern rumor. Broken Crown lit the old ash. Novigrad made the trail speak. Because Black Ink has learned the right words to do harm and too little truth to fear them. Because your old man's fear succeeded and failed in the same shape."
Geralt accepted that because denying it would have insulted the room.
Jack picked up the black disk from Kaer Morhen and placed it on the table. Asha saw it and, for the first time, lost color.
"Where did you find that?"
"Vesemir hid it."
She did not touch it. Her hand hovered over it as Yennefer's had once hovered over the red mark in the cellar. Then she withdrew.
"Guardian death-token," she said. "Given to a child if the house expected the line to travel under protection. It should have been with Helena."
"Was she alive when I was found?"

The question entered without warning and made several people look away. Jack did not. He turned to Asha because she was the one who had brought his mother into the room and therefore owed it the cruelty that kept truth intact.
Asha's throat moved once. "No."
"You saw her?"
"After."
"Say it."

Geralt moved slightly, but Yennefer stopped him with one glance. Protection at the wrong moment became theft. Geralt hated her for being right. He loved her history and recognized the shape of the hate and let it pass.

Asha said, "Helena died holding the east stair. Jacob died three paces from her with a broken sword and no shield. Zerrikanterment's body was not body by then, only light and ash and heat so great the stone remembered it for years. You were beneath the fallen lower wall. The signet was around your neck. You were breathing. We thought that was mercy. Later I learned mercy had teeth."
She tested him once more before she gave the dead their names.

It was a small cruelty. Necessary cruelties were still cruelties; Asha had stopped excusing them with prettier words decades ago. She took the iron ring from the table and rolled it toward the edge. It fell. Jack caught it before it struck the floor.
The ring burned him.

No flame. No visible mark beyond the red lines tightening under his bandage. But the smell changed: hot iron, old smoke, a courtyard in rain, a cradle that had been dragged too quickly over stone. Geralt stepped forward. Yennefer caught his sleeve without looking. Jack held the ring until the heat passed.
"You could have let it fall," Asha said.
"Yes."
"Why didn't you?"
"It mattered to you."
"You do not know me."
"I know how people look at things they have not forgiven themselves for keeping."

The room took that in carefully. Dandelion looked down. Zoltan muttered something into his beard. Triss's face softened and then sharpened because softness alone would not protect anyone here. Yennefer watched Asha now, not Jack, as if the test had revealed more about the examiner than the examined.

Asha accepted the ring back. Her fingers closed around it. "Helena wore this through three disguises. Handmaid, widow, trader's sister. None fit. She hated bad lies. She used them anyway because good lies take time and she was always spending time on other people's survival."
Jack said nothing.

Good again. Some men rushed grief as if claiming it quickly proved depth. Jack did not claim what he had not earned. That restraint hurt to watch. It meant the child Asha had failed to find had become a man without the memory that would make mourning easy.

"Jacob took the button from his coat the night he refused orders," she said. "He scraped off the sun because he said a man should not wear an empire on his heart after choosing against it. Helena told him it was theatrical. He told her theatrical men sometimes stood in front because practical men had already run. She laughed. Not loudly. She was not safe enough for loud laughter by then."
The button lay between them like a coin from a country that no longer existed.
Jack's voice came lower. "You knew them."
"I served her. I guarded her badly. I loved them in the way people love a household that gives them purpose and then asks too much."
"And me?"
Asha did not soften the facts. "I was told to find you after the fire. I failed for twenty-three years."
That was the first thing she gave him that was truly hers.
Jack studied the disk.
His hand did not shake. That was the problem.

Triss rose quietly and went to the sideboard. She poured water and placed it near him without touching his shoulder. It was such a small act that it almost escaped the room. Almost. Jack looked at the cup, then at her, then back to Asha.
"Why did no one come?"

Asha took the blow because it was deserved by the dead and the living alike. "We did. Too late. Then not at all, because our survivors were hunted, our routes watched, our rites broken. I searched through burn lists, port records, witcher rumors, grave mistakes, and a hundred boys with the wrong eyes. Then you vanished into Kaer Morhen's walls and became a rumor that refused to answer."
"Vesemir," Jack said.
"Yes."
Geralt closed his eyes for one breath.
Dandelion, very softly, said, "The past has dreadful punctuality. It always arrives after the chairs are set."
Zoltan turned to him. "That yours?"
"Unfortunately."
"Keep it."
Asha looked toward Dandelion. "You map songs."
"On my better days. On worse days I create evidence for future prosecution."

"Then map this carefully. No song. Not yet. The names I spoke are not for crowds. Black Ink will turn Helena into breeding stock, Jacob into imperial implication, Zerrikanterment into public dragon panic, and Vharakthul into cult bait before your printers finish drying ink."
Priscilla nodded. "Then we keep the public fight on ownership, not origin."
"Good," Asha said. "Someone in this city has ears."
"Two," Dandelion said. "Artistically shaped."
"One mouth too many."
Zoltan grinned. "You'll fit."
Jack left the room before the questions were done.

No one stopped him. That was perhaps the first mercy the night offered without demanding a witness. He went to the stable behind the Chameleon, where Buck had been given the largest stall after biting a groom only symbolically. The horse looked up as Jack entered, considered the smell of grief, and lowered his head over the stall door.
Jack rested his forehead against Buck's neck.
The horse stood still.

There were no words under the scent of hay and horse sweat. No old names, no diagrams, no key, no carrier, no Zerrikanterment, no Obsidian Crown. Only breath, warmth, the slow shift of a living animal deciding that movement could wait. Jack stayed there longer than discipline liked.
Geralt came after a while.

He stopped outside the stall. The lantern in his hand made the straw gold and the shadows merciful. He did not speak until Buck allowed him to stand close. That took two breaths and one skeptical ear.
"Asha is still in the room," Geralt said.
"Good for the room."
"Yennefer is interrogating her."
"Bad for Asha."
"Triss is keeping them from killing each other."
"Bad for Triss."
Geralt leaned against the stall door. "Dandelion is writing nothing and suffering visibly."
Jack's mouth moved against Buck's neck. Not quite a smile. "Good for art."
Silence returned. Geralt could have filled it with apology. He had what he needed. He did not, which was why Jack eventually spoke.
"My mother had a name."
"Yes."
"My father too."
"Yes."
"I don't remember either."
Geralt's hand tightened around the lantern handle. "No."
Jack lifted his head. His eyes looked darker in the stable light, less flame than wound. "Do names matter if there is no memory attached?"

Geralt thought of Ciri's name spoken by enemies, by friends, by fathers who were and were not fathers. He thought of Yennefer saying Cirilla with fury sharpened into love. He thought of Vesemir not writing Jack's name where others could find it, as if absence could protect a child from being wanted wrongly.
"Yes," Geralt said. "But not by themselves. You have to decide what they get to mean now."
"That advice?"
"Maybe."
"Needs work."
"Most of mine does."
Buck pushed his nose into Geralt's shoulder, not gently. Geralt accepted the correction.
Jack looked back toward the tavern. "Zerrikania."
"Eventually."
"Soon."
"Maybe. We still need to know what Black Ink will do with Ciri's file."
The name changed the air. Ciri remained absent and increasingly present, which was how dangerous names behaved.
"She should know," Jack said.
Geralt watched him without blinking. "Yes."
"From you?"
"If she'll hear it."
"From me?"
"Not yet."
Jack's expression sharpened.

Geralt raised one hand. "Not because you don't have the right. Because she is surrounded by people waiting to turn every meeting into a policy. We choose the room first. That is not hiding her from you."
"It sounds familiar."
"It should. That's why I'm saying it before it becomes easier to lie."
Jack studied him for a long time. Then he nodded once. It was not agreement. It was permission for the sentence to survive until tested.
Behind them, the Chameleon's back door opened. Yennefer stood there, black hair catching lantern light, face controlled and eyes less so.
"Ilyra has sent another message," she said.
Geralt straightened. "Ciri?"
"Not yet." Yennefer's mouth tightened. "But the dossier is moving. We have less time than I hoped, which is inconvenient because I had hoped for very little."
Jack stepped away from Buck.
The horse immediately bit the stable door.
"He objects," Geralt said.
"To what?" Jack asked.
"Probably history."
For once, Jack could not argue.
Asha told the story of the fire only after Yennefer stopped asking like a sorceress.

At first the questions came sharp and correct: dates, route markers, witness lines, rite components, whether Zerrikanterment was a name or title, whether Vharakthul's contamination could be separated from the Cinder-Seal, whether Jack's witcher mutations had worsened or stabilized the original architecture. Asha answered what she could and refused what had to be refused. The refusals made Yennefer colder. The cold made Asha harder. The room suffered accordingly.
Then Triss put bread on the table.

No spell. No strategy. Just bread, olives, watered wine, and a knife with a cracked handle. Yennefer regarded it as if it had interrupted a duel. Triss said nothing. Asha took a piece because the body had old authority over pride, and because hunger could make testimony theatrical if left untended.
Yennefer sat.
"Helena," she said, and this time it was not a question made for conquest.

Asha studied the bread in her hands. "She was not queen. That matters. Northern minds hear blood-house and make throne. House Morningstar was adjacent to power because power kept maps, wells, and guards. The custodians were not meant to rule. They were meant to be ignored until needed and remembered only by those who knew why forgetting was useful. Helena hated the arrangement and obeyed it better than any of us."
Jack stood near the window. He did not turn. Geralt watched him watching the street.
"Jacob?" Triss asked.

"Nilfgaardian. Deserter, if the empire wrote it. Oath-blade, if Helena wrote it. Traitor, if his first commander survived. Husband, though the rite used another word." Asha's mouth tightened. "He had a terrible singing voice and believed watered beer was proof the North lacked civilization. He taught me three Nilfgaardian curses and one prayer for horses."
