Jack's shoulders moved once. Too little to be grief. Too much not to be.

Asha continued because stopping would make the next words larger. "The fire came before dawn. Not wildfire. Prepared heat. Black oils, powdered bone, silver dust, prayer hooks, and a rite meant to stain the blood before the Last Warden could close around it. We held three doors. Lost two. Helena sent me with the child route, then called me back because the lower wall had fallen and the child was gone from the cradle."
Geralt's eyes closed.

"We found the cradle under stone," Asha said. "Empty. Blood on the cloth. Then Zerrikanterment came down through the smoke. Not as stories say dragons come. No wings breaking clouds. No golden sermon. Heat, light, and a pressure that made every liar in the courtyard scream. He knew the line had narrowed to one breathing child. He knew the enemy had touched the key. He chose compression over purity. He saved what could be saved."
"And trapped the contamination," Yennefer said.
"Yes."
Jack turned then. "Did he know?"
Asha held his gaze. "I think he understood the choice and hated it."
"That is not an answer."
"It is the only honest one left."
The room took that badly because it was true.

Later, when the bread had gone hard at the edges and the first candles burned low, Asha placed her bone charm beside Jack's hand. "I do not ask you to accept duty tonight. I do not ask you to trust me. I do not ask you to mourn people you cannot remember on command."
"What do you ask?"

"Do not let the North's fragments convince you they are the whole truth. Do not let Black Ink's hunger convince you your body is public infrastructure. Do not let our dead make you their obedient monument."
Jack studied the charm. "And if Zerrikania does?"
"Then I will have brought you to another cage and must help you break it."
Yennefer studied Asha for a long second. "That, at last, sounded like an answer."
"It was expensive," Asha said.
"Good answers usually are."
Jack picked up the charm. It did not burn. It weighed less than its history. That felt wrong. It also felt survivable.
They laid the evidence on Zoltan's table because the table was already scarred.

Fine tables encouraged lies. Polished surfaces asked people to behave as if history could be arranged symmetrically, with the clean papers on one side and the ugly ones on the other. Zoltan's table had knife marks, beer rings, wax scars, two gouges from an argument involving a halfling and a cheese invoice, and a burned corner Dandelion claimed was artistic. It accepted ugly things without pretending they were guests.

Kaer Morhen records went north. Novigrad ledgers went west. Triss's courier notes formed a precise line in the center. Yennefer's sketches of magical dead zones sat above them, black ink over fine paper, each mark sharp, like threats. Dandelion's song map covered the right side, all hooks, phrases, and arrows drawn with theatrical desperation. Zoltan's wax and coin trails anchored the bottom. Asha placed her bone charm beside the black disk from Vesemir's cache and made no attempt to explain why every candle leaned away from it.
Jack stood with his back to the wall.
Geralt stood beside him.
That was noticed by everyone and named by no one.
"Say it plainly," Zoltan said. "If I have to stare at one more decorative line on a mage map, I'll begin taxing elegance."

Triss touched the middle page. "Black Ink is not merely following Jack. They are testing which public and legal phrases create resonance. Host suitability, hereditary infrastructure, bloodline custody, voluntary cooperation, anomalous witcher asset. Each phrase appears near a physical event or a planned event."
"Words as bells," Jack said.
"Yes," Yennefer said. "And your name as a clapper."
Dandelion winced. "That metaphor is effective and unpleasant."
"Then remember it," Yennefer said.

Asha pointed to Yennefer's dead-zone sketches. "These are anchor sickness. Not full breaches. Old sites with wounded pressure. The North built over more than graves. It built over broken maintenance points and forgot the stones were not decorative."
Geralt studied the map. "Broken Crown. St. Luthar's well. Willenford mill."
"Not all anchor-sites," Asha said. "Some are echoes. Some are places where human rot made the old architecture easier to hear. That distinction matters."
"How much?" Zoltan asked.
"A thing people die over if misread."
"Helpful scale."

Triss added one more paper, Ilyra Sarn's latest note, delivered through a spice merchant who had not known he carried anything except pepper and a small private resentment against imperial tariffs. The note had been opened, resealed, and then opened again by Yennefer because trust, she explained, did not survive being lazy.
Geralt read it aloud.

The dossier has moved from advisory summary into restricted imperial circulation. It does not name Jack directly in the first paragraph. It names a crimson-eyed witcher, Geralt of Rivia, Kaer Morhen omissions, potential bloodline custody, and destabilizing association with Her Highness's private history. Your window to speak as family narrows. If you delay, the state will teach her the shape before you give her the facts.
No one moved when he finished.
Ciri's absence had become the largest person in the room.

Yennefer took the note back with fingers that did not tremble because she would not permit them the vanity. "Emhyr's people will see risk. Northern enemies will see leverage. Black Ink will see opportunity. Ciri will see betrayal if she learns everyone moved around her again."
Geralt looked down at the table. "Then I write."
"You write badly," Dandelion said, too gently to be joking.
"Good. She'll know it's mine."
Triss turned to him. "Too little. Ilyra said the room matters."
"What room?"
"Not court. Not Corvo Bianco if roads are watched. Not the Chameleon if Black Ink knows we use it. Somewhere she can arrive as Ciri before anyone makes her arrive as title."
Asha touched the bone charm. "North first. East after."
Jack turned to her. "Meaning?"

"She must be told in the North because the wound here is already moving toward her. You must go east because the doctrine that explains you was born there. Come north, come east. Two calls. One for truth before policy. One for origin before the seal worsens."
"Convenient phrasing," Dandelion said.

"Old phrasing," Asha replied. "From a maintenance verse children used to remember routes when maps were forbidden. Come north for witness, come east for water, come home only after the fire names you."
"That's worse," Zoltan said.
"Old songs usually are. People confuse age with quality."
Dandelion looked offended. "On behalf of songs, I object selectively."

Jack picked up Ilyra's note. He read the phrase destabilizing association with Her Highness's private history and felt anger arrive without heat. Cold anger was more useful. It sharpened edges without wasting blood.
"They are already using her around me," he said.
"Yes," Yennefer said.
"Then I should not meet her."
Geralt's head came up.
Jack continued before anyone could interrupt. "If the meeting creates policy leverage, don't give them the meeting. Send the file. Send warning. Send whatever words keep her clear."
Yennefer's expression became very still. "You are not the first person to think removing yourself from Ciri's life would protect her. The previous attempts did not impress me."
Geralt did not look away from Jack. That, more than Yennefer's accuracy, made the sentence land.
"I am not her life," Jack said.
"No," Triss said. "But you are becoming part of the danger around it. She deserves to know the difference."
"Knowing makes her vulnerable."
"Ignorance makes her governable," Yennefer said. "Choose which insult you prefer."
The room held the answer before Jack did. He hated that. He hated rooms that knew before he chose. He hated, more than that, how often the hate was simply fear wearing useful armor.

Geralt set both hands on the table. "Ciri survived because people helped her. They nearly killed her by confusing aid with control. I said that in Kaer Morhen. I am saying it again because I need to hear it too. We don't protect her by making another circle around the facts."
"And if truth pulls her into the trap?" Jack asked.
"Then we make sure she sees the trap before stepping."
"That sounds like hope."
"No," Geralt said. "Hope is what Dandelion spends on hats. This is preparation."
Dandelion touched his feather. "My hats are prepared for history."
"Your hats are evidence against democracy," Zoltan said.
The joke did not fix the room. It did what jokes were meant to do when used by people with sense: gave breath somewhere to stand.
Geralt wrote to Ciri in the early morning while the others argued over routes.

He chose a small room above the Chameleon's kitchen because the table was uneven and therefore honest. The first page went badly. He wrote Ciri, then stopped for so long the ink dried on the nib. He could write contracts, diagrams of monster nests, lists of oils, warnings, crude directions, and once, under duress, a thank-you note to a duchess. Writing to his daughter about a hidden young witcher he had helped keep from her made every word look like it had arrived carrying its own noose.
He began again.
Ciri,

He stared at cowardly. Too easy? Too indulgent? Men could turn self-accusation into a request for comfort if they were not careful. Ciri would see that. Yennefer would see it faster and with worse commentary.
He crossed out nothing. Let the ugly word work.

There is a witcher named Jack Morningstar. Vesemir found him as a child. I was there. We hid him from mages, courts, hunters, and from you. We believed two hunted children near each other would draw every predator with a map. We were not entirely wrong. We were not right.
The room blurred for a moment. Geralt blinked once and blamed the kitchen smoke below because age deserved at least one useful lie.

He wrote of Black Ink, of language turning a man into use, of Jack's body being treated as bloodline custody and public risk. He did not write everything Asha had said. Not in a letter that might be opened. He wrote enough for Ciri to choose whether to come and enough for her to know the people who loved her were no longer choosing around her without consequence.
At the end he paused again.
If you come, come as yourself before anyone makes you arrive as Empress-designate. If you do not come, I will understand. That is also a lie. I will try to understand. That is closer.
He sanded the page. Folded it. Sealed it with plain wax, no wolf mark. A father writing as a father could not afford symbols that invited offices to join the room.
When he opened the door, Yennefer stood outside.
"Were you listening?" he asked.
"No. I was considering whether to."
"And?"
"I decided virtue was less exhausting this morning. May I read it?"
He gave her the letter. She read without expression until the last line. Then the expression changed, not enough for most people to name.
"Closer," she said.
"What?"
"You wrote that is closer. Good. She trusts corrected lies more than polished ones."
Geralt took the letter back. "You writing too?"
"Yes. Mine will be less apologetic and more terrifying to intercept."
"Good."

Yennefer looked toward the stairs. The Chameleon was waking below: pots, muttering, Dandelion arguing with an invoice, Zoltan threatening a courier with honest pay, Triss asking for ordinary ink, Jack somewhere in the stable because grief and horses remained reliable conspirators.
"You understand," she said, "that when Ciri comes, she will be angry."
"Yes."
"At you. At me. At Triss perhaps, though less fairly. At the situation. At Jack for existing where old pain can find him. At herself for recognizing him too quickly."
"Yes."
"You will not defend yourself by saying you meant well."
Geralt turned to her. "No."
Yennefer nodded. "Progress. Appalling how long it takes men to become minimally useful."
"I'm sixty-one."
"Exactly."
He almost smiled. She did not, but the old shape of shared understanding passed between them and did not ask to be more than it was.
Jack accepted help in the stable because the stable gave him something to do with his hands.

Acceptance in a room with tables and watching eyes looked too much like surrender. Acceptance while checking Buck's hooves, counting feed, repairing a cracked strap, and listening to Zoltan explain safe routes felt more like strategy. That was perhaps cowardly. It was also workable, and Jack had survived too long to despise workable things.
Zoltan spread a road map over a feed bin. Buck tried to eat the eastern edge. Zoltan removed it just in time.
"Your horse has political opinions about Zerrikania," he said.
"He dislikes being left out."

"Sensible. Now listen. North route to the old meeting ground here." Zoltan tapped a spot beyond Oxenfurt, away from main imperial courier roads and near old witcher paths that Geralt could pretend he wasn't sentimental. "Ciri's people can reach it under cover if Ilyra has half the skill Triss says. You, Geralt, and whoever hasn't been arrested by then wait no longer than two days. Then east by stages. Not straight. Straight roads are for taxes and ambushes."
Asha, standing near the stall door, nodded. "We will need water routes after the Pontar. Then dry roads. Then someone who knows which border shrine is a shrine and which is a listening post."
"You?" Jack asked.
"Sometimes."
"Poor answer."
"True one."
He looked at Geralt, who had entered quietly enough that only Buck's ears and Jack's shoulders admitted it.
"Annoying, isn't it?" Geralt said.
"You both overuse that."
"Truth?"
"Short answers."

Triss came in with a packet of letters wrapped in cloth. Yennefer followed with another, sealed in black wax that seemed to threaten the fingers of anyone considering curiosity. Dandelion arrived last, carrying a smaller packet and a piece of bread he was pretending was breakfast rather than nervous habit. Priscilla stood behind him, hooded for travel, expression calm in a way that meant she had already considered the fear and given it no vote. Zoltan took all three packets and placed them in different bags.
"One through Ilyra," Triss said. "One through a Kovir banking route. One through a courier who thinks he carries theater gossip."
"Insulting," Dandelion said. "He carries excellent theater gossip."
Yennefer turned to Zoltan. "If any route is compromised, burn the outer wrapper and send the ash through the river code Triss described."
Zoltan grunted. "I've smuggled men, money, cursed idols, three priests, one entire printing press, and Dandelion out of places where he was not welcome. I can manage letters."
"The printing press was heroic," Dandelion said.
"The printing press complained less."
Jack tied the repaired strap. His hands were steady now. That did not mean his mind had settled. It meant the body had found a task small, and the body could obey it.
"Roles," he said.
The room turned toward him.
He kept his eyes on the knot. "If we are doing this, say roles plainly. No one drifts around me pretending not to guard, steer, study, or use."
Triss answered first, because Triss understood rooms. "I maintain courier lines and keep Ciri's arrival from becoming a state event. I also monitor Black Ink language and mage channels."
Yennefer said, "I identify magical pressure and prevent anyone in this charming catastrophe from confusing necessity with permission."
"That is not a role."
"It is when I do it."
Zoltan said, "Money, routes, forged marks, hostile debt correction."
Dandelion lifted a hand. "Public narrative suspicion, rumor infection control, and refusing, heroically, to write the obvious ballad."
Priscilla added, "Hooks. I hear them before he does."
"Humiliating but accurate," Dandelion said.
Asha turned to Jack. "Doctrine. Faithel memory. Testing whether the East will recognize you as bearer or mistake you for breach."
Geralt said nothing.
Jack let the silence examine him first.
Geralt's answer came slowly, which made it better. "Beside. Until you tell me otherwise. And sometimes after, if otherwise sounds like dying alone because you dislike needing people."
"That is ownership adjacent."
"Yes. I'll watch it. You watch it too."
The honesty made the stable colder and warmer at once.

Jack finished the knot. Buck nosed his shoulder, hard, pushing him half a step. The horse had opinions about most plans and respected none that did not include oats. Jack reached into the feed bag, gave him a handful, and let the small practical kindness stand without title.
"I accept help," Jack said.
No one moved.
"Not custody. Not management. Not ownership. Help. If that changes, I leave. If I try to leave because fear is easier than trust, you may argue. Once."
"Only once?" Dandelion asked.
"You get half."
"Cruel but tailored."
Geralt nodded. "Accepted."
Yennefer's eyes softened in a way that would have been invisible if anyone named it. "Witnessed."
Triss smiled faintly. "Recorded nowhere official."
Zoltan closed the map. "Good. Now someone pay for the oats before the horse classifies us as debtors."
The last thing Part III's road gave them before they left Novigrad was a file line.

It arrived through Merrow, though none of them knew his name yet. A copy placed in the wrong courier pouch. A mistake perhaps. Or conscience wearing the mask of poor sorting. The page had been folded twice, sealed once, opened, then resealed with wax too cheap for the office that had sent it. Zoltan found it because cheap wax offended him and because the courier had tried not to look at the packet after delivering it.
Yennefer read it aloud in the alley behind the Chameleon while the horses waited.

Senior review addendum. Subject's network has expanded beyond occupational association into emotional defense structure. Geralt of Rivia functions as obstructive paternal vector. Triss Merigold and Yennefer of Vengerberg constitute high-risk magical interference. Novigrad rumor control partially compromised. Faithel element suspected after public event. Recommended escalation: connect subject to Elder Blood advisory file before autonomous family disclosure occurs.
Geralt looked toward the north road.

Jack listened to the phrase emotional defense structure and felt something in him resist the insult by recognizing the fact beneath it. Black Ink had tried to make care sound like machinery. The horror was that care did have structure. It had routes, rooms, hands, debts, letters, horses, jokes, old guilt, and people willing to stand near danger without owning the person at its center.
That did not make it a cage.
Not yet.

He folded the page and put it beside Vesemir's note, Asha's bone charm, and the black disk from Kaer Morhen. Evidence. Not identity. He would have to keep making that distinction until the world tired of trying to make it for him.
At the city gate, Dandelion embraced Geralt again and Jack not at all, which proved he had learned something about survival. He instead offered Jack a folded scrap.
"Not a song," Dandelion said quickly. "A line. For emergencies."
Jack opened it.
A man may be useful and still belong first to himself.
Jack let the silence answer first.
Dandelion adjusted his feather. "It is not perfect. Perfection is expensive and often late."
"It's usable."
The bard placed a hand over his heart. "A review of devastating restraint. I shall treasure it in bitterness."
Zoltan handed Geralt a pouch. "Coin, permits, names. Don't spend the names unless you have to. They're worth more and complain after use."
Priscilla kissed Dandelion's cheek, then turned to Jack. "Do not let them make you easier to sing than to know."
"I'll try."
"Try harder when frightened."
He nodded. That was fair.

Triss and Yennefer did not say goodbye at the gate. They had learned the foolishness of dramatic departures. Triss checked the packet seams. Yennefer checked the road with magic and found three old watchers, two new ones, and one man so bad at hiding that she left him alone out of professional contempt. Geralt mounted Roach. Jack mounted Buck. Asha adjusted her cloak and looked east though they would go north first.
The road beyond Novigrad was muddy, crowded, and dishonest.
It was also theirs for the next few miles.
Geralt measured Jack's face. "Beside?"
Jack glanced toward the city, then toward the north, where Ciri's truth waited somewhere behind couriers, titles, love, and policy learning to speak first.
"Beside," he said.
They rode.
They left Novigrad in rain so thin it felt petty.

Rain had many characters. Storms made declarations. Downpours washed alleys clean for three minutes and then bragged about it. Mist pretended to be gentler than it was. This rain simply found collars, cuffs, saddle seams, boot tops, and the vulnerable space between patience and irritation. It turned the road out of the city into brown paste and made the guards at the gate twice as unpleasant because discomfort loved company and rarely had the courage to call it need.

Zoltan's permits worked. This surprised no one except the youngest guard, who read them three times because correct papers in Novigrad looked more suspicious than forged ones. Yennefer solved the delay by asking him to spell his superior's name for a complaint. His literacy improved dramatically. Dandelion waved from under the Chameleon's awning with Priscilla beside him, both already turning back toward the work of making the city less obedient. Triss rode with the group only to the first old shrine.
There she would turn toward the courier road and a chain of messages delicate and likely to break if anyone called it strategy too loudly.
Geralt noticed Jack counting riders.
"Still time to leave," Geralt said.
Jack looked ahead. "You offering?"
"Naming."
"Triss's influence."
"Probably."

They rode a while in silence. Buck disliked the mud but approved of leaving the city, which he showed by not trying to bite anyone for almost an hour. Roach seemed unimpressed by this moral progress. Asha rode a lean dun mare with desert tack altered for northern rain. The mare ignored Buck with priestly discipline, which offended him more than hostility would have.

At the old shrine, Triss dismounted. The shrine had once belonged to Melitele, then to the Eternal Fire, then to no one with a budget. Someone had left a clay cup of milk there anyway. The milk had soured. The gesture had not. Triss checked the road behind them before speaking, because she was warm, not careless.
"I will keep the letters moving," she said. "Ilyra first. Then Kovir. Then the false theater gossip, assuming Dandelion has not made it true out of vanity."
"He will try," Geralt said.
She touched his arm, careful of the bandage. "Do not let guilt make your decisions faster than your sense."
"Which sense?"
"Any. Use smell if the others fail."

He turned to her, and for a moment the rain, road, Asha, Jack, Yennefer, and the whole ugly machinery of Black Ink stepped back far enough for the house in Toussaint to exist between them. Triss kissed him. Briefly. Presently. No apology to history. No performance for it either.
Yennefer looked away because dignity and kindness occasionally shared a door. Jack saw that. Triss saw him seeing. Neither named it.
Triss came to Jack last. She adjusted the edge of his glove where the bandage would rub. He could have done it himself. He let her. That was the whole conversation until she looked up.
"Help does not require gratitude every time," she said. "But occasionally nod, or Geralt will think you are dying."
Jack nodded.
"See? Efficient."
She mounted and turned down the courier road. The group watched until the trees took her green cloak.

Yennefer's face was unreadable. Geralt's was not, if one knew where to look. Asha watched both and said nothing. Jack understood then that old love and present love were not two blades crossed for spectacle. They were roads that had survived different wars and still had to meet at bridges no one trusted.

They rode north after that, toward the place Ilyra's next message named only as the broken mill where no grain turns. It was not Willenford. Not Jack's first village. Another mill, another broken mechanism, another private room where Ciri might arrive as herself if the gods, roads, clerks, and fathers behaved better than history suggested.
At dusk, Geralt drew level with Jack.
"When she comes," he said, "do not let the title speak first."
"I don't know how to speak to her."
"Good. People who think they do usually want something."
"I want something."
Geralt studied the side of his face.
Jack kept his eyes on the road. "To not be another burden placed in her hands by people who love her."
Geralt's expression changed with the pain of an accurate cut. "Then don't be. Be a man with his own trouble. She respects that more than burdens."
"That advice?"
"Maybe."
"Still needs work."
"I know."

The rain stopped near dark. It left the road shining and the trees dripping. Somewhere ahead, a nightjar called once and fell silent. Buck lifted his head, listening. Jack felt the signet at his throat cool, not in warning, but in recognition of distance closing.
North for witness.
East for water.

The words did not come from him. They came from Asha's old verse, from Vesemir's paper, from Black Ink's files, from Ciri's approaching dossier, from the dead who had waited too long to be named. Jack did not like inheriting words. He liked less that some of them were useful.
He rode beside Geralt until the dark took the road's edges.
Extract from a sealed memorandum carried under the name Ilyra Sarn, copied in a cipher Triss Merigold considered serviceable and Yennefer of Vengerberg considered optimistic:
To my principal,

The language is familiar enough that I dislike writing it down. A hidden Wolf School witcher, name withheld in outer channels but recoverable if one follows Geralt of Rivia's recent movement, has become the center of overlapping administrative, magical, and rumor operations. Current hostile descriptors include host suitability, bloodline custody, hereditary infrastructure, voluntary cooperation preferred, and public-risk anomaly. I know you will notice the shape of the crime before I describe it.

He is not reported to have attacked civilians. Repeated accounts, including hostile ones, show him moving toward civilian danger even when that danger appears staged to produce a record against him. This does not make him harmless. It makes the people writing harmlessness and danger into legal costumes more dangerous.

Geralt is involved. Yennefer is involved. Triss Merigold is involved. The bard is involved, which means the songs are already either a problem or a weapon, depending on the hour. A Zerrikanian survivor has entered the matter and has spoken names I will not commit to open paper.
You once told me that the first sign of a cage is not iron, but people lowering their voices and calling it necessary.
They are lowering their voices now.
I await your decision.
I.S.

The memorandum traveled under three wrong names, through a courier who thought he carried theater gossip, a priest who believed he carried a list of orphan stipends, and a laundress who knew perfectly well she carried trouble and charged accordingly. By the time it neared Ciri's hands, the outer papers had become boring, which let them survive inspection. That was Triss's gift, Yennefer's suspicion, and Zoltan's contempt for official curiosity working in one narrow packet. It did not make the facts safe. It only made it arrive before the lie could sit down first.

part_subtitle: A title is another kind of cage.

paragraphs: Extract from an unsigned transitional memorandum delivered to the imperial apartments at dawn: Her Highness is not to be burdened with technical irregularities unless such irregularities threaten succession optics, mage safety, or the stability of northern settlement language. Her Highness is, however, to be reassured that all matters touching anomalous bloodlines are being handled with appropriate discretion.
Ciri read the word reassured twice and decided the writer had never survived being reassured by powerful men.

The memorandum lay among twelve cleaner lies on a black lacquered table in a room that smelled of ink, pressed linen, wax, and flowers forced to be beautiful indoors. Nilfgaardian flowers had discipline. They stood in porcelain vases as if awaiting inspection. Beyond the tall windows, Vizima's morning had the pearl-gray color of a city pretending fog was a political decision. Courtiers moved somewhere beyond the doors, quiet as knives in velvet. Ciri sat in the chair no one called a throne because everyone in the palace had learned that the most dangerous furniture did not need the name yet.

Ilyra Sarn stood across from her with both hands folded over a leather case. She was a narrow woman in sober black, neither old nor young in the useful way of intelligence people, with hair pinned so flat it seemed less styled than disciplined into silence. She did not fidget. She did not apologize. That was why Ciri had kept her.
"You woke me for reassurance," Ciri said.
"No, Highness. I woke you because men who write reassurance at dawn have usually done something by midnight."
"Good." Ciri pushed the memorandum aside. "Show me."

Ilyra opened the case and did not close it again after Ciri finished the first pass. Closed cases invited comfort. Open ones asked whether the reader had enough courage to go on. The packet contained copies, not originals, which was already a kind of warning. Originals made people foolish. Copies meant the person delivering them had chosen survival long enough to be useful.

Ciri saw words before she saw the shape of the whole file: unregistered Wolf School asset, bloodline custody, host suitability, voluntary surrender preferred, public-risk anomaly, hereditary infrastructure. The room remained warm. Her fingers went cold. A well-trained empire did not waste ugly words before breakfast. A well-trained office could make a person into a bridge, a door, a bloodline problem, a public concern, a chamber with legs, and never once write prison.
"Who wrote this?"

"Several hands," Ilyra said. "Same vocabulary family. Northern vassal corridors, Novigrad confiscation lots, at least one medical relay, and a Redanian post-purge archive. The final synthesis is associated with a man named Sorel Veyrane. He does not sign what matters."
"No one does if they think history might read it later."

Ciri lifted the page about hereditary infrastructure and saw how cleanly the phrase sat on the paper. It did not shout. It did not threaten. It did not even insult. That was what made it vile. She had been called Elder Blood by men who wanted her womb, her throne, her death, her gate, her name, and her obedience. Those men had never needed to hate her. Some had loved an idea of her with reverence enough to make hatred look honest.
"Tell me the person beneath it," she said.

Ilyra placed a sketch beside the file. It was bad work by a hurried hand: pale hair, scar at the left cheekbone, wolf medallion, red eyes noted three times as if repetition made the color safer. Beneath it was the name JACK MORNINGSTAR, copied in a clerk's neat script. Someone had underlined Morningstar. Someone else had drawn a small black oval beside it.

Ciri studied the sketch and did not move. That was the first lesson of courts. Movement told people where the blade had entered. The artist had failed the mouth. Files often did. They made dangerous people either too cruel or too blank because the middle would have required acknowledging personhood.
"Witcher?"

"Apparently. Hidden Wolf School training. Kaer Morhen references. Vesemir's name appears in a suppressed note. Geralt of Rivia is now with him. Yennefer of Vengerberg has been seen on the route. Triss Merigold's courier hand appears in two harmless letters that are not harmless."

Ciri's chest tightened at the names, not because they surprised her, but because they made the file personal before she had chosen where to put the pain. Geralt. Yennefer. Triss. Vesemir dead and still leaving doors locked behind him. She touched the page with the Wolf School phrase and remembered winter at Kaer Morhen, rough gloves, sword lessons, Geralt's silence when he had no answer and wanted the lack to look like wisdom.
"Geralt hid him from me," Ciri said.
"Yes."
"Do not soften that."
"I had not intended to."
Good. Ciri preferred useful cruelty to embroidered comfort.
"The man is twenty-three?"
"By available estimates."
"Then do not call him boy because a file does."
Ilyra bowed her head a fraction. "The man, then."

Ciri stood and went to the window. Vizima below looked washed and obedient. A black carriage moved through the courtyard with four riders around it. A servant carried a basket of bread across a side path, shoulders hunched as if bread might become treason by proximity to marble. This was the world Emhyr wanted her to inherit and govern, a world where even bread learned routes.
"What does my father know?" Ciri asked.
Ilyra did not ask which father. That also was why Ciri had kept her.

"Emhyr knows of a public-risk matter that might intersect succession optics. He does not, to my knowledge, have the full Morningstar language yet. Some of his men want to acquire it before rivals do. Some want to bury it until the coronation path is less fragile. Some want to use the northern panic as proof that imperial custody is the only civilized response."
"And you?"
"I want you to know before they learn which version to give you."
That was loyalty in the palace: not affection, not purity, not innocence, but speed toward truth before truth was dressed for her.
She set the sketch down. "Why did you bring this before speaking to Emhyr?"
"Because His Imperial Majesty would be tempted to protect you by controlling the problem."
"Jack."
Ilyra inclined her head. "The man. Yes."
"And you think I will not be tempted?"
"I think you know the smell of that temptation better than he does."

That was dangerously close to kindness. Ciri let it pass because the morning had already spent its allowance of humiliation. She crossed to the mirror. The woman in it looked too composed to be honest. Pale hair tied severely. Brown wool chosen by a chambermaid who had argued with three silks before surrendering to practicality. No emerald. No imperial black. No Cintran blue either. She would not wear a dead kingdom like a wound just to travel under one more set of eyes.
Ilyra watched her through the mirror. "Highness."
"Say the thought."
"If this man becomes connected to you publicly, your enemies will use him."
"They use my weather, my meals, my silences, my womb, my sword hand, my dead grandmother, and the angle of my head when I listen to Emhyr. They may take a number."
"This would be different."
"Yes." Ciri touched the folded page hidden in her sleeve. "Because this time I will know before they name it for me."

A servant knocked with court breakfast and withdrew after seeing Ilyra's face. The tray remained outside, cooling with imperial discipline. Somewhere beyond the antechamber a captain murmured to another man, and both fell silent when Ciri moved. The palace was full of people trained to hear rank through doors.
"Leave the outer memorandum," Ciri said. "Take the better copies. If I am stopped, I want the stupid paper on the table and the dangerous paper on the road."
"You expect to be stopped?"
"I expect to be loved, ruled, watched, managed, and improved by committee. Being stopped is only the honest version."

Ilyra folded the pages into a travel packet small enough to vanish inside a seam. "There are rumors already. Not court rumors yet. Stable rumors. Kitchen rumors. Two grooms argued whether the red wolf serves Nilfgaard or eats Nilfgaardian officers first."
"And the answer?"
"One said a proper wolf eats whatever stands closest. The other said a witcher charges extra."
Ciri laughed then, quickly and unwillingly. It saved nothing. It made the room breathe.
"Good," she said. "Let the kitchens be wiser than the court. It will not be the first time."
"Where is Jack now?"
"Moving north from Novigrad toward a meeting place named in Triss Merigold's routed note. A broken mill where no grain turns. That phrase may be code, or old local speech."

"It is both. Probably." Ciri returned to the files. "Arrange a covered departure. No imperial banners, no official escort beyond what is already used for my personal security. Two riders who know how to be quiet, one physician who thinks he is accompanying me for fatigue, and a trunk of dresses unsuitable for mud so anyone watching believes I would never take that road."
Ilyra's mouth almost moved. "At once."
"And if Emhyr asks?"
"He will."
"Tell him I went to inspect a matter of court gossip before it became policy. He will hate that because it sounds like something I might do."
"It is something you are doing, Highness."
"Then let him enjoy accuracy for once."

Before noon, Ciri was dressed in brown wool, a travel cloak, and a hood plain enough to offend three chambermaids and delight herself. The imperial physician complained about the weather until Ilyra told him the complaint would be recorded as loyalty to routine. He became silent and useful. The two riders knew better than to look at her too often. That pleased her. People who could not stop looking at rank rarely noticed danger.
They left through the side gate during a delivery of onions.
It was comforting, in a mean little way, that empire could be escaped briefly under the protection of vegetables.
Emhyr received the news of her departure before Ciri reached the outer city road.

That was expected. If he had not, she would have replaced three palace watchers by evening and enjoyed the paperwork. The emperor did not ride after her. That would have made him a father in public and a ruler in haste, both roles he preferred arranged with witnesses selected beforehand. Instead, a courier reached her at a shrine where the roof had collapsed and the saint beneath it had collected rain in both carved hands. The courier carried no imperial banner. He did carry fear, which was more identifying.
The letter was short, written in Emhyr's own hand, and therefore more dangerous than a decree.

Cirilla, you are walking toward a matter whose outlines I am not yet prepared to trust. Return if this is personal. Continue if this is political. If it is both, remember that the world will use whichever answer costs you more. E.

Ciri read it under the broken saint while Ilyra pretended not to read over her shoulder. Rainwater dripped from the saint's fingers onto the floor stone with the patient rhythm of a clerk counting objections.
"He is improving," Ilyra said.
"No. He is becoming harder to hate efficiently."
"A troubling development for governance."

Ciri folded the letter and placed it inside her sleeve with the hereditary infrastructure page. Father and file. One warned her about cost. The other tried to make a stranger into one. It was almost funny, if one had a damaged sense of humor and the morning available for cynicism.
"We continue," she said.
"Because it is political?"
"Because he asked the wrong distinction."
The physician, who had slept badly and understood nothing, cleared his throat. "Highness, the road east of here is known for fever in wet seasons."
Ciri looked at the rain, the broken saint, the two secret pages against her arm, and the narrow road ahead where a hidden witcher waited inside someone else's vocabulary.
"Then let us not catch the administrative kind," she said.
The physician did not know whether to laugh. Sensible man.
The broken mill stood in a hollow where three roads had once argued and all lost.

Rain had turned the lane to black paste. Willow trees leaned over the stream with the exhausted posture of old women listening to children lie. The mill wheel hung still, one side broken, green moss thick on the paddles. No grain had turned there for years, perhaps decades. Someone had scratched a wolf on the door and then crossed it out. Someone else had drawn a crown above it in charcoal. The crown had run in the damp and looked as if it were bleeding down the wood.

Ciri arrived before sunset and smelled wet rot, horse sweat, old stone, and a faint trace of something metallic under the stream. She noticed the watcher in the alder first, the second watcher near the cart shed, and the place in the mud where a third had waited and left before she arrived. Geralt would have noticed the same. Yennefer would have noticed the spell residue near the door and made a face. Triss would have noticed that the cart shed's latch had been recently oiled and asked who paid for oil in a dead mill.
Ciri missed them suddenly and hated the timing.
"Inside?" Ilyra asked.
"No. They will not enter until they know who else is outside."
"They?"
"Geralt taught me paranoia. Yennefer refined it. Triss made it polite enough for rooms."
Ilyra accepted this as tactical summary.

The first sign of them was not sound. It was the horses. Ciri's gelding lifted his head toward the north road, and the two escort horses followed. A moment later, a gray mare stepped out from between pines with Geralt in the saddle, white hair under a dark hood, shoulders carrying the old road as if it had never released him. Beside him rode a taller man on a dark horse with a blunt head and the expression of an animal prepared to dislike history on principle. The man's hair was silver-white, shorter than Geralt's, wind-tossed and rain-dark at the edges.
His eyes, when he came close enough, were crimson.
Not monster red. Not fever red. Ember under ash. A dangerous color made worse by the fact that he did not use it.

Asha rode behind him, scarred, watchful, with the stillness of someone whose body remembered vows more faithfully than language. Yennefer came last because she preferred to have the whole road inside her field of vision and because she had always known how to make arrival feel like judgment.
Geralt saw Ciri and stopped breathing badly for half a second.
That hurt more than any speech would have.
"Ciri," he said.
"Geralt."
The title did not enter. She refused to bring it. Not here. Not before this.

Yennefer dismounted first and crossed the mud with such precision that the mud seemed to apologize for existing. She touched Ciri's cheek once. Briefly. In public that was an embrace. In private it would have become something else. Ciri leaned into it just enough to tell her she was forgiven for arriving with fear, not enough to let the fear take charge.
"You should not have come without telling us," Yennefer said.
"You taught me that sentence. I learned its weaknesses."
Yennefer's mouth tightened. Pride and annoyance were sometimes difficult to separate in her face.

Geralt came to her next. He did not hug her at once. He looked at her boots first, because boots told the truth about travel and because fatherhood, with Geralt, often began at the ground. Then his attention reached her face.
"You're wet," he said.
"It rained. I survived."
"Still should dry your hair."
"I missed you too."
He hugged her then. It was awkward with armor, cloak, swords, and everything unsaid between them. Good. Clean embraces were for people with lighter lives.
Jack remained beside his horse.

Ciri stepped back from Geralt and faced him fully. The file had made him a category. The sketch had made him an outline. The man in the mud did neither. He stood with his weight balanced, left hand gloved, right hand near but not on his sword, body angled to keep his horse clear of strangers. He did not bow. He did not stare. He watched as if watching cost him nothing and trust would cost more than the road currently had in its purse.
"Jack Morningstar," she said.
"Cirilla Fiona Elen Riannon."
Geralt's face tightened at the full name. Yennefer's eyes sharpened. Ciri almost smiled.
"That's a great deal of name to use in a swamp," she said.
"I wanted to see which one made you angry."
"All of them, depending on mouth and hour."
"Useful."
"No," she said. "Not that word. Not with me."
His expression changed by less than a breath. Ciri saw it anyway.
"Fair," he said.
It was the right answer because it did not ask reward for understanding late.

They went inside the mill only after Yennefer burned a listening charm from the rafters and Jack found a wire under the threshold attached to a clay tube of powdered glass. Geralt cut the wire. Asha watched Ciri watching them and said nothing. Ilyra catalogued every movement without appearing to. The dead mill became a room full of people who had all been hunted by someone more organized than hunger.
Ciri placed the folded page on the cracked table.
"Hereditary infrastructure," she said.
No one pretended not to know the phrase. That was something.
Jack studied the paper. "I wondered which file would bring you."
"Not file. Vocabulary. Files are just where cowards keep their best clothes."
Asha made a small sound in the back of her throat. Not a laugh. Approval with scars.
Geralt turned to Ciri. "We were going to tell you."
"I know." She let the words sit long enough to become uncomfortable. "That is not the same as telling me."
Yennefer did not rescue him. Ciri loved her for it and hated that there was enough history for rescue to be required.
"I wanted the truth before anyone decided which version of truth would keep me calm," Ciri continued. "I also wanted to meet the man the continent is trying to turn into a noun."
Jack's gaze held hers. "And?"
"Too early. Files are ugly first dates."
Geralt made a sound that might have been pain or amusement. Yennefer looked toward the broken window. Ilyra, to her credit, wrote nothing down.
Jack almost smiled. Then he looked at the page again and the almost went cold. "I am not here to be another burden placed in your hands."
The sentence struck too near the road from Novigrad. Geralt looked down. Ciri did not.
"Then do not be," she said. "Stand there as a man with a problem. I have problems. Some of mine wear crowns. We can introduce them and see which bites first."
For the first time since he arrived, Jack's stillness altered. Not softened. Rebalanced.
Outside, something moved in the willows.

Everyone heard it. Everyone reached for something different: Geralt for a sword, Yennefer for a spell, Jack for the angle of the door, Asha for the knife hidden under her sleeve, Ciri for the space in the room that would let her draw if the door broke inward. Ilyra stepped back so no one would trip over her. That was intelligence, not cowardice.
A fox emerged from the reeds with a dead rat in its mouth. It looked at the room of armed legends, decided history was none of its business, and vanished.
"Good," Ciri said. "The fox has better politics than most courts."
After the fox vanished, the room did not become less dangerous. It became more honest.

A fox was easy. It wanted a rat and a road without witnesses. People wanted more elaborate things and felt superior for naming them policy. Ciri watched Jack clean a sliver of powdered glass from the threshold and wondered which part of him had learned to see traps before anyone admitted there were doors. Geralt crouched beside him without crowding. Yennefer stood behind Ciri, not quite close enough to touch, close enough that Ciri knew she had placed herself there deliberately.
Asha spoke from the darker corner. "Your file found you quickly."
Ciri turned to her. "I found the file."
"Same wound, different entrance."
"You knew my mother?"

The question entered the room too abruptly. Geralt looked up. Yennefer went very still. Jack's fingers paused over the wire. Asha's face did not move, but age seemed to arrive inside it, not on the skin, but under the scars.
"I knew Helena," Asha said. "Not enough. No one who loved her knew her enough. Duty took too much of the room."
"That sounds familiar," Ciri said.

Asha studied her, and for a moment Ciri felt measured by something older than courts and less impressed by them. "Yes. Your blood was hunted by people who called hunger destiny. His by people who call hunger custody. The languages differ. The mouth is the same."
Jack finished with the glass tube and set it on the table. "You told her more than me."
"You asked for less."
"I asked badly."
"You did."
Ciri liked Asha then. It was inconvenient, because liking severe survivors often ended in obedience one had not formally agreed to.
Ilyra leaned near the cracked shutter. "There were two watchers near the west alder. They have withdrawn."
"Because they saw me," Ciri said.
"Because they saw everyone see them see you," Ilyra corrected. "The difference will matter when the report is written."
Geralt made a low sound. "They will write one."
"Of course," Yennefer said. "Men who hide in wet shrubs have few other art forms."
Jack studied the glass tube. "Then our meeting is already evidence."
Ciri crossed the room and placed one hand flat on the table beside the hereditary infrastructure page. Not on Jack. Not on the file. Beside both. "Yes. So we decide what it proves before cowards do."
The words settled. They did not solve anything. That made them trustworthy.

Outside, the stream moved under the dead wheel. Inside, the dead mill acquired the first fragile shape of a company: not a family, not a court, not an escort, and certainly not a rescue party. A room full of people who understood that saving a man could become another method of ownership if no one watched the hands.
Ciri watched Jack watching the door.
Not afraid, exactly.
Prepared to leave before needing anyone became another trap.
Recognition was not desire yet. But it had taken off its cloak.
Before sleep, Ilyra gave Ciri the first report she had already written and not yet sent.

It named nothing that could be used cleanly if intercepted. It described the meeting as a convergence of private persons under weather. It called Jack "the man under hostile description." It called Geralt "the old wolf acting without title." It called Yennefer "maternal severity, active." Ciri read that phrase three times and decided she loved it enough to forbid Ilyra from knowing.
"You are amused," Ilyra said.
"No."
"Badly hidden, Highness."
"I was raised among witchers. My hiding is excellent. Your courage is simply inconvenient."
Ilyra accepted this with the grave face of a woman adding inconvenience to her list of usable virtues. "Do you want this sent?"
"Not yet."
"Because of Jack?"
"Because of everyone. If it leaves tonight, the palace learns I met him before he learns what meeting me costs. I will not have a file understand the price before the man does."
Ilyra's expression softened by less than a candle's width. "That distinction is dangerous."
"Most correct ones are."

Across the mill, Jack was speaking quietly with Geralt near the door. Geralt had his arms folded and the expression of a man receiving information he disliked from a younger man who had earned the right to give it. Yennefer watched them without seeming to. Asha sharpened a knife already sharp enough to embarrass metal. The stream below the floor murmured under all of them, turning no wheel, grinding no grain, carrying only rain and whatever rumors water took when humans spoke too close.
Ciri folded Ilyra's report and gave it back. "Seal it under health correspondence. Hold it until dawn. If I am dead by then, send it."
"I dislike that contingency."
"So do I. It remains administratively useful."
"You sound like him."
"Emhyr?"
"No. Like someone who learned statecraft by surviving it."
Ciri looked at the dead mill wheel through the broken wall. "Then write that down nowhere."
Jack did smile then, small and brief.
Ciri saw the man before the function.
That was dangerous enough to matter.

They spent the night in the broken mill because leaving immediately would have made the meeting look like panic and because the road had already swallowed one horse shoe from Ciri's escort. The physician, having been told nothing useful, diagnosed damp, politics, and possible exhaustion in everyone and then fell asleep sitting against a grain bin. Ilyra wrote by shuttered lantern. Asha walked the perimeter with Geralt and said almost nothing. Yennefer inspected the foundation stones and found a carved line under mold that made her mouth go thin.
Ciri found Jack outside near the silent wheel.

The stream moved beneath it, black and narrow, carrying leaves under the unmoving paddles. The wheel should have turned. It did not. Someone had jammed an iron spike between the axle and the frame years ago. Water pushed. Wood held. A little system of force and refusal, rotting in the rain.
"Do you always stand near things that explain the room too well?" Ciri asked.
Jack did not look at her at once. "Usually they find me."
"That sounds like Geralt. You should be worried."
"I am. About several things."
She came beside him, leaving enough space that neither could be accused of comfort by accident. The wheel groaned once as water struck it harder. Still it did not move.
"Did he hide me from you," Jack asked, "or you from me?"

There it was. A fairer question than the one she had been carrying. Ciri studied the wheel. "Both, probably. Geralt prefers one mistake that protects two people to two risks that explain themselves. He is wrong often enough to remain lovable and right often enough to be unbearable."
"You forgive him?"
"I choose him. Forgiveness is less stable. It has weather."
Jack considered that. "Useful distinction."
She turned her head slowly.
"Wrong word," he said.
"Learning already. Impressive. Triss will make you a certificate."
This time the small smile came easier. It vanished when he looked back toward the mill. "I don't know what I am to you."

Ciri followed his gaze to the lit cracks in the shutter where her family, such as the world had left and made it, moved around papers, scars, and old choices. "Neither do I. That may be why it has not yet been ruined by certainty."
They stood until the rain thickened. When Ciri went back inside, Geralt was pretending not to watch the door. Yennefer was openly watching it and therefore morally superior only by style.
Ciri said nothing to either of them.
Some truths needed the night to keep their shape.

chapters.chapter_title: THE WOMAN WHO WATCHES TOO STILL
paragraphs: From a villager's deposition taken near the hollow road: The pale witcher was there, and the ashen girl with the Nilfgaard cloak, and the old white wolf, and the black lady, and the scarred eastern woman. But the other woman, the quiet one near the stones, she was not with them. She was with the beasts. I cannot explain it better. The beasts knew and lowered their heads.
The first draconid lay in the road with its throat closed from the inside.

Jack found it at morning where the lane rose toward a ridge of bare stones and pine roots. It had been a forktail once, young, lean, not yet scarred into cleverness, with gray-green scales and wing membranes torn by old weather. No spear wound. No bolt. No silver. Its claws had dug four trenches into the mud, each trench pointing back toward the south as if the creature had tried to crawl away from the direction its body had chosen. Its mouth hung open. Black saliva had dried along the teeth.
The tongue was swollen and split in a line that looked too straight for sickness.

Buck refused to step within ten paces of it. Roach came closer and disliked herself for it. Ciri's gelding trembled but obeyed. Asha's mare watched the treeline, not the corpse, which told Jack what he needed; his hand stayed near steel.
"Poison?" Geralt asked.
"No smell of bait," Jack said. "No meat. No wolfsbane. No alder resin."
Yennefer crouched beside the body without touching it. "This is not ordinary sickness. Something pulled the heat inward until the tissues cooked where they should have cooled."

Ciri stood behind her, arms folded against the cold. She had not complained about the road, the rain, the mud, the lack of breakfast, the sleeping arrangement in a mill room with spiders large as property owners, or the fact that Geralt had woken twice to check the door. Jack respected all of that more than he wanted to.
"Draconids do not flee south this time of year," Geralt said.
"They flee pressure," Asha said.
The room turned toward her. She ignored the attention with professional contempt.
"What kind?" Ciri asked.
"The kind old scales feel before young men make names for it."
"Poetic."
"No. Translated badly."

Jack knelt near the forktail's head. The wolf medallion trembled, then stopped. The barbed-star signet under his shirt cooled, but not warning-cold. Recognition-cold. He had learned the difference badly and recently. He lifted a small scale with his knife. The underside bore a red line, not blood, not pigment, but pressure burned into the growth itself.
"It heard something," he said.
Yennefer's attention cut to him. "Heard?"
"Wrong word. Followed. Then resisted. Too late."
Ciri looked toward the ridge. "And us?"
"We're standing on the road it used."
Geralt sighed. "Convenient."
"Very," Jack said. "I hate it."
The second draconid found them an hour later.
The road beyond the second corpse entered a country where maps became suggestions and animals made better decisions than men.

At midday they found a nest under a limestone overhang, empty except for three cracked shells and a heap of warm black feathers. Yennefer identified the shells as draconid. Geralt identified the feathers as crow. Jack identified the footprints around both as human because the world, when it became interesting, usually did so by worsening.
"Poachers?" Ciri asked.
"Scavengers first," Geralt said. "Poachers after they realized the eggs were warm."
"After?"
Geralt pointed with the tip of his scabbard. "Knife marks. One shell opened. Two broken from inside. Something hatched wrong or was forced out too early."
Saesenthessis had not come down from the ridge. She watched the nest from above with the expression of a judge listening to a confession the defendant did not know he had made.

Jack touched the rock beside the nest. Warm. Too warm for shade. The barbed-star signet cooled at his throat. In the hollow of the overhang, someone had scratched a black oval beside a crude drawing of a wing. The mark was shallow and recent.
"They were here," he said.
"Black Ink?" Ciri asked.
"Or people hoping to sell them something with the same smell."
Asha crouched beside the broken shell and lifted a splinter between two fingers. "The young were called before they were ready."
"Called by what?"
Asha turned from Jack to the ridge. "By a hunger wearing a note too low for human ears."
Saesenthessis finally descended. "Not hunger. Imperative."
Yennefer's eyes narrowed. "That distinction comforts no one."

"It was not meant to." Saesenthessis took the shell from Asha. For the first time since her arrival, disgust entered her human face without disguise. "Someone is learning how to imitate ancient pressure with modern tools. Badly. The imitation harms the young first. It always does."
Geralt studied the scratched oval. "You know who teaches them?"
"I know the kind of mind that thinks an egg is a document if cracked with care."
"That is not an answer."
"No. It is an insult with direction."
Ciri folded her arms. "You could save time by telling us more."
"Time is not saved by pouring water into cracked jars."
"Then repair the jar."
Saesenthessis held her for three long beats. "You were raised by persistent people."
"And several impossible ones."
"That explains the tone."
The exchange nearly became amusing. Then the smallest shell moved.

Not hatch. Not life. Memory. A tremor passed through the broken curve and settled into Jack's wounded palm. He closed his fist before anyone could ask. Saesenthessis saw anyway. So did Ciri. So did Yennefer, whose habit of missing nothing had become personally exhausting to the rest of the world.
"It answers nests," Triss would have said, if she had been there. In her absence, Yennefer said the colder version.
"Your resonance is being taught by every site it touches."
Jack studied the shell. "And what is learning me in return?"
No one answered quickly.
Saesenthessis crushed the shell splinter in her palm. Pale dust fell through her fingers. "That is tomorrow's test."
At dawn, Saesenthessis took Jack to see what the others had slept beside.

The ridge behind camp dropped into a slate hollow where rainwater gathered in black pools. In one of those pools lay a basilisk, dead long enough for the eyes to film and fresh enough that warmth still rose from the open throat. It had crawled there from the east, dragging one wing, and placed its head beneath the water before dying. Not accident. Choice, or the nearest thing a creature in pain could make.
Jack crouched at the edge. "Drowning itself."
"Cooling itself," Saesenthessis said. "The pressure inside burned hotter than fever. It tried to put water between itself and the note."
"What note?"
"The one your blood hears without permission."

The words were cruel. Accurate words often were. Jack studied the dead basilisk's claws. The mud around them carried the same dragged half-circles he had seen at Broken Crown, at the shrieker's fall, at the nest under the overhang. A pattern large as ecology and precise as a trap.
Saesenthessis stepped into the hollow. The water did not ripple around her boots until she allowed it to. Jack decided not to ask. Some answers made a man's day worse.
"You think I am part of the disease," he said.
"I think you are the shape it was trained to seek."
"That is not better."
"No. Better is for children and politicians. We have only truer."
He turned to her. "Your father would have said that with a smile, according to Geralt."
"My father smiled when humans needed to be deceived into listening."
"And you?"
"I have found humans listen badly either way."

Jack touched the water with the tip of his knife. The surface warmed around steel, not his hand. He felt the signet at his throat tug once toward the basilisk, once toward his palm, and once toward the road where Ciri still slept. Three directions. One body.
Saesenthessis saw the calculation. "Do not make yourself the answer before the question has finished being ugly."
"I am not trying to."
"Men like you rarely try. You prepare, endure, and then call self-erasure efficient when enough people are watching."
That made him stand. "You know nothing about me."
"I know the posture of a creature deciding whether its usefulness is the same as its worth."
For a moment the hollow held no dragon, no witcher, no ancient seal. Only two beings too accustomed to survival to mistake it for innocence.
Jack wiped the knife clean. "Then tomorrow's test is yours too."
Saesenthessis's eyes warmed gold for less than a breath. "Yes."

When they returned, Ciri was awake and pretending she had not watched them leave. Yennefer was awake and did not bother pretending. Geralt was boiling water that had no intention of becoming drinkable. Asha looked at Jack once and said, "You saw the drowned scale."
"Yes."
"Then the old road has admitted it is sick."
Ciri took the cup Geralt handed her, sniffed it, and looked betrayed. "This road has many crimes."
Geralt nodded. "Tea is one."
The joke did not save the morning. It kept it human, which was sometimes the only saving available.
Asha found him later at the edge of camp, washing the knife too carefully.
"You are angry at the dragon," she said.
"Which one?"
"The living one. The dead one would be unfair."
Jack dried the blade. "She speaks as if people are slow tools."
"People often are."
"So you agree with her."
"I did not say I liked agreement."
Asha sat on a stone with the stiff care of old wounds. Dawn was spreading thinly over the ridge, making the prison stones look less ancient and more tired. "Saesenthessis is afraid."
Jack met her eyes.
"Do not mistake age for freedom from fear. Dragons hide fear better because they have had longer to practice arrogance."
"That was almost charitable."
"I am ill."
He almost smiled. The almost passed.

Asha took a length of cord from her wrist and tied one knot, then another. "In Faithel judgment, a witness is corrupt if she wants the result too badly. Saesenthessis wants you to prove a thing she does not yet dare hope."
"What?"
"That the last bearer can choose without becoming either weapon or martyr."
The word martyr made the knife feel heavier.
Jack put it away. "Everyone is very interested in what I become."
"Yes," Asha said. "That is why you must remain rudely interested in what you are."

From the camp, Ciri's voice cut through morning, accusing Geralt of boiling bark instead of tea. Geralt replied that bark had character. Yennefer said character was not flavor. Buck struck a hoof against stone, apparently agreeing with Yennefer.
Jack listened.
For a moment, what he was seemed less like a hidden bloodline and more like a man at the edge of an impossible camp, being kept from solitude by people with terrible manners.
It was not safety.
It was something to defend.
The old quarry they avoided had once supplied stone for three noble houses and one prison.

Saesenthessis said the prison had outlasted the houses, which struck everyone as likely and no one as surprising. Its outer wall remained in broken lengths along the ridge, moss over mortar, thorn roots through arrow slits, rain gathered in the sockets of carved faces that had probably been meant to frighten prisoners into order. Jack found a chain link half buried near the path. It was too large for a man's wrist and too small for a proper draconid.
"For what?" Ciri asked.
Saesenthessis studied the link. "For human confidence."
Geralt crouched beside it. "That includes many bad inventions."
"This one taught lesser wings that stone could command hunger when blood was near."
Yennefer's face hardened. "A training site."
"An attempt. Humans are fond of attempts that kill the lesson before the student."
Asha spat into the moss. Faithel disgust had few decorative stages.

Jack lifted the link with his knife. The metal hummed once, almost below hearing. Buck kicked the air behind him and tried to retreat from the sound. Jack dropped the link and stepped back, palm aching.
Ciri moved toward him before Geralt did, and then stopped because she remembered what stopping meant. Jack noticed. His face altered by a fraction, gratitude almost invisible under discipline.
The link had left a red stain on the knife tip.
Not rust. Not blood. Something in between, as if the metal had learned to remember injury without a body.
Saesenthessis took the knife from Jack, inspected the stain, and returned it handle-first. "Tomorrow's test will not be only scent."
"You said scent," Jack replied.
"I lied by omission. It is a venerable practice among species who dislike being interrupted."
Ciri gave the dragon a flat look. "I like her less by the hour."
"Good," Saesenthessis said. "Fondness clouds testimony."
"Fondness also keeps people from pushing witnesses into pits."
"That explains your court's inefficiency."
Yennefer made a sound too elegant to be laughter and too unwise to identify.

They camped beyond the prison stones. No one slept well. At midnight, the horses woke together and faced east. Their breath steamed white in warm air. From somewhere below the ridge came a note like a horn heard underwater. One note. Then none.
Jack was awake before the others rose.
His left hand had opened in his sleep.
The red lines glowed faintly across his palm.
Ciri saw it from her bedroll and said nothing. Silence, for once, was not concealment. It was the courtesy of allowing a man to wake before the world put his body on trial again.
Geralt remembered the first golden dragon he had met only after Saesenthessis used silence the same way.

It was not resemblance of face. She had little of Borch's warmth and none of his deliberate foolishness. It was the weight behind what she did not say. Borch had once hidden truth inside a smile until men revealed themselves by reaching for it. His daughter hid truth inside stillness and watched humans bruise their knuckles on their own assumptions.
They walked together at the edge of camp while the others watered horses.
"Your father talked more," Geralt said.
"My father liked people to underestimate him before they died of embarrassment."
"Sometimes they lived."
"Yes. His sentimentality was a known risk."
Geralt glanced toward Jack, who was pretending not to lean on Buck while Buck pretended not to support him. "You came because of him."
"I came because the small wings are dying where they should not die. He is not the cause. He is the shape the cause recognizes."
"Not comforting."
"You keep asking for comfort in places where accuracy is kinder."
Geralt accepted that because arguing would not improve the sentence. "Will you help him?"
Saesenthessis looked toward Jack, then toward Ciri. "If helping him does not become another human word for preparing him to be used."
Geralt stopped walking.

She did not. "You have already hidden one child because danger had too many hands. Now another danger has found him grown. If you love by building walls, witcher, learn where the door is before the person inside forgets he can leave."
Geralt watched her return to the stones.
He hated dragons a little then. Not for being cryptic.
For being right when a man needed them to be merely difficult.

It came from above, not diving to attack but falling as if the sky had rejected it. A shrieker, older, broader, one eye clouded, claws curled wrong. It hit the slope hard, breaking stones loose and slid toward the horses with wings beating mud into the air. Ciri's gelding reared. Buck lunged sideways, not away from Jack but toward him, trying to keep his rider's body between himself and the wrong thing, which was loyalty expressed with terrible strategy.
Jack drew silver. Geralt drew steel for the straps tangled near the horses. Yennefer lifted one hand and the air sharpened.
"Wait," Ciri said.
The shrieker was not attacking. It was choking.

Jack moved before argument could dress itself. He crossed the mud, slid under the beating wing, and drove one knee into the creature's shoulder joint to pin it without crushing the rib. The shrieker snapped at him by reflex. He caught the jaw with the flat of the blade and forced the head down. Black saliva bubbled at the throat. Under the scale plates, red pressure pulsed in broken intervals.
The old hunger in his blood answered.

For one breath, the road narrowed to heat, throat, red line, wingbeat, Ciri's horse screaming, Geralt shouting his name, Yennefer's spell held in a hand too controlled to release without necessity. Jack could have pushed. He knew it without knowing how. The shrieker's body would have obeyed. The horses would have gone still. The people might have too. Fear was a door. His blood had found the latch.
No.

He cut his own palm through the glove, pressed the blood to the mud beside the creature's mouth, and let the pressure move there instead of outward. The mud steamed. The shrieker convulsed, coughed a knot of black-red matter from its throat, and collapsed.
Alive.

Jack stood too quickly and nearly lost his balance. Ciri was beside him before Geralt, not because she was faster than the witcher but because she had been closer to the decision. She did not touch him. Good.
"You could have made it stop," she said.
"I did."
"That is not what I meant."
"I know."
Yennefer came to the clot in the mud. "Do not touch that."
"Wasn't planning to lick it," Geralt said.
"Your restraint continues to astonish scholars."
The old exchange might have been funny in another place. Here it was a handrail over a pit.
A woman's voice came from the stones above them. "He chose not to own fear. Good. One test survived contact with mud."
Jack looked up.

She stood on a fallen marker stone where no one had heard her arrive. Tall, dark-haired, wrapped in a plain cloak the color of dry bark, face calm in a way that was not human stillness but something wearing human stillness out of courtesy. Her eyes were not golden in any obvious sense. That would have been too easy and too theatrical. They were brown until they were not, until light shifted and a warmer depth moved behind them like a banked coal seen under clear water.
The shrieker lowered its head.
So did the wounded forktail lying dead behind them, though dead things should have been past manners. Its body settled as if relieved.
Geralt's expression became old and careful. "Saesenthessis."

Ciri's attention sharpened. Yennefer did not turn fully, because turning fully gave too much respect before respect had been priced. Asha placed her hand over the bone knots at her belt and bowed her head by a finger's width.
Jack kept his sword in hand. "You were watching."
"Yes."
"Helpful."
"Rarely."

She descended the rocks without hurry. Mud did not cling to her boots as much as it should have. Jack disliked that. He disliked more that the horses quieted as she approached. Buck watched her with fixed ears and no bite prepared. A horse refusing to threaten was serious evidence.
Saesenthessis stopped beside the shrieker and looked at Jack, not the wound. "This one should have died three ridges back. It came because you are a boundary it mistook for answer."
"I am not an answer."
"Good. Answers are often where thought goes to die."
Ciri made a small sound. It might have been approval. Jack kept his eyes on the scale.
Geralt sheathed his sword. "You followed the draconids."

"I followed their wrongness. Lesser wings are leaving nests. Eggs are cooling in warm stone. Young drakes bite their own shadows. Old ones sleep with heads toward the east and wake bleeding from the mouth. Humans call that omen because omen lets them stop looking for cause."
Yennefer studied the red line on the scale. "And the cause?"
Saesenthessis finally turned to her. "You are clever; you know I will not give you a whole truth merely because the room has become anxious."
"We are outside."
"Then the sky is anxious."

Geralt coughed into his glove. Ciri looked away. Jack watched Saesenthessis watch them and understood that she had not come to explain. She had come to measure who reached first and what they called the reaching.
"You know the signet," Jack said.
Her gaze lowered to his chest. The barbed star, hidden under cloth, grew cold against bone.
"I know the shape. Not the right to it."
"What's the difference?"
"Everything dragons worth remembering have killed to preserve."
Asha's breath changed. Saesenthessis heard it and turned to her.
"Faithel."
"Witness," Asha said.
"Still alive."
"Apparently."
"That is either devotion or stubbornness."
"In our order they are twins."
For the first time, Saesenthessis almost smiled. It did not warm her face. It gave it a blade's curve.

The shrieker stirred. Jack looked down and saw its one good eye fixed on the barbed-star hidden beneath his shirt. Not hunger. Not fear. Pleading, if a creature made of tooth and wing could plead without becoming less itself.
"It should be killed," Geralt said, not eagerly.
"Perhaps," Saesenthessis said. "But not because killing is easier to categorize."
"It's scale-sick," Jack said. "It will suffer. It may kill someone if it rises."
"Then decide as a witcher, not as a man afraid his mercy will be misfiled."

That struck. Saesenthessis had aimed it with a precision that proved cruelty or wisdom. Jack crouched beside the shrieker. The creature breathed in shallow pulls. The red pressure in its throat had not vanished. Only paused.
He killed it quickly.

The shrieker's body loosened under the blade. Ciri dropped her gaze to the ground, then returned to Jack. Geralt watched his hands. Yennefer watched his face. Saesenthessis watched the space after the choice.
"Good," she said.
Jack cleaned the blade. "You call that good?"
"No. I call the absence of theater good. Mercy does not require a witness to believe itself."
"You are a difficult guest," Ciri said.

Saesenthessis turned to her. "You are a young ruler under a borrowed cloak standing in mud beside a secret witcher, a sorceress who would burn empires to protect you, a witcher who pretends fatherhood is weather, a Faithel witness, and dead draconids that should not have found this road. You are not in a position to complain about guests."
Ciri held her for three beats.
"I like her," she said.
"That may pass," Geralt said.
"Most things do," Saesenthessis replied.
They made camp before the next ridge because the horses refused the old quarry and because Saesenthessis said the quarry remembered chains.

That was all she said at first. Remembered chains. Then she sat on a stone above the camp and watched the trees with such complete stillness that even Yennefer gave up asking questions for nearly half an hour. Asha sharpened a knife. Geralt checked the horses. Ciri helped without being asked and earned Buck's suspicious tolerance by offering him an apple with no ceremony. Jack saw the horse accept and considered it evidence against the world.
After supper, Saesenthessis came down from the stone.
"The next wrongness is not disease alone," she said. "It is invitation."
Yennefer studied the small fire. Its flame leaned east. "To what?"
"To something that hears through old anchors and answers through blood it does not own."
Ciri's jaw tightened. Jack felt it more than saw it because he was watching the fire too.
"Name it," Yennefer said.
"No."
The word was calm, complete, and infuriating.
Geralt looked up. "Because names have power?"
"Because humans use names like hooks. You catch a thing with them, then claim surprise when it drags you into water."
"We need something better than riddles," Ciri said.

Saesenthessis turned to her, and something old moved behind the human face. "Then earn better. Tomorrow I test the man with the signet. Not his blood. His restraint. If he fails, your files will be kinder than truth, and I will say so."
Jack held her gaze. "And if I refuse?"
"Then you choose not to be measured by me. That is a choice. I will then decide whether the world can survive your privacy."
Geralt's hand closed around the whetstone. "Careful."
"I am. That is why I am unpleasant before disaster rather than sorry after it."
Ciri stood. "He is not yours to test."
"No. Nor yours. Nor Geralt's. Nor Yennefer's. Nor the paper offices that are already making rooms for him. That is precisely the subject."
The camp went quiet.

Jack turned to Ciri. Her anger had not come from possession. That was where the danger lived. It came from recognition, from her own old vocabulary sharpening around another body. He wanted to tell her not to spend it on him. He also knew what she would do with that sentence.
"I choose the test," he said.
Ciri turned on him. "Do not make agreement sound like obedience."
"It isn't."
"Then say it better."
The fire leaned harder east. Asha made a sound that might have been a prayer becoming a curse halfway through.
Jack looked back at Saesenthessis. "I choose to know what I can refuse before others decide refusal is evidence."
Saesenthessis inclined her head. "Better."
Ciri did not sit. She looked at Jack as if he had become more irritating by surviving a sentence accurately.
That, too, mattered because of the danger in it.
Jack took the last watch because sleep had begun asking questions he did not want to answer.

The camp lay under thinning cloud. Geralt slept lightly with one hand near the knife under his cloak. Ciri slept badly and without apology, turned toward the fire as if daring dreams to approach through light. Yennefer did not sleep so much as reduce motion to a level most people mistook for rest. Asha sat with her back against a pine, eyes closed, lips moving once in a while over words too old to need an audience.
Saesenthessis stood beyond the firelight.
