Jack had known she was there for ten minutes before she chose to be visible. Knowing did not help. It was like noticing a mountain had decided to consider him personally.
"You watch them," she said.
"Watch keeps people alive."
"That is the small answer."
"Small answers fit most nights."
She looked toward Ciri. "That one was made into road and title before she could decide which name was shelter."
Jack's hand tightened around the whetstone. "She is not a subject for study."
"Everything is a subject for study. The question is whether study becomes ownership."
He hated that she kept making sense after sounding cruel. "Dragons always speak like this?"
"No. Some roar. It saves time and ruins nuance."
A small sound escaped him. Not quite laughter. Saesenthessis accepted it as if she had meant to draw a blade and found a coin instead.
"You know Zerrikanterment," Jack said.

"I know of a silence where a name should have been. I know golden dragons keep fewer records than humans desire and more memory than humans deserve. I know there are eastern stories my father treated with care, which for him meant saying almost nothing and making the nothing heavy."
"Your father."
She faced him then, and for a moment her human face seemed too small for what stood behind it. "Do not try to build a family tree from dragon reticence at midnight. You will dislike the fruit."
"I dislike most fruit."
"Then you and my father would have agreed on at least one matter."

The fire collapsed inward. Sparks climbed and died before reaching the wet branches above. Jack watched them, thinking of the cinder in his blood, of a golden thing dead before he had memory, of a black thing that had somehow survived inside the same last mercy.
"If you know so much about what should not be owned," he said, "why test me like property?"
Saesenthessis did not answer quickly. That was the first courtesy she had offered him without disguise.

"Because the world is already testing whether you can be used," she said. "I need to know whether you will use yourself first. There is a difference between a man choosing sacrifice and a man addicted to being the tool that makes everyone else safe. The first may save. The second becomes an argument for anyone with a handle."
Jack turned to Ciri again. Her sleep had tightened around some dream. Her hand moved once, searching for a sword that was within reach.
"And if I cannot tell the difference?"
"Then pray someone who loves you can."
"I don't pray."
"Then make better friends."
She returned to the dark before he could answer.
Jack kept watch until dawn, and when Ciri woke from the dream without crying out, he was looking away before she caught him looking.

Dandelion's discarded lyric fragment, found later in a wine-stained notebook: A wolf may wear the chain, or bite the hand, or run. But what of the wolf who lowers his teeth because the room is full of frightened children, and every man with a chain calls that proof he should be leashed?
Saesenthessis chose a place that had already been ruined by people, which proved she understood the continent better than she admitted.

The old tannery stood at the edge of a village abandoned after the last war, though abandoned was too clean a word for houses stripped of doors, wells filled with wagon wheels, and a shrine whose saint had been used for knife practice. Tannery pits lay behind the main building, flooded with rainwater, rot, and blue-green scum. The air smelled of old hides, lime, wet ash, animal fear, and the sour memory of labor no one had bothered to bury properly. Ciri hated it at once. That did not make it special. She had hated cleaner rooms.
"This is the test?" Geralt asked.
"This is the bowl," Saesenthessis said. "The test is what enters it."
"I preferred when dragons demanded riddles," Geralt said.
"That was never preference. You were younger and had better knees."
Ciri looked at Geralt because she enjoyed, briefly and sharply, watching him decide whether to take offense at accuracy. He chose silence. Wisely.
Yennefer walked the edge of the largest pit, nostrils flaring slightly at the smell. "There is draconid musk here. Not fresh. Distilled."
"Weaponized," Asha said.
"Lured," Saesenthessis corrected. "Weapon is a human compliment for fear with a handle."

Jack said nothing. He stood near the tannery door with his left hand bare and bandaged again after the road. The red lines beneath the skin had thinned but not vanished. Ciri had begun to notice when he closed his fist before looking at it. He treated his own body like a badly written contract, something to be monitored because the clauses might change when the room warmed.
Saesenthessis took a small clay vial from her sleeve and broke it against the threshold.

Scent moved before magic. Ciri felt it enter the air as heat behind the tongue, musk and iron and rain on stone, something reptile-old and territorial, something that told animal parts of the body to lower the head or bare the throat. Her medallion did not tremble because she had no medallion, but the scarred places of her life answered anyway. Cintra burning. A tower. Men saying princess as if it were a collar polished enough for ceremony. Elves calling her by blood and opening fate with knives in their eyes. Mages deciding the world would improve if her body became corridor, womb, answer.
Jack's head lifted.
The air around him warmed.
"What did you do?" Geralt asked.
"Made visible what was already being spoken under the hills," Saesenthessis said. "He is not the only thing that can call. He must know the difference between answer and appetite."
The first draconid came from the ruined cattle shed.

Not large. A cockatrice, young and half-starved, with feathers clotted by mud and scales mottled gray. It should have attacked the nearest movement. Instead it came low, trembling, beak open, eyes fixed on Jack. Behind it came another, then a third thing too malformed to name cleanly, draconid in bone and wrongness in growth. Their throats pulsed with the same red pressure. They did not challenge him. They approached as if drawn toward a fire in winter.
Jack backed one step.
They followed.
Ciri saw the moment his blood offered him the room.

It did not look grand. No lightning. No roar. The world simply waited for him to decide. The cockatrice lowered itself. The other two froze. Geralt's shoulders tightened. Yennefer's hand remained still with terrible effort. Asha's mouth moved silently over words older than fear. Saesenthessis watched without pity.

Jack could have made the creatures kneel. Ciri knew it. Worse, he knew it. Worse still, the part of the room built from frightened animals and frightened people wanted him to. Control promised quiet. Control promised safety. Control promised a clean line where everyone else saw panic.
He took out his knife and cut the bandage from his palm instead.

Blood appeared. The draconids hissed, not in attack but recognition. Jack placed his bleeding hand flat against the rotted doorpost of the tannery and let the heat move into wood. The old post blackened under his palm. He did not look heroic. He looked as if he were holding a door shut from the inside with his shoulder while men outside debated ownership of the house.
"Move behind me," Geralt said to Ciri.
"No."
"Ciri."
"No."

Jack heard. His eyes flicked toward her, and in that glance the room changed again. Not because of romance, not yet. Because he had seen the line Geralt tried to draw, the old protective line, the safe line, the line that said stand where I can lose you less. Ciri saw him see it and saw him refuse to reinforce it.
"No one behind me," Jack said. The words came through his teeth. "Not for this."
The cockatrice lunged.
Not at him. At Ciri.

The test turned cruel with the efficiency of things designed by old powers. Jack could have used the pressure then. He almost did. Ciri felt it strike her skin like heat through linen, felt the air tighten around her wrists, not holding, but ready to. Ready to stop her fall, her draw, her choice. She drew Zireael instead, fast enough that the blade sang. Geralt cursed. Yennefer's spell cracked the air but did not release. Jack's blood flared red, then contracted with visible violence.
He chose pain.

The cockatrice hit the flat of Ciri's sword and slid, wings beating, beak snapping inches from her face. Jack caught it by the neck from the side, not with resonance, not with command, just hand and strength and a witcher's terrible economy. He threw it into the scum pit and stepped back before the other two could turn the movement into permission. Geralt moved with him. Yennefer released a binding spell so narrow it wrapped only the malformed draconid's legs and left its throat free to breathe. Ciri drove the cockatrice down with the blade point at its chest.
"Yield," she said, ridiculous and furious, because some part of her had apparently decided even monsters deserved a verb before death.
The cockatrice hissed and lowered its head.
Saesenthessis turned to Jack. "You could have owned the room."
Jack's hand smoked against the doorpost. "Yes."
"Why didn't you?"
"Because fear is not consent."
The answer entered Ciri like a blade under armor.
They did not leave the tannery at once.

Saesenthessis made them stay among the pits until the last frightened draconid had either fled the false pressure or died resisting it. This was not mercy. This was accounting. Geralt hated it. Yennefer hated it more precisely. Ciri hated that she understood it.

Jack walked the boundary he had burned into the mud. Steam still rose where his blood had sunk into rot. Each time he passed the blackened doorpost, the cockatrice in the reeds hissed once and retreated farther. It had learned the line. That frightened him more than obedience would have.
"Learning is not owning," Saesenthessis said from behind him.
"You answer thoughts now?"
"Your face is less guarded when exhausted."
"Then stop looking."
"No."
He turned. The dragon stood near the largest pit, cloak untouched by filth, eyes too still. "You made it attack Ciri."
"I made the pressure choose the easiest proof."
"That is a clean way to say cruel."
"Yes."
Ciri reached them before Saesenthessis answered again. "If you ever make me someone else's test without warning, I will find a way to be educational about it."
Saesenthessis considered her. "You would try."
"I have moved between worlds. Do not make me curious about dragon anatomy."
Geralt, passing with a length of rope, muttered, "That is my daughter."
Yennefer replied, "Unnecessarily proud."
"Accurately proud."

Jack should have smiled. He did not. He was looking at the line in the mud where his blood had become barrier. It had held. The fact should have relieved him. Instead it gave the world another argument.
Asha came beside him. "In the old houses, a line like that would be praised."
"Should I be pleased?"
"No. Praise is often the first cloth wrapped around a chain."
"Your people have cheerful lessons."
"We had survival lessons. Cheer was seasonal."
She touched the doorpost where his palm had burned black into the wood. Her fingers did not enter the mark. "You refused command. That matters."
"Does it matter if command would have saved time?"
"Especially then."
Ciri heard. Jack wished she had not and was grateful she did. Desire had not begun in the test. Recognition had. Desire could be foolish; recognition had teeth.

When they finally left the tannery, the village behind it remained empty, but its walls had acquired witnesses: a burned ring in the mud, a dead malformed beast, two sets of tracks leading away, one red stain on old wood, and the story the world would make if left alone with those ingredients.
Dandelion was not there to poison the poison first. That troubled Jack.
It troubled Ciri that she knew it troubled him.
Saesenthessis did not smile. Her approval, if it existed, had no need of warmth. "Good. Now kill the ones that cannot leave the pressure and spare what can."
"You are a generous examiner," Yennefer said with ice in every syllable.
"No," Saesenthessis said. "I am a late one. The world has been examining him without asking for weeks."

They worked for an hour. It felt longer. The malformed creature died under Geralt's blade after Yennefer proved the red pressure had grown through bone and nerve. The second cockatrice fled when Jack burned a circle into the mud and gave it a direction the pressure could not cross. The first, wounded but sane, and hating them all, flapped into the reeds and vanished. Ciri wiped her sword clean on dead grass with hands steadier than she felt.

Jack was sitting against the tannery wall by then, left hand in a basin Yennefer had conjured and filled with water that steamed around his fingers. His face had gone pale in the witcher way, which meant not weak, only pushed farther than he intended to admit. Geralt stood near him with a cloth and the expression of a man who wished the cloth could solve more kinds of pain.
Ciri went to them. Geralt saw her and moved away, not far, but enough.
"You nearly held me," she said.
Jack looked up. "Yes."
"But didn't."
"No."
"Because fear is not consent."
"Because you said no before the world had the sense to ask."
That was the wrong sentence to say if he wanted safety. It was, unfortunately, the right one.
Ciri crouched before him. The mud soaked the hem of her cloak. Emhyr would have hated that. Good.
"Do not turn me into proof that you are good," she said.
His mouth tightened. "I wasn't."
"Good. Because I will not be your absolution."
"I don't want absolution."
"What do you want?"

He looked at the ruined pits, the dead creature, the blackened doorpost, the place where the cockatrice had lowered its head to her blade. "A road where every choice is not later used against someone else."
"Ambitious."
"Stupid, perhaps."
"Often the same thing before breakfast."

He almost smiled. Ciri felt the almost more than she wanted to. It had been years since she trusted an almost from a dangerous man. Geralt's almosts had raised her. Yennefer's almosts had taught her when tenderness was being rationed for survival. This one belonged to someone whose blood could make fear obey and who had chosen to burn his own hand rather than make the room kneel.
Saesenthessis watched from the ridge.
Ciri kept her attention on the test. Some witnesses did not deserve the satisfaction of knowing the precise moment their test had changed more than its subject.
The safe house that night had once belonged to a beekeeper, which made it more honest than most noble residences Ciri had slept in.

The hives behind the house were dead, tipped and gray with weather. Inside, the air held beeswax, dust, dried mint, old smoke, and the faint sweetness that clung to wood long after honey had been taken away. Rain began again after sunset, tapping the shutters and threading silver down the warped glass. Yennefer claimed the larger room for analysis with the authority of a conquering general. Geralt took first watch because fatherhood made him incapable of sitting still after fear. Saesenthessis vanished into the dark. Asha slept with her back to the wall and a knife in her sleeve.
Ciri found Jack in the smaller room with a basin, a lamp, and his left hand wrapped badly.
"That is ugly work," she said.
He looked up from the knot. "It holds."
"So does a prison door. Move."

He should have refused. He was exactly the sort of man who would refuse help because the word had teeth. Instead he moved his hand toward the lamp. That was not trust. It was exhaustion choosing the nearest competent witness, and Ciri respected that more than speech would have allowed.

The room had one bed, one narrow table, three chairs that had lost a war with time, and a cracked shelf holding six empty honey jars. The jars caught lamplight in dull amber circles. Old sweetness clung to them, faint and stubborn. Outside, rain tapped the dead hives as if asking permission to enter. The place felt used up, but not false. Ciri liked it for that. Empty palaces pretended at cleanliness. This room admitted it had once kept living things and failed them.

Ciri sat across from him. She cleaned the edge of the burn with watered spirits and felt his fingers tense once. He did not pull away. The lamp made the red lines under his skin look darker, nearly black at the center. Her own hand, the sword hand, smelled faintly of leather and cockatrice blood despite washing. The basin steamed between them, and for a while they let practical work speak because practical work had fewer ways to lie.
"I know what it is," she said.
"The burn?"
"No. The moment. When power offers to make the room easier."
He watched her then. Not like a file. Not like a ruler. Like someone listening with every scar he did not show.
"Does it stop offering?" he asked.
"No. You get better at recognizing the salesman."
The corner of his mouth moved. "And if the room truly needs saving?"
"Then you save it and pay. But do not pretend payment makes the choice pure."
"You sound like Yennefer."
"I survived her lessons. Some of them stayed in the wound."

She wrapped the hand properly. Cloth, pressure, knot. Practical things first, because practical things allowed tenderness to approach without looking directly at it. Jack's pulse moved under her fingers. Slower than hers. Too controlled. She disliked how much she wanted to make it less so, and disliked more that the want felt clean because no one had assigned it to her.
"Ciri," he said.
Her name in his mouth was better without the rest of it. That was the danger.
"Yes."
"If this is gratitude, don't."

She held him for a long moment. Then she laughed, not happily, but with enough sharpness to cut the room open. "You have been reading the wrong files if you think I confuse being rescued with desire."
"I think people confuse many things when afraid."

"I am afraid." She tied the bandage and did not let go. "I am also angry, wet, tired of titles, tired of men using my future as a box to store their better intentions, and perfectly capable of knowing when I want to cross a room."
His breath changed. Quietly. No performance, no conquest in it. Only the body understanding before the disciplined mind found a legal objection.
"And tomorrow?" he asked.

"Tomorrow I will still be Empress-designate. Geralt's daughter. Yennefer's daughter. Elder Blood to every fool who thinks naming me gives him a handle. None of that vanishes because I choose something tonight." She leaned closer. "That is precisely the point."
He did not reach for her first.
That mattered.
Ciri closed the distance and kissed him.

The first touch was not gentle in the way songs liked gentleness. It was deliberate. A chosen door opening on hinges rusted by too many hands forcing other doors. His mouth was warm, still with restraint, and for a moment she hated the restraint because it proved he understood the price. Then his right hand rose to her jaw and stopped there, waiting against her skin with pressure that was real and did not claim.
She answered by putting her hand over his.
"Yes," she said against his mouth, because some words deserved to be simple.

His breath left him slowly. The second kiss deepened. Rain filled the window. The house around them held its old wax smell and the small, stubborn heat of one lamp. Ciri felt the room narrow to fabric, skin warmth through cloth, the rough edge of his bandage near her wrist, the disciplined tremor he could not quite hide when she shifted closer. A soft sound escaped her before she shaped it, quiet and surprised by its own freedom.
"Mmh."
Jack paused at once.
She opened her eyes. "Do not make me punish you for being careful."
"Checking."
"Good. Checked. Continue."
This time the sound that left him almost became a laugh. Almost. She kissed it before it could retreat.

They moved slowly because speed would have lied about what mattered. His hand found her waist and stayed there, steady rather than possessive. Her fingers slid into the damp hair at the back of his neck. He was hot under the road-cold. Witcher heat, wound heat, something older banked under the ribs. Ciri did not flinch from it. Heat had chased her through worlds. This one asked before closing around her.
His mouth moved to her temple, her cheek, the place below her ear where breath turned traitor. Ciri's head tilted before she decided to permit it, and the small sound that followed came unguarded.

The lamp trembled. Not from magic. From the table taking his weight as he shifted closer and then stopped again because stopping was becoming part of the language between them. She pressed her forehead to his. Outside, the hives creaked in the rain, emptied cities of wax listening to a room where two living people refused to become symbols for anyone's comfort.
"I am not fragile," she said.
"I know."
"Then why do you touch me as if I might break?"
"Because people keep trying to use unbroken things."

For one moment the desire in the room turned its face and showed the grief under it. Ciri held his gaze. There was the man beneath the file. Beneath the wolf, key, bloodline, public risk, hereditary infrastructure. A man who killed quickly when mercy required it. A man who burned his own hand rather than command. A man who had been hidden from her so both of them would carry fewer hunters and had arrived anyway with hunters behind him.
She kissed him harder.

The restraint did not vanish. It changed. It became a frame strong, and she could lean against it. Cloth shifted in small, careful motions. Breath roughened. Her back met the wall and she chose the wall, chose the hand at her waist, chose the heat, chose the way his forehead lowered to her shoulder as if he needed one second not to be watched by anything old, imperial, draconic, or afraid.

Her own hands moved over him with certainty she had been denied too often by the world and refused to deny herself now. He made a sound when her fingers found the scar at his ribs, low and caught behind his teeth. Not pain. Not only wanting. Recognition that the body could be remembered without becoming evidence.
"Jack," she whispered.
He stilled at the name.

She did not let him retreat into discipline. She drew his face back to hers and kissed him again, slower now, letting each answer become clear before asking another. His bandaged hand remained careful even when breath shortened and the room warmed. Ciri took that hand and placed it where she wanted it, over cloth, over choice, over the living fact of her body being hers to offer or refuse.
His eyes went almost black around the crimson.
"Yes?" he asked.
She felt the question everywhere it did not touch.
"Yes."

What followed did not break the world open. The world was already open, already watching through titles, files, old loves, dead hives, wet roads, and rooms full of people who would bleed themselves stupid trying to keep her safe. That was why this had to be chosen inside it, not outside it. They stayed with each other, not past each other. Every pause was another permission. Every return was another answer. A loosened clasp. A breath against skin. His mouth at her shoulder. Her fingers in his hair. The low sound that left her when warmth gathered and stayed.
"Mmh... yes."

He answered with her name once, rougher now, almost broken. She caught his mouth before the sound could become apology. The lamp burned low. Rain thickened. The dead hives outside kept their ruined sweetness. Ciri heard her own breathing change first, uneven and open, no longer trained for court walls or battlefield silence. A small sound escaped her again, then another, softer, carried by movement, heat, closeness, and the staggering relief of wanting without being turned into anyone's solution.
"Ah... mm... stay."

Jack did not hurry her. That nearly undid her more than hunger would have. He let each reaction matter, let every pause ask and answer. His restraint was not refusal now. It was respect made physical. It held the space in which she could stop being symbol, daughter, title, gate, weapon, and future for the span of one deliberate breath, and be a woman choosing exactly what she wanted.
She touched his face when the intensity rose, grounding him as much as herself. "Stay with me."
"I am."
"No. Not as shield. Not as witness. With me."
His breath shook once. Then the guarded thing in him opened enough for heat to pass through without becoming command.
"With you," he said.

The words entered the room and changed it. After that, language thinned. There was breath, warmth, the weight of closeness, the soft scrape of fabric, the bed taking their joined weight with one tired complaint, and the long, low sounds Ciri no longer tried to train into silence. Nothing in the room took from her. Nothing renamed her. She chose, answered, guided, and was answered in turn until the world outside the shutters became only rain, dead hives, and a road that could wait one night to be cruel.

Later, when the fire had almost died and the rain had thinned to mist, Ciri lay with her head against Jack's shoulder, listening to the slow labor of his breathing as it returned to discipline. She disliked that return and understood it. His bandaged hand rested open beside her, palm up, no fist. She traced the clean edge of the cloth without touching the burn.
"Tomorrow," she said.
"Yes."
"No hiding this as if I am shameful."
His body went still under her cheek. "No."
"No deciding that protecting me means leaving me ignorant."
"No."
"No becoming noble and silent because the arithmetic hurts."
There was a longer pause.
"I'll fail that one," he said.
She lifted her head.
He faced her without ornament. "Not from lack of respect. From habit. Correct me before it becomes policy."
That was not romantic. It was better. It was a route drawn in bad country.
Ciri kissed him once, slow and tired and entirely hers. "I can do that."
Outside, somewhere in the wet dark, a draconid cried once and fell silent.
Neither of them slept quickly.
Morning made everything less private and therefore more expensive.

Ciri came down first, dressed before the house had warmed, hair braided properly this time, face so composed that composition became armor. Yennefer saw the braid and understood immediately that Ciri had needed to do something with her hands before entering the day. Triss, who had been mending a strap by the hearth, looked once and then looked away with such deliberate respect that Ciri wanted to thank her and could not bear the awkwardness of gratitude before breakfast.

Geralt entered from outside with damp shoulders and stopped for a fraction of a second when he saw her. That fraction held the whole idiotic tenderness of him. He checked the room, the door, Jack's absence, Ciri's face, the table, then finally a kettle that did not require supervision.
"Tea's bad," he said.
"A national tragedy," Ciri replied.
"Not sure which nation."
"Whichever annexes this inn first."

He nodded as if that were a reasonable geopolitical forecast and poured her a cup. The tea was indeed bad. She drank it because he had poured it and because love often arrived disguised as undrinkable herbs.

Jack entered last, bringing cold air and the smell of wet horse. He turned to Ciri once, not avoiding, not claiming. She looked back. The room noticed, because every person in it had spent too many years surviving on noticed things.
Saesenthessis appeared in the doorway behind him and said, "Good. No one has turned the night into a crown yet."
Geralt closed his eyes. "Could we have one morning without a proverb?"
"Certainly. Become less instructive."
Asha made a sound into her cup. It was not laughter by any legal standard, but it would have convicted her in a kinder court.

After breakfast, Ciri found Geralt outside the dead hives. Bees had once built whole cities there, waxed chambers, routes, work, hunger, sweetness, order. Now rain had entered through broken lids and the combs had collapsed into gray ruin. It seemed unnecessarily symbolic. The world had a vulgar streak.
"You're trying very hard," she said.
"At what?"
"Not asking questions. Not giving orders. Not looking as if you want to break Jack's jaw and tuck me behind a wall at the same time."
"Only thought about the wall twice."
"Progress."
He studied the dead hives. "You chose."
"Yes."
"He chose?"
"Yes."
"You know danger doesn't become kind because choice is involved."
"I learned that from you, usually while bleeding."
His mouth tightened. "Fair."
She took his hand before he could retreat into guilt and make a hobby of it. "You do not have to approve quickly. You do have to trust that I am not a girl being swept somewhere by a red-eyed story."
"I know."
"Say it better."
His eyes found hers. "I trust you. I don't trust the world near you."
"That one I accept."
He squeezed her hand once, not hard. "If he hurts you..."
"Then I will decide whether I need comfort, distance, a sword, or silence. You may offer all four and look miserable while doing it."
"I can do that."
"I know. You raised me."
That hurt him too, but it was a clean hurt. She left him there with the hives and went back before either of them turned the conversation into a shrine.
Before they left the dead hives, Ciri found Yennefer in the doorway of the larger room with a sealed pouch in one hand and the expression of a woman choosing which fear deserved to live.
"Ask," Ciri said.
Yennefer did not pretend not to understand. "Are you well?"
"No."
The answer landed cleanly because it did not arrive dressed for reassurance.
Yennefer lowered the pouch. "Good. If you had said yes, I would have become insufferable."
"You are already insufferable."
"Then I would have become creative."

Ciri leaned against the doorframe. The hall smelled of wax and damp wood. Jack was in the yard with Buck, checking a hoof that did not need checking. Geralt had chosen a place where he could see Jack and Ciri without appearing to guard either, which fooled no one and possibly comforted him. Triss pretended to inventory herbs so no one would have to thank her for restraint.
"I chose him," Ciri said.
"Yes."
"I chose myself too."
Yennefer's face changed at that. Barely. Ciri knew her anyway. "I know."
"No. You fear knowing."
"Yes."

Ciri looked through the door at Jack. He was speaking to Buck in the low, flat tone men used when they told animals the truths they could not yet entrust to people. The horse pressed his head against Jack's chest with such blunt affection that Ciri had to look away.
"If this becomes dangerous," Yennefer said, "do not decide you must protect me from your choice."
Ciri's mouth twisted. "That sentence sounds familiar."
"I am stealing from your lecture because it was competent."
"Flattery will fail."
"I was not flattering you. I was confirming my memory."

Ciri laughed once, and the laugh almost broke into something softer before she disciplined it. Yennefer reached out and touched her cheek with two fingers. Briefly. The gesture said more than the room could survive if translated.
"You are not shameful," Yennefer said.
"I know."
"Say it on days when knowing becomes less convincing."
That one went under armor.
Ciri looked down. "And you?"
Yennefer's hand fell. "I am many things. Shame is rarely useful."
"That is not what I asked."
"No."
"Will you tell me if your fear becomes desire, and desire becomes fear, and everyone in the room starts pretending the difference is obvious?"
Yennefer closed her eyes for half a breath. When she opened them, she was still Yennefer: severe, beautiful, tired of being readable by the one person she could not bear to keep ignorant.
"Yes," she said. "If it becomes that. I will tell you what honesty requires without making you custodian of my private life."
"Accepted."
"Generous ruler."
"Difficult mother."
"Correct daughter."
They stood there until Geralt dropped something in the yard. A bucket, from the sound. Buck snorted with judgment.
Ciri looked out. "He is trying very hard."
"They both are."
Jack had turned at the sound. Geralt was scowling at the bucket as if the object had betrayed him politically. The sight was so ordinary that it hurt.
Ciri went outside before the hurt became sentimental and therefore more dangerous.
Jack did not ask Ciri to ride beside him when they left.

He adjusted Buck's girth, checked the left stirrup, tightened the bedroll, and waited with the reins in hand until she brought her horse level. That was better than asking. It left the choice standing between them with its boots on.
Ciri mounted. "If you become noble today, I will be annoyed."
"I have been warned."
"Repeated warnings improve survival."
"That why Geralt is still alive?"
"Mostly. Yennefer did the difficult years. I contributed later."
Jack almost smiled. The almost stayed longer this time.

Behind them, the dead hives leaned in rain. Ahead, the road bent toward sickness, paper, and whatever archive waited beyond the next mistake. Ciri touched the hilt of Zireael and felt, beside her, the heat of Jack's wounded hand even through space.
Choice did not make danger kind.
It made the next danger answer to someone.
Jack rode behind Ciri for the first mile, then beside her for the second.

The change was small enough for pride to survive and deliberate enough for every watcher to notice. Ciri did not comment. Comment would have turned choice into a coin she was demanding be shown. Instead she let her horse find the easier ground, let Buck snort at a puddle with moral suspicion, and let the road make space where speech would have crowded.
After a while Jack said, "Geralt did not ask if I meant harm."
"No. He asked the bucket."
"He trusts you."
"He trusts me to choose. He does not trust the world to respect it. That is irritating and occasionally useful."
Jack looked ahead. "If the world uses this against you..."
"It already uses breathing against me when politics is bored. Finish the sentence only if it is not an apology for existing near me."
His mouth closed.
Good.

Ciri softened because victory without mercy was how courts made monsters with better clothes. "You are allowed to worry. You are not allowed to package your worry as a decision I am too precious to hear."
"Understood."
"That sounded official."
"I am trying not to be noble."
"Try harder. Nobility often begins with a man sounding as if he has signed himself into weather."
Buck flicked an ear back at them.
Jack glanced at the horse. "He thinks you are correct."
"Buck has sense."
"Do not encourage him."

The road opened briefly onto a stretch of high ground where they could see the country behind them: dead hives, tannery smoke, prison stones, the gray thread of road, and beyond it the wet north where songs and files were multiplying like rats with clerks. Ciri felt the old pull of gates in her blood, the knowledge that she could leave almost any place if the need was cruel enough. Beside her, Jack carried the opposite knowledge: that some rooms followed from within.
She reached across the small space between horses and touched his sleeve once.
Not a caress. Not a performance.
A marker.
He looked at the place her fingers had been after she withdrew them, then at the road.
"Daylight," he said.
She smiled. "Daylight."
Behind them, Yennefer saw. Triss saw Yennefer seeing. Geralt saw both and immediately became interested in a strap.
The world, Ciri decided, could write what it liked.
Some facts traveled badly through ink.
The next pause came at a stream where the bridge had given up on being useful.

Geralt tested the remaining planks, pronounced them treacherous, and crossed first because age had not made him less inclined to demonstrate bad ideas safely. Yennefer crossed after him without wetting her boots, which everyone found irritating and no one surprising. Buck refused the bridge until Ciri dismounted and spoke to him as if he were a difficult nobleman with better ears.
"You flatter him," Jack said.
"He responds to rank."
Buck blew air through his nose.
"He disputes that."
"He may file a petition."
The horse crossed.

On the far bank, Jack looked back at the water. The current pulled leaves into a narrow whirl beneath the broken middle of the bridge. For a moment the red lines in his palm warmed, then cooled. Not danger. Memory of pressure. He had begun to distinguish the shades of wrongness, which felt less like learning and more like being taught by wounds.
Ciri came beside him. "What?"
"Nothing ready to become a sentence."
"Good. Sentences are where men start building cages."
He faced her fully. "You make every conversation harder."
"Yes."
"That was not a complaint."
"I know."

They stood until Geralt called them both fools for letting rain start again while philosophical. It was practical advice, therefore nearly affectionate. Ciri mounted laughing under her breath. Jack heard it and carried the sound longer than weather required.

Triss Merigold's private notation, folded into a field ledger and never sent: Heat without fever. Obedience without spellwork. Calling without command. Containment without closure. The worst part is not that the categories fail. The worst part is that the wrong people will call the failure permission.
Yennefer knew before breakfast.

Not because Ciri smiled. Ciri did not. She came into the main room with damp hair braided badly, boots in hand, and the hard calm of a woman daring the furniture to comment. Jack entered three minutes later from the side door because he had gone outside to check the horses rather than be seen arriving from the room. That was considerate and therefore incriminating. Geralt noticed the timing, the bandage retied in Ciri's hand rather than Yennefer's, the absence of surprise between them, and immediately looked at the kettle as if tea had become tactically complex.
Triss would have called that proof if she had been present.

Triss arrived half an hour later with mud on her hem, courier dust on her cloak, and a sealed pouch tucked inside her bodice because no guard searched women properly when they were polite and looked tired. She took in the room in one glance: Geralt too quiet, Yennefer too still, Ciri daring judgment, Jack pretending horses had required far more grooming than any horse alive deserved, Asha watching everyone as if family systems were a form of battlefield geometry.
The analysis required three rooms, two basins, one locked trunk, five bad arguments, and a spoon Triss sacrificed in the name of science.

Yennefer objected to the spoon on aesthetic grounds. Triss objected to Yennefer's objection on methodological grounds. Geralt asked whether the spoon had offended anyone yet. Ciri said anything could be dangerous if used by a person with confidence. Jack, who had seen a man killed by a boot scraper in Velen, said nothing.

They chose the inn's washroom because it had stone walls and a drain. Triss placed the draconid clot in a blue-glazed bowl. Yennefer laid Black Ink's latest residue report beside it. The two things should not have known each other. The clot was dead matter, magic-sick and scale-born. The report was paper, ink, and lies wearing grammar. Yet when Yennefer moved the page within a hand's width of the bowl, the clot stiffened and the ink darkened around the words field stabilization.
"Again," Triss said.
Yennefer gave her a look. "Do not become Keira merely because the morning is ugly."
"I have never owned shoes that impractical."
"You have owned worse hats."
"Everyone has owned worse hats. That is not science."

The exchange steadied the room. Jack watched them work and understood what their style of competence demanded. Yennefer attacked mystery like an insult. Triss approached it as if the patient might hear even when the patient was a system. Neither softened the facts. Neither surrendered the living person to them.

Ciri stood beside the window, arms folded, saying less than her face wanted. The morning after had not made her uncertain. It had made her angrier at every force that would try to make certainty public property. Geralt noticed and pretended to inspect a latch.
Yennefer dipped the spoon into water touched by the clot. It blackened along the edge. Triss touched the handle with a pulse of magic and the bowl gave a sound like a distant hinge.
Jack's signet went cold.

Ciri's scarred places answered in a different language. She did not glow, vanish, or perform any convenient sign of Elder Blood for the benefit of anxious observers. She simply turned toward the bowl before anyone asked her to, as if a corridor had opened somewhere behind her ribs and a draft had moved through.
Yennefer saw it and stopped the test.
"Stop."
Triss looked up. "We need the interaction."
"We have it."
"We have an implication."
"We have my daughter reacting to poisoned draconid matter and administrative paper. That is too much implication for one basin."
Ciri's voice came low. "Do not decide the limit for me because you dislike the shape of the danger."
Yennefer's eyes flashed. "I dislike several shapes. This one has earned priority."
"Ask," Ciri said.
The room held still.
Yennefer turned to her. The change was slight and enormous. From mother as shield to mother as witness. "Will you stand nearer and tell me what you feel, stopping the moment you choose?"
"Yes."

Ciri came to the table. Jack moved back before she reached him, not because he feared her touch, but because the room already had enough pressure without his body adding a false center. Ciri saw. Approval passed over her face and hid quickly.
The bowl trembled when she stood beside it.
"Not a gate," she said.
Yennefer's voice sharpened. "What, then?"
"A gate would have direction. This is a room trying to become direction. It wants a person to define inside and outside."
Triss wrote with frightening speed.
Jack's left hand burned. He did not move it. Ciri turned to him. "You feel the opposite."
"Yes."
"What is it?"
"Not opposite. Complement. Lock looking for walls."
Yennefer swore softly in Elder Speech. Triss stopped writing.
Geralt looked from one to the other. "Explain."
"Ciri is gate-logic," Yennefer said. "Movement. Boundary traversal. World-suture."
"Beautiful and unpleasant," Triss added. "Jack is containment logic. Not a door by himself. A chamber waiting to be made from pressure."
Jack studied the Black Ink page. "Hereditary infrastructure."
"No," Ciri said immediately.
He met her eyes.
"That is their word," she said. "Not ours."
The bowl cracked.

Not shattered. Cracked. A red line ran through the glaze, then into the table beneath it. Jack cut his palm through the reopened bandage and pressed blood beside the crack before the line reached Ciri's hand. The pressure moved into him, not by spell but by horrible familiarity. For one breath every candle in the inn leaned inward. Ciri caught his wrist with both hands.
"Do not take it alone."
"It was moving toward you."
"And I said do not take it alone."
His attention dropped to her hands on his wrist. The room watched and pretended not to understand everything at once.
Yennefer sealed the bowl with a word that made the water turn white. Triss wrapped Jack's hand while Ciri held it steady. Geralt turned away to stop himself from doing something useless with a sword.
When the red line faded from the table, Triss returned to her notes.

"This is what Black Ink is synchronizing," she said. "Not only reports. Events. They file residue, residue is compared to public notices, public notices route witnesses, witnesses create pressure, pressure teaches the seal."
"Every attempt to measure me teaches the thing inside the lock how to be measured," Jack said.
Saesenthessis, standing in the open doorway as if she had always been there, answered, "Yes."
No one asked when she entered. Some discourtesies were too small for dragons.
Triss sent three letters after the washroom test and burned four drafts.

The first draft was too frightened and therefore too revealing. The second too careful and therefore useless. The third named Jack in a sentence that could be quoted by enemies. The fourth used the phrase dual resonance and made Yennefer say, "If you write that to anyone outside this room, I will feed the paper to the fire and the fire to you."
"Helpful critique," Triss said.
"Accurate critique."

The final letters were better. One went to Kovir under the shape of a request about post-war livestock fevers. One went to Dandelion disguised as a complaint about a verse that compared wolves to civic responsibility. One went to Zoltan and contained no disguise at all, only the instruction to find who was buying draconid musk, blackened copper, and clove-wax in the same week.
Zoltan, Triss wrote, if any man tells you this is not accounting, insult him for me.
Geralt read that line and said, "He will enjoy that."
"He deserves one pleasure."

Yennefer sealed the residue bowl in a warded trunk with more violence than the trunk deserved. "The scale-sickness is not disease in the ordinary sense. It is bad instruction traveling through animal bodies."
"Can it reach humans?" Ciri asked.
"Humans are tragically receptive to bad instruction," Yennefer said. "Magically, not in the same way. Politically, constantly."

Jack sat near the window, hand freshly wrapped, watching rain blur the yard into long gray strokes. The innkeeper had begun telling patrons the party in the parlor were tax auditors. This was effective. No one approached. Several people paid old debts at once.
Triss came to Jack with a cup of willowbark steeped too long. "Drink."
"Medical order?"
"Social threat. Yennefer made it. If you do not drink, I will tell her you respect neither medicine nor women with excellent aim."
He took the cup.
Ciri leaned against the mantel, watching him accept care without ceremony. That was new. Not easy. New. Geralt noticed too and looked away in time to preserve the moment from fatherhood.
Saesenthessis stood by the closed trunk. "The illness will spread along old anchor routes first. Hills, quarries, ruined fortresses, places where stone once agreed to hold pressure."
"Agreed?" Yennefer asked.
"Endured, then."
"That is not the same."
"No. That is why I changed the word."
Asha looked east. "If northern anchors are sick, the archive will have records of symptoms before it has truth. Black Ink will believe symptoms are control points."
"Then the archive comes first," Jack said.
Ciri's gaze moved to him. "Not Zerrikania?"
"Not yet. If they know my parents' names before I do, they will write the next road for us."
That answer did not come from destiny. It came from a man refusing to be driven by mystery while paperwork hunted his dead.
Triss nodded. "Then we need proof they filed more than you."
Yennefer's expression went cold. "We need proof they filed murder."
No one corrected her.
A Black Ink copy arrived before dusk, which proved the enemy had either excellent riders or shameless luck. No one in the room wished to credit luck.

The message was hidden in a shipment inventory for lamp oil. Zoltan's courier had marked the wrong line with a beer stain shaped suspiciously like a boot. Triss unfolded the inner paper and read without sitting.
"Observed effects after draconid-contact event suggest relational trigger. Female royal proximity may alter subject compliance threshold. Recommend separation if custody invitation fails."
The room changed.
Not loudly. Loudness would have been easier.

Geralt stood. Ciri's hand moved to her sword. Yennefer's face became so calm the fire seemed frightened of her. Jack looked at the paper with the awful stillness of a man watching his private life become a tactical note before he had learned where to put it.
Triss continued, because leaving the sentence unfinished would give it more power than it deserved.

"Addendum: sorceress interference probable. Do not antagonize Yennefer of Vengerberg unless containment environment prepared. Merigold to be redirected through humanitarian channels if possible. Geralt of Rivia unlikely to respond to formal authority. Leverage through dependents not advised until field captain confirms collateral tolerance."
"Dependents," Ciri said.
The word smelled worse than blood.
Asha took the paper and held it as if it were something dead but contagious. "They are learning who matters."
"No," Jack said. "They are learning what to threaten."
Yennefer turned toward him. "Those are not separate categories to men like this."
Ciri stepped beside Jack, not behind him. The motion was small and deliberate, becoming a correction to the report without needing ink.
"If they recommend separation," she said, "they have misunderstood proximity."
Geralt turned to her. Pride and terror made a poor mask on him. "Ciri."
"No."
He stopped.
Good, Triss thought. Painful, but good.
She folded the message into a square. "This proves Scale-Sickness is already feeding into policy language. The archive route cannot wait."
Yennefer's voice cut in. "And it proves every intimacy, every kindness, every argument in this company will become someone else's leverage if we let Black Ink write the minutes first."
Jack studied the fire. "Then we stop giving them minutes."
"How?" Geralt asked.
Jack lifted his eyes. "We make the next scene one they cannot explain before they arrive."
Saesenthessis, from the corner, looked almost pleased. "At last. A human proposes usefulness against the office rather than inside it."
No one thanked her. Dragons did not require encouragement.
That night Triss copied the Black Ink note into her own hand and changed one word in the margin: dependents became beloved.
Yennefer saw the alteration. "Sentimental."
"Accurate."
"Unwise."
"Also accurate."

The two women sat across from each other under a lamp that hissed whenever the wind reached the shutters. Between them lay files, draconid residue sealed in glass, and the map of a route that now bent toward an archive none of them had wanted to need. They had been romantic rivals once in the crude vocabulary of people who confused men with thrones and women with banners. The facts had been uglier, kinder, older, and less useful to gossip.
Triss tapped the margin. "They call people leverage because it helps them sleep."
Yennefer's mouth tightened. "You think Sorel sleeps?"
"I think men like him schedule rest."
"Worse."
"Yes."

For a while they worked without speaking. That, too, was a kind of alliance. Not friendship polished for a court. Not forgiveness made decorative. Competence beside competence while the people they loved became targets in someone else's sentence.
Finally Yennefer said, "Thank you for not leaving the room."
Triss did not look up. "Which one?"
"All of them."
The lamp trembled once.
Triss folded the copy and sealed it. "You are welcome."
Neither woman smiled. Both returned to work.
"Good," Triss said. "I see I missed several conversations and at least one mistake everyone will call a choice after lunch."
Ciri turned to her. "It was a choice before lunch."
"Then we are ahead of schedule."
Yennefer almost smiled. Almost. Then she held out a hand. "The pouch."
"No greeting?"
"The greeting is implicit in my not accusing you of taking three days to travel one."
"I took one and a half. One was occupied by a tollman with heroic interest in cheese."
Geralt looked up. "Did the cheese survive?"
"Better than the tollman. He remains alive but educationally improved."
That saved the minute, as small jokes often did when the room was built from knives no one wanted to pick up first.

The pouch contained three things: a Black Ink notice copied from a Temerian vassal corridor, a residue report from a Kovir mage contact willing to be paid in future discretion, and a scale wrapped in silk. The scale was black at the edge, green toward the center, and veined red underneath.
Jack's bandaged hand warmed visibly when Triss placed the scale on the table.
Ciri saw it and did not move. Yennefer saw Ciri not move. Geralt saw both and put the kettle down too hard.

"Scale-sickness," Triss said. "That is the field name now, though the field did not choose it. Draconids acting against territory, nests cooling, throats closing, heat moving inward. Public notices appear within a day of any confirmed case, sometimes before local reports are filed. Someone is synchronizing magical residue with civic language."
"Black Ink," Jack said.

"And something else," Yennefer said. She had not touched the scale. She did not need to. "The notices follow the sickness, yes, but the sickness follows pressure. The pressure follows anchors. The anchors follow..."
"Me," Jack said.
"No," Ciri said at once.
Every face in the room found her. She hated that. Good.
"No," she repeated. "That is the wrong grammar. It follows what his blood answers. That is not the same as saying it follows him."
Yennefer's expression shifted. Pride, fear, and a private grief she would deny under interrogation. "Correct."
Jack's attention touched Ciri for the briefest moment. The room pretended not to notice and failed with varying degrees of dignity.
Triss opened her ledger. "I have a map."
"Of course you do," Geralt said. "You bring maps the way Dandelion brings hats."

"Useful, portable, and less likely to frighten horses." She spread the folded sheet across the table. "Here are known scale-sickness reports. Here are contract notices using containment phrasing. Here are paid songs, Black Ink couriers, and residue events detected by Yennefer's stone fragments. They are not identical routes. They are converging routes."
Asha leaned over the map. "Toward old anchors."
"Yes," Triss said. "But the public papers move ahead of the magic in two places."
Yennefer's eyes narrowed. "Meaning someone knows where pressure will occur."
"Or wants Jack to be near, so everyone believes he caused it."
Geralt folded his arms. "Can they create the sickness?"

"Not fully," Yennefer said. "No. They can provoke residue, perhaps. Disturb an anchor. Move a draconid. Stage a witness. But this pressure is older than their offices. That may be the only comfort, and it is a poor one."
Jack touched the edge of the table with his uninjured hand. "Can you cut it out?"
The question was too calm. That gave anger nowhere clean to stand.
Ciri's chair moved back a finger's width. Geralt looked away. Triss lowered the pen. Yennefer did not soften. Sometimes the kindest answer wore no softness because softness invited bargaining.
"No," Yennefer said. "Not without possibly opening what it contains."
"Possibly."
"Certainly too much for me to gamble with your body to improve the quality of our ignorance."
Jack nodded once. "Then it is not a wound."
"It is a wound," Triss said. "But not all wounds can be closed without killing what grew around them."
He faced her, and she held his gaze because Triss had learned that warmth became useless if it fled difficulty.

Yennefer moved the scale with silver tongs. The red vein brightened when it neared Jack's bloodstained bandage and dimmed near Ciri's hand, then brightened again when Ciri touched the folded page marked hereditary infrastructure. The room went silent.
"Again," Triss said.

They repeated it. Scale near bandage: heat. Scale near Ciri's skin: faint tremor. Scale near Ciri's file page: red brightening. Scale near both Jack's bandage and Ciri's file page: the lamp leaned east and the old table creaked though no one touched it.
"It responds to blood and language," Ciri said.
Yennefer's face had gone cold. "It responds to recognition of function."
"Explain that as if I have not slept," Geralt said.

"Jack's blood carries pressure. Ciri's history carries a pattern of being named as function by magical and political structures. The residue is not reacting to Ciri's power in the simple sense. It is reacting to a grammar the world has used on both of them. Vessel. Key. Blood. Custody. Door. It is not intelligent as a man is intelligent. But old magic often understands shape before vocabulary."
"So the files matter magically," Jack said.

"The files matter because they teach people how to approach you. Magic and politics are both forms of approach when enough fear is involved." Yennefer's mouth tightened. "This is why words are not decoration."

Triss wrote quickly. "Rule one. His resonance calls and contains. Rule two. Draconid sickness increases around disturbed anchor sites. Rule three. Public language can align witnesses and rituals strongly; residue patterns answer to that. Rule four. Removing the seal force may free the contamination."
"Rule five," Ciri said. "No one calls him the cause because the sentence is convenient."
Triss wrote that too.
Geralt turned to Jack. "Rule six. You don't test the limits alone."
Jack's expression closed. "You making rules for me?"
"Yes. Badly. Argue after breakfast."
Ciri looked into her cup to hide the expression that wanted to become a smile. Jack saw it. Yennefer saw him see it. Triss saw everyone seeing everything and wrote nothing, which was perhaps mercy.
The analysis took the rest of the day and ruined three decent tablecloths.

Yennefer objected to calling them decent. Triss objected to treating domestic textiles as expendable. Geralt said the first tablecloth had already been stained by cockatrice bile, which gave it a warrior's death. Ciri said if cloth could be honored for service, perhaps the court should begin with the napkins because they had endured the most lies. Jack said nothing, which made Triss suspect he found the whole argument less irritating than he wished.

They tested scale, stone, bandage, old Black Ink paper, Saesenthessis's broken clay vial, and one piece of the black clot from the tannery pit. Each item responded to a different combination of heat, language, and blood. Yennefer grew sharper as the results worsened. Triss grew quieter. Ciri began pacing in the intervals, not from impatience but from a court-trained refusal to sit while other people made categories around her. Geralt checked Jack's bandage twice without comment. Jack let him once and refused the second, which counted as progress in no direction anyone could name.
By dusk they had a conclusion no one liked.

Jack's crimson resonance was not a power in the way Black Ink wished it were, and not an illness in the way healers would prefer. It called pressure because it recognized broken parts of the Barbed-Star lattice. It contained pressure because some golden remnant in the blood remembered duty. It contaminated every containment because something black and hungry had seeped into the same mechanism. Call and lock. Door and bolt. Wound and stitch. None of the metaphors held entirely. All of them cut.
"A contaminated lock," Triss said at last.
"A lock that bleeds," Asha said.
"A lock that is a man," Ciri said.
Saesenthessis had returned at some point and stood in the doorway. No one had heard her. Ciri planned to be annoyed about that later.
"Now you are beginning," the dragon-woman said.
Yennefer turned on her. "Beginning would have been more useful before we burned three tablecloths and nearly weaponized grammar."
"You are alive. The cloth is not. This is a favorable ratio."
Geralt rubbed his forehead. "I missed when riddles were shorter."
Saesenthessis turned to Jack. "Do you understand what they discovered?"
"They discovered I cannot be fixed."
"No." Ciri's voice cut across the room. "They discovered people who call you fixable are asking the wrong question."
Jack turned toward her. The room held its breath with appalling lack of subtlety.
Saesenthessis watched Ciri now. "And you understand why that matters?"
"Yes."
"Say it."
Yennefer's eyes flashed. "Careful."

Ciri stood straighter. "No, let her. Dragons are not the only creatures allowed to be unpleasant for educational purposes." She looked at Jack, not Saesenthessis. "It matters because if the world decides you are broken machinery, every repair becomes permitted. If the world decides you are dangerous blood, every cage becomes protection. If the world decides you are sacrifice walking, every affection becomes a delay to be overcome."
Geralt went very still.
Jack did too.
Triss wrote nothing. Some lines had to remain in the air first.
Saesenthessis inclined her head. "Better."
"Do not grade me," Ciri said.
"Then stop answering well."
Ciri almost laughed. It became something else before it escaped.
That night, Yennefer found Triss outside the house, washing ink from her fingers in a rain barrel under the eaves.
"You saw them," Yennefer said.
Triss dried her hands on a cloth already sacrificed to scholarship. "Everyone saw them. The bees in the dead hives saw them."
"Do you disapprove?"

"Of two adults choosing something in the middle of state violence and draconic residue? I disapprove of the timing, the danger, the inevitability, and the paperwork it will create. I do not disapprove of the choice."
Yennefer looked toward the dark window where Ciri's silhouette crossed once, then vanished. "You are kinder than I am."
"No. I count different debts first."

Inside, Geralt spoke quietly to Jack near the hearth. The words did not carry. The posture did: Geralt standing close to help and far enough not to claim. Triss watched that and felt an old ache soften into something more difficult. He was preparing to care for another young person who might be taken by destiny wearing new clothes. Geralt had never learned to survive that kind of arithmetic. He only kept standing near it.
"He is becoming fatherly," Triss said.
Yennefer followed her gaze. "Yes."
"That will hurt him."
"Yes."
"And Jack."
"Yes."
Triss wrapped the stained cloth around her fingers. "We are very good at identifying disasters after adopting them."
Yennefer's mouth curved without amusement. "It is one of our shared talents."

The rain barrel reflected both of them badly. Red hair, black hair, two women who had loved, lost, chosen, wounded, healed, and found themselves again beside a younger pair of people being turned into arguments by a world too frightened to ask permission.
"We need more than rules," Triss said.
"We need options," Yennefer replied. "And we are running out of northern ones."
Across the yard, Saesenthessis stood under the trees, looking east.
Triss saw the direction and understood what no one had yet said aloud.
Zerrikania was no longer a distant origin.
It was becoming a road.
Triss built the second map on the floor because the table had become prejudiced by blood.

She used bootlaces for courier routes, burnt matches for public incidents, crumbs for paid songs until Geralt objected that this made strategic planning vulnerable to mice, and three silver buttons for confirmed anchor signs. Yennefer contributed four black stones from sites that had steamed in rain and one hairpin when Triss ran out of straight lines. The hairpin marked Ciri. Yennefer placed it with such care that no one commented and everyone understood.

"Here," Triss said, pointing to the line between the tannery and the broken mill. "The public notices did not follow Jack. They followed expected witnesses. Wherever the story can be shaped, paper arrives first. Wherever the anchor pressure is strongest, draconids arrive first. Black Ink is not controlling the whole pattern. It is riding the portions it can explain afterward."

Yennefer crouched, black skirts gathered in one hand with irritated elegance. "So Sorel does not need omniscience. He needs punctual clerks, frightened witnesses, and enough old research to know where the road may become interesting."
"Exactly."
Geralt studied the crumbs. "Dandelion is here?"
"Dandelion is five crumbs and a badly paid fiddler."
"He'd say six."
"He always overvalues performance."

Ciri sat on a windowsill and watched Jack study the floor map without stepping near it. He had the expression of a man looking at a trap that had been built partly from his footprints and partly from other people's doors. She knew that expression. She had worn versions of it in courts, forests, deserts, towers, and once beside a frozen lake where the world expected her to be less frightened because destiny had finally become explicit.
"What happens if we stop moving?" Jack asked.

Triss looked up. "The public story moves without you. Black Ink improves its claim. Draconid sickness continues around anchors. Ciri becomes easier to separate as a political variable because the court will call stillness instability. Geralt becomes more tempted to do something violent and satisfying that solves nothing. Yennefer becomes unbearable."
"I am already unbearable," Yennefer said.
"More so."
"Ah. Catastrophe."
Jack nodded as if this were a normal forecast. "And if we move east?"
Asha spoke from the door. "We move toward memory with fewer translations."
Saesenthessis, seated on the windowsill opposite Ciri though no one had seen her sit, added, "And toward things that will resent being translated at all."
"Zerrikania," Ciri said.

The word changed the room. Barely. Heat noticed first. Heat entered the air that did not belong to the hearth. The barbed-star signet under Jack's shirt cooled. Asha bowed her head. Triss placed a silver button east of all known roads.

"Not yet," Yennefer said. "We still need northern proof. Archives. Jurisdiction. Who filed the old violence and who is repeating its handwriting now. If we go east with only myth, every court behind us will write the practical version before we return."
"Then we get proof," Jack said.
Geralt studied the map. "And try not to become it."
No one had a joke for that.

Private advisory drafted in Ilyra Sarn's cipher for later reconstruction: The principal refuses the premise that secrecy protects her. She distinguishes privacy from concealment with unusual force. Any handler attempting to manage the distinction for her should expect dismissal, injury, or both.
The inn called itself The Velvet Hart and had neither velvet nor, unless the stew was investigated by an honest natural philosopher, much evidence of hart.

It did have thick walls, a room with two exits, a stable owner who believed coin more faithfully than rumor, and a parlor large enough for arguments to stand without stepping on one another. That answered it. Outside, the road bent toward a Temerian vassal route where Black Ink permits were beginning to breed in offices that had once stamped Redanian confiscations. Inside, a fire smoked, rain worried the shutters, and a painted hunting scene above the mantel showed a stag looking resigned to aristocracy.
Ciri and Yennefer took the smaller parlor after the first argument because both understood that a room can become a weapon when too many people watch a woman choose her tone.

The smaller parlor smelled of stale lavender, damp velvet, and the faint smoke of a chimney that had never quite learned ambition. A painting of a noble child with a hunting falcon hung crooked above a cabinet. The child looked miserable. The falcon looked competent. Ciri approved of the falcon.
Yennefer closed the door. "Speak."
"Commanding already."
"Efficient."
"Jack says that when hurt."
Yennefer's expression altered by a hair. "Does he?"
Ciri sat on the arm of a chair instead of the chair because she had no interest in behaving for furniture. "You are afraid for me."
"Yes."
"You are also afraid because you understand him."
"Yes."
"And because wanting anyone in this knot feels like giving the world another thread to pull."
Yennefer studied the crooked painting. "You have become intolerably perceptive."
"I had teachers."
"Then blame Geralt. I taught poise, grammar, and how to make men regret condescension."
"You taught more than that."
The sentence stayed between them. Yennefer did not move toward tenderness. She let it come if it could survive the air.

Ciri softened first, which annoyed her and therefore made it true. "I am not angry that you feel something. I am angry at any version of the room where I am protected by not being told. I am angry at being treated as daughter when ignorance is convenient and as ruler when obedience is required."
Yennefer's mouth tightened. "That is just."
"Do not say it like a verdict."
"How shall I say it?"
"Like my mother."
Yennefer's control faltered. Only for a breath. Enough for Ciri to see the wound under the velvet.
"I am terrified," Yennefer said. "There. Maternal?"
"No. Honest."

They did not embrace. Not then. Yennefer reached out and corrected a loose strand of Ciri's hair with hands that had steadied spells, poisons, bodies, kingdoms, and one impossible girl. Ciri allowed it. That was more than an embrace in some languages.
"If you choose him," Yennefer said, "choose with your whole sight. Not because he mirrors your cage. Not because you wish to rescue a man from a word. Not because danger makes the blood impatient."
"I know."
"Do not say that like Geralt."
Ciri almost smiled. "I choose nothing blind. Not anymore."
Yennefer nodded. "Good."
"And you?"
The question struck exactly where Ciri meant it to.
Yennefer lowered her hand. "I choose nothing simple."
"That is not an answer."
"No. It is the most accurate thing I have."
In the larger parlor, Triss watched Geralt try to repair a saddle buckle that was not broken.
She let him fail for two minutes because love, in its kinder forms, sometimes allowed a man to embarrass himself privately before saving him from the public version.
"That buckle has survived several wars," she said.
"It squeaks."
"It does not."
"It might."
"Geralt."
He stopped with the tool in his hand.

The fire smoked behind them. Rain pressed against the shutters. Jack was outside checking Buck's fetlock because Buck had stepped on a stone and Jack preferred horse injuries to emotional parliaments. Yennefer and Ciri were behind the smaller door, speaking in low voices that turned Geralt's shoulders into a map of restraint.
Triss sat beside him. "History is not betrayal."
He studied the buckle. "Was not going to ask."
"No. You were going to carry the unasked question until it turned into something stupid with nobility attached."
"Everyone has become critical of nobility lately."
"It has earned scrutiny."
He almost smiled. Then the almost went out. "Yen and Jack."
"Yes."
"Ciri and Jack."
"Yes."
"It is a mess."
"Not yet. A mess requires secrecy, humiliation, ownership, or stupidity. At present, we mostly have danger, desire, history, fear, and several people too proud to say simple things."
"That sounds like a mess."
"It sounds like your social circle."
He put down the tool. "Does it hurt you?"
The question was plain, and it mattered. Triss took time with it.

"Yes," she said. "Sometimes. Not because Yennefer exists. She existed before me. Not because you remember loving her. I would distrust you if you claimed not to. It hurts because the world keeps making love a tactical liability and then pretending cruelty is the mature response."
Only then did he face her.
She held his gaze. "I chose you with eyes open. Do not insult me by acting as if my dignity depends on everyone else becoming less complicated."
Geralt's hand covered hers. Rough, warm, hesitant in the places speech had failed. "I would not."
"You would by accident."
"Fair."
"Then do better by intention."
He nodded. It was not a vow. It was more useful.
Outside, Buck snorted at something. Jack muttered back. The horse struck the stable door once. Triss smiled despite herself.
"There," she said. "A simpler relationship."
"Buck bites him less than most."
"High praise from a horse."
Geralt leaned back. For a moment, not long, the parlor became almost peaceful: smoky fire, bad painting, rain, and the woman he had chosen telling him the facts without asking to be worshiped for it.
Then someone knocked below, and the innkeeper shouted that a prayer book had been returned with one page too many.
Peace, as usual, had poor stamina.
The returned prayer book changed the shape of the argument before anyone opened it.

Ciri watched Jack pick it up with two fingers, saw Yennefer's nostrils flare at the seal, saw Triss glance first at the courier's hands rather than the paper. Geralt had already moved between the door and the stairs. Asha's knife was not visible. That did not mean it was absent. Saesenthessis looked bored in the way mountains might look bored before rockfall.
"Do we have one hour," Ciri asked, "or has the world become impatient?"
"The world was born impatient," Yennefer said.
Triss took the prayer book. "This was placed where the chapel boy would find it. Not given through staff. Whoever sent it wanted the inn to be implicated without being guilty."
Geralt measured Jack's face. "Trap."
"Invitation," Jack said.
"Same road in clean boots."
The innkeeper appeared in the doorway, pale and furious. "If that is politics, take it outside."
Ciri turned. "It is not politics."
The man relaxed by half a breath.
"It is probably several jurisdictions committing conspiracy through devotional literature."
He went pale again.
Yennefer looked pleased despite herself. "You are improving."
The innkeeper crossed himself, then remembered Ciri's face from no official portrait because she was too muddy and too angry for paint. "I want no trouble."
"Then you should have bought a monastery," Geralt said.
"Monasteries have worse cellars," Triss added.
Jack gave the innkeeper two coins. "For the room. And the door if someone damages it while being wrong."
The man took the money because class consciousness survived terror better than pride. "No blood on the parlor rug."
"There is a rug?" Ciri asked.
"There was."
"That may simplify matters."
Only after the man retreated did Jack open the prayer book.
The page inside smelled faintly of clove and cold iron.
They did not answer the invitation that night only with Yennefer's bead.

First they wrote the answer everyone wanted to send and burned it. Ciri's version contained three accusations, one legal threat, and a sentence Ilyra would later call "monarchically satisfying but strategically suicidal." Geralt's version had eight words, six of them rude by implication. Triss wrote a version so diplomatically lethal that even Yennefer admired it and then rejected it because admiration made it traceable. Asha suggested sending back a mourning cord knotted in the pattern for may your children inherit your lies. Saesenthessis said that was culturally rich but logistically obscure.
Jack wrote nothing for the longest time.
When he finally took the pen, he did not address Sorel. He did not address Black Ink. He wrote a single line on a strip cut from the margin of the invitation.
Voluntary language is not consent when refusal has been priced in advance.
Yennefer read it and said nothing.
Ciri read it next. Her face changed. "Send that."
"No," Triss said, softly. "That sentence is too much him."
Jack looked up.
She did not soften the point. "They are collecting you. Do not send them a clean piece."
For a moment the room threatened to become cruel in exactly the way care could become cruel when it wore caution too tightly. Then Jack nodded once and gave her the strip.
Triss burned it herself. Not because the sentence was wrong. Because it was his.

The final response contained no words. Yennefer's sealed grain, a line of burned glass, and a scrap of blank paper folded around nothing. Ciri approved of the nothing. Geralt said nothing often had better sense than people. Asha called it a refusal that did not perform. Saesenthessis said humans were finally learning to use silence with moderate competence.
Then Jack went outside with Yennefer, because the room had become too full of people trying to save him by managing the size of his voice.
Ciri stood before the painting and felt kinship with the stag.
"It knows," she said.
Yennefer, seated near the table with a cup she had not drunk from, did not ask what. "The painter lacked subtlety."
"The hunter or the hunted?"
"Both. Mediocrity is often democratic."
Ciri turned. "Are we speaking about paintings?"
"We may begin there. It is polite to give a conversation somewhere harmless to stand before killing it."

The room had been arranged badly on purpose. Geralt and Jack had gone to the stables to check horses, because men in emotional danger often discovered urgent tack maintenance. Triss had gone to confirm the innkeeper's ledger and whether the back road was as private as advertised. Asha sat outside the door, not guarding them exactly, but ensuring privacy did not become opportunity for others. Saesenthessis had vanished because dragons apparently considered scheduled conversations beneath dignity.
That left Ciri and Yennefer with the fire, the ugly painting, and everything mothers and daughters did not say when other people were bleeding nearby.
"You are worried," Ciri said.
"Observant."
"Do not do that."
Yennefer looked up. "Do what?"
"Make sharpness stand in for an answer because the answer has teeth."
For a moment, Yennefer's face became very still. Ciri had learned some of her cruelty from that stillness and most of her courage in answering it from surviving how much love lived beneath.

"I am worried," Yennefer said. "About Jack. About you. About the way old structures recognize each other in blood and language. About the fact that desire, when placed inside pursuit, becomes another route enemies can map."
"And about yourself."
The fire shifted. The stag on the wall continued suffering art.
Yennefer set the cup down. "Yes."
The answer should not have surprised Ciri. It did. She sat because standing had become performance.
"You want him," Ciri said.
"Yes."
No flinch. No confession dressed in apology. That was Yennefer. Truth, when she chose it, came perfectly armed.

Ciri studied her own hands. They were sword hands, court hands, scarred hands, hands that had held worlds too cold to name. "And you think that makes you monstrous because of Geralt. Because of me. Because you are supposed to be above wanting dangerous things after being wise about them."
"Do not become too skilled at my interior life. It is irritating."
"You made me. Complain to the craftswoman."

Yennefer looked toward the shuttered window. For once, her control did not vanish. It thinned enough for the old pain to show through. "Geralt and I are history. Real history. Not erased because he has a house with Triss, not revived because I remember how his silence sounds in three kinds of grief. Triss knows that. I know that. He knows it badly, but he knows."
"And Jack?"
"Jack is not a replacement. Not for Geralt. Not for what the years took. Not for any wound that would be vulgar if I handed it to a younger man and called the transfer healing."
"I know."
"Do you?"
There was the mother, finally. Not jealous. Not delicate. Afraid.

Ciri leaned back. "I know he looked at me yesterday like I was a choice, not a prophecy. I know he nearly controlled a room and chose pain instead. I know wanting him does not make him mine. I know you wanting him does not make me less. I also know I will cut the tongue from anyone who turns this into court gossip before I decide whether the tongue is worth preserving for intelligence purposes."
Yennefer watched her. Then, against all odds, laughed softly.
"You are very dear to me."
"That sounded like an accusation."
"Often the truest endearments do."
The laughter faded, but the room remained warmer for its brief existence.

Ciri leaned forward. "I do not want secrets used as kindness. Not with him. Not with you. Not with Geralt. I have had enough people arrange my life while praising my importance. If pain comes, let it arrive in daylight."
Yennefer reached across the small table and placed her hand over Ciri's. The gesture was simple. That made it harder to bear.
"Daylight, then," she said.
"And if I am hurt?"
"Then I will resist the urge to murder everyone involved while I ask if you want comfort first."
"Growth."
"Do not become impertinent."
"Too late."
Outside the door, Asha made the faintest sound. If Ciri had to name it, she would have called it old grief recognizing a younger room surviving itself.
