Triss found Geralt in the stable pretending the mare's left rear shoe required philosophical attention.

The shoe was fine. The horse knew it. Geralt knew it. Triss knew it, which meant the performance had become a domestic crime rather than a deception. Rain ticked on the stable roof. Lantern light turned the straw gold and the shadows brown. Buck occupied the far stall and had arranged his face into deep suspicion of a bucket. Roach chewed with the superior calm of a horse who had survived more of Geralt's emotional evasions than most people alive.
"The shoe looks oppressed," Triss said.
Geralt did not look up. "Could be a stone."
"Could be a man avoiding his own head."
"Less common in horses."
She leaned against the stall door. "Geralt."

He set the hoof down gently and stood. His hair had come loose at one side. He looked tired in the lantern light, not old exactly, though he was that too, but tired in the specific way of a man watching the past repeat with new names and realizing experience was not immunity.
"You know," he said.
"About Ciri and Jack? Everyone with eyes knows. Buck knows and is already judging us."
Buck struck the bucket with his nose. Judgment confirmed.
Geralt rubbed a hand over his face. "She is not a child."
"No."
"I know that."
"You do. And then you forget whenever danger stands near her with a human face."
He gave her a look. "Useful distinction?"
"Not always. But tonight it is." She moved closer, lowering her voice. "You are allowed to be afraid. You are not allowed to turn fear into authority and call it love."
The sentence hurt him. She saw it, hated that it had to, and refused to take it back. Love, if worth anything, occasionally had to stand with a blade and clean hands.
"I hid Jack from her," Geralt said. "Now he stands in front of her because of what I hid."
"Because of what Vesemir hid. What you agreed to hide. What Black Ink is exploiting. What older things made before you had choices. Do not make yourself the sole author because guilt wants a throne."
His mouth shifted. "Guilt wants a throne?"
"I spend time with Yennefer. Some phrasing is contagious."
"It was good."
"Do not tell her."
He almost smiled. Then the weight returned. "What if he hurts her?"
"Then she will hurt, and we will be there if she wants us."
"That's it?"

"No. Then you will go outside and consider killing him, not do it, come back in, fail to explain yourself, and check three doors. I will pretend not to notice the second door if you make tea afterward."
The smile came this time, reluctantly. "You make me sound predictable."
"Only in the places I love."

That stopped him. She had not meant to make the stable holy. She disliked when tenderness arrived without notice. It had poor manners and worse timing. Geralt stepped closer and pressed his forehead briefly against hers. The smell of hay, leather, rain, and horse surrounded them. No vineyard, no house, no warm study, and still, somehow, the same chosen peace held.
"And Yen?" he asked.
Triss had expected the question. Expectation did not make it easy.

"Yennefer is part of your history. Part of Ciri's life. Part of this. Pretending otherwise would make all of us smaller and more dangerous." She drew back to see him. "I am not a consolation prize, Geralt. Do not insult me by acting as if acknowledging her turns me into one."
His face changed. "Never."

"Good. Then hear the rest. If she wants Jack, and Jack wants her, and Ciri knows her own will, the problem is not desire. The problem is secrecy, ownership, and enemies who can make desire into leverage. We answer that with honesty and planning, not with men deciding which women should be protected from knowing their own hearts."
Geralt was silent for a long while. Roach chewed. Buck tried the bucket again, found it still disappointing, and gave up.
"You sound very calm," Geralt said.
"I am not."
"No?"

"No. I am frightened, jealous in small humiliating flashes, angry at the timing, sad for what will hurt, and still sure that making rules around other people's agency would turn us into the thing we are fighting." She exhaled. "It is possible to be dignified and annoyed. I am proving it at a price."
Geralt touched her hair. "I chose you with my eyes open."
"I know. I was there. You looked confused but determined."
"I often do."
"Yes. It has become endearing against my better judgment."

He kissed her. Not the kiss of a man apologizing for history. Not the kiss of a man asking permission to keep what he had already chosen. A present kiss, warm and tired and imperfect. Triss accepted it because the road ahead would take enough. She did not intend to donate clarity before being robbed.
When they left the stable, Jack was standing outside under the eaves.
Geralt stopped. Triss did not.
"If you heard anything private," she said, "pretend better."
Jack studied Buck's stall. "The horse was loud."
Buck snorted, offended by participation in diplomacy.
Geralt gave Jack a long look. Not accusation. Not permission. Something harder: the effort to let the young choose without abandoning him to the consequences.
"Ciri is not a secret," Geralt said.
Jack met his eyes. "No."
"Yennefer is not a solution."
"No."
"You are not a problem we all get to solve."
That one took longer.
"I'm learning," Jack said.
Geralt nodded. "Good. Learn faster."
Triss rolled her eyes and went inside before one of them mistook emotional competence for a habit.
The Velvet Hart had one good room, which it surrendered to Ciri because rank worked even when disguised, and because Ilyra could make a request sound like a future audit.

They used the room as a council chamber, though everyone hated the word. Saesenthessis returned near midnight and stood by the window. Asha placed a new map on the table, copied from Faithel memory over northern roads that did not understand what they crossed. Yennefer sat beside Ciri, not too close. Triss stood beside Geralt. Jack remained near the door until Ciri turned to him and then moved to the table, because some corrections did not need speech after the first time.
"There will be no hidden arrangements around intimacy," Ciri said.
Geralt closed his eyes very briefly. "Didn't expect a council agenda to begin there."
"Then you failed to study the room."

Yennefer turned to Jack. "No one in this room is comfort, prize, medicine, replacement, property, or consolation. If anyone begins behaving otherwise, I will name it. If I begin behaving otherwise, Ciri will enjoy naming it first."
"I have been waiting for a hobby," Ciri said.
Triss added, "And whatever happens, no one uses secrecy to spare someone from a choice that belongs to them. Privacy, yes. Concealment, no."
Asha studied them all with the grave expression of someone watching a new rite made from old injuries. "Your northern families argue like treaty councils."
"Treaties are easier," Geralt said. "Fewer feelings, more assassins."
Saesenthessis finally spoke from the window. "Good. You have made the emotional part nearly as tedious as the magical one. That means it may survive contact with fear."
"High praise," Jack said.
"No. A cautious omen."

They moved then to maps, routes, letters, draconid signs, Black Ink permits, and the troubling question of why the newest notices had begun using the phrase supervised mercy. No one liked the phrase. Dandelion would have hated it on rhythm alone. Zoltan would have asked who paid for the paper, then threatened the answer. Ciri, looking at it, thought of every time someone had offered to protect her from the burden of being free.
By the end, the shape of the next danger had arrived.

Black Ink would not seize Jack with nets while Geralt, Yennefer, Triss, Ciri, Asha, and a disguised dragon stood nearby. That would be theater and disaster. Sorel Veyrane preferred clean rooms. He would offer something. Legal identity. Medical safety. A route out of public panic. Silence purchased as mercy. A cage with velvet on the bars.
Ciri looked at the painted stag above the inn fireplace when they left the room.
It still looked resigned.
"Idiot," she told it.
Yennefer, passing beside her, said, "Be charitable. It had a poor painter."
Ciri smiled despite everything.
No one was safe. No one was innocent. No one was leaving the room smaller than they entered it.
For the moment, that had to hold.
Asha found Jack after the council, sitting on the inn's back step with Jacob's name not yet known and Helena's absence already waiting to hurt him.

He had a whetstone in one hand and no blade in the other. That was how she knew he had come outside to work and failed to find a task simple enough for the night. The yard smelled of wet straw, smoke, and the sour beer the stable boy had spilled while pretending not to listen at windows. Northern nights were too damp. They made every scar remember water.
"Your women argue bravely," Asha said.
His attention settled on her. "My women?"
"Bad northern grammar. The women around your fate. Better?"
"Less likely to get me stabbed."

She sat beside him without asking. Her knees hurt in the cold; she refused to let them say so aloud. "Helena argued like that when she was frightened into honesty. She would begin with etiquette and end with someone bleeding from the argument if they were unlucky."
Jack's fingers stilled around the stone. "You knew her well."
"I was assigned to guard her. Then I learned guarding a person without knowing her laugh is only inventory work."
He absorbed that the way he absorbed most truths, as if taking the blade by the edge and checking whether the cut was worth the information.
"What was she like?"

Asha looked toward the dark. There were questions survivors spent decades wanting to be asked and fearing the moment they were. "Tired of reverence. Quick with cups. Bad at pretending not to care. She hated songs that made duty sound clean. She would have liked Ciri, though the two of them might have burned a palace by accident before agreeing on method."
Jack looked down. "And Jacob?"
"Patient until patience became cowardice, then very fast. He had the face of a man officers sent to do practical work because they mistook silence for obedience."
"Sounds familiar."
"Yes," Asha said. "That is why memory hurts with such poor originality."
He almost smiled. She was grateful he did not, because the grief beneath it would have broken through too early.
"The cache we seek tomorrow may hold proof," she said. "Or ash. Or both. Do not decide before the stone opens what you need to find."
"Advice?"
"Warning. Advice is what people give when they think pain can be made efficient."

Inside the inn, Ciri laughed once at something Triss said, short and real. Jack looked toward the window. Asha saw the movement and decided not to name it. Some tenderness died if named before it had learned weather.
"You are gathering ties," she said instead.
"Unwise habit, apparently."
"So is breathing. The dead are very safe from consequences."
He turned the whetstone in his hand. "You Faithel comfort poorly."
"We trained under dragons and grieving women. Lower your expectations."
That time he did smile, brief and almost young. Asha looked away before he saw what it did to her.

Under seal of provisional civic review, delivered through a Temerian vassal courier with no declared sender: No party named herein is required to surrender dignity, trade, title, or lawful personal claim. The office offers supervised mercy, identity stabilization, protected medical oversight, and political silence for the prevention of wider panic. Voluntary compliance will be recorded as evidence of responsible personhood.
The invitation arrived folded inside a prayer book borrowed from the inn's chapel and returned with no prayers improved.
Jack found it because Buck bit the courier.

Not badly. Buck had standards and, in this case, excellent judgment. The courier was a young man with a Temerian accent, Nilfgaardian boots, Redanian paper in his satchel, and the pale face of someone who had been told the job involved delivering a devotional volume to a disguised noblewoman. When the horse took a professional interest in his sleeve, he dropped the prayer book, the book opened on the stable floor, and the paper slid out between a hymn to mercy and a woodcut of a saint holding what appeared to be a loaf of bread or a liver.
"He is getting better at intelligence work," Geralt said, looking at Buck.
"He prefers direct methods," Jack replied.
The courier, clutching his sleeve, looked between them. "I was paid at the south gate. I did not know it was hidden. I swear it."
Yennefer took the paper with two fingers. "Most people do not know the moment they become useful. That is why offices survive."
They brought the invitation to the inn parlor. Everyone read it. No one liked the same sentence first.
Before anyone spoke, Triss turned the invitation over and examined the fold.
"Three handlers," she said.
Yennefer leaned over her shoulder. "Four."
"One was not human?"
"One was not careful."
Jack stood near the window, because windows were honest about exits and dishonest about arrows. "Does that matter?"

"It matters because the page is trying to become a witness," Triss said. "See the pressure marks along the seam? It was folded around something small. Wax grain, powder, hair, anything that reacts to heat or magic. We do not burn it yet."
Ciri looked at the phrase responsible personhood again and wanted to put a knife through the word responsible. "They knew we would all touch it."
"No," Yennefer said. "They hoped. Hope is what bureaucrats call bait when they do not want to smell of fishing."
Geralt took the prayer book and inspected the saint. "Bad woodcut."
"That is what offends you?" Ciri asked.
"Several things offend me. Some need less explanation."
Asha had not moved. Her gaze stayed on supervised mercy. "In my order, mercy that arrives supervised is usually a cage brought by a man ashamed to carry iron."
Jack kept his eyes on the page. "If I refuse, they escalate."
"If you accept, they escalate with a cleaner conscience," Ciri said.
"If I ignore it, they choose the public version."
"Then we answer," Triss said. "Not as prey. Not as suspects. As people who understand the trap."
Yennefer glanced at her. "And how does one phrase that without giving them a wall to nail us to?"
Triss's smile had no warmth. "Carefully. Or not with words."
The discussion that followed was ugly because everyone loved someone into unreason and had the wit to disguise unreasonable as strategy.

Geralt wanted movement. The road at least admitted danger by having weather. Ciri wanted refusal sharp as a blade against the hand that had written the invitation. Yennefer wanted the author close and regretting the study of custody. Triss wanted the courier chain preserved until it named a counting house. Asha wanted the old words for oath-theft spoken aloud so the room would understand that this was not new evil, only northern tailoring. Saesenthessis wanted everyone to stop mistaking speed for superiority.
Jack listened until listening became another pressure around his ribs.
"They offer legal identity," he said at last.
Geralt's eyes found him.

Jack continued before interruption could become rescue. "My existence is off-record. Hidden. Useful to everyone who meant well, and everyone who did not. A legal identity could protect the people who ride with me from charges of harboring an unregistered mutant."
"No," Ciri said.
He held her gaze. "Let me finish."

"No," she repeated, not louder. "Not because I forbid you. Because that is their frame. You begin inside their sentence and then try to argue your way out. I know that room. It has imperial curtains."
Yennefer watched Ciri with fierce quiet.
Jack's jaw worked once. "Then give me a better sentence."

Ciri stepped closer. "You are a man whose existence was hidden by people who loved badly and hunted by people who classify well. You do not purchase personhood from the office that priced your refusal."
The room held still.

Geralt looked down, perhaps because the sentence had found him too. Triss's face softened. Asha murmured one Faithel word under her breath. Saesenthessis did not praise. That was how Ciri knew the dragon approved.
Jack read the invitation again. "Good sentence."
"Yes," Ciri said. "Do not ruin it by trying to pay me with gratitude."
He almost smiled. It failed, but honorably.
Yennefer took the page then. "Stop. The paper has had too long in the room."
She carried it out under the dead pear tree, and Jack followed because some arguments continued only after everyone else stopped trying to love them into safety.

Ciri hated responsible personhood. Triss hated identity stabilization. Geralt hated voluntary compliance. Asha hated supervised mercy with such stillness that even Saesenthessis glanced at her. Yennefer read protected medical oversight and the room felt colder.
Jack read political silence and understood the whole offer.
"They are not offering me safety," he said. "They are offering the rest of you quiet."
"They are offering ownership with warm gloves," Yennefer said.
"Warm gloves can still grip."
"Do not defend the diction."
He answered her stare. "I'm studying the door."
"It is a cage."
"Most cages have doors."
Ciri folded her arms. "Do not."
"Do not what?"
"Do not make that face. Geralt makes that face when he thinks ugly arithmetic becomes nobility if he says little enough."
Geralt looked offended, then considered the charge and lost confidence.
Jack placed the invitation on the table. "If I go, some pressure leaves you."
The room changed instantly.
Yennefer stood. "No."
"I said if."
"And I answered the version of you that thought saying if made it less idiotic."

Ciri's face had gone pale with anger. Triss looked at Jack with a sadness more dangerous than reprimand. Geralt leaned back, not relaxed, but measuring whether a fatherly intervention would become precisely the ownership they all claimed to oppose.
Jack saw all of it and hated that seeing did not solve anything.

"They have public language," he said. "Witnesses. Residue reports. Draconids dying in roads. Ciri's title can be dragged into it. Geralt's name. Yennefer's. Triss's. Asha's existence. Saesenthessis's disguise, if they even guess half of it. If one man walking into a room buys time..."
"No," Yennefer said again.
This time the word did not cut. It broke.
Jack let the silence answer first. "You don't get to forbid consideration."
"I get to despise it accurately."
"That isn't the same."
"No. It is the portion of restraint I am presently offering."
Ciri touched the invitation with one fingernail. "They want the record to say you chose it."
"Yes."
"So later, when they open you, bind you, drug you, parade you, or call you difficult, every clerk can begin with he agreed."
Jack's jaw tightened. "I know."
"Then stop speaking as if knowing makes it clean."
That landed. He did not answer.
Yennefer picked up the paper and turned toward the stairs. "I need air that has not listened to this."
"Yen," Geralt said.
"Do not follow me unless you have become less repetitive since supper."
Geralt remained where he was. Triss touched his wrist, a small intervention that saved him from a noble mistake. Ciri watched Yennefer leave, then turned to Jack.
"She is not angry because she wants to own the choice," Ciri said. "She is angry because she hears the room they are building around you and knows the instruments on the table."
Jack studied the invitation. "So do I."
"No. You hear the lock. She hears the hands."
Asha bowed her head once. "That is true."
Saesenthessis, from the window, added, "And dragons hear the language men use before they pretend the blood was inevitable."
Jack almost laughed. It would not have been humor. He took the invitation from the table and folded it slowly.
"I'll speak to her," he said.
Geralt watched him without blinking. "Speak. Not persuade."
"Yes."
"And don't be noble."
"I don't know what that means."
"Good. It's usually stupidity with a clean shirt."
That did make Jack almost smile.
Yennefer stood behind the inn under a dead pear tree, tearing the paper invitation apart without using her hands.

Small pieces lifted, folded, unfolded, and arranged themselves in the air around her like obedient insects preparing for execution. The rain had stopped. Water dripped from the branches at irregular intervals. The yard smelled of wet straw, horse manure, smoke from the kitchen, and the faint metallic tang of magic held too tightly. Jack stopped beneath the eaves and waited until three pieces of paper turned toward him like pale moths deciding whether he deserved fire.
"That is dramatic," he said.
"I am showing restraint."
"By vivisecting stationery."
"It volunteered to be symbolic."

He stepped into the yard. The mud took his boots with small, obscene sounds. The pear tree had borne no fruit that year, from the look of it. Perhaps not for several. Dead things remained useful to inns if they cast enough shade.
"You are angry," Jack said.
"Your powers of diagnosis continue to embarrass physicians."
"At me."
Yennefer let the paper pieces fall. They did not land in mud. They hovered an inch above it, because apparently even destroyed paper was not allowed to become dirty without permission.

"Yes," she said. "At you. At Sorel. At every school, court, mage, emperor, priest, and frightened functionary that ever discovered a body could be made into an answer. At myself, because part of me understands why you looked at the door instead of only at the cage."
Jack stood still. "Because sometimes going into the cage is tactical."
"Yes. And sometimes that sentence is the first chain."
The honesty between them had no fire to warm it. That was better. Fire made people sentimental before they had earned it.
"I do not want to be used," he said.
"I know."
"I also do not want everyone else torn apart because I refused a room."
"I know that too. Stop assuming disagreement is ignorance. It is tedious."

He looked away. Beyond the yard, the road ran black and wet under a clouded moon. Somewhere out there, Sorel Veyrane's men were waiting for responses, witnesses, delays, any movement that could be converted into policy. Inside, Ciri was probably so angry she might sharpen a blade that did not need sharpening. Geralt would be finding something practical to do with his hands. Triss would be making the practical work matter. Asha would be remembering dead people no one else yet knew how to mourn.
"I have been hidden, named, hunted, tested, and invited," Jack said. "Every person who touches this wants me to understand a different version of myself before I choose."
Yennefer stepped closer. "And what do you understand?"
"That I am tired of being understood."
Something in her face changed. A door opened, not to softness but to the room where softness had been locked for safety.
"Good," she said quietly. "That, at least, is yours."

The yard narrowed. Not by magic. By attention. Yennefer's hair was damp at the edges. One strand clung near her cheek and annoyed her by making her human. Jack wanted, with sudden sharpness, to move it aside. He did not. Want carried danger already; hands did not need to make proclamations.
She saw the restraint. Of course she did.
"Do not look at me as if I am another question you should avoid for everyone's comfort," she said.
His eyes returned to hers. "Are you?"
"Yes."
"Then I should avoid you."
"Probably."
Neither moved.
The dead pear tree dripped between them. A horse shifted in the stable. Somewhere inside, a chair scraped across a floor. The world remained full of witnesses even when no one watched.
Yennefer spoke first. "I am not a cure for your isolation."
"I know."
"You are not a cure for my grief."
"I know."

"Geralt is not absent from my history because he is present in Triss's life. Ciri is not diminished because I want something that frightens me. Triss is not made smaller by the fact that old pain still knows my name. If you cross this distance to escape any of that, do not."
Jack took one breath. Then another. His control, usually so clean it could be mistaken for absence, showed its seams.
"I don't want escape," he said. "I want one true thing that does not arrive through a file, a test, a title, or someone else's fear."
Yennefer held him in her attention for a long moment.
"That is a terrible reason," she said.
"Is it false?"
"No. That is why it is terrible."
She crossed the distance herself.

The first kiss was not gentle. It was precise, almost angry, a decision made by a woman who disliked needing anything and hated dishonesty more. Jack did not seize. He received, then answered, his hand rising to her waist with restraint sharp as a cut. Yennefer made a low sound against him, not surrender, not softness, but the body betraying how long it had been holding the line.
"Mm."
He stopped.
Her eyes opened, bright and furious. "If you ask whether I am certain, I will do something unkind to the next object within reach."
"Are you certain?"
The paper scraps burst into ash above the mud.
Jack's mouth curved. Barely.
"Yes," Yennefer said, and this time the word was not a weapon. It was a key turned by her own hand.

They reached the inn's side room without making the yard into theater. Yennefer had the good sense to choose a room with a lock, a hearth, one window, and no sentimental furniture. The air smelled of old wool, rain-damp stone, candle wax, and the bitter lavender she carried without admitting fondness for habits. A small fire burned low. It gave more light than heat, which suited the room. Some warmth had to be made honestly or not at all.
Jack stood just inside the door while she barred it.
"This changes trouble," he said.
"Everything worth doing changes trouble."
"Ciri knows?"
"Ciri knows what would make ignorance insulting and has the kindness to let privacy remain privacy. Do not confuse the two."
"Triss?"
"Triss knows Geralt's history and her own worth better than most courts know their borders."
"Geralt?"

Yennefer's face altered. Pain, memory, pride, affection, and a thousand unchosen endings moved through her and were gone before a lesser person would have found a name for one. "Geralt knows he cannot own the past by suffering near it. He is learning. Slowly. With terrible posture."
Jack let that stand.
When he reached for her, he did so openly.

Yennefer came to him with no softness wasted on uncertainty. Her hands took his face first, not gently, but with care disguised as command. The second kiss was deeper. Heat gathered between them, not sudden, not adolescent, but charged because both understood too much to claim innocence. His bandaged hand stayed away from her skin until she took it and placed it at her side.
"Do not make your wounds more polite than your wants," she said.

His breath changed. The control around him shifted under the words, not breaking, not vanishing, but allowing one visible seam. She felt it and made a soft sound when his hand settled, steady and hot through fabric.
"Ah... there."

The sound undid him more than any display would have. He kissed her throat, the line of her jaw, the place where pulse lived under pride. Yennefer's fingers tightened in his hair. Not to direct. To remain standing. Her head tilted back by half an inch, and the next breath left her unshaped.
"Mm... Jack."
He stopped at the name because in her voice it was not file, not strategy, not accusation. It was simply him, which had become so rare it hurt.
"Say it again," he said.
Her eyes opened. "Presumptuous."
"Yes."
She laughed once, low and astonished despite herself. Then she said it again, against his mouth, and let the name become warmth rather than evidence.

The room held. The fire burned lower. Rain began again at the window with the private rhythm of weather that had seen too much and offered no counsel. Their movements stayed slow because haste would have made the scene smaller than the choice. Yennefer's control did not vanish; it changed hands with her permission, returned, changed again. Jack's restraint did not disappear; it became the very thing that let her lean into danger without being taken by it.

When pleasure sharpened, it came through breath and sound rather than explanation. A small intake from her when his mouth found a place that made thought falter. A rougher exhale from him when her hands moved over scars he had not thought of as touchable. The low, broken "mmh" she failed to silence. The way she caught his wrist once, not to stop him, but to hold the moment still until she chose it again.
"Do not vanish into usefulness," she whispered.
"I am here."
"Say it as if you are not reporting for duty."
That hurt him. Good. Some wounds had to open before they could stop poisoning the blood.
"I am here," he said again, lower, rougher, no office in it.
Yennefer answered with a sound that would have ruined three courtiers and one minor philosopher if any had survived hearing it. "Ah... yes."

After that, language thinned. Breath and heat took more honest turns. His name in her mouth became less controlled and more permitted. Her name in his became an argument against every clean arrangement the world had offered him. There was the soft scrape of wool, the hearth's low collapse, the bed receiving their weight without ceremony, her hand at his shoulder when intensity threatened to turn him inward, his mouth at the place where pride became pulse, and her voice, lower now, open in a way that carried risk.
"Mmh... stay there. Yes."

He did, because she asked, because he wanted, because asking and wanting had finally entered the same room without being dressed as strategy. They did not pretend history left. It stayed by the hearth with its knives put away, watching as two people made something new without asking the old wound to approve.

Later, Yennefer sat on the edge of the bed with her robe around her shoulders and her hair loose, making her look like a rumor about herself. Jack knelt by the hearth, rebuilding the fire badly. She watched him place the logs in an arrangement that would smoke within five minutes.
"That is incompetent," she said.
"The fire or the aftermath?"
"The fire. The aftermath is merely volatile."
He moved the log. Smoke stopped threatening the room.

Silence came then. Not comfortable. Better than comfortable, perhaps. Honest. Yennefer looked at the invitation ash she had brought in unknowingly on her sleeve, a gray smear near the cuff. She rubbed it between two fingers and felt a grain resist.
Her face changed.
"What?" Jack asked.
She lifted the grain into the firelight. It gleamed black, then red. Not ash. Powdered seal-wax mixed with a listening reagent, dormant until warmed by body heat and magic.
Jack stood. "Tracking?"
"Witnessing. Perhaps both." Yennefer's mouth became a line. "The invitation was not only offer. It wanted to know who touched it, who destroyed it, who carried it near the heat."
"Me. You."
"Yes."
The room's warmth changed flavor.
Yennefer wrapped the grain in a scrap of linen and sealed it inside a glass bead with a sharp word that made the flame bow. Then she turned to Jack. The vulnerability did not vanish. It armed itself.
"Now our private choice has evidence," she said.
Jack looked toward the barred door. "Love is consequence."
"Do not make that sound like wisdom. It is mostly inconvenience with better lighting."
He almost smiled. She did not, but her hand found his and held it once before they returned to the others.
In the morning, Sorel's invitation would have an answer.
Not yes. Not no.
A fire line drawn around a black grain and mailed back without explanation.
Yennefer wrote the address herself.
When Yennefer and Jack returned, the room knew.

Not the details. Those were not for the room. But the change had entered with them in the way air enters after a storm: cooler, charged, carrying damage and relief in the same breath. Ciri saw the line of ash on Yennefer's sleeve. Triss saw the sealed bead in her hand. Geralt saw Jack's face and looked away before worry became trespass.
Yennefer placed the bead on the table. "They used a listening reagent."
"Of course they did," Triss said. "Mercy with ears."
Jack stood beside the door. "It reacted to heat and magic."

Ciri looked from him to Yennefer. She did not ask if it had reacted to intimacy. That would have been cruelty dressed as clarity. Instead she said, "Then the answer is stronger than refusal. They know they were seen."
"Yes," Yennefer said.
"And they know you saw them."
"Yes."
Geralt folded his arms. "They will move faster."
"They already were," Triss said.
Asha touched the table beside the bead, not the bead itself. "A listened-to room is a polluted room. Old law says nothing spoken there is binding unless repeated under open sky."
Saesenthessis looked toward the window. "An unusually sensible law."
Ciri went to Jack. Too distant to perform. At her side to refuse the report that would call distance prudence. "Under open sky, then. You are not going."
"I had decided that."
"Say it anyway."

He looked at the bead, at Yennefer's hand beside it, at Geralt pretending his silence was not desperate, at Triss with ink already staining her fingers, at Asha with mourning in her posture, at Saesenthessis waiting to condemn any pretty lie.
"I am not going into custody to buy anyone silence."
Outside, thunder moved beyond the hills though the rain had stopped.
"Good," Ciri said.
Yennefer's eyes remained on Jack. Whatever had happened between them had not softened her fear. It had given fear a name and therefore made it harder to dismiss.
Triss took out a fresh sheet. "Then we answer with the bead and move before the courier chain decides whether it is brave."
"Toward the cache?" Geralt asked.
Jack touched the barbed-star under his shirt. It had gone heavy again, pulling east. "Toward whatever my parents left before paperwork learned their names."
That made the room quiet.
The invitation had been answered.
Under open sky meant the courtyard behind the inn, between the stable pump and a wall where moss had grown over old knife marks.

They went there together because Asha insisted and because no one wanted to admit that old law had begun sounding more useful than new jurisdiction. The air smelled of rainwater, horse sweat, wet leather, and the sour cabbage soup the kitchen had failed to hide from the weather. Clouds moved low over the hills. No stars. No moon. Nothing grand to make the moment lie about itself.
Asha placed the bead on a flat stone. "Words spoken here bind only the speaker. No room owns them. No witness may carry them without naming itself witness."
"Practical," Geralt said.
"Civilized," Yennefer corrected.
Saesenthessis considered both. "Rare."
Ciri stood opposite Jack. "Say it again."
He did.
"I refuse to become a prisoner just to purchase quiet for others."
This time the words had weather on them. They sounded less like strategy and more like a man refusing to rent out his body to fear.

Ciri nodded. Yennefer's face did not soften, but some blade inside her lowered by a finger's width. Triss exhaled as if she had been holding the room together with one lung. Geralt looked at the stable roof because fatherhood sometimes required a man not to weep and not to pretend he was immune to the possibility.
Asha tied a knot in her red cord. "Heard."
Saesenthessis did not move. "Remembered."
That word landed heavier from her.
Jack studied the bead on the stone. "Do we send it now?"
Yennefer picked it up. "At dawn. Let Sorel spend one night wondering whether silence means surrender, contempt, or competence."
"Which is it?" Ciri asked.
"All three," Triss said.
Geralt grunted. "Good letter."
"No letter," Yennefer said.
"Best kind."
They almost laughed. Almost. The almost mattered. It meant the invitation had failed at one quiet thing: it had not made them speak only in fear.
When they returned inside, Jack paused at the threshold. Ciri paused beside him.
"What?" she asked.
He looked at the old doorframe, the mud on the floor, the company inside, the bead in Yennefer's hand. "A room can listen. Open sky can bind. Paper can lie. Doors can ask permission."
"You are becoming philosophical. It is alarming."
"Probably fever."
"I will tell Triss."
"Cruel."
She smiled once and entered before him, not because he held the door, but because he waited for her to choose the room first.
That, too, answered the invitation.
Ciri did not sleep after the open-sky answer.

She sat near the parlor window with Ilyra's unsent report on her knee and watched the road where the courier would leave at dawn. Jack was upstairs, or in the stable, or nowhere sleep would find him without an argument. Yennefer had retired to a room whose fire burned too bright under the door. Geralt remained outside for the third watch though it was not his turn. Triss had stopped correcting him because sometimes the kindest thing one could do for a witcher was allow him to be cold in the name of usefulness.
Ilyra appeared with a cup of water. Not wine. Not tea. Water. Intelligence, Ciri thought, had its tender moments.
"You intend to make this personal," Ilyra said.
"It became personal before I arrived."
"That is not the same as making it publicly yours."
"No."
Ilyra waited. She knew Ciri well; she let silence become a door rather than a wall.

Ciri touched the folded hereditary infrastructure page in her sleeve. "If I stand too close, they will call him imperial interest. If I stand too far, they will call distance proof he has no one worth angering. If I hide what I feel, they will use secrecy. If I name it, they will use scandal."
"Yes."
"Useful counsel."
"I thought honesty might be quicker."
Ciri looked out at the black road. "Then write this for the record you are not yet sending. I will not let fear of being used decide which truths I am permitted to stand near."
Ilyra's pen appeared as if summoned by loyalty. "Exact wording?"
"No. Make it dull so it survives capture."
"How dull?"
"Imperial."
Ilyra nodded gravely. "A severe standard."
The joke saved nothing. It carried the night one step closer to dawn.
The dead were about to speak next.
Sorel Veyrane received the bead
Sorel Veyrane received the bead of sealed listening ash in a room that had been scrubbed too clean for honesty.

Merrow placed it on the white dish with tongs. Halbreck stood by the window, arms folded, watching rain draw crooked lines down the glass. The office was temporarily housed in a former customs building where merchants had once lied about salt, fish oil, and cloth. Sorel approved of the location. Customs houses understood that civilization depended on declaring things accurately and punishing those who profited from omissions.
The bead contained no letter. No threat. No refusal. Only the black-red grain fused inside glass by a hand too controlled to be a hedge mage's and too angry to be merely professional.
"Yennefer of Vengerberg," Halbreck said.
"Almost certainly," Sorel replied.
Merrow adjusted his spectacles. "Is it a warning?"
"Yes."
"A rejection?"
"Not entirely."
Halbreck turned to him. "How can it be not entirely?"

Sorel turned the dish by a quarter inch. The bead caught the lamp and held a red point at its center. "If they meant only rejection, they would burn the courier chain, kill a minor clerk, or send no answer. This is evidence returned. It says they found the secondary reagent. It also says they are willing to communicate through objects when words are traps. That is useful."
"You are pleased they discovered a device you hid in a mercy offer."

"Pleased is imprecise. Their competence is confirmed. Their emotional entanglement deepens. Their willingness to avoid direct surrender remains high, as expected. The subject's consideration of compliance remains possible, or the invitation would not have caused such a reply."
Halbreck's face hardened. "You hear a man considering a cage and call it data."
"I hear a man weighing public consequence. That is not the same thing."
"No. It is worse. It means he has enough conscience for you to use."
Merrow looked down at the minutes and did not write that line. The best lines were often unusable, which was one of history's pettier cruelties.

Sorel covered the bead with a square of black cloth. "Prepare the archive request. Old Barbed-Star materials. Jacob var Moorlen. Helena of Morningstar. Any termination tags tied to eastern continuity custody. If the living subject is gathering family proof, the family proof will lead him to records. We should know which rooms he will enter before grief teaches him to kick doors instead."
Halbreck said, "And if the records prove we are repeating a crime?"
Sorel paused at the door.
"Then we will have the advantage of understanding the precedent."
After he left, Halbreck stood for a long time beside the covered bead. Merrow waited with his pen hovering over the page.
"Do not write that last sentence," she said.
"I was not going to."
"Good."
"Should it be preserved somewhere?"
She faced him then, too tired for anything but honesty. "It will preserve itself in what we do next."

Fragment translated by Asha from a Faithel mourning cord: The shield-man bought minutes. The bearer bought breath. The Last Warden bought silence with fire. The child bought nothing. Let no account place debt on the child.
The barbed-star necklace began pulling east before dawn.

Not visibly. It did not lift, glow, sing, or perform any other trick a tavern crowd would have found useful. It simply became heavier against Jack's chest whenever he faced away from the old imperial road and lighter when he turned toward a line of hills no map at the inn bothered naming correctly. He tested it twice in the yard. North, weight. South, weight. East, less. West, cold enough to hurt.
Asha watched him from beside the well.
"It has begun remembering near the wrong soil," she said.
"That explain anything?"
"Yes. Badly."
"Your order had a talent for that."
"We survived by keeping clean explanations away from dirty hands."
He could not argue with that. He disliked how often the old woman made sense after making none.

The others wanted to debate route logic. They were right to want it. Route logic kept people alive. But the necklace did not care about maps, and Saesenthessis, when consulted, only said that old keys sometimes pulled toward locks and sometimes toward the hand that lost them. Yennefer threatened to begin with the dragon if answers did not improve. Saesenthessis said improvement was a human superstition. Ciri told both of them that if the day began with an argument about epistemology she would side with the horse.
Buck, hearing none of the context and all of the tone, looked ready for office.
They rode east.

The road worsened quickly, which meant it was honest. Paved imperial confidence gave way to ruts, then to a hunter's track, then to an old quarry path swallowed by grass. The country here had been passed between crowns too often to retain loyalty to any of them. Broken boundary stones lay in ditches. A shrine to a local field goddess had been repaired with a soldier's shield. Apple trees grew wild where a manor garden had burned. Ciri rode with her hood up and no escort visible because Ilyra had taken the imperial riders on a false inspection route at dawn.

Triss rode beside Geralt, having refused to stay behind after the listening grain. Yennefer said nothing about the previous night and dared anyone else to value their life cheaply enough to make it necessary.
Jack did not look at her too often. He also did not avoid looking. Ciri noticed both and, after one long glance, rode closer to him.
"Daylight," she said quietly.
He nodded. "Daylight."
That was all. For now it was enough.

Asha led them to a collapsed watch-house by noon. The building had been old before the war and ruined before the last winter. Its lower stones were blackened by fire. The upper timbers had fallen inward and grown moss. A root had split the threshold. The place smelled of fox, damp ash, and an old mineral heat Jack felt in his teeth.
"Not the house," Asha said before anyone asked. "A way-station. Helena used it once. Jacob knew it later. Faithel marks were made for memory that could travel."
"A cache?" Triss asked.
"If no one found it."
Geralt studied the broken threshold. "People searched."
"People always search badly when they think stone is stupid," Asha replied.

Jack dismounted. The necklace had gone light as thread. That frightened him more than the weight. He crossed the threshold and felt the ruin answer under his boots with a slow inward breath. Not alive. Not waiting. Remembering, perhaps. He was beginning to hate that word.
Inside, Asha pointed to a wall where lichen had grown in a fan shape. "There."

Jack saw nothing at first. Then Ciri stepped beside him and angled her lantern low. The lichen shadow revealed five shallow cuts in the stone, not a star exactly, but the absence of one. A mark made to be seen only when someone brought light from the wrong direction. Jacob, if the cache was his, had known practical things. That made Jack feel something sharp and immediate he did not have a noun for.
"Do I touch it?" he asked.
Yennefer's face said no. Asha's said yes. Geralt's said he wanted to stand between both answers and the world. Ciri's said the choice is yours, do not make me repeat the whole revolution.
Jack touched it.
The stone did not open dramatically. It clicked like an old man clearing his throat.

A section of wall loosened enough for Geralt and Jack to pry it free. Behind it lay a narrow cavity lined with oiled leather gone stiff. Inside were four objects: a broken sword hilt wrapped in cloth, a small Nilfgaardian medallion blackened by fire, a sealed packet bound with red cord, and a child's bead made of pale blue glass.
Before Asha allowed anyone to touch the cache, she made them clean the room.

It was a strange order and therefore obeyed poorly at first. Geralt removed fallen stone from the threshold. Ciri swept damp leaves aside with the edge of an old board. Triss picked glass from a corner where some window had died years ago. Yennefer purified the air with one elegant twist of her fingers and then suffered Asha's disapproval because "clean" in a Faithel mouth apparently meant labor, not convenience. Saesenthessis watched this dispute with interest that would have made lesser beings nervous.
Jack cleaned nothing. Asha told him not to.
"That seems unfair," Ciri said, pushing a clump of wet moss away from the wall.
"It is," Asha replied. "Rites often are. Fairness is for markets and children who have not met inheritance."
Jack stood in the center of the ruin and listened to other people make space around the dead. He disliked it. He needed it. Both facts stood without canceling each other.

When the last ash had been brushed from the hidden wall, Asha took a strip of red thread from her sleeve and tied it around the first two fingers of her right hand. "Helena kept two kinds of caches. One for thieves, one for kin. Thieves see the object. Kin must see the work around it."
"What work?" Geralt asked.
"Threshold swept. Glass removed. Door acknowledged. Fire named. Water thanked. Blood kept inside the skin unless the stone asks otherwise."
"Practical religion," Triss murmured.
"The only kind that survives travel."
Asha turned to Jack. "If the cache is kin-marked, it may hurt less if you ask first."
"Hurt less."
"Yes."
"Comforting."
"No. Accurate."

Jack studied the hidden cuts. For once, he did not reach as if evidence might vanish if his hand took too long. He stood before the wall and spoke into stone that had known his parents better than he had.
"I do not know the proper words."
Asha's voice softened. Barely. "Then use improper ones honestly."
Jack swallowed once. The sound was small and worse than grief. "I am here. If this belonged to them, I will carry it. If it was meant for someone else, I will not steal it."
The ruin warmed.
Not much. Enough for the dead leaves near Ciri's boots to dry at the edges. Enough for Yennefer's gaze to sharpen. Enough for Saesenthessis to lower her head by a fraction.
Asha closed her eyes. "It knows enough."
Only then did Jack touch the stone.
Jack reached for the medallion first.

It was plain military issue, old enough that the eagle stamp had a slightly different wing shape from current imperial castings. The back had been scratched by a knife with one word: HELENA. Not title. Not house. Name.
Asha's breath failed.
"Jacob," she said.
The name entered Jack without permission.
Jacob.

A father should not have been able to arrive as a scratched word on cheap metal. Yet the room altered around it. Geralt took one step back, as if giving the dead space. Triss covered her mouth, then lowered her hand because hiding grief served no one. Ciri stood very still. Yennefer looked at Jack, not the object, because she knew objects could become knives if no one watched the hand holding them.
Jack set the medallion down carefully and unwrapped the sword hilt.

Nilfgaardian make. Practical. No gems. No vanity. The blade had snapped a hand's width above the guard. The grip was dark with age, worn on one side where a thumb had rested often. A small strip of leather had been tied beneath the pommel. On it, in faded ink, someone had written: Not orders. Her.
Jack read it once. Then again.

"He refused orders," Asha said. Her voice had changed. Less priestess. More survivor. "Jacob was assigned under trade security. A soldier with clean hands and a face that made officers underestimate him. He was told to deliver Helena to men with seals when the line narrowed. He did not."
"How do you know?" Jack asked.
"I was there for the refusing. Not for the first kiss. Helena threw a cup at him first. It was considered promising."
Ciri made a small sound, almost a laugh and almost a sob on behalf of people she had never known.

Jack studied the sealed packet. Red cord. Old wax. The barbed-star pressed into it, not with a ring, but by something sharper and less clean. The wax had cracked but held. He did not touch it at once.
"Open it," Geralt said softly.
Jack turned to him.
Geralt added, "Or don't."
Better. Painful, the effort behind it. Better.
Jack broke the seal.
Inside were two sheets. One in a strong, angular hand. One in a finer script with ink blurred at one edge. Asha closed her eyes when she saw the second.
"Helena," she said.

Jack gave the first sheet to Ciri before he could decide why. Perhaps because her hands knew files and cages. Perhaps because she had said daylight. Perhaps because if he held both pages at once, he would begin with the wrong one.
Ciri read aloud, not loudly.

"If this reaches the child grown, then I failed to carry the next truth myself. My name is Jacob var Moorlen, son of no house worth writing, officer by service, oath-blade by choice. I was ordered to escort Helena of Morningstar under merchant cover and later to surrender her under sealed authority. I refused the second order. If any man tells you I was bewitched, he is a coward.
"If any man tells you I betrayed the empire, ask which empire he means: the one on banners, or the one inside a man when he chooses what law cannot cleanly name."
Her voice faltered only once. On child. Jack spared her the witness of his face and fixed on the wall where the hidden star had been cut.
Ciri continued.

"Helena was not cargo, relic, priestess, or royal claim. She was a woman with duty enough to break a stronger world than ours. She loved badly in the beginning and fiercely after that. She feared the child would inherit a key and be called fortunate by fools. She said blood was not permission. Remember that if they come with kind language."
Yennefer turned away. Triss lowered her head. Geralt's face had become carved.

"I write quickly. They have reached the lower court. Zerrikanterment is here. He says minutes matter. I have spent my life obeying bells, horns, officers, decrees, and men who mistook clean boots for honor. The best thing I have ever done is disobey in time to love your mother. The second best will be buying her minutes. If you live, owe me nothing. If you carry my name, carry it only as proof that orders can be refused."
Ciri stopped.

The ruin breathed around them. Not magic. Or not only magic. Old air moving through old stone, carrying ash, fox, roots, the mineral heat of a buried thing, and the sudden unbearable fact that Jack Morningstar had once been someone's child in the simple way before every institution, seal, and prophecy arrived with better grammar.
"Read Helena," Jack said.
His voice sounded ordinary. That was how Ciri knew it had broken somewhere too deep for display.
Yennefer took the second page before anyone else could. She read the first line silently and then looked at Asha. The Faithel woman's face had gone gray under her scars.
"Please," Asha said.
Yennefer read.

"My son, if this reaches you, forgive the poverty of paper. A mother should leave a face, voice, scent, correction, song, temper, hand, and all the small tyrannies of love. I leave ink because men with seals are at the gate and ink runs faster than blood when hidden well. Your name is Jack because Jacob said a child should have a name a tired man could say while smiling.

"Your house-name is Morningstar, not because we were meant to rule, but because the morning star is seen before the sun and vanishes when the world thinks light belongs to something larger. Remember that. We were never crowns. We were warning."
Jack closed his eyes once.
Asha began a Faithel mourning verse under her breath. Saesenthessis, who had entered without sound, stood in the doorway and did not interrupt.
Yennefer continued.

"The line is narrow. That is not your fault. The seal is failing. That is not your fault. Zerrikanterment says he can fold the last cinder into you, make you hidden, make you survive if the world is merciful enough to be distracted. He does not say what it will cost because dragons mistake calm for kindness when grief would be more honest. I agreed because all other roads end with your small body in hands that already have vocabulary prepared. If I have damned you by saving you, then hate me cleanly.
"I would rather be hated by you alive than praised by no one over your cradle."
The page trembled. Yennefer's hand, not the paper. She steadied both by force.

"Jacob says I should write that I love you. As if that were not the reason for every word. As if love were a ribbon to tie around the knife. I love you. There. He is satisfied, arrogant man. Asha will know the old verse. If she lives, she will find you. If she does not, the verse may still. Blood is a vow, not a privilege. Power is a duty, not a crown. If anyone tells you different, break their teeth if you can and their argument if you cannot."
Asha laughed once through tears. "That was Helena."
Yennefer finished the final lines.

"You owe the dead remembrance, not obedience. You owe the world consideration, not ownership. You owe yourself a life, even if the locks inside you disagree. Live first if you can. Choose last if you must. Your mother, Helena of House Morningstar, last bearer by duty, frightened woman by truth."
No one spoke.

The silence was not empty. It was full of Jacob refusing orders, Helena writing faster than fear, Zerrikanterment compressing a cinder into a child, Asha running under command she would spend decades trying to fulfill, Geralt and Vesemir finding a boy and hiding him badly enough to save him and wound him, Ciri reading a father's letter aloud because the world had once tried to make her into the same kind of arithmetic.
Jack took both pages.
His hands did not shake. That was almost worse.
"They were real," he said.
Asha moved toward him, stopped before touching, and bowed her head. "Yes."
"Not theory. Not line. Not house."
"No."
"People."
"Yes."
He folded the letters with care so precise it hurt to watch.
Geralt took a breath. "Jack."
"No speeches," Jack said.
Geralt closed his mouth.
"Good," Ciri said softly, not to Geralt exactly.

Jack put Jacob's medallion and Helena's letter in his inner pouch. The broken hilt he held longer. The grip fit badly in his hand. Jacob had been smaller through the palm or held a sword differently. Evidence of a body. Evidence that a man had stood somewhere, loved someone, disobeyed something, and died buying minutes.
"Where did they die?" Jack asked.

Asha looked east. "Not here. This was a hand left behind in case the arm was cut off. The main house was farther than northern maps admit. Zerrikanian ground. Dry stone. Heat. A basement under a crumbling hall. Jacob left another letter there if fire did not eat it."
"Then why this cache?"

"Proof for the road before the road could reach home. Helena feared you would be told you belonged to crown, dragon, empire, or seal before anyone could prove you belonged first to people who loved you."
Jack studied the broken hilt. "Efficient woman."
Asha's face twisted. "Yes."
Ciri stepped close enough that their sleeves touched. Not more. Not in front of the letters unless invited by grief itself.
"You have parents now," she said.
He studied the floor. "They are dead."
"Yes."
"That is a poor kind of having."
"It is the only kind some of us get."
He faced her then, and whatever passed between them did not ask the room for translation.
The basement beneath the watch-house contained one more thing.

They found it because Triss noticed the ash under a stone had been swept inward rather than out. Geralt lifted the slab. Yennefer warded the edges. Asha sang one line of Helena's verse and the air warmed, not with threat, but with recognition. Under the slab lay a narrow tube of blackened copper and a strip of paper so dry it might have turned to dust if anyone breathed ambition near it.
The paper was not from Jacob or Helena.
It was a copied operational tag.

TERMINATION ACTION, BARBED-STAR CONTINUITY. Field categories: bearer, compromised protector, witness-servant, unknown golden draconic anomaly, infant continuity risk. Authority chain redacted. Transfer to archive on completion.
Triss looked at the words and went pale with anger.
"Completion," she said.
Yennefer's voice had no heat at all. "They filed the massacre."

Saesenthessis stared at unknown golden draconic anomaly and did not move. Jack saw the stillness and understood, in some new and bitter way, that dragons could grieve without lowering themselves into human gestures.
Geralt studied the tag, then Jack. "Part V," he would never say, because lives did not know parts. What he said was worse and better.
"We find the archive."
Jack placed Jacob's broken hilt beside the operational tag. Dead proof beside living paperwork. Father beside file.
He did not collapse. He did not rage. He became very precise.
"Yes," he said. "We do."
Outside, the horses shifted in the rain. Buck struck the ground once, impatient with grief that did not yet know where to run.
Jack took the letters, the medallion, the hilt, the child's blue bead, and the copper tube.
A child had bought nothing, the Faithel cord had said.
The world had still sent an invoice.

They buried nothing because there were no bodies, but Asha insisted on a rite, and no one in the ruin had the cruelty to argue with a woman who had carried four decades of unfinished mourning in her spine.

She chose a place beneath the split threshold where rain reached but did not pool. Jacob's broken hilt lay on a clean cloth. Helena's letter rested beside it under a flat stone so the wind could not perform scholarship on grief. The child's blue bead sat between them. Saesenthessis stood outside the doorway, not entering the rite and not leaving it. Yennefer held a candle that burned straight despite the rain. Triss held the second. Ciri stood at Jack's left. Geralt stood at his right and did not touch him. Good. He had learned the day's grammar.

Asha sang in a language that did not bend easily into the damp northern air. The melody was narrow, dry, almost without ornament, built for heat, stone, and memory carried in the mouth when paper would burn. Jack understood none of the words at first. Then one repeated often enough to become shape: Helena. Another came lower, with the rhythm of boots on hard ground: Jacob. The third was not a name, perhaps, but when Asha sang it the barbed-star signet cooled and Saesenthessis lowered her head.
Zerrikanterment.
The hidden name did not make thunder. It made the ruin listen.

When the song ended, Asha took the child's bead and pressed it into Jack's palm. "This was found in Helena's birthing cloth after the flight began. She said the child had gripped it and would not let go. Jacob said that proved judgment, because the bead was prettier than his finger."

Jack closed his hand around it. The glass was cold, ordinary, almost weightless. Of all the things in the cache, it hurt most. A sword hilt could belong to story. A medallion to service. Letters to the dead arranging themselves into dignity. A bead belonged to a child who had not yet learned that the world could file him.
Ciri's sleeve brushed his. This time he leaned back by a fraction. Not enough for the room to call it comfort. Enough for her to feel the choice.
Geralt studied the hilt. "Jacob bought minutes."
"Yes," Asha said.
"Vesemir bought years."
Jack held on his face for a moment.
Geralt did not look away. "Badly. Secretly. With mistakes that hurt you. But years."

The rite had not prepared space for that. Perhaps no rite could. Jack looked down at the bead in his fist and let the sentence stand without accepting or rejecting it. Some truths were like wounded animals. Touch too soon and they bit from fear.
"Years are not absolution," Jack said.
"No."
"But they are years."
Geralt nodded once. It was enough. For now.
Triss placed the operational tag inside a separate oilcloth. "This is the next road. Not east yet. Archive first."
Yennefer's mouth hardened. "Someone filed the murder of his parents and called it action. I intend to know which hand held the pen."
Saesenthessis looked toward the hills. "And I intend to know why a golden name reached a northern category before his own kin could bury him."
Ciri turned to Jack. "What do you intend?"

He opened his hand. The blue bead sat in the center of his palm. For a moment he did not look like a key, wound, weapon, or chamber. He looked like a man holding proof that he had once been small enough to love without usefulness.
"To keep the bead," he said.
It was not the whole answer. It was the only one that belonged entirely to him.
No one asked for more.
Jack returned to the ruin alone before they left.

Alone meant Ciri stopped at the broken threshold and pretended to study the road. Geralt remained with the horses and made Buck suffer a useless inspection. Yennefer spoke to Triss in low voices near the well. Asha watched from a place where she could intervene without admitting she had followed. Saesenthessis did not pretend at all. Dragons considered solitude a human courtesy and therefore optional.
Jack stood where the cache had been and placed his palm against the empty cavity.

No heat answered. No voice. No sudden memory of Helena's face or Jacob's hands. The world did not reward grief with visions just because grief had waited politely. He was grateful, then angry at the gratitude. A vision would have been another use. Absence at least belonged to the dead.
He took the blue bead from his pouch and set it in the hollow for one breath.
"I was told to live first," he said.
The cavity gave no reply.
"Difficult instruction."
Outside, Buck snorted with the vicious timing of a critic.
Jack almost smiled. Almost.

He took the bead back. The glass had warmed in his palm, not by magic, but by being held. That should not have mattered. It did. He understood, in the smallest and cruelest way, why people kept useless things from the dead. Usefulness was what the world demanded. Uselessness was sometimes proof that love had passed through.
Ciri was waiting when he came out.
She did not ask whether he was all right. Good. He was not, and the question would have required either lying or cruelty.
Instead she said, "We should wrap the letters against damp."
"Yes."
"And the hilt needs oil or it will rot further."
"Yes."
"And if anyone tries to turn your parents into a court argument before you are ready, I will be unpleasant."
His attention caught on her face. Rain had gathered in her lashes. The brown travel cloak made her look less imperial and more dangerous, which was probably closer to the truth.
"I can be unpleasant," he said.
"I know. I said I would."
He nodded once. The bead rested in his fist, small and warm.

That was how they left the watch-house: not healed, not enlightened, not strengthened in any heroic sense. A man with proof in his pocket. A woman with title hidden under mud. A witcher learning that fatherhood could mean standing close and not reaching. A sorceress carrying ash from a private consequence. A second sorceress already turning grief into routes and safeguards. A witness who had failed once and refused to fail quietly again. A dragon who watched the rain fall through a ruined roof and heard, perhaps, the shape of an old golden name in the dripping.
Behind them, the operational tag waited inside Triss's oilcloth.
The next road did not lead toward origin.
It led toward the office that had filed origin as completion.
The first archive name came before they reached the main road.
Not through magic. Through Zoltan.

A courier found them at an abandoned toll hut, half drunk from fear and fully sober from money. He carried a message written in a hand that looked as if it had wrestled the alphabet and won by biting. Triss opened it, saw the first line, and smiled without happiness.
"Zoltan found the counting route."
Geralt took the note. "Already?"
"He would object to the surprise."
Jack stood beside Buck with Jacob's medallion hidden under his glove. He had not meant to hold it while riding. He had not meant many things that day.
Triss read aloud.

"Clove-wax and black oval lots moved through a Temerian vassal archive under charitable reconstruction papers. One buyer used an ash-house near the old tannery road. Not a metaphor, apparently. Place burns confiscated documents by day and stores inconvenient ones by night. If this is not your trouble, I'll eat Dandelion's hat. Slowly, so he suffers."
Ciri studied the road ahead. "Archive of ash."
Yennefer's eyes went cold in the particular way that made wise people remember appointments elsewhere. "Good."
Asha touched the mourning cord at her wrist. "Helena feared paper would outlive bodies."
"It does," Jack said.
Geralt mounted slowly. "Then we make paper answer to bodies for once."
No one made that a speech. The road did not need one.
Buck stepped forward before Jack asked, as if the horse had decided grief was taking too long and ought to learn momentum.
Behind them, the watch-house disappeared into rain, carrying no bodies and too many names.
Ahead, the archive waited.
Not truth.
The courier from Zoltan also carried a second scrap, smaller, folded around a coin clipped so badly it could only have been chosen for insult.
Dandelion had written on it in an elegant hand that looked profoundly offended by the company it kept.

My dear witchers, sorceresses, monarchs-in-mud, witnesses, dragons pretending not to be dragons, and any horse with better judgment than the lot of you: the city has begun singing about a dead Nilfgaardian shield-man. I did not start this, which wounds me professionally. Someone else wants Jacob remembered before Jack is ready to own the memory. That means the archive is leaking, or being made to leak. Come quickly, preferably before the chorus rhymes Moorlen with forlorn men.
Zoltan had added underneath: I told him not to write that. He did anyway. Hurry.
Jack read the scrap once and folded it carefully.
Ciri watched him. "They are trying to take even grief's first telling."
"Yes."

His voice had become too calm again. Geralt heard it and went to tighten Roach's girth for the third time. Triss turned to Yennefer. Yennefer studied the road. Asha closed her eyes and seemed to count people not present. Saesenthessis turned her face toward the east, where hidden origin waited, then toward the west, where the archive of ash waited first.
"Grief is not slower because men hurry it," Asha said.
"No," Jack answered. "But witnesses are."

He tucked the scrap beside Helena's letter, not with it. Never with it. He was learning categories of his own now, and some of them mattered because they protected the dead from being used by the living too quickly.
Ciri rode beside him when they left the toll hut.

For a while neither spoke. The road gave them wet stones, cart ruts, a black dog that followed for half a mile and then wisely abandoned history, and one old woman selling turnips from a barrow who told Geralt he had the face of a man underfed by his own choices. He bought three turnips because the accusation was both accurate and affordable.
Jack put one in Buck's saddlebag.
"That is for the horse?" Ciri asked.
"For later judgment."
"Buck judges turnips?"
"Buck judges everything."
The horse flicked one ear, confirming nothing and condemning much.
Ciri let the small absurdity stand between them. It did not heal the day. It made space inside it. Sometimes that was the only form of mercy that did not lie.

The archive would not give him that mercy. Archives did not make space; they compressed it until names became columns and columns became permission. Jack knew that before seeing the ash-house because the road had taught him the shape of institutional hunger: a roof that did not leak, a clean desk, a careful clerk, a sealed shelf, and somewhere beneath all that neatness, a body no one had called a body while there was still time.

He touched the bead through his glove and thought of Helena refusing to be a line item, Jacob buying minutes with steel, Vesemir hiding a living child because secrecy had looked kinder than exposure, and Geralt now riding ahead with his shoulders set as if he could physically block the past from reaching them first. He could not. None of them could. That was the road's ugliest honesty. What they could do was arrive before the next hand corrected the record. Jack looked once at Ciri, once at Yennefer, once at Asha, and understood that grief had become company without asking permission.
He did not trust the comfort of that. He carried it anyway.
The room where truth had been filed incorrectly.
Outside, the rain stopped. The ruin dripped. The road waited with all the patience of a creditor.

part_subtitle: A father can be dead and still steer the blade.

paragraphs: Extract from a Black Ink transfer ledger, damaged at the lower edge: BARBED-STAR CONTINUITY, closed action inventory. Bearer-class adult female, terminated. Military protector, compromised by sentiment, terminated. Infant continuity risk, unresolved. Servant-witness category, unresolved. Golden draconic containment anomaly, status uncertain. Recommendation: recover or erase secondary cache before eastern custodial groups can contest custody doctrine.
The archive stood under a tannery because the living preferred bad smells above old crimes.

They reached it by taking four roads that did not admit they were roads. The first ran behind a row of dye houses where blue water leaked into the gutter and made the rats look royal. The second crossed a cooper's yard under an awning of split staves. The third was a covered passage used by fishwives who had mastered the art of seeing nothing while knowing exactly what everything was worth. The fourth was not a road at all, but a gap between two leaning walls where Jack had to turn his shoulders and Dandelion had to sacrifice a feather to masonry.
"A noble death," Dandelion whispered, looking at the torn plume.
"It was blue," Zoltan said. "Death improved it."

Jack noticed the choice before he noticed the door. Men who hid papers beneath banks wanted money to guard them. Men who hid papers beneath temples wanted guilt to make thieves hesitate. Men who hid papers beneath tanneries understood that rot had jurisdiction. No patrol wished to search a cellar where lime, urine, wet hide, old hair, and boiled fat sat in the throat like a punishment one had earned by breathing.

Zoltan had found the place through wax, debt, and an eel seller who did not believe in secrets after the third mug. Dandelion had found the door by insulting a municipal clerk until the man produced a key merely to make the argument end. Triss had found the false inventory number by comparing three ledgers and muttering in a voice that made the ink look guilty. Yennefer had found the ward on the threshold and removed it with two fingers, one cold glance, and a phrase in Elder Speech that made the ward reconsider its career.
Geralt studied the tannery steps, then Jack. "Smells worse than Kaer Morhen's west drain."
"No," Jack said. "This has ambition."

"You two compare filth like vintners compare grapes," Dandelion said from the alley. He wore a butcher's apron, a cap too small for him, and the expression of a man being forced to murder art in public. "It is one of your least marketable talents."
Zoltan, who had a hammer, three knives, and a sack of forged delivery tags, looked at the bard's apron. "You look respectable. It's disgusting."
"I feel morally diminished."
"Good. You blend in."

Ciri stood in the shadow beneath the overhanging upper floor, hood low, boots deliberately muddy. She had argued against coming for thirteen minutes and then won the argument by refusing to have it. Empress-designate, daughter, hunted girl, woman who knew files when they began salivating. She had left her two quiet riders at the far lane, because imperial protection entered rooms before fact and she wanted the evidence to trip over fewer banners.

Asha waited beside the stair with her hand near the bone knots at her belt. Saesenthessis had not entered the city. She had said stone that remembered gold would behave badly under too many roofs, which sounded like an answer until one noticed it was also a refusal. She watched from somewhere outside the walls, or perhaps not. Dragons made absence feel intentional.

The cellar door opened on hinges greased recently by a hand that respected silence more than law. Below, the air grew wet and chemical. Jack went first, because his blood had begun to cool against the signet, and cold that came from recognition should not be left at one's back. Geralt followed close to intervene and far enough not to insult the point of Jack going first. Triss came after him with a shaded lantern. Yennefer came last and made the stair feel as if it had been inspected and found wanting.

The archive was not grand. That was the obscenity of it. No vaulted chamber, no carved seals, no black-robed keepers murmuring over forbidden names. It was a low room with brick walls, three tables, eight shelves, a cabinet with warped doors, two stools, and a floor gritty with old lime dust. Boxes sat in rows by region, date, and category. Some had been scorched. Some had been sealed. Several had labels written in the same clean hand that had called dead people inventory.
"Ordinary," Triss said.
Jack studied the shelves. "Yes."
Her mouth tightened. She had meant it as accusation, and he had heard it as fact.
A dead rat lay beneath the cabinet, dried into a comma. Zoltan nudged it with his boot and looked offended. "Even the vermin gave up. That's how you know it's official."

Yennefer touched the nearest box without opening it. The lid trembled once. "These were moved after the purge years. Some from Redanian seizures, some from Temerian military stores, some from Nilfgaardian copies. Someone gathered fragments into one apparatus."
"Black Ink," Ciri said.
"Or the thing that became it," Triss answered. "Institutions have childhoods. Usually worse handwriting, same appetite."

Jack moved along the shelves. His left palm pulsed under the glove. Not pain. Not warning. A pressure that seemed to come from behind the knuckles, as if the blood remembered where the papers wanted him to stand. Labels passed under his eyes: WITCHER IRREGULARITIES, POST-PURGE RELIC LOTS, NON-HUMAN CUSTODIAL CULTS, DRACONID ANOMALY FRAGMENTS, CONTINUITY RISK INDEX.
He stopped at the last one.
Geralt saw him stop. "Jack."
"I know."
The second shelf gave them less truth and therefore more work.

That, Triss said, was the sign of a real archive. A false one handed over a single perfect confession and expected gratitude. A true one resisted by being dull, misfiled, misdated, and faithful to the cowardice of everyone who had touched it. She found the first contradiction in a bundle marked post-purge sanitation, which contained neither sanitation records nor dates from the purge. The ribbon had been tied by a left-handed clerk. The label had been written by a right-handed one.
The wax on the corner had clove in it, Novigrad office wax, far too expensive for a tannery cellar that pretended to be municipal waste storage.
Zoltan sniffed the page and looked offended. "I have known thieves with more respect for labeling."
"That is because thieves expect to retrieve what they hide," Yennefer said. "Officials expect someone else to suffer from the confusion."

Ciri stood beside the shelf without touching it. She had read the word terminated four times by then. Each reading made her quieter. The palace had trained her to hold anger behind the eyes, to make fury look like attention. Jack recognized the trick because he had learned a poorer version at Kaer Morhen. The difference was that Ciri's control had been polished for rooms with witnesses. His had been forged for rooms with straps.

Triss opened the bundle with a knife too small for combat and too sharp for forgiveness. Inside were shipping copies, field summaries, and a narrow slip of cloth wrapped around a brass clasp. The clasp was shaped like a little sun, cheap work, one hinge bent from heat. Not a relic. Not a weapon. Something from clothing. A child's cloak, perhaps, or a woman's satchel.
Asha saw it and lost color.
The smallest change, and still the archive felt it.
"Helena," Jack said.

Asha did not answer at once. She took the clasp from Triss with two fingers, as if it might accuse her if held too fully. "She used these on traveling sleeves. Morningstar fasteners were plain iron for household use. Brass for road work. The sun was not a royal sign. It was a joke. She said if the house could only keep a terrible night from coming, someone in it should be allowed to wear daylight."

The words did what the file could not. They put Helena in the room with weather on her cloak and wit still alive, making a joke about duty. Jack looked at the clasp longer than he had looked at the page calling her terminated.
Geralt saw that and looked away.
"The file missed it," Ciri said softly.
"Files miss everything that cannot help them win," Triss replied.
Yennefer took a second page. "Not everything. This one notes a recovered domestic fastener under non-actionable textile debris."
"Textile debris," Zoltan said. "I hope there is a special hell where clerks are beaten with their own adjectives."
"There is," Dandelion said from the door. "It is called patron correspondence."
No one laughed loudly. The joke survived anyway because the room needed something that was not a category.

Jack placed the clasp beside the blue bead from Jacob's broken hilt. Brass daylight. Blue bead. Two useless objects, therefore the most reliable things in the archive. He felt the old cold under his shirt answer the pairing. Not with pain. With a slow inward pressure, as if the barbed star understood objects better than words. The lantern flame leaned toward the table. Triss covered it with her hand until it steadied.
