"Price," she said before anyone asked. "Even listening has one."
The tied clerk behind the cabinet began breathing too quickly.
Geralt crouched before him. "Name."
"Ossen Birt. Assistant custodian under municipal archival transition."
"Bad name," Jack said without looking up.

Ossen swallowed. "I was given the position after three better men refused it. I did not know the contents of the sealed packets. I knew the odors, the shelf numbers, and the fact that gentlemen with clean gloves came twice a season to say the word continuity as if it were a prayer."
"Gentlemen," Yennefer said.

"One woman," Ossen corrected, then regretted accuracy as soon as the room sharpened. "A northern solicitor. Gray eyes. Surgical handwriting. She never removed her gloves. She said the dead were most useful when their paperwork became stable."
Ciri's fingers flattened on the table. "Useful."
Jack turned to her. She looked back. The word had become a shared enemy by now, a small bridge built over an ugly river.
"Did they remove anything?" Triss asked.

Ossen nodded toward the lowest shelf. "One index before you came. Barbed-Star eastern custodial references. The clerk who carried it wore no office color. He had a pilgrim badge inside his cuff. Black crown burned on tin. I noticed because it snagged the paper and he cursed like a soldier."
"Cazren," Dandelion said.
Asha closed her hand around the brass clasp until the bent hinge pressed into her palm. "Then they do not only want Jack. They are learning his prayers from stolen margins."
"They will not like what prayers do when stolen," Yennefer said.
"No," Asha answered. "They will like them very much. They will remove the parts that say no."

Jack took the living chamber page, folded it, and placed it with the clasp and bead. Evidence, object, wound. The archive had tried to make the dead into categories. It had failed in the way bad rooms sometimes failed when enough living people refused to read obediently.
"That's not why I said it."
"I know that too."

The box was narrow, bound with cracked black ribbon, and sealed with wax that had been broken once and repressed by someone who owned a better stamp than conscience. The oval mark sat deep in the surface. Jack touched it with the tip of his knife. The wax did not crack. It softened.
Triss drew in a small breath. "It answers to heat."
"It answers to him," Yennefer said.
Jack met her eyes.
"I did not say it should," she added.

He cut the ribbon. The lid opened with the soft sigh of paper that had survived longer than mercy. Inside lay a stack of reports, copied notices, redacted witness rolls, a piece of cloth stiff with old smoke, and one small envelope marked with a child's age rather than a name.
Three to four years. Pale hair. Signet attached.
The room went still in the particular way rooms did when everyone in them understood the knife had already entered and was merely waiting to be seen.
Jack did not open the envelope first. He took the top report.
Triss stepped closer, not touching him. "May I?"
He gave it to her because his hand had become too precise and precision, past a certain point, became another way to bleed.
She read silently. Her face changed by almost nothing. The nothing was terrible. Triss's warmth did not leave her when she was angry. It became brighter and less safe.
"This is a post-action summary," she said. "Not the original order. A summary. It assumes the action was authorized elsewhere."
"Read," Jack said.
She looked once at Ciri, once at Geralt, and then read.

"Operation designation: Barbed-Star Continuity. Objective: removal or acquisition of remaining custodial bloodline assets. Target adult female, Helena of suspected Morningstar descent, designated bearer-class. Associated Nilfgaardian military protector, Jacob var Jorek, compromised by sentiment, designated obstruction. Infant continuity risk, unidentified male, recovery preferred, termination acceptable if transfer compromised. Unidentified golden draconic containment anomaly encountered. Field doctrine insufficient. Authority chain redacted. Completion status unstable."
Dandelion, who had been quiet in the doorway because even poets could recognize when the room had no use for feathers, whispered a curse with no theater in it.
Asha made no sound. Her face had gone beyond grief into something older and drier. The hands at her sides did not tremble. That meant the tremor had gone somewhere more expensive.
Ciri turned to Jack. He did not look back.

Yennefer lifted the cloth from the box with two fingers. It had once been white or pale yellow. Fire had browned it. One corner carried a pattern stitched by hand: five barbed points around a tiny line of blue thread. Helena's hand, perhaps. Or another woman's. The file did not say, because files rarely understood where the soul of a thing had been placed.
"Terminated," Ciri said.
No one mistook the softness for weakness.
"They wrote terminated," she continued. "For his mother."
"Yes," Triss said.
"Compromised by sentiment for his father."
"Yes."
"Continuity risk for a child."
"Yes."

Ciri's hand rested on the table. Her fingers did not curl. The training of court held the gesture flat and elegant. Jack could smell the anger under her skin anyway. Witcher senses were sometimes a cruelty disguised as advantage.
Geralt reached for the edge of the table and missed it by half an inch before correcting the movement. Jack saw. So did Yennefer. Triss did not look away from the page, which was her kindness.
"There are margin notes," Triss said. "Later. Different hand. S. Veyrane, junior review."
The name made the room smaller.
"He was there?" Geralt asked.

"No," Triss said. "Too young, perhaps. Or not field-ranked. This looks like an archival interpretation. See here. He disagrees with the original failure category. He calls it not failed action, but incomplete custody event."
Zoltan spat on the floor. "That's a sentence that deserves a shovel."
"Several," Yennefer said.

Jack took the page back. The letters behaved themselves under his eyes. That was insulting. A page describing the ruin of his first life should have warped, burned, screamed, done anything except sit there with administrative patience.
A father could be dead and still steer the blade.

Jacob's hilt lay in Jack's pack. The blue bead lay in his inner pouch. Helena's letter had been folded twice and wrapped in oilcloth. Those things had weight. The page had weight too, but of a different sort. The dead had given him a name. The living had given him a category.
He chose the name.
"Next," he said.
"Jack," Ciri said.
"Next."
Triss did not argue. She knew the shape of men who asked for more pain because the alternative was feeling the pain already given. She took the second report.

This one held diagrams. Poor copies of better geometry. Five outer barbs. Inner anchor marks. A central chamber drawn as a circle, then crossed out in red ink. The translation beneath had three names for the same idea: vessel-prison, blood chamber, living hinge. The last line had been struck through but remained readable because whoever had redacted it had underestimated stubborn paper.
LIVING CHAMBER POSSIBILITY: REJECTED.
Yennefer took the sheet before anyone could ask. She did not ask permission because the line had insulted her so deeply that manners would have had to wait outside.
"Rejected," she said. "Not because of cruelty. They note cruelty in a separate column and mark it tolerable under emergency doctrine."
Geralt's mouth tightened.
"Why rejected?" Ciri asked.
Yennefer's eyes moved down the page. "Because the host could not be reliably governed afterward. They feared a living chamber capable of refusing future instruction."
The silence became violent.

Regis was not there yet, but the sentence seemed to summon the need for him. A living prison. A body asked to hold hunger. A man converted into architecture and found inconvenient because architecture might object.
Jack looked at the diagram and felt the seal under his shirt cool toward the center of his chest. Not cold from recognition now. Cold from direction.
"They considered it in 1249," Triss said quietly. "Before anyone alive in Black Ink fully understood what Jack is. Someone had enough doctrine to imagine using him as a prison."
"Or the cruelty to imagine everything," Ciri said.
"Cruelty is more inventive when afraid," Yennefer replied.

Asha reached for the edge of the table, then stopped herself. "The Faithel have words for this. Old words. Forbidden in my novice training except as failure theology. No child should carry chamber-law. No living body should replace stone unless stone, fire, blood, and witness have all failed."
His attention settled on her. "You knew."
"I knew of doctrine. Not of them writing it about you."
"But it exists."
"Because our ancestors had the honesty to name last horrors. Naming does not mean choosing."
Yennefer turned to Asha. "Men with files rarely respect that distinction."
"That is why we kept songs," Asha said. "Songs can forget safely. Files remember too obediently."
Dandelion opened his mouth, then closed it. The restraint showed on him. Priscilla would have been proud of him, and possibly suspicious.
Jack folded the living chamber page once. Then again. His fingers did not shake. That concerned Geralt more than shaking would have.
"This goes with us," Jack said.
"Everything goes with us," Triss said. "Copies, not originals if we can manage it. Originals where copies would be too slow."
"The archive keeper?" Zoltan asked.
"There isn't one," Jack said.
Geralt looked toward the stair. "There was."

They found him behind the cabinet, not dead, only tied, gagged, and frightened, smelling of vinegar and cheap wool. He was a clerk in his fifties with a bald crown, good ink stains, and the soft hands of a man who had chosen paper because swords were too honest. Ves cut him free with a knife she had not yet introduced into the story, because Ves had arrived without ceremony at the same time as the threat above.
She looked from the clerk to Geralt. "Roche says your bard makes too much noise."
Dandelion straightened. "Roche wounds from afar. Cowardly and efficient."
"He also says if you brought trouble, bring it quietly."
"We brought a tannery," Zoltan said. "It started loudly."

Ves did not smile. Her eyes moved to Jack, to the box, to Ciri's hood, and then back to Geralt. She saw rank, disguise, grief, and probable disaster in the space between breaths. That was why Roche trusted her. Men could talk for an hour and call it reconnaissance. Ves looked once and knew which door would matter when fire started.
"Two watchers upstairs," she said. "One Black Ink, one church. They are trying very hard not to notice each other."
"Church?" Yennefer asked.
"Red candles in the bag. Blackened crown stitched inside the coat. Bad sermon smell."
Dandelion rubbed his forehead. "I dislike it when metaphors recruit."
Jack studied the living chamber page. "So do I."
The tied clerk began trying to speak through the gag. Geralt removed it.
"I did not know what was in the sealed boxes," the clerk said immediately.
"Popular opening," Jack said.
"I catalog what arrives. I do not decide arrival."
"Rope says otherwise."
The man looked wounded by the logic. "They tied me because I objected to removal without entry correction."
Zoltan stared. "They kidnapped you for being tedious?"
"For being accurate," the clerk said. "There is a difference."
Triss knelt before him, gentler than the room deserved. "Who ordered removal?"
"Transfer note. South road. Temerian vassal stamp, but wrong wax. Resistance-era countermark under it. Someone used old patriot channels to move Black Ink stock."
Ves's face changed.
Geralt saw it. "Roche."
"Yes," Ves said. "Now."

Jack closed the box. The archive had given him what it had been built to deny: proof that his parents' deaths had entered a ledger before they had entered a grave. It had also given a road. Not east yet. Temeria first. Quiet country, false permits, men who survived by making ugly bargains and calling them necessary because the alternative had worse boots.
He put the living chamber page inside his coat.
Ciri watched the movement. She knew what it meant when a person carried the worst answer because no one else should have to look at it too often. She had carried prophecies in less visible pockets.
"Do not make that private," she said.
Jack left that unanswered.
"The page," Ciri said. "Not the pain. The pain is yours. The page is evidence."
He held her gaze long enough for the room to grow aware of the distance between them. "Fair."
That word had become a small bridge. Neither trusted bridges fully. Both crossed anyway when the water required it.
Above, something broke. A shout. A body against wood. The smell of smoke under tannery rot.
"Church watcher," Ves said.
"Or the other one," Zoltan replied.
"Both," Jack said.

They took the box, the clerk, the copies, and the knowledge that the massacre had been filed as work. They left through the waste chute because Dandelion's key no longer fit the civilized exit and because history, when honest, often traveled through sewage.

In the alley behind the tannery, rain washed lime dust from Jack's boots. He looked once at the black box in Zoltan's arms and thought of Helena as terminated, Jacob as compromised, Zerrikanterment as anomaly, himself as unresolved risk.
Then he thought of the blue bead.
The file had not known about that.
That was its first defeat.
They did not get clear of the tannery without paying for the defeat.

The first watcher came from the roof with a hand crossbow and the sincere expression of a man who had been promised hazard pay by someone who would later deny knowing his name. Ves saw the angle before the man fired. She moved Jack by striking his shoulder with the flat of her hand, not asking, not warning, just moving the most important target out of a quarrel with mathematics. The bolt struck the brick where his throat had been and broke with a sound too small for the room it changed.
Geralt threw a knife. The watcher dropped behind the roofline, not dead, judging from the quality of the curse, but suddenly less professional.

The second man wore no weapon anyone could charge him for. He stood at the mouth of the alley with both hands open, a pilgrim badge pinned to his coat, and red wax under one thumbnail. He looked at Jack and smiled as if seeing not a person but a long-delayed appointment.
"The door walks," he said.
Jack went still.

Ciri moved first this time. Not toward the man. Toward Jack, one step, close; her presence put a body between his attention and the sentence without pretending to shield him from it. Yennefer's hand lifted. The pilgrim's smile faltered because zealots understood fire as symbol until a sorceress offered them the practical version.
"Run," Yennefer said.
He did.
Zoltan watched him go and looked offended. "We're letting him?"
"Yes," Triss said, clutching the black box beneath her cloak. "A frightened messenger carries panic better than a corpse."
"I like corpses for clarity."
"I know. That's why we let other people do diplomacy."

Jack looked down the alley after the pilgrim. Rain had turned the stones black. The phrase remained after the man vanished, not as sound but as residue, a handprint left on the inside of the skull. The red door walks. He had heard worse words in cleaner rooms, but these were different. Black Ink classified him from above. The cult called from below. Both needed him to stop being a man in order for their sentences to work.
Ciri's shoulder brushed his. "Do not answer every name they throw."
"I didn't."
"You listened."
He turned to her. "Listening is how one stays alive."
"Not always. Sometimes it is how people teach you the cage before they build it."
He had no answer that did not make her right. The alley gave him rain, chemical stink, and Zoltan swearing at a cart wheel. He accepted those instead.
Triss made the copies in a safe room above a cooper's shop whose owner owed Zoltan money, Dandelion pride, and the city several unpaid fees.

The room smelled of fresh shavings, ink, hot glue, and rain caught in wool cloaks. Ciri sat by the window with her hood down for the first time since entering the district, watching the lane below as if courtiers might sprout from puddles if unsupervised. Yennefer stood at the table, one hand flat beside the living chamber diagram, her face so controlled that the cooper's apprentice refused to enter after bringing water. Geralt repaired a strap on Jack's pack that had not required repair until Geralt needed something smaller than murder to do with his hands.

Jack stood by the door and counted footsteps beyond it. Six regular, three drunk, one limp, one child dragging a stick, two soldiers pretending not to be soldiers, and Ves returning with news before she knocked.
Triss copied the categories with ordinary ink.
Bearer-class. Compromised by sentiment. Continuity custody. Golden draconic containment anomaly.
At the fourth repetition, her pen stopped.
"I hate this," she said.
No one gave her comfort. Comfort would have insulted the work.
"Good," Yennefer said. "If it ever becomes easy, burn the table."
Triss dipped the pen again. "I may burn it anyway."
"After copies," Zoltan said from the corner. "Tables are replaceable. Evidence charges more."

The clerk from the tannery sat on a stool under Geralt's supervision and looked gradually less dead. His name was Ossen Birt. He had confessed to no moral crime that deserved the noose and several small ones that deserved humiliation, a category Dandelion had offered to administer professionally. Ossen had explained that the vassal stamp came through a Temerian corridor using old resistance marks. That meant Roche. Not guilty. Not innocent. Relevant.
Ves had listened to Ossen's description once and left.
When she returned, her boots had acquired mud from a road outside the city. "Roche will meet you. No banners. No imperial escort. No bard."
Dandelion put a hand to his chest. "I am wounded."
"He said that too. He said he did not care."
"A traditional exchange."
Ves turned to Ciri. "Highness."
Ciri's face did the small tightening it always did when title entered a low ceiling. "Here, Ciri."
Ves considered that. "Here, the wrong ears turn names into markets."
Ciri nodded once. Respect, not agreement. "Then use what keeps people alive."
Ves's eyes moved to Jack. "He looks calmer than the file."
"Files are dramatic," Jack said.
"No. Files are dull. That's how they get past guards."
He almost smiled. "Fair."

The word made Ciri look down at her hands. Geralt pretended not to see. Yennefer saw and chose silence with a surgeon's precision. Triss saw and kept writing because sometimes ink was the most dignified curtain available.
Ossen cleared his throat. "If I may be permitted an observation."
"Probably not," Zoltan said.

"The transfer stamp is not merely Temerian. It uses an old royal courier distortion. Before the vassal compromise, it meant resistance mercy. A false permit for moving fugitives through hostile inspections. Someone has repurposed it."
Ves's face went colder. "How many?"
"I saw nine in the last month. Medical chests, legal cases, relic lots, one livestock certificate, though I suspect there was no livestock."
"There rarely is when papers mention it too carefully," Geralt said.
Jack thought of Willenford, geese, garkains, and all the small doors through which large violence entered. "What did the livestock certificate carry?"
Ossen studied the floor. "Manacles. Padded. Sized for wrists. Built for panic."
The room did not change temperature. It only felt as if it had.
Ciri stood. "Roche. Now."
"Not now," Ves said. "At dawn. The road is watched, the bridge is bought, and the patrol captain believes his own honesty, which makes him dangerous after dark."
Ciri's eyes sharpened. "You give orders well."
"I survived men who gave worse."
That ended the argument because it was not an argument. It was credential.

By midnight, Triss had made three sets of copies. Yennefer had burned the discarded scrap in a blue flame that left no ash. Geralt had repaired two straps, a torn glove, and a buckle on Buck's bridle after Jack told him twice the buckle was fine. Buck had bitten no one, which either meant good discipline or contempt too deep for expression.
Jack slept for one hour in a chair by the door with Jacob's hilt under his coat and the living chamber page sealed in Triss's copy packet, not his own.
Ciri noticed.
Good, he thought before sleep took him. Let the page have witnesses.
Vernon Roche had chosen a country without a throne and had the permanent expression of a man who expected someone to send him the bill.

He waited in a ruined counting house two miles from the old road to Tretogor, on ground that had been Temerian, Redanian, Nilfgaardian, and briefly owned by a gang of deserters who had discovered that collecting tolls required more arithmetic than stabbing. The counting house still had its stone strongroom, its cracked floor tiles, and a faded painted lily hidden under soot where someone had tried to erase it without kneeling. Roche had not cleaned it. Some marks deserved to remain half-buried and stubborn.
Geralt entered first with rain on his cloak and suspicion in his boots. That was polite, in Roche's opinion. The older he became, the more he distrusted men who entered dangerous rooms looking dry.
"Geralt," Roche said.
"Roche."
"You brought a small war."
"It followed."
"Small wars do. They get attached when fed."

Geralt stepped aside. Jack came in behind him, then Ciri under a plain hood, then Yennefer, then Triss, then Asha, then Ves, who had been outside checking whether anyone had remembered to be stupid. Zoltan remained with the horses because the road beyond the counting house had opinions about wheels. Dandelion had been forbidden to come and had therefore come halfway, then been intercepted by Priscilla with more sense and better timing.
Roche saw Ciri and did not bow too deeply. That was also polite. Men who bowed too deeply to young women with too many titles usually hoped the angle might hide the knife in their sleeve.
"Highness," he said.
"Roche."
"This room has leaks, rats, and no imperial furniture. I apologize only for the rats."
"The rats are probably more honest than furniture."
"Temeria agrees."

Jack looked around the room. Roche watched him do it. Door, window, ceiling gap, strongroom hinge, Ves's position, Geralt's distance, Ciri's sightline, Yennefer's left hand, Triss's satchel, Roche's boots. The boy was not a boy, but men learned to use the wrong word when a face was younger than the trouble attached to it.
"You trained him," Roche said to Geralt.
"Some."
"Vesemir hid him."
"Yes."
"And now everyone with a stamp wants him."
"Yes."
Roche grunted. "That is what happens when you let the state learn a noun."
Ciri removed her hood. "Black Ink is using Temerian corridors."

"So Ves said." Roche looked at the papers Triss placed on the old counting table. He did not touch them yet. A man who had lived as long as Roche had among documents knew better than to touch a snake merely because someone else said it was dead. "Show me."

Triss showed him the false transit orders, the old resistance countermark under the vassal stamp, the wax trail, the legal phrasing, and the livestock certificate Ossen had described. She did not over-explain. Roche liked her for that. Many mages spoke as if the world had been waiting for their footnotes. Triss spoke like someone who had learned that frightened people needed the sharp end first.
Roche did not begin with the permits. He began with boots.

He pointed at Jack's first, then at Ciri's, then at the mud drying on Geralt's cuffs. "That is the first lie papers tell. Papers pretend roads are straight. Boots remember otherwise. Your Black Ink men understand maps, stamps, and fear. They understand less about who must walk after the stamp is dry."
Ves placed three pairs of boots on the table.

Dandelion, who had been successfully kept away from the meeting for nearly an hour and had therefore become everyone's problem in spirit, would have called the display theatrical. It was not. The first pair belonged to a courier. Soles wrapped for silence, front leather polished, back leather cracked. A man who expected to be seen from ahead and forgotten from behind. The second pair were pilgrim boots, muddy above black soldier stitching. The third were small, padded on the inside, with leather loops hidden near the ankle.
Ciri's face did not change. "For restraints."
"For making restraints look like transport care," Ves said. "A child, an old woman, a wounded mage, or a man someone has decided should arrive unmarked."
"Jack's size?" Geralt asked.
"No," Ves said. "Smaller."
That made the room colder than if she had said yes.

Roche took one of the false permits from Triss and laid it beside the boots. "A defeated country keeps two governments. The one that signs where the victor points, and the one that remembers where the dead are buried. Sometimes they help each other. Sometimes they sell each other for flour. If Black Ink is using our quiet roads, it is not because Temeria invited them as a state. Temeria has no clean state left to invite anyone. It is because our old tricks have become valuable to new cowards."
"You make compromise sound like disease," Yennefer said.
"It spreads through necessity," Roche replied. "That is close."

Geralt leaned against the wall and looked at the lily under soot. The painted flower had survived occupation, burning, and someone too ashamed to erase it properly. Jack watched him watch it. Geralt's guilt had a way of standing beside older ruins and finding family there.
"You used these routes to save people," Geralt said.
"Yes."
"And now they use them to move chains."
"Yes."
"That all?"

Roche's jaw tightened. "No. I used them to move people worth saving and people useful to saving others. I told myself I knew the difference. Some days I did. Some days the difference wore a uniform I disliked and asked for mercy anyway."
Ciri turned to him then. The look was not imperial. It was the look of someone who knew what it meant to be handed ugly arithmetic and told maturity was learning to swallow the result.
"And when you were wrong?" she asked.
"Ves remembered," Roche said.
Ves did not soften. "Sometimes after."
"Usually after," Roche agreed.
The words should have made him smaller. They did not. The room trusted him more because he had not tried to make survival clean.
Triss turned over the permit. "The countermark here is altered. Not copied badly. Altered with knowledge. Someone had access to one of your original mercy ledgers."
Roche's eyes went to the strongroom door. "Three people alive know where those ledgers sleep."
"Alive," Jack said.
"A useful correction." Roche turned to Ves. "The dead one had a brother."
"Had two," Ves said. "One was hanged by Redanians. One became a customs assessor under the vassal office and began wearing gloves."
"Gloves again," Yennefer murmured.
"You remember hands when they take things from you," Ves said.

Roche opened the strongroom then, but not before making everyone wait while he listened to the road outside. The delay was not caution for show. Jack heard the same thing three breaths later: a wagon wheel, a cough, a crow, and beneath them a horse shifting weight with a rider trying not to move. Ves lifted her crossbow without looking at the window. Geralt's hand found his sword. Ciri did not reach for hers. She turned slightly so the cracked wall covered her left side and gave Jack space to move if the door broke inward.
He noticed.
So did Roche.
"You two will be expensive," Roche said.
Ciri's mouth tightened. "I am already expensive. The empire keeps reminding me."
"The empire prices you as symbol. Enemies will price you as lever. Friends should price you as person and plan accordingly."
"Is that advice?"
"That is the tax for standing in my ruined counting house. Advice is extra."

The horse outside moved away before anyone fired. A watcher, not an attacker. Ves made a mark on the shutter frame with the tip of her knife, one small line. Counted. Jack liked that better than a threat. Threats fed stories. Marks fed memory.
Only then did Roche lift the floor stone.

The tin box beneath it smelled of old oil, children's wool, and paper sealed against the kind of damp that had eaten better countries. Jack smelled the child's cloak before seeing it. Old smoke lived in the seams. A brass repair hook, too crude for noble use, had been worked into one elbow.
"Whose?" Ciri asked.
"No one's now," Ves said. "Which is why inspectors hate it. Dead children's clothes make even bastards imagine witnesses."
Geralt closed his eyes once. Too brief for mercy. Long as memory.
Roche handed Triss the permits. "Black Ink did not invent cruelty. They professionalized old habits. That is why they will last unless someone makes the habit expensive."
Jack studied the padded boots. "Then we make it expensive."
"No," Roche said. "First you make it visible. Then you make helping it shameful. Then expensive. If you reverse the order, martyrs breed faster than rats."
Zoltan, from the doorway, muttered, "Rats at least chew their own ropes."
Ves turned to him. "You were told to stay with the horses."
"The horses found me dull. I came where the politics smell worse."
"You chose correctly," Ciri said.

Roche looked from the future empress to the dwarf to the hidden witcher and seemed, for one tired second, almost amused by the absurdity of Temeria's latest council. Then the old expression returned, bill expected, bill unpaid.

"The chapel granary," he said, tapping the map. "If the chains are already there, we do not charge in as heroes. Heroes give priests a crowd. We arrive as auditors. Everyone fears auditors because they ask for receipts."
Roche read the first page. Then the second. His face did not change until he reached the countermark. Then it changed too little.
Ves saw it anyway. "Real?"
"The mark is real," Roche said. "The use is a bastard."
"That narrows nothing."
"It narrows a knife."
Geralt leaned against the wall, arms folded. "Old resistance channel?"

"Before the vassal compromise, we used three mercy marks. One for weapons, one for people, one for messages too ugly to write honestly. This is the second, altered. It meant the bearer was not to be delayed if found in a cart, coffin, wine crate, or livestock pen. It saved mages, children, deserters worth saving, and once a goat that was either very important or mislabeled."
"What happened to the goat?" Jack asked.
Roche studied him. "It bit a Redanian sergeant and became a local hero."
"Sensible goat."
"Temeria produces them."
For one breath the counting house remembered that humor could exist without betraying the dead. Then Roche placed the page flat on the table.

"After the war, some channels were folded into vassal administration. Not officially. Never officially. Temeria survives by having papers that say one thing, men who mean another, and women like Ves who check whether the road agrees."
Ves looked through the cracked window. "The road rarely does."
"But Black Ink found the old marks," Triss said.

"Or bought them from a clerk who once swore his mother taught him loyalty and then discovered his mother had rent." Roche tapped the countermark. "Do not romanticize defeated countries. Patriotism is cleaner in songs than in cupboards. People sell things. Sometimes because they are bastards. Sometimes because their children need boots. Sometimes because the empire tells them selling is cooperation and refusing is nostalgia."
Geralt's face had gone still in the way Roche knew well. It was the look of a man hearing one of his own defenses come from another mouth and disliking the fit.
"Ugly survival," Geralt said.

"Yes. We chose it. Temeria under vassal compromise, not ashes. Old colors in cupboards, not on fields. Taxes paid to men we used to kill. Boys alive because their fathers swallowed pride until it lodged somewhere permanent." Roche looked at Ciri, because only a fool pretended she did not sit at the center of some of that arithmetic. "I do not regret saving what could be saved. I regret what the saving taught people to accept."
Ciri did not flinch. "Good. That means you remain useful."
Roche almost smiled. "Your father says similar things with better gloves."
"My father owns too many gloves."
"Emperors do. They dislike fingerprints."
Yennefer's mouth curved by a blade's width. Geralt looked at the floor because the room had too many fathers in it already.

Jack had said nothing. Roche noticed that too. Quiet men in rooms full of politics were either bored, ignorant, or counting exits. Jack was counting the ways men explained necessary harm and deciding which explanations deserved to remain alive.
"You dislike this," Roche said to him.
Jack let the silence answer first. "I dislike how often men say necessary after the harm has been done."
"Before the harm, necessary is prediction. After, it is defense."
"You comfortable with that?"
"No. Comfort is for people who chose less." Roche leaned over the table. "But if you want clean hands, witcher, wash them before touching history. It won't help. History stains through soap."
Geralt glanced between them. "Roche."
"What?"
"Less charm."
"This is my charm."
"Explains the wars."
Ves snorted despite herself. Roche pretended not to notice. A commander did not always need obedience. Sometimes he needed proof that his people had not become furniture.

Triss unfolded the map. "These transit routes cross three places where Black Ink could move people or objects without standard inspection: Old Alder Ford, the chapel granary near Dravik, and a ferry at Marna's Bend. Which one carries manacles?"
"All could," Roche said.
"Which one would you use?" Ciri asked.
Roche pointed without hesitation. "Chapel granary."
Yennefer studied the mark. "Why?"

"Because men think chapels are watched by gods and therefore forget to watch the cart doors. Also because the priest there is dead, the replacement drinks, and the grain tithe records are so badly kept that a dragon could be logged as rye if it wore a sack."
Asha's face did not change at dragon. Saesenthessis was not present to object. The absence felt briefly amused.
Ves moved beside the map. "There is more."
Roche turned to her. "Say it."

"One of the altered marks went through a charity tied to war widows. The same charity Zoltan found in Novigrad. Same wax. Same clove-black compound. The courier making the last transfer wore a pilgrim badge with a blackened crown scratched on the back."
"Cult," Yennefer said.
"Or someone using cult marks to make Black Ink look less tidy," Triss said.
"Both can be true," Jack said.
Roche nodded once. "That is the sort of answer that gets men killed and investigations moving."

They went to the strongroom because Ves had insisted the real reason for meeting was not talk but proof. Roche unlocked three bolts, removed a fourth that had not been installed by the original builder, and lifted a floor stone with Geralt's help. Beneath lay a tin box wrapped in oilcloth and a child's old cloak, patched at the elbows.
"We hide things in what inspectors find sentimental," Ves said. "They dislike touching poor children's clothes. Makes their hands remember they have hands."

Inside the box were permits, wax impressions, and six names. Four clerks. One courier. One priest: Cazren of the Red Step, formerly attached to an Eternal Fire fringe house, removed for doctrinal fever after the pyres cooled.
Dandelion's absence became inconvenient at once. Priscilla's too.

"Cazren," Yennefer said. "I have heard the name. Pamphlets. Apocalypse sermons. He claimed the White Frost did not end because Ciri saved the world, but because the world had been granted time to prepare for judgment."
Ciri rolled her eyes in a way that made her look younger and more tired at once. "How generous of judgment."
"He disappeared after Novigrad's sermon houses became unfashionable," Triss said.
"Men like that do not disappear," Roche replied. "They discover basements."
Jack studied the pilgrim badge impression. A simple crown, burned black at the points. Beneath it, in a poor hand, someone had scratched five words.
THE RED DOOR WALKS NORTH.
His palm tightened.
Ciri saw and came closer. "Do not."
"I didn't."
"You started."
He met her eyes. The room practiced looking elsewhere with varying degrees of skill.
"Started what?" Roche asked, because tact had never been his favorite weapon.
"Becoming useful to the wrong sentence," Ciri said.
Roche looked from her to Jack and then, unexpectedly, to Geralt. "You have your hands full."
Geralt's face remained blank. "Had noticed."

"No, you hadn't. Not fully." Roche returned the badge to the table. "When a future empress cares about a man being hunted by a legal apparatus, the man becomes political. When the man cares back, she becomes leverage. When the sorceress with the history of making kings nervous stands beside him, he becomes magical leverage. When Geralt of Rivia stands there looking guilty, he becomes family leverage. Your enemy has too many handles. Start cutting some or stop pretending you can carry them all."
No one liked that. It had the smell of truth said by someone who had enjoyed too few opportunities to be gentle.
Geralt spoke first. "You offering help or indictment?"
"Temeria survived by learning to make one document do two jobs." Roche placed the permits in Triss's stack. "Help."

Ves pulled a second map from the box. "Old quiet roads. Safety had no place in it. Merely less expected. The chapel granary leads to Cazren's circle if the courier trail is honest. The Marna ferry leads to Black Ink's next legal holding point. If both enemies are touching the same routes, they are not yet allies."
"Good," Yennefer said.
"Or bad," Zoltan said from the doorway, having entered with mud on his beard and an expression of satisfaction. "Enemies sharing a road sometimes means they're both waiting at the bridge."
"You were outside," Roche said.
"I got bored. Also your lookout has a cough."
Ves's head turned. "Which lookout?"
"The one who thought a dead oak could serve as cover."
Ves cursed and left. Roche watched her go with the calm of a man who trusted only people he still worried about.

The discussion became practical after that, which was safer and worse. Routes. Names. Wax. How to move Ciri without announcing Ciri. How to move Jack without making every innkeeper rich in witness statements. How to let Yennefer work without leaving magical scent obvious enough for a half-trained tracker with a crystal and ambition. How to contact Dandelion without letting the cult hear the wrong song first.

Roche gave them two forged transit sheets and one real permit he said he had been saving for a day when Temeria needed to do something noble or stupid. Geralt asked which this was. Roche said the distinction had been difficult since the war.
Before they left, Roche and Geralt stood alone beside the cracked lily on the wall.
"You hid him," Roche said.
"Yes."
"For good reasons."
"Yes."
"And bad ones."
Geralt studied the half-erased lily. "Yes."
Roche nodded. "Ugly survival."
"You make it sound like a club."

"It is. No wine, poor songs, everyone hates the dues." Roche folded his arms. "Don't let the boy become the price of your old decision. Men like us get used to paying with other people's peace and calling it strategy."
Geralt's jaw worked once. "He's not a boy."
"No. That's why the warning matters."

Outside, rain had softened to mist. Jack stood with Buck in the yard, checking the horse's left foreleg while Ciri pretended to examine a saddlebag and watched him instead. Yennefer spoke with Triss near the cart, their heads bent over a paper as if the world could be argued into less cruelty by two women refusing to blink first.
Geralt saw all of it. Roche watched him see it.
"Family?" Roche asked.
Geralt did not answer quickly.
"Careful," Roche said. "States eat families first. Easier to call it policy afterward."
The chapel granary had been built by pious men with excellent drainage and poor imagination.

It stood on a low rise beyond fields that had once fed soldiers, then refugees, then crows. The chapel itself was roofless, its saint broken at the nose, its altar used for weighing grain until the new priest decided commerce needed less stone and more privacy. Three carts stood behind the granary with tarps pulled tight. One smelled of rye. One smelled of mold. The third smelled of oil, padded leather, and fear handled by men who wore gloves.
Jack found the manacles under three sacks of barley.

They were not ordinary shackles. Padded at the wrists, etched inside with phrases that looked legal until Yennefer read them aloud and the air seemed to grow teeth. Non-consensual custody under emergency doctrine. Public preservation restraint. Host stabilization measure.
Geralt stared at them. "Host stabilization."
"If they call it restraint, someone may imagine a person inside it," Triss said.
Jack touched the padding. Clean. New. Small enough for his wrists if the gloves were removed.

Ciri took one step forward and stopped. She did not touch them. Her face had gone imperial in the worst way, not cold because she did not feel, but cold because feeling had been locked inside armor and told to wait.
"These will not be used," she said.
Roche, who had come despite claiming he would not, turned to her. "That an order?"
"No." Ciri lifted her eyes from the manacles. "It is a promise. Orders require jurisdiction. Promises require consequence. I have plenty of both."
Ves, standing near the door with a crossbow, looked briefly pleased.
From the chapel ruin beyond the granary came singing.

Not Dandelion's kind. No clever rhyme, no warm vanity, no performance begging the room to be loved. This was low, repetitive, and hungry. A dozen voices perhaps, maybe more hidden under stone. The words came through rain and broken roof, rough and close.
Red door. Black crown. Blood hinge. Walk down.

Dandelion needed to hear this. Priscilla needed to hear this. Not because songs were beautiful. Because songs were routes, and this one led somewhere that wanted Jack kneeling before men who would call chains sacrament.
Jack closed the cart.
Roche looked toward the chapel. "Now your problem has priests."
"It had clerks," Jack said. "Priests are just clerks with candles."
"Say that in Novigrad and you'll have a fascinating afternoon."
"I dislike afternoons."
The singing grew louder.
Yennefer smiled without warmth. "Then let us ruin theirs."

They did not attack. That was the first victory. Jack wanted to move toward the sound with sword in hand because the words had put their fingers on his name without permission. Ciri wanted to tear the song out by the roots. Geralt wanted to put himself between both of them and everything, which was an old reflex and not always a wise one. Roche wanted prisoners. Ves wanted sightlines. Triss wanted the ledger that made the song move.
Triss won because she had the correct objective.

They left the cultists singing, stole the ledger from the cart's false bottom, and burned the manacles in a pit behind the granary. The fire burned blue at first, then red. Jack watched until the padding collapsed and the legal phrases blackened.
A rider came while the fire still had color.

He came from the east road at a trot too calm for weather and a posture too humble for innocence. His horse was poor, but the bridle was new. His cloak was pilgrim-brown. His boots were soldier-black under the mud. Ves raised her crossbow before anyone told her to. Roche stepped to the left of the road, where a man could speak without blocking a shot. Geralt's hand drifted near his sword.
The rider stopped. "Message for the chapel keeper."
"Dead," Roche said.
"Replacement, then."
"Drunk."

The rider looked at the burning manacles and made the error of understanding too quickly. Jack saw it. So did Ves. The man's hand moved toward his sleeve, not a weapon draw, a paper draw. Sometimes paper was worse.
Yennefer lifted one finger. The rider's sleeve froze to his wrist.
"Uncomfortable?" she asked.
The man stared at her. "Illegal restraint of a courier under vassal safe passage."
"How educational."

Triss took the paper from his sleeve. She read the outside first, then the angle of the fold, then the wax. "Black Ink holding notice. It names the granary as a temporary public preservation site. It authorizes non-injurious restraint of a subject fitting Jack's description. It is dated tomorrow."
Roche smiled without pleasure. "They were going to arrive after the chains were already here and call it emergency discovery."
Jack studied the courier. "You ride ahead of tomorrow."
The man said nothing.
"Smart," Ves said. "Or paid too well to look smart."

They did not kill him. Roche took his horse, his permit, and his boots because black soldier boots under pilgrim mud told stories better than confessions. Then they sent him west barefoot with a note pinned to his cloak stating that public preservation sites should preserve their own couriers.
Ciri watched him limp away. "That was petty."
"Temerian justice," Roche said. "Limited resources."
Ciri stood beside him. "Promises require consequence."
"You said that."
"I wanted to hear if it was foolish."
He studied the fire. "It was ugly."
"That was not my question."
"No."
"No, not foolish?"
"No, not safe."
She huffed once. It was almost a laugh and much too close to grief to be one. "You are very difficult when being careful."
"Professional courtesy."

Behind them, Geralt told Roche that burning the manacles without seizing the cultists would let the warning spread. Roche said yes. Geralt asked if that was intended. Roche said yes again. Men who wanted chains to look holy should learn that someone could burn them before witnesses. It would make the next singer afraid of his own refrain.
The ledger went to Dandelion.
The route went to Cazren.
The quiet country had spoken, and like all defeated countries, it had chosen evidence before courage and courage after evidence made cowardice too expensive.
Roche kept Geralt back when the others rode.

It was not dramatic. He did it by standing in the way of the narrow gate and pretending to examine a loose hinge. Geralt could have moved him. Roche knew that. Geralt knew Roche knew. Friendship between men with blood on their boots often worked by making the obvious too tedious to mention.
"The girl," Roche said.
Geralt looked toward the road where Ciri's hood moved beside Jack's dark horse. "Which one?"

"Don't be clever. It doesn't suit either of us." Roche pushed the hinge once. It squealed. "Ciri. If imperial men begin to call her judgment compromised, they will not need to control her by force. They will make every private feeling she has into an argument against her public mind."
"I know."
"No. You remember it from the old days. That is not the same as knowing how it works with a throne waiting. A hunted girl can run. An empress-designate running becomes a crisis with trumpets."

Geralt watched Ciri stop to adjust her stirrup. Jack did not help until she lifted one brow at him. Then he handed her the strap, and even that small courtesy seemed to create a line the world would one day try to interpret.
"She won't leave him," Geralt said.
"Then she needs more than love around her. Love is brave and stupid and leaks like a bad roof. She needs procedure she can weaponize before theirs closes around her."
"You giving imperial advice now?"

Roche's face hardened. "I am giving advice to the man who raised the young woman whose empire is currently walking over my country with polished boots. I dislike the sentence, but not the girl. If she is going to rule, let her learn which papers become manacles before some smiling adviser teaches her to call them safeguards."
Geralt nodded once. It was not thanks. Thanks would have embarrassed them both and improved neither.
"And Jack?" Geralt asked.
"He needs to learn that being hard to catch is not the same as being free." Roche stepped aside at last. "You may quote me badly."
"I usually do."
"So I have heard."
Brother Cazren had learned, while still a priest of the Eternal Fire's outer kitchens, that hungry people listened better when the sermon smelled of bread.

The trick was not kindness. Kindness gave food away and asked the soul to follow if it wished. Cazren had always considered that sloppy. He preferred lentils under salt, black rye, watered beer, and a room warm in a way that made poverty feel briefly chosen. Men who came for food stayed for heat. Women who came for heat stayed because their sons had bad dreams. Boys who came to mock remained because mockery was easier before a preacher named their fear in a voice that did not tremble.

He had been removed from three proper pulpits and two improper ones. The first removal came after he suggested that fire did not purify enough if the world kept producing the same rot. The second after he called Radovid's death proof that kings burned poorly unless opened first. The third after a canon with soft hands told him apocalypse fatigue was not doctrine. Cazren had thanked him, stolen his candle money, and discovered basements.

The basement beneath Saint Mered's abandoned almshouse was excellent. Low ceiling, good acoustics, two exits, one dry wall for scripture, and a store-room where donated flour could be weighed beside names. A saint with ledgers was better than a saint with miracles. Miracles could not be audited.
By dusk, thirty-three people had gathered there.

War widows. Dock men. Former witch hunters with their insignia removed and their habits intact. Two girls from a laundry who had both dreamed of red stone and woken with ash on their tongues. A cooper whose son had frozen during the White Frost and who hated every survivor of prophecy with a fairness no theologian could improve. Three men who wanted violence and had learned to kneel first because kneeling made violence look like service.
Cazren fed them lentils. Then he let them smell the red candles.

Not ordinary tallow. Ordinary tallow comforted. These had been mixed with powdered rust, dragon-bone fraud, ash from burned court records, and one black scale bought from a man who had promised draconid origin with such confidence that the lie deserved artistic respect. The candles smoked dark at the wick and red along the gutter. They made the low room look wounded.
On the table lay the ledger.

Names. Debts. Dreams. Witnesses. Phrases that repeated across unrelated mouths: red door, walking chamber, crown under stone, hinge in blood, wolf with a throat of iron, mother of ash, father with a broken sword. Cazren had not invented all of them. Invention was for poets. Revelation was for men clever at organizing what frightened people already brought.
"You have seen the sign," he said.
The room leaned toward him.
Good. Bodies had more honest theology than mouths.

"Not in temples. The gods do not always choose temples. Temples have schedules, roof fees, clerks, and broom cupboards full of arguments about candle wax. Judgment has better taste." A small ripple of laughter moved through the hungry. Cazren smiled gently because hunger liked being allowed to laugh before being told it was holy. "You have seen it in dreams, in cracked walls, in the way your children wake speaking names they never learned, in beasts hollowed from within, in the red wolf walking roads men with titles pretend are safe."
A woman near the back began to weep. Excellent. Not because tears proved truth. Because tears opened the throat and the throat loved company.

"The old fire failed," Cazren continued. "The White Frost came, and did kings stop it? Did priests? Did your tax receipts? Did the men who said wait, obey, endure? No. A girl of Elder Blood closed one door and left another breathing."
A former witch hunter shifted uneasily. Cazren saw. He corrected.
"Do not curse the girl. The girl did what a door does when used by hands stronger than mercy. She opened. She closed. She survived. Survival is not innocence. It is unfinished instruction."
The room accepted this because it let them honor and resent without choosing. Theology, done properly, did not remove contradiction. It yoked it.
He lifted the blackened crown from the table. Iron, cheap, ugly, made from a barrel hoop and seven nails. Every symbol began as bad craft until enough people bled around it.

"The Obsidian Crown teaches hierarchy. Not noble above peasant. Not man above elf. Not empire above broken kingdom. Those are children's ladders. The true order is hunger above denial, strength above lies, the ancient above the temporary. What cannot endure must kneel to what can."
The candles bent inward.
Cazren's sermon began before the room knew it had become one.

He did not climb onto a box. He did not raise his hands. Those were mistakes made by men who wanted to be seen wanting power. Cazren moved among bowls with a ladle, giving each person a little less than hunger desired and a little more than suspicion expected. A widow received lentils first. A former guard received watered beer. A child received black bread with the burnt edge cut off. Every gift was remembered publicly. Every need became a string.

"The world ended once," he said to a man missing two fingers, as if discussing weather. "You felt it. Snow in the wrong season. Cattle screaming at empty air. Kings dying badly. Mages hiding. Fires without warmth. Then they told you it was saved."
The man swallowed soup. Around him, others leaned closer without knowing they had done it.
"Was it?" Cazren asked.
No one answered. He smiled as if they had.

"A saved world should not leave widows counting rye in basements. A saved world should not let rulers trade borders like blankets stripped from fevered children. A saved world should not ask the poor to be grateful that apocalypse was postponed into taxes."

That won him the first murmur. He let it grow and did not feed it too quickly. Good preachers, Dandelion knew, understood tempo. Bad preachers shouted truth until it became noise. Cazren was worse than good. He listened to the room until the room believed it was speaking through him.
Priscilla's hand found Dandelion's sleeve in the dark above the stair.
"He is setting the refrain," she breathed.

Dandelion had heard battle songs and lullabies, coronation hymns and gutter rhymes, songs made for taverns and songs made to make men march toward arrows. This was stranger. Cazren was borrowing from harvest cadence, the old call and answer that let exhausted bodies move together without thinking. Thresh. Turn. Lift. Breathe. The rhythm was older than theology and more dangerous because the body trusted it before the mind asked who held the flail.
Below, Cazren set down the ladle.
"A door is not guilty for standing in a wall," he said.
A woman near the candles whispered, "A door opens."
"Only when taught," Cazren replied.
The room breathed with him.

"A hinge is not wicked for bearing weight. A chamber is not cruel for holding what would devour the house. But if a chamber walks, if a door takes flesh, if a hinge bleeds, then judgment has taken mercy by the throat and given us a shape we can follow."
"The red door," said someone.
"The red door walks," Cazren answered.
Not loud. Worse, certain.

Priscilla went pale enough that candlelight found her through the stair crack. She had once been hurt by men who thought a woman in a song had ceased being a person. Dandelion saw the memory move through her and felt his own vanity become useless in his hands.
"We should leave," he whispered.
"We should steal the ledger," she whispered back.
"I adore you. Your timing is monstrous."
"That is why you adore me."

The ledger sat on the left table, open beside sacks of charitable flour. Names were written in columns, not merely of those fed, but of dreams reported. Ash tongue. Red stone. Black crown. Wolf with door in ribs. Girl of green fire. Sea beast hollow. The handwriting was careful. Hunger had become data. Cazren had done what Black Ink did, but with a hymn instead of a seal.

Dandelion felt a professional anger then, clean and bright. Songs were allowed to lie. They were allowed to exaggerate, beautify, mock, seduce, preserve, flatter, and occasionally improve history against its will. But this was not song. This was a cage with rhythm.
Cazren lifted the blackened crown from the table.

It was not a real crown. Tin, perhaps iron under soot, hammered by someone with more devotion than skill. The points were uneven. Red candle wax had gathered in the dents like clotted light. Men in the room regarded it with reverence because poverty made symbols cheaper to make and harder to refuse.

"They will call him risk," Cazren said. "The offices will call him asset. Sorceresses will call him anomaly. Kings will call him jurisdiction. But we will call him by the name the dark taught our dreams."
The room answered before he finished.
"Red door."
"Blood hinge."
"Chamber that walks."

Dandelion wrote each phrase. His hand did not shake because he had spent decades training it to steal words under conditions less righteous and more drunk. Priscilla marked the exits, the candle near the ledger, the two men watching the stairs, and the woman at the back who did not chant. Dandelion noticed the woman last. Priscilla noticed first. The woman held a bowl in both hands and stared at Cazren with the despairing concentration of someone trying to believe because disbelief had not fed her child either.
"That one," Priscilla whispered. "She is not convinced. She is tired."
"Useful?"
"Human," Priscilla said. "Try not to confuse the two."
He deserved that. Unfortunately, he had no time to admire it.
A floorboard above them creaked because Zoltan, who had promised not to approach the almshouse, had approached the almshouse with the delicacy of a moral avalanche. Dandelion closed his eyes.
"Dwarven subtlety," he said.
"Dandelion," Priscilla whispered.
Below, Cazren paused.

That was how Dandelion knew the man had teeth. Not because he heard the creak. Many people heard the creak. Cazren heard the timing. The room's breath had been his instrument, and something had gone off beat.

Dandelion descended before the watchers could come up and discover the difference between espionage and farce. He chose posture first, face second, voice last. A minor inspector, bored by holiness and annoyed by damp stairs. Men feared confident irritation because it implied a department.
"Brother," he said from the third step. "Your soup appears to have developed a theology. There are forms for that."
The room turned.

Priscilla followed two steps behind him, slate hidden beneath her shawl, eyes lowered into harmlessness and open to miss nothing. Cazren took them in, and Dandelion saw recognition arrive, not of their names yet, but of their function. Public words had come to inspect private ones.
"Inspector," Cazren said.
"Temporarily," Dandelion answered. "I find permanence vulgar."
The ledger remained open. The black crown remained within reach. The crowd remained hungry. That was the problem with entering stories. One could never choose only the interesting parts.
By the time recognition found Dandelion's hat, the woman at the back had moved her bowl one inch from the candle.
Priscilla saw. Dandelion saw Priscilla see.
A plan, then. A terrible one, but plans often began as choreography performed by people pretending not to dance.
That had not been arranged.
Cazren felt a tremor move through the room and knew better than to claim credit too soon.
"The red door walks," he whispered.
They whispered back. "The red door walks."
"The blood hinge turns," Cazren said.
They whispered back. "The blood hinge turns."
"The chamber will open," he said.
They answered, "The chamber will open."
Above them, a floorboard creaked.
Cazren stopped. The room stopped with him. Silence, properly taught, could be more obedient than song.
A boy from the door leaned down and whispered, "Bard."
Cazren smiled.
That was also good. Poets were dangerous when they listened and vain when they thought themselves hidden. Both qualities could be used.
They did not leave the almshouse cleanly because clean exits belonged to stories sung after the taxes were paid.

Priscilla reached the ledger first, not by speed but by understanding shame. The woman at the back knocked the candle crooked with her bowl and cried out as if burned. Half the room turned toward the small human disaster of soup spilled on a skirt. The other half looked toward Cazren because crowds trained by hunger always checked whether permission was required before helping. In that divided breath, Priscilla slid the ledger under her shawl and replaced it with a charity register whose pages contained actual flour weights and therefore less theology.
Dandelion saw the exchange and nearly ruined it by admiration.

Cazren saw too much. His eyes moved from the candle to Priscilla's hands, then to the woman with the bowl. He did not shout. Shouting would have confessed loss. Instead he smiled with such kindness that the woman began to cry harder.
"Even accidents serve," he said.
That frightened Dandelion more than a knife.

A fanatic who could turn failure into proof before the room breathed again was not merely dangerous. He was durable. Black Ink made cages from paper. Cazren made them from interpretation. Every stumble, every spilled bowl, every hungry gasp could be drafted into his sermon if no one stole the rhythm first.
So Dandelion did what had ruined and saved him in equal measure across half the Continent.
He performed.

"Excellent," he announced, clapping once with bureaucratic despair. "Improper storage, irregular congregation, disputed soup, unauthorized crown, and now sacramental lentils on municipal flooring. I shall need three signatures and a mop. Possibly two mops. Holiness, I find, spreads."

The first laugh came from the dock man who had looked at his bowl earlier. The second came from the girl at the laundry. A third tried to rise and died when Cazren turned his head, but it had existed. That mattered. Reverence, like glass, remembered the first crack.
Priscilla passed behind Dandelion and touched his wrist once. Ledger secured. Left exit. Two men moving.
They ran then.

Not heroically. Through flour dust, stacked bowls, wet steps, and a side door that had been built for sacks rather than poets. Zoltan caught the first man who followed and introduced him to the wall with dwarven theology. Priscilla kept the ledger dry under her coat. Dandelion lost the rest of his feather and, for once, did not mourn it aloud.
Behind them, Cazren's voice rose again, warm and steady.
"The old world steals names because it fears the door. Let it steal. The door still walks."
Dandelion stopped in the rain only until the price became clear.
"He will use this," he said.
Priscilla looked back at the almshouse. "Then we use the ledger faster."
Dandelion had disguised himself as a flour inspector because dignity, having suffered butcher's aprons, had apparently decided to die thoroughly.

The badge was tin. The hat was gray. The ledger under his arm had three real pages and forty-seven pages of old theatrical accounts turned upside down. He had a pen behind one ear and a face arranged around bureaucratic boredom, which Priscilla said was his least convincing performance because it required suppressing every instinct that had kept him fed since adolescence.
Priscilla came as his clerk.

This was unfair. Priscilla looked like a clerk in the way a knife looked like tableware when laid beside bread. Plain dress, shawl, hair covered, eyes lowered when watched and awake when not. She carried a slate and a small knife. The knife was for string, she said. Dandelion believed this as much as he believed Zoltan when he claimed to enjoy moderate language.

They entered Saint Mered's almshouse through the upper kitchen. It smelled of stale flour, boiled lentils, candle smoke, damp stone, and people whose gratitude had made them easy to manipulate. The last smell was the worst. Dandelion knew crowds. He loved them, feared them, seduced them, robbed them gently, and occasionally let them save him from himself. This crowd had the wrong silence above it. Not boredom. Not prayer. Preparation.
"You hear it?" Priscilla asked.
"Rhythm," he said. "Four beats, then three. Easier to remember when frightened. Very old trick."
"Yours?"
"Madam, I am wounded. My tricks scan better."
She gave him a look.
"Some of them," he admitted.

They found the stair behind sacks of barley marked for the chapel granary Roche had spoiled. Dandelion could have sworn. He did not. Priscilla placed one hand on his sleeve. A signal, not comfort. He breathed and listened.
Cazren's voice rose from below, warm and rough and deliberate. The red door walks. The blood hinge turns. The chamber will open.
Dandelion wrote the lines down. His hand did not shake. That was professional pride, not courage.
"He stole the shape from work songs," Priscilla whispered. "Threshing cadence. Older women would know it without knowing why."
"Can it spread?"
"It already has."

Dandelion turned to her. Priscilla's face was pale in the dim kitchen light. Not fear of discovery. Recognition. Songs had nearly killed her once in ways men preferred not to understand because it made taverns less harmless. She knew what a crowd could become when its breath aligned.
"We need the ledger," she said.
"Naturally. I was hoping to steal theology before supper."
"You steal supper more often. Treat this as growth."
Below, the crowd repeated the line again. Blood hinge. Chamber. Crown.

Dandelion descended three steps, then four. Priscilla followed. The basement opened under them. Cazren stood at the table with the black crown in his hands, red candlelight making his face look carved from hunger and conviction. Dandelion had seen that face on actors who mistook applause for revelation, on rebels before speeches, on priests who enjoyed pyres too much, and on patrons after the third bottle when they decided funding art made them immortal.
A face built for damage.
Cazren saw him at once.
Of course he did. True fanatics were not fools. Fools were easier and rarely survived into ledgers.
"Inspector," Cazren said.

Dandelion bowed with the irritation of a minor official whose authority had been recognized incorrectly. "Brother. I am here regarding irregular flour movement under charitable exemption, devotional grain allotment, soup thickness, and possible false holiness applied to lentils."
One dock man frowned. Another studied his bowl.
Cazren smiled. "We keep careful accounts."
"So did several tyrants. It rarely improved their soup."
Priscilla made a tiny mark on the slate. Good. Ledger sighted. Left table. Two men within reach. One candle near paper. One exit behind hanging cloth.
Cazren set the black crown down beside the ledger. "You are not a flour man."
"Few of us are what our hats promise."
"You are a singer."
"Under favorable conditions. These are not."
A murmur moved through the room. Dandelion felt it strike his skin. Recognition could save or kill depending on who gave it first.

Cazren turned to the crowd. "See how quickly the old world sends ornament to mock hunger. A feather man. A court singer. A friend of white wolves and throne girls. He comes to weigh our bread and steal our words."
That was effective. Dandelion hated effective work done by bad men. It made professional disgust difficult to separate from moral urgency.
"I steal only when the words are mistreated," he said. "These are being beaten in a cellar. I may have to intervene."
A few people laughed. Too little.
Cazren's eyes sharpened. "Tell me then, poet. What does your red wolf call himself when no one sings?"
Dandelion let the silence hold. Jack's name had weight now. Names could lead chains.
"Tired, probably," he said. "Most men being hunted by clerks and candles become tired."

Priscilla had moved while he spoke. Three steps left. Downcast eyes. Slate held close. One hand near the ledger. The former witch hunter near the table watched Cazren, not her. Men with old habits watched the loudest man in the room and forgot women who moved as if permission had already been granted.
"He is not a man," Cazren said.
There it was. The sentence every enemy eventually found, the door through which all ownership entered wearing different shoes.
Dandelion's performance fell from him.
"Yes," he said, very clearly, "he is. That is what has upset everyone."
The room shifted.
Priscilla took the ledger.

The former witch hunter saw too late. His hand moved. Priscilla's small knife moved first, not to flesh, but to the candle. It toppled into a bowl of lentils and died in a wet hiss. Darkness broke the room's rhythm. Dandelion shouted something about flour seizure, doctrinal contamination, and rats in the tithe sack. It was nonsense. Good nonsense. Crowds needed shape, and nonsense with official posture could beat panic by three seconds.
They used the three seconds.

Up the stairs. Through the kitchen. Out under laundry lines. A boy tried to bar the door and changed his mind when Priscilla gave him one calm glance. Dandelion did not ask what expression she used. Some arts were private.
They ran through rain, flour dust, and the beginning of shouting.
In the alley, Zoltan stood with two horses and the expression of a dwarf who had expected trouble and been offended by its punctuality.
"Got it?"
Priscilla held up the ledger.
"Good. Bard?"
"Insulted, threatened, theologically underestimated. Otherwise radiant."
"Mount. Radiance later."
Behind them, Saint Mered's began to sing again. Louder now. Not because Cazren had recovered control, but because disruption had made belief more vivid. The words followed them over the wet stones.
The red door walks. The blood hinge turns.
Priscilla looked back once.
"We did not stop it," she said.
Dandelion heard the crowd and felt the old horror of public words leaving their maker. "No. But we learned the tune."
"Can you break it?"

He thought of Jack, of Ciri's face when public names got too close, of Geralt reading guilt into leather straps, of Yennefer's hatred for vessel, of Triss copying the word chamber until ink became a wound.
"No," he said. "But I can make people distrust anyone who sings it too cleanly."
"That may serve."
"It won't be."
Priscilla's hand touched his sleeve, brief and firm. "Then begin before the door closes."

They read the stolen ledger in Zoltan's back room above a warehouse where the ceiling leaked in four places and one of the leaks had been assigned a cup with a label. Dandelion objected to the label on artistic grounds because it read leak three and thus implied a bureaucracy of water. Zoltan said water had better administrative discipline than most aldermen and should be encouraged.
Priscilla ignored both and turned pages.

The ledger was worse than a sermon. Sermons admitted hunger. Ledgers organized it. Each name had a debt, a grief, a dream phrase, and a usefulness mark. Widow with dead son, hears crown in sleep, useful for weeping. Former guard, knows south gate, useful for transport. Laundress, two daughters, dream of red horse, useful for women's circle. Beggar child, repeats hinge rhyme, useful if fed.
Dandelion stopped performing. "He is scoring sorrow."

"Yes," Priscilla said. "And he understands cadence. Look here. The people with similar grief receive different phrases, but phrases that complete each other when sung together. He is making a crowd that feels as if it discovered the song by itself."
Zoltan leaned over the page and scowled. "Can you break that?"
"Not by mocking it," Priscilla said. "Mocking hunger makes the hungry defend the man who fed them."
Dandelion sank onto a crate. It creaked under velvet and despair. "Then what?"
"Witnesses. Counter-memory. Not a better song saying he is wrong. A song that makes people remember he wrote their grief into columns."
"A ledger song," Zoltan said.
Dandelion closed his eyes. "That phrase has injured me."
"Good," Priscilla said. "Pain may keep you honest."
He faced her then, the woman who had paid more than most for public words becoming violence. She did not look fragile. That was not the same as unhurt.
"We write it together," he said.
"No," she answered. "We listen first. Then we write what their own mouths can bear to sing without feeling mocked."
Dandelion touched the ledger with one finger. He had loved audiences all his life. He had rarely respected them and feared failing them. That, he discovered, had been vanity in a better hat.
"Begin," Priscilla said.
So he did, before the door closed.
Cazren did not punish the room after the bard fled.

Punishment wasted heat. Better to convert embarrassment. He lifted the black crown, stood among the spilled lentils, and let the people see that he was not angry. Anger would have made him ordinary. Mercy, performed correctly, made him necessary.
"He feared the ledger," Cazren said.
The crowd listened, hungry for the humiliation to become meaning.

"He feared what your hands would write. Your dreams. Your dead. Your children waking with ash on their tongues. Why would a court singer fear poor people's pages unless poor people had found the road kings denied?"
A woman whispered, "The red door."
"Yes." Cazren lowered his voice. "The red door walks. But doors are made to open. A door that refuses must be persuaded. A hinge that resists must be oiled with what first made it turn."
He touched the black crown to the table.

In his private pocket lay the page he had not left in the ledger. He was not foolish; scripture did not live in one book. The page had come from a dream shared by three women, one boy, and a dying draconid whose throat had smoked when it opened.
It showed a road east.
It showed a canyon of stars.
It showed a man with red eyes kneeling in black sand while a crown beneath the world breathed through him.
Cazren folded the page carefully.

After the room emptied, he counted the bowls. Thirty-three had eaten. Thirty-one had stayed through the interruption. Twenty-seven had repeated the final line. Five had wept. One had watched without moving his lips, which meant spy, skeptic, or future leader. Cazren marked him as useful and dangerous, a blessed combination if handled before pride grew roots.

He took the black crown from the table and set it over the ledger's empty space. The stolen book did not trouble him as much as it would trouble a man who confused records with truth. The bard had stolen accounts. Cazren still had hunger. Hunger wrote itself again if fed in the right room.
From the alley came a child's voice singing the refrain badly. Wrong pitch. Wrong pause. Strong memory.
Cazren smiled.
The first miracle of any faith was not fire from heaven. It was repetition in someone else's mouth.
Cazren folded the page carefully.
Black Ink wanted custody. Empires wanted caution. Sorceresses wanted analysis. Lovers wanted the man. Fathers wanted the boy.
Cazren wanted the door to remember its purpose.
He was wrong about almost everything except the direction.
That made him difficult to kill cleanly.

chapters.chapter_title: REGIS AND THE QUESTION OF APPETITE
paragraphs: Regis arrived with an umbrella, which made the situation worse.

It was not a large umbrella, nor a decorative one. It was plain, black, excellently maintained, and held at a sensible angle against the rain falling over Marna's Bend. The road there had become more mud than road, the ferry sat chained to the wrong bank, and a dead draconid lay under a tarp near the willow line because everyone present had agreed not to let Dandelion see it before breakfast. Regis stepped around a puddle, inclined his head to Geralt, and looked at the tarp with the tired courtesy of a physician invited to dinner and shown a corpse under the table.
"Geralt," he said.
"Regis."
"You said the matter was urgent. I assumed a certain range of unpleasantness."
"And?"
"You have exceeded expectations. This is rarely a compliment."
Geralt almost smiled. Almost was becoming a family dialect.

Jack stood beside Buck under a willow that dripped steadily down the back of his collar. His left hand was bandaged again because the old cut had opened during the granary fire, not much, only a reminder that his body had opinions about restraint. Ciri watched from the ferry post, cloak hood low, expression caught between impatience and the practiced stillness of a woman who had spent too much time being observed. Yennefer stood near the tarp. Triss held the living chamber copy in oilcloth. Asha stood where the road bent east, as if she had already begun leaving.
Regis saved Jack for last.
That was deliberate. Jack respected it despite himself. Monsters, truly old ones, knew the discourtesy of immediate hunger.
"Mr. Morningstar," Regis said.
"Regis."
"Technically, Emiel Regis Rohellec Terzieff-Godefroy, but in present weather I would accept several abbreviations and one dry room."
"No dry room," Geralt said.
"Then we must make do with accuracy."
Regis did not examine the living chamber page first.
He examined the cup beside it.

This irritated nearly everyone except Geralt, who knew old friends sometimes approached horror through the nearest harmless object because the harmless object was less likely to bite and more likely to reveal who in the room had patience.
"Bad tea," Regis said.
"We know," Geralt replied.
"No. You suspect. I have confirmed. There is willow bark, stale mint, and an unfortunate optimism about dried apple."
Zoltan grunted from the window. "It was boiled under pressure."
"So are confessions. That does not improve them."
Ciri laughed once before catching herself. The sound loosened the room by a thread. Regis heard it, acknowledged nothing, and set the cup aside as if concluding the first diagnostic.
Only then did he look at Jack.

He did not stare at the crimson eyes. People with manners did not, and monsters with age had better manners than many kings. He looked at Jack's left hand, at the bandage wrapped too neatly to have been tied by someone unconcerned, at the line of tension along the throat where the barbed star rested hidden, at the way Ciri had placed herself in the room with visibility to both Jack and the door. His attention reached Geralt last.
"You have become parental in several directions," Regis said. "This seems logistically unwise."
Geralt exhaled through his nose. "Missed you too."
"I would have brought a better tea had I known affection would be so badly expressed."

Yennefer stood near the table, fingers resting lightly beside the diagram. She had not sat since Regis entered. That was not discourtesy. That was Yennefer refusing to let the room decide whether civility had made her less dangerous. Regis bowed with precision that respected her without flattering her.
"Madam Vengerberg."
"Regis."
"Your reputation for disapproval remains restorative."
"Your reputation for politeness remains evasive."
"Then we are both consistent, a rare mercy."
Triss placed the packet before him. "We need an answer we will hate."

Regis's expression changed. The gentle surface remained, but the air beneath it cooled. "Then you should be careful not to reward yourselves for hating it. Some people mistake reluctance for morality."
Jack liked him less immediately, which was proof of either wisdom or bad timing.

Regis took up the living chamber page. He read all of it, including the lines others had skimmed because the words had begun repeating themselves inside the skull. Then he read it again. No one interrupted. Even Dandelion, for once, let silence keep its profession.
"This is not a prison design," Regis said at last.
