Asha's eyes narrowed. "It says chamber."

"Humans also call many marriages arrangements. We should not therefore assume consent has improved. This is a proposed metabolism. A living chamber is not merely a box with pulse. It must receive pressure, distinguish hunger from signal, absorb injury without identifying with the injurer, and continue choosing boundaries while part of it is being taught that boundaries are lies."
The room did not move.
Jack read the line again. "You make it sound alive."
"It would have to be. That is the cruelty. Dead stone can hold without understanding. A living chamber must understand what it holds, but not so deeply that refusal becomes self-destruction."
Geralt rubbed one hand over his mouth. "Could it work?"
Compassion crossed Regis's face, which made the answer worse before he gave it. "Many impossible things work briefly. That is why they kill."
Yennefer's voice cut through. "Briefly is not an answer."
"No," Regis said. "It is a warning."

He moved to the bowl Triss had prepared. Inside lay a clot from one of the scale-sick draconids, sealed under glass and spell-cold. The matter did not rot. It trembled when Jack entered the room and stilled when he left. Regis lifted the glass cover a finger's width. The smell that escaped was not decay. It was hunger translated poorly into flesh: hot copper, wet ash, old reptile musk, and a sweetness that made the mouth remember blood.
Regis closed his eyes.
Not in revulsion. In recognition.
Geralt saw. "Regis."
"I am here."
"That wasn't my question."
"No. It was your hand on the hilt before a question found language. I appreciate the efficiency."
Jack watched him more closely. "You feel it."
"Yes."
"Because you are a vampire."

"Because I have been hungry," Regis corrected. "The species is a detail, significant and often socially inconvenient, but still a detail. Hunger has grammar. This has grammar. It is not hunger exactly. It is dominion wearing hunger because hunger is a language bodies obey quickly."
Asha murmured something in Faithel. Jack knew none of the words, but the cadence made the barbed star cool against his chest.
Regis opened his eyes. "What did she say?"
"That a door is innocent until someone teaches it appetite," Asha said.
"A sensible people, your Faithel. Very unpleasant, I imagine, when correct."
"Often."
Ciri came to the table. "And Jack?"
No title. No file word. No asset, bearer, chamber, hinge. Just the name, placed between them like a drawn line.
Regis's attention moved from her to Jack. "At present, he is not appetite. He is boundary under stress. That distinction matters."
"But later?" Jack asked.
Regis did not soften the answer. "Later, if enough pressure teaches the boundary to survive by wanting what it holds, the distinction may begin to suffer."
Geralt's face went stone-still.
"No," Ciri said.

Regis inclined his head. "I would be grateful if your refusal could alter metaphysics. Unfortunately, it can only alter what people do before metaphysics narrows the room. Which is not nothing. It may be everything, if used early."
Yennefer took the page from him. "Then the living chamber is unacceptable."
"Morally, yes. Strategically, perhaps. Eventually, if every other door fails, one should beware words like unacceptable. They tend to become monuments after the dead have no use for principles."
Triss closed her eyes once. "I hate this answer."
"Then keep it honest," Regis said. "Do not let hatred of the answer become hatred of the person who may one day be forced to stand near it."
Jack pushed away from the wall. "No one is forcing me."
"Not yet," Regis said.
Those two words struck harder than accusation. Jack felt Ciri turn toward him. He did not look at her because if he did, the room might discover too much.

Regis continued, quieter. "You should also understand the other danger. A person can be forced by chains, spells, threats, or law. He can also be forced by love if he mistakes the desire to spare others pain for a command they gave him. That kind of coercion leaves no jailer to blame. It is very efficient."

Geralt turned to Jack then. Fully. The look said Ciri, and Yennefer, and Triss, and Asha, and perhaps even himself. It said every person in the room was becoming a possible lever, whether they deserved it or not.
Jack disliked being seen that accurately.
"You speak gently," he said.
Regis folded his hands. "A lifetime of evidence suggests harsh truths do not improve when shouted."
"Sometimes they move faster."
"So do fires."
Zoltan muttered, "He's worse than a priest. At least priests pass a plate."
"If it comforts you," Regis said, "I can request a donation for the improvement of tea."
That earned the room its second laugh. Brief. Necessary.
Then Regis took up Jacob's broken hilt from the table. Jack's hand moved before he stopped it. Regis noticed and did not touch the hilt further. He studied it where it lay.
"Your father died buying minutes," he said.
Jack's throat tightened. "Yes."

"Minutes are underestimated by people who have not needed them. A minute can be shelter, birth, escape, a letter hidden, a door barred, a child lifted over a wall. If one day you are asked for more than minutes, remember that the dead did not buy them so the living could spend themselves cheaply."
Silence followed with more weight than any argument.

Ciri studied the hilt. Yennefer watched Ciri. Geralt studied his hands. Triss looked at Jack and saw the place where grief had become calculation, and she hated the calculation because she had already learned to read its direction.
Regis covered the draconid clot again. "There. I have not helped."
"You have," Geralt said.
"Then I apologize."
Geralt followed Regis outside because old friendships sometimes required rain to keep witnesses honest.

The yard behind the safe house had once held chickens. Now it held two broken crates, one offended rooster who had survived enough wars to distrust white-haired men, and a trough full of rainwater reflecting a sky without useful stars. Regis stood beneath his umbrella. Geralt stood beside him without cover and pretended that choice meant something tactical.
"You're doing it," Regis said.
"Standing in rain?"
"Preparing yourself to accept the worst answer because you think preparation will make you less responsible for it."
Geralt stared at the trough. "You became more annoying after dying."
"One must improve where one can."

Inside the house, Jack's voice carried once, low and controlled, then Ciri's sharper answer. They were not arguing exactly. They were testing which words could be used without cutting. Geralt knew the sound. He had heard it years ago from Ciri when she was learning that refusal was sometimes the only room she owned.
"If it comes to him choosing," Geralt said, "I cannot stop him."
"No," Regis agreed. "You should not."
The agreement was worse than disagreement. Geralt studied him as if silence might find a flaw.

Regis's face remained calm, which did not mean gentle. "You can, however, make certain the choice has not been starved first. A person who sees only one honorable exit is not choosing freely. He is obeying a room that has hidden the doors."
Geralt's hand closed once, then opened. "You think I would let that happen?"

"I think you have loved children who were hunted by destiny and institutions, and that love has made you both brave and inventive. I also think guilt is a poor architect. It builds corridors toward sacrifice and labels them protection."
The rooster made a harsh, contemptuous sound from the crate.
Geralt studied it. "Even the poultry agrees."
"Poultry has long been underrepresented in moral philosophy."
That should have been funny. It was, faintly. It did not save him.
"Ciri won't forgive me if I let Jack spend himself," Geralt said.
"Ciri may not forgive you if you forbid him either. The tragedy of raising people with agency is that they eventually use it against your fear."

Geralt shut his eyes. Rain moved down his face and into old scars. He saw Ciri in Kaer Morhen's yard, furious because he had made her repeat a turn until her wrists shook. He saw Jack in a hidden trail, smaller, quiet, made invisible for reasons that had once seemed necessary. He saw both of them standing near some future fire where no father could stand between choice and consequence.
"I hate this," he said.
"Good," Regis replied. "Hatred may keep you from admiring your own endurance. That would be intolerable."
Geralt almost smiled. Almost.

When they went back inside, Jack found them waiting and knew, somehow, that rain had not improved anything. Geralt handed him a dry cloth anyway because cloth was what he had, and some forms of fatherhood were only a refusal to let a man drip on the floor while the world decided whether to make him a prison.
He reached for the bad tea and drank it. His face remained perfectly composed.
"You really are a monster," Zoltan said.
Regis set down the cup. "In this matter, my friend, the evidence is regrettably strong."

Regis knelt beside the tarp. He did not lift it at once. His fingers hovered above the canvas, not touching, sensing perhaps. Jack watched his face. It was civilized, gentle, grave, and arranged over something that did not need civilization to survive. That made him more honest than most men in the room. Monsters who admitted the effort of manners deserved more trust than humans who thought manners proved innocence.
"Before I look," Regis said, "tell me what you fear I will say. It saves time."
Geralt grunted. "No."
"Ah. Worse than usual, then."
Yennefer lifted the tarp.

The draconid had been a small wyvern, female, with a torn wing and eggs still inside her, all of them cold despite the body's heat. The throat was open from within. Not cut. Split. The chest had collapsed inward around a hollow that should have held lungs, heart, hunger, animal instinct, the ordinary architecture of living meat. Something had eaten the idea of appetite and left the rest undecided.
Regis looked for a long time.
Rain tapped the umbrella.
"No blood loss," he said.
"No," Yennefer answered.
"No feeding pattern. No external digestion. No predator claim. No territorial mark I recognize."
"The red line under the scales?"
Before he left, Regis asked for one more thing that was not a sample, not a diagram, and not a spell.
"The hand," he said.

Jack held it out only after looking at Ciri, which annoyed him because he had not meant to. Regis did not touch the palm. He held his own hand beneath it, near the heat and careful not to claim permission by accident.

"You are still resisting in the body before the mind arrives," Regis said. "That is good. It is also exhausting. Do not let anyone praise the exhaustion until it becomes your favorite proof of virtue."
"I dislike praise," Jack said.
"Many people do. They often accept being needed instead. It is worse because it sounds less vain."
Ciri looked away first. Geralt did not.

Regis examined the exposed underside. "Pressure. Directional. A call resisted too late. She came toward a source and tried to flee the source while moving toward it. That is a complex misery for an animal."
Jack's palm pulsed.
Regis studied the bandage. Not hungrily. No anger could stay simple after that. He looked as if he understood hunger well enough not to flatter it with drama.
"May I examine your hand?"
Jack glanced at Yennefer.
She raised one brow. "He asked properly. Do not look at me as if I trained the vampire."
"I remain sadly untrained," Regis said. "Ask several villages."
Jack held out his hand.

Regis took it with fingers cool and careful. The contact did not flare the mark. It quieted it. Not comfort. Recognition between restrained things. Regis leaned closer, inhaled once, and released Jack immediately.
"Interesting," he said.
"Treacherous word," Geralt said.
"Most true words are, if used before lunch."
Ciri stepped nearer. "What did you smell?"
"Restraint," Regis said. "And something that has learned restraint from imprisonment rather than ethics. There is a difference. Ethics says no. A cage says not yet."
Yennefer's face hardened. "Vharakthul."
"Perhaps. Or what remains of the pressure that names him. I would prefer not to be definitive when dealing with entities capable of making definitiveness look provincial."
"You always talk this much?" Jack asked.
Geralt answered before Regis could. "Yes."
"When worried, more," Regis added. "As I am fond of you all, I advise tolerating it."
The umbrella collected rain. Buck watched it with suspicion. Perhaps the horse had never seen a monster hold portable weather and remain polite.
Triss unfolded the living chamber page. "We found this."
Regis did not take it. He read where she held it.
His expression altered. The gentleness did not vanish. It drew back from the surface, revealing the old thing beneath, not savage, not cruel, simply older than human comfort.
"Ah," he said.
Geralt hated the sound. "Ah what?"
"Ah, as in the moment when the physician confirms the patient has been reading surgical notes without understanding which knife was sharpened for him."
Jack touched the edge of the file. "Living chamber."
"Yes."
"Can it work?"
Everyone turned toward him. Ciri's face changed first. Yennefer's next. Geralt's last because his horror had to cross more old roads before it found the surface.
"Do not answer that," Ciri said.
Regis turned to her. "I suspect he did not ask because he hopes for comfort."
"I know why he asked. That is the problem."

Jack's voice stayed even. "If the file considered it, someone understood the risk. If the Faithel named it, someone feared it so deeply they forbade it. If Vharakthul is learning the outer seal, then every forbidden thing becomes a possible route. I asked whether it can work."
Geralt stepped forward. "And I asked him not to answer."
"No," Jack said. "Ciri did. You only moved."
That struck. Geralt stopped. The road seemed to wait.

Regis folded his hands around the umbrella handle. "The answer is yes, in the most useless and dangerous sense of yes. A living containment can hold what stone fails to hold if the living structure shares enough sympathetic geometry with the prison and enough will to deny the prisoner. In your case, Mr. Morningstar, your body appears to possess both through no fault of your own."
Ciri's hand tightened on the ferry post.

"But," Regis said, and the word carried mercy like a bowl with cracks, "containment is not storage. One does not place hunger inside a body and expect the body to remain organized around previous habits. Hunger teaches architecture. It finds rooms. It makes corridors. It convinces the walls that opening is relief."
Yennefer studied the dead wyvern. "You are saying the chamber changes."

"I am saying both change. Prisoner and chamber. Appetite and restraint. If the thing held is old enough, hungry enough, ideological enough, then the person containing it may survive and still become arranged around keeping it. Eating because hunger must be answered. Sleeping because the prisoner sleeps. Loving because love becomes a lock and therefore a target."

The last sentence did what claws had not. It made Jack look at Ciri. Only once. Too quickly. Enough for Regis to see, Geralt to hate, Yennefer to store, and Triss to understand with a sadness that did not ask permission.
Regis lowered his voice. "Living prisons rarely die cleanly. They become duties that breathe."
Asha looked east. "Faithel law calls it last witness. The chamber must choose. The witnesses must refuse before they consent."
"A wise cruelty," Regis said. "Refusal proves everyone understands the horror. Consent proves they understand the alternative."
"Stop making it sound possible," Geralt said.
Regis regarded his old friend with genuine sorrow. "My dear Geralt, I am trying to make the price sound ruinous so no one mistakes possibility for solution."
Triss folded the page. Her hands were steady. "Then it remains unacceptable."
"For now," Regis said.
"No," Ciri replied. "Not for now. Unacceptable is not a postponement."
Jack turned to her. "Sometimes the world disagrees."
"Then the world can learn manners."

Zoltan would have liked that. Dandelion would have tried to write it down and been corrected by Priscilla. Geralt looked at Ciri as if she were a girl with ash in her hair at Kaer Morhen and a woman with a throne closing around her at once. Yennefer looked at Ciri as if pride were a wound she refused to dress.
Regis covered the wyvern again.
"What do we do with the body?" Triss asked.
"Burning may release more than smell," Yennefer said.
"Burying invites scavengers. Leaving it invites theology," Geralt said.
"Water?" Ciri asked.
Regis shook his head. "No. Water carries memory too well when old magic is involved."

Jack looked toward the ferry chain. The river ran swollen and brown beyond it, carrying leaves, mud, and the drowned patience of every upstream village. "Salt and lime. Deep pit. Iron above, not below."
Regis looked pleased in a subdued way. "A sensible ugliness."
"Witcher trade."
Yennefer kept Regis back for one question before the digging began.
"Can the hunger be separated from the seal-force?"

Regis held the question for a long time, not because he did not understand it, but because he understood all the hopes hiding in its edges. "Perhaps in theory. Theory is generous because it never has to hold the patient's hand while failing."
"That is not an answer."

"It is the only honest one I have. If the contamination entered at the moment of preservation, then removing it may be like removing smoke from a scar. One can cut around it. One can perfume it. One cannot restore the skin to the hour before burning."
Yennefer's face did not change. The lack of change hurt more than movement would have. "I dislike impossible medicine."
"So do I. It tends to make good people consider monstrous alternatives."
She looked at Jack, who was speaking quietly to Ciri beside Buck. "He will think of himself as alternative before he thinks of himself as good."
"Yes," Regis said. "That is why the rest of you must become extremely inconvenient."
Yennefer almost smiled. "At last, a treatment plan suited to my talents."

They buried the wyvern in the rain. It took two hours. The physician Ciri had dragged from Vizima would have fainted if present, so Ilyra had kept him elsewhere with a fabricated fever, a small mercy for everyone. Geralt and Jack dug. Roche's men brought lime. Ves kept watch. Yennefer warded the pit. Triss recorded the method in language no office could convert easily into custody doctrine. Ciri held a lantern when the light failed, and the flame leaned toward Jack no matter how she turned it.
When the body was covered, Regis placed one gloved hand on the iron bars laid across the soil.
"Rest," he said.
No one asked whether he spoke to the wyvern, the hunger, or himself.
Geralt found Regis by the river after midnight.

The rain had stopped. Mist sat low over the water. The ferry creaked against its chain on the far bank, useless until morning and perhaps after, because men who owned ferries learned early that inconvenience could be monetized. Regis stood under a willow with the umbrella closed at his side, looking less like a vampire than a tired scholar who had misplaced a kinder century.
"You should have lied," Geralt said.
"To whom?"
"Him. Ciri. Me. Pick one."
Regis smiled faintly. "I have lied to you before. You hated it with less accuracy then."
Geralt grunted.
For a while they listened to the river. Old friends did not always need to improve silence. Sometimes they had earned the right to stand inside it badly.
"He will consider it," Geralt said.
"Yes."
"Too calmly."
"Yes."
"And if the numbers turn ugly past a certain point, he will choose it."
"I suspect so."
Geralt turned on him. "You could sound less resigned."
Regis accepted the anger without moving. "Resignation is not agreement. It is recognition of another will. You taught me some of that, if you recall, while being deeply irritating and armed."
"This is different."
"Every beloved disaster is."

Geralt looked toward camp. Jack slept or pretended to. Ciri did not sleep. Yennefer did not either, but that had been true since the first century invented worry. Triss sat beside the sealed copies, warming her hands around tea gone cold. Asha watched the east like a sentence not yet translated.
"I hid him," Geralt said.
"Yes."
"Now he may hide the world in himself because men like me thought secrets were protection."

Regis's voice became very gentle. "Do not flatter yourself into sole guilt. It is an attractive vice among moral men. The world was unkind before your decision and would have found other cruelties without your assistance. You are responsible for what you did. Not for every hunger that found the road after."
Geralt hated how much he needed that to be true.
"If he chooses it," Geralt said, "I don't know whether I can let him."
"Then begin deciding what love means before the hour demands a definition."
"That's your advice?"

"It is less advice than warning. You love people with your hands. Swords, straps, food, doors, saddles, standing between. If the choice arrives, standing between may become another form of ownership."
Geralt watched him without blinking.
Regis held his gaze. "A terrible thought. I know. I brought an umbrella, not comfort."
Geralt almost laughed. It hurt more than it helped.
Behind them, something moved. Jack stood at the edge of the mist, not hiding, which meant he had heard what made hiding pointless.
"You talk loudly for old monsters," Jack said.
"Age affects volume unpredictably," Regis replied.
Geralt said nothing.
Jack came to the riverbank. His face was unreadable, but his left hand was wrapped too tightly. "If it comes to it, I choose."
"No," Geralt said.
"Yes."
"Not alone."
Jack faced him then, and the river between all their old choices seemed briefly easier to understand than the space between the two witchers.
"Not alone," Jack said. "But mine."
Regis closed his umbrella strap with unnecessary care.
The difference mattered.
The problem was that sometimes the world killed people through differences that mattered.
Before dawn, Regis found Jack sitting beside the salt-lime pit.

The pit had been covered with earth and iron, but it still changed the air. Not smell exactly. Shape. The space above it seemed unwilling to host insects, dew, or ordinary silence. Jack sat on a fallen log with his elbows on his knees and watched the place where the wyvern had been denied the river.
"I hope I am not intruding," Regis said.
"You are."
"Ah. Shall I leave?"
Jack considered. "No."
Regis sat at the other end of the log. He did not bring the umbrella this time, perhaps because the weather was clear or because even vampires understood when a joke had finished its work.
"You asked whether the Living Chamber can work," Regis said. "May I ask what answer you hoped for?"
"No."
"You hoped I would say no?"
"I hoped you would not ask the second question."
Regis nodded, accepting the hit as cleanly placed. "Then I will ask a different one. If you become the last prison, what do you imagine remains yours?"
Jack studied the iron bars over the pit. "Choice."
"Choice at the gate, perhaps. Afterward?"

The afterward had no proper shape. Jack could imagine pain, darkness, pressure, hunger learning him from within. He could imagine Ciri refusing, Yennefer furious, Geralt standing in a doorway the world had removed. He could imagine winning in the way a lock won, by continuing to be closed. He could not imagine what a man did after becoming a room.
"I don't know," he said.

"Good. Certainty would worry me more." Regis folded his hands. "I have lived too many years to believe restraint is one decision. It is a civilization maintained daily inside one body. There are mornings when the civilization is well governed. There are nights when barbarians reach the gates."
"And if the gates hold?"
"Then one still has to live near the gates. Do not underestimate that punishment. Do not romanticize it into sacrifice before you understand the maintenance."
Jack turned to him. "You think I want sacrifice."
"No. I think you trust loss more than comfort. That is common among people taught too early that comfort comes with hooks."
The words found places Jack had not named. He disliked Regis for that and respected him more in the same breath.
"If it comes," Jack said, "someone must hold."
"Perhaps. But if holding requires a man, then the man is not merely a lock. He is a citizen of his own suffering. Ask for laws before you accept the kingdom."
Regis rose. "That is my least poetic advice and therefore possibly my best."
The difference mattered.
Ciri learned that her affection had become a state concern from a woman carrying pears.

The woman was not actually a pear seller. The pears were real, because Ilyra disliked props that collapsed under inspection, but the seller's hands had no fruit stains and too much knife discipline for honest market work. She approached Ciri at the morning halt outside Marna's Bend with a wicker basket, a bowed head, and a voice pitched exactly between servant humility and trained urgency.
"Highness," she said, offering the basket.
Ciri considered the pears. "If those explode, I will be irritated."
The woman's face did not change. Good training. "Only one contains a note. The others are seasonal."
"That may be the most Nilfgaardian sentence I have heard this week."

Ilyra, standing near the horses, took one pear, turned it, found the hairline cut, and removed a tight roll of paper from the hollow around the stem. She gave the fruit back to the woman. "Waste nothing."
The woman bowed and left with eight pears, seven of them innocent and one now relieved of politics.

Ciri read the note under the patched canvas awning where the road crew had once kept tools. Rain threatened without commitment. The camp smelled of wet leather, horse sweat, cold ash, and the salt-lime pit where the wyvern had been buried. Jack stood by Buck with Roche's map in one hand and a look that said he knew a message had arrived and would rather face a monster than ask whether it concerned him. Geralt watched both road and daughter with the weary concentration of a man discovering that fatherhood had no retirement clause. Yennefer stood too still near a hawthorn.
Triss warmed a cup of tea between both hands and pretended the steam did not give away how cold she was.
The note was from Emhyr.

Cirilla, the pattern around your movements has become visible. Men who fear you are now less dangerous than men who fear for you in public language. I have received inquiries using the terms anomalous protector proximity, emotional vulnerability vector, and destabilizing private attachment. I do not ask you to return because asking what you will refuse wastes ink. I do ask whether the person drawing these terms understands what your closeness will do to him. E.
Ciri read it once. Then again. She considered throwing it into the ash pit and decided the ash pit had suffered enough.
Yennefer approached without needing to be called. "Well?"
Ciri handed her the note.
Yennefer read it and made a sound that was almost admiration and mostly contempt. "Your father has acquired a poetic bureaucrat."
"He wrote it himself."
"Worse. He is improving."
Geralt came over. Yennefer handed him the paper. He read slowly, lips barely moving at emotional vulnerability vector.
"Vector," he said.
"I know," Ciri said.
"I hate that one."
"Pick a number and stand in line."
Jack did not move. Buck did, pushing his nose against Jack's shoulder as if the horse understood that human correspondence was a predator with poor teeth and endless patience.
Ciri folded the note and put it in her sleeve. "They know."
"They knew you cared before you did," Yennefer said. "Institutions are vulgar that way."
"Do not start."
Ilyra brought the second warning in a box of pears because imperial gravity preferred sweet surfaces.

The pears were yellow, unbruised, and packed in straw too clean for the roads they claimed to have traveled. Each fruit carried a tiny black mark near the stem, not ink, not rot, only pressure from a signet ring pressed too carelessly during inspection. Ciri noticed because she had spent half her life learning that a court could hide a threat in a flower, a compliment, a prayer, or a tray.
"From Vizima," Ilyra said.
"The pears or the leash?"
"Both, Highness. The pears are better mannered."

Ciri lifted one and smelled wax, cellar straw, and the faint iron tang of a courier who had bled through a glove. Inside the box, beneath the fruit, lay a thin note folded into the invoice. No imperial seal. That meant it was worse. Seals announced power. Unsealed notes announced intimacy, or the wish to be able to deny it.

Cirilla, the note said, your movements have become a discussion in rooms where concern has learned to use your name softly. Return if you wish to choose the conversation. Remain if you wish others to choose its terms. E.
She read it twice. The second reading made her angrier because it was good advice.
"He is improving again," Ilyra said.
"He is threatening me politely."
"That may be what improvement means in certain families."
Ciri turned to her. Ilyra's face remained still. Intelligence handlers made dangerous jesters because they survived by saying true things at safe angles.
"Who else has written?"

"An adviser with too many syllables in his title wishes to know whether your northern inspection has become compromised by personal sympathy. A quartermaster wants to know whether your escort should be expanded. A priest attached to the imperial household sent a prayer for discernment, which I have quarantined on aesthetic grounds."
"Personal sympathy," Ciri said.

The phrase moved through her like a hand looking for a handle. Personal sympathy meant Jack. Personal sympathy meant Geralt. It meant Yennefer and Triss and the old impossibility of being daughter, ruler, survivor, and woman in the same body without someone calling one of those roles evidence against the others.
Ilyra waited. That was her gift. She did not fill silence merely because rank left room for it.
Ciri set the pear down. "What have they seen?"

"Stop there. You changed route after the broken mill. You delayed one diplomatic reply. You refused to identify Jack by file language in a rider's hearing. You sent a private instruction forbidding imperial assets from making custody approaches in your name. The last one has frightened the right people and reassured none."
"Good. Reassured people become creative."
"There is more." Ilyra took a second slip from her sleeve. "Someone reported that you and Jack rode side by side for half a mile without speaking."
Ciri stared at her.
"I agree," Ilyra said. "The empire's capacity for boredom remains formidable."
"Who wrote that?"
"A man who has never been allowed to ride beside anyone interesting."
Ciri almost smiled and hated that too. Humor made cages visible but did not break them.

Through the window of the rented upper room, she saw Jack in the yard below with Buck. He was checking the horse's left hind shoe. Geralt stood nearby pretending not to supervise. Yennefer spoke with Triss under the eaves, both women using low voices and precise hands, two forms of care that would deny kinship if accused. Asha watched the road. Regis stood in the rain with his umbrella and looked as if weather had disappointed him morally.

Jack straightened. Ciri could not hear what Geralt said, but she saw Jack answer with two words. Geralt's shoulders changed. Barely. His body always told on him before his mouth did. Fatherhood, with Geralt, made itself visible in badly hidden irritation and the repair of straps no one had asked him to touch.
"Highness," Ilyra said quietly.
Ciri did not look away from the yard. "Say it."

"If you love him, it is already political. If you do not love him, they will write that you do if it helps. If he loves you, he is a hostage to your choices. If he does not, he is still a man your enemies can place near you and call motive. There is no private answer now. Only more or less honest public handling."
Ciri closed her hand around the pear until the skin broke. Juice ran over her fingers. Sweet, sticky, absurd.
"I have not said love."
"No," Ilyra said. "You have said logistics several times with unusual hostility."
Ciri laughed then despite herself. It came out sharp as a blade. "Yennefer taught me that."
"It has lineage."

Below, Jack looked up. Not because he heard the laugh, perhaps. Because the world had changed pressure around it. His eyes found the window. He did not smile. She did not either. The distance between them held every word others might later weaponize.
Ciri wiped pear juice from her hand with a cloth and turned from the window.
"Write to Emhyr," she said.
Ilyra produced paper without comment.
"Not as daughter. Not as fugitive. As Empress-designate."
"Exact phrasing?"

Ciri thought of Jack being called hereditary infrastructure. Thought of herself being called succession optics. Thought of Yennefer's face when anyone said vessel. Thought of Geralt's warning silence before warnings had language.

"Any attempt by imperial personnel, formal or deniable, to classify, seize, bargain for, transport, medically claim, magically examine, or otherwise convert Jack Morningstar into a state asset under my presumed authority is forbidden. Any such action will be treated as an act against my person, my household, and the stability of the succession."
She told Jack before the order left.

Not in front of everyone. That would have made truth into theater. She found him behind the stable, where Buck was educating a post by ignoring it with contempt. The rain had stopped. Water fell from the eaves in slow drops, each one striking the mud with the patience of a clerk making a list.
"I have forbidden imperial custody action in my name," Ciri said.
Jack tightened the strap he was checking. "That is an order."
"Yes."
"To them."
"Yes."
"Not to me."
She heard the question hidden under grammar. Good. He had learned to make questions look like fences.
"Not to you," she said. "I do not command your body. I am warning anyone who thought my title could be used as a rope around it."

Then he let her see his face. The crimson of his eyes was duller in wet daylight, less flame than banked coal. It did not make him less frightening. It made him more human, which was often worse for people who wanted categories.
"This makes you vulnerable," he said.
"I was born vulnerable. Then everyone gave it ceremonial names."
"Ciri."
Her name in his mouth had become dangerous because he used it rarely and accurately. She folded her arms before her body could do something foolish with the sound.
"Do not thank me," she said.
"I wasn't going to."
"Good. Gratitude becomes debt too quickly."
He returned to Buck's strap. Buck nudged him once, hard, as if offended by unresolved emotional accounting.
"Your horse has opinions," Ciri said.
"He thinks both of us are making bad weather in a small yard."
"Sensible."

For a moment they stood with the horse between them, which was safer than no distance and less cowardly than a wall. Ciri could feel the shape of the order waiting inside her coat. Imperial words, imperial threat, imperial consequence. She had used the machine to keep another machine from touching him. That did not make her clean. It made her early.
"They will say my judgment is compromised," she said.
"Is it?"
"Yes."
He stopped.
Ciri held his gaze. "All judgment is compromised by what a person refuses to betray. I prefer to know my compromises by name."
Jack's mouth moved almost into a smile and failed, not from lack of feeling but because feeling had arrived under guard.
"Then write that in your order," he said.
"Ilyra would enjoy it too much."
"She sounds formidable."
"She is. I collect women who frighten sensible men. It improves rooms."
Buck snorted. The post remained unimpressed.
Ciri stepped closer by one pace, still outside touch. "Listen carefully. They may use me against you."
"I know."

"No. You know as strategy. I need you to know as promise. If someone places my name in your hand and tells you the only way to spare me is to become less yourself, you come to me first if breath remains. You do not answer a room that has learned my voice badly."
The yard seemed to still around the words.
Jack checked Buck, then her. "And if breath does not remain?"
"Then I will be angry to the point of inconveniencing gods."
That time he did smile, brief and quiet and gone before the world could claim it.
"Fair," he said.
It was their bridge again. Small. Unsteady. Crossed anyway.
Ilyra's pen paused only once. "That is strong."
"Good. Weak orders ask to be interpreted."
"Your father will read this as personal."
"He should. I learned statecraft from personal consequences."
Ilyra sanded the page. "And Jack?"
Ciri looked back through the window. Jack had returned to Buck's shoe. Geralt had taken the hoof knife from him. They were arguing now, badly, safely, about the angle of a nail.
"Jack receives no order from me," Ciri said. "Not this one. Not about himself."
"Then what does he receive?"
Ciri folded the stained cloth over the broken pear and placed it in the box, where all perfect fruit became less convincing by proximity.
"The facts before the order leaves," she said. "I will not let a file understand my choice before he does."
"I had not yet warmed properly."
Geralt turned to Jack. "He should hear it."
"He is standing four paces away with witcher hearing," Ciri said. "He has heard the part that offends him and not the part that earns trust. That is poor manners on our part."
Jack faced her then.

The camp, which had been trying not to notice, gave up and became a collection of people very interested in saddlebags, maps, bridles, clouds, and one irrelevant tree. Roche, from the cart, muttered something about young people and state collapse. Ves told him to shut up. Regis observed with the gentle face of a man who had watched centuries prove youth was not the only age capable of foolishness.
Ciri crossed to Jack.
"My father has received reports that you are an emotional vulnerability vector."
Jack met her eyes. Then at Buck. "The horse agrees."
"Buck has better political instincts than most of the court."
"He bites faster."
"So do I when cornered."
Jack's mouth moved, almost. "I know."
The almost smile made the next part worse.
Ciri held out the note. He took it. His eyes moved over the lines with no visible change until he reached private attachment. Then his hand went still.
"It is accurate," he said.
"Which part?"
"That closeness takes its due."
"That was not the insult."
"No. It was the useful part."

Ciri felt Yennefer watching, Geralt hurting, Triss understanding, and the road collecting witnesses. This was what titles did. They turned even private truth into a room full of consequences. She had wanted one night in the chapel to belong to herself. It had, and that was precisely why the world had begun pricing it.
"Do not make yourself smaller to reduce what I pay," she said.
Jack handed the note back. "I was considering making myself farther."
"Same cowardice. Different geography."
That landed. He did not flinch, but it landed.
"Ciri," Geralt said.

She turned on him before he could improve the damage into something kinder. "No. I know what I said. I know what it takes. I also know the difference between a man choosing distance from fear and a man choosing distance because everyone around him keeps calling his presence dangerous until he believes absence is a gift."
Jack's eyes sharpened. "Sometimes absence is a gift."
"Sometimes. Not when it is wrapped by enemies and delivered by guilt."
The camp quieted until rain became loud.

Yennefer's expression was unreadable. Triss looked down into her tea. Geralt's hand had closed around the strap he had been repairing until the leather creaked. Regis watched Jack with a sorrow that did not presume to speak. Asha watched Ciri as if measuring whether title and woman had finally become enemies in the same body.
Jack looked away first. Not defeat. Calculation aborted before it could become cruelty.
"Fair," he said.
Ciri hated how much the word had come to mean.
Ilyra reached them by noon in a covered carriage that looked like it belonged to a minor noblewoman with expensive nerves and uninteresting relatives.

This was deliberate. Minor noblewomen with expensive nerves were common at gates and inconvenient to detain. Ilyra stepped down in a gray travel dress, carrying a dispatch case and wearing the calm expression of someone who had spent the journey lying to patrols with such competence that honesty would have been an insult.
"Highness," she said. "Your schedule is now officially impossible."
"Only now?"
"Before, it was merely offensive."

Ciri took the case and opened it inside the cart while rain began properly. Yennefer, Triss, and Geralt joined her. Jack remained outside for three breaths before Ciri said, "Inside," without looking up.

He entered. Wet cloak, controlled expression, too much height for the cart ceiling. Buck pushed his head briefly under the canvas as if verifying where his witcher had been put, then withdrew after sniffing Ilyra and apparently deciding she contained no oats.
Ilyra laid out the problem.

Three imperial inquiries had moved toward Ciri's handlers. None named Jack directly. That was the danger. One asked about unregistered protectors near the future empress. One requested clarification on hostile custody doctrines in vassal territory. One suggested that if anomalous threats affected Her Highness's emotional judgment, temporary advisory supervision might be justified for succession stability.
Ciri read the last one and smiled.
It was a bad smile.
"They want to supervise my judgment by proving my judgment is compromised because I object to bodies being stolen. Elegant."
"Court elegance often resembles a snake eating its own proof," Yennefer said.
Triss pointed to the second note. "This one is not from Emhyr's inner hand."
"No," Ilyra said. "A northern liaison attached to settlement policy. The paper passed through a vassal corridor before entering imperial review."
"Black Ink," Geralt said.
"Likely. They are not attacking Jack first now. They are shaping the room around Ciri so any defense of him looks like private instability."

Ciri leaned back against the cart wall. The wood smelled of oil and old perfume. Someone had used this carriage for real luxury once. Now it held wet witchers, sorceresses, political treason, and one intelligence officer with sensible shoes. That was an improvement.
"Options," she said.

Ilyra did not waste time. "Return to Vizima and turn defense into policy. Bad. You will be trapped in process before you can protect anyone. Continue privately and risk the court building a version without you. Worse. Publicly name Jack under your protection. Ruinous. Publicly forbid non-consensual seizure of all free witchers, mages, non-human custodians, and unaffiliated anomalous persons under vassal emergency doctrine. Broad without naming him. Strong as a gate brace. It would slow them. Risky in a more useful way."
Yennefer looked pleased. "I like her."
"You like competence," Triss said.
"When it behaves."
Geralt turned to Ciri. "If you issue that, they'll know."
"They already know too much," Ciri replied. "It would poison the well." "I can either drink quietly or throw something larger in."
Jack's voice came low. "Do not spend imperial weight on me."

"There," Ciri said, too fast. "That. That sentence. You make yourself one person so the arithmetic can call you cheaper. It is the same trick they use, only you think it is noble because you do it from inside your own skin."
His face closed. "That is not what I meant."
"It is what the sentence does."
Regis, who had remained outside the cart until now, spoke through the canvas. "She is correct, though the weather makes my agreement less dramatic than it deserves."
Geralt opened the flap. "Regis."
"Yes?"
"Lurking?"
"Listening. Lurking has poorer posture."
Ciri almost laughed. The almost was useful.
Jack held her gaze for a long moment. "If you make it broad, not mine."
"Yes."
"If it protects others."
"Yes."
"If you do not call it love."

That hurt because it was generous and cruel in equal measure. He was not denying the feeling. He was protecting it from the document it would become. Ciri understood that so well she wanted to strike him for making understanding necessary.
"I will call it law," she said. "Privately, I reserve the right to call it whatever I please."
Yennefer looked toward the rain. Geralt studied the floor. Triss's eyes softened for one second and then returned to the paper.
Ilyra produced a clean sheet. "Then dictate."
Ciri dictated standing inside a carriage that smelled of damp wool and borrowed nobility.

No person under the protection of imperial transition, vassal settlement, free company, guild license, mage-recognition process, witcher contract, non-human custodial obligation, or private citizenship shall be placed under emergency restraint, medical custody, bloodline seizure, or anomalous-host classification without named charge, witnessed consent, and review by three authorities who do not share a funding chain.

Triss wrote quickly. Yennefer changed two phrases to survive hostile interpretation. Ilyra changed one to survive imperial procedure. Geralt objected to funding chain because it sounded like something that would make clerks multiply. Ciri kept it for that reason.
Jack said nothing until the end.
"They will find cracks," he said.
"Yes," Ciri replied. "But cracks slow rats if the walls are thick enough."
Ilyra sanded the page. "This will not save him."
"No," Ciri said. "But it will make theft take longer and involve witnesses. That is sometimes the beginning of civilization."

Outside, the rain turned hard. Inside, Ciri signed not as girl, not as daughter, not as lover, but with the long ugly line of a name the world had been trying to own since before she knew how to hold a sword.
Cirilla Fiona Elen Riannon.
Empress-designate, though she did not write the title.
The absence did more work than the word would have.
The response did not come from Emhyr.

That frightened Ilyra more than anger would have. It arrived by courier wearing no imperial colors, sealed with a temporary settlement mark, and written in a hand trained to make threats look like concern. The document acknowledged Ciri's draft, praised its humanitarian breadth, questioned its procedural feasibility, and suggested provisional advisory review for any order issued under conditions of emotional proximity to anomalous persons.
Yennefer read that sentence and said nothing.
Ciri had learned to fear Yennefer's silences more than most men's shouts.
"They moved quickly," Triss said.
"No," Ilyra answered. "They were waiting for her to defend someone. They did not know whom. The mechanism was prepared."
Geralt studied the settlement mark. "Can Emhyr stop it?"

Ciri laughed once. The sound was too short to be humor. "Of course. That is the problem. If he stops it openly, my protection becomes his indulgence. If he does not, the review becomes proof I need supervision."
"Then we bypass him," Yennefer said.
Ilyra's eyes lifted. "Legally?"
"Do not ask questions that insult both of us."

Triss took a clean page. "We answer through three channels: mage humanitarian language to make refusal look cruel, witcher guild-adjacent language to make enforcement look expensive, and Ciri's order through vassal settlement before the advisory review can claim sequence."
"That is not one answer," Jack said.
"No," Triss said. "It is a net. Nets are what one uses when the fish has lawyers."
Ciri turned to Jack. "See? I am not spending imperial weight on you. I am spending paperwork on everyone who hates paperwork."
"Generous."
"Vindictive, actually. Generosity is less organized."
Leaving it unsaid accomplished far more than speaking it out loud.
That night, Jack found her by the unfinished road marker east of camp.

It had once pointed toward three villages. Two names had been scratched out, not by war but by taxation, which was more final in certain districts. The remaining arm leaned east and said nothing useful. Ciri sat on the stone base with her cloak wrapped around her knees, watching mist move over the low fields. She had left the camp without escort because she wanted privacy and because everyone nearby was competent at pretending not to follow while following. Geralt was in the trees to the west. Yennefer watched from a place where no one would see her unless she wanted them to.
Jack heard both and chose not to mention either.
"You are being guarded," he said.
"I know."
"Badly?"
"Lovingly. It is a related problem."

He stood beside the marker, not too close. After a while, she patted the stone. He sat. The movement was careful, not because of injury but because closeness had become a political act and both were tired of giving politics free seating.

For a while they said nothing. The camp fire glowed through mist. Buck's silhouette moved once near the horses. Somewhere, Roche's men changed watch. An owl called and received no answer, which seemed sensible.
"I almost thought of the chapel today," Ciri said.
Jack looked ahead. "Almost."
"Yes. Then I stopped because once I thought it, they would have won something. They would have made a private room into evidence."
"Rooms can be both."
"I know. That is what hurts."
He said nothing because there was no clean answer.
Ciri studied his bandaged hand. "When I signed the order, I wanted to sign it for you. I made it broad because that was wiser. I still wanted it to be for you."
"I know."
"Do you hate that?"

He considered. She appreciated that he considered. Men often answered too quickly when women asked if their care had become a burden. They thought speed was kindness. It was usually fear wearing clean boots.
"No," he said. "I fear it."
"Good."
That surprised him.
"Good?"

"Yes. Fear means you understand it has weight. I am tired of men treating my choices as either gifts or disasters depending on whether they benefit. Sometimes they are blades. I know. I still hand them over."
Then his attention came back to her. The crimson in his eyes held the last of the camp light and made it look like something banked rather than burning.
"Then I will take it carefully," he said.
"You had better."
The almost smile returned between them. Not happiness. Something more durable and less safe.

Jack reached for her hand, stopped halfway, and waited. She placed her hand in his. No kiss. No heat beyond what skin carried. That made it harder to survive in some ways. Desire could be blamed on night, fear, bodies, old wounds, the need to feel alive. Holding hands in a misty field while the world tried to categorize the contact as leverage required a quieter defiance.
Ciri leaned her shoulder against his.
Barely. It steadied him anyway.
From the trees, Geralt looked away.
Yennefer did not.
Before dawn, Ilyra burned three drafts and kept the fourth.

Ciri found her by the cart, sleeves rolled, hair coming loose at one temple, the pear basket beside her now serving as document weight. Intelligence officers, Ciri had learned, became most honest when exhausted past the point of decorating caution.
"Bad?" Ciri asked.

"Manageable, which is the court word for bad with furniture." Ilyra handed her the draft. "Your order can move if we attach it to broader vassal settlement protections and avoid naming anomalous bodies in the first sentence. If we place witchers beside guild contractors and non-human custodians beside religious minorities, anyone opposing it has to admit which category they hate so openly that they expose it."
Ciri read the draft. "You learned cruelty from lawyers."
"I learned survival from watching them eat slower prey."
"And Jack?"

Ilyra's eyes flicked toward the road marker where he had sat with her hours before. "He becomes less visible under the order and more visible to anyone who reads absence well. That includes Emhyr, Yennefer, Triss, Black Ink, and every enemy worth fearing."
"So it helps and hurts."
"Most real tools do."

Ciri folded the draft. The word tool sat badly after everything, but Ilyra had not meant it that way and the difference mattered. She looked toward Jack, then toward the faint paling of the east. "Send it."
"As law?"
"As weather. Let them complain after it is already raining."
Yennefer did not.

Druidic packet delivered through Kovir courier route, salt-stained and resealed twice: To Yennefer of Vengerberg, Triss Merigold, and the white-haired witcher who still owes me a clear answer about a Leshen in Ard Skellig. The sea has begun returning what it should keep. Queen Cerys demands plain truth before she sends aid into another continent's secret. I agree with her, which will surprise no one with sense.

The first sign, according to the fisherman who found the carcass, was that the gulls would not touch it. Fishermen respected gulls the way priests respected omens: publicly with reverence, privately with insults and an eye to profit. Gulls touched everything. They stole bait, bread, fingers if the fingers were slow, and once, in a story Cerys had heard too many times, a nobleman's funeral ring before the widow finished crying. If gulls would not land, the thing below them had entered a category older than appetite.

Cerys arrived in riding leathers, hair braided back, crown absent because cliffs did not care for gold and neither did she when the work was honest. The wind off the sea cut through wool and made banners snap above the harbor. Rain had not yet fallen, but the air had the iron taste of weather preparing an argument. Ermion stood beside the covered shape on the stones with his staff planted in the shingle and his face set in the grim expression of a man who had been right too early and disliked the repetition.
"Draconid?" Cerys asked.
"Yes."
"Skellige kind?"
"No."
"Then why is it on my shore?"
"That is the expensive question."
Cerys turned to him. "You have been speaking with witchers again."
"One learns phrases from bad company."

The fisherman crossed himself twice, once in the Skellige way and once in a manner he had probably learned from a Novigrad merchant's frightened wife. Cerys waved him back before theology complicated the footprints.
Ermion lifted the tarp.

The carcass had once been a basilisk or near it, insulting taxonomy. Its head was too narrow, its chest too deep, its wing joints malformed by some inland breeding line that had no business reaching an island shore. The belly had not been opened. The skin remained whole. Yet the body sagged inward as if everything that made it hungry had been drawn through a hole smaller than thought. The eyes were intact and empty. Not dead empty. Rooms after furniture empty.

Cerys felt the old chill move under the weather. She had seen battlefields after raids, drowned men, plague, berserker aftermath, and the Wild Hunt's shadow when stories became hoofbeats. This was different. This was not violence done to flesh. It was instruction removed from flesh.
"No birds," she said.
"No lice either," Ermion replied. "No worms. No scavenger claim. Even rot is hesitating."
"Rot has more sense than half my jarls."
"Often. Less jewelry."
She crouched near the head. The smell was wrong. Brine, yes. Dead scale, yes. But beneath it lay hot stone, old smoke, and something like a forge heard from underwater. "You said dreams."

Ermion nodded toward the priestess waiting by the path. "Three women in separate villages. One priestess of Freya. One net-mender. One girl too young for politics and too old for fairy tales. Same phrase."
"Say it."
"The crown drinks through the door."
Cerys stood. Wind pulled at the braid over her shoulder. "I hate mainland secrets. They always arrive half-drowned and expecting hospitality."
"This one may have arrived from farther than the mainland."
"Do not become mystical before breakfast. It makes me violent."
Ermion covered the carcass. "Yennefer's packet names Jack Morningstar. Geralt is with him. Ciri too, unofficially enough that the official denial will be exhausting."
Cerys looked toward the harbor where men moved crates, nets, and lies with equal skill. "Ciri is never unofficial. She merely changes which office panics first."
"The packet asks for reports, not rescue."
"Good. Rescue across the sea is expensive and usually late." She looked back at the tarp. "But reports are not nothing. What does Yennefer want?"
"Truth before rumor. Signs of anchor sickness. Sea changes. Dream phrases. Any draconic disturbances. She also wants to know if Skellige hears the same words as the North."
"And do we?"
Ermion's silence answered.
Cerys cursed. It was a concise curse, suitable for weather, politics, and gods with poor timing.
The priestess of Freya was named Ragna, and she treated queen, druid, and dead beast with equal suspicion.

The scale fragments were sealed in wax mixed with salt. Triss set them apart from the papers because they made ink crawl toward the margins. That small movement frightened her more than the red glow had. Ink should not behave like an animal seeking a corner.
"Another witness," she said.
"Another argument," Yennefer corrected. "Witnesses can be ignored. Arguments find courts."

She lived above the harbor in a house that smelled of salt wool, dried fish, juniper smoke, and childbirth. Shells hung over the door, not for decoration but for warning. They clicked in the wind with a sound like small teeth. Ragna was broad-shouldered, gray-haired, and in possession of the sort of stare that had delivered children, shamed warriors, and argued with storms without finding any of those tasks spiritually separate.

"Dream came three nights," she said, pouring sour beer into cups no one had requested. "First night, black water under stone. Second, red door walking with horse hooves behind it. Third, a woman singing in a dry tongue while a child bit a blue star."
Cerys held the cup. "A blue star?"
"Bead, maybe. Dreams make poor jewelers."
Ermion's expression changed. Cerys saw it because queens survived by seeing what old men hoped their beards hid.
"You know that symbol," she said.
"Yennefer's packet mentioned a child's blue bead found with Morningstar proof."
Ragna spat into the hearth. The fire hissed but did not argue. "Then the dream is nosing around graves. Bad manners."
"Dreams are not known for etiquette," Ermion said.
"Men say that when they want dreams to be excused. Dreams have causes. Sometimes too many." Ragna leaned toward Cerys. "This red-eyed man. He yours?"
"No."
"Ciri's?"
Cerys raised one eyebrow. "That is not a question a priestess should ask before noon."
"Noon is for cowards."
Ermion looked into his cup as if the beer might offer diplomatic shelter.
Cerys answered because avoiding the question would give it more teeth. "He is a person under pressure from people who think usefulness is a claim. That is cause for concern."
"Good answer. Practiced?"
"Painfully."
Ragna grunted. "Dream said: the crown drinks through the door. Door is not gate. Gate opens both ways. Door belongs to a house. Houses have owners."
"He has no house," Ermion said.

"Everyone has a house in a dream. Sometimes it is a body. Sometimes a grave. Sometimes a country foolish, thinking crowns make roofs." Ragna drank. "Tell the black-haired sorceress that if she wants a clean omen, she should wash it herself. Freya sends what she sends."
"I will soften that," Ermion said.
"Do not. She sounds like a woman who dislikes softened things."
Cerys smiled despite the corpse waiting below. "She does."

Ragna turned to her. "You will be asked for aid. Maybe not by letter. Maybe by the sea putting another dead thing in your path. Give aid, but not blind. Skellige paid for secrets at Kaer Morhen, at battlefields, at the Hunt's edge, and in songs where mainlanders remember us only when they need ships. Demand names. Demand the whole wound."
Cerys set the cup down. "I intended to."
"Good. Saves me scolding. I am busy."
Outside, thunder moved across the water though the clouds had not darkened enough for it. Ermion and Cerys both looked toward the window.
In the harbor below, the covered carcass shifted.
Not rose. Not lived. Shifted, as if something inside the hollow had heard the thunder and tried to answer with a body no longer furnished for obedience.
Cerys stood. "I hate being right after breakfast."
"It is not yet breakfast," Ermion said.
"Then there is still time to ruin the whole day."
They burned the carcass on the black stones beyond the harbor because burying on Skellige meant arguing with the sea and the sea had already spoken too much.

Ermion drew circles in salt, ash, and powdered iron. Ragna sang a Freya song with the tenderness removed so that only function remained. Cerys kept the crowd back herself, not because no one else could, but because people obeyed a queen differently when danger smelled strange. Men watched her watching the fire and learned not to move closer because she did not.
The carcass burned wrong. Smoke bent east. Fat did not pop. Bone cracked inward. At the center of the body, where hunger should have lived, red light pulsed three times and died.
A child in the crowd began chanting under his breath.
The crown drinks through the door.
His mother clapped a hand over his mouth and began to cry.
Cerys turned to Ermion. "Write faster."
"I am writing."
"Write angrier. Yennefer reads anger."
"Everyone reads your anger, my queen. It is one of our more successful diplomatic exports."
"Good. Send some."

The final packet included Ermion's report, Ragna's dream statement, scale scrap sealed in wax, a charcoal rubbing of the red pulse mark, and Cerys's own letter written in a hand strong, making ink seem like a tool rather than a decoration.
Yennefer, Geralt, Ciri, Triss, and whoever Jack Morningstar allows near his shoulder to read,

Skellige has received one hollowed draconid, three shared dream phrases, one child repeating mainland cult words without contact, and enough bad weather to make even druids look smug. The phrase here is crown drinks through the door. Ermion says door is not gate, which is the sort of distinction that usually becomes expensive. Ragna says a body can be a house in dreams, and dreams have begun trespassing.
If this is your secret, it has reached my shore. That makes it less private.

I will not sail my people blind into another hidden war. Send truth, not comfort. If aid is needed, name the need. If ships are needed, say so. If silence is needed, explain why silence is not merely another rich person's curtain. Skellige has buried enough for other people's prophecies.
Cerys an Craite, Queen of Skellige
Ermion read it once. "Direct."
"I was restrained."
"By what?"
"Lack of larger paper."
He sealed the packet.
As the courier rode toward the inland post, the wind turned east again. Gulls settled at last on the rocks where the carcass had burned. They pecked at ordinary ash and avoided the center.
Even birds knew some hunger should not be inherited.
Ermion stayed after the others left and drew three shapes in the ash with the end of his staff.
The first was a gate. Two uprights, a cross-line, an opening. "This is passage," he said to Cerys, because queens deserved answers even when answers were only shapes.
The second was a wound. A split line, ragged, refusing symmetry. "This is damage. It does not decide direction. It merely hurts and leaks."
The third was a door. A rectangle with a dark center and one side marked for hinge. "This is intention. A door implies a maker, a room, a threshold, and someone who believes they may decide entry."
Cerys studied the shapes. "And Morningstar?"
"I do not know. That is the fear. The dreams say door. His friends say man. His enemies say key. The dead beast says hunger has begun confusing the terms."
Cerys ground the door shape with her boot. "Then write that too. Leave nothing polite."
"You ask a druid to be impolite in writing?"
"I ask an old man to be useful before the sea sends me another corpse. Choose whichever offends you less."
Ermion smiled with half his mouth. "Useful, then. Impoliteness is for younger knees."

The packet reached Triss three days later in a rain-stiffened satchel, carried by a Kovir merchant who believed he was transporting smoked herring invoices and therefore complained the entire way with convincing sincerity.

They read it in a barn outside Vengerberg because the inn nearby had too many ears and one bard too eager to prove he knew the second verse of a song Dandelion had not yet finished corrupting. The barn smelled of hay, damp wool, horses, and sheep resentment. Buck approved of the sheep's attitude and no other part of the arrangement.
Yennefer read Cerys's letter first. Her mouth moved at send truth, not comfort.
"She has improved," Yennefer said.
Geralt took the report. "She was always direct."
"Direct and improved are not enemies."

Ciri read the dream phrase. The crown drinks through the door. Her face went still at door. Jack saw it and knew why. Gate had haunted her all her life. Door was worse in a quieter way. A gate belonged to paths, worlds, crossing. A door belonged to a house. To ownership. To rooms where someone could decide who entered.
"Door," Ciri said.
Asha closed her eyes. "Faithel teaching says gate is passage, wound is damage, door is intention. A door belongs to a maker. Or a claimant."
"Vharakthul claims," Yennefer said.
Regis, who had stayed longer than he claimed he would, looked at the red pulse rubbing. "And drinks. Through hunger, through dream, through dead beasts, perhaps through fear."
Jack studied the scale scrap. It lay in wax like a dead black leaf. His left palm ached.

"The problem is not local," Triss said. "Not Novigrad. Not Temeria. Not northern roads. It touches Skellige. Draconids are reacting across distance. Shared phrases are spreading without normal travel."

"The outer seal," Asha said. "If the old anchors are sick, the doctrine in the North will never be enough. You have fragments. Fragments helped you live this long. They will not tell you how the prison fails."
"Zerrikania," Geralt said.
No one disagreed.

Jack studied the barn doors. Rain moved beyond them, gray and patient. The east had waited behind every answer since the first warm ground under Willenford. Helena, Jacob, Asha's scars, Saesenthessis's silences, the blue bead, the living chamber page, the draconid bodies, the cult's red door, Cerys's weather. Evidence had become motion. Motion had become a road.
"Not yet," he said.
Every face in the room found him.
He touched the pouch where the bead lay. "Burial first."
Asha bowed her head once. Not agreement. Recognition.
Geralt looked at Jack for a long moment, then down at the Skellige report. "Yes."
Ciri did not speak. She understood too well that some roads became survivable only after grief was given a place to stand.
Outside, Buck kicked the barn door.
Zoltan, from the far stall, said, "Horse votes for burial with decent oats."
"Horse votes against barns," Jack said.
"Horse can file a complaint with Cerys. She's collecting mainland problems."
Dandelion, who had indeed come despite claims of being elsewhere, lifted a finger. "I can make that rhyme."
Priscilla touched his wrist. "Don't."
He lowered the finger. "Wisdom arrives through cruelty."
The barn breathed. For one moment, the world remained terrible and also populated by people refusing to let terror have the only voice.
Then they planned the burial.

The plan had to account for things that should never have belonged in the same conversation: a symbolic grave, imperial pursuit, Temerian quiet roads, Skellige omens, a cult song, Black Ink routes, the eating habits of horses, and whether Dandelion could be trusted not to call the whole matter beautifully tragic within earshot of Jack. The answer to the last question was no. Priscilla took responsibility.

Triss spread the map on a barn door laid over barrels. "Cerys can send ships if we need them later, but east by sea risks ports, records, and too many eyes. We go overland until the road makes water unavoidable."
"Overland means Korath," Asha said.

"Eventually," Yennefer replied. "Before that it means every petty official between here and the last civilized bath asking why a future empress, two sorceresses, witchers, a Faithel survivor, and a horse with criminal tendencies are traveling together."
Buck struck the stall wall.
"He heard criminal," Jack said.
"He understood tendencies," Geralt replied.

Ciri studied the map. The route east had too many names and not enough certainty. Villages thinned. Roads lost confidence. Borders became less lines than arguments with armed witnesses. Beyond all that waited lands northern maps described with the arrogance of ignorance.
"I cannot remain with the main party after the burial," she said.
Jack looked up. Geralt did too quickly.

Ciri continued before either could let concern swell into something everyone had to step around. "Not far. Not gone. But visibly traveling with you gives Black Ink and the court the same handle. Ilyra can create a false westward movement. I can ride offset with two guards and rejoin at marked points."
"No," Jack said.
"That sounded almost like ownership. Try again."
He closed his mouth. The barn enjoyed the silence in a cruel way.
"Bad," he said after a moment.
"Better. Also true. Still necessary."
Geralt rubbed a hand over his face. "I hate plans that sound like something I would have suggested twenty years ago."
"Then improve it," Ciri said.

So they did. Marked inns. Dead drops. Bird routes Triss could trust. Witcher signs placed where only Geralt and Jack would look. A phrase Dandelion would carry west in case rumor needed bending. Asha's old Faithel markers for the eastern approach. It was not safe. It was threaded. In this world, threaded was sometimes the nearest safety came without lying.
They buried Jacob and Helena where no one could prove they were.

It was the best the North could offer, which was to say insufficient and damp. The place lay three hills east of the ruined watch-house, under a stand of birch that had grown white and thin from poor soil. A stream cut through the lower field, too shallow to drown in unless one was unlucky, drunk, or very tired. Someone had built a stone wall there once and abandoned it halfway, leaving a line of gray rocks that led nowhere and divided nothing. Jack chose the place because the ground was quiet.
Safety had no place in it. Quiet.

Buck approved after biting at one birch branch and finding it morally acceptable. Roach grazed beside him with the solemn patience of a mare who had watched men make ceremonies out of things horses solved by standing near. Ciri's gelding kept to the stream. The other horses shifted under light rain. Weather had followed them like a creditor from Marna's Bend, softer now, no longer trying to erase tracks, only making every object shine too clearly.
The grave needed lies to survive.

That was the first indignity. No name carved cleanly. No signpost. No heroic stones placed where enemies, clerks, pilgrims, or collectors could find them. The world had already proved it could turn a family into a doctrine if given enough ash and a label. So they chose an old boundary hollow between two dead orchards, where the roots had knitted through war rubble and the road bent away because cart wheels disliked the slope.

Asha said the place had no proper eastern meaning. Geralt said western graves rarely cared for proper. Yennefer said if anyone tried to disturb it she would leave enough curse on the soil to educate future centuries. Triss asked her to make the curse subtle enough not to attract a mage with ambition. Yennefer looked offended by the implication that subtlety required request.
Buck chose the exact spot by refusing three others and standing before a thorn tree with one ear turned toward Jack.
"Your witness has opinions," Regis said.
"He usually does," Jack replied.
"Are they reliable?"
Buck bared his teeth at a branch.
"More than most councils," Geralt said.

They dug with borrowed spades and one entrenching tool Roche had given them after calling it a gift for optimism. The ground was cold under wet leaves. Not frozen. Stubborn. Jack worked until his palms blistered under old calluses and the red lines beneath the skin pulsed from pressure, not power. Ciri tried to take the spade once. He let her for six strokes. Then he took it back because the work had to pass through his hands until it became real.
She did not argue. That was how he knew she understood.

Asha prepared the bundle. Not bodies. Never bodies. The North had not given him that mercy. It gave him a broken hilt, the blue bead, Helena's brass daylight clasp, a strip of cloth that may have touched her sleeve, Jacob's practical letter copied once and sealed, Helena's letter wrapped in oilcloth, and the Black Ink operational tag folded so the word terminated faced inward where the earth could correct it slowly.
"The tag should not go with them," Triss said. "It is evidence."
"Copy exists," Jack said.
"Evidence should remain available."
"So should insult."
Triss turned from him to the tag. She understood before she liked it. "You want the file buried under the names it failed to use."
"Yes."
Yennefer's mouth curved by less than a knife's edge. "A rare example of administrative justice."
Ciri knelt beside the bundle and placed one of the pears from Ilyra's warning box beside it, small, yellow, bruised now from travel. His attention settled on her.
"It came with a leash," she said. "It can stay with people who cut one."
He did not know what to say. Good. Too many words would have made the pear ridiculous. Silence let it remain strange and therefore true.
Asha prepared the circle.

She used no shovel for the last work. She walked the circle with a copper bowl in one hand and a strip of linen in the other, singing under her breath in the same dry language she had used beneath the watch-house threshold. The song did not suit birch, rain, or northern mud. That made it hurt more. It had been made for stone holding heat after sunset, for water measured by oath, for rooms where family lines were remembered through hands, not graves. Here, it crossed wet grass and learned exile.

After the first verse she translated only the parts that wounded the room properly. Blood remembers work, not glory. Stone remembers weight, not praise. A name hidden is not a name lost if one living mouth refuses to sell it.
Jack stood outside the circle with Jacob's broken hilt, Helena's folded letter, the blue bead, and the copied operational tag wrapped in separate cloths.
Geralt stood beside him. Not too close. Close; the distance meant something.
"You don't have to put the tag in," Geralt said.
"I know."
"It's filth."
"It's witness."
Geralt said nothing because that was true and because truth, at graves, rarely arrived politely.

Ciri came with two flat stones she had carried from the stream. Her hands were muddy at the fingertips. No one commented. Royal hands, imperial hands, Elder Blood hands, hands that had held swords, held reins, held Jack in a chapel and then watched the world try to price the holding. Today they carried stones. That was better work than many thrones allowed.
"These?" she asked.
Jack regarded them. One had a white vein through the middle. The other was dark, smooth, and ordinary except for a red fleck near the edge.
"Yes."
She placed them by the circle and stepped back.

Yennefer brought a small silver pin. Triss brought ordinary thread. Dandelion brought no song because Priscilla had told him, very softly, that if he sang before Jack asked, she would break his lute and later feel complicated about it. Zoltan brought a carved peg of dark wood for no reason he explained. Regis brought a sprig of rue and looked almost embarrassed by his own sentiment. Roche and Ves did not come into the circle. They watched from the road with the courtesy of soldiers who knew not every grief improved under witnesses.
Saesenthessis appeared after Ciri laid the stones by the circle.

No one saw her arrive. She stood near the birches, cloak brown, hair dark, eyes human until light made them otherwise. The horses noticed and did not startle. Buck regarded her, snorted once, and returned to dismantling the branch. Approval, perhaps. Or recognition that dragons were not edible and therefore not his current problem.
"This is not their place," Saesenthessis said.
Jack let the question spend itself. "No."
"Good. A false grave that knows it is false is less insulting than a true one made by liars."
Zoltan muttered, "Dragons even complain elegantly."
"We hear well," Saesenthessis said.
"I know. I muttered for survival, not secrecy."
For a moment, the circle almost smiled. Grief did not break. It loosened its hand from the throat.
Asha stopped singing. "Bring the hilt."
Jack entered the circle.

The ground seemed to shift under him, not physically, not with magic worth naming. The barbed-star signet cooled against his chest. The blue bead warmed in his palm. He knelt because there were some arguments standing could not improve.

He laid Jacob's broken hilt first. Steel without blade. Service without empire. A man who had died buying minutes because minutes were all love could afford and because sometimes minutes became twenty-three years if the right old witchers found the smoke.
Then Helena's letter. He did not open it. He had read it past usefulness. The paper had become a room he could not live in but could not abandon.
Then the blue bead.
His fingers did not want to release it.

That was the worst part. Not the file, not the hilt, not the letter. The bead had no rhetoric. It had belonged to a child's grip, a mother noticing, a father joking. It proved that before the seal, before the trials, before Black Ink, before Ciri and Yennefer and blood-hunger and roads turning into evidence, there had been a small hand closing around blue glass because blue glass was pretty.
He put it down.

Ciri's breath caught. He heard it though she tried to keep it. Yennefer looked away, perhaps because even sorceresses who had survived everything had limits around children stolen by old necessities. Geralt's hand moved once at his side and did not reach. Good. Not reaching was sometimes the harder tenderness.
Last, Jack placed the operational tag.
Asha's attention snapped to him. "That does not belong with them."
"No," Jack said. "It belongs under them."

He put the tag beneath the two stones, where rain would reach slowly and worms, if the world had justice, would eat the edges first. Helena and Jacob above. File below. Not erased. Not honored. Buried in the correct order.
Asha's face changed. She bowed her head.
"Say their names," she said.

Jack looked at the little arrangement of objects and stones. His throat did not close. He had expected it to. Instead the world became too clear: rain on birch leaves, Buck chewing, mud under his knee, Geralt breathing through old guilt, Ciri holding herself motionless, Yennefer's perfume fighting wet earth and losing nobly, Triss's thread wrapped around her fingers, Dandelion silent with visible effort, Zoltan shifting his weight, Regis still as old blood under glass, Saesenthessis listening like stone that had learned sorrow.
"Jacob," Jack said.
The name entered the rain.
"Helena."
The second name stayed longer.

Asha resumed the song. This time Ciri added a line in a voice barely above breath. Not the same language. A Cintran cadence, perhaps, or something Geralt had heard once and forgotten until pain reminded him. Yennefer closed her eyes.
