Triss tied the ordinary thread around the wood peg Zoltan had brought and set it beside the stones. Dandelion did not sing. He hummed one note, very low, and stopped before it became performance.
The grave became incomplete in the correct way.

When it was done, Jack remained kneeling. Rain darkened his hair. The scar on his cheek looked silver. His left hand rested open on his thigh, palm up, as if the body had forgotten to close around its weapons.
Geralt came into the circle then.
He did not touch Jack. He crouched beside him and adjusted one of the stones because it had begun to slide in the wet soil. The movement was small, practical, and almost unbearable.
"There," Geralt said.
Jack studied the stone. "It will move again."
"Then we'll fix it again if we pass back."
If. Not when. Honest and therefore kind.
Jack stood. His knee left a dark mark in the mud. For a moment, he looked less like a man leaving grief than a man giving grief instructions to remain behind until called.
"East," he said.
Asha turned toward the road. "Korath first. The Frying Pan. Then Elskerdeg Pass. Then the sanctuary if the pass does not kill us, sell us, or decide mercy is treason. After that, Canyon of Stars."

She drew the route in mud with a willow switch. Not a map as northerners understood it. No decorative mountains, no confident lines, no little castles pretending distance was polite. This was a memory of thirst: three wells that might be clean, one that must be paid for in salt or story, a dry wash that killed men who crossed it in daylight, a caravan stone where guides lied less if given bitter tea first, and the pass where guardians measured strangers as if mercy were a locked gate.

"Water law begins before the desert," Asha said. "Do not offer coin first. Coin says you think need can be bought without relation. Offer memory. Small truth. Nothing that gives power. It shows you know water is not merchandise."
Geralt studied the mud route. "And if they ask for too much?"
"Then you learn which kind of thief they are before they hold your waterskin."
Buck leaned over Jack's shoulder and attempted to eat the willow switch. Asha pulled it away without looking at him.
"The horse must be watched for salt loss," she added. "He is so stubborn he may die while blaming others for heat."
"He'll like you eventually," Jack said.
"I do not require affection from witnesses."
Buck snorted into her sleeve.
"He disagrees," Ciri said.
Asha looked briefly wrong-footed, which made her seem younger than scars allowed. "Then he may file complaint after Elskerdeg."
"Cheerful route," Zoltan said.
"It is honest."
"Cheerful was unlikely, then."
Buck lifted his head at Korath, though no horse should know a desert by name. He stamped once. Jack watched Buck's ears work for a moment.
"Yes," he said. "I know."
The horse snorted in the manner of someone who did not believe humans knew much of anything until hungry, wounded, or charged.
Geralt waited until the others had gone to ready the horses before speaking to Jack alone.

Alone was not accurate. Ciri was within sight near the stream, speaking with Yennefer in tones too low for ordinary ears and perfectly clear to a witcher who chose not to listen. Triss was with Ilyra, sealing copies. Asha stood by the road. Regis had tactfully become interested in a birch fungus. Saesenthessis had vanished, which for dragons was a form of commentary. Dandelion was being prevented by Priscilla from composing a burial verse on moral grounds. Zoltan was helping by insulting the mud.
Still, the circle held a privacy of purpose.
Geralt stood beside the half-wall that led nowhere. Jack checked Buck's girth though the horse was not saddled yet. Habit gave hands something to do when words became expensive.
"You care for her," Geralt said.
Jack's fingers stopped on the strap. "Which one?"
Geralt let the pause sharpen.
"Cruel question," Jack said. "There are several women here capable of ruining a careless answer."
"Ciri."
Jack resumed the strap. "Yes."
Geralt exhaled through his nose. Not relief. Not surprise. A man hearing an arrow hit the target he had watched leave the bow.
"Yennefer too," Geralt said.
Jack's hand stilled again.
The road seemed to lose all humor.
"Careful," Geralt added. "I am not accusing you."
"Good. It would be complicated to punch you at a grave."
"Lambert would manage."
"Lambert has broader social policies."
Geralt almost smiled. Then the almost died because the subject deserved more.
"I loved Yennefer," he said.
Jack faced him then. No evasion. Good. Pain preferred clean sightlines.
"I know."
"No. You know there was history. Songs. Arguments. Ciri. Things people say because they like making the past smaller than it was. I loved her. Not neatly. Not well, some days. But truly."
Jack said nothing.

Geralt looked toward the stream. Yennefer stood with Ciri, black against gray, one hand lifted to brush rain from Ciri's hair and stopping before public tenderness became too visible. She had always been like that. Love arriving as control, correction, precision, a room arranged so someone survived.
"I chose Triss," Geralt continued. "In this life, on this road. Not because Yennefer stopped mattering. Not because Triss was easier. She is not. She only hides the knife in warmth."
Jack's mouth moved faintly. "That seems accurate."

"Yennefer still matters. Ciri is my daughter in every way that would make blood feel redundant. Triss is my partner. Yennefer is Ciri's mother. All of that is true. All of it stands in the same room and breaks furniture if people pretend otherwise."
"Why tell me?"

Geralt looked back at him. "Because you walk into rooms and measure exits. This room has none. If Ciri chooses you, if Yennefer chooses closeness to you, if either of them gives you trust, desire, fear, loyalty, anything, you do not get to treat it as comfort."
Jack's face closed, then opened by a fraction because the words had hit the part of him trained to hear practical warnings.
Geralt stepped closer. "You treat it like a blade someone handed you hilt-first. Carefully. With both hands if needed. Never forgetting the edge faces them if you turn wrong."
Rain clicked on the birch leaves.
"You think I would use them," Jack said.

"No." Geralt's answer was immediate, and it mattered. "I think you would leave to spare them. I think you would decide your absence harms them less. I think if the arithmetic gets ugly enough, you will put yourself into the sum and call the result necessary before anyone can stop you."
Jack looked toward the grave. "You have developed opinions."
"I have experience with fools."
"Including yourself."
"Mostly."

The honesty made the warning harder to dismiss. Jack turned to Ciri. She had finished speaking with Yennefer and was now pretending not to watch him. Yennefer did not bother pretending. That, too, was a kind of mercy.
"What do you want from me?" Jack asked.
Geralt's expression tightened, because want had too many wrong answers.
"Do not make love another reason to disappear," he said.
Jack breathed once, slowly.
"That an order?"
"No."
"Request?"
"Warning."
"As a witcher?"

Geralt looked at the grave, the blue bead under stone, the road east, the horse waiting with all the impatience of living things that did not care for human tragedy unless it delayed feed. "As someone who is beginning to care whether you come back."
The words were clumsy. Too direct for Geralt. Too late for many things. Exactly on time for this one.
Jack looked down at the strap. His hand had tightened around it so hard the leather bent.
"That was almost a speech," he said.
"I know. I feel unwell."
"Sit down. It may pass."
Geralt did smile then. Briefly. Badly. There it was.
Jack released the strap. "I will not promise what I may not be able to keep."
"Good. Promises made to comfort the listener are usually lies wearing perfume."
"Yennefer say that?"
"No. She uses better perfume."
Jack looked toward the road. "I will remember the warning."
Geralt nodded. It still left the wound open. It was what they had.
They left the grave before sunset.

Not because grief was finished. Because unfinished grief traveled better than night roads in hostile country. Roche and Ves parted first, taking the quiet roads back toward Temerian business, false permits, and a country that survived by pretending its compromises were temporary. Roche gave Jack no embrace, no blessing, no patriotic nonsense. He gave him a folded paper with three names and said, "If any of these men offer help, ask what their children need before trusting the price."
Ves gave Ciri a look that contained a warning, a salute, and the practical assessment that the future empress needed better field boots. Ciri accepted all three without comment.

Dandelion and Priscilla went west with Zoltan to poison Cazren's song before it became the only tune poor grief remembered. Dandelion complained that no one appreciated the sacrifice of sending him away from the main tragedy. Priscilla told him tragedy was easier to survive at a distance and more difficult to rhyme honestly. Zoltan said both were idiots and checked the coin pouch twice.
Regis remained until the last moment.
"I will follow at a civilized distance," he told Geralt. "Which, in our present circumstances, means near to be useful and far from blame for everyone's mood."
"Too late," Geralt said.
"Yes, I feared as much."
He turned to Jack. "Remember what I said."
"You said many things."
"Then begin with the worst."
"Living prisons become duties that breathe."
"Very good. Horrifying, but retained accurately."
Regis inclined his head and walked into the trees with the quiet of something that did not need roads.

Saesenthessis appeared once more on the low ridge east of the birches. Ciri saw her first, or thought she did. The dragon-woman's cloak moved in wind that did not reach the field. She looked at Jack, then at the grave, then toward the east.
"The North has given you evidence," she said. "Zerrikania will give you context. Do not worship either. Evidence lies by omission. Context lies by pride."
Jack looked up at her. "And dragons?"
"We lie by silence. It is more dignified and often worse."
Then she was gone.
Buck sneezed, perhaps at dignity.

The eastern road began as mud, then stone, then a line beyond the last wet fields where the air seemed already drier though the sea, desert, pass, and sanctuary were still far beyond ordinary sight. Asha rode ahead for the first mile because she knew the road and because following her gave Jack time to look back without witnesses directly in front of him.
He looked back once.
The birches hid the grave almost immediately. Good. A false grave should not become a landmark for strangers. It should remain a place the living could fail to find unless grief remembered the turn.

Ciri rode beside him after the first ridge. Yennefer and Geralt followed behind, close for danger, distant for dignity. Triss rode with Ilyra and the copied files, every paper wrapped against rain as if paper itself had become a species she was determined to domesticate. Buck settled into the eastern road with resentment, endurance, and one backward ear listening for Jack's breath.
"Morningstar," Ciri said after a while.
Jack glanced at her.
"That is what Dandelion will call the burial if we do not threaten him properly."
"We can threaten him properly."
"Priscilla will be ahead of us."
"Good. She has better aim."
Ciri smiled. Small. Real. Gone before the road could charge for it.

Jack touched the pouch where the bead no longer sat. The absence had weight. Not emptiness. Placement. The bead was under stone now, above a file, beside a hilt and a letter, in a country that was not home but had agreed to hold a little grief until he could bring the full wound east.
Love was not shelter.

Geralt had said it without saying it. Ciri had proved it by signing law. Yennefer by refusing to soften danger. Triss by copying vile words until they could be used against their makers. Asha by walking toward the country that might judge her failure. Even Buck, in his horse way, by moving east despite disliking all human plans on principle.
Love was responsibility.

Jack looked ahead. The road narrowed between two dark pines and then opened toward hills the color of old iron under cloud. Beyond them waited Korath, Elskerdeg, Faithel songs, the sanctuary, the Canyon of Stars, and the thing beneath all of it learning the shape of his blood.
Readiness had begun to feel like another northern superstition: useful in stories, unreliable on roads.
Motion would have to do until courage decided whether to arrive.

At the last northern inn before the road turned from empire's memory into trader's rumor, Jack bought oats, salt, two skins of vinegar, and a coil of rope from a woman who asked no questions because she charged so much that curiosity became unnecessary. Geralt bought dried meat and checked the shoeing nails on every horse. Triss sent one more packet west. Yennefer argued with a map until the map lost. Ciri disappeared for an hour and returned with a plain cloak, two knives, and an expression that discouraged questions about how either had been acquired.
Asha watched all of this with the air of a woman seeing northerners prepare for heat by purchasing objects that would later teach humility.
"Too much?" Jack asked.
"Wrong much," Asha said. "But learning begins when leather cracks."
Buck bit the rope.
"Your witness is impatient," she added.
"He dislikes philosophical supplies."
"He will dislike Korath more."
Jack looked east. For the first time, the road ahead did not smell of rain. It smelled of dust under wet air, as if another country had sent a warning small and able to fit through the weather.
He did not feel ready.
That was probably the first honest preparation.
They rode east until the wet northern light thinned behind them and the road began to smell, faintly and impossibly, of dust.

part_subtitle: The land that made the bloodline will either claim Jack or reveal him.

paragraphs: Extract from a trader's weather account copied at the southern caravanserai: Northerners ask when the desert begins. The correct answer is not a place. The desert begins when water stops being a thing you own and becomes a thing that judges whether you are worth carrying farther.

In the North, water is a convenience, a commodity that flows from wells and rain clouds, bought with ordinary coins and forgotten as soon as it is swallowed. But in the vastness of Korath, it is the sole arbiter of existence.
It is the law that cannot be bribed, the judge that offers no appeals, and the quiet force that determines which travelers will see another sunrise and which will become part of the shifting dunes.
Korath began before the sand.

It began with the road forgetting puddles. It began with grass thinning into gray wire under the horses' hooves and stones taking heat from a sun still too low to earn such confidence. It began when Buck stopped complaining about mud because there was none, then started complaining about dust because horses, like priests and kings, preferred known grievances to new governments.

The transition was not marked by gates or banners, but by the gradual fading of green from the earth, replaced by a dry, barren expanse of cracked clay and skeletal shrubbery that seemed to shrink under the glare of the sky.

Jack noticed the change in the reins first. Leather dried faster here. Sweat left salt on glove seams before a man had finished pretending the morning was tolerable. The air had less mercy in it. It entered the mouth clean, hot, and accusatory, and it made every old wound feel as if someone had opened a ledger and requested payment in skin.

The silence of the desert was different from the silence of the northern forests; it was not the quiet of sleeping life, but the heavy, waiting silence of a place that had long since stripped away everything unnecessary. He felt the dry wind scratching at his throat, a constant reminder of the physical price of simply existing in this space.

Asha rode ahead in a hood the color of baked clay. She had said little since the last northern inn, which was not unusual, but the silence had changed. In the North she had withheld answers. Here she withheld memory. The distinction was small to anyone who had not lived by listening to breath, hand, and the angle of a horse's ear. Jack had not survived this long by being anyone.

He watched her back, the steady, rhythmic rise and fall of her shoulders, and felt the invisible weight she carried—a history that belonged to this soil and this heat, a legacy she was reluctant to share with the foreigners who rode behind her.

Ciri rode beside him for the first hour, then fell back to argue with Yennefer about the map. It was not a loud argument. Yennefer made loudness feel unnecessary by sharpening every word until volume would have been vulgar. Ciri answered with the clipped patience of a young ruler who had learned that if she shouted, men would call it proof of temperament rather than proof that the room had become stupid.

They held the map between them, a dry piece of parchment that seemed increasingly irrelevant in a landscape where the dunes shifted overnight and landmarks were nothing but memory and bone. Ciri's horse, a fine grey gelding, shook its head, its bridle clinking softly in the dry air.
"The map says there is a dry wash three miles south," Ciri said, her fingers tracing the faded ink. "But the guide is heading east."

"The guide has a cousin whose wrist is whole and a sister's son whose freedom depends on us arriving in one piece," Yennefer replied, her voice smooth and cold. "He does not look at maps. He looks at the color of the dunes."

Geralt rode behind Jack with Roach and watched the horses. Triss watched the riders. Regis, when he appeared at all, appeared where shade should not have held a person and then made polite remarks about the heat as if the heat might apologize under social pressure. Saesenthessis had left them three mornings earlier with the explanation that Zerrikanian skies disliked being observed by those who remembered older scales.

It was, Jack had decided, a dragon's way of saying she would arrive exactly when least convenient. The company moved like a slow caravan, each member locked in their own thoughts, their boots and hooves raising small clouds of dust that settled on their clothes and skin like a gray shroud.
By noon, the first water seller refused coin.

His stall stood under a cloth canopy at a dry crossing where two paths met and immediately regretted the intimacy. He was old, brown as roasted bark, and thin in the way desert people became thin without becoming weak. Three clay jars sat behind him in shadow. Two boys with knives at their belts watched the jars, not the travelers, which told Jack the important thing in the scene.

The water seller did not call out to them, did not offer his wares with the noisy enthusiasm of a city merchant. He simply sat in the shade of his canopy and watched them approach with eyes that had seen many caravans pass and many travelers fail.
"Water," Geralt said.
"Memory," the old man replied.
Ciri glanced at Jack. Yennefer looked as if she had just heard a legal argument disguised as folklore and was prepared to dismantle both. Asha dismounted before either could speak.
"He asks for custom," she said.
"He asks for a memory," Jack said.

"Custom is often inconvenient when translated accurately. Coin buys from wells owned by cities. Memory buys from wells that survived cities. You give what the water can carry. If it rejects you, we buy dust instead. Dust is cheaper and less useful."
The old man smiled with four teeth and no apology. "The witness remembers. Good."
Geralt measured Jack's face. "I have several bad memories. How picky is the well?"
"Very," Asha said.
"Then it has standards," Geralt said. "Unlike some innkeepers."
The old man did not laugh. The boys did. Briefly, because their grandfather fixed them in place and restored the regional government of silence.

Asha stepped to the jars, placed two fingers on the nearest clay lid, and spoke in Zerrikanian. Jack understood none of the words. He understood the shape. An introduction. A restraint. An apology not for wrong done today but for failing to return when expected. Her shoulders did not bend. Her voice did.

She spoke of the family she had left behind, the graves she had not visited, and the duty that had kept her in the cold, wet forests of the North while her own people lived and died under the burning sun.
The old man listened. When she finished, he lifted the lid.
"She gave enough," he said in the common tongue. "Not all. That will do."
"You sell water with judgment," Yennefer said.
"I sell water with memory. Judgment is free."
Ciri almost smiled. "Expensive gift."
"For rulers, always."

The line entered the shade and stayed there. Ciri's face did not change. Jack saw the stillness that replaced expression. Yennefer saw it too and moved one step closer, not protective in a way anyone could accuse, but present in a way that made accusation expensive.

Geralt stepped forward, his boots crunching on the dry clay. "I'll go next," he said quietly. He placed his calloused hand on the jar lid. He did not speak in a foreign tongue; he spoke in the flat, dry voice of a man who had lived too long on the road.

He told of Sodden Hill, of the smoke that smelled of burnt hair and old blood, of looking through the bodies for a child he had thought lost to the fire, and the silent realization that he was looking in the wrong graves.
He spoke of the guilt of surviving when better men had died, and the quiet horror of realizing that the child was alive and carrying a destiny that would make survival feel like a punishment.

The old man watched him, his eyes steady and unblinking. For a long moment, the only sound was the breathing of the horses and the hot wind rattling the canvas of the stall. Then the water seller nodded slowly. "The old wolf knows the weight of his skin," he said. "Take."

Yennefer did not touch the jar. She stood before the old man, her black hair catching the glare of the sun, her violet eyes dark and unreadable. She spoke of the night she had spent in the ruins of Aretuza after the coup, when the halls were empty of girls and full of ashes, and the silence had been so heavy she could hear the stone cooling.

She spoke of the choices she had made in the dark, choices that had taken more than blood, and the realization that she would make them again if it meant keeping Ciri from the hands of the mages who wanted to turn her into a weapon.

The old man did not move. He regarded her for a long time, as if measuring the depth of her anger and the strength of her will. "The sorceress carries her own fire," he said. "The water will not cool it, but it will not reject it either. Fill your skins."

Triss stepped up, her face pale but her voice steady. She spoke of the lodge meetings, of the whispered plans to divide kingdoms and trade lives like grain, and the feeling of her own hands shaking under the table as she signed her name to decisions she knew would burn villages.
She spoke of the shame of being useful to rulers who did not know her name and did not care who died as long as the borders changed.
The water seller nodded. "The red one remembers the shame. It is a good salt for water. It keeps it from going sweet and lazy. Take."

Ciri stood before the old man last. She did not place her hand on the jar. She faced him with the clear, direct gaze of someone who had survived the desert of Korath once before, lost and alone, drinking the blood of sand monsters and talking to a unicorn that had no words to give her.

She spoke of the heat that had turned her mind to ash, the hunger that had made her forget her name, and the realization that the empire her father wanted to give her was built on the bones of people who had died for lack of water.
The old man's expression did not soften, but his eyes grew dark. "The daughter of the elder blood has walked the Frying Pan," he said. "She knows that the sand does not care for crowns. Fill."
Jack gave his own memory when Asha told him to.

He chose Willenford, not the battle, not the red flare, not Helena's letter, not the grave. He spoke of the boy Miro, the broken wooden horse, the mill collapsing like a verdict, the ground remembering what people had buried. The old man watched him with narrowed eyes and no reverence. That was a relief. Reverence was another kind of appetite.

Jack described the smell of the wet wood, the sound of the river grinding the broken planks against the rocks, and the quiet realization that the child had died because he was in the way of a plan he did not understand.
When Jack finished, the nearest jar gave a soft click.
The old man opened it. "The water accepts a man who knows buildings can be guilty."
"Useful moral category," Triss said.
"In the North you make buildings innocent by writing dates on them," the old man said. "Here we do not trust walls that much."

Zoltan would have liked him, Jack thought, and then remembered the dwarf was still two days behind with Dandelion, the heavy wagon, and the rumor knives that would be useless if they arrived too late. The thought made the road widen strangely. Friendship had geography now. Unwelcome development. In the old days, a witcher had no friends to keep track of; there was only the contract, the coin, and the next village.
Now he had a map that was full of names he cared about, and every mile he traveled east made them harder to protect.

They filled skins. The old man refused extra coin from Ciri and accepted two copper coins from Geralt because, he explained, witchers smelled of practical poverty and should be allowed dignity in small payments. Geralt stared at him.
"I have been insulted better," Geralt said.
"You have paid more for it," the old man replied.

The boys laughed again. This time the old man allowed it. The travelers turned their horses back toward the dry path, their water skins heavy and cold against the leather of their saddles, a small weight of safety in a landscape that promised none.
Nadir el-Kharim found them in the late afternoon by arriving from a direction that should not have held road.

He came on a narrow mare whose ribs showed but whose eyes were clear. A string of bone charms hung from the saddle, not decorative, not entirely religious, each one polished where fingers had touched it often. Nadir wore a blue scarf over his lower face, a white outer robe dust-stained at the hem, and a knife at his hip with a handle too plain for vanity. His boots were patched.

His bridle was excellent. Jack liked the bridle more than the man at first sight. It was made of thick, oiled leather with brass buckles that had been kept clean despite the sand, proof that the rider knew which tools deserved respect and which were merely for display.
"You are late," Asha said.
"I am alive," Nadir answered. "In Korath, that is punctuality with ambition."
"You took the upper wash."
"Bandits took the lower. I did not wish to start our friendship by becoming inventory."
Geralt turned to Jack. "He'll fit in."
"We are not friends," Asha said.

"No," Nadir agreed, cheerful in a way that did not reach his eyes. "You are a woman who once broke my cousin's wrist for cheating a widow on salt weight, and I am a man whose cousin still complains when the weather changes. In families like mine, this is nearly intimacy."
Asha turned to Jack. "He is the guide."
"I'm reassured," Jack said.
"That is because you do not yet understand my fees," Nadir replied.

He dismounted and bowed to Ciri with exactly enough respect to acknowledge rank and exactly enough lack of fear to suggest he had already survived worse customers. "Princess, empress, rider in a plain cloak, whichever name travels safest today. Welcome to the edge of a place that does not care who your father is unless he owns a well."
"He owns several," Ciri said.
"Then may he choke on the paperwork."
Yennefer's eyebrow moved. "Careful."
"I am. That was my diplomatic version."

Nadir's humor was a cloth over a knife. Jack saw the pressure under it. Debt. Fear. Calculation. The man had agreed to guide them because Asha had sent the right sign and because someone else had pushed him hard, making agreement profitable or survivable. Those were not the same thing. Men like Nadir knew the price difference.
He had the nervous, shifting gaze of a debtor who knew exactly how many days he had left before the collectors stopped using paper and started using iron.

They made camp where Nadir chose, not where the map suggested. The map favored an old well marked with a black dot. Nadir said the well was honest, which made it dangerous because honest wells drew dishonest men.

He took them instead to a shallow basin under a shelf of red stone where wind had carved the rock into ribs and old smoke stains proved travelers had once been desperate, calling the place shelter. The red stone rose above them like a wave frozen in the act of breaking, blocking the wind and casting a deep, purple shadow over their camp.

"No fire after moonrise," he said. "No metal left uncovered. No water skin set directly on sand. No standing with your shadow across another man's bowl unless you want him to think of murder before breakfast. No singing unless you are paying the jackals to attend. No asking if the heat is always like this. It is not. Sometimes it becomes proud."
Dandelion would have died of several rules at once.

Triss checked Jack's palm under the stone shelf. The red lines had darkened during the afternoon. Not flared. Thickened, as if heat had made the blood remember old grammar. She used a cloth soaked in bitter water, touched only the edge, and said nothing until Yennefer turned to her.

The skin of his hand was hot to the touch, and the red markings seemed to hum with a faint, rhythmic pulse that matched his heartbeat. It was not the fast, frantic pulse of fever, but the slow, heavy resonance of a lock waiting for a key.
"It is responding to the land," Triss said.
"No," Asha said from the edge of the basin. "The land is responding to him. There is a difference, and both are impolite."
"That should comfort me?" Jack asked.
"Comfort is not among the desert's gifts."
"It has gifts?"
"Thirst. Truth. Sand in places you cannot negotiate with."
Geralt looked up from checking Roach's hoof. "Charming country."
"It did not invite you," Asha said.
Nadir placed a clay cup before Jack. The drink smelled of smoke, salt, and something root-bitter, discouraging hope. "Tea."
Jack lifted it. "This is punishment."
"Medicine. In Korath the distinction is mostly marketing."

He drank. It tasted like a burnt rope had been steeped in regret. His stomach objected, then settled. The pulse in his palm eased by a fraction. Nadir watched closely, too closely. The guide sat back on his heels, his hands resting on his knees, his eyes fixed on the cup in Jack's hand as if he were waiting for the clay to break or the liquid to boil.
Jack lowered the cup. "You expected something."
"I always expect something. It gives disappointment a schedule."
"Try again."

The guide's eyes moved to Asha, then to the darkening east. "Men came through twelve days ago. Black coats under pilgrim brown. They paid in northern silver and asked where a red-eyed witcher would enter the Frying Pan. I sold them a lie."
"Generous," Geralt said.
"Expensive," Nadir corrected. "They knew one of my debts. A sister's son. Taken for taxes that were not taxes, by men who used a seal no one local recognized."
Black Ink had crossed the maps before them.

Ciri's hands went still in her lap. Yennefer turned her head slightly. Triss stopped wrapping the cloth around Jack's palm and began listening with her whole face. The news was not unexpected, but it made the canyon feel narrower.

The Black Ink were not soldiers; they were administrators who used knives when the ink failed, and their presence here meant that Jack's blood was no longer a secret kept within the ruins of Kaer Morhen.
"You guide us because?" Jack asked.
"Because if you die in the wrong place, they keep the boy and sell his debt to a man with softer hands and worse imagination. If you live, perhaps the account changes."
"So I am payment."
"No. You are trouble. I am hoping trouble falls in the correct direction."
Asha looked toward the stars. "He was always this honest when cornered."
"You liked me better silent."
"I liked your cousin better with two working wrists."
"Most of us did."

Geralt came over and sat beside Jack, his knees groaning slightly from the long hours in the saddle. He picked up a stick and began tracing idle circles in the dust. "Vesemir always said the east was too dry for witchers," he murmured, his eyes reflecting the pale starlight. "Said the oils ruined faster and the silver went black from the salt flats.
He had a contract once near the borders—some sand beast that lived in the old canal beds. Took him three weeks to track it because the wind kept wiping the footprints."
"Did he kill it?" Jack asked.

"He settled it," Geralt replied, throwing the stick aside. "Sometimes in places like this, you don't kill the monster. You just make a deal with the stones to keep it quiet. Remember that when we reach the sanctuary. Zerrikania doesn't look for heroes. It looks for locks."

The desert night arrived with no softness. Heat fell out of the air as if someone had cut its purse. Cold rose from the sand, clean and sudden. Buck pressed closer to Jack than pride allowed and pretended he had discovered something interesting near the man's shoulder. Jack rested one hand against the horse's neck. Under the skin, Buck's heartbeat was steady, irritated, and alive. Good witness.

Jack pulled his wool cloak tight around his shoulders and watched the stars. They were different here—larger, brighter, and arranged in patterns that seemed to watch the earth with a cold, geometric curiosity.

He slept badly. The cold was a physical weight that pressed against his ribs, a reminder that the desert was never empty. In the dark, he could hear the breathing of the others—Geralt's slow, even breaths, Ciri's occasional shifts in her blankets, and Nadir's silent, watchful presence at the edge of the shadow.
The red stone above them seemed to hold the cold like it had held the heat, releasing it slowly into the night.
Near dawn, the carcass was found at the edge of camp.

It had been a draconid once, perhaps a sand basilisk, though the head had collapsed inward and the ribs had opened from inside with careful violence. Not torn. Emptied. The skin remained almost whole, a leather bag with bones arranged like a polite lie. No flies touched it. The eyes were gone. The tongue were gone. The heart had been removed without breaking the sternum.
The flesh had not been eaten; it had been dissolved, turned into a fine, gray ash that coated the interior of the skin like soot.
Buck screamed before any human spoke.

Jack crouched beside the carcass. The air smelled of old copper, hot stone, and hunger that had not needed teeth. The wolf medallion trembled once and stopped. The barbed-star signet under his shirt warmed with a sickening intimacy, like a hand recognizing a door it had used before. He reached out, his fingers hovering over the dry, leathery skin of the draconid.
There was no warmth left in the body, but there was a pressure—a lingering resonance of the force that had hollowed it out.
"Not feeding," Geralt said.
"Learning," Saesenthessis said from the ridge above them.

The dragon-woman stood against the pale light of the dawn, her shadow long and thin across the sand. She did not look at the carcass; she looked at Jack. "Vharakthul is not a beast that hunts for meat," she said, her voice carrying the flat, heavy tone of her true form. "He is an appetite that hunts for shape.
He is practicing on the lesser things, learning how to hold himself in the skin of this world before he tries the host."
Jack stood, his hand rising to touch the star signet through his shirt. It was cold again, but his palm still throbbed. "He's close," he said.
"He is where he has always been," Asha said. "But the lock is wearing thin. Every time you use the resonance, you give him another finger on the gate."

They crossed the first customs line under a sun that had already begun charging interest on every breath. The guards counted water skins before names, blades before titles, horses before riders. Ciri offered coin once and learned, with the visible irritation of a woman accustomed to currencies obeying her, that imperial silver could not purchase a cup from a well protected by memory.

The old water-keeper took one look at her sealed purse and said, in Nadir's careful translation, that double thirst remained thirst. Ciri put the purse away. Jack saw the relief flicker under her anger, there and gone: the strange mercy of being useless to a system for once.
The desert taught in objects because speeches wasted moisture. A cracked tally rod at the border. A bowl of bitter water at a shrine where a child asked Jack for the memory that followed him.

Jack had given the boy a copper coin and the memory of the cold rain on Kaer Morhen's walls, a thing the child had never seen and could not use, but which he had accepted as if it were silver. Buck's cracked hoof pick on the salt flats, warning them away from ground that had no visible track and every intention of swallowing a horse.

A red scarf dropped by false pilgrims who had called their knives devotion. A hollow draconid scale filled with ash. None of it was prophecy. That made it harder to dismiss. These were the small practical things a country used when it wanted strangers to stop pretending that danger announced itself like a court herald.

At the first caravanserai, shade became litigation. Two families claimed the same strip of blue canvas while a guard too young for his authority tried to turn thirst into procedure. The courtyard was built around a dead fig tree whose dry branches rattled in the wind like bones.
The canvas itself was dusty, patched with gray twine, and large, covering four horses or six men, but in the heat of noon, it was more valuable than a house in Novigrad.

Nadir translated only the necessary lies until Tala's seal appeared on a courier tag carried by the man who had claimed innocence with both hands. The tag was a small piece of copper marked with three parallel lines and a star, the sign of the Canyon of Stars and the Faithel sanctuary. The guard took one look at it, bowed, and stepped back, his procedure suddenly forgotten.

Zoltan arrived in a dust-colored supply cart before the argument finished, beard full of grit and temper fully armed. Dandelion climbed down after him dressed like cargo and declared that if Zerrikania charged for shade, it ought to issue receipts for bad decisions. The dwarf was grumbling about the axle of the cart, which had survived three dry riverbeds only by the grace of dwarf curses and thick grease.

"If I had known the road was this dry," Zoltan said, spitting dust into the sand, "I would have brought more beer and fewer mages. Mages are terrible for the axle weight. They don't help push, and they complain about the dust on their sleeves."
"The dust is historical," Dandelion said, shaking his cloak. "It has been here since the first landing. One should respect its age, even if it has no respect for velvet."
"It has respect for nothing," Zoltan grunted, checking the wooden spokes. "Especially not for wheels. If we don't find grease before tomorrow noon, this axle will become a sermon on friction."

The canvas returned to its owner before sunset. So did three names from the rumor trail, two samples of wax, and one song that had been made wrong on purpose to bait the men who paid for wrongness. Zoltan had bought the names from a trader in the caravanserai's lower yard, paid for in Temerian silver that the trader had accepted only because he wanted to melt it down for buttons.

"The pilgrims are ahead of us," Zoltan told Geralt. "Not the holy kind. The kind who carry ink jars and lists of names. They have been asking about a witcher with red eyes and a horse that bites. They have three guards with them who look like they were trained in Nilfgaard and paid in Novigrad."
"Black Ink," Yennefer said.
"They have a ledger," Zoltan agreed. "And a man who knows how to use it. They are calling it a census of the eastern border, but they are only counting one family."

After that, the company stopped pretending it was merely traveling. Asha read the desert as a wound that had learned manners. Triss counted pulse, water, sleep, and lies with the same tired tenderness. Yennefer watched every local phrase that tried to turn Jack into function. Geralt became quieter whenever the road narrowed, which meant he was thinking too much and would later claim he had been checking horses.

Ciri stayed near Jack when local law pressed too close, not as shield, not as owner, but as a person who knew the smell of vocabulary sharpening around blood. Jack noticed and said nothing because some kinds of care arrived without speech attached.

By the last dunes before Elskerdeg, the road had shed logistics and become politics with stone teeth. Smoke stood on the horizon in one thin vertical line, rising from the pass like an accusation. Nadir studied it for a long time and stopped making jokes. "Elskerdeg does not wait," he said. "It calculates." Geralt, whose hatred of arithmetic was mostly moral, sighed.

Ahead lay gates, factions, water law, and a sanctuary that had survived by learning whom not to welcome. Behind them, the carcass of the emptied draconid cooled in the dawn, proof that Vharakthul's hunger had entered flesh badly and intended to keep practicing.

Entry from Nadir el-Kharim's water book, disputed by three creditors: a customs line counts water skins before names. The northern party paid in coin, argument, and one useful silence. The horse was counted as a moral participant after biting the lip of a man who had overcharged for shade.

At first caravanserai, a dispute over stolen shade cloth became a trial before anyone had been allowed the courtesy of water. The courtyard was built around a dead fig tree and three living rules: shade belonged to whoever had paid for it, water belonged to whoever had protected it, and foreigners belonged to the road until a local person chose to risk a name for them.
A strip of blue canvas lay on the stones between two families, one knife, four witnesses, and a guard who looked young and still believing judgment could be tidy.

Asha translated only the necessary lies. Nadir translated the profitable ones, then stopped when Tala's seal appeared on a courier tag carried by the same man who claimed to have lost the shade cloth. Jack watched the man's hands. They were afraid of the tag, not the knife. That improved the question.

A dust-colored supply cart arrived while the guard was deciding whether truth required witnesses or merely better posture. Zoltan climbed down first, beard full of road grit and temper fully loaded. Dandelion followed with a scarf over his hair and the pained dignity of a man who had been told to dress like cargo for his own survival.

"If this country charges for shade," Zoltan said, looking at the blue canvas, "I hope it also issues receipts for bad decisions." Dandelion touched the torn edge of the cloth and sighed. "At last, politics with fabric. I can almost understand it."

By sunset, the canvas had been returned, the courier tag had been taken, and Nadir had begun to believe the northern party might survive more than one day for reasons other than luck. The arrival also repaired the road's arithmetic. Zoltan brought coin, wax samples, and three names from the rumor trail. Dandelion brought two songs, one wrong on purpose and one wrong because the world had paid a better liar.
No one had heard her arrive. Nadir swore with feeling. Asha bowed her head a finger's width. Ciri looked almost relieved, which said unpleasant things about the morning.
Saesenthessis descended through red light. "Vharakthul's hunger is teaching itself flesh again. Lesser draconids are becoming rehearsal."
Jack studied the opened ribs. "Hosting him does this?"
"Failing to host him does worse," the dragon-woman said.
The answer sat in the cold morning like a knife placed on a breakfast table.
Nadir pulled his scarf higher. "Welcome to Korath," he said. "Breakfast will be delayed."
No one laughed.
That was how Jack knew they had reached Zerrikania in truth.

Pass-keeper proverb, translated by a northern scholar and corrected in three different hands: A gate that opens for pity will one day open for fire. A gate that never opens becomes a tomb. The keeper's sin is choosing which dead can be counted. In the arid heights of the pass, mercy is not a feeling; it is a calculation written in water ledgers and paid in steel.

This dry wisdom had been carved into the lintels of Elskerdeg before the first northern kingdom had even drawn its first map, a reminder that in this land, survival is a cold arithmetic of resources and vigilance.
Elskerdeg Pass sold safety with the manners of a knife merchant.

It rose from Korath in tiers of red stone, pale stair cuts, wind-polished towers, and hanging bridges strung between cliffs too narrow for armies and too honest for diplomacy. The road bent three times before the first gate so that every traveler arrived with their horses tired, their water counted, and their pride rubbed thin by heat. Above the gate, bronze plates flashed in the sun. Not decoration. Signaling mirrors.

Jack counted six watchers before Nadir lifted one hand and told him to stop being obvious. The stone of the cliffs was a dark, bruised red, scored by centuries of wind that whistled through the narrow gaps like a warning.

The sun hung high and white in the sky, a flat plate of brass that seemed to drain the color from the cliffs, leaving only the dry, chalky red of the stone and the deep, violet shadows of the crevices.
"They know," Jack said, squinting up at the bronze glare.

"Yes," Nadir replied. "But there is politeness in not proving it. In Elskerdeg, looking too hard at a guard tower is considered a form of auditing. They don't like auditors. Especially not northern ones who carry swords and smell of old mud. In their eyes, you are not a traveler; you are a risk factor on horseback. A risk factor that has arrived with too many companions and too many weapons."

Buck disliked the pass before the guards disliked Buck. He stopped beneath the first carved arch, sniffed the stone, and showed his teeth to a painted dragon scale set above the lintel. The guard nearest him, a woman with a shaved head and a hooked spear, looked at the horse and then at Jack.
She had a long scar running from her ear to her jaw, white against her sun-browned skin, and her eyes were the color of flint.
"Your beast has opinions."
"He has standards," Jack said.
"Does he pay toll?"
"He bites receipts."

"Then he pays in critique. We accept several currencies. Mostly copper, sometimes water, occasionally the names of people who tried to enter without asking. The horse may pass, but if he bites one of the children, we will charge you for the salt to cure him. And the child's mother will likely have a few words for you that do not require translation. Zerrikanian mothers have very little patience for northern horses with poor manners."

Ciri's mouth moved. Yennefer noticed and pretended not to. Geralt looked at Buck with the grave solidarity of men who had both been taxed by strangers. Roach blew a soft breath through her nostrils, her hooves shifting on the dry stone.

Asha gave their names in Zerrikanian. She spoke in a flat, rhythmic voice that seemed to match the heat of the air. She gave some names fully and some with gaps, hiding the names of the mages and the princess under regional titles that suggested they were merely servants or companions of the Morningstar house. Jack heard his own name as Jack of the Morning Star House, hidden bearer, untested return.

The words changed the air. The guards did not kneel. Good. One spat over the side of the road, not at him, but near, expressing a political position. The shaved-headed woman looked at Jack's star signet through his thin shirt, her grip on the spear tightening by a fraction. The air grew tense, the heat of the sun reflecting off the red stone walls like a furnace.
"Good country," Geralt muttered.
"No worship," Jack said.
"You approve?"
"Greatly."

"I prefer a country where they throw flowers," Geralt said. "Or at least don't spit near my boots. It's better for the leather. And it saves me from having to decide whether to hit them. In my experience, people who spit near your boots are usually hoping you'll give them an excuse to use their spears."

They were taken to the middle court, where shade fell in blue strips from woven awnings and water ran in a channel guarded by three children with knives. The children watched every cup drawn from the channel and made tally marks on clay tablets. Water was law here, and law had smaller hands than Jack expected.
The court smelled of dry dust, roasted meat, and the faint, sweet scent of crushed mint leaves that someone had thrown into the water channel to cool the air.
The council of the pass waited under a stone roof supported by pillars carved with old names. There were nine seats. Only seven were occupied. Nadir whispered the factions as if reading weather.

"Protect," he said, nodding to three elders wearing sand-white sashes. "Led by Mother Varda, the old priestess who believes in the prophecy of Zerrikanterment. They believe you must be taught and prepared before foreigners use you. They are the ones who will want to keep you in a cell and read you old poems until your eyes bleed. Exploit, two seats with copper rings.

"That's Kaelen, the merchant who wants to sell your lock-force to the highest bidder—probably Nilfgaard or the mages in Kovir. They believe better local hands on the key than northern hands. They will try to marry you to a cousin and charge us for the wedding. Purge, two seats, black cords at the wrist. That's Soren, the veteran who lost his entire family to Vharakthul's last emergence.
"They believe a living key invites the lock to learn.

"They will speak of mercy while thinking of knives. They believe the only safe morningstar is one that has been buried under six feet of dry sand. They will try to make certain you do not see the Canyon of Stars."
"And the empty seats?" Ciri asked.

"Dead, undecided, or wisely absent. In politics those are cousins. Sometimes they are the same person, depending on how the night went. In Elskerdeg, an empty chair is often the most honest seat in the room. It means someone knew they were going to lie and had the decency to do it in their own garden."

While the council was in the inner chamber, arguing over water ledgers and old transit maps, Geralt and Yennefer stood together near the dry fountain in the middle court. The sorceress adjusted her black cuffs, her eyes fixed on the distant signaling mirrors.

"Vesemir kept his secrets well," Yennefer said, her voice quiet but sharp, cutting the heavy air. "He trained Jack at Kaer Morhen, under our noses, and never once mentioned the Morningstar bloodline. If I had known, I could have analyzed the seal years ago, before the Black Ink began their census. We could have found a containment rite that didn't involve Jack carrying a god in his ribs."

Geralt sighed, his hand resting on the pommel of his sword. "He was trying to protect him, Yen. Two children of prophecy in the same castle would have drawn mages and kings like flies to a carcass. He knew what the Lodge did to Ciri. He didn't want the same for Jack. He was a witcher, not a politician. He saw a child who needed training and shelter, and he gave him both."

"He was also containing him," Yennefer replied, her violet eyes turning to him, cold and brilliant. "A body is a poor container for a dragon-seal, Geralt. You know that. Every time Jack uses his power, he gives the Obsidian Crown another anchor. Ciri sees it too. She is terrified, not of the monster, but of the choices we will have to make if the lock fails.
"She knows what it's like when the world decides you are a gate instead of a person."
"We'll cross that bridge when we reach it," Geralt said.
"In Korath, bridges have a habit of being made of bone," Yennefer murmured, turning away to join Ciri.
Tala of Elskerdeg entered after the council had stared past courtesy.

She came through the side arch wearing loose black trousers, a sleeveless leather cuirass, and a scarf of deep red wound once around her throat. Her hair was dark and bound at the nape with copper wire. A curved blade hung at one hip. She had the kind of beauty that did not ask to be admired because it was too busy deciding whether admiration was a weakness in the admirer.

Her eyes went first to Jack's hands, then to his shoulders, then to Buck beyond the gate, and only after that to his face. She moved with the light, balanced stride of someone who spent her life on cliffs and bridges, her boots making no sound on the stone.
"This is the last bearer?" she asked in the common tongue. Her voice was low, carrying a slight, rough edge like sand moved by wind.
Asha answered before Jack could. "This is Jack."
Tala turned to her. "Your correction has teeth now. Good. It was late growing."
Asha's face did not change. Her grief had discipline. "So did your courtesy."
Nadir made a small delighted sound and looked at the ceiling, perhaps asking the gods to let him live long enough to repeat this.

The eldest of Protect raised one hand. "The pass recognizes the witness Asha. It recognizes the Faithel mark she carries. It recognizes the claim that this man bears Morningstar blood. Recognition is not welcome. The North is full of names that are useful until they arrive here. We have too many names already. Names carry ghosts, and ghosts are terrible for the water supply."
"Efficient," Jack said.
"That is a northern word," Tala said.
"It's a tired word. Travel improved it."
Her mouth curved a fraction. "Perhaps. Or perhaps travel merely made you lazy. We shall see."
The council argued for two hours.

They did not argue like northern courts. There was less velvet, less paper, fewer chairs designed to make lies comfortable. They argued over water ledgers, old maintenance songs, the price of closing the pass, whether outsiders could be allowed near sanctuary routes, whether Jack should be taught, bound, killed, guarded, or sent back north with supplies sufficient to fail somewhere that would not stain Elskerdeg.

Kaelen of Exploit leaned forward, his fingers twisting the copper ring on his hand. "A living anchor is a resource. Nilfgaard's administrators are already at the border. If we do not offer them a controlled key, they will bring their own, and their keys are made of iron and mages. We can sell the transit rights for Jack's resonance, buy grease for our wheels, and salt for the meat."

Ciri stood up, her green eyes flashing. "Nilfgaard does not buy keys, Kaelen. They confiscate them. I know their administration better than you know your water ledgers. If you open the pass to their scouts, they will not pay you in gold. They will bring three legions, name your gates after Nilfgaardian generals, and turn your council into a municipal office under the authority of a commissioner from Wyzima.
They will count your wells, draft your sons, and pay you in paperwork that you cannot eat."

Kaelen blinked, his mouth opening and closing as he studied her plain cloak and then at Yennefer, who was watching him with a cold, mocking smile. "Princess, you speak with the authority of the throne, but you have no army behind you."
"I have what happened," Ciri said, her voice dropping, clear and hard. "And I have seen what Nilfgaard does to borders when they find a local hand willing to open the gate."

"We do not sell keys to empires," Mother Varda said, her voice dry but carrying the weight of the temple. "The Morningstar belongs to the Sanctuary, not to the ledger books of a Nilfgaardian clerk. If you trade the seal for Nilfgaardian gold, you will find the gold turns to ash before the winter is out. We have kept the Canyon of Stars clean for three hundred years. We will not turn it into a Nilfgaardian province."

"He belongs to the grave," Soren of Purge said, his voice flat. "Every time a bearer has tried to use the resonance, the crown has breathed. We have three hundred graves in the Canyon of Stars that prove it. How many more do you want to dig, Kaelen? Will you sell the spades for profit? The man is contaminated. Vesemir training did not clean him; it only made the contamination faster."

Yennefer's face became elegant murder. Her hands rested on her lap, but her fingers were curved as if she were waiting for the signal to tear the room apart. Triss wrote notes in ordinary ink because rage, like magic, needed a place to go. Geralt listened with the expression of a man deciding how many people he could reach before the spears did.
Jack said little until Soren stood again, his black wrist cord catching the light.

"If the key carries corruption, the clean answer is to break the key. A dead bearer teaches no lock. The Obsidian Crown has eaten three families before this one. We do not need a fourth to teach us how to bleed."
"Dead men teach plenty," Geralt said.
The council turned toward him.

"Usually bad lessons," Geralt added. "Like how to make graves when you should be making dams. Or how to die because you were too busy counting your neighbors' cousins. In the North, we call that a normal Tuesday. Here, I thought you had better sense. Frightened fools who think knives can solve a leak in the roof.
"If you kill him, the dragon will still be in the stone, and you won't have a witcher to hold the gate."
"Witcher, this is not your court."
"No," Geralt said. "Yours has better ventilation. Same kind of fools."
A spear butt struck stone, the sound echoing under the roof. Tala raised one finger. The sound stopped immediately. That told Jack her rank more clearly than any title.
"Let the bearer answer," she said.
Jack studied the Purge elder. "You can try."
The room tightened. The guards at the archway shifted their weight, their spears catching the red light.
"That is not an argument," the elder said, his jaw tightening.

"No. It is information you should have before making policy with my blood. If you try to break the key, you might find the lock opens anyway, and I don't think your well has enough memory to wash that out. The dragon inside me doesn't care about your council, Soren. He only cares about the shape of the teeth.
"If you want to test whether I can hold him, send someone who knows how to hold a sword, not a ledger."
Ciri looked down. Not hiding amusement. Hiding recognition. Yennefer did not hide hers, which was less amusement than approval sharpened thin.
Tala stepped into the open floor. "Policy later. First, test."
"Of course," Geralt said.
"You object?"
"Always. Rarely helps. It's a habit I acquired in Velen. People there were very fond of tests. Most of them involved mud and bad poetry. Or worse, relatives."
"Good. Then you are experienced."

The test was too informal to comfort anyone. They took Jack to an upper training court cut into the cliff, open to wind and sky. Seven pass-keepers watched from shade. Asha stood at one end with her hands folded before her. Ciri, Yennefer, Triss, Geralt, Regis, Saesenthessis, and Nadir were not invited, which meant all of them arrived at different distances and pretended not to be present in different ways.
Ciri sat on a stone ledge, Yennefer stood under a small awning, and Geralt leaned against a wooden post, his hand resting on the hilt of his silver sword.
Tala removed her scarf and wrapped it around her left wrist.
"Rules," Jack said.
"You ask that before every room?"
"Rooms lie less when forced to define themselves."

"Good. No killing. No maiming unless stupidity demands education. No crimson unless I ask for it. No witcher signs after first blood. No touching the water channel. If you reach for ownership, I cut you. If you restrain yourself to impress me, I cut you. If you fight like a hero, I cut you twice."
"Simple."
"No. Simple would be a duel. This is a question with knives. I am asking what your blood remembers when it is cornered."
She came at him before the last word settled.

Tala fought like someone who had learned heat as a teacher. No wasted movement. No heroic leaps. She used the slope, glare, dust, and the fact that northerners blinked wrong under white sun. She kicked sand toward his eyes, then followed with a low sweep of her blade that Jack only parried by dropping his guard.

Jack parried the first cut, gave ground on the second, and let the third pass close; wind brushed his throat. Steel answered. Their blades touched in short phrases. Question. Refusal. Revision. She was faster than he expected, her blade moving like a red thread in the sun, her movements shifting with the dust.

Jack tried to maintain a standard defense, his boots sliding on the dry stone. He thought of Vesemir's training in Kaer Morhen's courtyard, the old witcher's voice shouting warnings about keeping the center of gravity low and the eyes fixed on the opponent's shoulder, not the blade. But the sun was in his eyes, and the wind from the canyon kept shifting, blowing grit into his face.
Tala noticed his hesitation and pressed her advantage, her blade flashing in a series of quick, rhythmic cuts that forced him back toward the water channel.

First blood came from Jack's forearm. Tala opened a shallow line where his guard shifted to protect the old palm scar. She saw the reason immediately and attacked that habit three more times. Good. Cruel, and useful. She was testing his limits, finding the places where his mutations made him rely on speed rather than skill.
He stopped using signs.

The fight became closer. Body, breath, wrist, foot, shoulder. Heat rose from the stone. Sweat salted Jack's lip. His crimson pressure stirred behind the eyes, not from rage, but from the old blood's dislike of being tested by a place that recognized it. He felt the reach. Not toward Tala's body. Toward the fear of the watchers, the water in the channel, the old law under the court. Power wanted structure.

Structure wanted consent to become a cage. The dragon-force inside him hummed, a low, black vibration that wanted to tear through the limitations of the training yard. It was a tempting hunger, a dark offer of strength that would let him shatter her blade and end the test in one violent movement.
No. He contained it, pulling the force back down, locking it behind his teeth.
Tala saw the refusal. Her next cut slowed by the width of a thought. She saw the tension in his shoulders, the way his muscles bunched as he contained the resonance, and she respected the restraint.

Jack disarmed her without striking her hand. He stepped inside her guard, his shoulder slamming into her chest to break her balance, then trapped her blade with his hilt, turned the wrist, and let her own momentum put the knife point against his ribs while his sword rested near her throat. The result was ugly, balanced, and honest. Both could have died if pride sneezed.
They stood chest to chest, their breath hot and fast, the sun beating down on their shoulders.
Tala studied the sword. "You could have owned the court."
"Yes."
"Why not?"
"Because I came for a road, not a throne. Thrones have too many guards and too little shade. And the cushions are usually full of fleas. A witcher does not look for a cage he has to sweep himself."

The answer traveled through the watchers. Protect heard hope. Exploit heard inconvenience. Purge heard danger pretending restraint. Tala heard something else. Jack saw it in the change around her eyes. The hard, flint-like glare softened by a fraction, replaced by a curiosity that was older than the council.
She stepped back. "Elskerdeg opens the second gate. Not the third. Not yet. The key is whole, but the door is still deciding."
"Progress," Nadir said from somewhere too close to have permission.
"You," Tala said without turning, "will pay for the water you stole during the argument."
"I sampled for quality. It was a service to the pass."

"You will pay double for scholarship. And triple if you speak of it to the bards. Bards have a habit of turning double payments into long songs. And I do not wish to hear my water described in three-part harmony."

The room Tala chose that night was not luxurious. Luxury would have turned the encounter into performance, and Tala had no patience for performance unless it frightened an enemy into a mistake. A low bed stood against the inner wall with sun-dried linen folded at its foot. A brass lamp threw small star-shaped fires over the stone.

Two cups, one bowl of water, and a knife placed flat on the floor between them made the room more honest than softness alone would have been. In Elskerdeg, even tenderness began by admitting where danger was kept. The air in the room was cool, carrying the scent of dry earth, old copper, and the faint, trace of the tea they had drunk at the Caravanserai.

Tala entered carrying the shallow copper bowl from the unfinished ritual. Salt clung to its rim. Crushed herb darkened the water. A red thread lay across the surface like a small wound refusing to sink. "You left before accepting the salt," she said, her voice quiet in the small room. Jack sat on the edge of the bed and unwrapped the cut she had given him in the court. "I did not know leaving was an answer."
Tala set the bowl down on the stone floor. "In this pass, all movement answers something. Even the silence. If you do not answer the salt, the salt answers you."

She cleaned the cut without making pain ceremonial. Her fingers were warm, rough with blade callus, and precise, insulting his habit of endurance. When he did not flinch, she looked annoyed rather than impressed. She dipped a clean linen cloth into the water, the salt stinging his skin. "Pain is not a language you need to perform for me. We are not in the council chamber. You do not need to prove you are made of iron."

He almost made a joke. The room did not deserve a coward's joke. "Habit," he said. "Bad habit." "Most that survive are. If you don't hold yourself tight, the world shakes you apart." She tied the red thread around his wrist below the wound. It scratched skin already too aware of heat, scent, and proximity. "This means you were tested and not accepted. Not yet. It also means you were not rejected. Ambiguity has clothing here."
"Useful for politics," Jack said, his voice low.

Tala's eyes did not leave his. "Useful for desire too." The word did not arrive coyly. It arrived clean, armed, and adult. Jack looked at the visible knife, the unlocked door, the water within reach, the absence of guards, the absence of rite, the absence of any song beneath the stone trying to make consent into destiny. Tala had arranged the room so that refusal had architecture. That moved him more than perfume or fire could have.
She was offering him a choice that was entirely his own, free of the burdens of his lineage.

She stepped back once. "Say no and I leave with the bowl. Say wait and I sit by the door. Say yes and understand that I am not comfort, prize, cure, or surrender. I am asking whether the man who refused the court can enter closeness without conquering it."

Jack stood slowly, feeling every wound count itself. The air between them grew thick, warm, and alive with anticipation. The scent of dried mint and heat rose from the stone floor, blending with the smell of the dry wind outside. "I want to stay."
Tala's breath changed. Barely. She heard it in herself before anyone else could. A soft, sudden intake of air that broke her composure.

They crossed the space by inches rather than drama. Her hand rose to his jaw and stopped before touching, asking without becoming small. Her fingertips hovered just above his skin, the heat of her hand radiating against his cheek. He leaned into the space she had left, closing the gap until her palm finally settled against his cheekbone.

The first contact was not gentle in the easy way; it was exact, a thumb against the scar at his cheekbone, a palm that read him without pretending marks were decoration. The breath he released was quiet, a long, slow sigh. Hers changed in answer, hitching slightly. When they kissed, it was like testing a bridge in darkness: first caution, then heat, then the sharp anger of realizing the bridge might hold.

Tala tasted of bitter tea, dust, and a discipline that did not dissolve simply because she wanted. Jack kept his hands at her waist, feeling the strong, lean muscle of her sides under the thin leather of her cuirass. She guided one of his hands to her shoulder and the other to the back of her neck, teaching him without surrendering command.
Her touch was demanding but honest, her fingers warm and certain as they slid under the collar of his shirt.
"There," she whispered against his mouth, her lips warm and parting. "Not worship. Not fear."
"Responsibility," he murmured, his thumb tracing the line of her throat.
She made a low sound at that, a soft, warm sigh that broke into a gasp as he pressed closer, and kissed him again, deeper this time.

What followed did not hurry, though desire tried several times to make fools of them. Tala stopped him once to move the remaining knives farther from the bed, each blade set aside with the care of a woman who knew trust was not proven by pretending danger had vanished.

Jack stopped her once because her breath caught on the bruise at her ribs, a dark mark from some training match he had not witnessed. Each pause strengthened the next beginning. Each answer came clearer than the last: a hand returning, a mouth finding warmth again, breath breaking and then choosing not to hide.

Her breathing changed before anything else. It grew audible, uneven, not uncontrolled but allowed. When Jack's mouth found the place where her pulse beat hard beneath her jaw, a sound slipped from her, low and surprised, then returned warmer as he lingered, his lips tracing the warm skin of her neck.
"Mmh..." she sighed, her head tilting back to expose the line of her throat. "No worship... stay with me. Not above me."
He answered by waiting, holding his weight on his elbows, his eyes fixed on hers in the dim starlight. The wait made her fingers tighten in his shirt, pulling him down.
"Yes," she murmured, a soft, ragged sound escaping her. "Just like that, mmhh..."

She stopped trying to silence herself. Her hands slid up his back, her palms warm and certain against his shoulders, tracing the old scars left by Kaer Morhen's trials. The restraint they had carried all day began to weaken, replaced by a rhythmic, physical closeness that needed no translation. The heat between them built slowly, a steady warmth that filled the small room and shut out the cold wind of the pass.

Her breathing grew louder now, open, unhidden. When his hands moved along her sides, her body responded fully, a visible trembling running through her shoulders before she pulled him down into a deeper embrace.
"Ahhh~ Mmh.."
The sounds came in waves, carried on breath rather than thought. She clung to him, her fingers curling into his hair, her voice a soft undercurrent that rose and fell with each movement.
"Oh... gods, Jack..."

She did not finish, because the sensation gathered faster than she could follow. They moved together, not past each other, but present in every contact, their bodies answering the heat and the wind with their own quiet rhythm.

"Yes, just like that, mmhh..." she whispered, her hands sliding down to his hips, guiding him with a rhythmic physical description that had no need for named anatomy. "Don't stop... oh, God! You feel so good!"

The heat between them was intense, a silent negotiation of skin and breath. Jack felt the pulse in his palms humming in response to her warmth, not the painful flare of the dragon, but the clean, human heat of two bodies meeting in the dark. They shifted back and forth, up and down, a slow, certain movement that was older than the pass and more honest than the council's laws.
"Ahhh~ Mmh... right there..." Tala whispered, her voice breaking as she clung to him. "Stay... just stay."

When the intensity finally softened, Tala lay with one hand over his heart as if making certain he had not become symbol while she was not watching. Her chest rose and fell in slow, even breaths, her skin damp with sweat that smelled of dust and mint.
"Still a man," she said quietly in the dark.
Jack closed his eyes because the sentence struck harder than desire had. "Unfortunately."
"Good. We have too many symbols. Symbols are terrible in bed. They don't know where to put their knees."

He stayed until the lamp died. When the dark came, it did not feel merciful, but it felt honest. Tala's breath warmed his shoulder. Outside, the pass wind moved along the stones with the patient sound of a place that had watched armies arrive important and leave as bones. Jack slept for less than an hour and woke when Tala woke. Neither pretended not to be listening for attack.
That, too, was intimacy in Elskerdeg. Trust was not assuming safety. Trust was knowing who reached for the knife first and why.
The attack reached the second gate before dawn.

Purge opened one postern from within. Black Ink field men came behind them with restraint gear wrapped in cold iron nets and heavy shields. Cultists followed with red ash on their tongues and black crowns burned into their palms, their voices rising in a frantic, rhythmic chant that sounded like the dry rattling of locusts.
Elskerdeg woke not with bells but with water channels slamming shut, gates grinding, children running clay tallies to war posts, and Tala's voice cutting through the pass like a blade drawn properly.

Jack fought beside her in the blue hour. No crimson. Not yet. Steel, signs, shoulders, stone dust, breath. Twice he almost reached inward to draw the resonance, and twice Tala struck his wrist with the flat of her blade hard; the sting carried the lesson. "Not to save my pride," she said, her voice raw with dust. "Save it for the sanctuary.
If you use it here, the Purge will be right, and I hate being wrong in front of elders. Fight like a witcher, not a god! Witcher signs and steel are what we paid for!"

Geralt and Yennefer broke the water-tunnel assault from below. Geralt's silver blade was a blur in the dim light, parrying spears and opening throats with the clean, indifferent efficiency of a man who had defended Kaer Morhen against worse than cultists. He moved in a low, defensive stance, his blade deflecting spear points and cutting through the leather straps of the attackers' armor.
Yennefer's magic flickered in sharp, blue arcs, freezing the water in the channels to block the invaders and shattering their iron shields with bursts of kinetic force.

Ciri cut the restraint lines before they could be thrown, her blink-strikes leaving trails of white dust in the air. She moved through the yard like a ghost, appearing behind the net-throwers and cutting their straps before they could release the iron mesh.

Triss turned a poisoned channel warm, revealing the dye in it, her hands glowing with a soft, protective light as she filtered the water, neutralizing the acid that the cultists had poured into the main well-line. Asha named the traitor who had sold the postern key, her voice cold and clear over the din of battle.

Zoltan and Dandelion defended the lower yard. Zoltan's war cry, a gutter-born dwarven oath, was louder than the clashing steel, his axe spliting shields and wooden posts with terrifying strength. Dandelion stood behind a stone pillar, his scarf wrapped around his head, his hands holding a iron rod he had found near the stable, shouting warnings that were mostly accurate and entirely panicked.
"Watch the left!" Dandelion screamed. "The one with the red ash! He has a knife and a very poor attitude! And he's trying to ruin my cloak!"
"I see him!" Zoltan grunted, his axe taking the man at the knee. "He's shorter now! And his attitude won't help him walk!"

By sunrise the attack was broken, not defeated, but broken into retreat, leaving bodies, dropped restraints, one captured Black Ink courier, and a report naming a local hand. Elskerdeg had opened two gates. The third opened only after the dead were counted.

By sunrise, the attack was broken. Not defeated. Broken into retreat, leaving bodies, dropped restraints, one captured Purge elder, and a single Black Ink field note stamped with a copied Zerrikanian transit mark.
Tala read it, then handed it to Jack.
"They have a local hand," she said.
Jack looked toward the third gate. Beyond it waited the sanctuary.
Elskerdeg had opened two gates.
It was only when the fallen had been tallied that the third lock gave way.

Fragment from a Faithel teaching tablet, later recited by a child who did not know why the adults wept: A house that keeps a lock is not a palace. A hand that tends a wound is not a crown. Blood is not privilege. Blood is maintenance.

The journey through the lower foothills of the mountain pass had been a silent test of endurance. For three days, the Zerrikanian sun had beaten down upon their small company, a relentless hammer striking a landscape of red clay, white salt flats, and jagged limestone ridges that seemed to tear at the sky.

The wind was a dry, choking sigh that carried the scent of dust, scorched sage, and the faint, bitter tang of alkali. Jack rode at the front beside Asha, his hand resting on the pommel of his saddle, watching the way the heat waves warped the horizon until the cliffs in the distance looked like liquid metal pouring down the mountainside.

Behind him, Geralt’s horse walked with a slow, rhythmic clop, the witcher’s eyes constantly scanning the ridges for signs of movement. Yennefer rode in silence, her black curls pinned back under a simple linen scarf, her fingers flexing against the leather of her reins as if she were constantly measuring the invisible currents of magic that drifted through the dry air.
Triss and Ciri kept their horses close, speaking in low whispers that were quickly swallowed by the wind.
The sanctuary did not rise from the desert.

It had been cut into the place where desert, mountain, and old fear had agreed to share a wall. From the outside it looked like a series of sand-polished doors set into a cliff of pale stone, each door lower than a king would have built, each lintel marked by a star shape that refused symmetry by the smallest possible amount. The wrongness was deliberate. Jack saw it before Yennefer named it.

Perfection invited worship. The Faithel had built correction into their beauty, perhaps as piety, perhaps as warning. The dry heat of the Zerrikanian desert pressed against the pale rock, shimmering in waves that made the horizon look like a frayed thread.

The wind was a constant, grit-laden sigh, whistling through the narrow crevices of the red cliffs and depositing a fine, orange powder over the leather of their boots and the straps of their gear. Jack stood with his hands resting on his sword belt, his eyes fixed on the low lintels. There was no grandeur here, only a stubborn, ancient utility that seemed to mock the kingdoms of the North.
Asha stopped before the first door and did not move.
