"But he will never be a man. He will be a chamber. He will carry the hunger of Vharakthul in his veins, and the lock will draw the heat from his blood until he is as cold as Elias. He will be a wall, Helena, and a wall cannot love."
"Let him live," she whispered, her hands shaking. "Please. Let him live. I will sing the maintenance beat. I will keep the stone from drawing."
"The stone always draws," the dragon said, his great eyes closing. "But I will try."
The raiders broke through the door.

They were not imperial soldiers; they were men in black robes, their faces covered by silver masks, their hands glowing with a corrupt, greasy magic. They carried bowls of draconic blood, preparing to complete the contamination rite that would turn the seal to their own use.

Zerrikanterment roared, a sound that shook the sanctuary to its foundations. He did not breathe fire; he breathed light—a pure, golden force that filled the room, blinding the raiders and turning their black robes to ash. At the same moment, the dragon’s gold seal-force turned inward, focusing on the infant Jack.
Jack felt the memory hit his own chest.

It was not a picture; it was a physical sensation. His ribs felt like they were being crushed by a golden vise, his skin burning as the Cinder-Seal compressed into his infant flesh. He could feel the golden force fighting the black contamination of the raiders, the two powers twisting together in his blood, forming the knot that had defined his life.

He saw the dying dragon’s eye, a massive gold orb that reflected his own face, and then the dragon’s scales turned to charcoal, the great beast collapsing into ash. The golden force settled in his sternum, a cold, heavy weight that began to draw the warmth from his heart.

"Asha," Helena sang, her voice rising above the roar of the collapsing stone. She was sitting on the floor, her legs broken by a falling beam, her hands still reaching toward the place where the baby had been. She was singing the maintenance verse, her voice steady and clear, correcting the third beat as the ceiling began to fall. Her song was the last thing Jack heard before the stone took him.
Jack tried to pull away from the stone.
The memory was too heavy, the pictures turning to smoke and ash that seemed to fill his lungs. He felt himself falling back into the dark, his hands losing their grip on the stone table.
Hands caught him.

Not his mother’s. Real hands, warm and solid. Ciri’s hand was on his right wrist, her grip tight and strong, her green eyes close to his. Yennefer’s fingers were pressed against his left palm, her magic a cool, silver shield that pushed the memory back into the stone. Geralt’s arm was around his shoulder, holding him upright, his yellow eyes steady and calm in the fog.

The witcher’s grip was heavy, his leather-clad fingers squeezing Jack’s shoulder until the pain forced the cold Faithel past to recede, dragging him back into the room where the oil lamps still flickered.
Jack woke.
His palms were smoking against the stone table, the gold veins in the rock dark and silent once more. He breathed hard, the air cold in his lungs, his forehead wet with sweat.

Asha was shaking. She sat on a wooden bench, her face buried in her hands, her shoulders heaving with silent sobs. Tala stood beside her, her hand resting on Asha’s shoulder, her face hard and set. Ciri’s hands were clenched into fists, her jaw tight. Yennefer’s face was white with a fury she did not try to hide, her violet eyes flashing. Triss was crying softly, her hand resting on Jack’s sleeve.
Geralt remained silent, his hand holding the doorframe, his eyes fixed on the black wall.
Saesenthessis turned away.
"You knew," Geralt said, his voice flat.
"I knew what my father did," she replied, without turning back. "I did not know the details of the raiders' rite. I did not know how much corruption had entered the seal."

"Zerrikanterment made him a prison component," Geralt said. "He didn't gift him power. He didn't make him a hero. He made him a lock because the outer prison was wounded and his blood was the only thing that could hold the seam. You called it assignment."

"It was assignment," Saesenthessis said, her voice cold. "My father was dying. The sanctuary was burning. The raiders were preparing to open the gate. If he had not compressed the Cinder-Seal into the boy, Vharakthul would have risen twenty-three years ago. The North would have been ash before the first witcher could have drawn a blade. It was a choice between a dead child and a dead world. I would make it again.
"My father would make it again. Even your sorceresses, if they had been standing in that room, would have chosen the baby over the god."

"We do not make children into locks," Yennefer said, her voice shaking with rage. She walked to Saesenthessis, her face inches from the dragon's. "We find other doors. We fight. We do not bury them alive in the stone because we are too tired to hold the shield. If your father was too weak to hold Vharakthul, he should not have asked the North for help.
"He should not have stolen a boy's life to buy his own peace."

"The North was busy fighting itself," Saesenthessis said, her voice flat. "As it always is. If we had asked the kings, they would have argued about who owned the mountain until the deep had swallowed the valley. My father did the only thing that was possible. He built a wall. If the wall is ugly, then you may paint it, but do not pretend it isn't the only thing keeping the roof from falling on your head."

"We are not stone," Ciri said, her hand resting on Jack’s sleeve. "And Jack is not your father's wall. If the anchors are failing, then we find a way to kill Vharakthul. We don't just wait for Jack to freeze."

"Kill a god?" Saesenthessis almost smiled, her slitted eyes turning to Ciri. "You have the Elder Blood, gate-child, but you do not have the power of the first war. Vharakthul is not a draconid that can be killed with silver and oil. He is the pressure of the stars, held by the stone. If you open the lock to fight him, you only let him out."

Regis stepped forward, his face serious. "The dragon is correct about the physical price, Yennefer. The Cinder-Seal is not a active containment; it is an active decay. It has been drawing heat from Jack's blood since the day he was born. It’s why his body runs cold, why his sleep is filled with doors, and why his signet reacts to the copper channels. The seal is... eating him. Slowly.

If the anchors continue to fail, the pressure will increase, and the seal will draw even more heat to compensate. If we do not find a way to stabilize the outer anchors, the lock will draw until there is nothing left but Elias's salt."

"Then we stabilize them," Triss said, her voice rising. "We have the files from the Third Department now. We have the map fragments. We can find the other four anchors and rebuild them. We don't have to use Jack's blood. If the empire has files on the living chambers, they must have studied how the Faithel built the gates. There might be a record of another way to transfer the seal without using a child."

"If they do, they won't hand them over for a song," Geralt said, his hand closing around the doorframe. "We'll have to take them. The Third Department doesn't keep their libraries open for northern guests. If we go to Vicovaro, we go with swords drawn."

"You can't rebuild them without the Morningstar blood," Sera said, her voice cold as the stone. "The anchors were keyed to Helena's line. Only her son can touch them without setting off the collapse. If you try to cast your northern magic on the Skellige cliff, the draconid bones will shatter, and the anchor will weep until the sea is black. It’s a closed loop. The blood is the key, and the blood is the lock."

Yennefer turned her back on them, her shoulders tight. "There are no closed loops. Only lazy mages. We will find the Skellige anchor first. If the sea-water is black, we will filter it. If the bones are cracked, we will weld them. But we are not going to let this boy become a room."
Jack stood up from the table. His hands were still red where they had touched the stone, the signet on his finger cold as ice. He looked at Saesenthessis, then at Geralt, and finally at Ciri.
"How many doors?" Jack asked.
Saesenthessis watched the heavy stone doors of the chamber begin to close, the mechanism grinding in the dark.
"Fewer than yesterday," she said.
Saesenthessis found him above the sanctuary before dawn.

Jack had climbed there because sleep had become a room full of burning doors, and because the path was narrow enough that anyone following would have to announce care by breathing too loudly. The eastern sky had begun to pale. Below, the sanctuary channels were dark lines in stone. Children crossed the lower court with baskets of bread. A woman laughed at a dropped jar.
Ordinary life moving under the shadow of a decision no one had yet named aloud.
"My father would have lied less," Saesenthessis said.
Jack did not turn. "About what?"
"About hope. He preferred brutal honesty. I have often preferred dignified omissions."
"You call that an apology?"
"No. Dragons apologize badly. Usually by standing where arrows land."
Only then did he turn to her. Her face held neither pride nor performance for once. The old draconic stillness remained, but it had been thinned by guilt.

"Zerrikanterment knew living chamber doctrine," she said. "All golden dragons old, remembering the first war knew the shape of the last horror. He did not intend it for you. That matters. It also does not save you."
"Does anything?"
"People confuse saving with preventing pain. This has caused many foolish policies and most love songs."
The corner of his mouth moved. "Dandelion would object."
"Then he may write a worse sentence."
They stood while the sun placed a thin copper edge on the cliffs.
"If it comes to it," Jack said, "you will say the words."
Saesenthessis closed her eyes.

"I will not ask Ciri," he continued. "I will not ask Yennefer to name the thing she hates. I will not ask Geralt. He would hear it as permission to stop me. Triss would search until the last second, and that is her work. Asha would break on the old sin. Tala would call it by the pass name and make it a challenge. You can make everyone hate you and remain standing."
"You have learned cruelty from us quickly."
"No. I learned assignment."

The Faithel prepared memory with salt, blood, and refusal. It was not trance, Asha said. Trance sounded too much like surrender. This was witness with teeth. Jack sat inside the circle while Ciri, Yennefer, Geralt, Triss, Tala, and Saesenthessis stood beyond it, close to stop the rite if it became murder, far enough that his mother's face, if it came, would not have to arrive before an audience too eager to claim her.

Memory did not begin with slaughter. That was the mercy and the cruelty. It began with Helena mending a strap under a window while Jacob argued that a child should inherit bread before duty. It began with a cup placed out of reach of an infant because duty did not excuse stupidity.

It began with a blue-threaded cloth, a brass fastener shaped like daylight, and the ordinary impatience of two people who had known they were carrying history and still complained about stale flour. The file had called them terminated and obstruction. The song gave them hands.

When the massacre came, it did not come as spectacle. It came as smoke forced under a door, boots on stairs, the wrong prayer spoken by men who had stolen enough doctrine to make murder feel ceremonial. Asha's younger self ran where she had been ordered to run. Helena did not. Jacob bought time with a sword that was already losing. Jack heard none of it as accusation.

The anger had nowhere clean to gather. Forgiveness would have been cleaner if the dead had demanded it. Instead, the last warden's song gave him people, not relics, and left him to carry the weight of that gift awake.

The price did not announce itself at once. They arrived later as a changed route, a different silence, a cup passed with the wrong hand, or a horse refusing ground it had crossed yesterday without complaint. The consequence was not an answer, and that made it more trustworthy. Answers were what frightened courts demanded before breakfast.

This was only a pressure change, a small alteration in how the company arranged itself when the road narrowed: Ciri nearer to Jack, Geralt a step behind rather than before, Yennefer watching language, Triss watching bodies, Asha watching memory, Tala watching permission. A nilfgaardian sword hilt wrapped in black leather had done that. It forced everyone to show what they protected first.
Even the silence afterward had weight, and Jack had learned to respect anything that made strong people count breaths.
Her eyes opened. "If I say it, they may never forgive me."
"Good," Jack said. "Then someone will have kept the price visible."
Below, Buck kicked the stall wall. The sound climbed to them, blunt and ordinary.
Saesenthessis almost smiled. "Your horse disapproves of prophecy."
"He disapproves of closed spaces, cheap oats, bad roads, and most people. Prophecy is included by principle."
"Sensible beast."
"Don't tell him."

When Jack returned to the lower court, Geralt looked at the ridge, then at him, and asked no question. That was good. Questions would have required lies, and the day had already begun collecting enough of those.

Recovered Black Ink field order, edges burned: Authority is clearest at crisis. Local objections, religious panic, and familial attachments must be converted into preservation language. Subject is to be acquired alive if containment remains viable. If hostile draconic manifestation prevents acquisition, priority shifts to preventing uncontrolled ownership by cult, Faithel, or imperial faction.
The last ordinary morning began with bitter tea.

The sanctuary of Elskerdeg Pass was never intended to be comfortable; it was built to endure. Long before the first Northern kingdoms drew borders in ink or Nilfgaard extended its black-clad arms across the Yaruga, the Faithel had carved these halls from the cold, iron-veined basalt of the canyon. At dawn, the light did not flood the stone; it crept, a thin, blue-gray needle that stitched the shadows together.

The air was thick with the scent of ancient dust, dry juniper, and the sharp, metallic tang of cold well water that had spent centuries under the weight of the earth. In the cracks of the high vaulted ceiling, the wind from the outer pass made a low, whistling sound, a patient note that had played since the first stone was laid.

The floorboards of the inner chambers, worn smooth by centuries of Faithel sandals and Witcher boots, answered the weight of those who walked them with a soft, dry creak, a small sound that felt like the room itself was breathing, remembering the countless feet that had crossed it in times of peace and times of ruin.

Asha gave the tea to Jack in a small clay cup before dawn, when the sanctuary still held the blue edge of night and the canyon beyond the third gate breathed cold through its cracks. The cup was crude, unglazed, and smelled of the kiln and scorched herbs.

The tea itself was dark as river silt, smelling worse than the dried wild mustard Nadir used for his stomach and tasting far more sincere. Jack drank it because refusing would have meant starting an argument, and he had already reached his daily tolerance for being discussed before sunrise.

His companions had spent the last three days analyzing him like an architectural drawing under threat of collapse; every breath, every twitch of his fingers, and every pulse of the crimson core beneath his collarbone had been categorized, debated, and filed away.
"This is vile," Jack said, his voice flat in the quiet of the inner chamber.

"It keeps blood from listening too quickly," Asha replied. She did not look up from her small brass mortar, where she was grinding dried root with a stone pestle. Her movements were rhythmic, steady, the practice of a woman who measured time in the scraping of stone. "The blood of the Morningstars has always been too eager to answer the earth. The tea slows the conversation."
"By frightening it?" Jack looked down into the dark, murky liquid.

"By reminding it that the body has older enemies than destiny," Asha said, her voice dropping into that quiet, heavy register the Faithel used when they spoke of things that had survived three empires. "If you do not frighten the blood, it will seek the anchor before the battle even begins. The seal is hungry, Jack. It knows you are here.
"It remembers the taste of your ancestors' devotion, and it will draw the heat from your chest if you give it the slightest opening."

Geralt of Rivia, standing near the heavy timber door with Jack’s sword belt in his hands, looked into the clay cup. The witcher’s pale eyes caught the faint light from the single tallow candle burning on the table. "Any left?"
"You do not need it," Asha said, without pausing her grinding.

"No," Geralt said, his voice a low rumble, "but I might deserve it. My knees are arguing with the weather, and the weather seems to be winning. The damp in these old stone chambers gets into the bone. I've felt it before every bad fight since Sodden."
"Later," Asha considered, her pestle clicking against the side of the brass bowl. "We keep punishments in order. First the boy, then the old wolf."

The joke landed badly and therefore honestly. It gave the room one breath of human shape before the day took it, a brief, fragile reminder that they were still people who could laugh, even if the laughter tasted of ash.
In the corner, a small pile of dried pine needles smoldered on a flat stone, sending up a thin thread of sweet smoke that tried, and failed, to mask the smell of damp earth and coming storm.

Ciri fixed Jack’s collar because the brass buckle had twisted under the heavy leather gorget. She did it without asking, stepping into his space with the quiet confidence of someone who had spent her life navigating close quarters and violent roads. Her fingers were quick, cool, and controlled. It was not a lover’s gesture in the open room; there was no soft lingering, no meeting of eyes that spoke of private promises.

It was not imperial either, nor ceremonial. It was the simple, practical act of a comrade correcting a small thing because the larger things—the army marching toward the pass, the ancient dragon sleeping under their feet, the fracturing of the world—had become entirely impossible to correct.

"There," she said, her voice quiet as she tucked the strap under the iron rim of his pauldrons. She leaned in closer, her brow furrowing as she adjusted the tension. The metal of the gorget was cold, but her breath was warm against his neck.
"You missed a strap," Jack noted, not moving.

"I did not," Ciri said, her green eyes lifting to meet his for a fraction of a second. "I chose not to improve you beyond tolerability. If you look too much like a soldier, the Black Ink will think we’ve hired professionals."
"Strategic restraint."

"I have been practicing," she said, her voice softening slightly. "The Nilfgaardians tell me it is the first rule of diplomacy. I prefer to think of it as keeping my hands busy so I do not have to think about how many of them we will have to kill today. Or worse, how many of them will try to write a report about us afterward."

Her fingers lingered one heartbeat too long at his throat, near the heavy silver signet that hung from his neck. She could feel the heat radiating from his skin, the strange, rhythmic vibration that was not a pulse but the hum of the crimson core answering the pressure in the canyon. It was like touching a stove that had been turned off but still held the memory of the fire.
Then she stepped back, her boots clicking on the flagstones, before anyone could look at the contact and turn it into public property.
Yennefer of Vengerberg checked his pulse next.
She did it for too long.

Jack did not comment at first. Her hand rested at his wrist, cool, precise, and smelling faintly of lilac and gooseberries, a scent that felt impossibly clean and foreign in this dusty, iron-bound sanctuary. Her thumb pressed over the place where his human pulse had begun to argue with the ancient, draconic pressure beneath.

Her eyes were not on his face; they were fixed on the pale skin of his wrist, watching the way the blue veins seemed to shiver slightly under her touch. She looked like a physician preparing to be disappointed by reality, and a sorceress preparing to punish it for failing her expectations.
"You are doing that thing," Jack said, his voice barely louder than the wind in the rafters.

"I do many things," Yennefer said, without releasing his wrist. Her voice was cool, but there was a sharp edge to it, the tone she used when the laws of magic refused to bend to her will. "Be precise, Jack. It is the only way we will survive your education."
"Pretending medical attention is not worry," he said.

Her eyes lifted, dark and violet, flashing with a sudden, cold fire that made him regret the words. "Do not become perceptive this early in the morning. It is irritating, and I have very little patience left for clever boys who think they understand the price of their own blood. I am checking the alignment of your resonance, not your emotions.

If the core starts to pull on your heart, you will bleed from your ears before Sorel Veyrane even reaches the gates. The magic we are using to contain this place is brittle; it will not tolerate a chaotic anchor."
"Too late," Jack murmured.

"Clearly," she said, releasing his wrist with a sudden, visible reluctance. She hid it instantly, her fingers moving to adjust the cuff of his leather glove, pulling the seam straight with a force that suggested the glove had offended her personally. "Your heart is beating like a trapped bird. If you cannot control the resonance before the Black Ink arrives, I will be forced to use a binding spell that you will find extremely uncomfortable.
"Do I make myself clear?"
"Perfectly," Jack said.
Geralt came last with the sword strap.

He had taken the scabbard the night before, saying nothing to anyone, and had returned it at dawn with a new line of heavy stitching done in thick, waxed black thread along the shoulder harness. The work was not pretty—Geralt was no tailor—but it was strong, the stitches even and deep.

Jack recognized the pattern; it was the same ugly, durable stitching he had seen on the old repaired straps at Corvo Bianco, the work of a man who spent his evenings in silence, preparing for the next hunt because he did not know how to say *stay alive* without making the sentence stumble.

Geralt buckled the strap across Jack’s chest, his thick, scarred hands moving with the slow, deliberate care of Vesemir. He adjusted the angle of the silver hilt so it sat exactly where Jack’s hand would find it, a fraction of an inch lower than the standard Witcher carriage.
It was the way Vesemir had buckled straps on boys at Kaer Morhen before the trials, before the hunts, and before the punishments that they had only later learned were lessons.
"Tight?" Geralt asked, his hand resting on the pommel of Jack's sword to check the draw.
"Stop," Jack said.
"Stop is vague."
"You dislike vagueness now?"

"In straps," Geralt said, his eyes fixed on the buckle. "Vague straps catch on brush. They let the scabbard shift when you roll. If a sword is half an inch off when you reach for it, you're dead. There’s no room for vagueness when things start moving. You need to know exactly where the steel is, and you need to know it without looking.
"It has to be an extension of your own shoulder, not a piece of gear you're carrying."

Jack studied him, taking in the deep lines around the witcher’s mouth, the silver hair falling over his forehead, the heavy shoulders that had carried the weight of the Continent for longer than Jack had been alive. "Geralt."
The older witcher’s hands stilled on the leather harness. "Don't."
"I didn't say anything," Jack said.

"You were preparing to," Geralt said, his voice dropping. "Your jaw goes tight when you're about to say something stupidly heroic. I've seen it in Ciri. I've seen it in myself. It’s an expensive habit, Jack. We aren't here to die for a pile of old stones. We're here to hold the line until we can find a way to break it.
"If Sorel Veyrane thinks he can buy a Witcher's life with Nile gold, he's about to learn a very hard lesson about currency."
"You becoming clairvoyant in your old age?"
"No," Geralt said, his eyes finally rising to meet Jack’s. They were old, tired, and entirely honest. "Just familiar with fools preparing farewell sentences. The strap is fine. Keep it that way."

Triss Merigold, sitting by the heavy oak table with her books of gate-theory and old Faithel maps, looked up. She saw Geralt's hands on the strap, saw the way his fingers lingered on the buckle, and understood something that passed across her face like pain choosing patience. She had known Geralt for decades; she knew the silence that came over him when he was preparing for a loss.

Jack had become one of the people Geralt might not save. The knowledge had been arriving in the room for weeks, a slow, cold draft that they had all ignored, but the stitch on the leather strap made it visible. Triss closed her book with a quiet sigh, her fingers tracing the gold leaf on the cover as if she could draw some comfort from the old paper.
Buck pressed his head against Jack’s shoulder when Jack finally reached the outer court.

The horse had been brushed, watered, and inspected twice by the Elskerdeg stable-hands. Nadir had spent twenty minutes insulting the beast’s intelligence, while a Faithel child had offered it a handful of wild oats and a compliment that the horse had ignored. Despite the attention, Buck still looked as if the entire eastern continent had been organized for the sole purpose of inconveniencing him personally.
He was a heavy, broad-chested gelding with a coat the color of wet sand and a temper like dry timber. When Jack approached, Buck shoved him hard, moving him half a step back against the stone wall.
"Yes," Jack said, reaching up to scratch the horse behind the ears, where the leather bridle had rubbed. "I know."
Buck shoved again, blowing a wet breath against Jack’s neck.
"Still know," Jack murmured.

"He says you are a stupid man," Nadir translated from a safe distance, leaning against a pile of empty grain sacks. He was chewing on a stalk of dry grass, his eyes dark and watchful. "He says the mountains are too steep, the water is too salt, and your companions have too many opinions for a quiet journey. He also thinks the oats are dusty and the wind smells of iron. He is a very literary horse."
"He says that often," Jack said.

"Then your horse is consistent," Nadir said, spat the grass out, and adjusted the long knife at his belt. "A rare virtue in companions. Most people change their minds when the arrows start arriving. The Elskerdeg guards are already arguing about who gets the water if the well is poisoned. They have very little faith in northern promises."
The siege began before the sun cleared the eastern ridge.
It did not begin with the sound of drums or the thunder of hooves. It began with the quiet, administrative click of iron horse-shoes on the causeway below the gate.
Black Ink came first as law.

They did not carry banners. They carried papers—long rolls of thick, white parchment sealed with heavy red wax and tied with blue ribbon. The riders were nine, dressed in clean, sand-colored cloaks that had not yet gathered the dust of the pass. They were accompanied by a field captain with a face like dry leather and a small squad of men carrying heavy wooden cases.
The cases did not contain swords or spears; they contained restraint gear, iron collars, containment grids, and the silver-threaded nets the Black Ink used to harvest "unregistered anomalies."

They halted at the outer causeway, their horses standing quiet in the cold air, their breath rising in white plumes. The field captain unrolled a declaration and began to read. His voice was flat, dry, and designed to survive moral contact. It was the voice of a clerk who had seen men die under tax warrants and felt nothing but the desire to finish his shift.
The words echoed against the high basalt cliffs of the pass with embarrassing clarity, carrying across the empty stone like a sermon in an empty church.

"Under the cross-border risk doctrine, the Bureau of Internal Security hereby declares emergency preservation jurisdiction over the territory of Elskerdeg Pass," the captain read. "The subject known as Jack Morningstar, unregistered crimson anomaly, is to be surrendered for public preservation, pending stabilized review by the joint commission. Local custodial groups will receive procedural recognition and compensation upon full compliance. Any interference will be treated as treaty violation under the peace of Novigrad."

On the walls, the Elskerdeg guards listened in silence. They were men and women who had spent their lives holding the pass against bandits and desert beasts; they knew how to fight a spear, but the clean, legal language of the North was a foreign weapon. Behind them, Faithel children with water tablets stood behind the skirts of their mothers, learning, perhaps too young, how clean language could arrive armed.
Ciri stepped onto the causeway.

She did not carry her sword in her hand, but she wore it on her back, and she did not wear the Nilfgaardian silver or the fancy leather of her court. She wore a plain, gray woolen cloak that had been patched at the hem, but the way she stood—shoulders back, chin high, feet set wide on the stones—made the plain wool look like an imperial mantle.
The captain saw the cloak, then the posture, and made the small mistake of understanding too late who he was speaking to. He began to adjust his papers, his fingers fumbling with the wax seal.

"You are speaking," Ciri said, her voice carrying through the cold morning air without effort, "to a sovereign adult, in a sanctuary that lies three miles outside your treaty jurisdiction, while using the word *subject* for a man who is currently standing within hearing. You may continue, Captain, if you wish to turn simple foolishness into international evidence."
The captain swallowed, his throat moving above his high leather collar. "Your Highness. The Bureau’s mandate—"

"The Bureau’s mandate," Ciri interrupted, her voice dropping into a register that made the horses shift their weight, "ends at the border of the Redania-Temeria customs line. If you step onto this causeway with those iron collars, you are not officers of the law. You are thieves. And I have very little respect for thieves who bring their own paperwork.

"If you attempt to cross the second gate, I will treat your presence as an act of war against the crown of Nilfgaard. Let Sorel Veyrane explain that to the council. He is very fond of paperwork; let him read a war warrant."
Behind her, Yennefer smiled. It was a small, sharp movement of her lips that improved nothing. It was the smile she wore before she turned a conversation into a graveyard.
Cultists came next as hunger.

They appeared on the northern ridge, rising from the dry juniper scrub like insects. They were dressed in pilgrim brown, their robes torn and stiff with dried mud. Their mouths were stained with red ash from the offerings they had burned at the lower shrines, and black crowns had been burned into their skin and their garments with hot iron.
They did not carry weapons of steel; they carried heavy walking staffs, rusted hooks, and the short, curved knives used for skinning goats.

Brother Cazren stood at their center. He had shaved his head since Jack had last seen him, and his scalp was white and scarred from the sun. His face was gaunt, the skin stretched tight over his cheekbones, and his eyes had the bright, unfocused fever of a man who had stopped looking at the world and started looking only at his own thoughts.
He did not wait for the Black Ink to finish their declaration. He did not wait for anyone to ask him why he was there. He lifted both hands, his fingers curled like claws, and began to preach.

"The red door stands among you!" Cazren cried, his voice cracking on the high notes. "The weak age ends! It does not end in frost, as the Northern fools believe. It does not end in the fire of the dragons. It ends in correction! The Crown breathes! The door walks! Kneel, you children of dry grass, kneel before the hierarchy that was made before your fragile laws learned how to dry ink!
"The Crimson Wolf is the key, and the key belongs to the altar! Give us the vessel, or we will turn these stone halls into a slaughterhouse! The Crown demands its flesh, and it will have it!"
Geralt sighed, the sound low and dry in his throat. "I miss drowners."
"No one misses drowners, Geralt," Triss said, her hands already beginning to glow with a faint, warm orange light beneath her cloak.

"I do now," Geralt said, his hand settling on the hilt of his steel sword. "Briefly. They don't preach. They don't have paper. They just try to eat your boot, and then you kill them, and then you go get a beer. It was a simpler time."
"Progress is very difficult," Nadir agreed, though he did not look up from his grass-chewing. "It brings many specialists."
Compromised guardians came last.

That was the part that hurt Asha worse than the Black Ink and Brother Cazren combined. They did not arrive in a body; they came from the side paths, the narrow goat tracks that the Elskerdeg Pass-keepers had used for generations to bring water and wood to the sanctuary.
They were men and women from Purge, the faction that believed the Morningstar line was a plague that had to be burned out, and a few from Exploit, who wanted the core for their own gates.

Three of them had taken Faithel training under Asha herself; they knew the rhythm of the guards' watch, they knew where the stone was soft, and they knew where the songs of maintenance had to be repeated to keep the gates from sliding shut.

They opened the lesser paths, not breaking the main sanctuary wall, but letting mercenaries in from the rear. Old fear made them efficient. When a man believes he is saving his children from a monster, he does not hesitate to betray his neighbor.

The mercenaries followed because ordinary coin never missed the chance to make history uglier. They were the Free Company of the Red Desert, men who had desert-rust on their mail and cared nothing for the Faithel or the Black Ink, but cared very much for the gold Sorel Veyrane had promised them for a living delivery.
The battle began as arguments and became dust.

The first arrow was fired by an Elskerdeg scout whose cousin had died in the well-house three nights ago. It struck the Black Ink captain’s horse in the neck. The horse reared, throwing the captain into the dry dirt, and the sand-colored cloaks vanished behind a line of iron-rimmed shields.

Yennefer cut a path through the first wave of cultists with a white fire so precise it seemed surgical. She did not cast the fire in broad sheets; she threw it in thin, blinding needles that took the eyes of the leaders and left the rest to stumble in the smoke. Triss shielded the water carriers who were trying to drag the storage skins into the inner keep.

She stood on the upper terrace, her red hair catching the morning sun, her hands weaving a web of orange light that turned the incoming crossbow bolts into harmless ash before they touched the children.
Ciri vanished.
One moment she was standing on the causeway, her hand on her cloak; the next, she was a green-blink three yards behind the Black Ink shield line. Her sword, Zireael, made a sound like a wet whip.

She did not kill the men if she could help it—she had promised Geralt she would try to keep the numbers down—but she cut their straps, their knees, their hands, and the leather leads of their restraint gear. The men fell back in confusion, their formation breaking before they could find a target for their crossbows.

Geralt moved through the causeway with economic violence. He did not use signs; he did not use bombs; he used the old, cold craft of the sword. He parried a spear, stepped inside the shaft, and broke the wielder's collarbone with the pommel. He turned, took a mercenary's sword on his silver guard, and kicked the man off the causeway into the dry ditch twenty feet below.
There was no flourish in his movements, no display for the watchers. He was just a man clearing a path, his face grey and expressionless under the dust.
Jack held the anchor gate.

That had been the plan. Bad plans, Jack had learned, often survived because all the better alternatives had died earlier in the week. The anchor gate was a narrow archway of dark, polished basalt that led to the central chamber where the seal was housed.
The stone here was carved with the names of the five original keepers, and the floor was grooved with channels that had once carried the sacrificial blood of the Faithel.

The gate needed his blood near it, not in it. Asha and Sera stood on the small stone platform above the arch, their voices rising in the Faithel tongue, a high, rhythmic song that sounded like water falling over dry shingles. The song was the maintenance line, the sequence of sounds that kept the basalt from expanding under the heat of the core.

Above them, Saesenthessis stood on the high ridge, her human shape flickering like a reflection on wind-blown water as she held the draconic pressure from above, denying Vharakthul's shadow the ability to settle into the canyon stone.
Every enemy knew why Jack had to be moved. Every ally knew why he had to remain, and hated the knowledge.
The first breach came from below.

A cultist boy, no older than fifteen, had crawled through a dry drainage cut under the gatehouse. His face was smeared with black soot, and a crude crown had been painted on his forehead in red clay. He had a rusted skinning knife between his teeth. When he came out of the hole, he was shaking so badly he could barely hold the blade.

Jack saw him before the boy could stand. He was close; he could see the dirt under the boy's fingernails and smell the sour sweat of his fear. Jack could have killed him; the silver sword was in his hand, and the Witcher reflexes were already moving his arm. Instead, he twisted his wrist, caught the boy's strike on the flat of his blade, and stepped into his guard.
He broke the boy's wrist with a short, upward snap of his forearm, took the knife from his fingers, and shoved him hard against the stone wall.
Tala, who had been guarding the inner door with her short Zerrikanian bow, stepped forward and struck the boy unconscious with the heavy brass flat of her blade.
"Too soft," she said, her voice tight as she notched another arrow.
"Alive," Jack said, his breath coming hard.
"For now."
"Best most of us get," Jack said, turning back to the gate.
Then the anchor cracked.

It did not make a loud sound. It was a dry, snapping noise, like a green branch breaking in the winter. But the moment the sound happened, the air in the canyon changed. The wind in the rafters stopped. The dust on the floor rose three inches into the air and stayed there, suspended in the silence.

It was not the boy's knife that had done it. It was the blood. Too much blood had been spilled on the causeway, wrong blood, right place, wrong hour. The outer stone had drunk the chaos of the battle and remembered its oldest instruction badly.
The Faithel had built the sanctuary to contain the dragon's hunger, but they had built it out of the dragon's own stone, and the stone was beginning to remember its master.

Asha's song faltered. She choked on a word, her hands flying to her throat as if the wind had turned to glass in her mouth. She fell to one knee on the upper platform, her mortar tumbling over the edge and clattering onto the flagstones below.
Jack reached without thinking.
He drew the silver blade across his left palm, cutting deep across the old scars, and pressed his bloody hand against the polished basalt of the gatehouse wall.
Geralt shouted his name from the causeway. "Jack! No!"

It was too late. The stone accepted his hand with a relief that was so intimate it felt obscene. It did not feel like cold rock; it felt like warm, dry skin that was pulling at his blood, drawing the crimson resonance out of his chest and down his arm.

The core in his chest flared hot, the red light shining through his linen shirt, but he held it back, refusing to let the power open fully. He was the key, but he was also the lock; he had to hold the gate closed even while the gate was trying to drink him.
The old prison recognized the maintenance. The stone beneath his palm shivered, the red-brown heat spreading through the basalt, and the dry crack closed.
Something beneath the stone laughed.

It was not a sound. It was a pressure behind Jack's eyes, a heavy, black amusement that smelled of old gold and scorched wings. It was Vharakthul, moving through the stone with the patience of an emperor who had just watched a child learn a new game.

*Little wolf,* the pressure said. *You hold the door. But the door is made of my bone. The more you stitch, the more of yourself you leave in the seam. We are becoming very close, you and I. Soon, there will be no difference between the wolf and the cage.*
The seal cracked elsewhere.

On the high ridge, Saesenthessis looked down. For the first time, Jack saw fear in her human face before her pride could cover it. She shivered, her hands curling into claws, her golden eyes widening as she felt the shifting of the dragon-weight below.
The outer prison was learning him. It was learning the shape of his blood, the rhythm of his resonance, the limits of his strength. Every time he sealed a crack, he was giving the dragon another key.

By noon, the causeway was burning in three places. The water channels ran red where the cultists had been thrown from the terrace, and Brother Cazren was still preaching, his left arm hanging broken and useless at his side, his voice a dry rattle that would not stop.
Sorel Veyrane’s captain had abandoned his papers and his declarations; he was trying to drag his men back to the horses, his face white under the dust.

Jack stood at the anchor gate, his left hand wrapped in a bloody rag, his right hand holding the silver sword. The pressure behind his eyes was a constant, throbbing ache, and the crimson core in his chest felt like a hot coal that was slowly burning through his ribs.
The seal cracked again.
This time, the sound was louder, and the basalt did not close when his blood touched it. The red stone stayed open, a dark, smoking line that led down into the dark.
By the third hour, the battle had lost its grand declarations and become a matter of administration with screaming.

The grand terms—jurisdiction, preservation, correction, heresy—had been rubbed away by the dry wind and the reality of iron hitting bone. The causeway was cluttered with the debris of a broken army: dropped spears, smashed wooden cases, torn cloaks, and the bodies of men who had come to claim a key and found only a grave.

Black Ink men, ever disciplined, tried to mark their retreat positions with small yellow flags, even while the Elskerdeg archers cut them down from the upper ledges. A field clerk, his sand-colored cloak stained with ink and grease, crouched behind a broken supply cart and tried to keep the casualty categories separate on his parchment sheets.
He worked with a frantic, bureaucratic intensity until a Faithel sling stone took him in the side of his helm, shattering the metal and improving the honesty of his afternoon by ending it.

The cultists did not retreat. They dragged their wounded toward the channel mouths because Cazren had told them that blood spilled near the old stones would receive promotion in the corrected age. They did it with a quiet, terrifying joy, singing fragments of the crown-verse even as they bled into the sand.

The mercenaries, discovering that corrected ages paid very poorly when everyone died in the first hour, began to reassess the terms of their contract. They fell back toward the causeway entrance, their shields locked, their eyes looking for a way out that did not involve meeting Geralt's sword.
Nadir moved through the wreckage with a goat-skin water bladder and a long, curved knife.

He did not look like a hero. He looked like an angry merchant who had been forced to clean his own shop after a riot. Twice he dragged wounded Faithel children out from under the broken stone of the lower terrace, his movements quick and rough.
Once he stopped by a dead mercenary, cut the purse from the man's belt, weighed it in his hand, and threw it to a pass-keeper whose brother had died holding the western gate.
Geralt, leaning against a basalt pillar with his steel sword dripping red onto the dust, saw him do it.
"Death settles debts quickly," Nadir said, not looking up as he wiped his knife on his sleeve.
"So does theft," Geralt replied, his voice dry.

"The distinction depends on documentation," Nadir said, his dark eyes flashing with a brief, humorless amusement. "I am learning from your northern friends. They call it preservation. I call it recovery of expenses. The difference is only the quality of the ink. If we survive the day, I will show you my ledger. You owe me three silver for the oats, and another five for the water skins I have ruined today."
The third breach came through the water channel.

It was not men this time. It was poison. Sorel Veyrane's men had learned enough of the pass's grammar to know that water was the law of the sanctuary, and enough of the Bureau's cruelty to know that the law could be attacked where the children guarded it.
They had thrown three vials of dark, thick dye into the upper flow, a compound that did not kill instantly but turned the water to a bitter, black sludge that made the throat swell and close.
Triss saw it first.

She did not look at Geralt or Yennefer; she ran down the steps to the channel before the poison could reach the lower cisterns where the families were hiding. She dropped to both knees on the wet stone, her hands driving deep into the flow.
The water was cold, but the magic she used was hot; she did not try to block the water, she coaxed the poison out of it, her fingers moving in the current like a healer feeling for a bone.

Steam rose from the channel, smelling of sulfur and burnt hair. Her skin blistered where the dye touched it, the white skin of her wrists turning red and raw, but she did not pull her hands back. Yennefer saw her from the terrace and sent a thin, white thread of containment magic down the channel wall, reinforcing Triss's circle.
Together they held the line, two sorceresses standing in the spray while the mercenaries' arrows rattled against the stone around them.
A Black Ink captain, seeing them occupied, shouted to his remaining men: "Recover the witcher! The mages are engaged! Use the nets!"
Ciri heard.

What happened next traveled later in four incompatible songs across the taverns of the Yaruga. In one she became a white flame that could not be touched by iron; in one she became a demon from the outer spheres; in Dandelion's private draft, which he later hid in a drawer at Corvo Bianco, she became a woman whose patience had run out and whose sword was simply too tired of political theory to allow any more speeches.
The last was closest.
She moved through the Black Ink riders in blinks that were too short for fear to find a shape. She did not use the Elder Blood to escape; she used it as an interruption.

A blink to the left, and a captain's horse-lead was cut; a blink to the right, and a sergeant's hand was broken before he could cast his net; a blink to the center, and her sword, Zireael, was through the throat of the man who had reached for Jack’s scabbard with a heavy iron hook.

When she stopped, she was breathing hard, her hair damp with sweat and red dust. Six men were down on the stones, and one stood alone, his restraint pole shaking so badly it rattled against his breastplate.
"Run," Ciri said, her voice dropping to a whisper that was louder than the wind.
He did not argue. He dropped the pole and ran toward the horses.
Tala watched from the gate. "Your empress fights like a bad promise."
Jack parried a spear and kicked the wielder down the channel steps. "She is not my empress."
"No?"
"Not here."
Tala smiled without looking away from the next attacker. "Good answer. Expensive, but good."
The poison in the channel cleared. Triss pulled her hands free, skin blistered. Yennefer's face went white with anger, not at the enemy now, but at the price of keeping water alive.
The sanctuary endured.
Then the anchor cracked.

Cult verse heard at the northern ridge before the breach: The crown is not worn. It wears. The throne is not built. It kneels the world beneath it. Red door, open. Black breath, teach the small races their correction.
Vharakthul rose wrong.

He did not burst from the earth in a single, clean motion, nor did he emerge from the center of the canyon like a monster obliging a hero with good staging. He rose through failure. He was a shadow at five anchor points, a black, oily pressure that seeped through every cracked water channel and postern stair.

He was a shape assembled from the old memory of his prison, the centuries of draconic hunger, the blood spilled on the causeway, and the catastrophic education of Jack's own crimson resonance. The stones themselves seemed to lose their resolve; the basalt canyon walls, which had stood for ten thousand years as the silent guardians of the pass, shivered and groaned as if the iron veins within them were turning to liquid.

The very geometry of the sanctuary began to warp, the angles of the walls appearing too sharp, the shadows stretching longer than the light should allow, as if the space were being folded by a heavy, unseen hand.

The canyon of Elskerdeg had been carved by water that had died a thousand years ago, leaving only dry, black basalt that caught the heat of the sun and held it like an oven. The rock was shot through with red veins of iron and pale lines of copper, natural channels that the Faithel had carved and reinforced with their own magic to serve as the prison's skeletal structure.

But now, under the pressure of the rising dragon, those veins were beginning to hum, a low, metallic vibration that rose from the floor and traveled up the boots of those who stood upon it. The air was thick, heavy with the smell of old dust, sulfur, and the sour sweat of terrified men.

The shadows did not lie flat on the stone; they seemed to hover, a fraction of an inch above the flagstones, shivering like oil on water. The dust that blew in from the eastern desert did not settle; it remained suspended in the heavy air, a fine, red grit that irritated the eyes and made every breath taste of rust.

The canyon floor softened at the edges, the basalt turning to dark glass, then to something that resembled dragon scale, then back to stone again, unable to decide which history it belonged to. The light did not change; it died, replaced by a thick, purplish haze that smelled of sulfur, wet iron, and old crowns buried in tar.

The wind from the pass stopped, but the air remained in motion, a low, silent vibration that set the teeth on edge and made the horses scream in the pens below. The silence was not peaceful; it was heavy, suffocating, the kind of quiet that precedes the collapse of a mountain, a physical weight that pressed against the chest and made every breath feel like drawing silt into the lungs.
The basalt underfoot shivered, a rhythmic, deep-seated vibration that felt less like an earthquake and more like a heartbeat, slow and massive, rising from the dark core of the earth.

Brother Cazren stood on the northern ridge, his gaunt frame silhouetted against the purple sky. His voice, hoarse and high-pitched, carried across the canyon like the sound of dry grass scraping against a tombstone.

"Kneel, you children of dust!" Cazren screamed, his arms raised toward the shaking peaks. "The three ages are ending! The Age of Scale was the beginning, when the lords of fire walked the earth and the small races hid in the caves! The Age of Stone was your illusion, a dream of gates and chains built by cowards who thought they could bind the sky in basalt! Now comes the Age of Correction!
"The Crown has returned, and it will wear you all! The blood of the key must flow, and if you do not pour it, the stone will drink it from your veins!"

Behind him, the cultists answered with a low, rhythmic chant, their voices rising in the crown-verse. They did not retreat from the rising shadow; they ran toward it. A young woman, her face painted with red clay and her eyes wide with fanatical devotion, flung herself from the upper terrace into the steaming crack of the secondary channel.

She did not scream as she fell; she laughed, her body vanishing into the black smoke. The smell of burning hair and scorched flesh rose instantly, a sweet, sickening odor that mixed with the sulfur and copper.

Geralt tried to catch a young boy who was preparing to follow her, his hand reaching out to grab the boy's dirty smock. But the boy twisted in his grip, his teeth sinking deep into Geralt's thumb, and threw himself over the edge.
"They're not fighting us," Geralt said, his voice low and dark as he looked down into the smoking rift. "They're... they're feeding the lock. They want the stones to drink."

Jack stood at the center of the causeway, the silver sword in his hand feeling transitionally light against the gathering pressure. He could feel the crimson core in his chest flaring, a hot, rhythmic throbbing that answered the shiver of the basalt.
It was no longer a hidden hum; it was a visible light, a dull red glow that seeped through the fabric of his shirt, painting the dust on his boots with the color of fresh blood.

The scars on his back—the old lines from the mill, the marks of his long flight, the memories of iron and fire—burned with a dry, prickling heat, as if the dragon's breath were tracing the paths of his old wounds. The silver of his blade caught the purple light, turning it to a muddy, violet reflection that shivered with the movement of his hands.

He could feel the pulse of the dragon's thoughts touching his own, a heavy, dark tide that tried to pull him down into the stone, to make him forget his human shape and remember only the ancient fire.
The first breath of the dragon corrected the air. Magic lost grammar.

Yennefer's white fire shield collapsed into pale sparks, reformed crooked, and shivered like wet paper. She cursed in the Elder Speech, her fingers twisting in a complex pattern to draw more power from the copper points, but the air itself resisted her. The magical lines she had spent three days drawing along the causeway were shivering, their white light turning to a muddy, yellow glow that smelled of ozone and burnt hair.

She could feel the pressure of the draconic presence pressing against her temples, a cold, sharp needle of pain that threatened to break her concentration. Her black hair, usually held in perfect, glossy curls, was loose, tangled with red dust and clinging to her damp cheeks. The scent of lilac and gooseberries was entirely gone, replaced by the bitter, metallic tang of sulfur and scorched copper.

She remembered her time at Aretuza, under the strict instruction of Tissaia de Vries, who had taught her that magic was order, a method of imposing human will on the formless chaos of the universe. But here, in this iron-veined canyon, the chaos was older than humanity, older than the elves, and it was imposing its own dark grammar on her.
Every spell she cast felt heavy, sluggish, as if she were trying to write in water.

"The magic is losing its structure," Yennefer muttered, her teeth clenched as she forced her hands to remain steady. "The dragon isn't breaking the spells; he's... he's rewriting the rules of the casting. The somatic lines are bending. A straight line is no longer the shortest distance between my fingers and the target. The power is leaking out of the circles before the lock can close. The focus points are drifting like sand."

Triss's stabilizing web, which she had woven across the water channel to keep the poison from spreading, dimmed to a dull orange, shivered, and came back warmer only because she changed her casting method faster than terror could become paralysis.

She did not use the standard Aretuzan formulas; she reached for the rougher, older spells of the Elder Blood, her hands shaking, her skin peeling in white flakes from the sulfurous heat of the air. She could feel the pressure of the dragon's presence pressing against her mind, a heavy, black weight that tried to turn her spells into nonsense.

The skin of her wrists was raw, blistered where the dark dye had touched it, but she did not let go of the magic; she wove the orange threads with a desperate, frantic energy, her teeth clenched against the pain.

She had stood on Sodden Hill, had felt the fire that burned her skin and the fear that had taken her voice, but this was different. This was not the fire of Nilfgaardian mages; this was the cold, patient hunger of a sleeping world that was waking up and finding its house occupied by insects.

"Yennefer!" Triss shouted, her voice tight with strain, her words barely carrying through the low hum of the stone. "The channels are shifting! The magic is... it's not holding the geometry! The stones are ignoring the lines! The pressure is pushing the spell back into my fingers! If I hold it any longer, the backlash will burn my arms to the elbow! The energy has nowhere to go!"

"I can see that, Triss!" Yennefer snapped, her voice cool but her eyes flashing violet in the purple haze. Her hands were trembling slightly as she drew a new circle of containment in the air. "Keep the containment on the water! If the children drink that sludge, we won't need a dragon to finish us! If you let the line break now, the entire lower ward will turn to ash before the sun reaches the ridge!
"We must hold the cisterns, whatever the cost! Do not let the children see you shake! We are Aretuzans, Triss; we do not run from geometry!"

Faithel lamps burst one by one along the terraces, their brass casings cracking with a sound like dry bone, the oil within them igniting in brief, green flashes that died in the heavy air. Ciri blinked across the broken causeway to reach a wounded guard, but the space between her departure and her arrival had been warped by the dragon's presence.

She appeared three paces from where she had intended, her boots missing the stone terrace entirely. She hit the stone steps hard, rolled down the basalt flags, and came up coughing dust, her sword Zireael drawn and her green eyes wide with fury.
The white hair she usually wore pinned back was loose, tangled with red dust and sweat, and a long scratch along her jaw was bleeding a thin line of red that ran down her neck.

"Space is thick," Ciri said, her voice raw as she spat dust onto the stone. "It feels like... like trying to swim through wet clay. Every jump takes twice as much out of me, and the landing points are shifting. The road is closed, Geralt. I tried to jump behind the ridge, and the space... it was like a wall. I almost ended up inside the basalt.
"The Elder Blood is arguing with the stones, and the stones are winning."

Geralt did not look back. He was watching the shadow-limbs that were forming along the channel walls, his pale eyes narrow, his face gray and expressionless. He remembered fighting the golden dragon Villentretenmerth in the mountains of Caingorn, remembered the lessons Vesemir had taught him about the ancient beasts, how they did not fight like beasts because they had minds that had survived empires.
A dragon was not a monster to be hunted; it was a force of nature that had to be survived.

"Then we don't jump. We stay on the stone. It's harder to warp what has weight. Keep your feet set, Ciri. If you blink, make it short. Half a yard is enough to clear a blow. Don't look for the road; look for the steel. If the space is thick, use it; let the weight of the air carry the strike."
Draconids in the sky screamed.

They were not Vharakthul's allies; they were his children, and they were terrified. Some knelt in midair, their wings folding as if a command had found their muscles and forced them to pray. Some tore at their own throats, their claws ripping through scale and flesh to escape the sound that was rising from the stone.

One fell from the ridge like a stone, its wings locked, and shattered against the dry bed of the water channel without spilling a drop of blood. The sound of their screaming was a constant, high-pitched shriek that filled the ears and made it impossible to hear the shouts of the guards or the orders of the captains, a wild, animal panic that seemed to infect the very air.

Buck reared in the outer court, his heavy shod hooves striking the basalt wall. He broke one of his leather reins with a sharp snap and lunged toward the gate where Jack stood. Nadir caught the remaining rein, his boots sliding through the red dirt as he was dragged three steps.

He was swearing in three languages, his words a stream of curses directed at the horse, the gods of the desert, the dragons of the deep, and the specific category of northern adventurers who brought such things into quiet passes.

"Stand, you brainless beast!" Nadir shouted, his voice hoarse. "Jack! Get your horse! If he breaks the second gate, he'll run straight into the cultists, and they'll eat him before they even look at you! He's too fat to run, and too stupid to hide! The reins are slick with sweat, I can't hold him! If he escapes, I'm charging you ten silver for the recovery, and I'll take the saddle as interest!"

Jack did not turn. The world had become too narrow for horses. He could feel the dragon's presence behind his eyes, a heavy, black amusement that seemed to be watching the horse's panic with the same indifference it felt for the men on the causeway. The beast was nothing to a god; the city was nothing; the pass was only a gate.
Jack attacked.

There was no council. There was no last-minute debate. No formal attempt to classify the threat or determine if the Bureau of Internal Security had a regulation for draconic manifestations. Vharakthul had manifested enough to make physics negotiable and morality simple in the temporary, brutal way that battle did.

Jack drank Swallow and Blizzard too close together. The potions tasted of copper, wintergreen, and his own stomach's rebellion, but the effect was immediate. The world slowed to a crawl. The falling dust stayed in the air like small, grey insects; the screams of the draconids became a low, drawn-out groan; and the purple haze of Vharakthul's breath separated into distinct currents of cold and heat.
The crimson core in his chest flared hot, a red pressure that tore at the edges of his vision, but he ignored the pain. He ran down the broken channel with his silver sword in hand.
Geralt moved with him on the left, his steel sword drawn, his face gray and hard under the dust.
"Bad idea," Geralt said, his voice coming slow and deep through the Blizzard-haze, the sound vibrating in Jack's chest.
"Yes," Jack said.

"Good. We agree. Watch the shadow-tendons. They don't have bones, but they have weight. If they catch your ankle, they'll drag you into the basalt before you can cast. And don't use Quen unless you're about to lose a limb. The feedback is too hot. Keep your silver low and parry only when the shadow turns solid. We are only trying to buy enough time for the mages to think of a better plan."

A black limb, formed from the stone of the channel wall, struck at them. Jack rolled under the blow, the stone scraping his shoulder through his leather pauldrons. He cast Aard into the basalt, the kinetic force turning the softened stone into a spray of dry shards, and Geralt cut the tendon-shape that appeared when the shadow-force turned solid for half a heartbeat.
The blow did not draw blood; it made heat, a brief, white flash that smelled of scorched bone and old tar.

Jack turned, his blade catching a second shadow-limb, the silver ringing like a bell in the quiet of his Blizzard-hearing. He could feel the dragon's presence behind the strike, a cold, hungry mind that was evaluating his reflexes. It was like fighting a man who could see three seconds into the future; every parry was anticipated, every cut was met with scale that formed exactly where the edge was going to land.
The silver blade shivered with the impact, the vibrations traveling up his arms and settling in his shoulders.
"He's not fighting!" Jack shouted to Geralt. "He's... he's checking the locks! He's trying to find the place where the resonance is weak! He's testing the limits of our resistance!"

"Then don't give him the keys!" Geralt replied, parrying a strike that threw him back two steps. The witcher's face was dark with the toxic veins of his own potions, his eyes pitch black, his teeth bared in a snarl. "Use the signs! Keep him moving! If he stays in one place, he'll turn the stone into scale! He's trying to settle his weight into the pass, to anchor himself in the iron veins!
"Once he gets a footing, we won't be able to lift him with all the magic in Aretuza!"

Yennefer opened a path with fire and compression, each of her spells anchored to a copper point that Sera's people had marked along the causeway. The magic was white, bright, and loud, striking Vharakthul's forming throat and breaking into black sparks that hissed in the dust. The dragon laughed then.

The sound was not heard with ears; it was a weight that settled into the bones of their legs, making their knees remember kneeling. It was the old hierarchy of the world, the law of the scale and the tooth, and it did not care for their spells or their swords.

*You play with fire, little sorceress,* the laughter said, the words settling in Yennefer's mind like cold oil. *But I am the fire that melted the first stone. Your circles are only scratches in the dirt. Your magic is only the stuttering of a child who has learned to mimic the wind.
I have watched empires burn their own books to keep their rooms warm; you think your little letters will hold me? You are only a tenant in this house, and the landlord has returned. *

Yennefer did not answer. She drew a deep breath, her chest rising under her black velvet bodice, and cast a lightning bolt that took the dragon in the center of his forming chest. The blast was loud enough to rattle the stones in the keep, but Vharakthul did not fall; he only turned his head toward her, his black eyes widening with amusement.

Ciri struck from behind through a blink-cut, her blade Zireael flashing silver-green in the haze. She bit deep into a scale that had not existed a second earlier, the metal of her sword ringing against the draconic armor.
Vharakthul turned toward her, his black eyes widening with an interest that made Jack’s blood go cold.

*Elder gate-child,* the dragon said. The words were not sound; they were an appraisal, a cold calculation of her value. *You carry the road in your blood. You could open the sky for us. Why do you fight for these small, dry things? Why do you bind yourself to a father who is already dead? Join me, and we will walk through the gates of the worlds you have lost.
You will never have to run again. The towers of Tir ná Lia are waiting; why do you choose to bleed in the dirt with peasants? *

Ciri spit blood onto the stone and smiled, her teeth white in the purple light. "Wrong door, you bastard. And my father is standing right there. He's the one with the ugly scars and the poor manners. I've seen better worlds than yours, and they all have one thing in common: they don't have you in them. If the towers of Tir ná Lia are waiting, let them wait; I'm busy."
She vanished in a green flash before the black breath could take the space where she had stood.
Saesenthessis hit him from above.

She did not use her full dragon shape—there was no room in the narrow canyon for two such mountains of flesh—but she brought the pressure of it down through the human form she allowed the world to see. She was a flash of golden scale, a wing-shadow that covered the terrace, and an ancient authority that had been condensed into the space of a single woman. The canyon shook.

The basalt walls groaned as the two draconic forces met. She remembered her father, Villentretenmerth, the lessons he taught her about the responsibility of dragons, how they must protect what is fragile because they are the only ones who can. She looked at Vharakthul and saw only decay, a crown that wanted to turn the living world into a tomb.

Vharakthul's forming head was bent sideways by the golden pressure. For one heartbeat, the black crown around his skull fractured, and something ancient and terrified inside him recoiled, recognizing a will that was older than his prison.
Then he pushed back.

Saesenthessis staggered on the ridge. Blood ran from her nose, bright and gold-red against her pale skin. She wiped it away with a sharp, angry gesture that would have been funny if the sky had not been turning to ink around her. Her eyes, usually the color of polished brass, had gone entirely gold, the pupils narrow slits that reflected the purple haze.
She stood on the edge of the basalt ridge, her fingers curled like talons, her breath coming in short, ragged gasps.

"He remembers too much," she said, her voice carrying down to the channel, her breathing shallow and ragged. "He has eaten the memory of the anchors. The prison is his mother now. He is not trying to break the wall, Jack! He is trying to wear it! He wants the sanctuary to become his body! He wants the basalt to be his bone and the wind to be his breath!
"He has spent three hundred years learning the shape of our locks! The stone is no longer a cage; it is his second skin!"

Regis appeared beside Triss, carrying a wounded Faithel boy whose eyes had gone black at the edges. The boy's skin was cold, and he was whispering the crown-verse in a voice that did not belong to a child.

"The lesser hungers are nesting in the injured," Regis said, his voice calm but his eyes dark as he looked at the black veins spreading across the boy's chest. "It is not possession in the theological sense. More like appetite looking for chairs. The resonance is drawing the shadow-things out of the stone. They are looking for flesh that has stopped refusing, and the wounded are too tired to argue.
"It is a biological opportunistic response, not a moral failure. The shadow feeds on the exhaustion of the host."

"Horrible metaphor, Regis," Triss said, her hands glowing as she pressed her magic into the boy's chest to drive the cold out. Her face was pale with exhaustion, and her fingers were trembling so badly she could barely hold the spell-shaping.

"I am open to improvement," the vampire said, adjusting his spectacles. "Though under the circumstances, accuracy seems more useful than elegance. The boy's pulse is slowing. If the shadow reaches his heart, he will cease to be a boy and become a door. And once the door is open, the dragon will have a dozen more keys than he needs. The Faithel's blood is too close to the stone's memory. We must purge the shadow before it sets."
"Hold him," Triss whispered.
Jack used everything.
Silver first, because Witcher habits existed to begin action before terror could find the words to stop it. He parried a shadow-strike, the silver blade ringing like a bell.

Signs next. Quen cracked twice under the black pressure, the golden shield shattering into dry flakes that smelled of ozone. Igni guttered as if ashamed, the orange flame dying in the purple haze. Yrden sank into the basalt and became a brief, shivering ring of red-white containment before Vharakthul stepped through it and made the stones smoke.

Bombs after that. Moon Dust broke the forming edge of the dragon's wing, the silver flakes clinging to the shadow-scale and keeping it from turning solid. Grapeshot did nothing but annoy the canyon, the iron shards rattling against the stone like hail.

Samum flashed, a brief, blinding light that showed, for a fraction of a second, the true shape inside the manifestation: a vast, black dragon folded inside too small a return, starving, brilliant, and entirely certain of its victory.
Crimson resonance came when Jack ran out of ordinary refusal.

It flooded him hot and thick, a red tide that rose from the core in his chest and filled his throat with the taste of copper. His scars burned, the old lines on his back and chest turning to white heat. Sound narrowed to his own heartbeat, the scrape of his boots on the stone, the breath in his lungs, and the voices of his companions.

He drove the resonance into the chain of anchor-stone shards that Tala had dragged across the causeway. The shards rose into the air, not by magic, but by the old, material recognition of the stone. He hurled them into Vharakthul's chest as the dragon-shape leaned forward.
They hurt him.

The canyon proved it. The black pressure recoiled, the purple haze thinning for three paces around the gate. The cultists on the ridge screamed as the red ash in their mouths ignited, their faces turning to white flame. Sorel Veyrane's Black Ink men fell to their knees, their hands clawing at their breastplates as their restraint gear suddenly became too hot to touch.
Cazren laughed while he burned, his voice a high, thin shriek that was cut short when the stone beneath him collapsed.
Jack drove his silver sword into the wound the shards had made.
For one breath, he thought they might kill a god with physics and enough spite.
Vharakthul watched him through the split scale.

*Little wall,* the dragon said. *You learned to stand. Good. Now learn to open. You are only the lid on my box. The lid does not argue with the gold inside. You think you are the hero of this pass, but you are only the bolt on the door. And I have the key. Your father's stitching will not hold you when I draw the thread. You are mine, Jack.
You have always been mine. *
The external prison died.

It did not shatter; it died. A machine that had lost its last argument with use simply stopped working. The five anchor channels turned black from center to edge. The lamps went out. The wind stopped. Every old repair, every Faithel song, every hidden line of blood and golden pressure that had held across the centuries collapsed into a single, inward pull.
Jack felt it aim at him.
Yennefer saw him begin to burn, the red light from his chest flaring so bright it turned the purple haze to blood-color. "Jack! Down!"

Ciri reached for him. Geralt reached for him. Triss abandoned her stabilizing spell to throw a warm line of orange containment around his ribs. Saesenthessis struck again from the ridge and was thrown back against the basalt cliff hard enough to break the stone.
Jack stayed upright.

He could not move. Not because he was trapped, but because he was the next piece of the machine. The core in his chest was no longer his; it was the anchor, and the anchor was pulling the dragon in. The heat was white, blinding, a dry fire that seemed to be melting the bones of his collarbone.
Vharakthul unfolded from the dying prison, less whole than he wanted, but more present than the world could survive.
Jack's sword slipped from his fingers, the silver blade clattering against the basalt.

Geralt caught him before he hit the ground, his arms strong and his voice low and terrified enough to be honest. "Not yet, Jack. Not yet. Hold on to the stone. Don't let him draw you. The witcher's hands were hot, his fingers digging into Jack's shoulders, his black eyes wide with a fear he had never shown before. The heat from Jack's chest was blistering, but Geralt did not release his grip."
Jack tasted blood, potion, ash, and old gold.
"He is out," Jack whispered.
Yennefer stood over them, her face white and her eyes violet fire, her hands glowing with a white light that was the only clean thing left in the canyon. "Then we put him back."
No one answered.
Because the room was gone, the canyon was broken, and the only door left was breathing.
They tried the old rite even after the crown breathed.

Asha insisted because refusal demanded proof, not panic. She stood on the lower platform with her mortar in her hands, her face grey with dust and her fingers stained with the green juice of the herbs. She refused to look at the sky, refused to acknowledge the black wings folding over the cliffs.

She kept her eyes on the stone mortar, her fingers grinding the dried thistle with a rhythm that was too steady to be anything but desperation. Sera agreed because a doctrine that had been hated for centuries still deserved the courtesy of failing in daylight before a worse doctrine replaced it.

The Faithel who could still stand formed a ring around the secondary channel, their voices rising in the song of repair. It was not Helena's song; it was older, rougher, a melody that had been designed for stone rather than children. The words were guttural, rhythmic, a sequence of sounds that had been carved into the basalt before the first Northern kings drew maps.

The song was a blueprint, a description of order that the basalt had been trained to obey. Tala held the northern point of the ring, her bow ready; Asha held the southern. Jack stood outside the circle, his left wrist in Triss's blistered hand, his pulse too hot and too slow.

"If this works," Triss said, her voice shaking, "you do nothing. You stay where you are, and you let the Faithel handle the masonry. You don't reach for the sword, and you don't call the core. Do you hear me? If you try to help them, the resonance will pull you into the line, and you'll become part of the mortar. I've seen mages try to fix gates by throwing themselves in; it never works, Jack.
"It only makes the stone heavier. You are a man, Jack, not a stone. Remember that."
"Yes," Jack said.
"Say it properly, Jack."
"If this works, I do nothing."

"Good," she said, her green eyes searching his face, her lips pale. "I will assume the lie was for my benefit and resent it later when we are both safe and have nothing better to do than complain about the dust in this pass. I've spent enough time in this desert to last three lifetimes, and the water here is terrible. If we survive today, I'm going back to Kovir.
"The weather is awful, but the stone doesn't speak."
He faced her, but she did not smile. Her face was ashen, her red hair damp with sweat, and her hands were covered in white linen wraps where the poison water had burned her.

Asha began the restoration verse. The channel answered, the basalt glowing with a red-brown heat that smelled of clay. Sera poured the prepared ash into the crack; Yennefer bound it with a white thread of containment; and Saesenthessis pressed from above, her teeth clenched and her golden eyes flashing in the haze. Ciri stood ready to cut any thread of gate-magic that formed, her sword Zireael held low.
Geralt stood beside her, his steel blade ready to cut anything that had a body.
For thirty heartbeats, the crack closed.
Hope arrived in the canyon like an enemy wearing a friend's cloak, making them breathe easier for half a minute.
Then Vharakthul breathed through the sealed line.
