The ash rose from the crack and arranged itself into a black crown in the air. The song in Asha's mouth changed; not by her choice, but because the rhythm bent under the pressure. Jack heard the third beat become Helena's, then Cazren's cult line, then something older and colder than both.
Asha choked, her hands flying to her mouth, and she fell forward onto the sand before the song could use her voice any longer.
Sera broke the mortar with her iron-tipped staff, ending the music.
The rite failed.

Asha coughed blood into the sand, her fingers curling into the dirt. "He learned... he learned through the repair. Every time we build the wall, he learns the shape of the stone. The song is his now. We are only teaching him the words. The anchors aren't holding the dragon; they're teaching him how to sing. The Faithel have spent centuries building his mouth. Every stone we laid was only a tooth in his jaw.
We thought we were the guards, but we were only the keepers of his cage."

The first breath of Vharakthul corrected the air. Magic lost grammar. The sorceress's barrier shattered into pale embers before rebuilding itself at a flawed angle. Triss's stabilizing web shivered, dimmed, and came back with gaps that looked too much like teeth. Draconids screamed overhead. Some folded their wings midflight as if command had found muscle. Others tore at their own throats to resist the command.
Saesenthessis rose against the pressure and named what everyone else had hoped not to name: not worship, but obedience wearing inheritance.

They tried every answer that still deserved the word answer. Geralt cut what could be cut and found no heart where a monster ought to keep one. Yennefer built a binding lattice and watched it become a ladder. Triss attempted dispersal and caught three wounded Faithel before the backlash killed them. Ciri opened no full door, only slivers, each one closed before the Crown could learn the taste of Elder Blood.

Regis found no body to poison, no appetite to starve, no clean anatomy to betray. Asha and Sera spoke the old repair and heard the Crown repeat the ending before they reached it. By the time the secondary channel shattered, hope had become too expensive to spend carelessly.

The breach changed the company before anyone found language for it. Ciri stayed nearer without announcing protection. Geralt began watching the rear as if the road itself had learned pursuit. Yennefer and Triss measured every word Jack spoke, not for weakness, but for the places where the Crown might have left a hook. Asha and Tala kept their own silence, old law and old guilt standing side by side.
Black smoke shaped like a crown had not won the field. It had made every survivor reveal what they would guard first.
Regis, kneeling beside her, looked at Jack with the quiet horror of a man who had just watched a disease learn medicine.
"Then no repair," Yennefer said.
Saesenthessis's silence became heavier.
Geralt saw it. "Still not saying it?"
"No," she said.
"Good," Ciri replied, voice raw. "Keep not saying it."
Vharakthul struck the ridge, and the secondary channel shattered.
After that, no one had enough hope left to mistake it for safety.

Later judicial summary from an imperial committee that failed to agree on jurisdiction: At the crisis point, all relevant authorities lost practical capacity. Surviving witnesses dispute whether the subject consented, whether consent could exist under catastrophic conditions, and whether refusal by associated parties constituted moral evidence or emotional obstruction.

The legal representatives of the Nilfgaardian Crown, led by the regional prosecutor Marcilly of Toussaint, argued that the subject, as an unregistered carrier of a Class-Four draconic resonance, was a ward of the state under the Decree of Northern Pacification, and that his consent was irrelevant to the survival of the province.

The Koviri jurists, representing Master Gerhart of the Koviri Guild of Merchants, counter-argued that the subject's status as a free citizen of Willenford had never been legally terminated, and that the use of his body as a containment vessel without prior contract constituted a violation of the Common Law of the North.

The Redanian delegates, having no army in the pass, contented themselves with filing a procedural protest against the use of unlicensed sorcery within the boundaries of the Elskerdeg Pass, which had, according to a treaty signed in 1262, been declared a neutral zone. The imperial transcripts record that the debate lasted three weeks, while the pass itself was already covered in three feet of black glass.
The first attempt to seize Jack came while Geralt was holding him upright.

That was the obscene part. Not the timing alone, though the timing deserved several creative punishments. The manner. Three Black Ink field men, faces gray with fear, hands shaking, still carrying restraint hooks because terror had not yet stripped them of doctrine. They saw the outer prison die, saw Vharakthul rise, saw the canyon become a wound large enough to swallow history, and concluded that the proper next action was custody.
They had been trained to view the world through the lens of Sorel Veyrane's handbooks—order was not something that grew from the ground, it was something that was clamped onto it with iron rings.

The three men moved forward in a loose formation, their leather armor squeaking under the weight of the red dust, their eyes shifting between the black shadow rising behind the causeway and the boy whose chest was glowing with a dull, crimson light.

The lead field man, a veteran with a scarred lip and the cold eyes of a tax collector, held a copper-shod restraint pole. The tip of the pole hummed with a low, blue magic designed to quiet the nerves of feral beasts and unruly prisoners.

The copper had been forged in the deep cellars of Oxenfurt, mixed with cold-iron and silver to create a channel that could siphon off the neural energy of mutated subjects. It was the same tool they used on rogue mages and feral draconids in the northern borderlands.

"Preserve the subject!" he shouted, his voice cracking slightly on the final syllable. "Under Section Four of the Special Security Mandate, we are authorized to take custody! Step back, witcher! The Bureau has jurisdiction over all draconic remnants! We have orders signed by Sorel Veyrane himself! We are only doing our duty! If you interfere, the Crown will hold you responsible for the loss of the asset!
"The law is clear on this, even in the middle of a breach!"

Geralt watched him through black, potion-dilated eyes, his teeth bared in a silent snarl. He had his left arm wrapped around Jack's ribs, holding him up as the boy's boots slipped on the grit. The heat from Jack's chest was blistering, the crimson light turning the witcher's gray face to a dull red.

His heart rate had dropped to forty beats a minute under the influence of the Blizzard potion, and his mutated ears could hear the minute fractures forming in the basalt causeway beneath their feet. He could smell the sweat of the three mercenaries, a sour, cold odor of men who knew they were out of their depth but were too terrified of Sorel's punishment to disobey.
"He's not an asset," Geralt said, his voice coming slow and deep, vibrating in his chest. "He's a boy. And you're standing in my way."

Ciri killed the hook before it reached Jack. Not the man. The hook. Zireael cut through the restraint shaft and the spell-thread inside it. The broken tool burst into sparks and legal ash. The blue magic dissipated with a sound like wet leather hitting a fire, leaving only the scent of scorched copper and dry ink.

Ciri did not pause; she closed the distance in a single step, her boots striking the basalt flags with a sharp, dry snap. She put the point of her sword at the man's throat, the white metal of Zireael catching the purple light of the rising dragon.
"Say subject again," she said.

Her green eyes were very wide, very bright, and entirely cold. The wind from the pass blew her white hair across her face, but her hand did not tremble. The point of the blade touched the skin of his throat, drawing a single, tiny bead of red.

She remembered the cages of Leo Bonhart, the feeling of the iron bars against her shins, the way the men had watched her as if she were a horse they were about to buy. She remembered the long nights she had spent in the dark, wondering if she would ever own her own name again.
She saw the same look in these men's eyes, and she hated them for it with a precision that was sharper than any witcher sign.
He wet himself. The dark stain spread quickly across the linen of his trousers, steam rising slightly from the warmth of it in the dry air.
"Sensible," Geralt said, his voice strained.
The second attempt came from Cazren's people.

Two cultists crawled through the rubble of the collapsed wall, their hands and knees bleeding from the sharp basalt shards. Their faces were painted with red ash, their eyes fixed on Jack with a love so poisoned it had become appetite.

They did not see the witcher, they did not see the sorceresses; they saw only the key that had been promised to them by Helena's old songs, the door that would let the fire out. They had been taught that the world was a cage, and the only way to be free was to let the monster eat the bars.

"Open," one whispered, her teeth black with the charcoal they had eaten before the breach. "Open, holy door. Crown within, crown above. Let the black breath teach us our correction. The key is in the bone. We are ready, Jack. We have spent our lives preparing for your mouth. Let the scale devour the flesh."
Yennefer turned them to white fire before they touched him.

She did not use the somatic gestures of the Aretuzan academy; her eyes simply found them, her eyes flashing violet, and the air between them became too hot for flesh to survive. The white flame was brief, silent, and hot enough to turn the basalt beneath the cultists to black glass. There were no screams; the heat was too sudden for the nerves to carry the message.
They became ash in the space of a heartbeat, the red dust of the canyon floor swallowing their memory before the wind could take it.

No one criticized the severity. Some sentences forfeited funerals. Yennefer did not look at the ashes; her focus was on the sky, where Vharakthul's shadow was beginning to stretch over the ridge like a hand. She remembered her training at Aretuza, how Tissaia de Vries had taught her that magic was order, a method of imposing human will on the formless chaos of the universe.
But here, in this iron-veined canyon, the chaos was older than humanity, and it was imposing its own dark grammar on her.
The third attempt came from a compromised guardian.

That hurt worse. A woman from Purge, one arm broken and hanging uselessly at her side, used an old Faithel side-channel to reach the center line. She was a woman who had worked the mortar with Asha for five years, her skin tanned to the color of old leather by the desert sun, her hair held back by a blue cloth.

She carried a mercy knife, curved and clean, the silver handle chased with the star-marks of her office. Asha recognized her and made a sound as if someone had cut her from inside, a sharp, choked gasp that was lost in the rumbling of the canyon.

"No living key," the woman said, her voice dry and steady. "No living chamber. End the old sin, Asha. The first Faithel told us: if the wall fails, we do not let the box walk. We kill the box. We do not let the Northern empire have him. If they take the core, they will turn the whole desert into a prison. We must be the keepers of our own end."
Asha met her halfway.

Their fight was short because grief was already tired. The two women had known each other's families, had sung the same songs over the dry channels, but the dragon had changed the weight of their legacy. Asha parried the curved blade with her mortar-pestle, the heavy iron striking the silver-chased handle with a dull clang.
She disarmed her with a quick, twisting motion, broke her knee with a short, brutal kick, and then held the mercy knife over her throat with both hands shaking.

"Do it," the woman said, her face pressed against the red grit of the stone. "Be useful late, Asha. Don't let them carry the key out of the pass. If Sorel Veyrane gets it, he'll build a larger cage, and the dragon will eat the world from inside. Let me be the last one who dies because we tried to keep the door shut. The Faithel have always paid their debts in blood."

Asha did not. She stood over her for three long breaths, her face grey with ash and failure. Then she struck her unconscious with the pommel of the knife and dropped the weapon onto the flagstones as if it had become venomous.
"I am done being useful to fear," Asha said, her voice hoarse and raw.
The words traveled farther than a shout, settling into the quiet that lay between the rumbles of the mountain.
Vharakthul rose behind them.
Yennefer tried containment first.

Not a cage. She knew better than to try to build a wall around a god. Instead, she built a layered compression out of heat, stone, and reflected draconic pressure. She reached out with her mind to the copper points that Sera's people had marked along the causeway, using them as lightning rods to siphon off the dragon's own energy and turn it back upon him.

She wove Saesenthessis's wounded gold pressure into the weave, using the ancient authority of the golden dragon to give the spell weight. She used her own rage—the cold, disciplined anger that had survived Sodden Hill and Vengerberg—to sharpen the edges of the containment.

The spell closed around the black dragon-shape, a dome of white-hot light that shivered and hummed with the vibration of the stone. For eight breaths, the shadow stayed inside. The air within the dome was so dense it looked like purple glass, and the dragon's head was pressed against the top of it, his black eyes narrow and amused.
On the ninth breath, the spell turned inside out.

The white light turned black, the compression reversed, and the magical force was thrown back along the lines of casting. Yennefer fell to one knee, the stone cracking under her boot. Blood ran from her mouth, bright and hot against her pale chin.
Ciri moved toward her, her hand reaching out, but she stopped because the field between them had become lethal, a network of black sparks that hissed in the dust and turned the grit to glass.
Jack tried to stand, his chest flaring so bright it turned Yennefer's face red.
Geralt held him down with one hand, his fingers digging into Jack's shoulder.
"No," Geralt said.
"You cannot hold me here," Jack whispered, his voice sounding hollow, as if he were speaking from the bottom of a dry well.
"Watch me try."
Geralt tried to cut a solution next.

No one called it that. He simply rose, gave Jack's weight to Regis and Ciri, and moved into the broken channel with both swords drawn. When Geralt had no answer left, when the magic failed and the walls fell, he returned to the oldest thing he knew: the weight of the steel in his right hand, the silver in his left, and the simple, physical presence of his body between the danger and the people he had sworn to protect.

He did not attack Vharakthul as if the dragon-god could be slain by three feet of metal; he attacked the points where the manifestation touched the stone of the pass. He parried the shadow-tendons as they rose from the channels, cut the scale-edges where they tried to turn the basalt into skin, and broke the pressure-anchors with short, precise strikes.

For a moment, it worked. The shadow-tendons recoiled, the purple smoke thinning where his blades cut. Geralt moved with the fluid, silent grace of a man who had spent his life parrying death, his boots barely touching the stone as he rolled and struck. His steel blade left lines of sparks in the dark, and his silver blade rang with the high, clear pitch of a bell.

He remembered the Trial of the Grasses, the terrible fever that had melted his childhood memories and replaced them with the instincts of a predator. He could feel the toxic weight of the Swallow and Blizzard potions grinding against his liver, his vision shifting to monochrome, the heat of the dragon's breath showing up as a pale, shimmering white against the black basalt.
He could hear his own heartbeat—slow, heavy, forty beats a minute—and the sound of Yennefer's breath, ragged and wet with blood, from the terrace behind him.
Then Vharakthul struck him aside.

It was not a claw; it was a wave of pressure, a single, heavy pulse of air that took Geralt in the chest and lifted him off his feet. He hit the basalt wall hard, the sound of his ribs cracking like dry wood. He rolled down the steps, his swords clattering against the stone. Roach screamed from somewhere beyond the gate, a wild, horse-panic that echoed through the rocks.

Jack stood so fast Regis failed to stop him, the vampire's hand slipping from his arm. The world narrowed to Geralt on the ground, his face grey under the red dust, and the black dragon turning toward him with a slow, heavy interest.
Ciri blinked in.

She did not blink to attack; she blinked to save. She appeared between Geralt and the dragon, grabbed the collar of his armor, and vanished in a flash of green sparks. They reappeared half a dozen paces away, both of them hitting the stone steps badly. Ciri coughed, rolled over, and looked at Jack before he could take another step.
"No," she said.
Her face was smeared with soot and blood, her hands shaking as she held her sword.
Jack stopped.

Not because she ordered him to. Because she knew what he was about to do, knew that he was going to offer his own chest as a lock to save the witcher, and she hated him for the choice with a clarity that was sharper than any blade.
Triss tried to stabilize the field.

She could not hold it forever. She knew it and kept working anyway, which was one kind of courage people underestimated because it had no sword in it. She moved between the wounded guards, the failing channel nodes, and the lamps that were bursting along the walls. Her hands were warm with magic, her face pale with concentration as she wove the orange threads of her spells.

She kept the children in the lower court breathing; she kept the magical backlashes from burning Ciri when her Elder Blood scraped against the warped space; and she kept Jack's heart from answering the rhythmic hum of the dead prison. Her fingers were blistered, the skin of her wrists raw where the dark dye had touched it, but she did not let go of the magic.

She remembered Sodden Hill, the heat of the fire that had taken her skin, the smell of burning hair, and the way the world had seemed to dissolve into pain. She did not want to see these people burn. She did not want to see Jack become part of the stone.
"Three minutes," she said, her voice tight with strain.
"For what?" Geralt asked from the ground, his hand pressed against his side as he tried to sit up.
"Something better than this," Triss said, her eyes wet with tears she refused to let fall.

Regis stood beside Jack, his spectacles reflecting the purple light of the canyon. "I have no kinder biological answer. If a living containment occurs, the chamber remains alive, and the prisoner remains aware enough to press against it. The physical identity of the host will gradually fracture, the mind becoming a map of the prison rather than a collection of memories. Survival may be another form of punishment. For both.
The dragon's will is a parasite, Jack; it will feed on your thoughts, your names, the faces of your friends, until there is nothing left but the cage. It is a slow consumption, not a clean death."
"Thank you," Jack said, his eyes fixed on the dragon. "Comforting."
"I am rarely employed for comfort, though I aspire to politeness under all circumstances. I have watched the infection of the blood in many species; it is never a gentle transition."
Saesenthessis came down from the ridge, bleeding gold-red from her side.

She stood between them and Vharakthul, her human shape flickering at the edges like a candle in the wind. The gold scales along her arms and throat were cracked, the gold-red blood running down her skin and dripping onto the black basalt. She looked older than she had three days ago, her golden eyes narrow and dark.
She remembered her father, Villentretenmerth, the lessons he taught her about the gold, how a dragon must protect what is fragile because a dragon is the only one who can.

"Stone will not hold him now," Saesenthessis said, her voice dropping into the cold basalt. "He carries the anchors in him now. He knows the songs we used to build them. The pass is his body now. The basalt is his bone, and the wind is his breath. If we do not make the room, he will walk."

Yennefer looked up from one knee, her voice cold and sharp. She had her hand pressed to her throat, her violet magic flickering weakly around her fingers. She turned from Ciri to Jack. "Listen to me, Ciri. Do not try to blink him out. The Elder Blood is a road, but it is also a beacon. If you open a full door now under this pressure, the dragon's shadow will leak into the void between worlds.
The Wild Hunt will follow the scent, and they will find you before the first moon rises. We cannot use the gate as an exit; it is a sieve."

"Blood opened the last door," Saesenthessis replied, her eyes fixed on Jack. "Only blood can become the room. You know this, sorceress. The Morningstars were not chosen because they were wise; they were chosen because their blood was thick enough to hold the gold. The crimson resonance is the only lock that has the same weight as the key."

Ciri's face changed. The girl who had run through the swamps of Cintra, the empress who had walked the halls of Vizima, the survivor who had fought the Wild Hunt, the woman who had learned to love a witcher—all of them were struck by the same sentence. She looked at Jack, her eyes wide with a horror that was older than the pass.
"No," Ciri said.

Saesenthessis did not look away. "I accept your hatred, Princess. I would prefer it to your ignorance. If we do not make the room now, the dragon will walk out of this pass, and your worlds will not have walls thick enough to keep him out. You cannot blink everyone away, Ciri. The road is closed."

"No," Yennefer said, her voice colder, worse than Ciri's. "You will not dress body-ownership in ancient necessity and call it wisdom. We have spent too many centuries letting the old races tell us which children must be burned to keep the frost away. We are not Faithel; we do not build temples out of bones."
"I am calling it last horror," Saesenthessis said, her voice flat. "Wisdom failed earlier, when we thought we could keep a god in a box."
Geralt got to his feet, one hand against his ribs, his breath coming in short, painful gasps. "Find another answer."

Triss, still holding the orange field, had tears running down her cheeks, but her hands stayed steady on the magic. "I'm looking. I'm trying to find... to find a way to ground the resonance without using the boy. But the copper is melting. The stone isn't accepting the charge. The lines are dead, Geralt."
"Look faster," Geralt said.
"I am," she replied, and the words broke the room more than shouting would have, her voice carrying the weight of all the hills they had buried their friends upon.

Asha's voice was hoarse as she stood beside Sera. "It is an old sin. The living chamber is named in the texts only so we know the shape of what must be refused. It was never meant to be a plan; it was a warning. The first Faithel wrote that the vessel must be human so that the vessel could refuse. If the vessel cannot refuse, the prison becomes a throne. Asha's face was gray with dust.

She faced Jack. The first Morningstar was a blacksmith, you know. He was chosen because his blood was thick with iron from the forge, and he spent his life binding the heat of the Faithel's anchors. They branded his chest with a red-hot key, and every first-born son since then has carried the mark. It was never an honor, Jack; it was a tax paid to keep the fire from the town."

"Every refusal has been honored," Saesenthessis said. "The stone failed. The rite failed. Magic failed. Blade failed. Elder Blood cannot move him without teaching him the roads. Draconic pressure cannot dominate him. Biological restraint cannot make it kind. If we do not act, the decision will be made for us by the sky."
"Then we die," Ciri said.
Jack met her eyes.

She meant it. That was the worst part. There was no melodrama in her face, no heroic stance; it was simple arithmetic. She would rather die in the red dust of the pass than watch another person be told that their body was the only thing that stood between the world and the dark.
She had seen too many sacrifices, had been the target of too many containment plans herself, and she was done with the logic of the lesser evil.

Vharakthul advanced. The broken canyon bent around him, the basalt turning to glass and sludge as his shadow touched it. The sky above was entirely black, the stars gone, replaced by the heavy, purplish light of the crown.
Jack felt the decision before he allowed the words to find his tongue.

He had been deciding since Willenford. Since the day his father had handed him the silver sword; since the mill where Miro had died; since the wooden horse Jacob had carved; since Mara's warm hands had held his wrists; since Geralt's leather strap had marked his shoulders; since Ciri's refusal to let him disappear; since Jacob's last letter had warned him of the anchors; since Helena's song had taught him the rhythm of the pass.

Every road he had walked had put another stone in the scale. He did not want to die. He did not want to become a room. He did not want to be useful enough to justify every thief, every bureaucrat, every sorcerer who had ever reached for his collar.
He also did not want them dead.
That was not destiny. That was choice, ugly, awake, and his own.
"I decide," he said.
Everyone turned to look at him.
"No," Ciri said. This time it was not an argument. It was pain, a sharp, choked sound that was lost in the wind.
Jack turned to Saesenthessis. "What is needed?"

Geralt moved toward him, his face dark with potion-veins. But Triss caught Geralt's wrist, her orange magic wrapping around his fingers. She was not holding him easily; she was holding him because if he crossed the space now, if he tried to pull Jack back by force, the feedback from the dragon's breath would ignite the crimson core, and the world would lose the one thing Jack was trying to preserve in the choice.
"Do not make love another reason to disappear," Geralt said, his black eyes fixed on Jack's face.

Jack met his eyes, the red light from his chest reflecting in the witcher's pupils. "I remembered, Geralt. I remembered what you told me about the road. The road is just a way to get to the place where you have to stand."
"This looks like forgetting."

"No. This is me staying where the monster is. You told me that's what a witcher does. He stays between the beast and the gate. If I run now, the road will follow me, and it will follow you too. You can't fight a god in every town, Geralt."
Geralt's face broke by the smallest possible amount, the hard lines around his mouth shivering.

Yennefer stood, shaking with rage and exhaustion, her black hair tangled with dust. "Consent under catastrophe is not clean, Jack. You are choosing because you think there is no other path. That is not choice; that is submission. We can fight. We can find another way."

"No," Jack said, his hand touching the silver sword at his belt. "Make it dirty. Make it witnessed. Make everyone hate it. My father recommended that. He said if you have to pay, make sure the shopkeeper knows the color of your blood. If I don't pay now, Sorel Veyrane will buy the pass anyway, and he'll pay with the children's bones. He still believes in the files, Yennefer.
"He thinks the files will protect him from the fire."
Ciri made a sound like a blade refusing the sheath, her fingers clenching the hilt of Zireael until her knuckles were white.
Saesenthessis waited.
She did not reach out her hand. She did not offer him a bargain. That was the only mercy she had left to give him: she let him walk the distance alone.
Jack turned toward Vharakthul.
The black crown breathed.
And Jack walked toward it before anyone could give him permission.
Sorel Veyrane arrived through a speaking crystal and cowardice.

The crystal was found in the hand of the Black Ink field captain after Ves, half a continent away in Vizima, would later describe the man's courage as largely theoretical. The captain had dropped the device as he fled the causeway, and it had rolled into a crack in the basalt near the secondary channel.

It flared to life while the dragon was still pressing against the last viable lines of Yennefer's compression. The image that rose above the blue glass was pale, distorted by the sulfurous drafts of the canyon, and calm in the way only men who were three hundred leagues away could afford to be.

"Subject preservation remains imperative," Sorel's voice said, sounding thin and tinny through the static. "The assets of the Bureau must not be abandoned to local negligence. Captain, report status of custody."
Ciri stared at the blue image, her face cold. "You are late, Veyrane. Your captain is gone, your hooks are broken, and your jurisdiction is currently melting."

"Your Highness," Sorel said, the image flickering as the basalt shivered. "This event only proves the necessity of structured containment. If the subject had been secured in Willenford under our protocols, the resonance would not have reached critical density. Unregulated sentiment has brought us to this pass. We must salvage the core; the empire cannot afford to lose the potential of the resonance. The cost of recovery is secondary to the security of the asset."

Yennefer laughed, a sharp, bitter sound that had no amusement in it. She was leaning against a broken pillar, wiping the blood from her lip. "Listen to him. He is trying to build a courtroom while the mountain falls on his head. He wants to audit the ashes. He wants to weigh the dust and tell us the tax on the ruins. The bureau will have its balance sheet, Veyrane, even if the ledger is written in smoke."

"The world often ends badly because jurisdiction is absent," Sorel replied, his image turning its pale, grey eyes toward her. "If we do not maintain the files, how do we know what we have lost? Sentimental attachment to the individual is a luxury the empire cannot support during a draconic event. The boy's survival is secondary to the preservation of the containment properties.
"A single vessel is a small price to pay for the security of the Northern trade routes."
Geralt stepped closer to the crystal, his face very still. "You think this happened because people cared for him?"

"I think concealment, familial compromise, unlicensed mage intervention, imperial confusion, and local ritual secrecy produced preventable escalation," Sorel said, his voice level and dry. "A coordinated authority could have contained the subject earlier and avoided the destruction of the sanctuary. The boy is not a person, witcher; he is a container for a dangerous property. Your attempt to treat him as a son is a category error. A father's duty is to submit his children to the law.
"You have allowed your emotions to cloud your contract."

Jack listened. The words felt cold, dry, and clean, like old parchment. Subject. Contained earlier. Category error. Sorel's voice made every old theft seem like a filing system. The man still believed it, even now, when the sky was turning to ink and the dragon was breathing fire through the channels.

That was the true horror of the Bureau: not that they were monsters, but that they had built a room inside their minds where the theft of a person remained responsible if done before witnesses grew emotional.
Ciri lifted the crystal in her hand, the blue light reflecting in her green eyes.

"Listen carefully, Veyrane," she said, her voice dropping into the low hum of the stone. "If I live through this day, I will find every office that learned grammar from you. I will strip its seals, its warrants, its accounts, and its ability to use public safety as a mask for ownership. I will make sure your name is written in the books as a thief, and nothing more.
"You think you are the law, but you are only the rust on the lock."
Yennefer inclined her head. "Accurate. And I will provide the ink."
Ciri crushed the crystal under her boot, the blue glass shattering into a thousand tiny shards that were instantly swallowed by the red dust.

The first attempt to seize Jack proved what the battle had been trying to hide: humans would always be quicker than monsters to claim a surviving body. Veyrane's men came with custody chains slick with sand and orders to preserve him intact. Cazren's cultists came through the same corridor muttering open him beneath their breath. Office and altar wanted different futures and the same man at the center of them.
That kinship made Ciri's face go beautifully cold.

She did not merely defend Jack. She corrected the room. Hooks were cut before hands. Warrants burned before names. A Black Ink officer tried subject and discovered that Ciri could place a sword through a restraint shaft close enough to his fingers to teach theology without killing him.

Geralt made the line no closer with nothing more decorative than his body and the look of a father who had finally learned that love could mean not reaching first. Yennefer let Sorel Veyrane speak through a crystal long enough to hang himself with grammar. When he called emotional proximity a compromise, Ciri smiled with the part of empire that belonged only to her and crushed the crystal under her boot.
The clean chains finally had a face. That did not make the next choice easy. It made it easier to hate correctly.

The failed seizure left its mark in arrangements rather than speeches. Ciri did not step away from Jack until the corridor was clear. Geralt took the rear without being asked. Yennefer held her anger so tightly it became useful, and Triss counted breaths instead of wounds. Asha and Tala watched the old rites with new suspicion. The room had not been solved; it had been exposed.
Every person in it now knew what they would protect before law, rank, or fear.
Sorel's image flickered. "Your Highness, emotional proximity is compromising your assessment."
Ciri smiled then. It was not a kind smile. It was imperial at last, but the empire in it belonged to her, not Emhyr, not Nilfgaard, not any man who had ever mistaken title for leash.
"No," she said. "It is informing my sentence."
She crushed the crystal under her boot.
Jack studied the shards. Some part of him, exhausted and close to breaking, was glad Sorel had spoken. The clean chain had shown its face one last time. It made the dirty choice easier to name.
Not easy.
Never easy.
Easier to hate correctly.
"Then we do not walk," Yennefer said, her fingers stained with raw ash from the secondary line. "We crawl. But we do not stop."
Saesenthessis did not look at the sky.
"The gate is open," she said, her voice dropping into the cold basalt. "But the key is still turning."
Geralt adjusted Jack's shoulder harness one last time before the descent.
"Still too loose?" Jack asked.
"No," Geralt said, his face grey under the dust. "Just enough."
The wind from the lower valley was salt, and behind them, the red shore was already beginning to cool.

Unreliable song draft found among Dandelion's papers, heavily crossed out: He made himself the wall, they say. No. Worse. Better. A wall does not know the names of those who pound against it from the safe side. He did.

By the time Vharakthul had a body, every cleaner solution had failed in public. The sword had found no organ worth the name. Magic had given the Crown tools. Elder Blood could open routes but not guarantee that what followed would remain small enough to close. Dragon force could wound him and could not contain him. The old external anchor had cracked.

The Faithel repair had been learned and spoiled by the thing it was meant to bind. Regis had looked at the problem with a healer's terrible honesty and found no biological mercy. No answer remained except the one everyone had been circling with hatred: the living chamber, chosen or not at all.

The Canyon of Stars did not look like stone at night; it looked like frozen pressure. The wind that scraped through the deep waterless channels did not sound like wind, but like the dry, hollow rattling of old bones in a copper box. For centuries, the Faithel had scrubbed these stones, marking them with green copper bands and ancient anchor runes that had once promised to keep the sky from falling.

Now, the turquoise corrosion on the old bronze gear plates looked like dried poison under the cold light of the stars. The air tasted of dry dust, old salt, and the faint, bitter smell of sulfur that always came when the earth began to tear itself apart. It was a place where people came to die when they wanted the desert to keep their secrets.
The silence here was not empty; it was a weight that pressed against the ears, filled with the static hum of ancient machinery buried deep within the red sandstone.

They sat around a small fire of dry thorn-wood, the smoke rising thin and gray toward the cold stars. The flames did not leap; they crawled along the gnarled wood, casting long, trembling shadows against the canyon wall. The warmth was small and fragile, easily stolen by the wind that swept down from the high plateaus. No one spoke of the morning.
To speak of the morning was to pretend that time was still a straight line, rather than a circle that was rapidly tightening around them.

Jack sat on a low ledge, his knees drawn up, his back against the cold, vertical stone. He was listening to the wind, but he was also listening to the fire. The wood was old, salt-bitten, and it burned with a faint, green hiss that sounded like whispering.

Geralt stood a few paces away, near the shadow of a fallen pillar that had once supported a bronze axle. He had his silver sword across his knees, the whetstone in his right hand. Shh, shh, shh. The sound was steady, regular as a heartbeat, and just as stubborn.
He did not look at Jack, but every few minutes, his yellow eyes would slide toward the boy's left hand, where the glove was torn and the skin was white from the wind.

"Vesemir told me about a contract in Malleore," Geralt said, his voice flat, barely carrying over the wind's rattle. "A foglet had nested in a village well. Simple enough, usually. You throw in some salt, you use Yrden to slow the vapor, you draw the silver. But this one had been there thirty years. The villagers had been feeding it their sheep, then their dogs, then their children's teeth when the sheep ran out.

"They thought it was a god because it kept the well from freezing in winter. When I got there, the well wasn't water anymore. It was just a gray grease that smelled like old lard. Vesemir told me to walk away. He said some places have spent so much time being rotten that if you clean them out, the walls collapse because the rot was the only thing holding the timber together.
"The people there didn't want a witcher. They wanted an auditor who would tell them their debts were paid in a language they couldn't read."
Jack did not move. "Is that what I am? The rot?"

"You're the timber," Geralt said, the whetstone hitting the tip of the blade with a sharp, clear ring. "And we're the idiots trying to scrape the mold off without dropping the roof on our heads. I've spent fifty years looking at things that were made wrong. Some were born in the mud, some were made in the laboratory at Kaer Morhen, and some were made by wizards who had too much ink and too little sense.

"But they all had one thing in common: they didn't ask to be the wall. The wall is what you build when you don't have the courage to stand in the field. When I was ten, Vesemir locked me in the lower cellar for three days with nothing but a bucket of salt and a rusted dagger. He said he wanted me to learn the shape of a corner.

"He said a witcher who doesn't know where the wall ends will spend his life fighting the dark in a circle, and the dark has a lot more room than we do. I hated him for it. I spent those three days drawing lines on the floor with the salt, trying to figure out if there was a way to make the corners round. There wasn't.
"A corner is just two walls that have decided they can't go any further without hitting each other."

"My father kept a ledger," Jack said. "He kept it in a drawer under the dry flour. Every night after the mill stopped, he would sit with a candle and write down the names of the men who had brought their grain. He wrote down the weight, the dampness, the price of the sacks, and the number of coppers he had paid in taxes.

"He did it because he believed that if the numbers balanced, the world was safe. He thought that if he could account for every grain of wheat, the soldiers wouldn't come. But they came anyway. They burned the mill, they took the sacks, and they used the pages of the ledger to light their pipes. When I found him, he was still holding the quill. His fingers were stiff, and the ink had dried black on his knuckles."

"A ledger is the only honest thing the North ever built," Geralt grunted, finally setting the whetstone down on the dry stone. He stood up, his leather armor creaking, and walked over to Jack. He reached down, took Jack's left wrist, and turned it over. The skin was cold, the black veins of the Cinder-Seal showing faint and dark beneath the surface, like pencil lines drawn under the skin. "You have too many debts, Jack.

"Your father kept a ledger because he thought if he counted the salt, the king wouldn't come for the horse. But the king always comes for the horse. And he doesn't care about the ledger. A witcher doesn't write down his names because he knows that if he writes them down, someone will find the page and use it to bill him. We move because the road doesn't have an auditor.
"We move because if you stay in one place long enough, they build a fence around you and call it your house."
"A fence keeps the wolves out," Jack said.

"It keeps the horse in," Geralt said. His grip tightened on Jack's wrist, just enough to feel the quick, irregular jump of the witcher pulse beneath the skin. "You think you're being practical because you're writing the number down. But you're just making the page look neat. If you climb into the stone, you're not saving the road. You're just letting them use your body to pave it.

"You think you can balance this ledger, but there aren't enough numbers in the world to buy back a life once you've given it away. Vesemir used to say that the only contract you never sign is the one where the reward is your own shadow. You're trying to sign it, Jack. And you're doing it with your own blood."

Yennefer approached them, her skirts whispering against the gravel. The smell of lilac and gooseberries was so strong it made Jack's nose itch, a sharp, clean scent that belonged in a high chamber in Vengerberg, not in this dry gutter of red stone. Her face was pale, her dark curls pinned back with silver pins that caught the starlight like tiny, frozen sparks.
"Leave the boy's wrist alone, Geralt," she said, her voice quiet but sharp enough to cut the wind. "You are not a physician, and your touch is not comforting. It smells of horse-grease and old iron."
Geralt let go of Jack's hand and stepped back, his face returning to the shadow of the fallen column.

Yennefer sat on the stone beside Jack. She did not touch him, but she sat close enough that he could feel the dry, static warmth of her magic, a faint prickling on his skin like wool before a storm. "I have read the tablets from the third sanctuary," she said, her eyes fixed on the fire. "The Zerrikanians were very thorough. They kept records of every warden they compressed. They called them 'the willing stones.'

They believed that if a man chose to become the chamber, his mind would remain structured. But they were writing in stone, and stone does not know what it is like to have a headache. They did not write about the noise. They did not write about the way the dragon's thoughts will crawl through your head like beetles in a rotten log.

He is not a guest who sits in the corner and keeps his boots clean, Jack. He is an ideology that has spent four centuries trying to find a door. He will search your memory for every time you were cold, every time you were hungry, every time you wanted to run, and he will make those moments into a room where you can rest.
And if you rest, even for the length of a breath, the chamber will open. The wall must be constant. A wall cannot have a bad night. A wall cannot decide it wants a cup of tea."
"I've had several bad nights," Jack said. "Most of them had worse company than a dragon."

"Do not make jokes," she said, her voice suddenly breaking, the violet in her eyes dark and wet. "You are trying to look like Geralt, but you are not Geralt. You do not have fifty years of calluses to hide behind. You are Helena's child, and she was a foolish woman who believed that if she sang the song correctly, the king would listen. The king did not listen. He just built a larger forge.

"When I was in Aretuza, they taught us that power is a fluid. They said that if you do not shape the vessel, the water will find the cracks and split the clay. They spent three years teaching us how to make our walls thick, how to make our skin into iron, how to make our voices sound like bells.

"But they didn't tell us that when you make the vessel that strong, the water inside stays cold forever. You never warm up, Jack. Even when you are sitting by the fire, your hands are always like ice. And now, you want to become the stone itself.

"You want to make yourself so hard that no one can ever hurt you, but you don't see that once you're that hard, you can't feel the warmth of the fire either. You'll just sit in the dark, keeping the dragon cold, while the rest of us are left to wonder if we should have been the ones to break the clay."
"If we don't build it," Jack said, "we'll be the ones inside."
"We are already inside," she whispered. "We've been inside since the day we decided that one life could be traded for a clean sky. It's a merchant's trade, Jack. And I have always hated merchants."

Ciri came over from the edge of the circle. She had a cup of water in her hand, but she did not offer it to Jack. She just held it, the water still and dark under the starlight. "I spoke to Saesenthessis," she said. "She is standing near the upper ridge. She says the dragon's shadow is already touching the wells. The water in the lower channel is tasting of copper.

She says we have less than an hour before the pressure reaches the sanctuary gates. The guardians are already standing near the steps, but they look like men who are waiting for a funeral. They aren't looking at the road. They're looking at their own boots."
"We don't need an hour," Jack said.

Ciri faced him, her green eyes wide and angry. "You always say that. You say it as if it were a virtue. 'We don't need time. We don't need help. We don't need water.' You sound like a man who is trying to prove he doesn't have a stomach. It's not brave, Jack. It's just lonely. When I was in the desert of Korath, I had no water. I had no food.

I had nothing but a horse that was dying and a little monster that wanted to eat my eyes if I fell asleep. I spent three days licking the dew off the rocks, and I hated the sky because it was so blue and so clean while I was covered in dirt and horse-blood. I thought that if I survived, I would never let myself be thirsty again.

I thought I would spend the rest of my life sitting near a well with a bucket. But when I got out, the first thing they did was put a crown on my head and tell me that the well belonged to the empire. They said I couldn't drink unless I signed the ledger.

I spent two years trying to find a road that didn't have a gate, and now I'm here, helping you build the biggest gate of all. We're locking you in, Jack. And we're doing it because we don't know what else to do with the key. It's the same thing they did to me. They didn't want Cirilla; they wanted the blood. And now, they don't want Jack; they want the stone."
"The gate is for the dragon," Jack said.

"The gate is for you," she said, setting the cup down on the stone with a sharp clack. "You're the one who will be behind the bar. You're the one who will have to sit in the dark while the rest of us are walking on the road. You think because you're a witcher, you don't need the sun. But I've seen your face when the rain comes from the north.
"You look like you're trying to remember the smell of the pines. You look like you're trying to find a page in the ledger that isn't written in ink."
"The pines smelled like turpentine," Jack said. "And the rain was always cold."
"It was real rain," Ciri said. "And it fell on a real road."

Triss came toward them from the small fire, holding a copper pot that smelled of boiled dandelion roots and tallow. Her red hair was tied back with a rough string, and her face was red from the heat of the fire. She looked tired, the shadows under her blue eyes dark and heavy.

"The warming field is stable," Triss said, her voice careful and businesslike, though she did not look at Geralt. "I've placed three anchors near the inner circle and two near the channel. If the dragon's pressure rises too fast, the field will absorb the vibration. But it will draw from my own store. If I go quiet, Yennefer, you'll have to take the third line. I've calculated the drift.

"The crimson resonance is going to push the field outward, like oil on water. We have to keep it compressed, or the Faithel on the outer ridge will have their bones turned to chalk before the seal even closes. I've seen field compression fail before, Jack. In Sodden, we had a circle of twelve sorceresses trying to hold the line against Nilfgaardian fire-gems.

"The field looked like a gold dome, beautiful and solid, but the fire-gems weren't hitting the dome. They were hitting the grass outside. The heat rose through the soil, and before we knew it, our boots were melting. We were standing in hot pitch, trying to cast spells while our toes were burning. That's what Vharakthul does. He won't hit your sword; he'll hit the stone beneath your feet. He'll make the ground too hot to stand on."
"I've fought on hot stone before," Jack said.

"Not stone that wants to eat your knees," Triss said. "You must stay in the circle, Jack. If you step outside, even by an inch, the alignment will slip, and the field will collapse on top of us. It won't be a quiet death. It will be like being ground between two millstones that have run out of grease."
"I'll stay," Jack said.
"You'd better," she said, her voice trembling. "I didn't spend three hours boiling these roots just to have you turned to lime because you wanted to take a longer step."

Regis stepped forward, the small wooden box in his hands. He opened the lid, revealing three small green glass vials. "The mandrake is pure," he said, his voice quiet. "I gathered it near the ruins of Willenford, under the old wall where the soil has been turned by the plow. It has a high copper content. It will slow the heart, Jack. It will make your breath feel like lead in your throat.

But it will keep the veins from breaking under the pressure. You must take it when the dragon's shadow reaches the first step of the ritual circle. If you take it too early, you won't have the strength to hold the silver sword. If you take it too late, your heart will simply burst like an overripe plum. Mandrake is a strange herb.

It grows where men have died in pain, and it remembers the shape of their blood. It will try to make your heart match their silence. You must fight that silence, Jack. You must keep the pulse moving, even if it feels like you're dragging a wagon through mud."
"I've dragged worse," Jack said.
"I am sure you have," Regis said. "But a wagon does not try to swallow your legs while you're pulling it."

Regis reached out, his cool, pale fingers brushing against Jack's collar before moving to trace the edge of the Cinder-Seal scar that rose from beneath his coat. "The structural lines are... altered," the vampire murmured, his eyes dark with clinical interest. "The scar tissue has grown around the magic, locking the resonance into the marrow. It mirrors the carvings on the temple gates of Zerrikania.

The artisans who built those gates were Aen Elle exiles, men who had spent their youth carving the gates of Tir na Lia. When they came here, they had no stone but this soft sandstone, which crumbles under the chisel. So they mixed the sand with their own blood and grease, making a paste that hardened under the sun.

They believed that if you want a door to stay closed, you must paint it with something that was once alive. The Cinder-Seal is that paste, Jack. It is blood and sand, and it has had four hundred years to dry. If you pull too hard on the alignment, the sand will dissolve, and you will be left with nothing but the blood."
"The blood is mine," Jack said.
"For now," Regis said. "But the dragon has a very long throat. And he is very thirsty."

They fell silent again. The wind had shifted, coming now from the east, carrying the sharp, cold scent of the distant sea. The starlight was very thin, like salt spilled on black velvet. Far down the canyon, the shadow of Vharakthul was moving, a slow, greasy tide that seemed to swallow the stones as it crawled.

"The wind is from the east," Asha said, her hand tracing the copper rim of the bowl in her lap. "That is the wind of the sea. The Faithel called it the 'breath of the iron.' They believed that when the wind shifted to the east, the seal was calling for its wage. The first warden was a man from the mountains who had no name.

"He sat in the stone for forty years, and when they dug him out, his bones had turned to copper. They used his ribs to mend the gear plates on the second well. The second warden was a woman who had three children. She sat for ten years, and when she died, her voice stayed in the water channels.
"If you listen near the third well, you can still hear her complaining about the price of barley.

"They weren't heroes, Jack. They were just people who had no other way to keep their fields from turning to salt. They traded their names for three bags of seed and a year without the crown-officers."
"It's a fair trade," Jack said.
"It's only fair if you have the seed," Asha said. "We don't have the seed. We only have the canyon. And the canyon is very hungry."
"Then let it eat," Jack said. "I've been told I'm very tough."

Asha held him in her dark gaze. "You're tough because you're thin, Jack. But thin things break when the wind blows too hard. And the wind tonight is very strong. My grandmother used to tell me that when the first Faithel came to the canyon, they didn't have swords. They had copper knives that were so soft they bent when you hit a bone. They had to sharpen them on their own teeth.

They believed that the only way to make the metal obey was to teach it the taste of your mouth. That's why we drink the bitter tea before we sing. It's not for the throat. It's for the steel. We are teaching the blades that they belong to the body, not the market."

Tala stood near the fire, her red scarf wrapped tight around her throat, her hand resting on the hilt of her blackened blade. She had been checking the outer steps, her boots white with limestone dust. "The cultists are gathering near the lower gate," she said, her voice low. "They have three banners of black cloth, and they are singing the verse of the third well. They don't have weapons, most of them, but they have their hands.

They will try to throw themselves into the circle. They want to be the ashes, Jack. They believe that if they burn with the dragon, they will become the shadow. I'll hold them back, but they are many, and they don't care about the blade. A man who wants to be burned is very hard to stop with steel.

I saw a man in the valley of Elskerdeg who had set fire to his own hair because he believed the smoke would carry his prayers to the obsidian crown. He was laughing while his skin was melting. You can't argue with a man like that, Geralt. You can only cut him down before he gets to the flour."
"Use the flat," Geralt said. "They aren't soldiers. They're just idiots who have had too much smoke."

"I'll use what works," Tala said. "But if they get past the steps, the circle will be spoiled. Jack, do not look at them. If you look at their faces, you'll see someone you know. They have the faces of every man who ever bought flour from your father. They are the ones who couldn't pay their taxes, and they think the dragon is the only one who doesn't keep a ledger.
"They are the ones who have spent their lives in the mud, and they want the world to become mud so they don't have to look at the clean stone anymore."
"He keeps one," Jack said. "He just writes the names in soot."
"Then do not let him write yours," she said.

The fire clicked, a single piece of thorn-wood splitting in the heat, sending a tiny shower of green sparks up into the dark. The wind took them, and they were gone before they could reach the ledge. The canyon seemed to grow narrower, the red sandstone walls pressing in from the sides like the palms of two huge, silent hands.

The air was thick now, heavy with the smell of old copper and wet sheep, and the silence was so deep that Jack could hear the slow, dry clicking of the grasshoppers in the dry weeds near the steps. They were waiting for the rain too, but the rain in the desert was always late, and it always brought more salt than water.

Jack met Ciri's gaze. She had not sat down. She stood near the ledge, her green cloak blowing around her boots, her face turned toward the east where the shadow was rising. She looked like she wanted to run. She looked like she wanted to blink through the sky and never look back.
"Do you remember the lake?" she asked quietly.
"Which one?" Jack said.

"The one near Corvo Bianco," she said. "The one where the water was so blue it looked like Yennefer's eyes when she's angry. We went there after the horse died. You sat on the log and tried to skip stones, but you were too stiff. You threw them like you were trying to kill the water."
"I skipped three," Jack said.

"You skipped two," she said, a small, brief smile touching her mouth before it vanished. "The third one was just a splash. But the water was warm. And you didn't have the glove on. I remember looking at your hand, and the skin was just skin. There were no black lines. There was no seal. There was just the scar from the skinning knife, and it was white and neat.

"I thought that if we stayed there, the skin would grow back. I thought the road would stop asking for the wage. We spent that whole afternoon listening to the cicadas, and the air smelled of warm grass and horses. I didn't think about the empire once. I didn't think about Emhyr, or the crown-officers, or the files they were keeping in Novigrad.
"I just thought about how the water felt on my feet.
"And now, I have to stand here and watch you climb into a stone."
"The road never stops," Jack said. "It just gets wider."
"Then I want a narrow one," she said. "A road that only has room for two horses. And no gates."
"We'll find one," Jack said.
"No," she said, her voice dropping until it was barely a whisper against the wind. "We won't. We'll just find another well. And another ledger."
She turned away.
The shadow reached the first step. The starlight died. The canyon vanished into the black fleece, and the wind went quiet, leaving only the heavy, greasy heat that smelled of wet iron.

Jack stood up. His chest was tight, the Cinder-Seal pulling at his skin like a hand trying to turn him inside out. The Blizzard was working, the world slowing until the red coals of the fire were static, frozen in their gray ash. He took the small vial of mandrake oil from Regis's box, pulled the cork, and let three drops fall onto his tongue.

It tasted of dry earth, rot, and the bitter copper of an old coin left in a well. His heart slowed, the heavy, frantic thudding turning into a steady, cold march—thud... thud... thud. His vision split, the darkness of the canyon turning into a high-contrast monochrome where every stone was outlined in a thin, silver line of pressure.
"The enemy is here," Asha said, her voice rising in a high, clear chant. "The seal is open. The warden is ready."
The battle was about to begin.

Vharakthul rose from the center of the canyon, his physical aspect massive and terrifying. He was not a beast to be measured by scales and claws; he was an ancient ideology made physical, a monument of black dark that seemed to drink the starlight and spit it back as ash. The sky did not change color; it curdled, turning the shade of a wet sheep-fleece that had been left in the mud.

The air grew so hot Jack could feel the sweat running down his ribs under his wool coat, smelling of vinegar, toxic herbs, and the sharp, sour tang of the Blizzard potion that was already turning his spit to iron.

Jack stood at the edge of the circle, his silver sword held low. His vision had split into a cold, monochrome grid, the stone walls of the canyon outlined in thin, silver-white needles of pressure. Under the influence of the Blizzard, the dragon's movements were slow, almost majestic—the massive wings folding like heavy sail-cloth, the long, scale-sheathed neck turning with the patient grind of a millstone.
But Jack's own muscles were screaming, the mutagens driving his heart to a slow, heavy thud—thud... thud... thud—that made his ears ring and his teeth ache.

He reached for the next vial in his kit. The Full Moon potion. The fluid was pale, smelling of crushed bone and honey. He drank it down, the glass clicking against his teeth. Instantly, his lungs expanded, his chest feeling as if it were bound by bands of cold iron that prevented his ribs from collapse. His vision grew sharper, the silver lines of pressure turning into thick, glowing cords.

Next was the Golden Oriole, a bitter, yellow oil that smelled of mint and vinegar. As it hit his throat, the burning in his lungs eased, the toxic sulfur of the dragon's breath neutralized by the potion's clean, chemical heat.

Finally, he drank the Thunderbolt, the burning mutagens of wolfsbane and drowner brain making his muscles feel tight as iron wires, his crimson resonance humming in his chest like an angry hornets' nest. His face was a mask of black, swollen veins, his eyes entirely dark.

The dragon struck first, not with a claw, but with a wave of black pressure that smelled of sulfur and wet iron. Jack threw his left hand forward, his fingers twisting into the sign of Quen. The gold-yellow hemisphere of light formed in the air, humming with a static charge that made his hair stand on end.
The shield did not hold; it cracked with a dry, splintering sound, and the impact threw Jack thirty feet across the broken sandstone.

He hit the gravel hard, rolling to his knees as the dust rose in a gray cloud. His left side was a furnace of pain, two ribs cracked and rubbing together under his skin like broken dry twigs. The Swallow potion was working, the tissue itching and burning as it tried to knit itself together, but the heat of it was too high, making his breath rattle in his throat.

"Stay on your feet!" Geralt roared, his boots crunching on the stone as he pivoted to the left. He pulled a Moon Dust bomb from his belt and threw it into the forming joint of Vharakthul's shoulder. The bomb burst with a soft, metallic pop, filling the air with a thick cloud of silver flakes that settled on the black scales like frost.

Yrden runes flared on the canyon floor, Triss's field humming in a low, purple circle that slowed the dragon's joints. Jack ran through the opening before the black dark could close again, his silver sword flashing in the purple light. The runes on his blade—old, cut by a smith in Cintra who had died before the war—bit into the silvered scales.

Jack swung in a wide, two-handed arc, the silver blade slicing through the frost-like Moon Dust on Vharakthul's shoulder. The stone-like scales resisted, the shock of the impact running up Jack's arms, bruising his wrists and elbows, splitting the leather of his sleeves. The blade bit three inches deep, and a thick, black smoke poured from the wound, hot as molten lead. The smoke smelled of scorched fat and old tin.
Jack yanked the sword free, pivoting on his heel to avoid a sweep of the dragon's tail that shattered a fallen pillar behind him.

He drove Aard into the heap of broken stone. The concussive blast of air threw a shower of sharp sandstone shards into Vharakthul's face, distracting the beast for the fraction of a second Jack needed to regain his footing. He cast Igni, a torrent of white-hot fire washing over the dragon's front leg.
The flame did not burn the obsidian scales, but it heated the silver flakes of the Moon Dust, melting them into the joints, making the dragon's movements stutter.

Vharakthul did not bleed. He remembered bleeding, and that memory was hot enough to burn Jack's leather glove to a crisp. The dark heat poured from the wound, smelling of scorched leather and old fat. Jack cut again, his blade ringing against the obsidian scales like a hammer on an anvil.
First offer.

The canyon vanished. The starlight, the fire, the smell of sulfur—all of it was gone. Jack stood in a hall that seemed to have no ceiling, only a high, vaulted darkness supported by columns of polished black marble that reflected a red, sluggish light. The floor was clean, so clean it looked like ice.

Kneeling before him were rows of men—clerks in neat wool coats, their hands folded in their laps; soldiers in steel plates, their swords laid flat on the stone; cultists with their faces pressed against the marble, their fingers twitching in silent prayer. On a raised dais of black stone sat a chair. It was simple, carved from a single block of dark oak, but it looked heavier than the mountain.

Rule, little wall, the thought came. It was not a voice, but a pressure in Jack's skull, the taste of cold ink and the smell of old paper. A throne is the only place where no one can touch you. The Black Ink offices are empty. The files are burned. The captains who wrote your name in their ledgers are dead. You may write theirs now.
You may decide who eats and who stays in the dry well. No one will ever ask you to show your hand. No one will ever look at your neck for a seal.

Jack walked down the aisle between the kneeling ranks. He saw the clerks from the Novigrad treasury, their inkwells dry, their sheepskin ledger pages white and blank. He saw Sorel Veyrane, his hands bound with red thread, his face pale and smudged with soot. He saw the captains of the temple guard, their armor rusted, their banners torn.

They were all silent, their breathing shallow and regular, like men who had forgotten how to speak. The dark crown on the dais hummed with the same crimson resonance that was burning in Jack's chest. It was a promise of absolute silence. A promise that no paper would ever find him again.

Jack studied the kneeling clerks. He saw the back of Nadir's head, the gray hair thin and dirty. He saw Roche's scarred face, still and pale. He saw the red light of the sky outside the high windows, a sky that looked like old blood. He spit onto the polished black stone.
"Too much furniture," he said.
The vision shattered like dry glass.

Vharakthul struck again, the spear of black pressure cutting through Jack's side. The old Cinder-Seal took the blow, and Jack fell to one knee, the silver sword slipping from his fingers. Darkness crowded the edges of his sight, and the starlight broke apart into thin white needles.
Second offer.
The canyon disappeared again.

Jack stood in the small room of the mill in Willenford. The light was yellow and warm, coming from a candle that sat in a brass holder on the table. The smell of saffron bread was thick, sweet, mixed with the damp scent of wet wool that hung from the rafters.

Helena was standing by the window, her apron white with flour, her fingers tracing the edge of a song draft. Her copper eyes were bright when they found him. "You're late, Jack," she said, her voice soft and dry. "Your father has been waiting for the dry pine. He says the wet wood makes the chimney smoke, and the smoke makes his eyes water."

Jacob was in the corner, his woolen coat smelling of grease. He was using his curved knife to repair a leather harness strap, his calloused thumb moving with the slow, steady rhythm of a man who had spent forty years doing the same work. "No child should be forced to inherit rhythm before he can walk," he grunted, without looking up. "The boy has no ears for the third beat.
He sounds like a horse with a loose shoe."
"The pine was wet because of the rain," Jack said.

"The rain is always wet," Jacob said, his knife scraping the leather. "That's why you keep it in the shed. If you leave the door open, the water gets in, and the wood is no good for the hearth. Sit, Jack. Eat the bread before it goes cold."

Jack stared at the bread. The crust was split, the yellow saffron showing through the cracks. It looked so real, so heavy. He could see the dust motes floating in the candle-light. He could hear the waterwheel turning outside—creak, splash, creak, splash. He wanted to sit.

He wanted to take his boots off, to feel the warmth of the fire on his cold toes, to listen to his mother hum the third verse of the warden's song. He wanted to believe that the grave under the northern birches was just a bad dream he had had during the winter.
He reached for the bread.

But his hand was covered in black veins. The skin was hard, witcher-marked, and the glove was missing the index finger where the silver had burned it. His father's hands were calloused, but they were clean of magic. His mother's eyes were copper, but they did not have the yellow slit of the cat.
"She didn't like saffron," Jack said, his voice flat. "She said it tasted like brass. And she always used salt in the flour."
He cut.

The room vanished. The spear of black pressure struck him through the left side, right where the Cinder-Seal met the skin. The impact was not physical, but it felt as if someone had driven a frozen iron bar through his liver. Jack fell to one knee, the silver sword slipping from his fingers. Blackness pressed in around his sight, and the stars frayed into a white blur.
Ciri appeared in front of him, the green-white light of her Elder Blood flashing like summer lightning. Her blade—Zireael—cut through the black pressure line with a sound like wet silk tearing.
"Do not listen to the dead when they sound convenient," she said, her breath coming fast through her teeth. Her forehead was wet with sweat, and her sleeve was torn at the elbow.
"That's your advice?" Jack gasped, his hand pressed to his side. The Blizzard was starting to wear off, and the toxicity was making his teeth rattle.
"It's excellent advice," Ciri said, her eyes fixed on the dragon's red coal-eyes. "I have several dead and none are convenient. Get up, Jack. Geralt has the chain."

Yennefer pulled him back with a spell that felt like a cold hand grabbing his collar and dragging him through the gravel. "If you fall now, I will revive you just to be angry in person," she snarled, her fingers twisting in the air as she threw a violet shield between them and the dragon's breath.
"Threat noted," Jack said, his throat dry as ash.
"It was a promise," she said.
Triss pressed a small, warm clay charm against his side. The magic was fierce and hot, smelling of dried clover and tallow. "Thirty heartbeats," she said, her voice shaking. "Do not waste them."
"Only thirty?"
"You keep using your body as public infrastructure," she said, her eyes bright with tears she did not have time to let fall. "There are administrative limits. Even for witchers."
Geralt handed him the chain.

It was heavy, three links to the foot, the iron dark and pitted with rust. The Faithel had used it to secure the old bronze gear plates to the anchor stones. The links were cold, smelling of old grease and wet earth. Geralt did not say anything. He only looked at Jack, his yellow eyes flat and empty of everything except the next move. Vesemir's lessons. Witcher ugliness.
If the god would not obey the silver, make him obey the weight of the stone.
Jack ran.

He used the broken water channel, sliding down the dry sandstone chute to get beneath Vharakthul's forming shoulder. The dragon was huge now, a mountain of dark oil and bone-scales that seemed to drink the starlight. Jack wrapped the chain around his left forearm, the iron biting through the sleeve of his coat into the skin.
Vharakthul offered Ciri safe.

The canyon shifted again, but only for a second, like a shutter opening and closing. A small, white house near a lake. No Nilfgaardian banners. No imperial clerks. Geralt was sitting on a wooden bench by the water, old and slow, his hair entirely white, laughing as he mended a fishing net. Yennefer was standing in the doorway, her black hair loose, her hands free of magic and silver thread.

Triss was walking up the path with a basket of yellow apples, her face red from the sun. Ciri was there, her sword hung on the wall of the porch, her boots covered in garden mud. She looked like a woman who had never heard the word destiny.
"I can give her this," Vharakthul whispered in his mind. "A road with no names written in smoke. No courts. No crown. She will sleep until the sun comes up."
Jack saw it.
So did Ciri.
Her face twisted in the dark, her green eyes wide and dark with anger. "Bastard," she spat.
"Him or me?" Jack asked, his voice cracking.
"Currently both," she said.
"Fair," Jack said.

The offer died because she refused it first. That was the difference. Vharakthul wanted Jack's desire to be solitary, to be a secret he could use to buy him. Ciri's refusal made the desire less lonely, and therefore harder to turn into a key.
Vharakthul offered Yennefer safe. Geralt spared. Triss untouched. Buck alive. A world where no one he loved had to stand in the canyon and help make him a prison.
Jack wanted it.

There was no nobility in pretending otherwise. The want was not a thought; it was a physical hunger that tore at his ribs like a wild dog. He wanted Buck's warm, stupid breath against his shoulder. He wanted Geralt's bad repairs on the saddle straps, the leather stitched with thick, uneven twine. He wanted Ciri's sharp, mocking smile when he missed a parry.

He wanted Yennefer's hand staying too long at his pulse, her fingers cool and smelling of lilac. He wanted Triss's soup-and-strategy courage, the way she talked about tax law as if it were a weapon. He wanted Asha's bitter tea and Tala's red thread. He wanted Regis's awful, quiet honesty.

He wanted a road with no ancient thing breathing through his lungs, no red light in his palm, no papers with his name on them. He wanted to be a man who took contracts for three coppers and left before the villagers could thank him.
He wanted to live.
That was why the refusal mattered.
"Every offer is ownership wearing mercy," Jack said.
He drove the iron chain hook into the open wound in Vharakthul's shoulder, where the Moon Dust had silvered the joint, and wrapped the other end three times around his own left forearm.
Geralt understood first. "Jack!" he roared, his boots crunching on the stone as he started forward.
"Stay back!" Jack screamed.
He pulled.

The body did not have the strength to move a god, but the body did not need to. The soul only performed the gesture so it had something to believe. Jack pulled with the crimson resonance at full burn, the red light flaring from his skin until the canyon walls looked like they were made of fresh blood.
The golden seal pressure and the black contamination ground together in his chest like two millstones, the heat so intense he could hear his own blood singing in his ears.

Witcher mutations kept his heart beating past sanity. The potions turned his blood into a dark, toxic argument. Helena's song gave the rhythm—one, two, three, pause. Jacob's stubbornness gave the insult. Vesemir's training gave the angle. Geralt's tactics gave the leverage. Ciri's Elder Blood gave the route inward, cutting through the space between scale and spirit without opening a door for the dragon to escape.

Yennefer held his body together with magic so precise and sharp it felt like being sewn with iron wire. Triss stabilized the field, her golden light wrapping around them both, though she was crying now, the tears running down her dusty cheeks. Asha spoke the forbidden rite, her voice rising above the wind, her nose bleeding onto her chin. Tala and the Faithel held the circle, their blades dark, their faces still.
Saesenthessis named the draconic binding in a voice that sounded like stone moving under stone. Regis watched for the moment Jack stopped being only Jack.
Jack felt that moment come.
The red light in his eyes began to settle, turning into a cold, dark amber. His breath was no longer his own; it was heavy, hot, smelling of old iron.
He turned once.

Ciri was nearest, because she had refused to stay behind the line. Yennefer stood behind her, her face white as bone, her hands shaking as she held the violet threads. Geralt was three steps away. He had his silver sword in his hand, but the tip was touching the stone.
He was close enough to stop Jack, and far enough to respect the choice, which was the cruelest distance Jack had ever asked of a man.
"I know what I'm asking," Jack said.
No one answered.
"I know what it costs."
Ciri shook her head once. Not denial. She was refusing to make it easy for him. She was refusing to say it was right.
"I know you hate me for it."
Geralt's face went still, the firelight catching the yellow of his eyes.
Jack's voice broke only on the last word.
"Do it anyway. Please."
The please broke them.
Ciri opened the inward route.

It was not a portal. It was not a blue light in the air. She used Zireael to cut a line through the pressure itself, a path through possibility that turned inward, into Jack's crimson core. Her face showed every old crime that had been committed against her blood, and the one unbearable difference: this time she was not being used. She was helping someone she loved choose a cage.
Yennefer held his body together.

The spell tore the skin of her hands, the blood running down her wrists in dark, thin lines. She did not stop. Her black hair whipped around her face like smoke. She swore in three languages, her voice shrill with rage and horror, keeping his heart from rupturing under the pressure of the dragon's entry.
Triss held the others.

She kept Geralt from crossing the circle, her hand tight on his arm, her magic warm and heavy. Geralt did not move, but the effort cost him; his teeth were clenched so hard a drop of blood appeared at the corner of his mouth.
Asha spoke until the blood ran from her nose, her voice steady and cold.
Tala answered, her red scarf torn, her blade blackened by the heat.
Saesenthessis named the binding, stripping Vharakthul of his crown and his names until only the prisoner remained.
