Warmth met him through linen. Her breath changed immediately, audible now, each exhale fuller than the last.
"Mmh... yes. There."
The words came uneven, shaped by breath more than command.

He moved with her instruction, not past it. The lesson of mortality, he thought dimly, was not only that the body failed. It was that the body had to ask for time, and time, if loved well, could become tenderness instead of humiliation. Ciri seemed to understand that before he did. She kissed him slowly when he needed breath. She pressed him back when standing became too costly.
She laughed once against his throat when his hand shook and then closed her own over it, not to steady him like a patient, but to keep the tremor with her.
"Do not hide that," she murmured.
"It is not decorative."
"Neither am I. We endure."

Her mouth found his again. The heat gathered without haste and without mercy. It came through her hands, through the sound of linen shifting, through the small broken breaths she stopped trying to swallow. She had silenced herself in courts, on roads, in war rooms, in imperial corridors where every feeling became material for men who thought themselves clever. Here she stopped.
The first time his mouth moved to her throat and she tilted into it, the sound left her low and open.
Then softer, because the first had surprised her. "Mm... don't stop."
He did not.

The world reduced itself to touch answered by touch. Her fingers slid into his hair, tightened, released, tightened again. His breath roughened against her skin. She shifted closer and drew a sharper sound from herself when the closeness became more than thought.
"Oh... gods, Jack."
She laughed after it, breathless and not at all ashamed. "I am going to blame recovery for making me sentimental."
"Reasonable."
"You are not allowed to agree."
"Then unreasonable."
"Better."

She kissed him again, and the humor dissolved. The warmth deepened. Jack kept one hand at her back, one at her waist, holding her to him with enough strength to be promise and not enough to become claim. Ciri answered by moving with him in slow increments, every shift shaped by care around his wounds and want around the care. The two did not cancel each other.
Mercy, when it arrived, looked strange in exactly that way. Desire did not need him unbroken. It found him where he was.
Her voice became an undercurrent, no longer made of sentences alone. "Mm... ah... there. Stay. Stay with me."
He had no clever answer left.
He stayed.

The heat rose and held, wave after wave of breath and sound, of her mouth against his, of his name breaking in her voice and becoming less a call than proof. Nothing in the room opened. Nothing answered from beneath the earth. No fate took notes. If the walls remembered, they remembered only that two people had survived long enough to be foolish with tenderness.

When the intensity finally softened, Ciri lowered her forehead to his shoulder and breathed like someone returning from a fight she had chosen and won by refusing to make victory the point. Her fingers remained at his pulse.
"Still there," she whispered.
"You keep checking."
"Yes."
"Will that stop?"
She considered. "No."
He closed his eyes, and the smile came before he could hide it.

Later, when the light had shifted across the floor and the room smelled of warm linen, rain, and the last bitterness of tea, Ciri lay beside him with one hand on his chest and one leg thrown across his with proprietary care she would have denied in front of anyone useful. Her breathing had slowed but not settled completely.
Now and then it caught, as if her body remembered a sound and chose not to be embarrassed by it.
"I thought," she said into the quiet, "that if you lived, I would stop being angry."
"Did it work?"
"No."
"Good. I would not recognize you."
Her fingers pressed once over his heart. "I am angry because you lived and are still mortal. I am angry because I can lose you in smaller ways now. Fever. Bad roads. Infection. Geralt's cooking."
"That last one is serious."
"Do not joke while I am being honest."
He turned his head toward her. "I am listening."

She looked younger for one dangerous second, not in years, but in the unarmored space grief sometimes opened before shame could close it. "They spent my life wanting my blood to matter. I hated it. I still hate it. But when yours went quiet, I was afraid there would be less of you to hold. That makes no sense. I know."
"It makes sense."
"Do not be kind because I am naked under a blanket and politically vulnerable."
"I am kind because I am afraid of you."
She laughed softly, then hid her face against his shoulder. The laugh turned into one rough breath. "Good."
He touched her hair.
No power moved through him.
Only the hand.
Only her warmth.
Only morning continuing without asking permission.
"Ciri," he said.
She lifted her head.
"I am not less."
Her mouth trembled once before she stopped it. "I know."
"But I may need reminding."

That undid her more than any declaration would have. She kissed him then with a tenderness so fierce it almost hurt, and when she pulled back, her eyes had the look she wore before stepping through a door no one else could see.
"Then I will remind you," she said. "Badly, loudly, and often."
"Imperial policy?"
"Personal decree."
Outside, Buck screamed again at some innocent arrangement of the yard.
Ciri rested her forehead against Jack's and smiled.
"Even the horse agrees."
"The horse agrees with no one."
"Then he disapproves supportively."

Jack closed his eyes, held her, and let the room remain what it was for a little longer: not sanctuary, not prophecy, not aftermath written for witnesses, but a bed in a stubborn house where the woman beside him had chosen life loudly enough that death, for the moment, had no place to sit.
Yennefer came at dusk, when the day had already spent its noise.

The house had settled into the cautious rhythm of recovery. Below, someone washed bowls. Rain spoke against the roof in thin, persistent lines. Buck had finally ceased prosecuting the saddle and now stood in the stable yard with the grim dignity of a creature convinced victory had been achieved by exhaustion. Geralt and Triss were somewhere downstairs, which meant silence had witnesses and restraint had company.
Ciri had gone to the lower room after making Jack swear, with insulting specificity, that he would not stand without calling someone, fall without making noise, or die privately for dramatic effect.
He had promised two of the three.
Yennefer entered without knocking.
That, too, was a kind of honesty between them.

She wore black, of course, but not the court-black that made rooms rearrange themselves around her. This was travel black, softer at the sleeve, rain-dark at the hem, practical enough to admit the world existed and foolish enough to continue defying it. The scent of lilac and gooseberry reached him first, then the faint mineral sharpness of spell residue, then rain on wool.
She closed the door with two fingers and watched him for longer than comfort allowed.
"You are sitting badly," she said.
"Good evening."
"That was the charitable version."
"I am recovering."
"You are slouching with moral intent."
He shifted against the pillows. Pain answered from the ribs, dull and ordinary. Yennefer saw the flicker before it became a grimace. Her eyes narrowed.
"There," she said. "That. You still think pain is a private correspondence."
"It usually is."
"Not with me. I intercept letters."

She crossed the room and set a small black case on the table. Inside were glass vials, folded cloth, a needle, a silver hook, and a stoppered bottle that smelled of winter herbs and expensive punishment. Jack regarded the case as if it had come to accuse him.
"Medicine?"
"Discipline disguised as mercy."
"Popular combination."
"With you, necessary."

She sat on the edge of the bed. Not far. Not close enough to hide from what close meant. Her hand went to his wrist first, not because she needed to check the pulse again, but because she had made fear into procedure and procedure into permission. Her fingers were cool. His pulse beat steady beneath them.
Yennefer's mouth tightened.
"Still ordinary," he said.
"Do not gloat. It is unbecoming in invalids."
"I thought you wanted ordinary."
"I wanted you alive. Ordinary is the bill the universe attached afterward. I am examining the fine print."
Her thumb moved once over the pale scars where red lines had been. The touch was clinical for half a heartbeat. Then it stopped being able to lie.
Jack studied her hand. "Yennefer."
"No."
"I had not said anything."
"You were preparing to be noble. I have developed a rash to nobility."
"Dangerous condition."
"Often fatal to men near me."

The humor held for one breath and then failed. She did not look away, which cost her more. Jack had seen Yennefer angry at kings, monsters, sorceresses, rooms, weather, and fate itself. This was not anger. This was anger's stripped frame, the thing beneath it that made fury useful because useless fear was unbearable.
"I hate this," she said.
"Mortality?"

"Do not broaden the subject to escape the room. I hate that I can feel your pulse and it tells me so little. Before, danger announced itself in you like bad architecture. Heat, crimson, pressure, resonance. Now your body keeps human secrets. Infection can be quiet. Exhaustion can be polite. A wound can lie until morning."
"Humanity sounds poorly designed."
"It is atrocious. I have said so for decades. No one has improved it."

She released his wrist and began to unwrap the bandage at his side. Her movements were precise and gentle only because gentleness had been given strict orders to behave. The wound beneath had closed cleanly, puckered at the edges, purple fading into yellow. Yennefer inspected it with the severity of a magistrate judging a repeat offender.
"Healing," she said.
"That sounded reluctant."
"I dislike agreeing with tissue."
He almost laughed. The motion pulled at the ribs. She placed a hand flat against his chest before he could hide the pain.
"There again," she whispered.
The room changed.

Not suddenly. Yennefer did not permit suddenness unless she had caused it. It changed by pressure. Her hand remained where it was. His breath moved under her palm. Rain touched the roof. Somewhere below, Geralt said something too low to hear and Triss answered with the brisk tone of a woman refusing to let men turn concern into furniture repair.
Yennefer's eyes lifted to his.
"Tell me no if you want me to leave," she said.
The words were simple. That made them dangerous.
Jack's breath left slowly. "I do not want you to leave."
"Tell me wait if you need distance."
"I do not need distance."
"Do not answer as if this is another wound to tolerate."
"It is not."
"Then what is it?"

His gaze moved over her face first: the black hair loosened by rain, the bandage still wrapped around two fingers from the final battle, the proud mouth that had threatened gods and the almost invisible tremor in the hand she kept on his chest.
"A choice," he said. "If you still want it."
Yennefer's face closed for a moment, not against him, but against the force of wanting something after nearly losing it. When it opened again, her eyes had gone darker.
"Still," she said. "Unfortunately. Inconveniently. With poor judgment and excellent memory."
He reached for her hand.
She let him take it.

The first kiss was almost austere. It tasted faintly of rain and cloves, of restraint sharpened until restraint itself became intimacy. Yennefer did not melt into him. She would have considered the metaphor an insult. She arrived. Fully. Deliberately. Her hand stayed against his chest, feeling the mortal beat while her mouth gave him an answer no diagnosis could hold.
When she drew back, her breath had changed.
Only slightly.
Enough to make truth visible.
"Again," Jack said.
Her eyebrow moved. "Recovering men should not give orders."
"Request."
"Better."

She kissed him again, and this time severity warmed at the edges. Her lips parted on a quiet exhale. The sound entered him more deeply than a spell could have. Not because it was loud. Because Yennefer rarely allowed sound to escape without purpose.
"Mm..." she breathed against his mouth, and frowned as if her own body had made an argument without submitting it for review.
Jack smiled.
"Do not," she said.
"I did not."
"Your mouth did."
"It lies badly."
"It is learning from your jaw."
She kissed the smile away.

The contact deepened by degrees. Yennefer controlled the pace at first because control was the language in which she had smuggled tenderness past too many enemies. Her hand moved from his chest to his shoulder, then to the back of his neck. She did not pull. She invited with pressure and waited for answer.
When he gave it, when his hand settled at her waist and held there without demand, her breath caught.
The sound was too small to be performance and too honest to ignore.
Jack stopped.
Yennefer opened her eyes. "Why?"
"You made a sound."
"Astute."
"Checking."
Her expression shifted, irritation and tenderness cutting each other until neither won. "If I object, you will know. I am not famously subtle when displeased."
"True."
"If I ask you to slow, you slow."
"Yes."
"If I tell you not to stop, you will have the intellectual courage to understand that also."
His hand tightened once at her waist. "Yes."
"Good."
She leaned closer, and the next kiss carried more heat.

The rain thickened outside. The room smelled of storm, lilac, bitter medicine, and the clean linen Triss had bullied into service that morning. Yennefer shifted one knee onto the bed with measured grace, then paused when Jack's ribs made him draw breath through his teeth. Her eyes sharpened immediately.
"Too much."
"No."
"That is not an answer I accept from men with fresh wounds and a theatrical relationship with pain."
"A little."
"Better."

She changed the angle herself, guiding him back against the pillows with a hand behind his shoulder and another at his chest. It should have made him feel diminished. It did not. There was nothing patronizing in her care. She arranged him as she arranged spells, with exactness and intent, because collapse offended her and comfort deserved competence.
When she settled beside him, close but not careless, the heat returned in a different shape.
Slower.
Deeper.
Less like taking the world back and more like proving it had not taken everything.

Her fingers moved over his scars, pausing at each one as if refusing to let history become decoration. The old cheek mark. The shoulder. The faded lines at his palm. The place near his ribs where ordinary bruising had replaced ancient fire. She touched all of it with a sorceress's precision and a woman's barely controlled hunger, and each time Jack answered with breath rather than speech.
"There," she murmured when his eyes closed. "You see? You can be readable."
"I object."
"Your objection is noted and dismissed."

Her mouth followed her hand to his throat. Not far. Not fast. Enough that the warmth of her breath struck his skin before the kiss did. Jack felt it travel through him, not as power, but as want finding old locked rooms and discovering they had no guards left.
Yennefer heard the rough sound he made.
She stilled.
"Good?" she asked.
The question, in her voice, nearly undid him.
"Yes."
Her lips curved against his skin. "I require better vocabulary from a man who survived a god."
"Very good."
"Improvement."
She kissed him again. The sound she made this time was lower, warmed by satisfaction she would later deny if anyone had the poor survival instinct to mention it.

Her hand found his and drew it to her waist. Then higher, to the line of her shoulder, then to the loosened edge of black fabric where skin held the day's last warmth. She did not let him guess. She gave permission as a series of exact mercies, and each one made her breath less even.
"There," she whispered. "Slowly."
He obeyed.

Fabric shifted. The lamp trembled. Rain blurred the world beyond the shutters into gray and silver. Yennefer's breathing became audible, no longer quite disciplined, each inhale drawn too carefully, each exhale leaving her with a sound she did not completely own. Jack moved with her pace, with the limits of his body and the direction of hers.
He felt her trying to remain composed and felt the instant she decided composition had lost its argument.
"Ah... Jack."
His name in her voice was not soft. It was worse. It was exposed.

He kissed her then, and the exposed thing answered. Her fingers threaded into his hair. Her body leaned into his without forgetting the wound beneath his ribs. Desire and care moved together, awkward at first, then natural, then necessary. Each pause sharpened the next touch. Each breath asked again. Each answer came warmer.
"Do not vanish into politeness," she said, breathless against his mouth.
"I am here."
"Then be here more honestly."
He let his hand settle more fully at her back, drawing her closer within the safe limit of pain. She came with a sound that broke before she could refine it.
"Oh... mm."

The sound stayed between them, warming the space under her chin, under his hand, under the ruined pride both of them had mistaken for armor too many times. Yennefer lowered her forehead to his and laughed once, almost silently.
"This is absurd," she whispered.
"Recovery?"
"Wanting. After everything. As if the body is some optimistic idiot with no respect for context."
"Is it wrong?"
Her fingers tightened at his shoulder. "No. That is what makes it intolerable."
She kissed him again before he could answer.

The room narrowed. Breath became the measure of time. Her voice, when it returned, did so in fragments, quieter than the rain but clearer than any spell she had cast in the battle. "Mmh... yes. There. Not fast. Stay with me."
He stayed.

The heat gathered and held, not rushed toward ending, not arranged for performance. It moved through the slow press of her body near his, the careful slide of her hand over his scars, the way she paused when pain touched him and resumed only when his breath said yes. Jack heard himself answer her, low and rough, and felt her shiver at the sound. That response was its own confession.
Yennefer's restraint failed beautifully and in pieces.
A breath that became a moan against his mouth.
A curse in Elder Speech so soft it sounded almost devotional.
A tremor in the hand she had kept steady through battle, politics, and catastrophe.
"Ahh..." she breathed, then lower, "Do not stop. Not yet."
He did not.

The world did not become innocent. It did not forgive them their histories. Geralt existed downstairs, part of Yennefer's past in ways neither contempt nor affection could simplify. Triss existed there too, old wound and present kindness both. Ciri existed in the house, fierce and beloved and impossible to place in any clean category without lying. The dead existed. The choices existed.
The chamber existed behind them like a scar in the world's stone.
None of that left.
That was why the moment mattered.

Yennefer did not come to him empty of history. Jack did not hold her as if history were an inconvenience that desire could burn away. They brought all of it into the room and still chose the next breath.

When the intensity finally eased, Yennefer lowered her face against his shoulder and remained there, breathing unevenly. Her hair spilled across him, black and damp with rain's memory. One hand rested over his heart again, not checking now. Keeping.
For a long while, neither spoke.
Then she said, very quietly, "I had prepared for you to die."
Jack studied the darkening ceiling.
"I know."

"No. You know the shape. You do not know the labor. I prepared arguments, contingencies, threats, spells I had no intention of surviving, lies for Ciri, lies for Geralt, lies for myself. I prepared a face. Several, actually. One for each audience."
"And now?"
Her fingers moved once over his chest. "Now I have a living problem with a pulse and poor posture."
"Disappointing."
"Humiliatingly preferable."
He turned enough to look at her. The movement hurt. He did it anyway. She saw the pain and did not scold him this time. Her expression had gone too open for scolding.
"Yennefer."
"Careful," she said. "I am in a sentimental condition. It makes me vindictive."
"Stay."
The word entered the room without armor.
Her eyes closed.

For a moment he thought he had asked too much. Then she moved closer, careful with his side, and laid her cheek over his heart. The gesture was not surrender. Nothing about Yennefer surrendered. It was a placement of trust, and because trust had never come easily to either of them, it filled the room more completely than heat had.
"Until the rain stops," she said.
"And if it rains all night?"
"Then the weather will have made one intelligent contribution to history."
He smiled into her hair.

Her breath warmed his skin. Once, in the dark, she made a small sound, not desire now but relief so private it should not have had a witness. Jack heard it and did not name it. Naming would have made it defend itself.
Later still, when the lamp had burned low and the rain had settled into the softer language of water finding eaves, Yennefer lifted her head.
"You are not absolved," she said.
"For what?"
"For making us love something breakable."
He touched her face, thumb resting near the sharp line of her cheek. "I was breakable before."
"Yes," she said. "But now you are offensively honest about it."
"I will try to be less offensive."
"Do not."
The answer came too quickly.
She did not take it back.

Jack held her gaze in the dimness, and the mortal quiet inside him no longer felt empty. It felt occupied. Not by power. By consequence. By hands, breath, voices, rain, a horse angry in the yard, and a woman in black who had stayed because leaving would have been easier to explain.
Yennefer kissed him once more, slow enough to be remembered without becoming a promise she would have to defend in daylight.
"Sleep," she said.
"Command?"
"Mercy."
"Worse."
"Usually."
He slept with her hand still over his heart, while rain kept the house from sounding too much like silence.

On the final morning, Jack mounted slowly because mortal bodies had opinions that witcher discipline could no longer bully into silence. Buck's rebuilt bridle creaked under his hand, newly stitched with saddle leather Geralt had pretended was only practical. The yard smelled of sunlight, horse breath, damp linen, and the soup Triss had insisted was breakfast because recovery required tyranny in bowls.

Geralt stood by the stirrup and studied it for too long. "Your stirrup is still wrong," he said. Jack set his boot in it carefully. "Some things survived." Buck snorted with enough contempt to qualify as testimony.

Ciri rode on his left. Yennefer stood in the doorway with her arms folded, looking as if she had invented restraint and already found it disappointing. Triss handed Jack a packet of medicines and a list of instructions written in a hand so firm it had become law. Asha gave him a travel knot. Tala tied the red thread again because some ambiguities deserved renewal.
Regis offered a farewell so tactful it almost concealed grief. Dandelion was not allowed to sing. Zoltan threatened him with friendship if he tried.

By the time they reached the lower gate, the road had failed to recognize him. No hidden pressure rose through stone. No crimson answered in his blood. The world did not open, bow, accuse, or call. It merely waited, dusty and unreasonable, as roads had always done. Jack touched the pouch where Jacob's letter rested, then the red thread at his wrist, then Buck's mane.
"Ready?" Ciri asked.
"No."
She smiled. "Good. Honest preparation."
Buck stepped forward.
The lower gate opened.
The road did not remember him anymore.
Jack smiled at that, tired and alive, and rode on anyway.
